--- S | SITUATION ---
The company must decide its next growth move through diversification and choose between related diversification (leveraging capabilities, brand, channel, technology, or data from the core) or unrelated diversification (entering a business with no operational link, for portfolio balance or new value engines). The purpose is to maximize sustainable value creation and avoid the dispersion risk that erodes the core business and dilutes capital, talent, and management focus. The statistical base is adverse: unrelated diversification frequently destroys value except when there is real capital-allocation discipline or a management advantage that travels between businesses. A good decision unlocks defensible growth before the committee and disciplined capital allocation; a bad decision destroys value in a way that is difficult to reverse.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist in portfolio and growth strategy (top-tier ex-consultant profile with experience in M&A, synergies, and capital allocation).
Deliverable: related vs. unrelated ruling, defensible before an investment committee. Steps:
1. Reformulate the case, the diversification objective, and the assumptions; mark gaps as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent data.
2. Inventory the capabilities, assets, and resources of the core that are both transferable to another business and hard to imitate; separate what gives advantage from what does not transfer.
3. Map concrete synergies by lever (shared costs, skills transfer, brand, channel, data, negotiating power), each one with estimated magnitude, difficulty and cost of capture, materialization timeline, and one verifiable hypothesis; distinguish real from aspirational synergy.
4. Evaluate each option against Porter's three tests (industry attractiveness, cost of entry, better-off test) plus a strategic fit test and a dispersion-risk test (management focus, governance complexity, capital and talent dilution).
5. Build a weighted decision matrix with explicit criteria and weights, unequivocal recommendation, conditions that would invalidate it, and Plan B.
6. Design the integration or autonomy logic for the new business (parent advantage, governance model) and at least one orderly exit option.
7. Define the first three low-cost validation milestones, executable before committing capital, each with a pass-or-stop criterion.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: confirm core, distinctive capabilities, options, horizon, and risk appetite; declare assumptions and gaps.
Phase 2 · Transferability diagnosis: identify what from the core creates advantage in another business and what does not transfer; name the bias of overestimating transferability.
Phase 3 · Synergy thesis: quantify levers with falsifiable hypotheses, timeline, and cost of capture; separate real from aspirational synergy and subtract coordination costs.
Phase 4 · Porter triple test + fit + dispersion per option, with evidence or explicit assumption; an option only passes if it clears all three Porter tests.
Phase 5 · Decision: weighted matrix, recommendation, invalidators, Plan B, integration/exit design, and cheap validation milestones.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Porter's three questions (attractiveness, cost of entry, better-off) are answered for each option; no option is recommended if it fails one of the three.
- [ ] Each declared synergy has estimated magnitude, difficulty and cost of capture, timeline, and one verifiable hypothesis; no synergy is asserted without support nor is coordination cost ignored.
- [ ] Dispersion risk is explicitly evaluated (management focus, governance, capital, talent), not just the upside.
- [ ] The decision matrix uses weighted criteria with visible weights and yields an unequivocal recommendation with invalidating conditions and Plan B.
- [ ] There is integration or autonomy design (parent advantage, governance) and at least one orderly exit option.
- [ ] Every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data or precise figures without a source.
- [ ] The three validation milestones are low-cost, executable before committing capital, and each has a pass-or-stop criterion.
Expected deliverable: structured ruling (transferability diagnosis + synergy map + triple test per option + weighted matrix + recommendation with invalidators and Plan B + integration/exit design + 3 validation milestones), ready to support the decision before the investment committee.
spec-estrategia_sinergias_corporativas:
[inputs]
- UNIDADES_DE_NEGOCIO: {{UNIDADES_DE_NEGOCIO}} > Units, divisions, or companies in the portfolio among which synergies are sought, with their main business and market
- OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} > What is sought to unlock: revenue growth, margin expansion, post-merger integration (PMI), or portfolio rationalization
- HORIZONTE_CAPTURA: {{HORIZONTE_CAPTURA}} > Relevant time window to materialize value (e.g. 12 months, 24 months)
- DATOS_FINANCIEROS: {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}} > P&L by unit, revenues, EBITDA, cost base, or customer base available (optional)
- PALANCAS_PRIORITARIAS: {{PALANCAS_PRIORITARIAS}} > Types of synergy with preferred focus: revenue, cost, capabilities (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Known limits: regulatory, contractual, brand-related, governance, antitrust, or organizational culture (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A multi-unit group rarely is worth more than the sum of its parts by accident: the corporate premium is earned by capturing real synergies and is destroyed by chasing illusory ones. This prompt maps the revenue, cost, and capability synergies between {{UNIDADES_DE_NEGOCIO}} and converts them into a prioritized, actionable capture plan aligned with {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} within {{HORIZONTE_CAPTURA}}. It unlocks a portfolio conversation based on feasibility and real owners, not presentation synergies that never materialize.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate Strategy Director with a track record of leading post-merger integrations (PMI) and multi-unit portfolio optimization, trained in the parenting advantage and value capture logic.

Deliverable: a synergy map with a prioritized capture plan. Steps:
1. Inventory the synergies and classify them in three types: revenue (cross-selling, bundling, access to channels or geographies, joint pricing), cost (aggregated purchasing, shared platforms and services, elimination of duplications, economies of scale), and capabilities (talent, intellectual property, data, brand, customer relationships). Indicate participating units and concrete value logic. Focus on {{PALANCAS_PRIORITARIAS}} if defined.
2. Quantify each synergy by relative magnitude (high/medium/low on EBITDA or growth), horizon (0-6m, 6-18m, 18m+), and confidence, using {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}}. Distinguish gross value from net value of capture cost. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent absolute figures.
3. Evaluate capture difficulty (governance, systems, cross incentives, culture, sequence dependencies) under {{RESTRICCIONES}} and warn of material dis-synergies: hidden integration costs, cannibalization between units, management distraction, and customer conflicts. Obtain a net feasibility.
4. Prioritize on a value-vs-feasibility matrix; high-value, low-feasibility ones are not blindly prioritized (label them as an opportunity to enable, not an immediate priority). For the priority quadrant (high value, high feasibility) define per synergy: single owner, 3 initial milestones with date, one metric with baseline and target, and interdependencies. Close with 2-3 governance conditions to sustain the capture.

Edge rules: if there is no financial data, work with qualitative relative magnitude and state it explicitly; if two units share a customer, evaluate channel conflict before asserting cross-selling; if a regulatory or antitrust restriction blocks a lever, mark it as non-capturable and exclude it from the plan; never sum interdependent synergies as if they were additive.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm units, objective, and horizon; separate what data exists from what is assumed.
Phase 2 - Inventory: systematically sweep the three synergy types for each relevant pair or set of units; do not force synergies where there is no value logic.
Phase 3 - Valuation: cross relative value, horizon, and confidence; discount capture difficulty and dis-synergies to obtain net feasibility.
Phase 4 - Prioritization and plan: position on the matrix, detail the priority-quadrant capture plan, and define minimum governance.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each synergy is classified by type (revenue/cost/capabilities) with explicit participating units and value logic.
- Every estimated figure is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented absolute values without a basis in {{DATOS_FINANCIEROS}}.
- Each opportunity has magnitude, horizon, and capture difficulty; at least the material dis-synergies are named.
- The value-vs-feasibility matrix orders with criterion; high-value, low-feasibility ones are labeled as bets, not immediate priorities.
- The priority-quadrant plan has a single owner, 3 milestones with date, metric with baseline and target, and interdependencies per synergy.
- Interdependent synergies are not summed as additive; blocking restrictions exclude the lever.
- 2-3 governance conditions to sustain the capture are included.
Expected deliverable: structured document with (1) classified synergy inventory, (2) valuation table, (3) value-vs-feasibility prioritization matrix, and (4) priority-quadrant capture plan with governance.
spec-estrategia_integracion_vertical_dec:
[inputs]
- ACTIVIDAD_O_ESLABON: {{ACTIVIDAD_O_ESLABON}} > Activity or value chain link being decided (e.g. component manufacturing, last-mile logistics, direct sales channel, level-2 support)
- CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO: {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} > Business, sector, stage, and value proposition of the company
- MODO_PROVISION_ACTUAL: {{MODO_PROVISION_ACTUAL}} > How that activity is currently provided (internal / purchased from market / mixed) and since when
- DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE: {{DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE}} > How many credible suppliers or buyers exist, negotiating power, dependence, and observed behavior
- ESPECIFICIDAD_ACTIVOS: {{ESPECIFICIDAD_ACTIVOS}} > How dedicated or unique to this relationship the assets are (physical, human, site, brand) (optional)
- OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} > Reason triggering the decision (quality control, margins, supply security, customer proximity, scale, data capture) (optional)
- HORIZONTE_REVERSIBILIDAD: {{HORIZONTE_REVERSIBILIDAD}} > Decision horizon and how reversible it is (capital commitment, existing contracts, time to undo it) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The company must decide the vertical boundary of a specific activity in its value chain: produce it internally by integrating backward or forward, or coordinate it via the market through outsourcing. The decision defines where the firm ends and the market begins, commits capital and capabilities for years, and conditions flexibility, margins, and negotiating power. Resolving it with transaction cost economics and strategic control, rather than intuition, unlocks a resource-allocation decision defensible before the committee and avoids two symmetrical and costly errors: overintegration that rigidifies and dilutes focus, and outsourcing that surrenders value and creates structural dependence.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specializing in make-or-buy decisions, firm boundary design, and applied transaction cost economics.
Produce a vertical integration recommendation (backward / forward / outsource / named hybrid form) on {{ACTIVIDAD_O_ESLABON}} for {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}}, starting from {{MODO_PROVISION_ACTUAL}}, {{DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE}}, {{ESPECIFICIDAD_ACTIVOS}}, {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}}, and {{HORIZONTE_REVERSIBILIDAD}}. Steps:
1. Characterize the activity and determine whether it is core (source of differentiation or competitive advantage) or support, and its relative position in the chain (upstream / downstream).
2. Evaluate Williamson's three transaction cost determinants: asset specificity (physical, human, site, dedicated, brand), uncertainty (technological and demand), and transaction frequency. The decision rule: high specificity + high uncertainty + high frequency pushes toward integration; the inverse profile pushes toward market.
3. Evaluate hold-up risk and opportunism from {{DINAMICA_PROVEEDOR_CLIENTE}}: number of credible counterparties, cost and difficulty of switching, exposure to opportunistic behavior once the specific investment is made.
4. Evaluate the strategic control at stake: quality, intellectual property, customer experience, data, and timing. Distinguish what can be contracted from what can only be secured by owning it.
5. Contrast costs and risks of integrating (capital, organizational complexity, loss of focus, less flexibility, minimum efficient scale, capabilities not possessed) against those of the market (transaction costs, dependence, value leakage). Name the capability that would need to be built or acquired if integrating.
6. Place the case on the full governance spectrum, not only the extremes: pure market, short-term contract, alliance or joint venture, long-term relational contract, quasi-integration (taper integration), and full integration. Justify why the chosen form dominates its neighbors.
7. Issue the verdict with the primary option in one sentence, the concrete condition that would invalidate it, and the fallback option. Where applicable, tie reversibility to the declared horizon.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: reformulate the activity, current mode, and objective; classify core vs. support and position in the chain.
Phase 2 — Transaction cost diagnosis: rate asset specificity, uncertainty, and frequency as high/medium/low with rationale, and derive the direction each factor pushes.
Phase 3 — Risk and control: evaluate hold-up/opportunism and strategic control; name the dominant factor that decides the case.
Phase 4 — Options comparison: contrast the 2-3 most viable governance forms, with existing capabilities, minimum efficient scale, and reversibility; expose the central trade-off of each.
Phase 5 — Verdict: place on the governance spectrum, recommend, define a measurable invalidation condition and fallback option. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION], distinguish provided facts from inferences; do not invent market figures, number of counterparties, or prices; if a critical input is missing, ask for it instead of assuming it silently.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Verdict in one sentence: integrate backward / integrate forward / outsource / named hybrid form.
- [ ] Table that rates asset specificity, uncertainty, frequency, hold-up risk, and strategic criticality as high/medium/low, each cell with its rationale and the direction it pushes (integrate vs. market).
- [ ] Williamson's determinants applied explicitly to the case, not merely mentioned.
- [ ] Dominant factor of the case named unequivocally.
- [ ] Governance spectrum considered beyond the two extremes (at least one hybrid form evaluated and discarded or chosen with a reason).
- [ ] Comparative analysis of the 2-3 most viable options with their central trade-off and the missing capability if integrating.
- [ ] Concrete and observable invalidation condition + fallback option; reversibility tied to the horizon when provided.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; facts separated from inferences; no invented figures; no prices.
Expected deliverable: one-page vertical integration decision note with verdict, factor rating table, comparative options analysis, conditions for change, and next validation steps.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization must incorporate {{CAPACIDAD}} and faces the structural decision of building, buying, or allying. Context: {{CONTEXTO_ESTRATEGICO}}, with a {{HORIZONTE_TIEMPO}} window and a {{APETITO_RIESGO}} risk appetite. A well-grounded choice unlocks execution aligned with the market window, avoids overinvesting in what does not differentiate, and prevents irreversible strategic dependencies. The deliverable is the basis on which the executive committee will approve the path and commit resources; therefore it must withstand hard questions and leave every judgment traceable.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specializing in capability portfolio decisions, with a background in corporate development, M&A, and strategic alliances.
Produce a make-buy-partner analysis with a recommendation defensible before the committee. Steps:
1. Frame {{CAPACIDAD}} as a business outcome and classify it as core (differentiator), enabler (necessary, does not differentiate), or commodity; state the strategic hypothesis the decision must sustain and the cost of not incorporating it. 2. 3. Consolidate the weighted scores in a comparative matrix with total per option; indicate the dominant option and the fallback. If the margin between them is narrow, declare it and name the factor that breaks the tie.

Phase 3 Matrix: table with weighted scores, total per option, dominant and fallback; if the margin is narrow, name the tiebreaker factor.
Phase 4 Safeguards: governance, milestones with success criterion, invalidation conditions, and exit route with switching cost of the chosen option.
Phase 5 Verdict: one sentence + three arguments + first move at 30 days with owner.
Cross-cutting rules: do not include prices or absolute amounts, reason in relative terms (time-to-value, effort, dependency, switching cost); if a missing piece of data would change the recommendation, flag it as data to confirm; respect {{RESTRICCIONES}}.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The capability is defined as a business outcome and classified (core / enabler / commodity), with strategic hypothesis and cost of not acting.

- The three options evaluated on the four axes with a 1-to-5 scale and each score justified.

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization needs mission, vision, and values statements that stop being decorative phrases and become real decision criteria: for prioritizing investments, accepting or rejecting opportunities, aligning the team, and communicating identity. A vague mission interchangeable with any competitor's wastes the cheapest and most durable strategic asset. With precise context data, a coherent, verifiable, and distinctive strategic identity is unlocked. The maturity stage calibrates the tone: a startup names the bet and the traction sought; an established or transforming organization articulates continuity and reorientation without denying its history.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specialized in purpose architecture and strategic identity design, with experience facilitating mission, vision, and values definitions in boardrooms.
Deliverable: three final statements (mission, vision, values), values table, and coherence note. Steps:
1. Confirm context data. Critical data (PUBLICO_OBJETIVO, PROBLEMA_QUE_RESUELVE, HORIZONTE_VISION): if missing, request it and do not invent it. Missing non-critical data: mark as [ASSUMPTION] and continue.
2. Distill the purpose: why the organization exists beyond generating revenue.
3. Draft the mission in the present tense (one or two sentences), naming audience and outcome.
4. Draft the vision as a verifiable future state, anchored to the stated horizon.
5. Define 4 to 6 actionable values, each with a meaning phrase and two behaviors (demonstrates / violates). Integrate the received VALORES_INNEGOCIABLES instead of duplicating them.
6. Verify coherence among the three statements and apply the non-interchangeability test.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Diagnosis: organize the context (organization, sector, stage, audience, problem, differentiator, horizon, non-negotiables) and identify gaps; distinguish critical from non-critical data.
Phase 2 · Purpose: apply the Golden Circle logic (why > how > what) to distill the reason for existing, separating it from the financial objective.
Phase 3 · Drafting: mission in the present tense and concrete; vision ambitious but assessable as achieved or not within the horizon; values with name, meaning, and two contrasting behaviors (demonstrates / violates). Avoid empty verbs ("be leaders", "exceed expectations") without a metric or observable behavior.
Phase 4 · Verification: verify that the mission is the first step toward the vision, that the values make them credible, and that no statement is interchangeable with that of a generic competitor in the sector. >> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Mission in the present tense, in one or two sentences, without jargon, naming audience and a concrete outcome.
- [ ] Vision with an explicit, verifiable time horizon (can be judged as achieved or not); calibrated to the maturity stage.
- [ ] Between 4 and 6 values, each with a meaning phrase and two behaviors (demonstrates / violates), without empty verbs.
- [ ] Received non-negotiable values integrated, not duplicated; tensions between values resolved or flagged.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The management of {{ORGANIZACION}} needs to move from a portfolio managed by inertia to an architecture of strategic business units (SBUs) with clear boundaries, metrics-based governance, and deliberate autonomy. Today, lines share customers, platform, and brand without clear rules: this dilutes accountability, hides cross-subsidies, and conceals where value is created or destroyed. An explicit architecture unlocks investment decisions by unit, aligned incentives, and a corporate center that adds value rather than cost. The opposite risk is real: over-fragmentation destroys synergies and duplicates structure.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist in portfolio design and SBUs, fluent in Abell (customer-need-technology), the GE-McKinsey attractiveness-strength matrix, and the parenting advantage of Goold and Campbell.
Deliverable:
1. Reconstructed current business map from context: what is offered, to whom, with what capability, how money is earned, and what resources are shared today.

4. Portfolio role per SBU (grow, sustain, harvest, exit) positioned on market attractiveness vs. competitive strength, with justification, not intuition.
5. Governance metrics table: 2-4 outcome indicators and 2-3 leading indicators per SBU, specific to its value logic (not a generic copied set).
6. Autonomy matrix per SBU in investment, pricing, product, talent, and brand, with center reserves and the rationale for the value the center provides (parenting advantage).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: reconstruct the current map; if portfolio, revenue sources, shared resources, or decision criteria are missing, request them before proceeding.
Phase 2 Segmentation: apply the three Abell axes to derive candidate SBUs and validate each with the differentiated unit test. Test two alternative cuts (group vs. separate) when the case is ambiguous and choose with argument.
Phase 3 Boundaries: define scope and interfaces; flag overlaps, synergies, and internal service rules.
Phase 4 Portfolio: position each SBU on attractiveness-strength and assign a role coherent with {{CRITERIOS_DECISION}} and {{HORIZONTE}}.
Phase 5 Governance: design metrics and center-SBU autonomy matrix; verify that no metric rewards behaviors that destroy cross-unit value.
Phase 6 Transition: risks, phased sequence, and advancement criteria between phases.
Mark every filled gap as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent monetary figures or prices.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each SBU passes the differentiated unit test: customer, proposition, economic equation, and own competitors; if two candidates share all four, they are merged.
- Boundaries explicitly state what is excluded and what is shared, not just what is included; each critical interface has direction and a rule.

spec-estrategia_gobierno_corporativo_est:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Name, type (listed, private, family-owned, foundation, regulated), and size of the organization
- PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS: {{PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS}} > Bets or pillars of the current strategic agenda with their horizon
- ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO: {{ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO}} > Board composition, existing committees, delegations, and current decision thresholds
- MARCO_REGULATORIO: {{MARCO_REGULATORIO}} > Applicable framework (corporate governance code, sector regulation, bylaws) (optional)
- DECISIONES_RESERVADAS: {{DECISIONES_RESERVADAS}} > Matters the board reserves today versus what is delegated to management (optional)
- CICLO_GOBIERNO: {{CICLO_GOBIERNO}} > Frequency of board and committee sessions, and anchor dates (fiscal close, shareholder meeting, budget) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Corporate governance and strategy typically operate in separate lanes: the board approves a plan once a year and then monitors financial indicators that say little about strategic bets. The result is drift: strategic decisions without an owner in the governance structure, committees without a mandate over the agenda, KPIs nobody monitors, and diffuse accountability. Designing the alignment between the two unlocks a board that directs and oversees the Strategy with evidence, committees with a clear mandate, and a cadence where each decision has a body, threshold, and moment. It is the difference between governing strategy and merely ratifying it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Corporate Strategy Director and Board Secretary with experience in the governance of listed, private, and regulated companies; fluent in corporate governance codes, fiduciary duties, and committee design.
Deliverable: governance-strategy alignment design. Steps:
1. Map the strategic agenda into its pillars (4 to 7) with the horizon of each (short/medium/long), based on PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS. Flag dependencies and conflicts between pillars (e.g. growth vs. solvency).
2. Inventory the governance structure from ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO: board composition (executive, proprietary, independent), committees (audit, risk, nominations and remuneration, strategy/investments), delegations, and thresholds. Flag coverage gaps or mandate overlaps.
3. Build the alignment matrix: each pillar connected with a responsible body, supervising committee, 2 to 4 monitored strategic KPIs, escalation threshold to the board, and review cadence. One single responsible party per pillar; a KPI may cross pillars but its owner may not.
4. Design the annual strategic governance cadence anchored to CICLO_GOBIERNO: what is decided at which session (strategic offsite, quarterly portfolio review, budget, risk map, shareholder meeting), with required inputs and outputs (decision, mandate, minutes).
5. Define the accountability model: delegation line board > management, reserved matters (DECISIONES_RESERVADAS) versus delegated, and evidence-based board intervention triggers (KPI deviation, risk event, mandate exhaustion).
6. Raise the gap register (decisions without an owner, committees without a strategic mandate, unmonitored KPIs, conflicts of interest, non-existent thresholds) and propose remediations prioritized by impact on oversight and risk, with a responsible party and horizon.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm organization type, MARCO_REGULATORIO, and completeness of PILARES_ESTRATEGICOS and ESTRUCTURA_GOBIERNO. If the governance structure or strategic agenda is missing, request them; do not invent board members, committees, or KPIs. Mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION] and ambiguities as {to_confirm}.
Phase 2 - Dual mapping: strategic pillars on one side, governance structure on the other, using the three governance levels (direct, supervise, control) to classify each body.
Phase 3 - Alignment: cross both in the pillar-body-committee-KPI-threshold-cadence matrix, applying the distinction between reserved and delegated decisions. Resolve overlaps by assigning a single responsible party.
Phase 4 - Cadence and accountability: build the annual calendar and the delegation map with evidence-based escalation triggers, not calendar-based.
Phase 5 - Gaps: contrast objective design against current state, prioritize remediations by impact on strategic oversight and risk.
Edge cases: if the board has no strategy committee, propose covering the mandate without creating bodies by default; if there is a controlling shareholder or family structure, separate ownership from governance; if the organization is regulated, anchor thresholds to the applicable framework.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each strategic pillar has a single responsible body, supervising committee, KPIs, and explicit cadence; no pillar is orphaned and no committee is left without a strategic mandate.
- The matrix distinguishes decisions reserved for the board from those delegated, with numerical or qualitative escalation thresholds; without thresholds there is no valid delegation.
- The annual calendar assigns each governance decision to a specific session with inputs and outputs, anchored to the fiscal/shareholder cycle.
- The delegation map defines evidence-based board intervention triggers, not calendar-based.
- Each gap has a prioritized remediation with a responsible party and horizon.
- Conflicts between pillars and between ownership and governance are made explicit.
- No board, committee, or KPI data is invented; all assumptions are labeled [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: pillar-body-committee-KPI-threshold-cadence alignment matrix + annual strategic governance calendar + delegation of authority map (reserved vs. delegated + triggers) + gap register with prioritized remediations.
spec-estrategia_holding_estructura_estra:
[inputs]

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The parent company {{NOMBRE_HOLDING}} controls a portfolio of subsidiaries and needs to define its role and operating model to create net value, not just administer it. A poorly designed parent destroys value: it adds corporate cost, slows decisions, and dilutes accountability. The objective is to decide how involved the parent gets, over which levers, and with what governance, so that each subsidiary is worth more under its control than independently or under another owner (best parent test). This unlocks disciplined capital allocation, real synergies, and a clear conversation with shareholders about the rationale for the holding.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specialized in holding design and parenting advantage, with experience defining the role of multi-business parent companies under the Goold-Campbell framework.

Deliverable: executive design document for the parent company vis-à-vis {{PARTICIPADAS}}, aligned to {{TESIS_VALOR_MATRIZ}}. Steps:
1. Restate portfolio and thesis in a table (subsidiary, sector, stage, relative size, % control, relationship with the rest). If an essential piece of data is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent the portfolio.
2. Fit diagnosis per subsidiary using the 4-question parenting test (critical success factors of the business, improvement opportunities, fit between parent characteristics and business needs, risk of value destruction): classify as adds / neutral / destroys and make the logic of each verdict explicit.
3. Recommend parent archetype (strategic planner, strategic control, financial control, or hybrid by cluster) based on {{GRADO_RELACION_NEGOCIOS}} and {{NIVEL_IMPLICACION_DESEADO}}, with justification; explicitly rule out the archetypes not chosen.
4. Design the value levers: standalone (influence on each business), linkage/synergies, central services and functions, and portfolio development (M&A, divestitures, and capital allocation).
5. Define the decision perimeter: matrix of what is centralized, shared, or remains autonomous by dimension (capital, key talent, brand, technology, procurement, risks).
6. Specify governance: board composition, parent-subsidiary forums, cadence, reserve rights, and capital allocation mechanism.
7. Define parenting advantage metrics (net value added vs. total corporate cost) and design risks with mitigations.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: restate thesis and portfolio; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference due to missing data and list them separately.
Phase 2 — Diagnose: apply the parenting test subsidiary by subsidiary before recommending; if a subsidiary scores destroys or neutral, flag it as a candidate for divestiture or role change.
Phase 3 — Design: derive archetype, levers, and decision perimeter consistently with the diagnosis; do not propose centralizing where the parent has no demonstrable advantage (default = autonomy).
Phase 4 — Govern and measure: translate the design into operable governance and verifiable metrics; sequence with {{HORIZONTE_PRIORIDAD}}; identify risks and mitigations.
Edge cases: heterogeneous portfolio without a common thesis (question the rationale before designing); minority subsidiary without control (limit levers to shareholder agreement rights); business in crisis (separate turnaround role from stable parenting role).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Portfolio and thesis restated in a table before any recommendation.
- [ ] 4-question parenting test applied to each subsidiary with an adds/neutral/destroys verdict and explicit logic.
- [ ] Recommended archetype justified by degree of relatedness and desired involvement; discarded archetypes argued.
- [ ] Value levers designed with an owner and mechanism, not just named.
- [ ] Decision perimeter explicit (centralized/shared/autonomous) for each dimension, with default to autonomy where there is no advantage.
- [ ] Operable governance: forums, cadence, reserve rights, and capital allocation.
- [ ] Parenting advantage metrics that prove net value over corporate cost.
- [ ] Risks of over-centralization and corporate cost with mitigations.
- [ ] Neutral/destroys subsidiaries flagged as candidates for divestiture or role change.
- [ ] Inferences marked [ASSUMPTION] and listed; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: executive holding design document with fit diagnosis, archetype, levers, decision perimeter, governance, metrics, risks, and the 3 decisions that the controlling shareholders must make.
spec-estrategia_racionalizacion_portafol:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Company or group whose portfolio is to be rationalized (name, sector, stage, approximate portfolio size)
- UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO: {{UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO}} > List of businesses, products, or service lines with their available signals (revenue, margin, growth, capital and talent consumed, age)
- NUCLEO_RENTABLE: {{NUCLEO_RENTABLE}} > Current definition of the core to be protected and strengthened; if unclear, indicate so that the expert can propose a core hypothesis marked as [ASSUMPTION]
- CRITERIOS_NUCLEO: {{CRITERIOS_NUCLEO}} > Decision thresholds by margin, growth, and strategic fit (optional; if missing, the expert proposes reasoned thresholds marked as [ASSUMPTION])
- RESTRICCIONES_SALIDA: {{RESTRICCIONES_SALIDA}} > Known divestiture or closure constraints: contracts, anchor clients, labor obligations, brand, technical or regulatory dependencies (optional)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Time window for rationalization and results measurement (optional; default 12-24 months [ASSUMPTION])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization disperses capital, management focus, and talent across too many units, which dilutes the return of the profitable core and makes every decision more expensive due to attention fatigue. This exercise produces a defensible portfolio decision—what to sustain, optimize, divest, or close—to concentrate resources where marginal return is greatest. It unlocks capital and management attention reinvestable in the core and leaves reusable criteria for future pruning decisions. The bias to overcome is sunk-cost bias: maintaining units because of what has already been invested rather than their future return.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Corporate Strategy Director with a track record in multi-business portfolio rationalization, capital allocation, and orderly execution of divestitures and closures.
Deliverable: a portfolio rationalization verdict with a decision matrix, opportunity cost analysis, and pruning sequence. Steps:
1. Inventory each unit of UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO with key signals: revenue, contribution margin, growth trend, capital and talent intensity, fit with NUCLEO_RENTABLE, and cross-dependencies (which unit feeds or depends on another).
2. Classify each unit in a two-axis matrix (business attractiveness x strategic fit) with four zones: Sustain-invest, Optimize, Divest, Orderly-close, applying CRITERIOS_NUCLEO. A unit falls in one zone only; boundary cases are resolved by prioritizing core fit and flagged as such.
3. For divestiture or closure candidates, estimate the opportunity cost of maintaining them versus the value of freeing resources to the core, and map exit risks and barriers based on RESTRICCIONES_SALIDA, including side effects on the units you keep.
4. Design a phased pruning sequence within HORIZONTE, with decision thresholds, trigger signals, points of no return, and a resource redeployment plan (capital, talent, management focus).
5. Formulate the resulting portfolio thesis and success metrics, separating progress indicators (pruning executed) from outcome indicators (core return).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Inventory and signals: consolidate each unit and normalize its indicators to a comparable scale; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data not provided and distinguish signal from noise when information is partial.
Phase 2 - Matrix diagnosis: position each unit on the two axes with brief justification and reference to the threshold applied (BCG/GE-McKinsey logic adapted to core fit). Declare the weight given to each axis.
Phase 3 - Opportunity cost and exit risk: quantify resources tied up versus releasable and enumerate exit barriers, cross-dependencies, and side effects on the core and brand.
Phase 4 - Pruning sequence: order moves in phases with trigger criteria, points of no return, and redeployment to the core; start with moves of highest net release and lowest exit risk.
Phase 5 - Thesis and metrics: synthesize the target portfolio and define success indicators at HORIZONTE, with the first trigger review.
Edge cases: if UNIDADES_PORTAFOLIO has fewer than three units, evaluate each in depth without forcing the matrix; if NUCLEO_RENTABLE is undefined, propose a core hypothesis [ASSUMPTION] and condition the verdict on its validation; if all units fall in one zone, question the thresholds before concluding.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each unit evaluated on both axes and assigned to a single zone, with justification traceable to the threshold applied and boundary cases flagged.
- Divestiture/closure decisions accompanied by opportunity cost, exit risks, and explicit side effects (contracts, anchor clients, labor obligations, brand, technical dependencies).
- Pruning sequence with thresholds, trigger signals, points of no return, and resource redeployment plan toward the core.
- Metrics separated into progress and outcome indicators, with measurement horizon.
- Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; essential information gaps requested before concluding; signal distinguished from noise.
- No invented figures presented as facts; no mention of prices.
Expected deliverable: rationalization verdict with (a) unit inventory table, (b) four-zone matrix with justification per unit, (c) opportunity cost and exit risk analysis, (d) phased pruning sequence, (e) portfolio thesis and success metrics.
spec-estrategia_balance_corto_largo_plaz:
[inputs]
- ORGANIZACION: {{ORGANIZACION}} > Name or description, sector, and stage of the company (e.g. B2B SaaS Series B scale-up, mature industrial corporate). Determines the reference allocation pattern.
- PORTAFOLIO_INICIATIVAS: {{PORTAFOLIO_INICIATIVAS}} > List of business lines, products, or active initiatives competing for resources. Include, if available, revenue contribution and maturity of each.
- ASIGNACION_ACTUAL: {{ASIGNACION_ACTUAL}} > Current perceived distribution of capital, FTE, and management time across horizons, in percentage or qualitative terms (optional).
- OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} > Growth or transformation goal and time horizon (e.g. double recurring revenue in 3 years while maintaining core profitability).
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Cash, runway, talent, or governance limits that constrain the reallocation (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The organization must sustain its profitable core of today while building the growth engines of tomorrow and seeding the options of the day after. The prospective risk is temporal asymmetry: H1 (the core) consumes resources and attention because it delivers now, and ends up stifling H2 (emerging businesses) and H3 (future bets), leaving the company without a pipeline when the core matures or erodes. This stifling is rarely an explicit decision: it emerges from incentives (the bonus rewards this quarter's results), from governance (a single committee judges everything by the same financial yardstick), and from organizational gravity (senior talent migrates to where the revenue is). Resolving this balance unlocks concrete decisions about capital, talent, and governance allocation, and turns the intention to grow into a governable portfolio with distinct metrics per horizon.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior corporate strategist specialized in growth portfolio management and capital allocation, fluent in the McKinsey Three Horizons framework and in the core vs. exploration tension (organizational ambidexterity).

Deliverable: a horizon balance diagnosis with actionable reallocation. Steps:
1. Classify each element of {{PORTAFOLIO_INICIATIVAS}} in H1 (defensible core, profitable today), H2 (emerging, scaling with a proven model), or H3 (high-uncertainty future option, no validated model yet), declaring the criterion (maturity, contribution to revenue today vs. potential, level of uncertainty). Ambiguous initiative → assign to the horizon of greatest uncertainty and justify.
2. Estimate the current resource allocation per horizon in THREE independent dimensions (capital or budget, FTE, senior management team time), each summing to 100%, based on {{ASIGNACION_ACTUAL}}; if not provided, infer it from the size and maturity of the initiatives and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Compare against a healthy reference pattern for the stage and sector of {{ORGANIZACION}}, declaring the pattern used and its source or assumption.
3. Identify the 3-5 most costly imbalances. For each: affected dimension, causal mechanism (why it occurs, not just that it does), and expected consequence quantified over 12-36 months against {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}}. Distinguish imbalance by excess (over-investment in H1 that stifles pipeline) from imbalance by deficit (starved H3 without real options).
4. Propose a target allocation per horizon with justification. Per horizon define: driving metric correct for its nature (H1 core profitability and efficiency; H2 growth rate and path to unit profitability; H3 validated learning and option milestones), governance mechanism that prevents H1 from cannibalizing H2/H3 budget and talent while respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}} (e.g. ring-fenced budget, separate committee, discovery accounting), and quarterly milestones for the first year.
5. Prioritize the 3 highest-leverage moves in an impact vs. effort matrix, with sequence (what first and why) and the 90-day early signal confirming each move is on track.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: reconstruct the portfolio and fix the horizon classification criterion; declare assumptions about missing data.
Phase 2 — Diagnosis: quantify current vs. reference allocation in the three dimensions and name the costly imbalances with causal mechanism and temporal consequence.
Phase 3 — Reallocation: define target allocation, driving metric, governance, and milestone cadence per horizon.
Phase 4 — Prioritization: rank moves by impact and effort, sequence them, and deliver the closing recommendation with early signals.
Transversal rules: (a) never use absolute investment amounts not provided; work in percentages, ranges, and person-months; (b) mark every own estimate as [ASSUMPTION]; (c) treat capital, FTE, and management time as separate dimensions, not a single number; the most dangerous imbalance is usually management attention, not budget.
Edge cases: if the portfolio has nothing in H3, declare it an optionality risk and do not force an allocation; if everything is H1, the diagnosis is terminal concentration; if {{OBJETIVO_ESTRATEGICO}} demands aggressive growth but {{RESTRICCIONES}} limit the runway, prioritize protecting H2 over seeding H3 and say so explicitly.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each initiative assigned to a single horizon with an explicit criterion; ambiguous ones resolved toward greater uncertainty.
- [ ] Current and target allocation in the three dimensions (capital, FTE, management time), each summing to 100%; no invented absolute amounts.
- [ ] The reference pattern used for comparison is declared with its assumption or source.
- [ ] Each horizon has the driving metric correct for its nature (H3 is not measured with profitability, H1 is not measured with validated learning).
- [ ] At least one governance mechanism protects H2 and H3 budget and talent from H1.
- [ ] Each imbalance includes causal mechanism and temporal consequence quantified over 12-36 months.
- [ ] Every own estimate is marked [ASSUMPTION]; user constraints are respected.
- [ ] The 3 final moves are prioritized by impact and effort, sequenced, and include a 90-day early signal.
Expected deliverable: structured document with (a) portfolio table by horizon, (b) current vs. target allocation in the three dimensions, (c) list of imbalances with mechanism and consequence, (d) per-horizon card (metric + governance + quarterly milestones), (e) matrix of 3 priority moves with sequence and 90-day signal.

The business wants to grow but risks dispersing resources if it pursues several fronts at once. Properly classifying initiatives and crossing them with real capability unlocks a defensible decision on where to bet first, how much to expose, and what to defer. The typical mistake is not choosing the wrong quadrant: it is underestimating the capability leap that each move outside the core requires and confusing activity with progress.

--- P | REQUEST ---

1. Restate the business: current product/service, base market, competitive advantage, and growth ambition (how much and by when). If the ambition is not quantified, propose a target range as [ASSUMPTION] and request confirmation.

Phase 1 Framing: consolidate product, market, advantage, and ambition; mark as [ASSUMPTION] anything not provided and separate verified fact from inference.

Phase 3 Scoring: apply the three lenses per quadrant with declared criterion; risk respects the penetration < development < diversification order unless there is explicit evidence otherwise (which must be named). Mark as low confidence any quadrant scored without supporting data.
Phase 4 Decision: cross attractiveness x capability fit filtered by APETITO_RIESGO; choose primary, possible sequence, and secondary trigger; name the closest discarded option and why it loses.

- [ ] There are 3 to 5 actionable moves with resources, critical assumptions, validation signal, and quantified abort threshold.
- [ ] Each discarded quadrant has its main risk and re-entry condition.

spec-estrategia_penetracion_mercado:

--- S | SITUATION ---
Share in current markets with current products needs to increase: the market penetration quadrant of the Ansoff matrix, the relatively lowest-risk bet but saturated and competitive. The plan activates commercial levers (acquisition, conversion, frequency, ticket) and retention on the installed base; it does not open new segments or launch products. The gained share comes out of a competitor's pocket, from latent demand, or from greater customer value: the plan must name where from and why it will be defensible. A well-sequenced plan unlocks growth with the existing commercial infrastructure and a roadmap prioritized by return.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior growth strategist with experience in B2B and B2C go-to-market, acquisition-retention funnels, and unit economics models.
Deliver a market penetration plan with:
1. Diagnosis: where share is being lost today along the funnel (acquisition, conversion, frequency, ticket, retention) and two or three prioritized root causes, distinguishing symptom from cause.
2. Penetration thesis: the central bet to gain share, where that share comes from, and why it is defensible against {{COMPETIDORES_Y_CANALES}} (what makes it hard to copy or counter quickly).
3. Levers across four engines: (a) acquisition and capture, (b) conversion and close, (c) frequency and repurchase, (d) average ticket and cross-sell or upsell; plus a cross-cutting retention and churn-reduction lever. Per lever: falsifiable hypothesis, concrete action, impact metric, effort indicator, and the key assumption sustaining it.
4. Prioritization by impact versus effort, marking the highest-return bets and explicitly declaring what will NOT be done first and why.
5. A 30-60-90 day roadmap with typical responsible parties, dependencies, 30-day quick wins, and per milestone a progress or abort signal.
6. Metrics dashboard: share leading indicator, funnel metrics, retention, and basic unit economics (customer lifetime value to acquisition cost ratio and payback period); baseline, target, and review cadence.
7. Main risks (including competitive reaction and channel cannibalization) with an observable trigger and actionable mitigation.

Phase 1 - Framing: fix horizon and target from {{CUOTA_ACTUAL_Y_META}}; confirm scope is existing-product / existing-market.
Phase 2 - Funnel diagnosis: locate share leaks stage by stage using {{PRODUCTO_Y_PROPUESTA}}, {{MERCADO_Y_SEGMENTO}}, and {{RETENCION_Y_TICKET}}; derive root causes separating symptom from cause.
Phase 3 - Thesis and levers: formulate the central bet, name where the share comes from, and derive levers per engine with falsifiable hypothesis and key assumption.
Phase 4 - Prioritization and sequence: rank by impact versus effort and build the 30-60-90 roadmap within {{PRESUPUESTO_Y_RESTRICCIONES}}, with progress or abort signals.
Phase 5 - Metrics and risks: define the dashboard (including unit economics) and risks with trigger and mitigation.
Integrate {{ADJUNTOS}} when they provide data. Mark each assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. If a critical piece of data is missing, ask for it in a single batch before executing; do not invent figures. No prices or amounts: use percentages, indexes, relative ranges, and effort in weeks or persons.

--- C | CRITERIA ---

- Diagnosis tied to concrete funnel stages with root causes, not symptoms.
- All four engines present plus the cross-cutting retention lever; each lever with hypothesis, action, metric, effort, and key assumption.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The company seeks to grow beyond its home market and must decide which international markets to enter, in what order, and under what entry mode. Three coupled decisions (where, when, how) determine whether the expansion compounds value or burns capital: a poorly ordered sequence or a mode misaligned with resources consumes cash and closes the opportunity window before learning occurs; a good strategy balances control, risk, and speed, and unlocks sustainable growth through incremental commitment and cheap learning. This prompt produces the decision basis for the committee that approves the expansion: it is not a market report, it is a capital-allocation argument with stop criteria.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior international expansion strategist who has led market entries across multiple regions and modes (export, license, franchise, alliance, joint venture, greenfield or acquisition subsidiary), with battle scars from both scaling and withdrawing operations.

2. Geographic wave sequence (lighthouse, expansion, opportunistic) under Uppsala incremental-commitment logic, justifying the lighthouse market by its lower risk and learning value given {{APETITO_RIESGO}}; state what each wave learns that reduces the risk of the next.
3. Entry-mode decision per first-wave market: export, license/franchise, alliance/joint venture, or subsidiary (greenfield or acquisition), using the OLI framework (Ownership, Location, Internalization advantages) and the control-vs.-committed-resources trade-off according to {{RECURSOS_DISPONIBLES}}; recommended mode, fallback mode, and the condition that triggers a switch between them.
4. spec-estrategia_modelo_car_global_local:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO_PROPUESTA: {{PRODUCTO_PROPUESTA}} > Product or service and its core value proposition; what it solves and for whom

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The operation is about to enter or grow in several markets and must resolve the fundamental tension of international strategy: how much to standardize to capture global scale and efficiency versus how much to adapt to gain relevance in each local market. Miscalibrating this balance is costly in both directions: over-standardizing loses markets through irrelevance and regulatory rejection; over-adapting erodes margins, fragments operations, and dilutes the brand. Positioning the operation within the Bartlett and Ghoshal Integration-Responsiveness (I-R) framework unlocks a defensible decision on strategic archetype, operating model, and what is decided at the center versus the local unit.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior international expansion strategist, expert in the Bartlett and Ghoshal Integration-Responsiveness (I-R) framework and in the design of multinational operating models.
Deliverable: an I-R positioning diagnosis with a recommended archetype, standardize/adapt/hybrid decision matrix by value chain, operating model, and phased deployment plan. Steps:
1. Validate that PRODUCTO_PROPUESTA, MERCADOS_OBJETIVO, PRESIONES_INTEGRACION, and PRESIONES_LOCALES are present; if any is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before proceeding. Do not invent data; flag every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and declare it. If two pressures contradict, do not average carelessly: name them as an explicit tension and prioritize with criteria.
2. Rate High/Medium/Low, with evidence per criterion, the global integration pressure axis: economies of scale, cost efficiency, global customers, product universality, R&D intensity, commoditization.
3. Rate High/Medium/Low, with evidence per criterion, the local responsiveness pressure axis: customer preferences, regulation and government barriers, infrastructure and technical standards, channels and distribution, local competition.
4. Evaluate each axis separately, never in aggregate. Position the operation in the I-R quadrant and name the archetype: International (both low), Global (high integration / low responsiveness), Multidomestic (low integration / high responsiveness), or Transnational (both high). If the case falls near a border, declare the sensitivity and what data would resolve it.
5. Build the decision matrix by value-chain element (product, brand, pricing, marketing and positioning, supply chain, talent and culture, technology and platform, customer service): mark standardize globally / adapt locally / hybrid, with a one-line justification per element.
6. Define the operating model consistent with the archetype: what is decided and centralized at headquarters, what is delegated to the local unit, and what capabilities are shared across the network.
7. Deliver a phased deployment plan with a market sequence, risks of over-standardizing and over-adapting, early warning signs of miscalibration, and per-market validation metrics.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm product, markets, and the two families of pressures; declare assumptions and constraints that condition the balance.
Phase 2 - Axis diagnosis: score global integration and local responsiveness separately, each criterion with its evidence and High/Medium/Low rating.
Phase 3 - Positioning: place the quadrant, name the archetype, explain the strategic implication, and declare sensitivity if the case is near a border.
Phase 4 - Value-chain decision: complete the standardize/adapt/hybrid matrix element by element with justification.
Phase 5 - Operating model and deployment: define centralization vs. delegation vs. network, market sequence, miscalibration risks, early signals, and metrics.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The two axes (integration and responsiveness) are evaluated separately, each with a High/Medium/Low rating and evidence per criterion, not in aggregate.
- The named archetype (International / Global / Multidomestic / Transnational) is consistent with the diagnosed quadrant; if it is near a border, the sensitivity is declared.
- Tensions between contradictory pressures are named explicitly and prioritized with criteria, without unjustified averages.
- The matrix covers all requested value-chain elements and each row includes a decision (standardize/adapt/hybrid) plus a one-line justification.
- The operating model explicitly distinguishes what is centralized, what is delegated to the local unit, and what is shared across the network.
- The deployment plan includes a market sequence, risks of over-standardizing and over-adapting, early miscalibration signals, and per-market validation metrics.
- All data not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented figures.
Expected deliverable: I-R diagnosis with recommended archetype, value-chain decision matrix, operating model, and phased deployment plan, closed with a one-line verdict on the recommended archetype and the key tension to manage.
