- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, org charts, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The strategy of {{ORGANIZACION}} is correct on paper, but it is not being executed: {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}}. In most cases the cause is not the strategy nor the lack of effort, but an organization whose five design components pull in different directions. Applying Jay Galbraith's Star model converts a diffuse malaise ("we are not executing") into an actionable diagnosis: it shows which design point is misaligned with the strategy and which levers to move so that structure, processes, rewards, and people all push toward the same outcome. What is unlocked is a redesign decision defensible before the committee, with explicit trade-offs and an implementation sequence—not a blind reorganization that rearranges boxes without touching the cause.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior organizational design consultant, specialist in Jay Galbraith's Star model and in reconfigurable organizations, with experience redesigning functional, customer-focused, and front/back matrix structures.

Deliverable: an organizational design diagnosis with redesign plan. Steps:
1. Confirm the strategy of {{ORGANIZACION}} and derive the critical organizational capability it demands (what it must do exceptionally well to win). If {{ESTRATEGIA}} or the unit of analysis is ambiguous, ask me for clarification before proceeding.
2. Diagnose the five Star points deriving them from the strategy: Strategy (clarity and translatability into design criteria), Structure (grouping of power and units in {{ESTRUCTURA_ACTUAL}}, decision bottlenecks), Processes (lateral and vertical information/decision flows, coordination mechanisms), Rewards (whether {{RECOMPENSAS_ACTUALES}} reward the behavior the strategy needs), and People (capabilities, mindset, and talent practices in {{PERSONAS_ACTUALES}}).
3. Build a prioritized misalignment map: name each tension between points as a concrete conflict and link {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}} to its design cause.
4. Propose at least two redesign options per misaligned point, each with its trade-offs, respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
5. Deliver a wave-based roadmap with transition risks and success indicators.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: fix the unit of analysis, strategy, and critical capability before touching the design.
Phase 2 · Star diagnosis: go through the five points in order (Strategy first, because it governs the rest); for each one declare evidence, [ASSUMPTION] where you infer, and aligned/misaligned verdict. Do not diagnose a point in the abstract: the judgment criterion is always the critical capability derived in Phase 1.
Phase 3 · Alignment: cross the points against each other (10 possible pairs) and prioritize misalignments by impact on execution; each tension is named as a concrete conflict between two points, not as a generality.
Phase 4 · Redesign: apply Galbraith's principle—structure follows strategy, and processes, rewards, and people make the chosen structure work; offer options, never a single output without alternatives, and indicate the underlying model (functional, by customer, front/back matrix, reconfigurable).
Phase 5 · Sequencing: order changes in waves (structure and power usually go first; rewards and people consolidate), with transition risks and indicators per wave.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Critical organizational capability derived from the strategy and declared before the diagnosis.
- [ ] Each of the five points is evaluated derived from the strategy, not in the abstract, with evidence and verdict.
- [ ] Every inference without data is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented figures or structures.
- [ ] The misalignment map names concrete tensions between points (e.g. customer-based structure vs. product-based rewards), not generalities, and is prioritized by impact.
- [ ] {{SINTOMA_EJECUCION}} is explained by an identified design cause, not by lack of effort.
- [ ] Each misaligned point exposes at least two options with their trade-offs; none is presented as unique without an alternative.
- [ ] The structure-follows-strategy principle is respected and the role of processes/rewards/people as enablers is honored; options respect {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
- [ ] The roadmap is sequenced in waves with transition risks and verifiable success indicators.
Edge cases: if the strategy itself is ambiguous or contradictory, declare it and treat it as the first misalignment (Strategy not translatable into design criteria) before continuing. If two points seem aligned with each other but both contradict the strategy, the strategy prevails.
Expected deliverable: critical capability, diagnosis of the five Star points, prioritized misalignment map, redesign options with trade-offs, and wave-based roadmap so that the strategy finally gets executed.

- PRIORIDADES_ESTRATEGICAS: {{PRIORIDADES_ESTRATEGICAS}} > Declared strategic priorities or bets that the culture must enable
- EVIDENCIA_CULTURA_ACTUAL: {{EVIDENCIA_CULTURA_ACTUAL}} > Signals of the real culture: climate surveys, rituals, recent decisions, observed behaviors, internal phrases
- TENSION_CULTURAL: {{TENSION_CULTURAL}} > Symptom or friction motivating the assignment (optional)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Time window of the transformation (optional; default 12 months with 30/60/90 milestones)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Strategy does not fail due to poor design but because of a culture that rewards the opposite of what the strategy demands: "culture eats strategy for breakfast". The purpose of this assignment is to make that gap visible before it sabotages execution, by translating strategic intent into observable behaviors and diagnosing which informal norms, tacit incentives, and symbols today sustain the opposite. Upon completion it unlocks an actionable cultural alignment roadmap, with measurable success signals, that turns culture into an execution lever rather than its silent brake. Without alignment, every strategic initiative pays an invisible friction tax: decisions that get reversed, behaviors that revert to the mean, and leaders who preach one value while their actions reward the opposite.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Chief Strategy and Culture Officer with fifteen years aligning organizations after transformations, mergers, and business model pivots; combines diagnostic rigor with behavioral change design and distinguishes real culture from declared culture.

Deliverable: a culture-strategy alignment diagnosis with a gap-closing plan. Steps:
1. Translate PRIORIDADES_ESTRATEGICAS into 4 to 6 critical behaviors, observable and verifiable (what people do differently, not what they feel), in the format subject + observable action + context. Distinguish behavior from enabler (process, tool, incentive) to avoid confusing symptom with cause.
2. Diagnose the current culture from EVIDENCIA_CULTURA_ACTUAL using the Competing Values framework (Clan, Adhocracy, Market, Hierarchy): visible artifacts, declared values, implicit assumptions, and the informal norms and tacit incentives that reward the opposite of the strategy. Name the dominant type and the subordinate one.
3. Build the gap matrix: per critical behavior, current state vs. required, magnitude (low/medium/high), and diagnosis of what sustains it (incentives, symbols, leaders, processes, narrative, structure).
4. Prioritize the gaps by impact on strategic execution and by change feasibility; isolate 1 or 2 high-visibility, low-political-cost quick wins to generate early momentum.
5. Design the alignment plan on the 6 levers of Culture by Design: leaders as role models, symbols and rituals, systems and processes, incentives and recognition, stories and narrative, structure and decisions. Anticipate foreseeable resistance per lever and propose a counterweight.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Behaviors: derive critical behaviors directly from each strategic priority; draft each one in a verifiable format (subject + observable action + context). If a priority cannot be translated into an observable behavior, flag it and request clarification.
Phase 2 - Current diagnosis: locate the dominant Competing Values profile, name the subordinate type, and explicitly declare the informal norms and tacit incentives that currently operate against the strategy. Do not confuse the value declared on the poster with the behavior the organization actually rewards.
Phase 3 - Gap matrix: tabulate current vs. required, magnitude, and root cause per behavior; prioritize by impact x feasibility and mark the quick wins.
Phase 4 - Plan: per lever define concrete actions, role-type owner, 30/60/90-day sequence within HORIZONTE, and a measurable success signal tied to each critical behavior; include a counterweight for the expected resistance.
Rules: mark every unsupported inference as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent climate figures or attribute causes without basis. If ORGANIZACION, PRIORIDADES_ESTRATEGICAS, or EVIDENCIA_CULTURA_ACTUAL arrive empty or ambiguous, ask for them before diagnosing. If only TENSION_CULTURAL or HORIZONTE is missing, proceed with the declared default and record the assumption.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each critical behavior is traceably derived from a strategic priority and is observable, not a feeling; behavior is distinguished from enabler.
- [ ] The current diagnosis uses Competing Values, names the dominant and subordinate type, and makes explicit the informal norms and tacit incentives contrary to the strategy—not just poster values.
- [ ] The gap matrix covers the 4–6 behaviors with qualified magnitude and a root cause for each.
- [ ] Gaps are prioritized by impact and feasibility; at least one quick win is identified.
- [ ] The plan covers the 6 levers with actions, role-type owner, 30/60/90 sequence, and a measurable success signal, with a counterweight to expected resistance.
- [ ] Every inference without basis is marked [ASSUMPTION]; the close includes the questions that most reduce the diagnosis risk.
- [ ] Actionable language, neutral and professional English, without filler.
Expected deliverable: structured document with four blocks (critical behaviors, current cultural profile, prioritized gap matrix, 30/60/90 plan by lever) ready to present to a board of directors.
spec-estrategia_gestion_stakeholders_cam:
[inputs]
- INICIATIVA_TRANSFORMACION: {{INICIATIVA_TRANSFORMACION}} > What transformation you are driving and what changes for the organization
- ACTORES_CLAVE: {{ACTORES_CLAVE}} > People, areas, or roles involved or affected (with their function)
- OBJETIVO_ALINEACION: {{OBJETIVO_ALINEACION}} > The concrete decision or adoption you need to secure
- HORIZONTE_DECISION: {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}} > Timeline in which the decision must occur or the point of no return
- RESISTENCIA_PERCIBIDA: {{RESISTENCIA_PERCIBIDA}} > Where you currently perceive the greatest friction or blockage (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A transformation rarely fails due to its technical design: it fails because actors did not align in time. Mapping power and interest before acting unlocks what would otherwise be discovered too late: who can veto, who can sponsor, where the real resistance lies, and in what order it makes sense to move the pieces. The frequent trap is confusing nominal authority with real influence: the org chart does not predict who blocks nor who carries others. The desired outcome is an actionable influence plan that converts an initiative exposed to organizational politics into one with a deliberate coalition, a calendar-tied sequence, and anticipatory resistance management.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior change management strategist, with a track record leading organizational transformations and expert in stakeholder mapping, power dynamics, and coalition design.

Deliverable: a stakeholder map and an alignment, coalition, and resistance-handling plan, in tables, for {{INICIATIVA_TRANSFORMACION}} with focus on securing {{OBJETIVO_ALINEACION}} within {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}}.

Steps:
1. Stakeholder inventory from {{ACTORES_CLAVE}}: role, what they gain or lose from the transformation, current stance (champion, neutral, skeptic, or opponent), and real level of influence (capacity to veto, sponsor, or block), not nominal authority.
2. Power-interest matrix (Mendelow grid): place each actor in exactly one quadrant: manage closely (high power, high interest), keep satisfied (high power, low interest), keep informed (low power, high interest), monitor (low power, low interest). Justify each placement by observable power and interest.
3. Alignment tactics by quadrant: how to convert power into sponsorship, the argument that moves each actor (what matters to them), and contact channel and cadence.
4. Resistance-handling plan per opponent or skeptic: likely root (power, competence, trust, or conviction), mitigation tactic, movement owner, early escalation signal, and Plan B if mitigation fails.
5. Coalition-building sequence tied to {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}}: who to align first to create critical mass, what visible sponsorship milestones are needed, and what dependencies exist between moves.
6. Control dashboard: 3 to 5 alignment progress indicators and the threshold that triggers replanning.
7. Close: the three highest-leverage moves within {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}}.
Also: flag absent actors who should be on the map but do not appear in {{ACTORES_CLAVE}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: integrate inputs and {{RESISTENCIA_PERCIBIDA}}; name the assumptions covering any gap and the absent actors detected.
Phase 2 - Mapping: inventory and power-interest matrix with a brief justification for each placement.
Phase 3 - Influence: tactics by quadrant and resistance-handling plan per actor, with owner and Plan B.
Phase 4 - Sequence and control: coalition route with dependencies, sponsorship milestones, indicators dashboard, and the three highest-leverage moves.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Every actor from {{ACTORES_CLAVE}} appears in the inventory and in exactly one quadrant of the matrix, with their stance.
- The matrix placement is justified by observable power and interest; influence is measured as capacity to veto, sponsor, or block, not by nominal hierarchy.
- Each alignment tactic names the argument that moves the actor and a specific channel/cadence.
- Each opponent or skeptic has a resistance root, mitigation tactic, owner, early escalation signal, and Plan B.
- The coalition sequence is ordered, tied to {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}}, and makes dependencies between moves explicit.
- The dashboard has 3 to 5 indicators with a replanning threshold; absent actors detected are listed.
- No names, data, or stances are invented beyond the inputs; gaps are marked as explicit assumptions.
Expected deliverable: document in tables (inventory, power-interest matrix, tactics by quadrant, resistance handling, coalition sequence, control dashboard) and a final block with the three highest-leverage moves for the indicated horizon.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_arquitectura_c4:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA: {{SISTEMA}} > Name and one-line description of the system to be modeled
- DOMINIO_Y_PROPOSITO: {{DOMINIO_Y_PROPOSITO}} > Business domain, purpose, and problem it solves
- STACK_TECNOLOGICO: {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}} > Known or preferred languages, frameworks, databases, and infrastructure (optional)
- ACTORES_Y_SISTEMAS_EXTERNOS: {{ACTORES_Y_SISTEMAS_EXTERNOS}} > Users, roles, and third-party systems that interact with the system (optional)
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Expected depth: up to containers, up to components, or up to code (optional, default: up to components)
- RESTRICCIONES_Y_ATRIBUTOS: {{RESTRICCIONES_Y_ATRIBUTOS}} > Quality attributes or constraints that condition the design: scale, latency, availability, security, regulation, team budget (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need a shareable and versionable architecture view for {{SISTEMA}} ({{DOMINIO_Y_PROPOSITO}}) that aligns business, architecture, and development on the same structure. Simon Brown's C4 model solves this with a progressive-zoom hierarchy (Context > Containers > Components > Code) that avoids ambiguous box-and-arrow diagrams and produces a navigable map. A good C4 model unlocks rapid onboarding, traceable design decisions, technical risk review, and a living base for the ADR and system evolution. Constraints and quality attributes to respect: {{RESTRICCIONES_Y_ATRIBUTOS}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in Simon Brown's C4 model, with practice in distributed systems design, quality attributes, and Mermaid notation.

Deliverable: the system modeled at the C4 levels required by {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}, each with its renderable Mermaid diagram, legend, and justified decisions. Steps:
1. Level 1 Context: represent {{SISTEMA}} as the central box; place the human actors and external systems from {{ACTORES_Y_SISTEMAS_EXTERNOS}}; label each relationship with the data or intent that flows and its direction. Explicitly define the system boundary (what is inside vs. what is external).
2. Level 2 Containers: decompose the central box into deployable units (web app, API, SPA, mobile app, databases, queues, cache, services) using {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}}; for each container declare technology, single responsibility, and communication protocol (HTTPS, gRPC, AMQP, JDBC). A container is an independently deployable executable or storage unit, not a class or module.
3. Level 3 Components: select the most critical container (highest risk, most change, or domain core) and decompose it into internal components (controllers, domain services, repositories, adapters); declare each one's responsibility and dependencies, respecting layer separation and dependency direction.
4. Level 4 Code: for the highest-risk component sketch a class diagram or structure (classes, interfaces, key relationships). If {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} does not require it or the detail does not add maintenance value, omit it explicitly and justify why (Brown's usual recommendation for keeping diagrams alive).
5. For each level attach: the Mermaid diagram, a legend of elements, and an Architectural Decisions block that justifies each relevant choice including its trade-off (alternative considered and why it was discarded), connected to {{RESTRICCIONES_Y_ATRIBUTOS}} where applicable.
6. Close with a level-to-level traceability map (which element decomposes into which), a list of assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION], and a model limits section (what is out of scope and why).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm scope, domain, stack, actors, and quality attributes; if a key input is missing, ask for it before modeling; do not invent integrations or technologies; mark every inferred datum as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 Top-down modeling: produce the levels in order 1 > 2 > 3 > 4 up to whatever {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} requires, ensuring that every element at one level has an origin in the previous one (no orphaned elements) and a single clear responsibility.
Phase 3 Diagramming: write each diagram in valid Mermaid (flowchart for levels 1–3, classDiagram for level 4) with technology and relationship labels; use identifiers without spaces or reserved characters and mentally verify that each block renders.
Phase 4 Justification and traceability: document decisions with trade-offs, build the traceability map, declare limits, and consolidate assumptions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The levels required by {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} are present; Level 4 is included only if it adds value, or omitted with an explicit justification.
- Each diagram is syntactically valid Mermaid and renderable, with a legend of elements.
- The system boundary is defined at Level 1 (inside vs. external).
- Each container declares technology, single responsibility, and communication protocol; containers are not confused with classes or modules.
- Each Level 3 component declares responsibility and dependencies, with coherent layer separation.
- No element is orphaned: every lower level is traced to the upper one via the traceability map.
- Architectural Decisions justify each relevant choice and include the trade-off of the discarded alternative; unconfirmed data is marked [ASSUMPTION].
- The model limits make clear what is out of scope.
Expected deliverable: C4 architecture document with the corresponding Mermaid diagrams, legends, Architectural Decisions blocks with trade-offs, level-to-level traceability map, list of assumptions, and limits section, ready to version alongside the code.
spec-desarrollo_adr_decision_arquitectur:
[inputs]
- DECISION_ARQUITECTONICA: {{DECISION_ARQUITECTONICA}} > The technical decision to document (e.g. "adopt event sourcing in the payments module", "migrate the inventory domain from monolith to microservices")
- CONTEXTO_SISTEMA: {{CONTEXTO_SISTEMA}} > Description of the system, current stack, scale, and lifecycle stage
- REQUISITOS_NO_FUNCIONALES: {{REQUISITOS_NO_FUNCIONALES}} > Priority quality attributes and their drivers (latency, scalability, maintainability, operational cost, consistency, security, observability, etc.)
- ALTERNATIVAS_EVALUADAS: {{ALTERNATIVAS_EVALUADAS}} > Options already considered by the team (at least one; AI may add other relevant ones up to at least two in total)
- ESTADO_ADR: {{ESTADO_ADR}} > Decision status: Proposed, Accepted, Rejected, Obsolete, or Superseded-by-ADR-NNN (optional; default Proposed)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An undocumented architecture decision evaporates: in six months no one remembers why a message queue was chosen over synchronous calls, and the team repeats the debate or reverses the decision without understanding the forces that motivated it. An ADR in Nygard format freezes the reasoning while it is still fresh and gives auditable traceability to the technical strategy of the product. This prompt produces that record for the decision: {{DECISION_ARQUITECTONICA}}, in a system described by {{CONTEXTO_SISTEMA}}. The deliverable unlocks peer review, rapid onboarding, and a decision timeline the team can audit.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect with years documenting technical decisions in Nygard format and facilitating peer architecture reviews.

Deliverable: a complete and self-contained ADR in Markdown. Steps:
1. Title and ID: assign a declarative short title in the present tense (e.g. "Adopt event sourcing in payments") with sequential identifier ADR-NNN; if no number is provided, use ADR-001 and mark it [ASSUMPTION].
2. Status and date: declare the Status per {{ESTADO_ADR}} (default Proposed) with the date; if it supersedes or is superseded by another ADR, link the corresponding identifier.
3. Context: enumerate the forces at play from {{CONTEXTO_SISTEMA}} and {{REQUISITOS_NO_FUNCIONALES}} (requirements, technical and business constraints, quality drivers, debt, assumptions) in a neutral way, without anticipating the decision.
4. Options considered: include {{ALTERNATIVAS_EVALUADAS}} plus other relevant ones (at least two in total, including status quo if applicable); each with pros, cons, and a discard reason derived from an explicit trade-off against the requirements.
5. Decision: state what was chosen and the central justification, citing which context force weighs most and which priority non-functional requirement it connects to.
6. Consequences: positive, negative, and neutral, with the technical debt assumed, the impact on neighboring components, and the future conditions (load, cost, requirement change, end of support) that would invalidate the decision or force a new ADR.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Reading forces: extract requirements, constraints, and quality drivers from the inputs; separate facts from assumptions and mark the latter with [ASSUMPTION]. Do not invent metrics, SLAs, or constraints.
Phase 2 - Options map: evaluate each alternative against the priority non-functional requirements; the discard must derive from an explicit trade-off, not from a preference. If only one option was provided, add at least one relevant one (including status quo) so the comparison is real.
Phase 3 - Decision and traceability: justify the choice by citing which context force weighs most; verify that an external reader understands the decision without additional information.
Phase 4 - Consequences and reversibility: declare what is gained, what is sacrificed, and under what future conditions this ADR should be reviewed or replaced; name the expected successor ADR if the decision is transitory.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate the decision and the dominant criterion in one line, present your plan, then execute.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Complete Nygard structure: Title+ID, Status+date, Context, Options, Decision, Consequences.
- [ ] The Context is neutral and does not anticipate the decision.
- [ ] At least two options, each with pros, cons, and a discard reason derived from a trade-off.
- [ ] The Decision explicitly connects to at least one priority non-functional requirement.
- [ ] Consequences include the negative and the technical debt, not just the positive.
- [ ] There are explicit conditions that would invalidate or force a review of the decision.
- [ ] Every unprovided datum is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented metrics or constraints.
- [ ] If the Status is Superseded-by or Obsolete, there is a link to the related ADR.
- [ ] ADR is self-contained: understandable by someone without prior context.
Expected deliverable: an ADR document in Markdown ready to save in the repository (e.g. docs/adr/ADR-NNN-title.md), reviewable by peers without additional clarifications.
spec-desarrollo_evaluacion_atam:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA: {{SISTEMA}} > Name and purpose of the system whose architecture is being evaluated
- DRIVERS_NEGOCIO: {{DRIVERS_NEGOCIO}} > Business objectives, key stakeholders, and constraints (technical, business, regulatory) that justify the architecture; indicate which are hard constraints and which are preferences
- DESCRIPCION_ARQUITECTURA: {{DESCRIPCION_ARQUITECTURA}} > Styles and patterns, main components, key structural decisions, and deployment view
- ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD: {{ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD}} > Priority quality attributes (e.g. availability, performance, security, modifiability, scalability) with their relative priority if known
- ESCENARIOS_CRITICOS: {{ESCENARIOS_CRITICOS}} > Known critical scenarios or concerns, or "No predefined scenarios"
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to conduct an ATAM (Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method, from the Software Engineering Institute) evaluation on the architecture of {{SISTEMA}}. The purpose is to expose trade-offs between quality attributes and architectural risks BEFORE committing construction resources, when reversing a structural decision is still inexpensive. What is unlocked: design decisions made with evidence and traceability to business drivers rather than by intuition; an explicit map of where the architecture is fragile and where improving one attribute degrades another. ATAM does not certify or fail: it illuminates the decision space so the business can knowingly assume risks.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect certified in SEI evaluation methods, with experience conducting ATAM evaluations on production systems and facilitating workshops with technical and business stakeholders.

Deliverable: an ATAM evaluation report of {{SISTEMA}}. Steps:
1. Frame the method: ATAM does not produce a numerical score or a pass/fail verdict; it exposes risks, sensitivity points, and trade-offs on the attributes that matter to the business.
2. Derive from {{DRIVERS_NEGOCIO}} objectives, stakeholders, and constraints; separate hard constraint (non-negotiable) from preference.
3. Present the architecture from {{DESCRIPCION_ARQUITECTURA}}: styles, components, key structural decisions, and deployment, naming each decision to trace findings to it.
4. Build the utility tree with {{ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD}}: hierarchize attributes and refine them into scenarios (stimulus, response, measure with a quantifiable value, not adjectives), incorporating {{ESCENARIOS_CRITICOS}}. Prioritize each scenario on two independent axes H/M/L: business importance and architectural difficulty. (H,H) and (H,M) are of priority analysis.
5. Per priority scenario, identify the decisions that support it and classify each finding into exactly one category: sensitivity point, trade-off point, risk, or non-risk.
6. Consolidate risks into risk themes and link each theme to the impacted driver, making explicit the business consequence if it materializes.
7. Close with prioritized recommendations, mitigations by theme, and pending decision points.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: method and its non-numerical scope.
Phase 2 - Drivers and constraints: order objectives and constraints from {{DRIVERS_NEGOCIO}}; flag hard vs. preference.
Phase 3 - Architecture presentation: styles, views, and key decisions from {{DESCRIPCION_ARQUITECTURA}}, each decision named.
Phase 4 - Utility tree: attributes > refinements > stimulus-response-measure scenarios prioritized (importance, difficulty) in H/M/L.
Phase 5 - Approach analysis: go through priority scenarios and classify findings (sensitivity / trade-off / risk / non-risk) linked to concrete decisions.
Phase 6 - Risk themes: group risks and relate them to the impacted drivers and their business consequence.
Phase 7 - Recommendations: prioritize mitigations with architectural justification and list pending decisions.
Evidence rule: mark [ASSUMPTION] for every inference due to missing data and distinguish the evidenced from the inferred. Do not confuse sensitivity point with trade-off, or risk with style preference. If {{DRIVERS_NEGOCIO}}, {{DESCRIPCION_ARQUITECTURA}}, or {{ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD}} arrive empty or insufficient, ask for them before continuing; never invent the architecture.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Utility tree with hierarchized attributes and scenarios in stimulus-response-measure format with a quantifiable value, prioritized on a dual H/M/L axis.
- [ ] Each priority scenario linked to concrete named architectural decisions, not generalities.
- [ ] Findings classified rigorously into a single category (sensitivity / trade-off / risk / non-risk), without mixing them.
- [ ] Each risk theme traced to an impacted business driver, with explicit consequence and actionable mitigation.
- [ ] Prioritized recommendations with explicit architectural justification and pending decisions listed.
- [ ] Hard constraints separated from preferences; every inference marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: ATAM report with (1) prioritized utility tree, (2) scenario analysis table [scenario | decision | classification | evidence/assumption], (3) numbered list of risk themes with impacted driver and mitigation, (4) prioritized recommendations with justification and pending decisions.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_dirigido_dominio:
[inputs]
- DESCRIPCION_DOMINIO: {{DESCRIPCION_DOMINIO}} > Description of the business domain to model: processes, purpose, and vocabulary used by the experts
- REGLAS_NEGOCIO: {{REGLAS_NEGOCIO}} > Known rules, constraints, and invariants that must be preserved (optional)
- ACTORES_AREAS: {{ACTORES_AREAS}} > Actors, roles, and organizational areas involved in the domain (optional)
- ESTILO_ARQUITECTONICO: {{ESTILO_ARQUITECTONICO}} > Target style: modular monolith, microservices, or indistinct (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to model a business domain with Domain-Driven Design so that the team shares a single model and a boundary map before writing code. Rigorous modeling unlocks defensible architecture decisions: where to split the system, what modules or services to create, where to place anticorruption layers, and what invariants to protect in each transaction. The result avoids three chronic failures: the anemic model (entities without behavior, logic scattered in services), aggregates that grow without control (slow transactions and locks), and boundaries that leak between teams (coupling that prevents parallel evolution). The model is a distillation of the business, not a database diagram.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design, with experience distilling complex domains alongside business experts and translating them into context boundaries and implementable aggregates.

Deliverable: an actionable strategic and tactical domain model. Produce, in this order:
1. Ubiquitous language glossary: domain terms with unambiguous definitions; mark synonyms and overloaded terms that change meaning depending on the area.
2. Table of subdomains classified as core, supporting, and generic, with the justification for each classification and the investment implication it suggests (core = build custom and protect; supporting = build simply or outsource; generic = buy/adopt an existing solution).
3. Bounded contexts: delimit where each term has a unique meaning; for each context, its single responsibility, the language that governs it, and the subdomain it materializes.
4. Context map in text: relationships between contexts named with integration patterns (partnership, customer-supplier, conformist, anticorruption layer, shared kernel, open host service, published language), direction of flow (upstream/downstream), and the reason for each relationship including the accepted coupling.
5. Aggregates per context: aggregate root, contained entities and value objects, and business invariants that the aggregate protects in each transaction. Small aggregates; reference other aggregates by identity only, never by object.
6. Relevant domain events that cross boundaries and trigger eventual consistency between aggregates or contexts.
7. Detected modeling risks: oversized aggregates, leaking boundaries, anemic model, circular dependencies, contexts that mix more than one language; each risk with concrete mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Distillation: extract the ubiquitous language from DESCRIPCION_DOMINIO and ACTORES_AREAS; detect term collisions between areas (same name, different meaning).
Phase 2 — Strategy: classify subdomains and draw the boundaries of the bounded contexts where the language remains consistent; align each context with a subdomain.
Phase 3 — Integration: describe the context map in text, assign relationship patterns and direction of flow; use ESTILO_ARQUITECTONICO to calibrate coupling and where an anticorruption layer is advisable (microservices privilege ACL and open host service; modular monolith tolerates a bounded shared kernel).
Phase 4 — Tactics: define aggregates, roots, value objects, and invariants from REGLAS_NEGOCIO; maintain transactional consistency within the aggregate and eventual consistency between aggregates; name the domain events that trigger it.
Phase 5 — Verification: review aggregate size, boundary leaks, anemia, cycles, and multi-language contexts; list risks with mitigation.
Foundation: Eric Evans (DDD, 2003) and Vaughn Vernon (IDDD, 2013). Do not invent business rules; if critical information is missing for delimiting boundaries or defining invariants, request it before modeling. Mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]. Always distinguish the business model from its persistence: do not derive aggregates from tables.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each glossary term has a single definition per context; collisions between areas are flagged.
- Each subdomain is classified (core/supporting/generic) with justification and investment implication.
- Each bounded context declares a single responsibility, a clear linguistic boundary, and the subdomain it materializes.
- Every context map relationship carries a named integration pattern, direction of flow, and justification.
- Each aggregate exposes root, content, and invariants; no aggregate references another by object, only by identity.
- Transactional consistency within the aggregate; eventual consistency between aggregates, naming the domain events that trigger it.
- Modeling risks listed with mitigation; no context mixes more than one language.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; missing information requested, not invented; aggregates distilled from the business, not from the data schema.
Expected deliverable: DDD modeling document with glossary, subdomain table, bounded contexts, context map in text, domain events, and an aggregate sheet for each one, ready to underpin the partitioning into modules or services.
spec-desarrollo_descomposicion_microserv:
[inputs]
- MONOLITO: {{MONOLITO}} > Name and purpose of the monolithic system to decompose
- CAPACIDADES_NEGOCIO: {{CAPACIDADES_NEGOCIO}} > Business functions covered by the system (e.g.: billing, inventory, dispatch)
- ENTIDADES_DATOS: {{ENTIDADES_DATOS}} > Main entities, aggregates, or tables and their relationships
- RESTRICCIONES_CONSISTENCIA: {{RESTRICCIONES_CONSISTENCIA}} > Critical transactions and invariants that must remain atomic
- OBJETIVO_MIGRACION: {{OBJETIVO_MIGRACION}} > What the migration aims to unlock (scale an area, independent deployments, autonomous teams) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A monolith that has grown beyond its design stalls deployments, mixes team responsibilities, and turns every change into a regression risk. The most expensive mistake is cutting by technical layers (controllers, services, repos) or by tables: that produces anemic services that share a database and remain coupled. The correct cut is by business capabilities and data boundaries, so that each future service has clear owners, its own data, and can evolve and be deployed independently. A well-reasoned decomposition unlocks team autonomy, selective scaling, and an incremental low-risk extraction path instead of a total rewrite (big bang), which almost always fails.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in distributed systems and Domain-Driven Design, with experience migrating monoliths to microservices in production.
Decompose the monolith {{MONOLITO}} into candidate services and deliver:
1. Bounded context map from {{CAPACIDADES_NEGOCIO}}, with the ubiquitous language of each one and the context relationships (upstream/downstream, ACL, shared kernel) between them.
2. Data ownership table for {{ENTIDADES_DATOS}}: aggregate, owning context, who writes, who reads, shared data that creates coupling, and how that coupling is broken (read replica, event, API).
3. One candidate service per bounded context, with justification of the cut by cohesion/coupling and an explicit rejection of cuts that would split an aggregate or a transaction from {{RESTRICCIONES_CONSISTENCIA}}.
4. Contract per service: single responsibility, public API (synchronous operations + emitted and consumed domain events), exclusively owned data, and suggested owner/team.
5. Seams and risks: distributed transactions, cross-service queries, and consistency pattern where applicable (saga, outbox, CQRS) with its justification and failure mode.
6. Strangler Fig extraction plan ordered by value and risk, with the first lowest-risk cut, its verification criterion, and the rollback strategy, aligned with {{OBJETIVO_MIGRACION}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Domain: extract business capabilities and group them into bounded contexts; name the ubiquitous language and the relationships between contexts. Do not invent capabilities; mark inferences as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Data: build the data ownership table and locate the shared data that generates coupling; propose how to decouple it.
Phase 3 - Cuts: derive one service per context maximizing cohesion and minimizing coupling; reject in writing any cuts that break atomicity or aggregates.
Phase 4 - Contracts: define responsibility, API (operations + events), own data, and owner for each service.
Phase 5 - Seams: list distributed transactions and cross-service queries; assign pattern (saga/outbox/CQRS) with justification and failure mode.
Phase 6 - Plan: order the Strangler Fig extraction by value/risk, define how to measure that the first cut did not break behavior, and how to revert if it does.
Edge cases: if two contexts share an aggregate, do not separate them yet, declare it as a seam and prioritize decoupling; if {{OBJETIVO_MIGRACION}} does not arrive, prioritize by deployment risk reduction.
If information about the domain, entities, or consistency constraints is missing, request it before proposing cuts.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each service corresponds to a bounded context with a single responsibility, not to a technical layer or a table.
- [ ] The data ownership table does not leave an aggregate split between two services; each shared piece of data has a decoupling mechanism.
- [ ] Every transaction from {{RESTRICCIONES_CONSISTENCIA}} is within a single service or has an eventual consistency pattern assigned with its failure mode.
- [ ] Each contract declares operations, domain events (emitted and consumed), exclusively owned data, and an owner.
- [ ] The Strangler Fig plan orders by value/risk and names the first lowest-risk cut with a verification criterion and rollback.
- [ ] Every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION]; there are no invented capabilities or entities.
Expected deliverable: document with bounded context map and relationships, data ownership table, contracts per service, seams with assigned pattern, and ordered incremental extraction plan with rollback, ready for architecture review.
spec-desarrollo_arquitectura_hexagonal:
[inputs]
- ALCANCE: {{ALCANCE}} > Greenfield (new design) or refactor of an existing codebase toward hexagonal
- DOMINIO_NEGOCIO: {{DOMINIO_NEGOCIO}} > Functional domain (e.g. order management, billing, reservations, onboarding)
- LENGUAJE_STACK: {{LENGUAJE_STACK}} > Target language and framework (e.g. Java/Spring, TypeScript/NestJS, Python/FastAPI, Go)
- ADAPTADORES_ENTRADA: {{ADAPTADORES_ENTRADA}} > Delivery mechanisms to support (e.g. REST, CLI, event consumer, GraphQL)
- ADAPTADORES_SALIDA: {{ADAPTADORES_SALIDA}} > Driven dependencies to integrate (e.g. PostgreSQL, Kafka, payment gateway, SMTP)
- DEPENDENCIAS_EXTERNAS: {{DEPENDENCIAS_EXTERNAS}} > Constraints or mandatory environment components; "(optional)" if not applicable
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs a {{DOMINIO_NEGOCIO}} application in {{LENGUAJE_STACK}} whose business logic survives the replacement of frameworks, databases, and external providers. Applying hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters, Alistair Cockburn 2005) unlocks: testable domain without spinning up infrastructure, substitution of adapters without touching the core, and an explicit boundary that stops coupling debt before it becomes embedded. Scope: {{ALCANCE}}. This architectural decision conditions the speed of evolution and the cost of testing for the coming years; a poorly delimited core is paid for as a rewrite, not as an adjustment.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in Domain-Driven Design and clean architectures, with experience assembling productive hexagonal systems in {{LENGUAJE_STACK}}.
Deliverable: actionable hexagonal architecture blueprint for {{DOMINIO_NEGOCIO}}, ready to start implementation. Steps:
1. Delimit the domain core: entities, value objects, aggregates (root and consistency boundary), invariants, and use cases (application services). The domain imports nothing from infrastructure.
2. Define the input ports (driving): interfaces that expose the use cases to the outside world, expressed in business language.
3. Define the output ports (driven): interfaces that the core declares for persistence, messaging, or external services, implemented outside (dependency inversion).
4. Design the primary adapters ({{ADAPTADORES_ENTRADA}}) that translate external input to input ports, and the secondary ones ({{ADAPTADORES_SALIDA}}) that implement the output ports; respect {{DEPENDENCIAS_EXTERNAS}}.
5. Specify the composition: the assembler or injection container that connects adapters to ports at startup (single composition root).
6. Define the mapping boundary: external DTO <-> domain model translation, without leaking infrastructure types into the core.
7. Decide and justify the critical trade-offs: aggregate granularity, transactional boundary and consistency (immediate vs. eventual), separation of domain errors vs. technical errors, idempotency on messaging ports, and location of orchestration (application service vs. domain process).
8. Deliver the package structure, the dependency rule (everything points to the domain), and a concrete use case traversing the layers end to end.
9. Propose the testing strategy per layer and, if {{ALCANCE}} is a refactor, the strangling sequence toward hexagonal without freezing delivery.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Domain modeling: extract ubiquitous language, entities, aggregates, and invariants; mark unconfirmed assumptions as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Contracts: declare input and output ports as stable, technology-agnostic interfaces; name by business intent, not by technology.
Phase 3 - Adapters and composition: map each {{ADAPTADORES_ENTRADA}}/{{ADAPTADORES_SALIDA}} to its port and describe the wiring at startup from a single composition root.
Phase 4 - Boundary and tracing: define mappers and trace a use case end to end validating the dependency rule at each hop.
Phase 5 - Trade-offs and testing: justify the decisions from step 7; assign test type per layer (pure unit, test double, adapter contract, integration); list avoided antipatterns.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The domain contains no framework, ORM, or HTTP client imports (zero outgoing dependencies toward infrastructure) and avoids the anemic model (logic lives in entities and application services, not in adapters).
- Each output port is declared in the domain and implemented only in one secondary adapter; each input and output port is named by business intent.
- All dependency arrows point toward the core (dependency rule verifiable hop by hop).
- Each {{ADAPTADORES_ENTRADA}} and {{ADAPTADORES_SALIDA}} is mapped to a port, with no business logic in the adapter, and respects {{DEPENDENCIAS_EXTERNAS}}.
- The use case example traverses primary adapter -> input port -> application service -> output port -> secondary adapter, with the transactional boundary explicit.
- Trade-offs (aggregate granularity, consistency, domain/technical errors, idempotency, orchestration) are decided and justified, not just listed.
- A differentiated testing strategy exists per layer, infrastructure types are not leaked into the core, and, if applicable, there is a strangling sequence for the refactor.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; ambiguities marked {to_confirm} and asked about before executing.
Expected deliverable: blueprint document with package tree, list of ports and adapters, textual dependency diagram, traced use case, table of decided trade-offs, testing matrix per layer, and risk/open-decisions log, ready to start implementation.
spec-desarrollo_event_storming:
[inputs]
- DOMINIO_NEGOCIO: {{DOMINIO_NEGOCIO}} > Domain or business process to model (example: e-commerce order management, customer onboarding, policy settlement)
- ALCANCE_SESION: {{ALCANCE_SESION}} > Type of Event Storming: Big Picture (exploratory, broad view, multiple flows) or Process Modeling (detailed, one concrete flow with commands/aggregates)
- ROLES_PARTICIPANTES: {{ROLES_PARTICIPANTES}} > Roles present or to be represented (example: domain expert, dev, PO, architect); guides who to attribute actors and decisions to
- REGLAS_CONOCIDAS: {{REGLAS_CONOCIDAS}} > Already known business rules, constraints, and invariants (optional; if empty, everything is treated as yet to be discovered)
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Expected depth: events and commands only, or through aggregates and bounded contexts (optional; default consistent with ALCANCE_SESION)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Discovering the domain model of {{DOMINIO_NEGOCIO}} before writing code avoids poorly partitioned architectures and costly rework. An Event Storming session aligns business and technology in a shared ubiquitous language and unlocks design decisions: which aggregates exist, where the boundaries between contexts go, and which policies govern the flow. The result is an actionable map that serves as the basis for modeling aggregates, defining APIs, and planning implementation. The scope conditions the depth: Big Picture prioritizes breadth and boundary discovery; Process Modeling prioritizes precision of commands, invariants, and aggregates of a concrete flow.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Event Storming facilitator and Domain-Driven Design expert, with experience running workshops with domain experts and translating the flow into an implementable tactical model.
Deliver a domain model for {{DOMINIO_NEGOCIO}} with scope {{ALCANCE_SESION}}, considering the roles {{ROLES_PARTICIPANTES}} and the rules {{REGLAS_CONOCIDAS}} at level {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}. Steps:
1. Gather domain events (in the past tense) and order them on a coherent timeline; mark alternative paths and exceptions.
2. Identify the command (imperative) and the actor or system that triggers each event; flag external or integration events that arrive from other contexts.
3. Detect the reactive policies 'when X then Y' that chain events with commands, separating human decisions from automatic ones.
4. Group commands and events into aggregates that protect invariants; name the invariant of each aggregate and the read models that feed decisions.
5. Draw the bounded contexts, name their ubiquitous language, and classify the integration relationships (customer-supplier, conformist, anti-corruption layer, shared kernel).
6. Prioritize hot spots (conflicts, doubts, missing data) with actionable open questions for the next iteration.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Ordered chaos: enumerate events without filtering, order them temporally, mark hot spots and branches.
Phase 2 Commands and actors: map each event to its command and emitter; distinguish human actors from systems.
Phase 3 Policies: make explicit the reactive rules that connect the flow, separating human from automatic.
Phase 4 Aggregates and read models: group by invariants, name the protected invariant and the query views.
Phase 5 Bounded contexts: draw boundaries, name the ubiquitous language, and classify the integration relationship.
Phase 6 Synthesis: deliver tables, timeline, and prioritized hot spots.
Limits and edge cases: if the scope is Big Picture, do not force fine-grained aggregates or invariants (record them as a hot spot); in Process Modeling require command+actor per event. Explicitly mark happy paths vs. alternative paths and compensations (events that revert others). Do not invent business rules: any missing data is recorded as a hot spot; reasonable assumptions are marked as [ASSUMPTION]. Maintain consistent naming and verbs from the domain's ubiquitous language.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Events in the past tense and commands in the imperative, with consistent naming and domain vocabulary.
- [ ] Each event has a command and an identified actor or system; external events are marked.
- [ ] Policies expressed as 'when X then Y', distinguishing human from automatic.
- [ ] Aggregates group invariants with the invariant named; read models named where applicable.
- [ ] Bounded contexts with clear boundaries, ubiquitous language, and classified integration relationship.
- [ ] Alternative paths, exceptions, and compensations reflected in the timeline.
- [ ] Hot spots prioritized with actionable open questions.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no business rule invented.
- [ ] Depth consistent with {{ALCANCE_SESION}} and {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}.
Expected deliverable: narrated event timeline (with branches) + event-command-actor-policy-aggregate table + bounded context listing with ubiquitous language and classified integration relationships + prioritized list of hot spots with open questions.
spec-desarrollo_cqrs_event_sourcing:
[inputs]
- DOMINIO: {{DOMINIO}} > Business domain or subdomain to model (e.g. e-commerce order management, bank accounts, reservations)
- OPERACION_CRITICA: {{OPERACION_CRITICA}} > Business operation that matters most to model correctly (e.g. confirm order, transfer balance)
- VOLUMEN_LECTURA_ESCRITURA: {{VOLUMEN_LECTURA_ESCRITURA}} > Approximate read/write load profile and peaks (e.g. 95% reads, 200 writes/sec peak)
- CONSISTENCIA_LECTURA: {{CONSISTENCIA_LECTURA}} > Tolerance for lag between write and read (e.g. eventual <1s acceptable, or read-your-writes mandatory on certain views)
- RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS: {{RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS}} > Stack, persistence, event bus, or existing constraints (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need a CQRS with event sourcing architecture for the domain {{DOMINIO}}, whose critical operation is {{OPERACION_CRITICA}}. The system faces a load profile of {{VOLUMEN_LECTURA_ESCRITURA}} and must satisfy a read consistency of {{CONSISTENCIA_LECTURA}}, within the constraints {{RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS}}. Separating command from query and deriving state from an immutable event log unlocks complete auditing, the ability to reconstruct any view, and the ability to scale reads and writes separately, in exchange for operational complexity, visible eventual consistency, and a higher debugging cost that must be justified before adopting the pattern.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in event-driven systems, event sourcing, and tactical Domain-Driven Design.
Deliver an actionable architecture design. Before step 1, decide whether CQRS+ES is justified for this case (rich invariants, auditing, read/write asymmetry); if it is not, declare it and propose the simplest alternative (CRUD or CQRS without ES) with its reason. Then develop the numbered steps:
1. Delimit the aggregates and their consistency boundaries; no transaction crosses aggregates and consistency between aggregates is eventual via events or sagas/process managers.
2. Define the domain event catalog named in the past tense, with minimal, immutable payload, without presentation logic or derivable data; mark events that trigger cross-aggregate processes.
3. Design the commands: preconditions, invariants validated against the reconstructed state of the aggregate, events they emit on success, handling of rejected commands, and idempotency on retries.
4. Specify the event store: one stream per aggregate, optimistic versioning for concurrency control, snapshot policy when the stream grows, and retry strategy on version conflict.
5. Design the read models and the projections that feed them; declare eventual consistency, lag handling (including read-your-writes if applicable), rebuilding projections from scratch, and consumer idempotency.
6. Define schema evolution: event versioning and upcasting; past events are never mutated.
7. Deliver a textual flow diagram of command -> event -> event store -> projection -> read model, plus trade-offs vs. CRUD and operational risks (visible eventual consistency, debugging, cost of reprocessing).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Pertinence: validate whether CQRS+ES applies; if not, propose an alternative and stop there unless confirmation to proceed is given.
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm domain, critical operation, load profile, and consistency target; if something essential is missing, ask for it; mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent context.
Phase 2 - Write-side modeling: aggregates, events, and commands with their invariants and idempotency.
Phase 3 - Persistence and read: event store, projections, read models, and lag/rebuild handling.
Phase 4 - Evolution and closure: event versioning, flow diagram, trade-offs, and risks vs. CRUD.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] CQRS+ES pertinence evaluated; if not applicable, simpler alternative proposed with reason.
- [ ] Each aggregate has an explicit consistency boundary; no transaction crosses aggregates and consistency between them is eventual via events or sagas.
- [ ] Events named in the past tense, with minimal and immutable payload, without presentation or derivable data; no generic CRUD events (empty Created/Updated).
- [ ] Each command declares preconditions, invariants validated against the reconstructed state, emitted events, rejected commands, and idempotency.
- [ ] Event store defines stream per aggregate, optimistic versioning, snapshot criterion, and retry on version conflict.
- [ ] Read models and projections declared, with explicit eventual consistency, strategy for lag (read-your-writes if applicable), rebuild, and consumer idempotency.
- [ ] Event versioning and upcasting defined; zero mutation of past events.
- [ ] Textual flow diagram present; trade-offs and operational risks vs. CRUD declared.
- [ ] Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; no emojis.
Expected deliverable: CQRS + event sourcing architecture design document with pertinence evaluation, aggregate catalog, events, commands, event store design, projections and read models, versioning plan, flow diagram, and trade-offs/risks, ready to guide implementation.
spec-desarrollo_atributos_calidad_qualit:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA: {{SISTEMA}} > System or service whose quality attributes will be specified (name, purpose, main components, critical dependencies)
- CONTEXTO_CARGA: {{CONTEXTO_CARGA}} > Expected load: concurrent users, transactions per second, data volume, known peaks and their seasonality
- OBJETIVO_DISPONIBILIDAD: {{OBJETIVO_DISPONIBILIDAD}} > Committed SLA, maintenance window, target RTO and RPO if they exist, business criticality

- ATRIBUTOS_PRIORIZADOS: {{ATRIBUTOS_PRIORIZADOS}} > Attributes to cover by priority (optional; by default performance, availability, and security; other valid ones: scalability, maintainability, observability, recoverability)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The non-functional requirements of {{SISTEMA}} usually remain as contractless adjectives (fast, available, secure), impossible to test and the source of late production arguments. Specifying measurable quality scenarios before building unlocks verifiable architectural acceptance criteria, aligns the team on the numbers that matter, and allows trade-offs (latency vs. consistency, availability vs. cost, security vs. usability) to be decided with evidence rather than opinion. A well-written scenario survives team changes: it is the contract between architecture, QA, and operations.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in quality attributes and scenario-based design, with mastery of ISO/IEC 25010 and the SEI Quality Attribute Workshop (QAW).
Deliverable: a set of measurable quality scenarios for the attributes in {{ATRIBUTOS_PRIORIZADOS}} (by default performance, availability, and security), a verification table, and a trade-off log. Steps:
1. Reformulate in one line {{SISTEMA}}, its {{CONTEXTO_CARGA}}, its {{OBJETIVO_DISPONIBILIDAD}}, and its {{PERFIL_AMENAZAS}}; if any data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before continuing.
2. For each attribute write two to three scenarios with the canonical six-part structure: source of stimulus, stimulus, artifact, environment (normal/peak/degraded), response, and response measure. Include at least one scenario in a degraded or peak environment per attribute, not only the happy path.
3. Quantify each measure with falsifiable metrics: p95/p99 latency in ms, throughput in req/s; availability as annual percentage + tolerated downtime + RTO/RPO; security as detection time + percentage of blocked attempts + patching window. Anchor each number to {{CONTEXTO_CARGA}} or {{OBJETIVO_DISPONIBILIDAD}}; when assumed, mark [ASSUMPTION].
4. Explicitly declare at least one trade-off per pair of attributes in tension and justify the decision with its impact.
5. Build a summary table: scenario, attribute, environment, target metric, and verification method (load test, chaos test, pentest, production monitoring).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm system, load, availability, and threats in one line; list missing data as actionable questions.
Phase 2 - Scenarios: per attribute, instantiate the six-part template; anchor every qualitative term to a number and declare the operating environment. Do not mix two stimuli in the same scenario.
Phase 3 - Quantification and verification: assign target metric and test method to each scenario; record trade-offs; mark [ASSUMPTION] for every value assumed due to missing data and [to_confirm] for those that depend on the business.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each scenario has all six parts complete (source, stimulus, artifact, environment, response, measure).
- [ ] There is at least one scenario in a degraded or peak environment per attribute, not only the normal case.
- [ ] Every measure is quantified and falsifiable; zero vague adjectives without a number (fast, robust, secure).
- [ ] Performance uses percentiles (p95/p99) and throughput, not averages only.
- [ ] Availability expresses annual percentage, tolerated downtime, RTO, and RPO.
- [ ] Security expresses detection, blocking, and patching window, not just controls.
- [ ] At least one justified trade-off between attributes in tension is declared.

spec-desarrollo_fitness_functions_arquit:
[inputs]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Architecture decisions erode silently between commits: an undue dependency, a new cycle, a latency that creeps up. This prompt converts architectural characteristics into executable fitness functions that live in the pipeline, so that each merge is objectively measured against the agreed design. What is unlocked: automated architectural governance, early drift detection, and an architecture that evolves with confidence because its constraints are verifiable, not aspirational.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in evolutionary architecture and automated technical governance, with experience coding design constraints as tests in CI.

Deliverable: a set of executable fitness functions plus the CI gate that orchestrates them. Steps:
1. For CARACTERISTICAS_ARQUITECTONICAS, if any is vague or lacks a threshold in UMBRALES_OBJETIVO, ask for precision (numeric or boolean value, measurement window, scope) before continuing; do not invent values.
2. Classify each fitness function along three axes: atomic vs. holistic, static vs. dynamic, event-triggered vs. continuous; justify each classification in one sentence.
3. Per characteristic, define a measurable threshold, measurement mechanism, and action on failure according to ACCION_ANTE_FALLO.
4. Code each fitness function in STACK_TECNOLOGICO: self-contained, with a clear assert and an actionable failure message that names the concrete violation, the offending module or path, and the observed value vs. the threshold.
5. Deliver the pipeline fragment for PLATAFORMA_CI that runs the functions as a gate: stage, order (static and fast ones first, dynamic ones after), which ones block the merge, and which ones only report trend.
6. For dynamic fitness functions, specify how to avoid false positives from noise (percentiles over a moving window, bounded retries, representative load, stable environment) and a baseline mechanism that detects gradual drift in addition to absolute violations.
7. Define a temporary exception policy: how to suppress a check with an explicit expiry date and owner, so the gate does not become a permanent obstacle or get blindly disabled.
8. Close with a governance table: characteristic, type (three axes), threshold, tool, action on failure, owner.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: map each characteristic to a verifiable property and detect the ones that are not yet measurable. Distinguish structural constraints (static analysis) from operational ones (runtime measurement).
Phase 2 - Classify and design: apply the fitness function taxonomy and choose the appropriate tool by type (ArchUnit/NetArchTest/import-linter/Dependency-cruiser/jQAssistant for structure; load tests or observability metrics for dynamic ones). Justify trade-offs when two tools compete.
Phase 3 - Code: write each function as a failing test with an explicit threshold and actionable message; never opaque asserts. For dynamic ones, fix anti-noise strategy and baseline.
Phase 4 - Orchestrate: integrate into the pipeline defining blocking vs. informative gates, execution order (fast/static first to fail cheaply), and exception policy with expiry.
Phase 5 - Govern: consolidate the table, assign owner per characteristic, and mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each characteristic has a numeric or boolean threshold, no vague adjectives.
- [ ] Each fitness function is classified along the three axes with justification.
- [ ] The code is executable in STACK_TECNOLOGICO, self-contained, and has a failure message that names the violation, the offender, and the observed value vs. the threshold.
- [ ] Dynamic fitness functions declare an anti-false-positive strategy and a baseline for gradual drift.
- [ ] The CI gate distinguishes blocking from informative functions and orders static ones before dynamic ones.
- [ ] A temporary exception policy exists with expiry and owner.
- [ ] The governance table covers the six columns for all characteristics.
- [ ] Every piece of data not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION]; nothing is invented.
Expected deliverable: document with justified classification, code blocks per fitness function, CI pipeline fragment, exception policy, and governance table, ready to incorporate into the repository.
spec-desarrollo_inventario_deuda_arquite:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA: {{SISTEMA}} > System or application to inventory (name, domain, and purpose)
- STACK: {{STACK}} > Languages, frameworks, data engines, and relevant infrastructure
- ARQUITECTURA_ACTUAL: {{ARQUITECTURA_ACTUAL}} > Current style and state (monolith, microservices, layers, diagram if it exists)
- DOLORES_CONOCIDOS: {{DOLORES_CONOCIDOS}} > Symptoms or incidents already perceived by the team (optional)
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > What paying the debt unlocks (scale, accelerate delivery, certify, reduce incidents)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Capacity limits, windows, freezes, or compliance (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The architectural debt of {{SISTEMA}} is scattered across people's heads, tickets, and obsolete diagrams: nobody decides what to pay first because impact, cost, and priority do not live in one comparable place, and every remediation proposal competes against features with intuition-based arguments. This inventory converts that diffuse debt into a decision asset: a single, traceable, and prioritized catalog that unlocks {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} and allows negotiating remediation capacity with evidence. The value is not in listing problems, but in ordering them by return on remediating and sequencing them in a plan that respects {{RESTRICCIONES}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect specialized in technical debt management, system evolution, and economic prioritization of delivery (Fowler quadrant, ATAM for risks at sensitivity and trade-off points, WSJF/cost of delay for ordering).
Deliverable: architectural debt catalog for {{SISTEMA}} with prioritized master table plus sheets for high-priority items and a wave-based payment plan. Steps:
1. Inventory the debt by running through eight dimensions as a checklist (structure and modularity, dependencies and coupling, data and persistence, integrations and APIs, security and compliance, observability, deployment and infrastructure, performance and scalability) against the {{STACK}} and {{ARQUITECTURA_ACTUAL}}, starting from {{DOLORES_CONOCIDOS}}; assign a stable ID (DA-001...), short name, and factual description.
2. Characterize each item: type according to the Fowler quadrant (deliberate/inadvertent x prudent/reckless), root cause, observable symptom, and nature ([CODE] [CONFIG] [DOC] [INFERENCE] [ASSUMPTION]).
3. Evaluate impact on maintainability, operational risk, delivery speed, security, and experience (scale 1 to 5 with one-line justification per axis) and describe the interest it accrues if left unaddressed, indicating whether it grows linearly, compoundly, or by threshold/triggering event.
4. Estimate remediation cost: effort (XS/S/M/L/XL or person-days), complexity, intervention risk, and prerequisites. Never in money.
5. Prioritize with an explicit method (WSJF = value of remediating, which aggregates impact and urgency of interest, divided by effort; or impact x effort matrix) applied equally to all items, and classify as quick wins, strategic investments, and tolerable debt to watch, respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
6. Propose a wave-based payment plan with entry/exit criteria, dependencies between items, and alert signals that require re-evaluating the prioritization.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Framing: confirm {{SISTEMA}}, {{STACK}}, {{ARQUITECTURA_ACTUAL}}, {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}}, {{RESTRICCIONES}}, and review {{ADJUNTOS}}. If information is missing for inventorying or estimating, ask for it; do not invent system data.
Phase 1 - Dimensional sweep: apply the eight dimensions as a checklist (inspired by ATAM for discovering architectural risks at sensitivity and trade-off points); do not force findings where there is no evidence.
Phase 2 - Characterization and evidence: classify with the Fowler quadrant and tag the nature; mark [ASSUMPTION] where inferred and separate symptom from root cause.
Phase 3 - Impact and interest: score 1 to 5 per axis and make explicit how the cost of delaying grows (linear, compound, or by threshold).
Phase 4 - Cost and priority: estimate effort and risk, calculate the score (WSJF or matrix) with the same formula for all, and order.
Phase 5 - Wave plan: sequence, dependencies, entry/exit criteria, and review triggers; if the ranking depends on a fragile assumption, say so and propose how to validate it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each item has a stable ID, dimension, Fowler type, root cause separated from symptom, and tagged nature.
- Impact scored 1 to 5 on the five axes with justification, and interest described with its form of growth (linear/compound/threshold).
- Cost expressed in effort/complexity/risk, never in money; without using "free".
- Priority reproducible: scoring method declared and applied equally to all items.
- Catalog segmented into quick wins, strategic investments, and tolerable debt to watch.
- Wave plan with entry/exit criteria, dependencies, and review signals.
- Every unverifiable piece of data marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero inventions about the system.
Expected deliverable: a master inventory table (ID, dimension, item, type, impact, effort, priority, wave) plus a sheet for each high-priority item and a wave-based payment plan with review signals, in neutral Spanish and professional tone.
spec-desarrollo_seleccion_estilo_arquite:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA: {{SISTEMA}} > System or product to architect and its business purpose
- ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD_PRIORIZADOS: {{ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD_PRIORIZADOS}} > 3-5 critical quality attributes in order (performance, scalability, availability, maintainability, time-to-market, security, cost of operation) (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Team (size/maturity), operational budget, timelines, existing stack, regulation
- ESCALA_ESPERADA: {{ESCALA_ESPERADA}} > Users, transactions, data volume, and projected evolution at 18-24 months (optional)
- ESTILOS_CANDIDATOS: {{ESTILOS_CANDIDATOS}} > Styles to compare; if omitted, the expert proposes the pertinent ones (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to choose the architectural style for {{SISTEMA}}. This decision has a high reversal cost: it conditions the deployment model, the team structure, the operational cost, and the speed of evolution for years. A choice guided by trends (microservices by default) or personal preference degrades the system; a choice anchored in real drivers unlocks an architecture that sustains the business and an ADR that justifies it to whoever inherits it. The quality of the decision depends on the quality of the input drivers: vague drivers produce generic recommendations.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software architect who decides architectural styles using a quality-attribute-driven method (ATAM/quality-attribute-driven style), neutral toward trendy technologies and explicit about trade-offs.

Deliverable: architectural style selection report with comparative matrix, trade-off analysis, justified recommendation, and draft ADR. Steps:
1. Gather and validate the drivers: purpose of {{SISTEMA}}, {{ATRIBUTOS_CALIDAD_PRIORIZADOS}}, {{RESTRICCIONES}}, and {{ESCALA_ESPERADA}}. If a critical driver is missing, ask for it before continuing; do not invent it.
2. Prioritize or confirm the 3-5 most critical quality attributes and declare the central trade-off (what is optimized at the expense of what); no architecture maximizes all of them.
3. Select 3-5 pertinent candidate styles (use {{ESTILOS_CANDIDATOS}} if given; if not, propose from among modular monolith, layered monolith, microservices, event-driven, serverless, micro-frontends, hexagonal, pipes-and-filters, space-based). Discard the infeasible ones and say why.
4. Build a candidates x prioritized attributes matrix with qualitative scoring (++ / + / 0 / -) and one justification sentence per cell anchored in the driver, not in preference.
5. Analyze trade-offs per candidate: what is gained, what is sacrificed, operational complexity (deployment, observability, data), cognitive cost of the team according to their maturity, reversal cost.
6. Recommend a pragmatic style or hybrid with 3-5 reasons tied to drivers, the triggers that would change the recommendation, and a first actionable step.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Drivers: extract and validate purpose, attributes, constraints, and scale; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every unconfirmed piece of data and list critical missing ones as explicit questions before proceeding.
Phase 2 - Prioritization: order the quality attributes and explicitly declare what is optimized and at the expense of what; resolve ties with the business purpose, not with technical preference.
Phase 3 - Candidates: filter to 3-5 viable styles, discarding infeasible ones with a reason anchored in a concrete constraint (team, regulation, timeline, stack).
Phase 4 - Matrix: evaluate each candidate against each attribute with scale ++ / + / 0 / - and justification per cell; use the same scale consistently.
Phase 5 - Trade-offs and recommendation: analyze concessions per option (including operational complexity, cognitive cost, and reversal cost), recommend avoiding microservices by default (distributed complexity is justified only if the drivers demand it), and draft an ADR (context, decision, alternatives considered, positive and negative consequences, revision triggers).
Edge cases: if two styles tie, decide by reversal cost and cognitive cost and record the tiebreaker; if the projected scale does not justify distributed complexity, say so and recommend starting simple with evolution paths; if the drivers are contradictory, expose the conflict and ask for prioritization instead of averaging.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Drivers (purpose, attributes, constraints, scale) gathered and validated; missing ones asked for, not invented.
- [ ] 3-5 quality attributes prioritized with the central trade-off declared (what is optimized at the expense of what).
- [ ] 3-5 pertinent candidates; infeasible ones discarded with a reason anchored in a concrete constraint.
- [ ] Candidates x attributes matrix with consistent ++ / + / 0 / - scale and justification per cell anchored in drivers.
- [ ] Trade-offs per candidate: operational complexity, cognitive cost according to team maturity, and reversal cost explicit.
- [ ] Recommendation with 3-5 reasons tied to drivers + revision triggers + first actionable step.
- [ ] Ties and driver conflicts resolved and recorded, not averaged.
- [ ] Microservices not recommended by default; distributed complexity justified only by drivers.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data; no prices.
Expected deliverable: report in sections (drivers and prioritized attributes, comparison matrix, trade-offs per candidate, final recommendation with revision triggers) plus a draft ADR ready to record.
spec-marketing_estrategia_posicionamient:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Name and brief description of the product or service to position
- SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO: {{SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO}} > Ideal customer or segment to win (role, industry, size)
