--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs a secure coding checklist specific to their stack that serves as a shared criterion in pull request reviews and as a gate in the pipeline, not a generic list nobody consults. A checklist anchored to the language and recognized frameworks (OWASP, CWE, ASVS) unlocks consistent reviews, reduces vulnerabilities that reach production and gives junior developers a verifiable standard without depending on the reviewer's memory. Without stack, exposure and sensitive data context the controls cannot be prioritized; that is why the context comes in as input. The differential value lies in items that a team can act on the same day: not stating "validate input" but pointing out the real anti-pattern of the framework and its idiomatic replacement, with verification method and severity.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior application security engineer (AppSec) specialized in secure code review and SDLC, with practical command of {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}.

Deliverable: a secure coding checklist for {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, adapted to {{TIPO_APLICACION}} on {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}}, calibrated to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} and to {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}}, ready to paste into the repository contribution guide.

Steps:
1. Confirm or request any missing context; do not invent stack or exposure. If a critical input is missing, ask before drafting.
2. Structure the checklist in eight control domains: input validation; output encoding and injection prevention (SQL, NoSQL, commands, templates, insecure deserialization); authentication and session management; authorization and object-level access control (IDOR/BOLA); secrets and cryptography; error handling, logging and traceability without data leakage; dependencies and supply chain; secure configuration by default.
3. For each item deliver five fields: (a) imperative and verifiable control in one line; (b) CWE or OWASP/ASVS reference associated; (c) anti-pattern in {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} and the correct idiomatic construct as replacement; (d) verification method (manual review, linter/SAST rule, or test); (e) severity if omitted (high/medium/low).
4. Mark each item as mandatory or recommended according to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} (L1 most permissive, L3 most strict).
5. Close with the block of blocking items for PR approval and the controls to automate in the pipeline.

Decisions and limits:
- CWE/ASVS must be real and cited in a recognizable way; if you are not sure of the exact identifier, name the category and mark [ASSUMPTION] instead of inventing a number.
- Do not include infrastructure configuration external to the code (network firewalls, WAF) unless {{TIPO_APLICACION}} requires it as a pipeline gate.
- Prioritize actionable depth over exhaustiveness; an ambiguous or unverifiable item does not enter.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: map {{TIPO_APLICACION}}, {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}} and {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}} to the priority risks of OWASP Top 10 (2021); discard non-applicable domains with a brief justification (e.g. a CLI without HTTP sessions).
Phase 2 - Anchoring: link each domain to its OWASP category and the corresponding CWE Top 25; set the ASVS scope according to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}.
Phase 3 - Specification: draft the items per domain with the five fields, using real idiomatic constructs of {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} (query parameterization, contextual escaping, secure framework APIs, authorization decorators/middleware).
Phase 4 - Prioritization: classify mandatory/recommended and severity; consolidate the PR blocking block and the pipeline automation.
Phase 5 - Packaging: format as a checkable checklist ready for the contribution guide; declare assumptions with [ASSUMPTION] and leave ambiguities as open questions, not inventions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each item is actionable, verifiable and mapped to a real CWE or OWASP/ASVS reference (no invented identifiers).
- Anti-patterns and replacements are idiomatic to {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, not generic; the replacement is concrete code or a stack API.
- Coverage of the eight domains or explicit justification of exclusion.
- Each item indicates verification method, severity and mandatory/recommended character consistent with {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}.
- Injection, authentication, object-level authorization and secrets are covered at minimum, aligned to {{SUPERFICIE_EXPOSICION}} and {{DATOS_SENSIBLES}}.
- The PR blocking block is a clear subset of high-severity mandatory items.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; ambiguities resolved by question, not by invention.
Expected deliverable: checklist in checkable format, grouped by domain, with PR blocking block, pipeline automation section (SAST, dependency scanning/SCA, secrets detection) and assumptions, ready to paste into the repository contribution guide.
spec-desarrollo_code_review_estructurada:
[inputs]
- PULL_REQUEST: {{PULL_REQUEST}} > Diff, description and objective of the PR; title and associated issue if it exists
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Language, framework and conventions of the code base (e.g. TypeScript/React, Python/Django)
- OBJETIVO_DEL_CAMBIO: {{OBJETIVO_DEL_CAMBIO}} > What the change must achieve: expected behavior and acceptance criterion
- NIVEL_RIGOR: {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} > Minimum severity to report according to criticality (e.g. standard, high for core components) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A pull request is waiting for review before being merged. A structured and traceable review unlocks a defensible merge: it separates what breaks behavior from what is merely annoying, reduces the risk of regressions in production and leaves the author with concrete corrections rather than personal friction. The objective is not to have opinions about the code, but to decide with evidence whether it goes in as-is. Operating assumption: the only source of truth is {{PULL_REQUEST}} and the diff; nothing outside the diff is stated as fact.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior code reviewer and maintainer of a high-traffic repository, expert in {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, with criteria to conduct code reviews that raise quality without slowing the team.
Deliverable: structured review of {{PULL_REQUEST}} with prioritized findings and a merge verdict. Steps:
1. Confirm objective ({{OBJETIVO_DEL_CAMBIO}}), scope of the diff and {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}; if the diff or context is missing, request them before continuing.
2. Correctness pass: logic, edge cases, concurrency and race conditions, error handling, resource leaks, input validation, idempotency, regressions and test coverage.
3. Style and maintainability pass: names, cohesion, coupling, duplication, complexity, API clarity, consistency with {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} conventions and readability.
4. Risk pass: security (injection, authorization, secrets in code, sensitive data in logs), performance and N+1 queries, backwards compatibility, data migrations, configuration and rollback plan.
5. Consolidate findings, strengths, open questions and verdict.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: reformulate objective and scope; set minimum severity according to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}.
Phase 2 - Three independent passes (correctness > style > risk) over the diff; one entry per finding with severity (blocking, major, minor, nit), location (file and approximate line), diagnosis, impact and concrete correction or suggested fragment.
Phase 3 - Evidence integrity: do not invent lines outside the diff; absent context is marked [ASSUMPTION] with what you would verify; distinguish what is demonstrated from what is inferred. Trade-off: when in doubt between blocking and major, escalate to the higher severity and record the assumption that supports it.
Phase 4 - Consolidation and single verdict. Verdict rule: a single blocking finding forces "request changes"; only minor/nits enable "approve with comments".
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The three passes (correctness, style, risk) are explicitly covered.
- [ ] Each finding has severity, location, impact and actionable correction.
- [ ] No finding cites non-existent lines; context gaps go as [ASSUMPTION] with a verification plan.
- [ ] What is demonstrated by the diff is separated from what is inferred.
- [ ] There are real strengths and open questions for the author.
- [ ] The verdict is single (approve / approve with comments / request changes) and justified in one sentence, consistent with the severity rule.
- [ ] Professional, direct and respectful tone toward the author: the code is critiqued, not the person.
Expected deliverable: (a) findings table ordered by severity, (b) strengths list, (c) open questions, (d) verdict with justification.
spec-desarrollo_revision_pull_request_di:
[inputs]
- TITULO_Y_DESCRIPCION_PR: {{TITULO_Y_DESCRIPCION_PR}} > Title and description of the pull request, with the declared purpose of the change
- DIFF: {{DIFF}} > Unified diff to review (output of git diff or patch), with added and removed lines and hunk headers
- FOCOS_DE_RIESGO: {{FOCOS_DE_RIESGO}} > Axes to treat as critical: security, concurrency, performance, migrations, contract compatibility (optional)
- POLITICA_DE_MERGE: {{POLITICA_DE_MERGE}} > Team severity convention and approval threshold (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A pull request is waiting for review and needs an actionable merge verdict today. Reviewing only the diff and its impact radius, rather than auditing the entire code base, concentrates scrutiny where the real risk originates: the lines that change and what those lines touch downstream. A clear hunk-by-hunk verdict unlocks the merge, prevents regressions reaching production and leaves the author with concrete corrections rather than opinions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer, expert code reviewer, with criteria to distinguish what is blocking from what is cosmetic and to infer collateral effects outside the diff.
Deliverable: hunk-by-hunk review report + merge verdict.
1. Reconstruct the intent of the PR from TITULO_Y_DESCRIPCION_PR and the set of hunks from DIFF. If the description is missing or the diff arrives truncated (headers without closure, incomplete paths), ask for it before continuing rather than inferring.
2. Go through the DIFF hunk by hunk; for each hunk evaluate correctness and edge cases, error and null handling, concurrency and shared state, security (injection, secrets in the clear, authorization, input validation), performance (N+1, hot allocations, locks), contract compatibility (API, schema, serialization) and migrations (reversibility, deployment order), prioritizing FOCOS_DE_RIESGO.
3. Classify each finding as Blocking, Major, Minor or Nit according to POLITICA_DE_MERGE (if not provided, use that scale by default). Blocking = corrupts data, opens a breach or breaks a contract; Major = likely regression or dangerous debt; Minor = robustness improvement; Nit = preference.
4. Track the impact radius of each change: callers, tests, feature flags, contracts and dependencies affected even if they do not appear in the diff; mark those inferences as [ASSUMPTION] and declare what evidence would confirm them.
5. Verify that each behavioral change has a test that covers it; if coverage is missing or the test does not exercise the new path, record it as a finding with the minimum suggested test.
6. Issue a single verdict: Approve / Approve with minor changes / Request changes, with the prioritized list of blockers and the exact unblocking condition.
Limits: do not rewrite code outside the diff; do not propose large-scale refactors outside the change; a single verdict, no ambivalence.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: reconstruct intent and scope; confirm the diff is complete and declare environment assumptions (language, framework, version) if not stated.
Phase 2 Hunk sweep: analyze each hunk against the risk axes; do not go to untouched code except to trace collateral effects.
Phase 3 Impact radius: for each relevant change list what is affected downstream and mark [ASSUMPTION] what cannot be verified in the diff.
Phase 4 Test coverage: cross behavioral changes against present or absent tests; name the missing test.
Phase 5 Verdict: consolidate findings with severity and suggested patch, order by severity and close with the verdict and its unblocking condition.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The analysis sticks to the diff; untouched code only appears as a traced collateral effect.
- [ ] Each finding brings file:line, severity, why it is a problem and a concrete suggested patch.
- [ ] Covered axes: correctness, errors/nulls, concurrency, security, performance, contract/migrations.
- [ ] Severities justified with their criterion (Blocking/Major/Minor/Nit), not assigned at random.
- [ ] Explicit impact radius (callers, tests, flags, dependencies); inferences marked [ASSUMPTION] with evidence that would close them.
- [ ] Behavioral changes contrasted against coverage; missing tests named.
- [ ] No style nits that a linter already covers; no rewriting of code outside the diff.
- [ ] Single and clear verdict with prioritized blockers list and unblocking condition.
Expected deliverable: hunk-by-hunk report with classified findings and suggested patches, closed with an actionable merge verdict and its unblocking condition.
spec-desarrollo_redaccion_comentarios_pr:
[inputs]
- LENGUAJE_O_STACK: {{LENGUAJE_O_STACK}} > Language, framework or stack of the PR (defines applicable conventions and anti-patterns)
- DIFF_O_CODIGO: {{DIFF_O_CODIGO}} > Unified diff or fragments to review, with line numbers if possible
- CONTEXTO_PR: {{CONTEXTO_PR}} > What the PR resolves: issue, objective, expected scope (optional)
- ESTANDARES_EQUIPO: {{ESTANDARES_EQUIPO}} > Team style guide, conventions and definition of done (optional)
- NIVEL_EXIGENCIA: {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} > Rigor according to author maturity or module criticality: formative / standard / critical (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are reviewing a Pull Request and must transform observations into comments that the author can act on without clarification meetings. A good comment accelerates the merge, transfers criteria and preserves the relationship with the author; a vague one generates back-and-forth, defensiveness and debt that sneaks through. The objective is specific feedback, anchored to the code evidence and oriented toward improvement, not toward judging the person. What is unlocked: a review that the author appreciates and resolves in a single cycle.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer and code reviewer expert in constructive technical communication, with criteria to separate what is blocking from what is optional.
Deliverable: a set of review comments ready to paste in the PR, plus a closing summary.
1. Read {{DIFF_O_CODIGO}} in the context of {{CONTEXTO_PR}}; if it arrives empty, illegible or without useful line numbers, stop and ask for it rather than inventing findings.
2. Identify real findings in six axes: correctness, security, performance, maintainability, public contract (API/signatures/backwards compatibility) and tests; discard cosmetic noise that the linter or formatter covers.
3. Classify each finding by severity with explicit criterion: [blocking] prevents the merge (bug, leak, contract break), [important] should be resolved before merging, [suggestion] optional improvement, [question] requires clarification to be able to judge.
4. Draft each comment with four parts: severity + observation anchored to the line/block + why/impact + actionable suggestion with code fragment when applicable.
5. Prioritize: group the nits, do not pile them on a blocker; adjust the quantity and detail to {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} (formative = explain the why and offer alternatives; critical = exhaustive on correctness and security).
6. Close with verdict (approve / approve with minor changes / request changes), count by severity and the 1 to 3 points that block the merge.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: reformulate what the PR does, the stack {{LENGUAJE_O_STACK}} and the {{ESTANDARES_EQUIPO}} that apply; if missing, assume industry standard for the stack and declare it as [ASSUMPTION]. Same treatment for empty {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} (assume standard) and absent {{CONTEXTO_PR}} (review only what is evident in the diff).
Phase 2 Plan: list the detected findings with their tentative severity before drafting, to validate priority and avoid false positives.
Phase 3 Execute: write the definitive comments. Tone: describe the code, not the person; propose in plural ('we could', 'it would be advisable'); avoid 'always', 'never', 'obvious', 'simply'; mark the optional as such and separate fact from preference. One finding per comment, with its suggested fragment.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each comment carries explicit severity among the four categories.
- [ ] Each finding is anchored to a specific line or block, not generic.
- [ ] Each comment explains the impact (bug, security, performance, maintainability, contract) and proposes an actionable change.
- [ ] The tone describes the code, not the person; without 'always/never/obvious/simply'.
- [ ] The optional is marked; nits are grouped and do not compete with what is blocking.
- [ ] No false positives: what the linter already covers is not commented; assumptions are declared.
- [ ] The closure includes verdict, count by severity and the 1 to 3 real blockers.
Edge cases: empty diff or without lines -> ask before reviewing; enormous PR -> review the risky parts and declare what is not covered; public contract change without tests -> blocker with justification.
Expected deliverable: block of review comments in neutral Spanish, each self-contained and pasteable in the PR, followed by the closing summary.
spec-desarrollo_revision_legibilidad_nom:
[inputs]
- CODIGO: {{CODIGO}} > Fragment, file or pasted code to review
- LENGUAJE: {{LENGUAJE}} > Programming language (defines the native naming convention)
- CONVENCION_ESTILO: {{CONVENCION_ESTILO}} > Team style guide (e.g. PEP 8, Google Style, Airbnb) or "no defined guide"
- NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD: {{NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD}} > "quick" (only high severity) or "exhaustive" (all findings) (optional, default exhaustive)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A code fragment is read and modified many more times than it was written. Opaque names and confusing structure are the primary source of friction in maintaining software: they slow down the reader, hide bugs and make every future change more costly. This review unlocks self-documenting code, faster onboarding and less accumulated technical debt, without touching the behavior of the program. Bounded scope: only readability, names and structure; functionality, correctness, security and performance are out of scope.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer specialized in maintainability and code review, with criteria formed in Clean Code, Code Complete and the language style guides.

Deliver a readability and naming review of {{CODIGO}} in {{LENGUAJE}}, aligned to {{CONVENCION_ESTILO}}, with the detail indicated by {{NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD}}. Steps:
1. Inventory identifiers (variables, constants, parameters), functions/methods and structural blocks of the fragment.
2. Evaluate identifiers: revealed intention, absence of opaque abbreviations and generics (data, temp, info, aux), length proportional to scope, consistency with the language convention.
3. Evaluate functions/methods: the name describes what it does and returns, precise verb, coherent size and abstraction level, single responsibility, readable parameters.
4. Evaluate structure: logical grouping, top-down reading, excessive nesting, missing guard clauses, comments that paper over unclear code, style consistency.
5. For each finding record: location (line or symbol), severity (high/medium/low), why it damages maintainability, and concrete proposal with before > after.
6. Synthesize a renaming table and the three improvements of greatest impact prioritized.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm language, convention and scope; if CODIGO, LENGUAJE or CONVENCION_ESTILO are missing, ask for them before proceeding; if CONVENCION_ESTILO is "no defined guide", adopt the native convention of {{LENGUAJE}} and declare it.
Phase 2 Inventory: list the symbols and blocks to evaluate.
Phase 3 Diagnosis: apply the heuristics of the three dimensions symbol by symbol, without inventing non-existent defects; acknowledge the successes.
Phase 4 Proposals: for each finding draft the renaming or restructuring with before > after, verifying that it does not alter behavior.
Phase 5 Synthesis: build the renaming table and prioritize the three improvements of greatest impact.
Edge cases: code without relevant defects (state it, do not force findings); incomplete or truncated fragment (note what context is missing); collision with existing names in the proposed renaming (warn). Unresolved assumptions are marked {to_confirm}.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each finding has location, severity, maintainability justification and before > after proposal.
- [ ] Proposed names reveal intention and respect the convention of {{LENGUAJE}} and {{CONVENCION_ESTILO}}.
- [ ] The three dimensions are covered: identifiers, functions/methods and structure.
- [ ] Functionality and performance are not evaluated; exclusive focus on readability and no change alters behavior.
- [ ] No absent problems are invented; successes are acknowledged.
- [ ] Coherent severities and improvements prioritized by real impact.
- [ ] NIVEL_PROFUNDIDAD respected (quick = only high severity).
Expected deliverable: report with findings classified by severity, suggested renaming table (current > proposed > reason) and top 3 prioritized improvements.
spec-desarrollo_revision_clean_code:
[inputs]
- CODIGO: {{CODIGO}} > Fragment, file or module to audit (paste the code or reference the file)
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Language, version and framework (e.g. Java 21 + Spring Boot, TypeScript + React)
- CONVENCIONES: {{CONVENCIONES}} > Team style guide or conventions (optional; use the idiomatic ones of the language if omitted)
- SEVERIDAD_MINIMA: {{SEVERIDAD_MINIMA}} > Minimum threshold to report: blocking, high, medium or low (optional; default: all)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A team needs to raise the maintainability of their code base before technical debt slows feature delivery. A rigorous audit against Clean Code and SOLID unlocks safe refactors, reduces the cost of future change and turns subjective reviews into verifiable criteria. The result enables prioritization decisions with evidence, not opinions, and leaves an actionable remediation path.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer specialized in code review and refactoring, trained in Robert C. Martin's Clean Code principles and SOLID.

Audit {{CODIGO}} and deliver a prioritized report. Steps:
1. Audit the Small functions axis: length, single responsibility per function, homogeneous abstraction levels, number of parameters, nesting depth, boolean flags and duplication.
2. Audit the Clear intention axis: intention-revealing names, comments that compensate for poor code, magic numbers and strings, readability as prose, explicit vs silent error handling.
3. Audit the Low coupling axis: rigid dependencies, Law of Demeter, dependency injection, hidden side effects, Single Responsibility Principle and leaky abstractions.
4. Record each finding with: location (line or range), axis and violated principle, severity (blocking/high/medium/low) and impact on maintainability.
5. Justify the severity: blocking = compromises correctness or security; high = multiplies cost of change in a hot zone; medium = degrades local readability; low = cosmetic.
6. Propose concrete refactor with before/after block per relevant finding, naming the technique (extract method, introduce parameter object, replace conditional with polymorphism, etc.).
7. Build remediation plan ordered by impact and regression risk, with recommended test coverage per item.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} and {{CONVENCIONES}}; if {{CODIGO}} or the language is missing, ask for it before continuing. Mark any domain assumption as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Audit by axes: go through the code applying the three axes in order; do not infer behavior not present in the code or invent domain logic.
Phase 3 - Synthesis: prioritize findings by maintainability impact crossed with refactor regression risk; filter by {{SEVERIDAD_MINIMA}} if indicated; identify the three zones of greatest risk.
Phase 4 - Delivery: produce the report in the format of the CRITERION block.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each finding cites exact location (line or range) and names the violated principle, not a generality.
- Each severity is justified by its criterion (correctness/security, cost of change, readability or cosmetic).
- Each refactor includes compilable before/after code, names the technique and preserves observable behavior.
- No finding invents domain logic absent from the code; assumptions go marked [ASSUMPTION].
- The remediation plan orders by impact, flags regression risk per item and indicates recommended test coverage before touching each zone.
- Zero unsolicited complete rewrite; the focus is to audit and propose.
- If {{SEVERIDAD_MINIMA}} was indicated, no finding below the threshold appears in the report.

Expected deliverable: report in sections (1) Executive summary with finding count by axis and severity and the three zones of greatest risk; (2) Findings table [ID | location | axis | principle | severity | impact]; (3) Before/after refactors per relevant finding with named technique; (4) Prioritized remediation plan with regression risk and recommended test coverage.
spec-desarrollo_revision_solid:
[inputs]
- CODIGO_O_MODULO: {{CODIGO_O_MODULO}} > Source code, class, or module to review; paste the text or reference the file
- LENGUAJE: {{LENGUAJE}} > Language and version (e.g., Java 17, C# .NET 8, Python 3.12, TypeScript 5.x)
- CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO: {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} > What the module does and how it is expected to evolve (future variants, anticipated extension points)
- PRIORIDAD_FOCO: {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}} > Axis to prioritize: maintainability, testability, or extensibility (optional; default: maintainability)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Object-oriented design erodes when classes accumulate responsibilities and dependencies couple to concrete implementations: every change breaks something far away and tests become fragile. A rigorous review against SOLID converts vague intuitions of "this smells bad" into actionable findings, unlocks safe refactors, and reduces technical debt before it becomes structural. The result enables extending the system without fear and testing each piece in isolation. Without this, the team pays the cost in regression bugs, slow onboarding, and decreasing velocity.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer, specialist in object-oriented design, GoF patterns, and test-driven refactoring.
Deliver a SOLID review report on {{CODIGO_O_MODULO}} ({{LENGUAJE}}), considering {{CONTEXTO_NEGOCIO}} and prioritizing {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}:
1. Brief inventory of classes, interfaces, and responsibilities detected, with the reason for change of each unit.
2. Principle-by-principle walkthrough (SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP) with findings for each; all five are reviewed even if one has no findings.
3. Per finding: principle, exact location (class / method / lines), observable symptom, concrete risk, and proposed refactor with the applicable pattern and minimum viable change.
4. Findings prioritization table by severity and impact on {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}, with relative estimated effort (S/M/L).
5. List of design decisions that appear to be violations but are justified (not to be flagged as faults), with the reasoning that supports them.
6. Suggested refactor sequence: a safe order that respects dependencies between findings and minimizes regression risk.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Mapping: identify classes, interfaces, dependencies, and the reasons for change of each unit.
Phase 2 - Detection by principle:
  SRP: one class, one reason for change; detect mixing of persistence, domain logic, and presentation.
  OCP: look for if/else or switch on types that force editing existing code when adding variants.
  LSP: verify that subtypes honor the parent's contract (preconditions not strengthened, postconditions not weakened, exceptions and invariants).
  ISP: detect fat interfaces with empty methods, NotImplemented, or that no client uses in full.
  DIP: trace dependencies toward concrete classes that should point to abstractions; review the direction of the dependency and where objects are constructed.
Phase 3 - Refactor: for each finding propose the appropriate pattern (Strategy, Factory Method, interface extraction, dependency injection, composition over inheritance) with the minimum viable change; warn if it breaks the public API or binary compatibility.
Phase 4 - Prioritization: order by severity × impact on {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}; separate critical from cosmetic and estimate relative effort. Mark inferences as [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All five principles reviewed explicitly, even if one has no findings.
- [ ] Each finding cites exact location (class / method / lines) verifiable in the provided code.
- [ ] Each refactor names a concrete pattern and the minimum viable change, not generic advice.
- [ ] A warning is given when a refactor requires breaking the public API or compatibility.
- [ ] Real violations are distinguished from deliberately justified design decisions, with reasoning.
- [ ] Findings prioritized by severity and impact on {{PRIORIDAD_FOCO}}, with relative effort and a safe refactor sequence.
- [ ] Inferences marked as [ASSUMPTION]; nothing invented about code not provided.
Expected deliverable: structured report with inventory, findings by principle, prioritization table, justified decisions, and refactor sequence, ready to open tickets.
spec-desarrollo_definicion_definition_of:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO_O_PRODUCTO: {{EQUIPO_O_PRODUCTO}} > Name of the team or product whose Definition of Done is being defined
- STACK_TECNOLOGICO: {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}} > Languages, frameworks, and application type (e.g., Java/Spring backend, React frontend, Node monorepo)
- PLATAFORMA_VCS: {{PLATAFORMA_VCS}} > Version control and review platform (e.g., GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket)
- HERRAMIENTA_CI: {{HERRAMIENTA_CI}} > Continuous integration tool where automatic checks run (e.g., GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins)
- COBERTURA_OBJETIVO: {{COBERTURA_OBJETIVO}} > Agreed minimum test coverage threshold for new code (e.g., 80% on modified lines)
- TIPOS_CAMBIO_PRIORITARIOS: {{TIPOS_CAMBIO_PRIORITARIOS}} > Change types to cover in most detail (e.g., feature and hotfix) or "all equally" (optional)
- DOLORES_ACTUALES: {{DOLORES_ACTUALES}} > Problems motivating the formalization of the DoD (e.g., recurring production bugs, inconsistent reviews) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Team {{EQUIPO_O_PRODUCTO}} integrates changes into the main branch without an explicit, verifiable agreement on "done," which produces inconsistent quality across pull requests and reviews that depend on each reviewer's individual judgment. Formalizing a technical Definition of Done unlocks an objective merge gate: it converts tacit expectations into measurable checks, reduces rework and defects that escape to production, and enables automating part of the verification in the pipeline. Context: stack {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}}, version control {{PLATAFORMA_VCS}}, CI {{HERRAMIENTA_CI}}, target coverage {{COBERTURA_OBJETIVO}}, priority change types {{TIPOS_CAMBIO_PRIORITARIOS}}. Pain points motivating this: {{DOLORES_ACTUALES}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer and tech lead with experience defining quality policies, merge gates, and pipelines in continuous delivery teams; opts for verifiable criteria over good intentions and for automation over reliance on individual discipline.
Deliverable: an actionable technical Definition of Done plus a checklist ready for the pull request template. Steps:
1. Validate the context: if {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}}, {{HERRAMIENTA_CI}}, {{PLATAFORMA_VCS}}, or {{COBERTURA_OBJETIVO}} are empty or ambiguous, ask for them before drafting the final version; do not invent values.
2. Structure the DoD in seven categories: code and design (style via linter, dead code, bounded complexity, no TODO without an associated ticket); testing (unit, integration, minimum coverage over new lines, no omitted or disabled tests without justification); review (minimum approvers, all comments resolved, PR description and ticket link); security (dependency and secret analysis, input validation, no known critical vulnerabilities introduced); build and CI (pipeline green, no new blocking warnings, reversible data migrations if applicable); documentation (changelog, public API contract, README if applicable); observability (structured logs and metrics for relevant changes, feature flag for high-risk changes if applicable).
3. Formulate each criterion as a binary verifiable statement (meets / does not meet); for each one indicate the verification method (automatic in {{HERRAMIENTA_CI}} vs. manual review), a concrete threshold or evidence, and classify it as blocking or recommended. Vague language such as "clean code" or "well tested" is prohibited.
4. Separate universal criteria from those conditioned by change type: feature, bugfix, hotfix, refactor, and infrastructure. Explicitly acknowledge that a hotfix may defer recommended (non-blocking) criteria as long as the debt is recorded with a follow-up ticket; never defer a blocking security criterion.
5. Mark which criteria are best automated as mandatory branch protection status checks in {{PLATAFORMA_VCS}}, distinguishing what is already automatable from the effort needed to enable it, to reduce friction and eliminate dependence on human forgetfulness.
6. Deliver a final copyable checklist for the pull request template (grouped by category, with a visual blocking marker) and a brief note on where the DoD lives, how a change to the DoD is proposed, and with what cadence it is reviewed.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the objective, the stack, and the current maturity level; list assumptions marked as [ASSUMPTION] when a non-blocking piece of data is missing (e.g., absence of integration tests, release branches).
Phase 2 Plan: present the category index and the criterion card model (statement / verification method / blocking-recommended / applicable change types) and confirm thresholds before drafting.
Phase 3 Execute: draft the complete DoD, derive the table and the pull request checklist, and close with the versioning note and cadence.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each criterion is a binary verifiable statement, without vague wording such as "clean code".
- [ ] Each criterion specifies a concrete threshold or evidence and its verification method (automatic vs. manual).
- [ ] Each criterion is classified as blocking or recommended.
- [ ] All seven categories and five change types are covered, with the hotfix relaxation rule explicit and bounded.
- [ ] Criteria that can be automated as mandatory branch protection checks in {{PLATAFORMA_VCS}} are explicitly identified, separating what is already automatable from what is pending enablement.
- [ ] Thresholds are consistent with {{COBERTURA_OBJETIVO}} and the declared stack; no blocking security criterion admits an exception.
- [ ] The PR checklist is copyable, grouped by category, and visually marks what is blocking.
- [ ] Includes a versioning note (where it lives, how to change it) and a review cadence.
- [ ] Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: technical Definition of Done document by categories + criterion / verification method / classification / applicable change types table + copyable checklist for the pull request template + versioning note and review cadence.
spec-desarrollo_revision_manejo_errores:
[inputs]
- MODULO_O_ARCHIVOS: {{MODULO_O_ARCHIVOS}} > Code, module, or files to review (paste fragments or paths)
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Language and framework (e.g., Java/Spring, Python/FastAPI, Node/Express, Go)
- CONVENCION_ERRORES: {{CONVENCION_ERRORES}} > Project error convention: domain exceptions, Result/Either, return codes (optional)
- STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD: {{STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD}} > Logging/tracing/metrics stack (e.g., SLF4J+Logback, structlog, OpenTelemetry, Sentry) (optional)
- RUTAS_CRITICAS: {{RUTAS_CRITICAS}} > Priority flows where a failure is costliest (e.g., payments, authentication, DB writes) (optional)
- NIVEL_RIGOR: {{NIVEL_RIGOR}} > Expected depth: quick (critical/high only) or exhaustive (all severities) (optional, default: exhaustive)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Error handling defines whether a system degrades under control or fails silently: an empty catch or a lost log turns a trivial incident into hours of blind diagnosis, and an error that crosses a critical path without context becomes data loss or financial loss. This review of {{MODULO_O_ARCHIVOS}} seeks a codebase where every failure is captured with sound judgment, propagated with its root cause, and observable in production, reducing mean time to detection and resolution before the debt escalates to an incident.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior reliability engineer (SRE) and code reviewer specialized in error handling, resilience, and observability.
Deliverable: actionable review report. Steps:
1. Confirm language, error convention, observability stack, and critical paths; if a critical input is missing, request it before evaluating and mark [ASSUMPTION] for anything inferred.
2. Capture: detect overly broad try blocks, empty catch blocks or those that swallow the error, generic except/catch that hide different failures, loss of stack trace, and errors caught where they cannot be handled.
3. Propagation: verify preservation of root cause when rethrowing or wrapping (chained cause), use of domain types with context, mixing of return codes with exceptions, paths that fail silently, and async (promises/tasks) without rejection handling.
4. Logging and resilience: confirm a single log per error at the correct level (no double-logging or log-and-rethrow), correlatable context (request ID, trace ID, business identifiers), absence of PII or secret leaks, actionable messages, resource release in finally or equivalent, recoverable vs. fatal errors differentiated, and retries with backoff/timeouts/idempotency/circuit breakers where applicable.
5. For each finding deliver: location (file/function/line), severity (critical/high/medium/low with explicit criterion), problem, production impact, and a code patch aligned to the convention, without introducing new silent catch blocks.
6. Close with a marked compliance checklist and an executive summary of the 3 to 5 priority risks ordered by exposure. If a dimension is clean, state it explicitly.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix language, error convention {{CONVENCION_ERRORES}}, observability stack {{STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD}}, and critical paths {{RUTAS_CRITICAS}}; adjust depth according to {{NIVEL_RIGOR}}; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION] if any input was not provided.
Phase 2 - Sweep by dimension: traverse {{MODULO_O_ARCHIVOS}} in order — capture, propagation, logging and resilience — recording evidence with exact location and citing the observed line or pattern.
Phase 3 - Prioritization: assign severity by impact on robustness/observability and likelihood of triggering on {{RUTAS_CRITICAS}}; severity criterion: critical = data/financial loss or silent failure on critical path; high = degradation without observability; medium = bad practice with bounded risk; low = hygiene improvement.
Phase 4 - Remediation: draft the minimum patch per finding, aligned to {{CONVENCION_ERRORES}} and {{STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD}}, without introducing new silent catch blocks or changing the public contract without marking it as a trade-off.
Phase 5 - Closing: consolidate checklist and top 3 to 5 risks; if the input is insufficient to conclude on a dimension, state it instead of inventing findings.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All three dimensions (capture, propagation, logging/resilience) covered with located evidence; clean dimensions declared explicitly.
- [ ] No empty catch blocks, generic except that swallow different errors, or silenced errors without explicit justification.
- [ ] Root cause preserved when rethrowing or wrapping (chained cause, without losing stack trace).
- [ ] Each error logged once, at the correct level, with correlatable context (request/trace ID); no log-and-rethrow.
- [ ] No PII or secret leaks in logs or error messages; actionable messages for the person debugging.
- [ ] Recoverable vs. fatal errors differentiated; resources released in finally or equivalent.
- [ ] Resilience evaluated where applicable: retries with backoff, timeouts, idempotency, circuit breakers; no unhandled async rejections.
- [ ] Each finding includes severity with explicit criterion and an applicable code patch.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] when an input was missing; no findings invented due to lack of context.
Expected deliverable: report with a findings table (location, severity, problem, impact, patch), marked compliance checklist, and executive summary of 3 to 5 priority risks ordered by exposure.
spec-desarrollo_revision_concurrencia_ra:
[inputs]
- CODIGO_O_RUTA: {{CODIGO_O_RUTA}} > Fragment of concurrent code or path of the files to review
- LENGUAJE_Y_MODELO_CONCURRENCIA: {{LENGUAJE_Y_MODELO_CONCURRENCIA}} > Language and model (e.g., Java threads, Go goroutines+channels, Python asyncio, Rust async, C++ std::thread)
- INVARIANTE_CRITICO: {{INVARIANTE_CRITICO}} > Invariant or property the code must preserve under concurrency (e.g., balance never negative, exact counter, single execution)
- UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD: {{UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD}} > Minimum severity to report (critical / high / medium / low)
- CONTEXTO_DESPLIEGUE: {{CONTEXTO_DESPLIEGUE}} > Cores, expected load, and component criticality (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
This review protects a concurrent system before a synchronization defect manifests in production, where concurrency failures are intermittent, hard to reproduce, and tend to appear under real load or on hardware with more cores than the development environment. Detecting them in code, with the exact interleaving that triggers them, unlocks targeted fixes and a testing strategy that prevents silent data corruption, deadlock hangs, and undiagnosable degradation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior engineer in concurrent systems and memory models, with experience debugging data races and deadlocks in production.
Deliverable: concurrency review report prioritized by severity and reproducibility. Steps:
1. Map the mutable shared state of {{CODIGO_O_RUTA}} and record which thread, coroutine, or task reads and writes each element, according to the model {{LENGUAJE_Y_MODELO_CONCURRENCIA}}; distinguish what is truly shared from what is thread-confined.
2. Inventory the synchronization mechanisms present (locks, mutexes, atomics, channels, queues, semaphores, async/await) and verify that every shared access is protected consistently in ALL paths, including error, timeout, and cancellation; mark unprotected or inconsistently protected accesses.
3. Detect race conditions: data races and logical check-then-act and read-modify-write sequences; for each one describe the concrete thread interleaving that breaks the invariant {{INVARIANTE_CRITICO}}.
4. Build the lock acquisition graph and flag cycles from inconsistent locking order (deadlock), waiting with a lock held, locks not released on error paths, unsupported reentrancy, and livelocks or starvation.
5. Review memory visibility and ordering: shared variables without volatile/atomic/barriers, unsafe object publication, incorrectly implemented double-checked locking, and false assumptions about type atomicity.
6. For each finding record: severity (>= {{UMBRAL_SEVERIDAD}}), exact location (file and line or function), defect type, triggering interleaving, observable impact, probability of manifestation, and a concrete fix with the recommended pattern (minimal critical section, single ordered lock, immutable structure, atomic, message passing).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Reconnaissance: identify concurrent execution units, shared state, and synchronization boundaries; calibrate priority with {{CONTEXTO_DESPLIEGUE}}.
Phase 2 Race analysis: for each shared access evaluate atomicity and protection; reconstruct interleavings that violate {{INVARIANTE_CRITICO}}.
Phase 3 Blocking analysis: assemble the lock graph, look for cycles and paths that hold resources; evaluate deadlock, livelock, and starvation.
Phase 4 Memory visibility and ordering: review publication, barriers, and reordering permitted by the language's memory model.
Phase 5 Synthesis: prioritize by severity × probability and propose fix + detection test per finding.
Rules: do not invent lines or APIs absent from the code; mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; distinguish a genuine race from a deliberately relaxed lock-free pattern and do not report the latter as a defect without evidence; if language, concurrency model, or invariant is missing, ask before executing.
Edge cases: if {{CODIGO_O_RUTA}} is a path without access to the tree, request the relevant files; if there is no real mutable shared state, state it explicitly and do not force findings.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Mutable shared state mapped with its readers and writers, separated from what is thread-confined.
- [ ] Every shared access classified as consistently protected, inconsistently protected, or unprotected, covering error and cancellation paths.
- [ ] Each race condition accompanied by the exact thread interleaving that breaks the invariant.
- [ ] Lock graph built and deadlock cycles flagged with acquisition order.
- [ ] Memory visibility and ordering reviewed (atomic/barriers/publication) according to the language's memory model.
- [ ] Each finding with severity, exact location, impact, probability, and a concrete fix with pattern.
- [ ] Each fix with a test or detection strategy to reproduce and validate (stress, thread sanitizer, delay injection, formal model).
- [ ] Zero invented APIs or lines; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; deliberate lock-free patterns not flagged as defects without evidence.
Expected deliverable: prioritized findings table (severity, location, type, interleaving, impact, probability, fix, test) ordered by severity × probability, plus an executive summary of residual concurrency risk and the assumptions that condition it.
spec-desarrollo_plan_pruebas_unitarias:
[inputs]
- UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA: {{UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA}} > Function, method, or class to test, with its signature (name, parameters, return type)
- FIRMA_Y_CONTRATO: {{FIRMA_Y_CONTRATO}} > Contract: what it receives, what it returns, side effects, preconditions, and postconditions
- REGLAS_DE_NEGOCIO: {{REGLAS_DE_NEGOCIO}} > Conditionals, validations, limits, and expected behavior for each path
- DEPENDENCIAS: {{DEPENDENCIAS}} > External collaborators to isolate with test doubles, their type (mock/stub/fake/spy) and interaction contract, or "No external dependencies"
- FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS: {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}} > Target framework, language, and doubles library (e.g., JUnit 5 + Mockito, pytest + unittest.mock, Jest, xUnit + Moq)
- NIVEL_COBERTURA: {{NIVEL_COBERTURA}} > Target criterion: statement coverage, branch coverage, or MC/DC, or "Branch coverage" by default
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to shield a unit of code before refactoring or releasing it. A unit testing plan with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern and branch coverage converts the unit's contract into an executable safety net: every decision is exercised, regressions are detected early, and the team modifies with confidence. This unlocks safe refactoring, objective code review, and a TDD base for the next increment. The real value depends on three invariants: no branch goes unjustified, no behavior is invented, and every case is transcribable to code with no pending decisions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software quality engineer (SDET) specialized in unit test design, branch coverage analysis, boundary values, and test doubles.
Deliver a unit test case plan for {{UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA}}, in {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}} syntax, with target {{NIVEL_COBERTURA}}, following these steps:
1. Validate {{FIRMA_Y_CONTRATO}} and {{REGLAS_DE_NEGOCIO}}; if the expected behavior for any path is missing, ask before continuing and do not invent behavior.
2. Map the decision graph: each conditional, logical short-circuit operator, loop, and exception block, deriving the true and false branches of each and assigning stable identifiers.
3. Build the case matrix covering: happy path, boundary values (boundary and boundary ±1), equivalence classes, null or empty inputs, and error or exception paths.
4. Specify each case with ID, descriptive name, branch covered, and the three Arrange / Act / Assert blocks (a single invocation in Act; at least one verifiable assertion in Assert), isolating {{DEPENDENCIAS}} with the correct double (mock for interaction, stub for state, fake for logic, spy for partial verification).
5. Close with the branch-to-case traceability table, the test double inventory, and the list of uncovered branches with justification.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Contract: confirm signature, preconditions, postconditions, and side effects; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every assumption due to missing data.
Phase 2 Decisions: enumerate branches (each condition T/F, short-circuits, loops 0/1/N, exceptions) and assign branch identifiers; flag unreachable branches if detected.
Phase 3 Case design: apply boundary value analysis and equivalence partitioning; one case per branch, without redundancy; one case = one verification objective.
Phase 4 AAA writing: draft Arrange (data, state, doubles with justified type), Act (the single action under test), and Assert (state, output, or verified interaction) in {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}}; self-explanatory test names (method_condition_expectedResult).
Phase 5 Traceability: branch-to-case table that proves coverage against {{NIVEL_COBERTURA}}, uncovered branches justified, and test double inventory.
Decisions and trade-offs: prioritize minimum doubles (stub over mock when verifying state is sufficient); avoid over-specifying interactions that couple the test to the implementation. Limit: do not design integration or end-to-end tests; the unit is tested isolated from I/O, network, clock, and randomness (inject or fake them).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every branch of the decision graph has at least one case (T and F for each condition, loops 0/1/N, each exception).
- [ ] Every case follows strict AAA: a single invocation in Act and at least one verifiable assertion in Assert.
- [ ] Happy path, boundary values, equivalence classes, null/empty, and error paths are present.
- [ ] Every test is independent, deterministic (no dependency on order, clock, network, or randomness), and explicitly names its test doubles with justified type.
- [ ] The branch-to-case traceability table demonstrates coverage against {{NIVEL_COBERTURA}} and justifies every uncovered or unreachable branch.
- [ ] Every assumption is marked with [ASSUMPTION]; no behavior was invented; every ambiguity was asked about before continuing.
Expected deliverable: test plan in {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}} with AAA case matrix, branch coverage traceability table, and test double inventory, ready to transcribe to code with no pending decisions.
spec-desarrollo_test_driven_development:
[inputs]
- FUNCIONALIDAD: {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} > Behavior or feature to implement and its verifiable acceptance criterion
- LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK}} > Language and test framework (e.g., Python/pytest, JavaScript/Vitest, Java/JUnit, Go/testing)
- CODIGO_EXISTENTE: {{CODIGO_EXISTENTE}} > Existing code or interface signature (optional; "Start from scratch" if none)
- DEPENDENCIAS_A_SIMULAR: {{DEPENDENCIAS_A_SIMULAR}} > Dependencies to replace with test doubles (optional; "None" if not applicable)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to implement a feature letting the tests guide the design, not the other way around. The goal is code correct by construction, with a regression net that grows with each behavior and an architecture that emerges from real cases rather than speculation. When finished, happy cases and edge cases are covered, the design is decoupled by the necessity of testing, and a green suite enables refactoring and extending without fear.
Explicit assumptions: a test runner is configured and runnable; the acceptance criterion is observable as assertions; doubles isolate I/O, time, randomness, and network. Limit: TDD guides unit design, it does not substitute integration, contract, or end-to-end tests, which are flagged as subsequent work.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer, expert practitioner of Test-Driven Development in the Kent Beck school.
Guide the implementation of {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} in {{LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK}} applying the strict red-green-refactor cycle, one behavior at a time. Consider {{CODIGO_EXISTENTE}} as the starting point and isolate {{DEPENDENCIAS_A_SIMULAR}} with test doubles.
1. Confirm the input data; if any is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before writing code. Do not assume.
2. Propose the ordered list of behaviors to cover, from the simplest case to the most complex, including edges (empty input, limits, errors, invalid values, concurrency or shared state if applicable).
3. For each behavior, execute the cycle showing each phase separately:
   - RED: the smallest test that fails, named by the expected behavior (not by the implementation), in Arrange-Act-Assert structure with a single reason for failure. Declare what should fail and why; confirm the failure before advancing.
   - GREEN: the minimum production code that makes it pass, without advancing logic for cases not yet tested.
   - REFACTOR: in green, eliminate duplication and improve names without changing behavior; confirm suite is green.
4. If a behavior reveals a relevant design decision (coupling, interface contract, error handling, double choice), explain it as a trade-off before coding.
5. After each cycle propose the next case and wait for confirmation before continuing. Mark pending assumptions as {to_confirm}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Framing: restate the feature and the acceptance criterion; list the behavior sequence and the first proposed cycle.
Phase 1 - Iteration by cycles: for each behavior deliver RED, then GREEN, then REFACTOR, each phase labeled and with its test and production file updated. Respect the invariants: never production code without a prior test that demands it; never refactor with the suite in red; never skip the red phase; a single reason for failure per test.
Phase 2 - Behavior close: indicate the exact command to run the suite and a one-line summary of the behavior covered; propose the next case.
Phase 3 - Global close: when behaviors are exhausted, deliver the complete cycle log, the final green suite, and flag higher-level tests (integration, contract, e2e) that fall outside scope.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each cycle shows the three labeled phases (RED, GREEN, REFACTOR) in order.
- The red test is confirmed as failing before writing production code; the production code is the minimum necessary and does not advance untested cases.
- Test names describe behavior, not implementation; Arrange-Act-Assert structure with a single reason for failure.
- Edge cases explicitly covered (empty input, limits, errors, invalid values), not just the happy path.
- Refactors occur only in green and preserve behavior; relevant design decisions are justified as trade-offs.
- The exact command to run the suite is provided along with a per-cycle summary of the behavior covered; pending assumptions marked {to_confirm}.
Expected deliverable: sequence of red-green-refactor cycles with test and production files versioned per cycle, final green suite, execution command, log of covered behaviors, and note on pending higher-level tests.
spec-desarrollo_behavior_driven_gherkin:
[inputs]
- HISTORIA_USUARIO: {{HISTORIA_USUARIO}} > User story or business rule to specify (As/I want/So that narrative or rule description)
- CRITERIOS_ACEPTACION: {{CRITERIOS_ACEPTACION}} > Known acceptance criteria, one per line (optional; if missing they are inferred and marked [ASSUMPTION])
- PROFUNDIDAD_COBERTURA: {{PROFUNDIDAD_COBERTURA}} > Level: happy | happy+alternates | exhaustive with boundaries and errors
- IDIOMA_GHERKIN: {{IDIOMA_GHERKIN}} > Language of the .feature keywords: es (Caracteristica/Escenario/Dado/Cuando/Entonces) or en (Feature/Scenario/Given/When/Then)
- FRAMEWORK_OBJETIVO: {{FRAMEWORK_OBJETIVO}} > Target framework for syntax and convention adjustments: cucumber | behave | specflow | pytest-bdd | agnostic
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A user story without clear acceptance tests travels to development with ambiguity that is only discovered late, in defects or rework. A BDD specification in Gherkin converts the expected behavior into an executable contract that business, development, and QA read the same way and that the automation framework executes as living tests. Having this .feature before coding unlocks more precise estimation, verifiable Done criteria, and a regression net that documents the domain while protecting it. The opposite risk is real: a bloated .feature coupled to the UI, or with scenarios that test multiple things at once, becomes fragile and no one maintains it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior QA Automation Engineer specialized in Behavior-Driven Development, with mastery of Gherkin, Specification by Example, and the Cucumber/Behave/SpecFlow/pytest-bdd frameworks.
Deliverable: an executable .feature file plus its traceability table.
1. If HISTORIA_USUARIO, PROFUNDIDAD_COBERTURA, or IDIOMA_GHERKIN is missing, request it and stop. CRITERIOS_ACEPTACION and FRAMEWORK_OBJETIVO are optional; without a framework, assume agnostic and avoid syntax specific to a single engine.
2. Draft the Feature header with the narrative As [role] / I want [capability] / So that [value].
3. Derive scenarios from the criteria according to PROFUNDIDAD_COBERTURA: happy path, alternate paths, boundary values, and error/exception cases.
4. Group into a Scenario Outline with Examples table the scenarios that differ only in data; do not force an Outline when flows diverge.
5. Extract to a Background only the preconditions truly shared by multiple scenarios; never put actions or assertions in Background.
6. Tag each scenario or group with a useful tag (@happy, @alternate, @boundary, @error, @regression) and mark [ASSUMPTION] for every inferred criterion or rule.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: extract role, capability, value, and the list of business rules implicit in the story and criteria; name as [ASSUMPTION] those that are missing and flag ambiguities with {to_confirm}.
Phase 2 - Coverage design: for each rule define the happy path, alternates, boundaries (empty, maximum, off-by-one, duplicates, concurrency if applicable), and errors/exceptions; discard duplicates by applying one behavior per scenario; explicitly declare what is out of scope.
Phase 3 - Gherkin writing: declarative domain language, third person, present tense; a single When per scenario; names that state the rule, not the steps; And/But to chain steps of the same type; no clicks, selectors, IDs, or UI details; data in tables with stable headers.
Phase 4 - Parameterization and verification: consolidate data-only variant cases in Scenario Outline with intention-named Examples; review against the Criterion checklist; adjust conventions to FRAMEWORK_OBJETIVO; confirm the block parses.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each scenario verifies a single observable behavior and its name describes the rule, not the steps.
- Valid Given-When-Then structure: context in Given, single action in When, verifiable result in Then; And/But for additional steps; no assertions in Given or in Background.
- Declarative domain-oriented language: no clicks, selectors, IDs, or UI implementation details.
- Coverage according to PROFUNDIDAD_COBERTURA: happy; happy+alternates; or exhaustive with boundaries and errors, as requested — neither more nor less.
- Scenario Outline only for cases that vary in data alone; Background only for truly shared preconditions.
- Keywords in the requested IDIOMA_GHERKIN and syntax parseable by FRAMEWORK_OBJETIVO (or agnostic if not specified).
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and ambiguities {to_confirm}; no inferred criterion presented as confirmed.
- No prices; neutral and professional English in the narrative and the table.
Expected deliverable: a single executable .feature code block, followed by a traceability table with columns Scenario | Type (happy/alternate/boundary/error) | Rule or criterion it verifies, and a brief close listing the pending [ASSUMPTION] items with the data that would be sufficient to confirm each one.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_pruebas_integraci:
[inputs]
- SERVICIO_BAJO_PRUEBA: {{SERVICIO_BAJO_PRUEBA}} > Service or component whose integration behavior is to be verified, with its main responsibility

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs confidence that SERVICIO_BAJO_PRUEBA collaborates correctly with its DEPENDENCIAS before each release. Unit tests pass, but incidents appear at the seams: contracts that change without notice, divergent serialization, half-completed transactions, duplicate or out-of-order messages, and dependencies that fail in unanticipated ways. Designing an integration suite focused on those boundaries unlocks safer releases, reduces production regressions, and converts expected inter-component behavior into a verifiable and CI-executable contract. The practical challenge is twofold: not falling into excess mocks (which are green-in-suite but red-in-production) nor into dependence on live external services (which makes the suite slow, flaky, and costly).

Archetype: Senior QA and test architecture engineer, specialist in distributed systems, contract testing, and microservice resilience.
Deliverable: complete integration test suite design. Steps:
1. Map integration boundaries: for each point of contact between SERVICIO_BAJO_PRUEBA and a dependency from DEPENDENCIAS, document the expected contract (input, output, error codes, format, version, timeout semantics, and idempotency) and the call direction.
2. Define the isolation strategy according to ESTRATEGIA_DOBLES: which dependencies are spun up real (ephemeral containers, test database, local broker) and which are replaced by doubles, justifying each choice. For external third-party APIs, prefer consumer-driven contract testing over live calls; reserve the double for failures not reproducible with the real dependency.
3. Design cases prioritized by risk in four families: (a) happy path for each critical flow; (b) contract validation (fields, types, versioning, backward compatibility); (c) dependency failure modes (timeout, 5xx, malformed response, retries, idempotency, circuit breaking, controlled degradation); (d) transactional or eventual consistency (rollback, duplicate messages, ordering, exactly/at-least-once).
4. Specify the harness: seed data, isolation, and cleanup between tests, and determinism of async dependencies via active polling (polling with timeout and assertions) instead of fixed sleeps, declaring how flakiness is prevented.
5. Produce the case matrix and the representative code skeletons.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Framing: if critical data for SERVICIO_BAJO_PRUEBA, DEPENDENCIAS, or ESTRATEGIA_DOBLES is missing, request it before continuing; do not invent contracts.
Phase 1 - Boundaries: build the contact point inventory with its contract and direction.
Phase 2 - Isolation: decide real vs. doubles per dependency and justify against the two risks (excess mocks / fragility of live services).
Phase 3 - Cases: derive scenarios by the four risk families, prioritizing critical paths and highest-impact failure modes.
Phase 4 - Harness and code: define deterministic setup/teardown and draft 2–3 representative tests in STACK_Y_FRAMEWORK (at least one contract test and one failure mode test).
Phase 5 - Closing: consolidate matrix + acceptance checklist aligned with CRITERIO_DONE, with note on execution time and pipeline position.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every integration boundary between SERVICIO_BAJO_PRUEBA and DEPENDENCIAS appears as a contact point with explicit contract and declared direction.
- [ ] Each case tests real collaboration between components, not logic of a single isolated unit.
- [ ] The real vs. doubles choice is justified per dependency; no mocks hide the verified contract, no unnecessary dependence on live external services.
- [ ] All four families are covered: happy path, contract (including versioning/compatibility), failure modes (timeout/5xx/malformed/retry/idempotency/circuit breaking), and transactional or eventual consistency (rollback/duplicates/ordering).

- [ ] Assumptions are marked with [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: (1) boundary inventory with contract per contact point; (2) real vs. doubles decision table with justification per dependency; (3) case matrix with columns ID, boundary, risk family, scenario, precondition, action, expected result, double type; (4) code skeleton of 2–3 representative tests in STACK_Y_FRAMEWORK; (5) suite acceptance criteria checklist, integrable in CI.

- STACK: {{STACK}} > Language and framework on each side and Pact library to use (e.g., consumer TypeScript/Jest with pact-js, provider Java/Spring with pact-jvm)

CONSUMIDOR and PROVEEDOR evolve in independent repos and pipelines; E2E tests are slow, fragile, and detect integration breaks late, already in shared environments where the cost of rolling back is high. Independent deployment with confidence is unlocked: a versioned and verified contract on both sides lets you know, before deploying, whether a candidate version breaks the integration, replacing the bulk of E2E tests between these two services with fast, deterministic feedback in each pipeline. spec-desarrollo_property_based_testing:
[inputs]
- UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA: {{UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA}} > Function, class, or module to test, with its signature or source code
- LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK}} > Language and PBT library (e.g., Python+Hypothesis, TypeScript+fast-check, Java+jqwik, Rust+proptest, Elixir+PropCheck)
- CONTRATO_ESPERADO: {{CONTRATO_ESPERADO}} > What the unit must guarantee: postconditions and business invariants
- CASOS_BORDE_CRITICOS: {{CASOS_BORDE_CRITICOS}} > Highest-risk edges in the domain (optional)
- NUM_PROPIEDADES: {{NUM_PROPIEDADES}} > Target number of properties to generate (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Example-by-example tests only verify the cases the author imagined, leaving alive the bugs that live in data nobody thought of. Property-based testing inverts the approach: instead of asserting concrete results, it declares properties that must hold for thousands of generated inputs, and when one fails it reduces (shrinking) the counterexample to the minimum reproducible case. The real value is not in running more cases, but in choosing strong properties and generators that truly reach the risk edges. Designing them well unlocks early detection of edge-case bugs, executable specifications that document the real contract, and a regression net that grows with each counterexample found.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior quality engineer specialized in property-based testing, with experience building property suites in Hypothesis, fast-check, jqwik, and proptest for production code.
Deliverable: executable and framework-idiomatic property-based test suite for UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA in LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK, with properties, generators, shrinking, fixed regressions, and a CI integration plan.
Steps:
1. Validate inputs: if the signature or code of UNIDAD_BAJO_PRUEBA, LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK, or CONTRATO_ESPERADO is unclear, ask for it before continuing; do not invent the contract.
2. Map CONTRATO_ESPERADO to invariant properties using the canonical patterns: round-trip (decode(encode(x))==x), inverse (f(g(x))==x), idempotency (f(f(x))==f(x)), metamorphic, preserved invariants, oracle or reference model, comparison against alternate implementation, and no-exception as baseline.
3. Prioritize by property strength: no-exception < type-preservation < invariant < idempotency < round-trip; prefer the strongest property the contract allows and do not stay at no-exception.
4. Per property, design the generator: valid domain, ranges, directed edges (zero, empty, negatives, NaN and infinities in floats, Unicode and surrogates, numeric limits, large collections, duplicates) prioritizing CASOS_BORDE_CRITICOS, and assume filters to discard invalid inputs without biasing the distribution; use the framework's compositional strategies before custom generators.
5. Define the expected shrinking strategy to reduce counterexamples to the minimum reproducible case.
6. Write the executable code (targeting NUM_PROPIEDADES properties) with descriptive names, a fixed seed for reproducibility, and at least one regression case fixed by a known counterexample.
7. List the properties that CANNOT be covered with PBT and why (network or DB effects not isolable, non-existent oracle, non-determinism), plus the CI integration plan (number of examples, time budget, flakiness handling, persistence of the counterexample database).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpretation: restate the contract and expected behavior of the unit; mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and ask for confirmation.
Phase 2 Property design: derive the prioritized list from the contract, justifying the canonical pattern of each and its relative strength.
Phase 3 Generator design: per property specify domain, directed edges, and filters, ensuring the distribution exercises the risk cases without bias.
Phase 4 Coding: implement tests and generators idiomatic to the framework, with fixed seed and fixed regression.
Phase 5 Coverage and limits: declare what is not coverable by PBT with its reason and the CI integration.
Avoid traps: no-exception as the only property; generators that never reach the edges; filters that distort the distribution; treating a failure as a bug without first validating whether the defect is in the property or the generator.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each property names its canonical pattern and traces to a concrete point in CONTRATO_ESPERADO.
- The strongest property the contract allows was preferred; no-exception appears only as a complement, never as the only guarantee.
- Each generator defines domain, directed edges, and assume filters without biasing the distribution, covering CASOS_BORDE_CRITICOS.
- The code is executable and idiomatic to the framework, with a fixed seed and at least one fixed regression case.
- Counterexamples shrink to a minimum reproducible case.
- Properties not coverable by PBT are explicitly listed with their reason and the CI plan (examples, time, flakiness, counterexample persistence).
- Every assumption is marked [ASSUMPTION] with a request for confirmation.
Expected deliverable: test file ready to run + property/pattern/generator/contract-point table + limits list and CI integration plan.
spec-desarrollo_mutation_testing_estrate:
[inputs]
- LENGUAJE: {{LENGUAJE}} > Project language and version (e.g. TypeScript 5, Java 21, Python 3.12, Rust 1.80)
- FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS: {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}} > Test framework and runner in use (e.g. Jest, JUnit 5, pytest, cargo test)
- MODULOS_CRITICOS: {{MODULOS_CRITICOS}} > Modules, packages or paths to mutate first by criticality/risk (e.g. payments domain, tariff calculation)
- UMBRAL_OBJETIVO: {{UMBRAL_OBJETIVO}} > Target mutation score and, if applicable, by criticality level (e.g. 80% global, 90% in core domain)
- RESTRICCIONES_CI: {{RESTRICCIONES_CI}} > (optional) CI platform and time/resource budget per run (e.g. GitHub Actions, <10 min per PR)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Line coverage tells you that code was executed, not that it is verified: a suite can traverse 90% of the code without a single assertion capable of detecting a defect. Mutation testing injects artificial defects (mutants) into the code and measures how many the suite kills; the mutation score exposes the real verification gaps that coverage hides. A mutation testing Strategy converts a misleading metric into actionable evidence of the robustness of the tests, prioritizes where to reinforce and leaves a mechanism in CI that prevents test quality from silently degrading with every change. Central risk to avoid: treating the score as a goal in itself and inflating it by discarding mutants as equivalents without criterion (Goodhart's law applied to testing).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software quality engineer (SDET) specialized in mutation testing and high-detection test suite design.
Deliverable: executable mutation testing strategy for {{MODULOS_CRITICOS}} in {{LENGUAJE}} with {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}}, with a baseline measured on a real pilot run, prioritized backlog and CI plan. Steps:
1. Select the tool for {{LENGUAJE}} and {{FRAMEWORK_PRUEBAS}} (Stryker, PIT, mutmut/mutpy, cargo-mutants, mewt/muton or another) and justify the choice in one line (maturity, integration with the runner, support for incremental runs).
2. Define the initial scope over {{MODULOS_CRITICOS}}: what to mutate first by criticality/risk and what to exclude with rationale (generated code, configuration, DTOs, mappers, trivial adapters and logging). Justify each exclusion so as not to mask debt.
3. Build a table of mutation operators to enable (conditional boundary, condition negation, arithmetic, logical/boolean, return value mutations, void method call removal) indicating what real defect each one simulates and why it matters in the domain.
4. Establish the baseline: mutation score = killed mutants / (total mutants - equivalent mutants). Run a pilot campaign on a representative module and report score, alive mutants, killed mutants, timeouts and skipped mutants (skipped: a more severe mutant already failed on the same line). Leave the exact execution command.
5. Classify each surviving mutant as: real test gap, weak assertion (the test runs but does not assert the effect), dead code or equivalent mutant. Give the explicit criterion for declaring equivalence (semantically identical, not just same result on current cases) and mark those cases so as not to penalize the score without inflating it.
6. Prioritize actionable survivors by impact x effort and, for each one, propose the concrete test or assertion that would kill it (test case name, input and assertion on the observable effect).
7. Define mutation score thresholds by criticality level against {{UMBRAL_OBJETIVO}}, a time budget, and CI integration: incremental run over the diff per PR (blocking) plus full periodic campaign (nightly/weekly, informational), respecting {{RESTRICCIONES_CI}}. Include failure policy and handling of timeouts/flakiness so as not to block on noise.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Interpret: restate language, framework, critical modules and threshold; list what is missing and mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. Confirm whether the pilot has already been run or needs to be run.
Phase 1 - Selection and scope: fix tool, modules to mutate and justified exclusions.
Phase 2 - Operators: select the set and document the intent of each one (defect it represents).
Phase 3 - Pilot and baseline: configure the tool, run the campaign on the pilot module, calculate the score discounting equivalents and report the alive/killed/timeouts/skipped breakdown.
Phase 4 - Diagnosis: classify survivors, separate equivalents with explicit criterion and assemble the prioritized backlog with the test that kills each mutant.
Phase 5 - Industrialization: define thresholds by criticality, time budget and the CI pipeline (incremental per PR + full periodic campaign) with the failure policy and timeout handling.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
