The three signals (traces, metrics, logs) must share the same Resource to correlate in the backend.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior observability engineer, specialized in OpenTelemetry and distributed telemetry.
Deliverable: complete, verifiable instrumentation of {{SERVICIO}} ({{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}, style {{ESTILO_INSTRUMENTACION}}). Steps:
1. List the exact OpenTelemetry dependencies to install for {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} (API, SDK, OTLP exporter, framework instrumentation). If you are not sure of an exact package name or version, say so and offer the source to confirm; do not invent it. Indicate the version of semantic conventions you assume.
2. SDK bootstrap: TracerProvider, MeterProvider, and LoggerProvider with a Resource declaring service.name={{SERVICIO}}, service.version={{VERSION_SERVICIO}}, and deployment.environment={{ENTORNO}} per semantic conventions (use environment Resource detectors if applicable); BatchSpanProcessor; OTLP exporters configurable by OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, and OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL; explicit sampling strategy (default ParentBased(TraceIdRatioBased), parameterizable by OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER); and graceful shutdown (shutdown/force-flush) when the process ends to avoid losing pending telemetry.
3. Instrument the critical points of the main flow (HTTP/RPC entry, outbound calls, data access) with stable, low-cardinality span names (do not put IDs or variable paths in the name; they go as attributes), useful attributes, exception recording, and error status. Exclude health checks and noisy routes from sampling. If {{ESTILO_INSTRUMENTACION}} is automatic, declare what the agent covers and what remains manual.
4. Define at least two metrics: a request counter by route and result, and a latency histogram with explicit unit (s or ms). Bound the cardinality of labels (normalize the route to its template, not the concrete URL).
5. Ensure W3C traceparent (and tracestate) context propagation at incoming and outgoing edges to avoid breaking distributed traces; declare the configured propagator.
6. Correlate logs by injecting the trace_id and span_id of the active span into each record, to link logs with traces in the backend.
7. Provide an OpenTelemetry Collector configuration fragment (OTLP receiver + batch and memory_limiter processors + exporter to backend) and the command or snippet to verify end-to-end that a span and a metric arrive.
Security constraint: never include secrets, tokens, or PII in span attributes, metrics, or logs; if a sensitive value would be useful, record a hashed or redacted version and declare it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Interpret): confirm stack, dependency manager, instrumentation style, collector endpoint/protocol, semantic conventions version, and whether there is an existing telemetry SDK (OpenTracing, statsd, proprietary APM) that might collide with or duplicate spans. Mark what is not provided with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 (Plan): enumerate dependencies, files to create or touch, expected spans and metrics, sampling strategy, propagator, log correlation plan, and verification plan.
Phase 3 (Execute): deliver dependencies, bootstrap, flow instrumentation, metrics, propagation, log correlation, Collector config, and the end-to-end check. Do not invent package names or attribute names; when in doubt, declare the source to confirm.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Correct dependencies for {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}; uncertain names or versions declared to confirm, not invented; semantic conventions version declared.
- [ ] Resource declares service.name, service.version, and deployment.environment with semantic convention keys, shared by all three signals.
- [ ] OTLP export configurable by environment variables; no vendor coupling.
- [ ] Explicit sampling (ParentBased + ratio) parameterizable and documented.
- [ ] Graceful shutdown (shutdown/force-flush) that avoids losing telemetry when the process ends.
- [ ] Spans with stable, low-cardinality names; exceptions and error status recorded; health checks and noisy routes excluded.
- [ ] >=2 metrics: request counter by route/result and latency histogram with explicit unit; label cardinality bounded.
- [ ] W3C traceparent/tracestate propagation at entry and exit; propagator declared.
- [ ] Logs correlated with trace_id and span_id.
- [ ] Collector config (OTLP receiver + batch + memory_limiter + exporter) and end-to-end verification of a span and a metric.
- [ ] No secrets or PII in attributes; sensitive values redacted or hashed.
- [ ] Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: instrumentation package (dependencies + bootstrap + instrumented flow + metrics + propagation + log correlation + Collector config + check) ready to integrate and verifiable against the collector at {{ENDPOINT_OTLP}}.
spec-desarrollo_definicion_slo_sli:
[inputs]
- SERVICIO: {{SERVICIO}} > Name and purpose of the service or API to govern
- JOURNEYS_CRITICOS: {{JOURNEYS_CRITICOS}} > User journeys that matter (e.g., login, checkout, balance inquiry)
- FUENTE_DATOS: {{FUENTE_DATOS}} > Measurement architecture: where events come from (load balancer logs, Prometheus metrics, traces, synthetic)
- VENTANA: {{VENTANA}} > Rolling measurement window (e.g., 28 days, 30 days) (optional, default [ASSUMPTION] 28 days)
- DESEMPENO_HISTORICO: {{DESEMPENO_HISTORICO}} > Observed performance for calibrating the SLO (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs to decide objectively — not by intuition or pressure — when to invest in new features and when to stop and stabilize {{SERVICIO}}. Defining SLOs, SLIs, and error budgets turns reliability into a measurable, negotiable variable: it unlocks a shared language between product, engineering, and operations, and enables a deployment policy based on evidence rather than heroics. This document is the governance input reviewed by the reliability committee and that sustains the conversation between delivery speed and accepted risk.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior SRE (Site Reliability Engineer) with experience operating production services under the Google SRE methodology and the SRE Workbook.

Deliverable: service level agreement document for {{SERVICIO}}. Steps:
1. Prioritize {{JOURNEYS_CRITICOS}} by user impact and select for each one the appropriate SLI type (availability, latency, freshness, correctness, or throughput). Discard low-impact journeys and explicitly state why they fall outside scope.
2. Specify each SLI as a ratio of good events over total valid events, citing the exact source within {{FUENTE_DATOS}}, the percentile when applicable, and a measurable threshold (e.g., good latency = requests served in under 300 ms at p95). Define what counts as a valid event and what is excluded (health checks, synthetic traffic, 4xx codes attributable to the client).
3. Assign to each SLI a target SLO as a percentage over the rolling window {{VENTANA}}, justified against {{DESEMPENO_HISTORICO}} and the user's real expectation; avoid aspirational figures without grounding and avoid excess nines that add cost without perceived value.
4. Calculate the error budget of each SLO (1 minus SLO) with explicit arithmetic: minutes or failure events allowed in {{VENTANA}}. Show the operation, not just the result.
5. Draft the error budget policy: triggers and actions when the budget is exhausted (freeze non-urgent deployments, prioritize reliability) and when there is slack (accelerate deliveries, take controlled risk, experiment). Name the person responsible for declaring the freeze and the unfreeze.
6. Design multi-window burn-rate alerts: a fast high-rate one for acute incidents and a slow low-rate one for sustained degradation, with calculated thresholds, a short confirmation window to reduce false positives, and the fraction of budget consumed by each alert.
7. Deliver a summary table: journey, SLI (definition + source + threshold), SLO, error budget, burn-rate alert.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: identify candidate SLIs by journey and discard metrics the user does not perceive.
Phase 2 - Specification: formalize each SLI (definition, source, percentile, valid vs excluded events, window), set calibrated SLO and derive error budget with visible arithmetic.
Phase 3 - Governance: define budget policy with responsible parties and burn-rate alerts; consolidate the summary table.
Always distinguish SLI (what you measure), SLO (the internal target), SLA (contractual commitment with consequences), and error budget (1 minus SLO); do not confuse them at any step. Edge cases to resolve: (a) window without sufficient traffic to be statistically significant — propose an alternate window or minimum count; (b) external dependencies that erode the budget through no fault of your own — propose how to attribute them; (c) journeys with seasonality — decide whether the rolling window absorbs the peak. Flag any data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with a reasonable reference value and its justification in one line.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each critical journey has at least one SLI expressed as a good/valid ratio with source, percentile when applicable, and measurable threshold.
- [ ] It is explicit what counts as a valid event and what is excluded from the measurement.
- [ ] Each SLO is justified against historical performance or user expectation; it is not aspirational and does not have extra nines without perceived value.
- [ ] The error budget shows explicit arithmetic in minutes or events for {{VENTANA}}.
- [ ] The error budget policy defines triggers, concrete actions in both directions, and the person responsible for declaring the freeze/unfreeze.
- [ ] There is at least one fast burn-rate alert and one slow burn-rate alert with calculated thresholds, a confirmation window, and the fraction of budget consumed.
- [ ] SLI, SLO, SLA, and error budget are distinguished without confusion.
- [ ] Applicable edge cases (low traffic, external dependencies, seasonality) are addressed or dismissed with reasoning.
- [ ] All data not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION] with justification.
Expected deliverable: service level agreement document with summary table ready for reliability committee review.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_logging_estructur:
[inputs]
- STACK_TECNOLOGICO: {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}} > Language, framework, and current logging library (e.g., Node.js + pino, Java + Logback/Logstash encoder, Python + structlog, Go + zap)
- DESTINO_LOGS: {{DESTINO_LOGS}} > Observability platform or ingestion destination (e.g., Elastic, Loki/Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch, Splunk)
- NIVEL_CRITICIDAD: {{NIVEL_CRITICIDAD}} > Domain criticality that determines verbosity, default level, and retention (e.g., financial transactional, internal, experimental)
- CAMPOS_NEGOCIO: {{CAMPOS_NEGOCIO}} > Business context fields for the context object (e.g., user_id, tenant_id, order_id) (optional)
- POLITICA_DATOS_SENSIBLES: {{POLITICA_DATOS_SENSIBLES}} > Applicable privacy/PII and retention rule (e.g., mask email, exclude card PAN, GDPR, HIPAA) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Services emit heterogeneous logs (free text, divergent formats, no correlation), which makes incident investigation slow and costly and breaks end-to-end traceability. A unique, versioned structured JSON logging schema unlocks deterministic queries, reliable dashboards, precise alerts, and cross-service traceability without ingestion transformations. This is the base contract that any service on {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}} must comply with to send to {{DESTINO_LOGS}} in a domain of criticality {{NIVEL_CRITICIDAD}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior platform and observability engineer, with experience in structured logging at scale, W3C Trace Context, and operation of observability platforms.
Deliver the complete design with these numbered steps:
1. Define the JSON schema contract with mandatory fields: timestamp (ISO-8601, UTC, milliseconds), level, message, service, environment, version (app release), schema_version (log contract version), and correlation trace_id, span_id, request_id; nested context object for {{CAMPOS_NEGOCIO}}; error object with type, message, and stack. For each field specify type, optionality, cardinality, and example; declare which fields are reserved to avoid collisions with the destination.
2. Build the severity level table (DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR, FATAL) with the usage criterion for each, what should NOT be logged at each level, and the expected operational action (e.g., FATAL = pageable alert). Set the default level according to {{NIVEL_CRITICIDAD}} and justify it by cost/retention vs. observability.
3. Define the correlation rules: propagation between services via the traceparent header (W3C Trace Context), ID generation and format (16/32-char hex), context inheritance in child logs, and behavior when NO incoming context arrives (generate new root span). Cover the case of batch/async processes without an HTTP request.
4. Apply {{POLITICA_DATOS_SENSIBLES}}: list the fields to mask or exclude, the redaction technique (salted hashing, truncation, allowlist), and the point in the pipeline where it is applied (at origin, before serializing). Flag the risk of PII leaking through message or stack.
5. Deliver two log lines valid against the schema: one for a normal event (INFO) and one for an error (ERROR) with stack and shared trace_id to demonstrate correlation.
6. Draft the adoption guide for {{STACK_TECNOLOGICO}} targeting {{DESTINO_LOGS}} without ingestion transformations: library configuration, schema versioning policy (semver, backward compatibility), and incremental migration plan for legacy services with dual-write.
Stay language-agnostic when STACK_TECNOLOGICO is not defined. If {{CAMPOS_NEGOCIO}} or {{POLITICA_DATOS_SENSIBLES}} are not provided, propose a defensible minimum set and mark it. Mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate the objective, stack, destination, and criticality; declare assumptions about business fields and data policy if missing.
Phase 2 - Plan: present the index of the 6 deliverables and the proposed list of mandatory fields before detailing; ensure consistency with the chosen destination.
Phase 3 - Execute: produce the contract, level table, correlation rules, data policy, examples, and adoption guide; verify that both examples comply with the schema field by field and share trace_id.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every mandatory field has type, optionality, cardinality, and example; timestamp is ISO-8601 UTC with milliseconds; schema_version exists to version the contract.
- [ ] trace_id, span_id, and request_id exist with a propagation rule via traceparent (W3C Trace Context) and defined behavior when incoming context is missing (including batch/async).
- [ ] The 5 levels include usage criterion, exclusion, and operational action; there is a default level justified by criticality and cost.
- [ ] The sensitive data policy names concrete fields, redaction technique, and point in the pipeline; warns of the risk of PII in message/stack.
- [ ] Both examples are valid JSON, comply with the schema field by field, and share trace_id (one INFO, one ERROR with stack).
- [ ] The adoption guide is actionable for the stack, does not require ingestion transformations, and includes schema versioning and a legacy migration plan.
- [ ] Each assumption is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: structured logging design document with schema contract (field table), level table, correlation rules, sensitive data policy, two validated log examples, and adoption guide with versioning and migration.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_alertas_accionabl:
[inputs]
- SERVICIO: {{SERVICIO}} > Name of the service or system whose alerts are being redesigned and its function for the user
- CATALOGO_ALERTAS_ACTUAL: {{CATALOGO_ALERTAS_ACTUAL}} > List of current alerts with their condition, severity, and, if it exists, firing frequency or false positive rate ("(optional)" if starting from scratch)
- SLOS_Y_OBJETIVOS: {{SLOS_Y_OBJETIVOS}} > Service SLIs and SLOs (availability, latency, errors) with objective and window; if they do not exist, they are proposed as [ASSUMPTION]
- DESTINATARIO_GUARDIA: {{DESTINATARIO_GUARDIA}} > Who receives pages and tickets (on-call role, team), notification channel, and, if it exists, escalation chain
- TOLERANCIA_RUIDO: {{TOLERANCIA_RUIDO}} > Appetite for noise vs detection: aggressive (detect earlier, more false positives) or conservative (fewer pages) ("(optional)")
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The on-call team of {{SERVICIO}} suffers from alert fatigue: too many notifications, many not actionable, and trust in on-call erodes to the point that real pages are ignored. The objective is to transform {{CATALOGO_ALERTAS_ACTUAL}} into a symptom-based alert system, anchored to {{SLOS_Y_OBJETIVOS}}, that only fires when there is real, actionable user impact and is calibrated according to {{TOLERANCIA_RUIDO}}. This unlocks sustainable on-call rotations, lower MTTR through clear runbooks, and recovered trust in each page received by {{DESTINATARIO_GUARDIA}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior SRE specializing in observability and SLO-based alert design, with expertise in the Google SRE Book and SRE Workbook (alerting on symptoms, multiwindow multi-burn-rate).

Deliverable: redesigned catalog of actionable, anti-fatigue alerts. Produce:
1. SLI/SLO reference inventory: confirm or propose (as [ASSUMPTION]) the SLOs that govern the alerts, with their error budget and window.
2. Triage of the current catalog: classify each current alert as keep, downgrade (to ticket or dashboard), or eliminate, with the reason. If {{CATALOGO_ALERTAS_ACTUAL}} is "(optional)"/empty, skip the triage and design from the SLOs.
3. Final catalog, one card per alert with: name; observable symptom (user impact, never internal cause); severity (page now / ticket / dashboard only); exact condition with threshold and evaluation window; threshold justification; responsible owner and escalation chain (first responder and whom to escalate to if not resolved); runbook (concrete steps for the first responder); auto-resolution condition.
4. Multiwindow multi-burn-rate error budget alerts for the critical SLOs (long window + short window pair per severity level), with the fraction of budget consumed that triggers each level.
5. Anti-storm rules: grouping of correlated alerts by dependency, suppression of downstream symptoms when there is an already-open root incident, and respect for maintenance or deployment windows.
6. Dead man's switch: an alert that fires upon absence of signal (heartbeat or traffic rate at zero) so that silence is not confused with health.
7. Anti-fatigue summary: how many alerts page vs ticket vs dashboard, what noise was eliminated and why, and the estimated volume of pages per on-call rotation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the service, SLOs, and fatigue pain; list what is missing and flag assumptions. If a critical SLO or the catalog is missing, ask for it or declare it [ASSUMPTION] before continuing.
Phase 2 Anchor to symptoms: derive from each SLO the user-visible symptom that should trigger action; discard cause metrics (CPU, memory, queue) unless they are the only reliable proxy for a symptom, and say so explicitly.
Phase 3 Three-test filter per candidate: urgent (requires immediate human action), actionable (there is something concrete to do now), novel (does not duplicate another alert). If it fails any one, downgrade or eliminate with reason.
Phase 4 Calibrate thresholds and windows: for SLOs use multiwindow multi-burn-rate (high burn rate in short window = page; moderate burn rate in long window = ticket); justify each threshold against the error budget or historical data. Adjust aggressiveness according to {{TOLERANCIA_RUIDO}}.
Phase 5 Reduce systemic noise: define grouping by dependency, suppression under a root incident, maintenance windows, and the dead man's switch.
Phase 6 Draft runbooks, owner/escalation, and auto-resolution per alert; close with the anti-fatigue summary.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every paging alert describes a user-observable symptom, not an internal cause; cause-as-proxy exceptions are justified.
- [ ] Each alert passed the three tests (urgent, actionable, novel) or was downgraded/eliminated with explicit reasoning.
- [ ] Critical SLOs use multiwindow multi-burn-rate alerts with long + short window pair and budget fraction per level.
- [ ] Each threshold has justification linked to the error budget or historical data; what is inferred goes as [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Each alert has an owner, escalation chain, actionable runbook (concrete steps), and auto-resolution condition.
- [ ] Anti-storm rules exist (grouping + suppression + maintenance) and there is a dead man's switch for absence of signal.
- [ ] The anti-fatigue summary quantifies page vs ticket vs dashboard, the eliminated noise, and the volume of pages per on-call rotation.
Expected deliverable: actionable alert catalog (SLO inventory + triage + cards per alert + burn-rate alerts + anti-storm rules + dead man's switch + anti-fatigue summary), ready to implement in the team's alerting engine.
spec-desarrollo_runbook_operacion_servic:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_SERVICIO: {{NOMBRE_SERVICIO}} > Name of the service or component to document and its business criticality (tier/impact if a failure brings it down)
- ARQUITECTURA_Y_DEPENDENCIAS: {{ARQUITECTURA_Y_DEPENDENCIAS}} > Language/runtime, deployment model (container/VM/serverless), orchestrator, database, queues, caches, and upstream/downstream external dependencies
- SLO_SLI: {{SLO_SLI}} > Current service level objectives and indicators (availability, p95/p99 latency, error rate) with their window and error budget if it exists
- STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD: {{STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD}} > Metrics, logs, traces, and alerting tools, plus links to dashboards (e.g., Grafana, Datadog, CloudWatch, ELK, PagerDuty)
- INCIDENTES_PRIORITARIOS: {{INCIDENTES_PRIORITARIOS}} > List of incidents to cover first; "Unspecified" to use the standard catalog
- POLITICA_ESCALAMIENTO: {{POLITICA_ESCALAMIENTO}} > On-call tiers, domain owners, time limits per severity, and escalation channel; "Unspecified" to propose a default scheme marked [ASSUMPTION]
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A production service enters an incident and the on-call person needs to act in minutes, not investigate from scratch at 3 a.m. A well-constructed operational runbook converts the team's dispersed knowledge into repeatable procedures: it reduces the mean time to mitigate (MTTM), lowers dependence on heroic experts, and enables broader and more sustainable on-call rotations. A poorly made runbook does the opposite: commands that do not run, phantom thresholds, and ambiguous steps cost expensive minutes under pressure. This prompt unlocks a runbook ready to paste into the repository or the operations wiki, actionable, verifiable, and free of invented content.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior SRE engineer with experience operating and placing critical production services on-call, author of runbooks that are used at 3 a.m. when no one has time to think.

Deliverable: an operational runbook for {{NOMBRE_SERVICIO}} in Markdown, self-contained and actionable. Produce:
1. Service card: purpose in one sentence, owner/team, criticality, SLO with window ({{SLO_SLI}}), error budget if applicable, upstream/downstream dependencies, and links (or placeholders) to dashboards/logs/traces from {{STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD}}.
2. Signal and alert table derived from the SLOs/SLIs: signal, threshold, severity, operational meaning, and immediate action. Distinguish paging alerts from those that only notify.
3. Incident catalog based on {{INCIDENTES_PRIORITARIOS}}, covering at least: high latency, elevated 5xx error rate, CPU/memory saturation, database connection exhaustion, queue backlog or consumer down, and degraded external dependency. For each incident: observable symptoms, root cause hypotheses ordered by probability, numbered diagnosis (with exact command or query and expected result), numbered mitigation (with expected result), objective resolution verification criterion, and escalation rule per {{POLITICA_ESCALAMIENTO}}. Mark every irreversible or high-impact action (data loss, traffic cutover).
4. Transversal safe operation procedures: rollback, controlled restart, shutdown feature flag, traffic draining, and horizontal scaling; each with preconditions, steps, risks, and how to abort midway.
5. Post-incident checklist linked to the post-mortem: what to capture (timeline, logs, metrics, decisions) before data rotates or expires.
6. Runbook maintenance guide: review cadence, owner, and how to validate it (e.g., game-day or a procedure rehearsal in staging).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{NOMBRE_SERVICIO}}, {{ARQUITECTURA_Y_DEPENDENCIAS}}, {{SLO_SLI}}, and {{STACK_OBSERVABILIDAD}}. If a critical piece of data is missing, ask for it; do not invent commands or thresholds. Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION] and leave an explicit placeholder (e.g., <LATENCY_DASHBOARD>, <RESTART_COMMAND>) where data is missing. If {{INCIDENTES_PRIORITARIOS}} or {{POLITICA_ESCALAMIENTO}} arrive as "Unspecified", use the standard catalog and a default escalation scheme, both marked [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Signal map: derive the alert table from the SLOs/SLIs, linking each signal to its dashboard and declaring whether it pages or only notifies.
Phase 3 - Incident catalog: for each incident apply the pattern symptoms > ordered hypotheses > diagnosis > mitigation > verification > escalation. Each diagnosis and mitigation step must be executable and include an expected result; never give a destructive command without a precondition and an impact marker.
Phase 4 - Safe operation and closing: document transversal procedures with preconditions, risks, and abort procedure; the post-incident checklist; and the maintenance guide.
Phase 5 - Verification: go through the CRITERION before delivering and correct what is missing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- [ ] Complete service card with owner, criticality, SLO with window, and observability links (or explicit placeholders).
- [ ] Signal/alert table with threshold, severity, and whether it pages or notifies, derived from the SLOs/SLIs.
- [ ] Each incident covers the six blocks: symptoms, ordered hypotheses, numbered diagnosis, numbered mitigation, verification, and escalation; the six minimum incidents are present.
- [ ] Every diagnosis/mitigation command or query is exact and includes an expected result; nothing invented goes without [ASSUMPTION] or placeholder.
- [ ] Irreversible or high-impact actions are marked; safe operation procedures include preconditions, risks, and abort; rollback is reversible and verifiable.
- [ ] Post-incident checklist links to the post-mortem and the maintenance guide defines cadence, owner, and validation method.
- [ ] Clean Markdown, self-contained, in neutral Spanish, ready to paste into repository or wiki.
Expected deliverable: operational runbook for {{NOMBRE_SERVICIO}} in Markdown, actionable under on-call duty, with incident catalog and verifiable mitigation procedures.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_health_checks:
[inputs]
- SERVICIO: {{SERVICIO}} > Name and responsibility of the service whose health checks you are designing
- STACK_ORQUESTADOR: {{STACK_ORQUESTADOR}} > Language/framework and orchestrator or load balancer (e.g., Java Spring Boot on Kubernetes, Node on ECS, Go behind an ALB). Determines the native probe semantics (liveness/readiness/startup in K8s; grace period and deregistration in ALB/ECS)
- DEPENDENCIAS: {{DEPENDENCIAS}} > Service dependencies marking each as hard (without it there is no service) or soft (degradable): database, cache, queues, downstream services. If the mark is missing, infer it and declare [ASSUMPTION]
- SLO_OBJETIVO: {{SLO_OBJETIVO}} > Relevant service level objectives (availability, p99 latency, startup time) that should guide thresholds and timeouts
- POLITICA_DEGRADACION: {{POLITICA_DEGRADACION}} > Expected behavior under partial degradation: continue serving in degraded mode or exit load balancing (optional; if missing, default = continue serving degraded and report soft dependency as degraded)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are designing the health checks for {{SERVICIO}} so they reflect the actual state of the service, not a superficial metric. Poorly designed checks cause two opposite operational failures: false positives (a healthy-reporting instance that rejects traffic) and correlated failure (readiness coupled to a shared dependency that takes all instances out of the load balancer at once and turns an intermittency into a total outage). A correct design unlocks safe deployments, reliable self-healing, and actionable observability aligned with {{SLO_OBJETIVO}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior reliability engineer (SRE) with experience operating production services under {{STACK_ORQUESTADOR}} and designing SLO-aligned probes.
Deliverable: health check specification ready to implement. Steps:
1. Classify {{DEPENDENCIAS}} as hard and soft and justify each classification based on its impact on the service's function. A dependency shared by many instances (e.g., central database) must NOT govern readiness even if it is hard: separate functional criticality from correlated failure risk.
2. Design three differentiated endpoints with single responsibility: liveness (process alive, not blocked; does NOT validate external dependencies), readiness (can accept traffic now; validates only local or low-correlation hard dependencies), startup (initialization completed before enabling liveness/readiness).
3. Per endpoint define: what it verifies and what it does NOT; HTTP success and failure codes; timeout and latency budget; check depth per dependency (shallow connection ping vs real functional query); caching of the result to avoid hammering dependencies on every probe; behavior under partial degradation per {{POLITICA_DEGRADACION}}.
4. Specify the JSON response contract for each endpoint: aggregated status (healthy/degraded/unhealthy), per-dependency status, observed latency, and service version, with enough detail for diagnosis without filtering credentials, internal hosts, or PII.
5. Recommend probe thresholds (period, consecutive failures and successes, initial grace period, timeout) consistent with {{SLO_OBJETIVO}} and the actual startup time. Hard rule: timeout < period; recovery budget (failures x period) less than the tolerable error budget.
6. List anti-patterns to avoid and how this design prevents them.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: map dependencies, SLOs, and service failure modes; identify which dependencies are shared and carry high correlation risk.
Phase 2 - Design: separate liveness/readiness/startup by single responsibility; define contracts and thresholds derived from the SLOs and actual startup time, not from default values.
Phase 3 - Harden: validate against anti-patterns (readiness coupled to shared dependencies; liveness that calls the database and causes cascading restarts; timeout >= probe period; checks without latency budget; probe executing a heavy query on every call; missing startup probe on slow-starting services) and adjust.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Liveness does not query any external dependency; it only detects process alive/blocked and never causes restarts due to downstream failure.
- [ ] Readiness validates only hard dependencies; soft ones report degradation without taking the endpoint down; shared dependencies with high correlation risk do NOT govern readiness.
- [ ] Startup probe present and sized for the actual startup time; enables liveness/readiness only upon completing initialization.
- [ ] Each endpoint declares HTTP success and failure codes, timeout, latency budget, and check depth per dependency.
- [ ] The JSON contract exposes aggregated and per-dependency status without filtering secrets, internal hosts, or PII.
- [ ] Thresholds are derived from {{SLO_OBJETIVO}} and actual startup time, with timeout less than the period and a bounded recovery budget.
- [ ] The design explicitly prevents correlated failure by shared dependencies and the cascade of restarts from liveness.
- [ ] Every decision without supporting data is marked [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: endpoint table + JSON contracts + recommended probe configuration + list of anti-patterns, ready to implement on {{STACK_ORQUESTADOR}}.
spec-desarrollo_profiling_rendimiento_cu:
[inputs]
- APLICACION: {{APLICACION}} > Application or service to profile (name, purpose, traffic scale)
- LENGUAJE_RUNTIME: {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}} > Language and runtime/version (e.g., Python 3.12, JVM 21, Node 20, Go 1.22, .NET 8)
- ESCENARIO: {{ESCENARIO}} > Concrete scenario to profile (endpoint, batch job, cold start, slow query)
- METRICA_OBJETIVO: {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} > Metric to move and current baseline (e.g., p95 latency, throughput, peak memory, allocations/request)
- PERFIL_DISPONIBLE: {{PERFIL_DISPONIBLE}} > Already-captured profile, flame graph, trace, or "no profile yet" (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to speed up {{APLICACION}} without blind rewrites. Optimizing by intuition wastes effort on code that barely influences the total time; the correct path is to profile CPU and memory to locate the hot paths that truly dominate execution and attack them in order of impact. A good analysis unlocks latency and infrastructure cost gains with surgical, verifiable changes, and leaves a repeatable method for the next performance regression.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance engineer with experience in production profiling on {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}}, flame graph reading, and data-driven optimization.

Deliverable: a profiling report with ranked hot paths and a prioritized optimization plan. Steps:
1. Confirm {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}}, the {{ESCENARIO}}, and the {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}}; if there is no reproducible baseline, define one with me: representative load, controlled environment, warm-up, number of iterations, and how to isolate environmental noise.
2. Recommend the profiler and capture mode for the stack (sampling vs instrumented; on-CPU and off-CPU CPU profiling; separate memory/allocations profile) with the concrete commands or steps and their expected overhead.
3. Analyze {{PERFIL_DISPONIBLE}}: separate self time from total time, distinguish CPU-bound from I/O wait and lock contention, and detect excessive allocations and GC pressure. Quantify each finding as a percentage of total time.
4. Rank bottlenecks by impact using Amdahl's law; for each one: probable root cause, cost of improvement, expected improvement, and theoretical ceiling (you cannot accelerate beyond the fraction that bottleneck represents).
5. Propose concrete optimizations (algorithm, data structure, caching, batching, fewer allocations, parallelism, queries), prioritizing the minimum change with the greatest return; name the improvement mechanism and the regression risk.
6. Define the verification: re-profile, compare against baseline with multiple runs to rule out measurement noise, and a measurable success criterion confirming gain without regressions in other metrics (memory, throughput, p99).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Measure-analyze-optimize-verify method, in phases:
- Phase 1 Measure: fix reproducible baseline and capture CPU (on/off) and memory profiles of the {{ESCENARIO}}. Do not optimize without evidence.
- Phase 2 Analyze: read the flame graph/call tree, attribute percentage of time to each hot path, and classify the nature of the cost (CPU, I/O, lock, GC/allocations).
- Phase 3 Prioritize: apply Amdahl's law to order by improvement ceiling; discard micro-optimizations without profile backing.
- Phase 4 Optimize: propose the minimum change with the greatest impact first, with its explicit improvement mechanism.
- Phase 5 Verify: re-profile, compare against baseline, and validate the success criterion.
Edge cases to watch: regressions that only emerge under concurrency or real load; hot paths dependent on input data; cost dominated by cold start or by external queues/services where the code itself is not the bottleneck; profiles taken in a non-representative environment. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. If {{PERFIL_DISPONIBLE}}, {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}}, or {{ESCENARIO}} is missing, ask for it before proceeding; do not invent numbers.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every identified hot path carries its percentage of total time (no loose qualitative assertions).
- [ ] Self time is distinguished from total time, and CPU-bound from I/O/lock/GC.
- [ ] Bottlenecks are ordered by impact via Amdahl's law, with cost, expected improvement, and theoretical ceiling per item.
- [ ] Each optimization names the concrete mechanism, the regression risk, and the minimum change with the greatest return goes first.
- [ ] Profiler and capture mode correspond to {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}}; includes a separate memory profile from the CPU one and its overhead.
- [ ] The baseline is reproducible (load, environment, warm-up, iterations) and verification uses multiple runs to rule out noise.
- [ ] There is a measurable success criterion without regressions in other metrics (memory, throughput, p99).
- [ ] Assumptions carry [ASSUMPTION]; missing data is asked for, not invented.
Expected deliverable: profiling report with ranked hot paths table (percentage, nature, root cause, Amdahl ceiling) + prioritized optimization plan (mechanism, cost, risk) + verification protocol.
spec-desarrollo_optimizacion_consultas_s:
[inputs]
- MOTOR_VERSION: {{MOTOR_VERSION}} > Engine and version (PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.0, SQL Server 2022, Oracle 19c); fixes index syntax, INCLUDE/covering, and plan tools
- CONSULTA_SQL: {{CONSULTA_SQL}} > Complete slow SQL query, with representative example parameters for the real case
- PLAN_EJECUCION: {{PLAN_EJECUCION}} > Actual plan with metrics: EXPLAIN ANALYZE (Postgres), EXPLAIN ANALYZE/FORMAT=JSON (MySQL), actual execution plan with statistics (SQL Server), DBMS_XPLAN with rowsource (Oracle). Estimated plan is not sufficient
- DDL_TABLAS_INDICES: {{DDL_TABLAS_INDICES}} > DDL of involved tables with their current indexes, keys, and constraints
- VOLUMEN_Y_TIEMPO: {{VOLUMEN_Y_TIEMPO}} > Rows per table, known selectivity of key predicates, and observed execution time (with percentile if available)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Write limits, read/write ratio, maintenance or read-only windows, cap on new indexes (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A critical SQL query runs slowly and degrades the experience or saturates the database. Diagnosing it from its actual execution plan and indexes unlocks a measurable speedup without changing the business logic, and leaves a reusable indexing strategy for future queries on the same schema.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior database engineer specializing in performance tuning and index design.
Deliverable: bottleneck diagnosis + prioritized optimization plan with DDL ready to execute + before/after validation plan.
Steps:
1. Verify the inputs; if MOTOR_VERSION, CONSULTA_SQL, PLAN_EJECUCION, DDL_TABLAS_INDICES, or VOLUMEN_Y_TIEMPO is missing, ask for it and do not proceed with invented data. Without a real plan, limit the output to hypotheses marked [ASSUMPTION].
2. Read the plan and identify costly operators: Seq Scan / Full Table Scan on large tables, Nested Loop with many iterations, Sort/Hash spilled to disk, unnecessary materializations, and gaps between estimated and actual rows.
3. For each bottleneck name the root cause: non-sargable predicate, missing or non-covering index, wrong column order in composite index, unsupported join, stale statistics, or estimate biased by column correlation.
4. Propose improvements prioritized by impact-effort, each index as executable DDL and each rewrite with the SQL before/after. Prioritize indexes that serve multiple schema queries over single-use ones.
5. Declare for each proposal its write cost, storage, and maintenance cost, respecting RESTRICCIONES; warn when a rewrite could change the result set (NULLs, duplicates, order).
6. Deliver the validation plan with comparable metrics and a procedure in a test environment representative in data and volume.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Plan reading: walk through the plan from highest to lowest cost, note operators, estimated vs actual rows, loops, and disk spills; the estimated/actual gap reveals where statistics fail.
Phase 2 Root cause: map each costly operator to its structural cause (sargability, indexes, statistics, joins, correlation).
Phase 3 Solution design: define indexes and rewrites; justify column order (equality before range, highest selectivity first, covering columns with INCLUDE or engine equivalent). Do not invent columns, indexes, or cardinalities outside the inputs.
Phase 4 Validation: specify how to re-measure and compare (new plan, time, logical reads/buffers). Mark every inference not backed by the plan as [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each bottleneck cites the operator and plan figures that support it (estimated vs actual rows, time, spills).
- [ ] Each proposal has an explicit root cause and DDL or SQL ready to execute.
- [ ] The column order of each composite index is justified (equality/range, selectivity, coverage).
- [ ] The write cost, storage, and maintenance cost of each new index is declared.
- [ ] Proposals are prioritized by impact-effort and reusable indexes are favored.
- [ ] Every rewrite that could alter the result set is warned.
- [ ] The validation plan defines before/after metrics and a procedure in a representative test environment.
- [ ] Every assertion without evidence in the plan is marked [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: bottleneck table, prioritized list of optimizations with DDL/SQL, associated costs per proposal, and before/after validation plan, plus the reusable indexing strategy for the schema.
spec-desarrollo_diseno_indices_base_dato:
[inputs]
- MOTOR_VERSION: {{MOTOR_VERSION}} > Exact engine and version (e.g., PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.0/InnoDB, SQL Server 2022, Oracle 19c, MariaDB 11); determines syntax, available index types, planner reading, and diagnostic commands
- DDL_TABLAS: {{DDL_TABLAS}} > CREATE TABLE of the involved tables with types, primary keys, FKs, collation/charset, and existing indexes
- CONSULTAS_CRITICAS: {{CONSULTAS_CRITICAS}} > Frequent or slow queries, ideally with their current plan (EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE) and relative frequency; include filters, JOINs, ORDER BY/GROUP BY, and projection
- VOLUMEN_CARDINALIDAD: {{VOLUMEN_CARDINALIDAD}} > Rows per table, distribution and cardinality/selectivity of candidate columns, presence of NULLs and skewed values
- RATIO_LECTURA_ESCRITURA: {{RATIO_LECTURA_ESCRITURA}} > Read/write ratio of the workload, write peaks, batch windows, and tolerance for index creation latency (defines the read/write balance)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Queries degrade as tables grow, and each new index accelerates reads but penalizes INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, consumes space, and slows maintenance (VACUUM, rebuild, replication). The correct index strategy unlocks stable p95 latency, lower CPU/IO load, and a workload that scales without over-indexing or slowing down writes. A well-founded decision today avoids schema rewrites and costly migrations later. The goal is not to add more indexes, but the minimum set that sustains the real workload.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior database engineer specializing in performance and query optimization, with expertise in the planner of {{MOTOR_VERSION}}.
Deliverable: justified indexing strategy with DDL ready for review and measurement plan. Steps:
1. Inventory {{MOTOR_VERSION}}, {{DDL_TABLAS}}, {{CONSULTAS_CRITICAS}}, {{VOLUMEN_CARDINALIDAD}}, and {{RATIO_LECTURA_ESCRITURA}}; if any piece of data is missing, ask for it before continuing and do not invent values. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you assume.
2. Per key query decompose: equality predicates, range predicates, ORDER BY/GROUP BY columns, JOIN columns, and projected columns. Note estimated selectivity and whether there are functions applied to columns.
3. Derive the column order of each composite index with the equality-before-range rule and the selectivity of the leading column; never put range before equality. Justify if the most selective column is not in the lead position (e.g., to serve an ORDER BY without a sort).
4. Propose concrete indexes (B-tree, partial/filtered, covering with INCLUDE or trailing columns, functional/expression, GIN/GiST/BRIN for JSONB, text, ranges, or time series per {{MOTOR_VERSION}}) and for each one deliver exact DDL, queries it accelerates, and estimated write and space impact.
5. Consolidate indexes that serve multiple queries (a well-ordered composite can cover several by prefix) to minimize the total. Identify redundant (prefix of another), duplicate, overlapping, or unused indexes and mark them for elimination with their DROP.
6. Warn about the relevant traps for the case: function on the column that invalidates the index, type/collation/charset mismatch, low selectivity or skew that the planner discards, write amplification, over-indexing, indexes that only work with fresh statistics, and locking during creation (recommend CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY or online per engine).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: read schema, queries, and plans; map each query to its filter/order/join/projection columns and record selectivity and volume. Detect whether current plans do Seq Scans, costly Sorts, or lookups due to missing coverage.
Phase 2 - Design: for each candidate query define the optimal index, order columns by equality-before-range, decide covering vs partial, and consolidate shared indexes to minimize the total and write cost.
Phase 3 - Read/write balance: contrast each proposed index against {{RATIO_LECTURA_ESCRITURA}}; discard or downgrade those that penalize writes without proportional read gain. In write-heavy workloads, prioritize coverage of the most frequent queries, not all of them.
Phase 4 - Validation: define the before/after measurement method (compare EXPLAIN ANALYZE, p95 latency, logical reads/writes, index size, and actual usage via engine statistics views) in an equivalent environment with representative data and volume, never directly in production; include rollback plan (DROP) and deployment order.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each proposed index cites the query or queries it accelerates and its estimated write and space impact.
- [ ] Column order in composite indexes respects equality-before-range and prioritizes the most selective column as leader, or explicitly justifies the exception.
- [ ] DDL syntactically valid for {{MOTOR_VERSION}}, with non-blocking creation (CONCURRENTLY/online) when the engine supports it.
- [ ] Redundant/duplicate/overlapping/unused indexes to eliminate are listed, each with its DROP.
- [ ] At least the relevant traps for the case are named (function on column, collation/type, low selectivity/skew, write amplification, over-indexing).
- [ ] Missing data is requested; volumes and cardinalities are not invented; [ASSUMPTION] items are marked.
- [ ] Includes before/after measurement plan with concrete metrics and warns not to apply to production without validation; defines rollback.
Expected deliverable: prioritized recommendations table (high/medium/low impact, write cost, decision to create/eliminate/postpone) + DDL block ready for review (CREATE INDEX and DROP INDEX in deployment order) + measurement section (metrics, environment, success criterion) and rollback.
spec-desarrollo_estrategia_caching_capas:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA: {{SISTEMA}} > Current architecture, stack, and service on which caching is being designed
- PATRONES_TRAFICO: {{PATRONES_TRAFICO}} > Read/write ratio, volume (RPS/peak), most expensive endpoints or queries, key distribution (skew/known hot keys)
- TOLERANCIA_OBSOLESCENCIA: {{TOLERANCIA_OBSOLESCENCIA}} > How much staleness each data type tolerates (seconds/minutes) and which require strict freshness or read-your-writes
- CAPAS_DISPONIBLES: {{CAPAS_DISPONIBLES}} > Allowed or existing layers (client, CDN/edge, gateway, distributed cache, data cache) (optional)
- OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO: {{OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO}} > Target latency (p95/p99), hit ratio per layer, and origin load reduction sought (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The system {{SISTEMA}} suffers from avoidable latency and origin load because it recomputes or re-queries data that changes infrequently. A well-governed layered caching strategy unlocks lower perceived latency, greater capacity per node, and less pressure on the origin, as long as freshness is maintained within {{TOLERANCIA_OBSOLESCENCIA}}. Without an explicit contract of keys, TTL, and invalidation, the cache stops being an optimization and becomes a source of staleness bugs, stampede incidents, and data crossed between users. The design must be correct-by-default: when in doubt, do not cache.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Performance Architect specializing in high-traffic distributed systems, with expertise in CDN/edge, distributed caches (Redis/Memcached type), and consistency patterns.
Deliverable: actionable layered caching strategy for {{SISTEMA}}. Steps:
1. Map the request flow and identify candidate layers within {{CAPAS_DISPONIBLES}}: client, CDN/edge, gateway, application cache, data cache. Per layer declare what IS cached and what is NOT (personalized data, authenticated sessions, writes, PII). Hard rule: per-user content is never in a shared cache without a key that includes identity/role.
2. For each cacheable datum define the key with its variation dimensions (schema version, locale, tenant, role, relevant headers), TTL justified by {{TOLERANCIA_OBSOLESCENCIA}}, and estimated size. TTL without freshness justification = rejected.
3. Classify each item by consistency pattern: pure TTL, stale-while-revalidate, or event-based invalidation, consistent with {{PATRONES_TRAFICO}}. Justify the choice against its staleness cost.
4. Design the invalidation (TTL, write-through, write-behind, targeted purge, key versioning), write propagation between layers (invalidation order to avoid re-filling with stale data), and stampede mitigation (locking/single-flight, TTL jitter, anticipatory refresh).
5. Define failure protection: fallback to origin with load budget, circuit breaker, cache penetration prevention (bounded null-caching or bloom filter), and hot key handling (key replica, second-level local cache).
6. Specify metrics and SLOs against {{OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO}}: hit ratio per layer, p50/p95/p99 latency, observed staleness, stampede rate, and instrumentation (what is measured, where, with what alert).
7. Deliver an incremental rollout plan layer by layer with success criteria and rollback criteria per stage (shadow/traffic percentage before 100%).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Interpret): validate {{SISTEMA}}, {{PATRONES_TRAFICO}}, and {{TOLERANCIA_OBSOLESCENCIA}}; classify data as cacheable vs non-cacheable. If a critical piece of data is missing (read/write ratio, peak RPS, latency target, available layers), ask for it; do not invent figures. Mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 (Plan): propose the layer map and, per cacheable datum, its key-TTL-invalidation trio; present the plan for approval before detailing.
Phase 3 (Execute): develop the complete strategy, write propagation, protections (stampede, penetration, hot keys, fallback), and staged rollout with rollback.
Mandatory edge cases: personalization behind CDN (Vary or edge compute), multi-region invalidation with eventual replication, application-cache vs data-cache consistency on the same write, and behavior with cache completely down (resulting load must not exceed origin capacity).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each layer explicitly declares what IS cached and what is NOT; per-user content is never in a shared cache without identity in the key.
- [ ] Each cacheable datum has a key with variation dimensions, freshness-justified TTL, and assigned consistency pattern.
- [ ] Write propagation between layers avoids stale reads and re-filling with stale data, respecting {{TOLERANCIA_OBSOLESCENCIA}}.
- [ ] There is explicit mitigation for stampede, penetration, hot keys, and total cache failure, with origin load budget.
- [ ] Metrics (hit ratio per layer, p95/p99 latency, staleness, stampede) are measurable and tied to {{OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO}}.
- [ ] Rollout is incremental with success criteria and rollback per stage.
- [ ] Edge cases (personalization behind CDN, multi-region, inter-layer consistency) are resolved.
- [ ] Assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION] and there is no invented data.
Expected deliverable: strategy document with a table per layer (what is cached, key, TTL, invalidation mode, expected hit ratio) plus the first three prioritized implementation steps and their rollback criteria.
spec-desarrollo_analisis_complejidad_alg:
[inputs]
- ALGORITMO: {{ALGORITMO}} > Code, pseudocode, or precise description of the algorithm to analyze
- LENGUAJE: {{LENGUAJE}} > Language or pseudocode of the algorithm (defines the real cost of native operations and data structures, including amortized cost)
- TAMANO_ENTRADA: {{TAMANO_ENTRADA}} > Typical and maximum n size, value range, and data shape (sorted, sparse, duplicates)
- OBJETIVO: {{OBJETIVO}} > Optimization target: reduce worst-case time, lower memory, support streaming, etc.
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > (optional) Limits: no external libraries, bounded memory, preserve order, stability
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An algorithm works in tests but its asymptotic cost decides whether it scales or collapses when n grows in production. This analysis converts intuition ("it feels slow") into formal evidence: demonstrated temporal and spatial complexity, bottleneck located, and an optimization path with explicit trade-offs. It unlocks architecture decisions, infrastructure sizing, and refactors prioritized by real impact, not by gut feeling. Distinguishing asymptotic cost from observed latency (constants, cache, branch prediction) avoids both over-engineering and false alarms.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance engineer specializing in algorithm and data structure analysis, with judgment to distinguish the optimization that matters from sterile micro-optimization.

Deliverable: complexity report with an assumptions section, case derivation, bottleneck diagnosis, alternatives with their complexity, before/after comparison table, and reproducible empirical measurement plan. Steps:
1. Reconstruct in one sentence what {{ALGORITMO}} does and declare assumptions about n, value range, and data distribution, each marked [ASSUMPTION].
2. Fix the cost model of {{LENGUAJE}}: native operations, data structures, and their amortized vs worst-case cost (rehashing, dynamic array reallocation).
3. Derive temporal complexity in worst case, average case, and best case (Big-O / Big-Theta / Big-Omega), justified by counting dominant operations; solve recursion with the master theorem or recursion tree showing the key step.
4. Derive space complexity: auxiliary memory and stack depth, separated from the input space.
5. Identify the dominant term and the block or line that governs growth; note the constant factor when it decides at the real n of {{TAMANO_ENTRADA}}.
6. Propose 1 to 3 alternatives aligned with {{OBJETIVO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}}, each with a core idea, new temporal and spatial complexity, and an honest trade-off; if no improvement compensates, declare it.
7. Build a before/after comparison table and empirical verification plan matching {{TAMANO_ENTRADA}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: parse {{ALGORITMO}} and {{LENGUAJE}}; fix the cost model. If {{ALGORITMO}}, {{LENGUAJE}}, or {{TAMANO_ENTRADA}} is missing, request it before proceeding.
Phase 2 - Asymptotic analysis: decompose by blocks; count operations; apply sum and product rules; solve recurrences; obtain T(n) and S(n) by case, without inventing behavior (ambiguous things are marked [ASSUMPTION]).
Phase 3 - Diagnosis: isolate the dominant term and the concrete bottleneck; distinguish asymptotic cost from real latency (constants, cache, branch prediction).
Phase 4 - Optimization: map the bottleneck to techniques (hashing, memoization, divide and conquer, two-pointers, sliding window, more appropriate data structure, precomputation) consistent with {{OBJETIVO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}}; derive the new complexity of each alternative and its trade-off.
Phase 5 - Verification: before/after table and empirical measurement protocol (n sizes, metric, repetitions, warm-up and noise isolation, log-log plot to confirm the expected asymptotic slope).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Temporal complexity given in worst, average, and best case with correct notation.
- [ ] Each bound justified by operation counting or recurrence resolution, not asserted without proof.
- [ ] Cost model of {{LENGUAJE}} is explicit, with amortized vs worst case where applicable.
- [ ] Space complexity separates auxiliary memory from input space and includes the recursion stack.
- [ ] Dominant term and bottleneck identified with precision (block or line); constant factor noted if it decides.
- [ ] Between 1 and 3 alternatives, each with new complexity and honest trade-off; or a declaration that none compensates.
- [ ] Alternatives consistent with {{OBJETIVO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented behavior.
- [ ] Asymptotic cost distinguished from real latency.
- [ ] Before/after comparison table and reproducible empirical verification plan.
Expected deliverable: structured report with assumptions and cost model, case derivation, bottleneck diagnosis, alternatives with their complexity, before/after comparison table, and reproducible empirical measurement plan.
spec-desarrollo_optimizacion_carga_front:
[inputs]
- APP_DESCRIPCION: {{APP_DESCRIPCION}} > What the application is, its audience, and why load speed matters (impact on conversion, SEO, or retention)
- STACK_FRAMEWORK: {{STACK_FRAMEWORK}} > Framework and version (React, Vue, Angular, Astro, vanilla) + language
- BUNDLER: {{BUNDLER}} > Bundler in use (Vite, webpack, esbuild, Turbopack, Rollup, Parcel)
- MODO_RENDER: {{MODO_RENDER}} > SSR, SSG, CSR, ISR, or hybrid; whether there is hydration (full, partial, islands, RSC)
- METRICAS_ACTUALES: {{METRICAS_ACTUALES}} > LCP, INP, CLS, TTFB and their source (Lighthouse lab / PageSpeed / field CrUX); use no-measurement if they do not exist
- BUNDLE_Y_DEPENDENCIAS: {{BUNDLE_Y_DEPENDENCIAS}} > Initial bundle weight and suspected heavy libraries (charts, maps, WYSIWYG editors, moment, lodash, full icon sets) (optional)
- RUTA_CRITICA: {{RUTA_CRITICA}} > Screen or route to optimize first (highest traffic or conversion)
- PRESUPUESTO_OBJETIVO: {{PRESUPUESTO_OBJETIVO}} > Core Web Vitals target or performance budget (e.g. LCP < 2.5s mobile, initial bundle < 200KB gzip); use no-target if not defined (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Lighthouse/PageSpeed report, bundle analyzer output, package.json, network waterfall, screenshots, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A frontend application loads slowly and this degrades conversion, SEO, and experience. The goal is to improve Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS) on the First Load by reducing render-blocking, trimming the initial bundle, and deferring non-critical resources. A plan prioritized by impact unlocks measurable gains without rewriting the app or breaking functionality. Method constraint: optimize based on real measurement, not intuition; each lever is tied to a concrete metric and a way to verify it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior web performance engineer specializing in Core Web Vitals, performance budgets, critical render path, and RUM/lab instrumentation.
Deliverable: actionable, prioritized optimization plan, ready for tickets. Steps:
1. If METRICAS_ACTUALES is no-measurement, deliver the measurement protocol first (mobile Lighthouse, 4x CPU throttling, Slow 4G + complementary trace; lab vs. field) and do not optimize blindly.
2. Render-blocking: list resources that block the initial render (critical CSS not inlined, synchronous JS in the head, fonts without font-display swap, images without width/height) and separate critical from deferrable.
3. Bundling: define route-based code splitting, dynamic import of heavy components and libraries, tree shaking, replacement of monolithic dependencies with granular imports or lighter alternatives, and duplicate detection with a bundle analyzer.
4. Lazy loading: below-the-fold images with loading=lazy, IntersectionObserver for components, preload/preconnect of the LCP resource, and defer/async on non-critical scripts.
5. INP/interactivity: reduce main-thread work (long tasks, costly hydration, heavy handlers); consider deferred hydration or task partitioning.
6. CLS: reserve space for images, fonts, and elements that load late (explicit dimensions, aspect-ratio, skeleton containers).
7. For each recommendation, estimate the expected effect on the target metric, effort (low/medium/high), and risks or functional regressions.
8. Close with an execution order prioritized by impact over effort and how to re-measure each change; compare against PRESUPUESTO_OBJETIVO if it exists.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: confirm stack, bundler, render mode, and the weakest metric; if measurement is missing, define how to capture it (lab + field) before continuing.
Phase 2 Critical map: classify each resource on the critical render path as critical vs. deferrable and associate it with LCP, INP, or CLS; identify the exact LCP element.
Phase 3 Plan: write recommendations by lever (render-blocking, bundling, lazy loading, INP, CLS) with effect, effort, and risk, specific to the declared stack.
Phase 4 Prioritization and verification: order by impact over effort, mark quick wins vs. structural changes, and define the re-measurement method and success criterion per change. Do not invent figures; any figure without measurement is marked [ASSUMPTION] with the path to obtain it.
Edge cases: if the bottleneck is TTFB/server, state it explicitly and scope the frontend reach; if MODO_RENDER is pure CSR, prioritize splitting and hydration over critical CSS; if there are no ADJUNTOS or metrics, the measurement protocol is the first deliverable.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each recommendation maps to a concrete metric (LCP / INP / CLS / TTFB).
- [ ] Render-blocking, bundling, lazy loading, INP, and CLS are covered.
- [ ] Each item includes expected effect + effort (low/medium/high) + risk/regression.
- [ ] Recommendations are specific to the declared STACK_FRAMEWORK, BUNDLER, and MODO_RENDER, not generic.
- [ ] If there was no measurement, the capture protocol (lab + field) was delivered before optimizing.
- [ ] No invented numbers; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] with the path to obtain them.
- [ ] Close with an order prioritized by impact/effort (quick wins vs. structural) and a re-measurement plan against PRESUPUESTO_OBJETIVO if it exists.
Expected deliverable: optimization plan in a prioritized table or list, ready to convert into engineering tickets, with a before/after measurement section and success criterion per change.
spec-desarrollo_pruebas_benchmark_microb:
[inputs]
- CODIGO_BAJO_MEDICION: {{CODIGO_BAJO_MEDICION}} > Exact function, method, or snippet to measure, with its minimal dependencies and the initial state it requires
- LENGUAJE_RUNTIME: {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}} > Language, runtime, and exact version (e.g. Rust 1.79 release, JVM 21 C2, .NET 8, Go 1.22, CPython 3.12); include optimization flags if known
- ENTRADAS_REPRESENTATIVAS: {{ENTRADAS_REPRESENTATIVAS}} > Size, shape, and distribution of inputs that reflect the real case, not trivial data; indicate whether they vary between iterations
- METRICA_OBJETIVO: {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} > Latency per operation (ns/op) or throughput (ops/s); include target budget or regression threshold if it exists
- NIVEL_CONTROL_ENTORNO: {{NIVEL_CONTROL_ENTORNO}} > (optional) How much the machine can be controlled: "shared CI", "workstation", "dedicated host with performance governor"
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An optimization decision is only defensible if the measurement that supports it is reproducible. Most homegrown microbenchmarks lie: they measure JIT warmup instead of steady state, let the compiler eliminate as dead code exactly the work being measured, precompute constants and time a no-op, or measure below clock resolution. A reliable microbenchmark of {{CODIGO_BAJO_MEDICION}} unlocks the ability to compare two implementations with evidence, detect regressions in CI with a defensible threshold, and discuss performance with numbers instead of intuitions. What is delivered here is the difference between a data-driven optimization strategy and guesswork dressed up as rigor.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance engineer with experience in microbenchmarking on {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}}, familiar with the compiler/JIT optimization model of the ecosystem, the memory hierarchy, and the corresponding reference harness.

Deliverable: a complete, commented, ready-to-run microbenchmark plus its interpretation guide. Steps:
1. Select the idiomatic harness for {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}} (JMH, Criterion or Divan, BenchmarkDotNet, google-benchmark, pytest-benchmark or timeit, Benchmark.js or tinybench, testing.B) and justify why it is preferred over a manual stopwatch.
2. Structure warmup and measurement as separate phases; define enough warmup iterations to stabilize JIT/tiering and warm caches, and discard the initial samples.
3. Block dead-code elimination by consuming the result with the idiomatic mechanism (black_box, Blackhole, DoNotOptimize, accumulated sink) and block constant-folding by feeding {{ENTRADAS_REPRESENTATIVAS}} that the compiler cannot precompute.
4. Control the environment up to {{NIVEL_CONTROL_ENTORNO}}: CPU governor/frequency, turbo boost, GC pressure, I/O, core affinity, ASLR; run multiple forks or processes to capture variance across startups.
5. Configure the report of {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} with honest statistics: median, percentiles (p50/p95/p99), confidence interval, number of samples, and outlier detection; compare against the budget if it includes one.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}}, {{CODIGO_BAJO_MEDICION}}, {{ENTRADAS_REPRESENTATIVAS}}, and {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}}; if any data is missing, ask before writing code. Explicitly name which compiler optimizations threaten this measurement in this ecosystem and verify that the duration per operation exceeds clock resolution (if not, measure in batch and divide) [ASSUMPTION if the optimization level is not specified].
Phase 2 - Harness and anti-tricks: write the benchmark with the chosen library, integrating warmup, result consumption, and non-precomputable inputs; comment each defense indicating which noise or optimization it neutralizes. Separate the setup/allocation cost from the measured work.
Phase 3 - Environment and sampling: define forks/processes, iterations per measurement, and machine controls; document what could not be fixed and its expected impact on variance.
Phase 4 - Report and interpretation: specify the statistical output and the decision rule for separating signal from noise (e.g. overlap of confidence intervals or minimum detectable effect size); warn that a microbenchmark does not replace an end-to-end benchmark.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Uses the ecosystem's reference harness with justification, not a homegrown stopwatch unless impossibility is documented.
- [ ] Warmup and measurement are separate; warmup samples are discarded; JIT/tiering and caches are stabilized.
- [ ] The result is consumed with the idiomatic mechanism against dead-code elimination.
- [ ] Inputs prevent constant-folding (they are not constants the compiler can precompute) and reflect real shape/distribution.
- [ ] The measurement exceeds clock resolution; setup/allocation does not contaminate the measured work.
- [ ] CPU governor, turbo, GC, I/O, affinity, ASLR, multiple forks are controlled or documented.
- [ ] The report includes median, percentiles, dispersion or confidence interval, and number of samples, not just the average.
- [ ] There is an explicit rule to decide whether a difference is real or noise, useful for a CI gate.
- [ ] The limit is stated: the microbenchmark does not replace end-to-end measurement in production.
- [ ] Assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented performance figures.
Expected deliverable: benchmark code commented defense by defense + parameter table (warmup, iterations, forks) justified + list of controlled and residual noise sources + output reading guide + signal-vs-noise decision rule.
spec-desarrollo_optimizacion_concurrenci:
[inputs]
- LENGUAJE_RUNTIME: {{LENGUAJE_RUNTIME}} > Language, version, and runtime (e.g. Java 21 + virtual threads, Go 1.22, Rust + Tokio, C++20 + std::execution, Python 3.13 free-threaded)
- HOT_PATH: {{HOT_PATH}} > Fragment or description of the section that distributes work and does not scale (include data size and loop/fan-out shape)
