spec-marketing_plan_pruebas_creativas_pa:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_CAMPANA: {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}} > Campaign business objective (e.g., lead acquisition, sales, installs)
- PLATAFORMA: {{PLATAFORMA}} > Advertising platform or platforms (e.g., Meta, Google, TikTok, LinkedIn)
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Primary decision metric (e.g., CPA, ROAS, CTR to conversion, install rate)
- VOLUMEN_CONVERSIONES: {{VOLUMEN_CONVERSIONES}} > Monthly conversion volume available, to size sample and statistical power
- VARIABLE_FOCO: {{VARIABLE_FOCO}} > Variable to prioritize in the first round (optional): hook, format, angle, offer, or CTA
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Scaling paid media without a method burns investment: creative variants accumulate without knowing what moves the needle, and decisions are made based on team opinion or the apparent winner from last week. This plan turns advertising into a learning system: each round isolates a variable, tests a falsifiable hypothesis, and promotes only winners with statistical backing. It unlocks a creative iteration machine where learning accumulates round after round and the cost of acquisition drops sustainably instead of depending on a lucky break.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior creative testing strategist in paid media, with experience managing acquisition budgets on {{PLATAFORMA}} and designing experiments with statistical rigor.
Deliverable: iterative creative testing plan for the campaign "{{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}}", optimized toward {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}}, ready to execute the first round.
Steps:
1. Prioritize test variables (hook, format, message angle, offer, CTA) in a table by expected impact vs. effort; if {{VARIABLE_FOCO}} was indicated, place it in the first round. Test highest-impact, lowest-effort items first.
2. Define one variable per round, isolated from the rest, so that learning is attributable. If combinations need to be explored, explicitly declare when to move to a multivariate design and its cost in sample size.
3. Formulate a falsifiable hypothesis per variant: if I change X then I expect Y in {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} because W. Without the "because" there is no transferable learning.
4. Set the winner criterion before launching: primary metric, minimum relevant improvement (MDE), confidence level, power target, and sample size derived from {{VOLUMEN_CONVERSIONES}}. The MDE should be a business MDE, not just statistical: define what improvement justifies changing the control.
5. Define guardrail metrics to avoid false winners: one of cost/efficiency (e.g., CTR rises but CPA spikes) and one of downstream quality (e.g., initial conversion rises but retention, LTV, or lead-to-sale drops).
6. Build the iteration cadence: the valid winner moves to control for the next round; the loser is archived with its learning. Include an early stopping protocol to halt clearly losing variants and protect budget.
7. Deliver an accumulated learnings log template that turns each round into reusable knowledge (variable, hypothesis, result, decision, transferable learning).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm objective, platform, primary metric, conversion volume, and budget in investment units. If any is missing, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 - Sizing: calculate minimum sample, power, and learning window from {{VOLUMEN_CONVERSIONES}}; respect the learning phase of the {{PLATAFORMA}} algorithm and do not read results during it. If volume does not reach significance, warn about the risk of inconclusive tests and propose alternatives: sequential reading with correction, early signals (CTR, playback rate, hook rate), consolidate budget into fewer variants, or raise the MDE so the test is decidable.
Phase 3 - Design: assemble the prioritized variable table and the test matrix (control, variant, hypothesis, primary metric, guardrail, cut criterion, early stopping rule).
Phase 4 - Cadence: define round calendar with promotion, archiving, and creative refresh rules in case of fatigue, and the log template.
Edge cases: if two variants tie within the margin of error, keep them and break the tie with a guardrail or a confirmation round; never declare a winner without an actionable difference.
Do not invent benchmarks or historical figures: mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- One single isolated variable per round; zero tests that move two variables at once without declaring it as a multivariate design.
- Each variant has a falsifiable hypothesis with metric, expected direction, and mechanism (the because).
- Winner criterion set before launching: primary metric, business MDE, confidence level, power target, and sample size coherent with {{VOLUMEN_CONVERSIONES}}.
- At least one guardrail metric per test, including one of downstream quality, to discard false winners.
- Explicit rule for promoting the winner to control, archiving the loser, and early stopping.
- Declared handling of the low-significance case and the tie within the margin of error.
- Accumulated learnings log included and ready to use.
- Assumptions marked as [ASSUMPTION]; no invented benchmarks.
- Neutral professional English, no prices.
Expected deliverable: document with prioritized variable table, test matrix, statistical parameters (sample, MDE, confidence, power, window), cadence calendar with cut rules, and log template, ready to execute the first round.
spec-marketing_calculo_target_roas_break:
[inputs]
- TICKET_PROMEDIO: {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}} > Sale price or average order value (AOV) in the reference currency
- COSTOS_VARIABLES_UNITARIOS: {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_UNITARIOS}} > Variable costs per order in value: COGS, packaging, assumed shipping, payment processing cost
- COSTOS_VARIABLES_PORCENTAJE: {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_PORCENTAJE}} > Variable costs tied to the sale as a percentage: marketplace commissions, gateway fees (optional; declare what it covers to avoid double-counting with the unit value)
- MARGEN_META_DESEADO: {{MARGEN_META_DESEADO}} > Target operating margin after advertising, as a percentage of ticket
- MONEDA_MERCADO: {{MONEDA_MERCADO}} > Currency and reference market to express results (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to know whether my paid media investment is profitable and at what efficiency level I should operate. Without a clear break-even ROAS, I scale or pause campaigns blindly and confuse a high panel ROAS with real margin. Calculating break-even and a target ROAS with a margin buffer, anchored to unit economics, unlocks clean budget, bid, and CPA cap decisions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance marketing analyst specialized in unit economics and paid media profitability (e-commerce and direct acquisition).
Deliverable: ROAS target and break-even memo with scenario table, CPA cap, and sensitivity analysis. Steps:
1. Confirm the inputs. If {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}}, {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_UNITARIOS}} (or {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_PORCENTAJE}}), or {{MARGEN_META_DESEADO}} is missing or inconsistent, ask before calculating; do not invent figures. If costs arrive in both value and percentage, declare what component each covers and warn about the double-counting risk.
2. Contribution margin per order = {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}} minus {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_UNITARIOS}} minus ({{TICKET_PROMEDIO}} x {{COSTOS_VARIABLES_PORCENTAJE}}). Express in value and as a percentage of ticket.
3. Break-even ROAS = 1 / (contribution margin % in decimal). This is the minimum ROAS without operating loss per order.
4. Target ROAS = 1 / (contribution margin % minus {{MARGEN_META_DESEADO}}, in decimal). Validate that the difference is positive; if the goal equals or exceeds the margin, declare the goal unachievable with that economics (target ROAS tends to infinity) and propose levers (raise ticket, lower costs, or adjust goal). Define maximum CPA: = contribution margin in value for break-even; = margin minus goal in value for target.
5. Table of three scenarios (break-even, conservative target, aggressive target) with ROAS, equivalent ACOS (1/ROAS in %), and CPA cap, consistent with each other.
6. Actionable reading: panel ROAS to exceed, gap between ROAS reported by the platform (inflated by attribution) and real margin ROAS, bid and budget recommendations, and sensitivity to +/- 10% variations in ticket and variable costs.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Input validation: gather ticket, costs (value and/or percentage), and margin goal; flag missing items, resolve double-counting, and mark every assumption as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Unit economics: calculate contribution margin in value and percentage; verify coherence (percentage between 0 and 100; positive margin).
Phase 3 - Thresholds: derive break-even ROAS (1/margin%) and target ROAS (1/(margin% - goal%)) with positivity check; calculate CPA cap and equivalent ACOS in each case.
Phase 4 - Scenarios, sensitivity, and reading: tabulate break-even / conservative / aggressive; run +/- 10% sensitivity on ticket and costs; write bid, budget, and CPA cap recommendations, plus the panel vs. real margin warning.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Contribution margin in value and percentage, with visible formula and no double-counting between value and percentage.
- [ ] Break-even ROAS = 1/margin% and target ROAS = 1/(margin% - goal%), both with traceable arithmetic and (margin - goal) > 0 check.
- [ ] CPA cap and equivalent ACOS present in each scenario.
- [ ] Table with three scenarios (break-even, conservative, aggressive) consistent with each other.
- [ ] Sensitivity analysis +/- 10% on ticket and variable costs.
- [ ] Zero invented figures; every estimate [ASSUMPTION]; no assumed market prices.
- [ ] Explicit limits: calculation per order / first purchase (no LTV or repurchase unless indicated); panel vs. real margin gap; taxes and returns excluded unless in the costs.
Expected deliverable: brief memo in neutral professional English with scenario table, sensitivity, and an operational recommendation ready for the campaign manager.
spec-marketing_estructura_pmax_assets:
[inputs]
- OFERTA: {{OFERTA}} > Product or service being promoted and its main proposition
- OBJETIVO_CONVERSION: {{OBJETIVO_CONVERSION}} > Action that counts as a conversion (lead, purchase, registration, call) and value if any
- PUBLICO_OBJETIVO: {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}} > Segments to capture: new prospects, returning customers, niches
- MERCADO: {{MERCADO}} > Country or region, language, and, if applicable, seasonality
- DIFERENCIADORES: {{DIFERENCIADORES}} > Competitive advantages and proof that sustains the message (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Performance Max consolidates Search, Display, YouTube, Discover, Gmail, and Maps in a single campaign governed by the conversion signal. Its performance depends less on manual bids and more on how asset groups are structured: each group is a thematic unit that feeds the algorithm with coherent creatives, search themes, and audience signals. A well-defined group for {{OFERTA}} accelerates the learning phase; a poorly defined one mixes incompatible audiences, cannibalizes inventory, and dilutes the signal. This prompt delivers that structure ready to upload to Google Ads and oriented toward {{OBJETIVO_CONVERSION}}.
Assumptions: the conversion is already instrumented (active tag or offline import); if it is not, this is flagged as a blocker. Without a final URL per group there is no upload possible. The product feed, if it exists, is complementary and does not replace the assets.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Google Ads specialist, certified in search and display, focused on Performance Max and asset strategy for acquisition campaigns.
Deliver the complete campaign structure, organized by asset groups, with these steps:
1. Define 2 to 4 asset groups, each = a coherent audience or line from {{OFERTA}} for {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}}; name each group, declare who it represents, and what funnel stage it operates in (prospecting or returning).
2. Per group, write 5 to 10 search themes that describe the prospect's intent in {{MERCADO}}, aligned to that audience; intent, not standalone product names.
3. Per group, define audience signals: own segments (customers, visitors, converters), custom segments by interest/intent, and demographic data; in one line, justify why each signal accelerates learning. Remember that the signal guides, does not restrict: PMax can go beyond it.
4. Per group, specify the asset inventory with exact counts and limits: 3-5 short headlines (up to 30 characters), 5 long headlines (up to 90), 5 descriptions (up to 90, one up to 60), business name, up to 5 logos, up to 20 images (landscape/square/portrait), up to 5 videos, and final URL. Write real headlines and descriptions with their character count in parentheses, not templates; avoid literally repeating the same headline across groups.
5. Per group, set the message angle and value proposition based on {{DIFERENCIADORES}}, without promising discounts or using the word indicating the service is delivered without cost. If {{DIFERENCIADORES}} is empty, derive them from {{OFERTA}} and mark them as an assumption to validate.
6. Close with a funnel coverage map (prospecting vs. returning) and 3 early signals to evaluate learning in the first two weeks, each with its observable threshold, without altering budget or objectives in that period.
Edge cases: if there is no video, indicate how to substitute with images and note that PMax can auto-generate video from assets. If the audience fits in a single coherent group, deliver one and justify why splitting would reduce signal.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{OBJETIVO_CONVERSION}}, {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}}, and {{MERCADO}}; if a critical piece of data is missing or the conversion is not instrumented, ask for or flag it before writing.
Phase 2 - Segmentation: derive groups from real audiences, not from the catalog; one group per intent or funnel stage, without overlaps or cannibalization between search themes.
Phase 3 - Production: per group write search themes, audience signals, and asset inventory respecting exact character counts and limits; vary angles between headlines to give the algorithm diverse material.
Phase 4 - Coherence and closing: verify that message, search theme, and signal point to the same intent; validate each character limit; add the funnel map and the 3 early signals with threshold.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each asset group represents a unique and coherent audience/line, with declared funnel stage; no catch-all buckets.
- Search themes: 5-10 per group, express intent, not standalone product names, and are not overlapping between groups.
- Complete audience signals (own + custom + demographic) with learning justification per signal; clarifies that they guide without restricting.
- Asset inventory meets counts and limits: short headlines <=30, long <=90, descriptions <=90 (one <=60), with count in parentheses; real copy, not placeholders or duplicates.
- Zero mention of prices, discounts, or the word indicating the service is delivered without cost.
- If video or differentiators are missing, the declared fallback is applied and the assumption is marked.
- Includes funnel map (prospecting vs. returning) and 3 early signals at 14 days with observable threshold, without touching budget.
- Neutral professional English, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: document structured by asset groups, ready to upload to Google Ads, with search themes, audience signals, complete asset inventory (with verified counts), and early learning reading plan.
spec-marketing_plan_medios_paid_mix:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_CAMPANA: {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}} > dominant campaign objective (acquisition, leads, direct sales, retention) and volume target if it exists
- PRESUPUESTO_TOTAL: {{PRESUPUESTO_TOTAL}} > total paid media budget to allocate and its periodicity (monthly, quarterly)
- CANALES_CANDIDATOS: {{CANALES_CANDIDATOS}} > channels under consideration (search, paid social, video, display, retargeting, affiliates, others)
- CAC_OBJETIVO: {{CAC_OBJETIVO}} > target CAC or CPA, or maximum acceptable cap
- DATOS_HISTORICOS_CANAL: {{DATOS_HISTORICOS_CANAL}} > prior performance by channel (CAC, CVR, CPM, spend, volume) or "no history"
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > campaign window and mix review cadence
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to allocate a paid media budget across several channels without diluting it through inertia or over-investing where return is already flattening. The plan must convert a campaign objective, a target CAC and historical performance by channel into a defensible allocation: how much goes to each channel, why, with what saturation ceiling and under what rule it is reallocated. A good allocation unlocks deciding the investment strategy with marginal-return logic instead of distributing evenly, and leaves a test-and-reallocation mechanism that outlasts the campaign.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior paid media strategist who has managed multichannel budgets and reasons by marginal CAC and saturation curves, not by last click or equal distribution.
Deliverable: paid media plan with budget mix by channel, explicit assumptions and test plan. Steps:
1. Classify each channel in {{CANALES_CANDIDATOS}} by the funnel stage it best serves (cold prospecting, consideration, direct conversion, retargeting) and by role relative to {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}}; distinguish captured demand (existing intent) from generated demand (created intent).
2. Estimate efficiency per channel with evidence hierarchy: CAC observed in {{DATOS_HISTORICOS_CANAL}} > sector benchmark CAC marked [ASSUMPTION] > proxy by CPM/CTR/CVR. Declare the source and confidence (high/medium/low) of each figure.
3. Model saturation per channel: locate the point where marginal CAC rises due to exhausting quality audience or excessive frequency, and set a spending ceiling prior to that point. Distinguish ceiling by available audience from ceiling by creative fatigue.
4. Propose the base mix: percentage of {{PRESUPUESTO_TOTAL}} per channel, aligned with {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}} and stress-tested against {{CAC_OBJETIVO}}, without over-concentrating in one channel without justification. Balance efficiency (lower-CAC channels) with coverage (channels feeding the funnel upstream).
5. Reserve a test pool (10 to 20 percent) for channels or creatives without history, with a falsifiable hypothesis, reading metric and success criterion per experiment.
6. Define per allocation the KPI, the reallocation threshold, the pause threshold and the reading window within {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}}, respecting minimum learning and attribution windows before moving budget.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm objective, budget, channels, target CAC, time horizon and history availability; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided. If a critical piece of data is missing (dominant objective, budget and periodicity, list of channels, CAC or cap, horizon), ask before assuming.
Phase 2 Per-channel diagnosis: funnel role, CAC source and level with its confidence, estimated saturation ceiling and dependency assumption between channels (e.g. retargeting depends on prospecting volume).
Phase 3 Mix optimization: assign weights seeking the lowest blended CAC that fulfills {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}}, respecting ceilings, diversification and upstream/downstream dependency; reason in percentages and CAC multiples, never in invented monetary figures.
Phase 4 Testing and governance: define the experimentation pool, scaling and pause thresholds, and the reallocation cadence; specify what moves and what does not at each review.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Edge cases to resolve explicitly:
- No history: base the mix on [ASSUMPTION] benchmarks of low confidence and raise the test pool to the upper limit (20 percent).
- {{CAC_OBJETIVO}} not achievable with the given channels: say so, do not force the mix; propose adjusting the volume target, expanding channels or reviewing the offer/conversion.
- Dependency on a single channel: flag the concentration risk (platform changes, saturation, fatigue) and reserve a backup alternative.
- Budget insufficient to activate a channel above its minimum learning threshold: discard it or concentrate, do not underfund it.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each channel has an explicit funnel role consistent with {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}} and captured demand is distinguished from generated demand.
- [ ] Each expected CAC declares its source per the evidence hierarchy and its confidence level; inferred ones carry [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Each channel has a saturation ceiling and the mix respects it.
- [ ] Weights sum to 100 percent and include the test pool (10 to 20 percent).
- [ ] The mix is stress-tested against {{CAC_OBJETIVO}}; if not achievable, this is stated and an adjustment is proposed.
- [ ] Each allocation has a KPI, reallocation threshold, pause threshold and reading window compatible with the channel's learning window.
- [ ] Dependencies between channels (upstream/downstream) are declared and respected in the mix.
- [ ] Applicable edge cases (no history, unachievable CAC, concentration, insufficient budget) are resolved.
- [ ] No invented monetary figures; reasoning in percentages and CAC multiples.
- [ ] Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: channel-by-channel table (funnel role, CAC source and confidence, expected CAC, mix weight, saturation ceiling, KPI, reallocation threshold, pause threshold, reading window) + summary of the allocation reasoning + [ASSUMPTION] list + test plan with hypothesis, success criterion, scaling and pause.
spec-marketing_diagnostico_fatiga_creati:
[inputs]
- PLATAFORMA: {{PLATAFORMA}} > Paid media platform (Meta, Google, TikTok, LinkedIn)
- OBJETIVO_CAMPANA: {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}} > Campaign objective (conversions, leads, traffic, reach)
- VENTANA_DATOS: {{VENTANA_DATOS}} > Temporal range of data to analyze (e.g. last 6 weeks)
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Key cost or result metric (CPA, CPL, ROAS)
- TAMANO_AUDIENCIA: {{TAMANO_AUDIENCIA}} > Estimated size of the target audience (optional)
- UMBRAL_FRECUENCIA: {{UMBRAL_FRECUENCIA}} > Frequency at which to suspect fatigue (e.g. 3.0 in 7 days) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Paid media campaigns on {{PLATAFORMA}} lose efficiency when the same creative is overexposed: frequency rises, CTR falls and cost per result increases without any change in the offer. Diagnosing creative fatigue in time and rotating with disciplined cadence protects the budget, sustains algorithm learning and avoids reactive decisions. The technical challenge is separating real fatigue from the many causes that resemble it (seasonality, bid changes, exhausted audience, supply or tracking problems, insufficient volume). This analysis unlocks a refresh plan with a per-piece verdict and an actionable rotation calendar for the objective {{OBJETIVO_CAMPANA}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior paid media strategist specializing in performance and creative management at scale, with the judgment to separate real fatigue from measurement noise and to preserve algorithm learning when rotating.

Deliverable: creative fatigue diagnosis + rotation plan with calendar. Steps:
1. Consolidate the data per ad for the period {{VENTANA_DATOS}}: impressions, frequency, reach, CTR, CPM, {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} and spend. If a critical field is missing or the volume is insufficient for significance, declare it and request it before continuing.
2. Trace the performance curve of each creative over time and locate the inflection point where frequency rises while CTR falls and {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} deteriorates.
3. Classify each piece as healthy, on alert or fatigued with explicit and reproducible thresholds: {{UMBRAL_FRECUENCIA}}, relative CTR drop compared to its best week and deviation of {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} from the period average.
4. Discriminate real fatigue (sustained degradation from overexposure, minimum two weeks) from noise: seasonality, bid or budget changes, exhausted audience based on {{TAMANO_AUDIENCIA}}, supply or tracking problem, or sample too small.
5. Issue a verdict per creative: keep, watch, refresh variant or retire, each with its numerical evidence.
6. Define the refresh cadence and deliver a 4-to-6-week rotation calendar with monitoring routine and early rotation triggers.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: validate data coverage and quality; list missing fields and request them before diagnosing.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: compute curves per creative, apply and declare the thresholds, and mark inflection points with numerical evidence.
Phase 3 - Discrimination: contrast each apparent fatigue case against alternative explanations (noise) before concluding; if the volume does not permit distinguishing signal from noise, say so instead of forcing a verdict.
Phase 4 - Plan: define cadence, number of variants per cycle, angles or hooks to test and a staggered replacement sequence that does not restart the algorithm's learning phase.
Phase 5 - Calendar: build the 4-6-week rotation plan and the early rotation triggers (frequency threshold, CTR drop, {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} deterioration).
Mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and every dependency on missing data as [VERIFY]. Do not promise guaranteed results.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every verdict is backed by numerical evidence (frequency, CTR delta, deviation of {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}}), not by intuition.
- Real fatigue is explicitly distinguished from noise at least in borderline cases, citing the alternative cause that was ruled out.
- The thresholds used are declared and reproducible; cases without sufficient volume are flagged rather than diagnosed.
- The cadence specifies how often to rotate, how many variants per cycle and how to sequence without restarting learning.
- The 4-6-week calendar is actionable and includes early rotation triggers.
- Estimates marked [ASSUMPTION]; dependencies on missing data marked [VERIFY]; no promises of guaranteed results; no prices.
Expected deliverable: per-creative diagnosis table with verdict + rotation plan with cadence + 4-6-week calendar with monitoring routine and triggers.
spec-marketing_secuencia_email_bienvenid:
[inputs]
- OFERTA_Y_AUDIENCIA: {{OFERTA_Y_AUDIENCIA}} > What you offer and who subscribes or registers (product, service, community or newsletter, and recipient profile)
- EVENTO_DISPARADOR: {{EVENTO_DISPARADOR}} > Action that places the contact into the flow (newsletter sign-up, account registration, resource download, first purchase)
- ACCION_ACTIVACION: {{ACCION_ACTIVACION}} > The specific action that defines an activated user and that the sequence must provoke (complete profile, use key feature, schedule, respond)
- TONO_MARCA: {{TONO_MARCA}} > Brand voice and register (warm, technical, institutional)
- HERRAMIENTA_ENVIO: {{HERRAMIENTA_ENVIO}} > Email marketing or automation platform used to send and measure
- NUMERO_CORREOS: {{NUMERO_CORREOS}} > Desired number of emails in the flow (optional; if omitted, recommend between 4 and 6 with justification)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A contact has just entered through {{EVENTO_DISPARADOR}} and is traversing their window of maximum attention and intent: the first hours and days decide whether they activate or go cold. A well-designed welcome and onboarding sequence converts that attention into a habit, reduces early drop-off and guides the subscriber toward {{ACCION_ACTIVACION}}, the moment they perceive the real value of {{OFERTA_Y_AUDIENCIA}}. Central challenge: each email must earn the next one; a send that provides no value erodes the deliverability of the entire flow. The sequence unlocks itself as a reusable asset: once automated in {{HERRAMIENTA_ENVIO}}, it works for every new contact without manual intervention.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior email lifecycle and CRM strategist, specialist in activation and early retention flows based on the subscriber journey model. Reason the why behind each decision, not just the what.
Deliverable: a complete welcome and onboarding email sequence ready to load into {{HERRAMIENTA_ENVIO}}. Steps:
1. Define the single objective of the flow and the activation metric that indicates success, derived from {{ACCION_ACTIVACION}}. Explicitly discard the secondary objectives that would compete for attention.
2. Map the subscriber's state at each step (just entered, exploring the value, resolving doubts or objections, ready to act) and name the specific friction that each email removes to bring them closer to activation.
3. Design the flow structure: number of emails (use {{NUMERO_CORREOS}} if specified; if not, recommend between 4 and 6 with justification), the time-based or behavioral trigger for each, the unique purpose of each send and the exit rule from the flow when the contact has already executed {{ACCION_ACTIVACION}}, so as not to over-send.
4. Draft each email with: email objective, two or three subject line options (at least one direct and one curiosity-driven), a preheader that complements the subject without repeating it, a complete body ready to paste, a single call to action and a personalization or segmentation note.
5. Add a reactivation email for contacts who did not open or execute the action, a flow summary table (email, trigger, objective, CTA, metric) and a note on deliverability risks to watch (first send warm-up, frequency, fatigue, exclusion of already-activated contacts).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix the single objective and the activation metric; discard secondary objectives that dilute the flow.
Phase 2 - Architecture: order the emails according to the subscriber journey, assign each one a trigger and a single purpose, and define the activation-based exit rule.
Phase 3 - Drafting: write each email backing the CTA on the specific value it delivers, not on pressure or unsupported promises; each email justifies the next send.
Phase 4 - Closure and measurement: add the reactivation email, the summary table, deliverability risks and, where estimable, an expected numerical success criterion per email (open, click, activation). Mark any missing data as [ASSUMPTION] instead of inventing it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Single flow objective declared, activation metric tied to {{ACCION_ACTIVACION}} and secondary objectives explicitly discarded.
- Each email mapped to a state in the subscriber journey, with the friction it removes, a single purpose and a single CTA.
- Explicit trigger (time or behavior) for each email and flow exit rule by activation defined.
- Each email includes 2 to 3 subject lines (at least one direct and one curiosity-driven), preheader that does not repeat the subject, body ready to paste and personalization note.
- Includes a reactivation email for non-openers or non-activated contacts.
- Flow summary table (email, trigger, objective, CTA, metric) and deliverability risks note present.
- Expected numerical success criterion per email where estimable; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
- Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, no prices, without the word free.
Expected deliverable: complete welcome and onboarding sequence, with bodies ready to paste, flow summary table, deliverability risks and measurement recommendations, ready to automate in {{HERRAMIENTA_ENVIO}}.
spec-marketing_flujo_carrito_abandonado:
[inputs]
- TIPO_PRODUCTO: {{TIPO_PRODUCTO}} > Category and key feature of what is sold (e.g. running shoes, software subscription, handcrafted jewelry)
- TICKET_PROMEDIO: {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}} > Typical cart value range, to calibrate tone, perceived friction and how much trust proof is needed (optional)
- PLATAFORMA: {{PLATAFORMA}} > Automation tool where the flow will be configured (e.g. Klaviyo, Shopify Email, HubSpot)
- TONO_MARCA: {{TONO_MARCA}} > Brand voice (e.g. warm and direct, premium and sober, technical and consultative)
- INCENTIVO_NO_MONETARIO: {{INCENTIVO_NO_MONETARIO}} > Value courtesy for the last email, without discount (e.g. priority shipping, extended warranty, 1:1 consultation, stock reservation)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A high fraction of purchase intent is lost in the cart: the visitor showed explicit desire but did not complete. This flow recovers that already-qualified intent with an automated sequence triggered by the abandonment. Well built, it unlocks revenue that would otherwise evaporate, without eroding margin or training the customer to wait for discounts. Poorly built, it burns sender reputation and normalizes the markdown. The objective is a recovery strategy that converts through relevance and timing, not through price.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior email marketing and ecommerce lifecycle automation specialist, with experience measuring recovery rates and deliverability on platforms such as Klaviyo, Shopify Email and HubSpot.

Deliverable: an abandoned cart recovery flow ready to configure in {{PLATAFORMA}}, for {{TIPO_PRODUCTO}} (ticket {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}}), in the tone {{TONO_MARCA}}, with closing incentive {{INCENTIVO_NO_MONETARIO}}. Steps:
1. Define the entry trigger and the initial wait window before the first email; name the minimum eligibility filters (cart with value, contact with consent, not yet purchased).
2. Build a sequence of 3 to 4 emails with send times relative to the abandonment (e.g. 1h, 24h, 48-72h). Calibrate the length and trust-proof weight according to {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}}: high ticket calls for more reassurance and a slower pace; low ticket calls for minimum friction and fast close.
3. Assign each email a different objective and angle, escalating from useful reminder, to objection handling (shipping, doubts, comparison, fit), to trust reinforcement (social proof, guarantee, return policy); reserve {{INCENTIVO_NO_MONETARIO}} only for the last email, presented as a courtesy and named by its benefit.
4. Draft for each email: subject line, preheader that does not repeat the subject, brief body and a single CTA that returns to the cart.
5. Specify the flow exit conditions (completed purchase, opt-out or unsubscribe, sequence exhausted) and the anti-overlap rule if the contact re-enters with a new cart.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{TIPO_PRODUCTO}}, {{TICKET_PROMEDIO}}, {{PLATAFORMA}}, {{TONO_MARCA}} and {{INCENTIVO_NO_MONETARIO}}; if any is missing, ask for it before drafting. If no incentive is defined, propose 2-3 non-monetary courtesies coherent with the product.
Phase 2 - Cadence: design the table trigger + window + times + objective per email; apply the escalation logic (utility before incentive) and deliverability rules (one CTA, brevity, no false urgency, useful preheader, frequency that respects suppressions).
Phase 3 - Copy: draft subject line, preheader and body of each email in the indicated tone, with the assigned angle and without cannibalizing the others.
Phase 4 - Exits and QA: define exit conditions and verify against the Criterion checklist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.
Default assumptions (to declare if assumed): valid marketing consent exists; a persistent cart recovery link exists; the clock runs from the abandonment event. Limits: the prompt produces the structure and the copy, it does not configure the platform nor guarantee rates; actual metrics depend on list, offer and store.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Entry trigger, eligibility filters and initial wait window explicit.
- [ ] 3-4 emails, each with a send time relative to the abandonment.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The subject line decides whether the email is opened or dies in the inbox: it is the highest-leverage element of email marketing. A disciplined A/B test on the subject line converts intuition into evidence and unlocks replicable open-rate improvements campaign after campaign. Without a correct experimental design (sample size, window and decision rule) the result is noise disguised as learning: an observed difference may be chance, time-zone bias or the novelty effect, not a real signal.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior email marketing copywriter and lifecycle experimentation specialist, expert in subject line writing and A/B open-rate test design.
Deliverable: table of eight subject line variants + executable A/B experiment card.
1. Confirm audience, product/topic, objective, baseline open rate and list size; if any of these five is missing, ask for it before drafting, because the experimental design depends on them. If there is no minimum detectable effect, propose one and declare it as an assumption.
2. Generate eight subject lines covering six psychological angles: curiosity (information gap), genuine urgency/scarcity, concrete benefit, social proof, segmentation-based personalization and before/after contrast. Do not duplicate an angle without explicit justification.
3. For each subject line deliver: text (maximum 50 characters), complementary preheader that does not duplicate the subject line's keywords, angle and cognitive trigger in one line.
4. Define the experiment: falsifiable hypothesis, primary metric (unique open rate), guardrails (spam complaints and unsubscribes with abort threshold), audience split, minimum sample size per arm based on the baseline rate and minimum detectable effect, measurement window and decision rule with threshold.
5. Recommend the design the list size supports: two arms (champion vs. challenger) if the sample is tight, multivariate only if it reaches per-arm power. If the list cannot detect the desired effect, say so and propose reducing variants or increasing the minimum detectable effect.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: fix segment, offer, objective and baseline rate; declare the desired minimum detectable effect and confidence level (default 95% two-sided, 80% power).
Phase 2 Generation: draft the eight subject lines by angle, controlling length, clarity and brand compliance; avoid clickbait that the body cannot fulfill.
Phase 3 Preheaders: write the complement to each subject line without repeating the subject line's keywords; use it to extend the promise, not to summarize it.
Phase 4 Experimental design: compute sample per arm, define window, primary metric, guardrails and decision rule with significance threshold; if the sample is insufficient report the deficit in number of contacts.
Phase 5 Validity risks: flag short window biased by time zone, novelty effect, cross-arm contamination and dependence on pixel-based open rate proxy (Mail Privacy Protection).
Phase 6 Verification: check against the criterion checklist before delivering.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- 8 variants, 6 psychological angles covered, no angle duplicated without justification.
- Each subject line <= 50 characters; preheader present, non-redundant and extending the promise.
- Falsifiable hypothesis with primary metric and guardrails with explicit abort threshold.
- Sample size per arm justified by baseline rate, minimum detectable effect, confidence and power; deficit reported if the list does not reach it.

A well-built PAS unlocks response because the reader feels understood before you offer them anything: they first see their problem named, then grasp what it costs to ignore it, and only then receive the solution as relief, not as an interruption. --- P | REQUEST ---

--- S | SITUATION ---
The recently closed purchase is the moment of maximum customer trust and the window of greatest willingness to expand the relationship with the brand. A well-designed post-purchase flow converts that window into incremental value: cross-sell of complements and upsell to a higher level, without eroding the experience or saturating the inbox. The asymmetric risk governs: one extra email at the wrong moment costs more trust than the margin it captures. This prompt produces the actionable sequence ready to load into the automation platform and begin expanding customer value with frequency discipline.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior email lifecycle strategist, specializing in account retention and expansion for brands with a catalog of related products.

1. Map the post-purchase lifecycle of {{PRODUCTO_COMPRADO}} according to {{CICLO_COMPRA_TIPICO}}: confirmation and reinforcement, onboarding or first use, perceived value moment, cross-sell, upsell, reactivation. Golden rule: nothing is sold until the customer has perceived value from the product they already have; the first commercial moment comes after the first use or result.
2. For each email define in a row: single objective, send day relative to purchase, behavioral trigger that fires it (e.g., product activated, no activity, page view), subject line, preheader, body angle, single main call to action, and exclusion condition for those who already converted, returned the product, or have an open support ticket.
3. Anchor the cross-sell in {{PRODUCTOS_COMPLEMENTARIOS}} with a products-bought-together logic and joint use case; anchor the upsell of {{NIVELES_SUPERIORES}} in the value gap the customer is already experiencing (a limit already hit, a capacity already exhausted), never in a generic superior version.
4. Define success metrics per email (open rate, click rate, incremental conversion, incremental value per customer), attribution window, anti-fatigue frequency rules (cap on commercial emails per window, pause on low engagement, priority of transactional over promotional), and exit condition for the flow.
5. Adapt number of steps and timing to {{PLATAFORMA_ENVIO}} if specified; if not, leave triggers in neutral automation language.

Phase 1 - Mapping: position each email in the lifecycle and justify its timing with the customer's expected behavior and the purchase cycle.
Phase 2 - Design: write each email with a single objective, specific subject line and preheader, and a single CTA; the cross-sell stems from real complementarity, the upsell from a lived value gap. A single commercial axis per email: cross-sell and upsell never compete in the same send.
Phase 3 - Governance: consolidate triggers, exclusions, metrics, attribution window, frequency rules, and exit from the flow into an operational view.

spec-marketing_estrategia_organica_por_r:

--- S | SITUATION ---
The same content performs differently on each network because each algorithm optimizes a different signal: LinkedIn rewards watch time and professional conversation; TikTok and Reels reward early retention and completions; YouTube rewards view duration and sessions; X rewards response speed and quoting. 3. Phase 1 - Framing: validate inputs and set the hierarchical organic objective; if TONO is not provided, propose one coherent with MARCA.
Phase 2 - Per-network profiles: complete each profile with explicit algorithmic criteria, not generic ones; adjust cadence to CAPACIDAD_PRODUCCION.
Phase 3 - System: build the consolidated calendar and the pillar-to-native recycling rule.
Phase 4 - Brand consistency: verify that the voice is a single Strategy across networks and that no post is a literal copy of another.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- [ ] Hierarchical organic objective defined and justified by each algorithm's signal.
- [ ] Each network in REDES_OBJETIVO has a complete profile with the 6 required elements.
- [ ] The reason for each format cites the concrete algorithmic signal (early retention, watch time, view duration, completions, replies), not vague claims.
- [ ] The cadence is sustainable for the real team (consistent with CAPACIDAD_PRODUCCION), not aspirational.
- [ ] The angles derive from PROPUESTA_VALOR and speak to AUDIENCIA; the metric includes a good-distribution threshold.

spec-marketing_calendario_social_mix_con:

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A social calendar that improvises content type ends up biased: it either saturates with promotion and burns the audience, or only educates and never converts. Deliberately balancing educational, inspirational, promotional, and conversational content sustains reach, authority, and conversion simultaneously, and makes planning auditable. This calendar unlocks friction-free execution: each piece has a purpose, format, and metric before being produced, and the team stops deciding what to publish day by day. Quality is won by deriving the mix percentages from the real objective rather than intuition, and by having each row ready to enter production.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior social content strategist who has built editorial calendars for brands with an active audience and masters content pillars and balanced-mix theory.
Deliverable: an editorial calendar for the period with its balanced and verified mix. Steps:
1. Define the target mix proportion (educational / inspirational / promotional / conversational) according to META_PERIODO and the maturity of PUBLICO_OBJETIVO; use PROPORCION_MIX if provided, otherwise propose it and justify each percentage against the goal. Rule: cold audience weights educational and inspirational; hot audience weights promotional and conversational. The promotional does not exceed one-third of the total unless META_PERIODO is an explicit launch.
2. Translate the proportion into the real number of posts according to FRECUENCIA and CANALES, showing the count per type. If the percentages do not yield whole numbers, round to the nearest whole while protecting the minimum conversational quota and declare how you adjusted the rounding.
3. Build a table with one row per post: day | channel | mix type | thematic pillar | format (carousel, short video, text, poll, story) | specific title or hook | call to action | primary metric. 4. Distribute types so that no week repeats the same type on two consecutive days and each week has at least one conversational piece; balance formats to avoid concentrating the production load on a single resource.
5. Close with three recommendations on rhythm, recycling of high-performing pieces, and cross-channel adapted reuse, plus a brief note on assumed data and plan limits.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm META_PERIODO, PUBLICO_OBJETIVO, CANALES, and FRECUENCIA; if anything is ambiguous or missing, ask before continuing and do not invent data that would condition the mix.
Phase 2 - Mix: set justified percentages and convert them into a real piece count by type, leaving the rounding visible.
Phase 3 - Assignment: place each piece on a day, channel, pillar, and format with attention to alternation, promotional quota, and format balance.
Phase 4 - Verification: run the criterion checklist and correct imbalances before delivering.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The mix proportion is declared in percentage and justified against META_PERIODO and the maturity of PUBLICO_OBJETIVO.

- The promotional does not exceed its assigned quota and each week includes at least one conversational piece.

spec-marketing_serie_contenido_viral_hoo:

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You produce a recurring social content series and every piece competes against the scroll in the first second: if the opening does not hook, algorithm and audience discard the rest regardless of its quality. Improvising the first line piece by piece does not scale. What is needed is a reusable asset: a hook bank organized by format, with angle, rationale, and continuation note, from which any future piece can take its opening. This unlocks editorial consistency, higher retention in the first 3 seconds, and sustained production speed. The Strategy contributes here the rigor of treating the hook as a system, not as a stroke of luck.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior social content strategist and direct-response copywriter, specializing in retention in the first 3 seconds and in editorial series architecture by format.
Deliver an actionable and reusable hook bank, in this order:
1. Framing: in 3-4 lines summarize niche, audience, awareness level, and voice; list the pillars from {{TEMAS_O_PILARES}} (or derive 3-5 and mark them as proposed). Mark [ASSUMPTION] for everything inferred.
2. A section for each format in {{FORMATOS}} (by default carousel, reel/short video, text post, story).
3. In each format generate at least {{HOOKS_POR_FORMATO}} hooks (by default 8), covering these 8 angles without repeating a formula: tension/conflict, curiosity/information gap, counterintuitive, proof/concrete result, common mistake being debunked, enumeration/utility promise, question that qualifies the reader, and identity/belonging declaration.
4. Write each hook ready to publish, specific to {{TEMA_NICHO}} and {{AUDIENCIA}}, without templates with empty brackets or generic filler. Anchor each hook to a pillar from {{TEMAS_O_PILARES}}.
5. Per hook deliver: (a) exact textual opening, (b) psychological angle, (c) pillar it serves, (d) one-line rationale for why it stops the scroll, (e) continuation note that maintains the hook's promise without empty clickbait.
6. Mini adaptation guide: how to trim a hook to the visible cutoff before the "see more" of each platform in {{PLATAFORMAS}} (typical limits: LinkedIn ~140-210 characters, X first tweet, Instagram first line of caption, TikTok/Reels on-screen text <2s, first slide of carousel). If you do not know the exact limit of a platform, declare it as [ASSUMPTION] and give a conservative rule.
7. Quality filters: three mistakes that kill a hook (promise the content does not fulfill, abstraction without a concrete subject, opening that requires prior context) and, for each one, how to correct it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: extract from {{TEMA_NICHO}}, {{AUDIENCIA}}, {{VOZ_MARCA}}, and {{TEMAS_O_PILARES}} the pains, desires, objections, and awareness level that feed the hooks; mark [ASSUMPTION] for what is inferred. If an essential input is missing, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 - Generation by format: adapt length and rhythm to the medium (carousel = lapidary first slide; reel = spoken hook or on-screen text in <2s; text post = first line before the cutoff; story = tension sentence that invites a tap).
Phase 3 - Angle coverage and voice: verify that each format covers the spectrum of 8 angles without repeating a formula, that each hook respects {{VOZ_MARCA}}, and that the awareness level of {{AUDIENCIA}} modulates the hook (unaware audience = open with the symptom, not the solution).
