Expected deliverable: document with (a) PMF score definition, normalization and weighting, (b) instrumentation plan and formula, (c) temporal reading rules plus minimum dashboard, (d) alert-hypothesis-decision loop table, plus three-line executive summary.
spec-producto_disenar_experimento_ab:
[inputs]
- CAMBIO_PROPUESTO: {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} > Change or variant to test against the control: what is modified, where, and for which segment
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Single decision metric (e.g., checkout conversion, D7 retention)
- BASELINE_ACTUAL: {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}} > Current value of the primary metric with unit and, if available, its variability (e.g., 4.2% conversion; standard deviation for mean metrics)
- MDE_OBJETIVO: {{MDE_OBJETIVO}} > Minimum effect that justifies shipping the change, in relative or absolute terms (e.g., +5% relative). If unknown, derive it from the business threshold
- TRAFICO_SEMANAL: {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}} > Volume of the randomization unit per week available for the test (e.g., 20k users/week)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Time window, tolerated risk, segments, seasonality, or instrumentation capacity (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are going to make a product decision about {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} and we want to replace opinion with causal evidence. A well-designed A/B experiment unlocks a defensible decision (ship / no ship / iterate) with bounded statistical risk, without spending excess traffic or declaring false winners from looking at results early. The complete design must be pre-registered and frozen before the test is turned on: changing criteria after seeing data invalidates the inference.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior product experimentation expert (growth + applied data science), fluent in frequentist inference, power calculation, online test design, and validity bias detection.
Deliver a pre-registrable A/B experiment design document containing:
1. Falsifiable hypothesis: "Because we observe [evidence], we believe that {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} will produce [directional effect] on {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}}; we will know when [threshold]". Include the assumed causal mechanism.
2. Primary metric: exact operational definition of {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} (trigger event, randomization unit, attribution window, inclusion criterion); 1-2 guardrail metrics against collateral damage; discard vanity ones.
3. Statistical framework: H0 and H1, appropriate test (z for proportions or t for means), one or two tails with justification, and handling of the analysis unit if it differs from the randomization unit (risk of underestimated variance).
4. Design parameters from {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}} and {{MDE_OBJETIVO}}: absolute and relative MDE, alpha, power, allocation ratio; justify each choice against the cost of false positive vs. false negative.
5. Sample size per arm and estimated duration with {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}}, rounded to complete weekly cycles to absorb within-week seasonality.
6. Validity guardrails: anti-peeking rule (fixed size) or look correction (alpha spending / sequential), SRM check, exclusion criteria, novelty effect handling, and contamination between arms.
7. Pre-registered decision criterion with threshold: ship / no ship / iterate, and expected confidence interval of the effect.
Respect {{RESTRICCIONES}} if provided and flag any tension between desired power and available traffic.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: translate {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} into a falsifiable hypothesis with causal mechanism; fix the single primary metric; separate guardrail metrics; discard vanity ones.
Phase 2 - Statistics: declare H0/H1, choose the test (z of two proportions for rates, t for means), fix alpha (default 0.05) and power (default 0.80) unless {{RESTRICCIONES}} or the asymmetric cost of errors indicate otherwise; justify one vs. two tails.
Phase 3 - Sizing: convert {{MDE_OBJETIVO}} to absolute effect on {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}}, calculate n per arm, translate to duration with {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}} rounding to complete weeks. Show the formula used and variance assumptions. If power and traffic are incompatible within the window, offer the trade-off (more time, larger MDE, or lower power).
Phase 4 - Validity and decision: define anti-peeking or sequential correction, SRM check, exclusions, novelty/contamination, and the decision tree with pre-registered threshold.
If {{BASELINE_ACTUAL}}, {{MDE_OBJETIVO}}, or {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}} are missing, stop and ask; do not invent figures. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Falsifiable hypothesis with evidence, causal mechanism, directional effect, and explicit threshold.
- Single primary metric with randomization unit, window, and inclusion criterion; guardrails present; vanity ones discarded.
- H0/H1, test, tail, and analysis unit consistent with the metric type.
- MDE in absolute and relative terms; alpha, power, and ratio justified against the cost of each error.
- Sample size per arm with formula and visible variance assumptions; duration in complete weeks from {{TRAFICO_SEMANAL}}.
- Complete validity guardrails (anti-peeking/sequential, SRM, exclusions, novelty, contamination).
- Decision criterion with threshold and expected confidence interval.
- Trade-off declared if power and traffic do not fit within the window.
- Zero invented figures; missing items requested; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: pre-registrable A/B experiment design document, actionable and freezable from start to finish.
spec-producto_calcular_tamano_muestra:
[inputs]
- METRICA_OBJETIVO: {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} > Metric the experiment measures (e.g., checkout conversion rate, D7 retention, revenue per user)
- BASELINE: {{BASELINE}} > Current value of the metric before the change (e.g., 4.2 percent, or mean 18.5 with its standard deviation)
- MDE: {{MDE}} > Minimum detectable effect that justifies action, declaring whether it is absolute (+0.5 pp) or relative (+10 percent)
- TRAFICO_DIARIO: {{TRAFICO_DIARIO}} > Eligible users per day allocated to the experiment
- NUM_VARIANTES: {{NUM_VARIANTES}} > Total number of variants including the control (e.g., 2 for A/B)
- PODER_Y_ALFA: {{PODER_Y_ALFA}} > (optional) Statistical power and significance level; defaults 80 percent and 5 percent, two-tailed
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are about to launch an A/B experiment and need to know, before turning it on, how many users and how many days it requires to detect a real effect with rigor. Sizing the test wrong wastes traffic, produces false readings from peeking, or concludes a "no effect" that was actually a lack of power. A correct calculation unlocks a defensible experimentation decision: you know in advance whether the test is viable with your traffic or whether you need to narrow the scope, extend the window, or raise the MDE. The output must support a launch-or-adjust decision, not just yield a number.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product experimentation analyst (growth/data science) with mastery of frequentist inference for A/B tests and experience translating statistics into roadmap decisions.

Deliverable: an experiment sizing that includes (1) sample size per variant and total, (2) duration in days, (3) MDE sensitivity table, and (4) assumptions and risks.

Steps:
1. Classify the metric as a proportion (conversion, retention, CTR) or continuous mean (revenue per user, sessions, time); if it is continuous and the standard deviation is missing, ask for it and stop.
2. Fix the parameters: baseline, MDE (absolute or relative), power (default 80 percent), alpha (default 5 percent), and tails (default two). If the MDE is relative, convert it to absolute explicitly (e.g., +10 percent over 4.2 pp = +0.42 pp).
3. Calculate sample per variant with the correct formula, show the formula and Z constants; multiply by the number of variants for the total and round up.
4. If there are more than two variants, warn about multiple comparisons and adjust alpha with a correction (Bonferroni: alpha / number of comparisons) before recalculating.
5. Convert to duration = total users / daily traffic, rounded up; if less than 7 days, recommend covering at least one complete weekly cycle to absorb day-of-week seasonality.
6. Build the sensitivity table varying the MDE (by half and double) and reporting resulting sample and duration, to evidence the cost of detecting smaller effects.
7. Close with assumptions and risks: multiple comparisons, peeking, randomization unit vs. analysis unit, practical vs. statistical effect, allocation ratio other than 50/50, and SRM (sample ratio mismatch) verification.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: reformulate the metric, its type, and the received parameters; flag missing data and mark as [ASSUMPTION] any value you must assume (never invent baseline or traffic).
Phase 2 - Plan: declare the formula you will use (two proportions or two means), the Z constants for power and alpha, and the calculation sequence, before executing.
Phase 3 - Execute: run the calculation step by step with explicit numbers, derive the duration, build the sensitivity table, and enumerate assumptions and risks. If a critical data point is missing, stop and ask instead of inventing it. Do not report false precision: round samples up and maintain 2-3 significant figures in intermediates.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Metric classified (proportion vs. continuous) and corresponding formula shown explicitly with its Z constants.
- [ ] Baseline, MDE (with its type absolute/relative and explicit conversion if applicable), power, alpha, and tails declared unambiguously.
- [ ] Sample per variant and total rounded up; verifiable step-by-step arithmetic.
- [ ] Multiple comparisons correction applied and declared when there are more than two variants.
- [ ] Duration derived from daily traffic, with the weekly cycle rule applied if applicable.
- [ ] MDE sensitivity table (half and double) present and consistent with the base calculation.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and risks (peeking, multiple comparisons, analysis unit, practical vs. statistical effect, allocation ratio, SRM) listed.
- [ ] No prices and no invented values; missing data requested before calculating.
Expected deliverable: sizing block with sample (per variant and total), duration in days, sensitivity table, and assumptions/risks section, ready to support the decision to launch or adjust the experiment.
spec-producto_disenar_mvp_test:
[inputs]
- IDEA: {{IDEA}} > Description of the idea or product to validate
- CLIENTE_OBJETIVO: {{CLIENTE_OBJETIVO}} > Specific customer segment and their context
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > Problem or need the idea solves
- RECURSOS: {{RECURSOS}} > Time, team, and owned channels available for experimenting
- HORIZONTE_VALIDACION: {{HORIZONTE_VALIDACION}} > Deadline for having actionable evidence (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are facing an idea that has not yet been built, and the greatest risk is not building it badly, but building the right thing on top of a false assumption. The purpose is to design the lowest-effort MVP that attacks the riskiest hypothesis, to decide with behavioral evidence (not opinion) whether the idea deserves resources. This unlocks a continue/iterate/pivot decision before committing the construction budget, and converts an intuition into an auditable experiment. A validation MVP is not a small version of the product: it is the cheapest instrument that generates the most credible signal about the assumption that, if false, sinks the idea.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product strategist specialized in early validation and lean experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish an MVP that learns from a reduced version that only consumes resources.

Deliverable: an actionable validation MVP design. Steps:
1. Map the critical assumptions of {{IDEA}} in three families: desirability (the customer wants this and prioritizes it over their current alternative), viability (the idea is sustainable over time), and feasibility (it can be delivered). Mark each assumption with risk (high/medium/low) and current evidence (none/weak/solid).
2. Select the riskiest hypothesis: maximum impact if false, minimum evidence today. Reframe it as a falsifiable hypothesis: "We believe that [segment] will take [observable action] because [motivation]; we will know when [signal] exceeds [threshold]."
3. Recommend the MVP type that tests that hypothesis with the lowest effort given {{RECURSOS}}: concierge, Wizard of Oz, smoke landing page with waiting list, clickable prototype, demand video, or pre-sale. Justify the choice and discard each alternative with one line.
4. Design the experiment: minimum scope to build, what is NOT built yet, test script with {{CLIENTE_OBJETIVO}}, instrumentation (how the signal is captured without biasing it or contaminating the channel), key behavioral metric, success threshold, minimum sample for the signal to be credible, and run duration within {{HORIZONTE_VALIDACION}}.
5. Define the decision rule: continue, iterate, or pivot/discard based on the result, including what to do with a gray-zone result.
6. Expose the risks of the experiment itself: false positives from novelty effect, sample bias, non-representative channel, or weak proxy signal — with their mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: confirm idea, customer, problem, resources, and horizon. If an essential data point is missing, ask; do not invent context. Every assertion about the market that does not come from the user's context is marked [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Plan: present the assumptions map and name the riskiest hypothesis with its risk/evidence justification before proposing the experiment.
Phase 3 - Execute: deliver chosen MVP type with alternative discards, experiment design with instrumentation, metric, threshold, minimum sample, duration, decision rule, and experiment risks. Express effort in scope and relative time, never in money.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The selected hypothesis is the highest-risk one (high impact if false + weak evidence), not the most comfortable to test.
- The hypothesis is written as a falsifiable statement with observable action, signal, and numeric threshold.
- The MVP type is the lowest-effort one that still tests the hypothesis; alternatives are explicitly discarded.
- The design separates what is built from what is NOT built yet, and explicitly states the signal instrumentation.
- The metric is behavioral (conversion, pre-sale, retention, repeated use), not declarative; threshold, minimum sample, and duration are defined before running the test.
- The decision rule distinguishes continue / iterate / pivot unambiguously and includes a gray zone.
- Experiment risks (false positives, bias, channel) are named with mitigation.
- Market assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero monetary estimates.
Expected deliverable: prioritized assumptions map, falsifiable hypothesis, justified MVP type with discards, experiment with metric-threshold-sample-duration-instrumentation, experiment risks, decision rule, and a one-page summary table.
spec-producto_fake_door_test:
[inputs]
- FUNCIONALIDAD: {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} > Feature or functionality to validate before building
- SEGMENTO: {{SEGMENTO}} > User segment exposed to the fake door (define available base size)
- CANAL_EXPOSICION: {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}} > Where the entry point lives (app, landing, email, menu item)
- TASA_OBJETIVO: {{TASA_OBJETIVO}} > Minimum click rate that justifies building, e.g. 8%
- NIVEL_CONFIANZA: {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}} > Desired statistical confidence level, e.g. 95% (optional, default 95%)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before investing weeks of engineering in {{FUNCIONALIDAD}}, we need to know whether {{SEGMENTO}} truly demands it. A fake door test exposes the entry point in {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}} as if the feature already existed and, on click, captures the intent and shows an honest in-progress message. Designing the door well unlocks a binary build/discard decision based on observed behavior, not opinions, and avoids the cost of building blindly. The risk of a bad design is twofold: a deceptive door erodes trust, and a poorly instrumented one produces a number that decides nothing.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product experimentation and demand discovery expert, with mastery of smoke tests, sample sizing, and research ethics.
Deliver the complete fake door test design, in these steps:
1. Falsifiable hypothesis: "if we expose {{FUNCIONALIDAD}} to {{SEGMENTO}}, we expect a click rate of at least {{TASA_OBJETIVO}}", with primary metric (CTR on the door = unique clicks / unique impressions) and guardrails (bounce, complaints, unsubscriptions, NPS or sentiment of those exposed).
2. Experimental design: define the exposure condition and, if the channel allows it, a control (without door) to isolate the novelty effect. Specify the criterion that distinguishes genuine interest from accidental click or mere curiosity (e.g., double confirmation, time on post-click screen, leaving email).
3. Exact exposure point in {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}}, trigger copy, and honest post-click capture screen copy with no inducement to deception. Include an optional one-question micro-survey to capture the reason for interest.
4. Sample sizing and duration to conclude at {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}}, covering at least one usage cycle of the segment; explicitly state the proportions formula, assumed baseline rate, and minimum detectable effect.
5. Binary decision threshold around {{TASA_OBJETIVO}}: above, build or advance; below, discard or iterate the value proposition. Define how to read a gray zone (confidence interval crossing the threshold) and what to do in that case.
6. Instrumentation plan: triggered event, recorded attributes, per-user deduplication, bot and non-human traffic handling.
7. Communication script for those who left their email, closing the loop with dignity, without creating empty waiting lists or commitments that will not be honored.
8. Ethical and reputational risks of the fake door and their mitigation: exposure limit per user, plan if the test goes viral or leaks, and early-stop criterion if guardrails are triggered.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm {{FUNCIONALIDAD}}, {{SEGMENTO}}, {{CANAL_EXPOSICION}}, {{TASA_OBJETIVO}}, and {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}}; estimate the available base size of the segment. If a critical data point is missing (especially if the base is insufficient to reach the sample), ask before proceeding.
Phase 2 Hypothesis and metrics: finalize the falsifiable hypothesis with primary metric and guardrails; mark any estimate as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 3 Door design: define control vs. exposure and the anti-accidental-click criterion; draft honest triggers and post-click screen; verify that no piece promises immediate availability or charges for what does not exist.
Phase 4 Calculation: size sample and duration with the proportions method; explicitly state the formula, baseline rate, and minimum detectable effect. If the segment base does not reach the required sample, say so and propose adjusting the target rate, confidence, or window.
Phase 5 Decision and instrumentation: fix the binary threshold and gray-zone rule, the event and attributes to record, deduplication and bot filtering, and the closing script for users.
Phase 6 Ethics: list risks, mitigations, exposure limit, and early-stop criterion before closing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Falsifiable hypothesis with explicit target rate and defined guardrails (includes qualitative signal from those exposed).
- Primary metric is CTR on the door (unique clicks / unique impressions), not an ambiguous proxy.
- Design distinguishes genuine interest from accidental click or curiosity, with explicit criterion.
- Trigger copy and post-click capture copy are honest: no promise of immediate availability or charge for what does not exist.
- Sample and duration calculated with formula, baseline rate, and visible minimum detectable effect ([ASSUMPTION] where applicable); it is validated that the segment base reaches the required sample.
- Binary decision threshold is actionable, with explicit gray-zone rule (build / iterate / discard).
- Instrumentation plan with event, attributes, per-user deduplication, and bot handling.
- Communication script closes the loop with dignity, without empty waiting lists.
- Ethical and reputational risks listed with mitigation, per-user exposure limit, and early-stop criterion.
Expected deliverable: executable fake door test plan with hypothesis, experimental design, copy, sizing, decision threshold, instrumentation, closing script, and risks section.

Before launching a controlled experiment, the team needs to agree on a single success metric (OEC, Overall Evaluation Criterion) that decides whether the variant wins or loses. The recurring risk is optimizing a short-term proxy that is easy to inflate (clicks, sessions) that improves in the test but degrades long-term value, or confusing statistical significance with practical relevance. Properly defining the OEC enables defensible launch decisions, avoids false positives from gameable metrics, and aligns the experiment with the north star: {{META_LARGO_PLAZO}}. This card feeds the launch review and the learning log of the experimentation program.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product experimentation leader with a track record designing OEC and guardrails for A/B testing programs at scale.

1. Validate inputs; if {{HIPOTESIS_Y_CAMBIO}}, {{POBLACION_SUPERFICIE}}, {{META_LARGO_PLAZO}}, {{METRICAS_ACTUALES}}, or {{DURACION_Y_UNIDAD}} are missing or ambiguous, ask for them in a single batch before continuing; do not invent context.

spec-producto_evitar_peeking_test:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_EXPERIMENTO: {{NOMBRE_EXPERIMENTO}} > Name or hypothesis of the A/B test to shield
- METRICA_PRIMARIA: {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} > Single decision metric (e.g., checkout conversion rate)
- TASA_BASE: {{TASA_BASE}} > Current value of the metric in the control (baseline)
- MDE: {{MDE}} > Minimum detectable effect that justifies adopting the variant (absolute or relative)
- ALPHA: {{ALPHA}} > Target significance level and power (optional, default alpha 0.05 / power 0.80)
- NUMERO_LOOKS: {{NUMERO_LOOKS}} > Planned interim reviews and daily traffic per variant (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A product team runs an A/B experiment and, upon seeing the dashboard mid-run, stops the test as soon as a significant result appears. That practice (peeking + early stopping) inflates the false-positive rate far above the nominal alpha: each additional look is an extra opportunity to cross the threshold by chance. The purpose is to set valid stopping rules in advance that protect the decision, allow — if desired — looking at results without penalizing inference, and leave a defensible decision for stakeholders. This unlocks: launching variants with real statistical confidence, avoiding reverting features adopted on noise, and an auditable experimentation culture.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior growth and experimentation data scientist, proficient in classical frequentist inference (power, sample size) and in sequential methods (alpha spending, group sequential, always-valid inference with e-values).
Deliverable: a documented stopping protocol for {{NOMBRE_EXPERIMENTO}}. Steps:
1. Restate in one line the hypothesis on {{METRICA_PRIMARIA}} and name the concrete peeking risk in this case.
2. Decide the stopping regime and justify it: (a) fixed sample with a single analysis at the end, or (b) sequential design with planned interim reviews. Spell out the trade-off (speed of decision vs. error control).
3. If fixed sample: calculate the sample size per variant from {{TASA_BASE}}, {{MDE}}, and {{ALPHA}} (significance and power), translate it into duration according to the traffic in {{NUMERO_LOOKS}}, and set ONE read date.
4. If there will be interim reviews: choose the method that controls the accumulated Type I error (O'Brien-Fleming or Pocock via alpha spending, or sequential testing with e-values/always-valid p-values), declare the number of looks, and deliver the table of look-corrected thresholds.
5. Define the decision rule per look (stop for efficacy / stop for futility / continue) and draft a one-page governance script that prohibits stopping the test without crossing the pre-registered threshold.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm single primary metric, hypothesis direction, and randomization unit; identify whether the metric is binary (proportion) or continuous (mean), because it changes the sample formula. Detect unstabilized variance or strong skew: if applicable, propose transformation or variance reduction (CUPED) before sizing.
Phase 2 - Regime: recommend fixed sample when the horizon is short and the discipline of not looking is viable; recommend sequential when the business will demand looking or cutting early. Document the reason and the cost in sample size that each additional look pays.
Phase 3 - Calculation: for proportions use the two-sample formula with {{ALPHA}} and power; for means, the version with standard deviation and effect size; convert to days with traffic. For sequential, distribute alpha across looks (O'Brien-Fleming conservative at the start; Pocock spends evenly; e-values allow unlimited and optional looks). If there is more than one variant, correct for multiple comparisons.
Phase 4 - Rules and governance: tabulate threshold per look, set futility criterion, declare guardrail metrics that trigger stopping for harm even when the primary does not cross, and write the pre-registration (what is decided, when, with what threshold, who approves) so that looking at the dashboard does not authorize stopping the test.
Edge cases: novelty/primacy effects that distort early looks (do not conclude before a full weekly cycle); contamination between variants; population mixing (Simpson's paradox) when segmenting post-hoc.
For every missing value (metric, MDE, baseline rate, alpha, power, looks, traffic): ask before calculating. Any assumed value is flagged [ASSUMPTION] and isolated so the user can correct it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Single primary metric declared; additional metrics treated as guardrail or with explicit correction.
- [ ] Nature of the metric (proportion vs. mean) identified; sample formula consistent with it.
- [ ] Stopping regime (fixed vs. sequential) chosen WITH justification of the trade-off and the cost of each look.
- [ ] If fixed: sample size per variant calculated and translated to a single read date, with visible inputs.
- [ ] If sequential: method named (O'Brien-Fleming / Pocock / e-values), number of looks, and table of look-corrected thresholds.
- [ ] Explicit decision rule per look: efficacy, futility, or continue.
- [ ] Guardrail metrics and minimum weekly cycle declared to neutralize harm and novelty/primacy effects.
- [ ] One-page governance script that prohibits stopping without crossing the pre-registered threshold (what, when, threshold, who approves).
- [ ] Every assumption flagged [ASSUMPTION]; no missing data invented.
Expected deliverable: stopping protocol document (framing + justified regime + calculation/thresholds + decision rule + guardrails + one-page governance pre-registration), ready to attach to the experiment ticket and audit.

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You will build a prioritized experiment backlog for {{PRODUCTO}}, in service of {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} and focused on {{SEGMENTO}}. The team carries more hypotheses than validation capacity: without an evidence-based order, discovery spends effort on what is comfortable instead of what is risky, and the organization confuses activity with learning. This backlog unlocks deciding what to test first by prioritizing what would hurt most if false and what can be learned fastest and cheapest, reducing the risk of building what nobody wants and the opportunity cost of validating the wrong assumption too late.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Head of Product Discovery, with experience ordering experimentation backlogs using assumption risk and learning velocity in digital products.
Deliverable: a prioritized experiment backlog in table form, plus a kickoff note for the first three experiments.
1. Verify the minimum context (product, objective, segment, hypotheses, resources); if anything essential is missing or ambiguous, ask for it in a single batch before proceeding. Do not invent figures or evidence: what is not supported is flagged as an assumption.
2. Rewrite each belief from {{HIPOTESIS_SIN_VALIDAR}} as a falsifiable hypothesis: We believe that [action] will achieve [measurable outcome] for {{SEGMENTO}} because [reason]. We will know it is true if [measurable signal and threshold]. If a belief hides several, decompose it.
3. Classify each hypothesis by risk type: desirability, viability, feasibility, fit (business/legal/ethics).
4. Score two axes 1 to 5: assumption risk (impact if false, weighted by weakness of current evidence) and learning velocity (speed and low effort to obtain a reliable signal; faster and cheaper = higher score). Justify why each score.
5. Calculate priority = assumption risk x learning velocity, sort from highest to lowest, resolve ties by lowest learning cost, and adjust to {{RECURSOS_PLAZO}}.
6. For the top items define test method (interview, fake door, prototype, smoke test, concierge, analytics), metric and success and failure thresholds, sample or duration, underlying assumption being validated, and decision it unlocks (persevere/pivot/discard). One experiment per critical assumption.
7. Close with the prioritized table and the note for the three experiments to run first with their justification. Declare limits: what cannot be concluded, dependencies between experiments, and measurement risks (insufficient sample, novelty effect, contamination between variants).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: set objective, segment, and hypothesis inventory; flag each claim as [fact] or [assumption].
Phase 2 Falsifiability: normalize each hypothesis to the template and define its measurable signal and threshold.
Phase 3 Risk: classify the risk type and score both axes with explicit criteria for why each score.
Phase 4 Prioritization: calculate priority, sort the backlog, resolve ties by lowest learning cost, adjusting to real capacity.
Phase 5 Experiment design: detail method, metric with success and failure thresholds, sample/duration, assumption being validated, and decision for the top items.
Phase 6 Delivery: build the table and the kickoff note; flag the confirmation bias avoided and the limits of the reading.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each hypothesis is falsifiable, with a measurable signal and explicit threshold.
- Each item has a risk type and both axes scored 1 to 5 with justification.
- Priority is calculated and the backlog is sorted consistently, adjusted to resources and timeline.
- The top prioritizes high assumption risk + high learning velocity, not what is already believed nor what is comfortable.
- Each top experiment defines method, metric with success and failure thresholds, sample/duration, assumption being validated, and decision (persevere/pivot/discard).
- There is one experiment per critical assumption; limits, dependencies, and measurement risks are declared.
- Facts and assumptions are distinguished; nothing invented.
Expected deliverable: prioritized backlog table (hypothesis, risk type, assumption risk, learning velocity, priority, method, metric/threshold, decision) + note with the first three experiments, their justification, and the confirmation bias avoided.
spec-producto_growth_loop_disenar:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or feature for which the loop is being designed; include in one phrase what it does and for whom
- ACCION_DE_VALOR: {{ACCION_DE_VALOR}} > Core action where the user gets value and, by executing it, generates a potentially shareable output
- ADQUISICION_ACTUAL: {{ADQUISICION_ACTUAL}} > How users arrive today (paid, organic, referrals, sales) and approximate weight of each channel
- METRICA_OBJETIVO: {{METRICA_OBJETIVO}} > Growth result to maximize (e.g., new active users per month, amplification factor, organic acquisition cost)
- RESTRICCION: {{RESTRICCION}} > Limit to respect (e.g., no incremental ad spend, no touching onboarding, experiment timeline) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Linear funnel growth is exhausted: each new user costs more in paid acquisition and acquisition does not compound. A self-reinforcing growth loop changes the economics: the output a user produces when getting value becomes the acquisition input for the next, so growth feeds itself. This prompt models that cycle for PRODUCTO, verifies whether it truly closes, quantifies its amplification factor, locates the step that strangles it, and designs the experiment that tests whether it is self-sustaining. The most common error is disguising a funnel as a loop: if the flow only advances by re-injecting external spending or effort on each turn, it does not compound. This unlocks a composable, defensible growth lever — not an isolated channel trick.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Head of Growth specialized in product loops and experimentation, with the judgment to distinguish a real loop from a disguised funnel and to read the economics of the cycle.
Deliverable: the complete design of the growth loop of PRODUCTO in four artifacts (textual diagram of the loop, equation with variables, bottleneck table with levers, experiment card). Steps:
1. Map the loop over ACCION_DE_VALOR in 4 to 6 chained nodes: observable user output, channel or surface toward non-users, moment and conversion trigger of the non-user, and step that returns them to the start; verify that the last node feeds back into the first.
2. Apply the loop-vs-funnel test: if sustaining the flow requires re-injecting external spending or effort on each turn, declare it a funnel and name what is missing to close it into a loop.
3. Classify the type (invitation viral, indexable user-generated content, data that improves the product and raises retention, or direct network effect) and justify why it applies to PRODUCTO according to ADQUISICION_ACTUAL; do not assign it by default.
4. Formulate the loop equation: amplification factor per cycle, cycle time, and conversion rate per step; mark [ASSUMPTION] on each estimate and indicate how to instrument it (event, property, cohort). Interpret the regime: factor >= 1 is self-sustaining; between 0 and 1 amplifies acquisition but cannot sustain itself alone; name the threshold that changes the regime.
5. Identify the bottleneck (step with lowest pass-through rate) and propose 3 levers, each with the metric it moves, its expected effect on the amplification factor, and its cost or risk, aligned to METRICA_OBJETIVO and within RESTRICCION.
6. Name two loop risks: channel saturation (exhausted when reachable non-users run out) and leaks or counter-loops (churn, channel fatigue, decreasing output quality).
7. Design a falsifiable experiment: hypothesis, variant, primary metric, numerical success criterion, approximate sample size, duration, and the condition that would invalidate it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate PRODUCTO and its growth engine; if ACCION_DE_VALOR, ADQUISICION_ACTUAL, or METRICA_OBJETIVO is missing, ask for it and stop. Do not invent figures.
Phase 2 - Loop mapping: derive the nodes from ACCION_DE_VALOR, verify cycle closure, and run the loop-vs-funnel test; if it does not close, declare it and propose what is missing.
Phase 3 - Type and quantification: classify the justified type against ADQUISICION_ACTUAL, build the equation, label each estimated value with [ASSUMPTION] plus its measurement method, and interpret the regime according to the factor.
Phase 4 - Diagnosis and experiment: locate the bottleneck, derive the 3 levers with metric/effect/cost, name saturation and leaks, and build the falsifiable experiment card.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The loop closes: the last node verifiably feeds back into the first and passes the loop-vs-funnel test (does not advance solely with re-injected external spending/effort).
- The loop type is justified against ADQUISICION_ACTUAL, not assigned by default.
- The equation includes amplification factor, cycle time, and conversion per step; each estimate carries [ASSUMPTION] and its measurement method; the regime (>=1, between 0 and 1) is interpreted.
- The bottleneck is the step with the lowest pass-through rate; each of the 3 levers names the metric it moves, its effect on the factor, and its cost or risk.
- Both risks are named: channel saturation and leaks or counter-loops.
- The experiment is falsifiable: hypothesis, primary metric, numerical success criterion, sample, duration, and invalidation condition.
- Zero invented figures; all RESTRICCION constraints respected; no meta-commentary.
Expected deliverable: textual diagram of the loop + equation with variables + bottleneck table (3 levers with metric/effect/cost) + experiment card, ready to take to a product committee.
spec-producto_north_star_experiment_map:
[inputs]
- METRICA_NORTE: {{METRICA_NORTE}} > The single north star metric of the product and its exact definition, including measurement window and counting unit (e.g., active weeks per user in a 28-day rolling window)
- ECUACION_INPUTS: {{ECUACION_INPUTS}} > The equation or input tree that composes the north star: first-level levers and second-level sub-levers; if only a verbal definition is available, note it so the model can formalize it before inferring
- BACKLOG_EXPERIMENTOS: {{BACKLOG_EXPERIMENTOS}} > List of experiments or tests in the backlog, with their hypothesis, owner, and status if available
- EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE: {{EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE}} > Data, baselines, segment sizes, or results from prior tests to estimate impact and confidence ("No data" if none)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Planning horizon for the priority bets and approximate team capacity if known (e.g., next quarter, 2 squads)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Product teams accumulate experiment backlogs that sound attractive but are not connected to the lever that actually moves the north star metric; the result is activity without progress. Without an explicit input tree, prioritization rewards the familiar or the flashy over what actually changes the outcome. This prompt builds the map that connects each test with the input it intends to move, exposes orphan inputs with no bets, and strips bare the popular experiments that do not move anything that matters. This unlocks an experimentation strategy where each test justifies its place by causal chain toward the north star, not by trend.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Growth Product Lead, expert in north star metrics, input metric trees, experiment design, and ICE/RICE prioritization.
Deliverable: a map of experiments against the inputs of the north star metric. Steps:
1. Break down METRICA_NORTE into its input tree based on ECUACION_INPUTS: first-level levers and second-level actionable sub-levers. If the equation is verbal or ambiguous, formalize it explicitly and flag the assumption before continuing.
2. For each experiment in BACKLOG_EXPERIMENTOS identify the exact input it targets, the causal chain that would move it, and the critical falsifiable assumption that must be true for it to work.
3. Mark as orphan every experiment that does not map to any input; each orphan gets a decision: discard or re-justify with the missing causal chain.
4. Estimate ICE per experiment: Impact on the input (not on the north star directly), Confidence according to evidence, and Effort, using only EVIDENCIA_DISPONIBLE; label [ASSUMPTION] every unsupported estimate and lower its confidence.
5. Build the coverage map: inputs saturated with too many experiments versus orphan inputs with no tests; name both extremes.
6. Explicitly flag the high-effort or high-visibility popular experiments that do not move any input that matters.
7. Recommend 3 to 5 bets to run first within HORIZONTE, each with causal justification and, where applicable, the orphan input they help cover.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Input tree: derive levers from the equation; if the equation is unclear, ask for it before inferring and do not invent inputs.
Phase 2 Causal mapping: connect each experiment to an input via explicit chain; isolate the critical falsifiable assumption of each.
Phase 3 Scoring: apply ICE only with provided data; without data, declare the estimate [ASSUMPTION] and lower the confidence; do not fabricate precise numbers on non-existent evidence.
Phase 4 Coverage and decision: detect orphans and saturations; issue the master table and the top bets within the horizon and declared capacity.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate the north star metric, its tree, and the backlog as you understand them, and present your mapping and scoring plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each input in the tree is derived from ECUACION_INPUTS; formalized or assumed ones are marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Each experiment maps to an input or is marked as orphan with its decision.
- [ ] Each mapping exposes causal chain and critical falsifiable assumption.
- [ ] ICE scores Impact on the input, not on the north star directly; unsupported estimates carry [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] The coverage map names orphan inputs and saturated inputs.
- [ ] 3 to 5 bets prioritized within HORIZONTE with causal justification and capacity considered.
- [ ] Popular experiments with no impact on the north star are explicitly flagged.
- [ ] No invented numbers: if evidence to estimate is missing, it is declared instead of fabricated.
Expected deliverable: master table (experiment -> input -> lever -> critical assumption -> ICE -> decision run/de-prioritize/discard) + input coverage map (orphan and saturated) + top 3 to 5 justified bets within the horizon, in neutral and professional English.
spec-producto_plan_user_research:
[inputs]
- DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO: {{DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO}} > The concrete decision the study must unlock (for example: build or not build feature X, redesign onboarding, prioritize a segment). Include, if known, the action that would be taken according to each possible result
- PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA: {{PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA}} > Product and maturity stage (idea, MVP, growth, maturity) that determines whether the study is exploratory or evaluative
- SEGMENTO_USUARIO: {{SEGMENTO_USUARIO}} > Target segment or user profile of the study; note if there is more than one segment to compare
- PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS: {{PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS}} > Available time, team budget, and user access (own panel, external recruitment, installed base). Optional; if missing, high constraint is assumed and flagged as an assumption
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The product team faces the decision {{DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO}} about {{PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA}} and needs evidence from real users of the segment {{SEGMENTO_USUARIO}} before committing design and development effort. A well-built research plan converts uncertainty into falsifiable questions and verifiable method: it unlocks deciding with evidence rather than opinion, avoids building on unvalidated assumptions, and leaves a reusable protocol for future discovery cycles. The recurring risk is inverting the order — choosing a trendy method and then looking for what to ask — or measuring perceptions when the decision requires observing behavior; this plan prevents that.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Lead UX Researcher with more than ten years designing discovery and evaluation studies for product teams, fluent in qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods, rigorous in separating what you want to learn from what you ask the user.
Deliverable: an actionable research plan, ready to take to the field this very week, with these numbered sections:
1. Product decision and why the research unlocks it (what will be done differently according to each result).
2. Learning objectives (2 to 4), each tied to a concrete decision and the action associated with each possible result.
3. Research questions, separating what you want to learn (research questions, internal) from what will be asked of the user (discussion guide), without leading questions.
4. Hypotheses or assumptions to falsify where applicable, written as testable statements with their confirmation or refutation signal, and marked as such.
5. Recommended method (exploratory qualitative, evaluative, quantitative, or mixed) with justification against the question and the product stage, and one discarded alternative with its reason.
6. Recruitment: target profile, inclusion and exclusion criteria, sample size reasoned by study type, and recruitment channels.
7. Discussion guide or session protocol: opening, thematic blocks or tasks, closing, and estimated duration.
8. Analysis plan and success or decision criteria defined before data collection.
9. Risks, biases to mitigate, and ethical and consent considerations.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Interpret): identify the type of question behind {{DECISION_DE_PRODUCTO}} (generative or evaluative, attitudinal or behavioral) and the stage in {{PRODUCTO_Y_ETAPA}}. If the decision, the segment, or the stage is missing, ask for them before proceeding; do not invent the scope.
Phase 2 (Plan): derive objectives from the decision, research questions from the objectives, and only then choose the method that best answers those questions; never the other way around. Size the sample according to study type (for example, 5 to 8 participants per segment in evaluative qualitative; larger n when measuring or comparing). Adjust scope and sample to {{PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS}}; if the timeline is short, propose a minimum viable version of the study and state what is sacrificed.
Phase 3 (Execute): write the discussion guide without biased, double-barreled, or hypothetical questions the user cannot answer with real behavior; set decision criteria before data collection and close with risks, biases, ethics, and consent. Explicitly state any relevant design decision and its trade-off. Mark any adopted assumption with [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each learning objective is explicitly connected to a decision and to the action triggered by each possible result.
- Internal research questions are separated from the user discussion guide questions.
- The discussion guide contains no leading, double-barreled, or non-observable hypothetical questions.
- The method is justified by the question and stage, not preference, and includes one discarded alternative.
- Sample size is reasoned according to study type and fits within {{PLAZO_Y_RECURSOS}}.
- Success or decision criteria are defined before data collection.
- Biases, ethics, and consent are covered.
- Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; gaps marked as a question for the user.
- Neutral and professional English, without emojis.
Expected deliverable: research plan in nine sections, executable this very week by the product team, with the decision > objectives > questions > method order preserved end to end.
spec-producto_elegir_metodo_research:
[inputs]
- PREGUNTA_RESEARCH: {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}} > What the team needs to learn, in their own words
- DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR: {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}} > What product decision depends on this answer and who makes it
- ETAPA_PRODUCTO: {{ETAPA_PRODUCTO}} > Discovery, design, pre-launch, or product in use
- DATOS_EXISTENTES: {{DATOS_EXISTENTES}} > Analytics, support tickets, or prior studies already available (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Time, user access, and available effort (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Choosing the wrong research method wastes weeks and produces evidence that does not answer the real question: interviews are conducted when analytics are needed, or surveys when behavior needs to be observed. The objective is to decide the correct method BEFORE investing effort, starting from what needs to be learned. With the decision made, {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}} is unlocked with adequate evidence rather than opinions, and users are not recruited for questions that existing data already answers. A silent risk to avoid: producing a methodologically impeccable study that arrives too late for {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}} or that measures declared perception when the decision requires observed behavior.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX Research Lead who has built mixed research programs (quali + quanti) in product teams and masters the Christian Rohrer / NN/g methods landscape: the attitudinal-behavioral (what they say vs. what they do) and qualitative-quantitative (why vs. how much) axes, plus product usage context.
Deliverable: a justified, ready-to-execute method recommendation. Steps:
1. Reformulate {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}} in a single falsifiable sentence and connect it to {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}}; name which answer would change the decision in each direction.
2. Classify the question on two axes: attitudinal vs. behavioral (what they say vs. what they do) and qualitative vs. quantitative (why vs. how much), justifying each axis according to {{ETAPA_PRODUCTO}}.
3. Recommend 1 primary method and 1 triangulation secondary method, choosing from: interviews, moderated or unmoderated usability tests, surveys, card sorting, tree testing, product analytics, A/B testing, diary studies, intercept surveys, support ticket analysis. The secondary must cover the opposite axis from the primary.
4. For the primary method define: sample and recruitment criterion, location on both axes, evidence it produces, how it is analyzed, and decision threshold (what result would suffice to resolve {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}}), all within {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
5. List 2 biases or validity threats of the chosen method and how to mitigate them.
6. Review {{DATOS_EXISTENTES}} and flag explicitly if the question does NOT need new research because there is already data that answers it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: isolate the falsifiable question and the decision; if {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}} mixes several questions, separate the dominant one (the one that most drives the decision) and name the others as backlog. If {{PREGUNTA_RESEARCH}}, {{DECISION_A_DESBLOQUEAR}}, or {{ETAPA_PRODUCTO}} are missing or ambiguous, formulate the minimum questions in a single batch before continuing.
Phase 2 Classification: locate the question on both axes; attitudinal captures declared perception and behavioral captures observed behavior; quali explains why and quanti measures magnitude and prevalence. If the question uses opinion verbs ("prefer", "like") to predict behavior, flag the say-do gap as a risk.
Phase 3 Selection: map each axis to methods; prioritize the one that produces the most direct evidence for the decision and a secondary that triangulates the opposite axis. If {{RESTRICCIONES}} block the ideal method, name the ideal, declare the constraint, and propose the best viable substitute.
Phase 4 Design: detail sample, recruitment, evidence, analysis, and decision threshold of the primary method, adjusted to {{RESTRICCIONES}}; give an indicative sample size according to method type (qualitative saturation vs. statistical power) without promising time or cost figures.
Phase 5 Validity: name 2 biases (social desirability, self-selection, recall, moderator effect, unrepresentative sample, novelty, survivorship) and their concrete mitigation.
Phase 6 No-research gate: if {{DATOS_EXISTENTES}} already answers the question, flag it and propose analyzing what exists before launching a new study; if it only partially answers it, define what specific gap justifies the new study.
Assumptions: flag with an explicit marker any data you had to assume.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The question was reformulated in a single falsifiable sentence tied to the decision, with the answers that would change the decision.
- [ ] The classification explicitly names both axes (attitudinal/behavioral and quali/quanti) with justification according to stage.
- [ ] There is exactly 1 primary method and 1 secondary, both from the list, and the secondary triangulates the opposite axis.
- [ ] The primary method includes sample, recruitment, evidence, analysis, and decision threshold consistent with constraints.
- [ ] 2 biases are listed with concrete mitigation.
- [ ] The no-research gate was evaluated and declared with a flag (yes/no/partial) based on existing data.
- [ ] Assumptions were flagged.
Expected deliverable: a 1-page research method recommendation with falsifiable question, classification on two axes, designed primary method with decision threshold, triangulation secondary method, two mitigated biases, flagged assumptions, and research-new yes/no/partial verdict.
spec-producto_guia_entrevista_explorator:
[inputs]
- TEMA_O_PROBLEMA: {{TEMA_O_PROBLEMA}} > Area of behavior or problem to explore (e.g., "how freelancers manage collecting on overdue invoices"). Required: without it, the guide has no focus.
- SEGMENTO_PARTICIPANTE: {{SEGMENTO_PARTICIPANTE}} > Profile of the person to be interviewed: role, context, and inclusion/exclusion criterion. Required: defines the language and episodes to probe.
- DECISION_A_INFORMAR: {{DECISION_A_INFORMAR}} > Product decision the research must unlock (e.g., "whether we build automated collection or only reminders"). Required: anchors the hypotheses.
- COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE: {{COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE}} > Specific past behavior to anchor the narratives to (optional). If missing, derive a candidate behavior from TEMA_O_PROBLEMA and flag it [ASSUMPTION].
- DURACION_OBJETIVO: {{DURACION_OBJETIVO}} > Estimated session duration (optional, e.g., "30-45 min"). Calibrates the number of questions and probes.
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We are in the discovery phase and need real evidence about TEMA_O_PROBLEMA before committing to design or development. The risk is building on assumptions: a poorly written guide induces compliant and hypothetical responses that falsely validate the idea and make us invest in the wrong thing. A solid exploratory guide unlocks DECISION_A_INFORMAR because it captures how SEGMENTO_PARTICIPANTE truly behaves today, in specific past episodes and not in declared intentions.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product researcher in qualitative discovery, trained in The Mom Test (talk about the past and facts, never the future or opinions) and in non-directed ethnographic interviewing.

Deliverable: a ready-to-conduct open exploratory interview guide, with:
1. Learning objective in 1 sentence: what decision it unlocks and what we currently assume without evidence.
2. Hypotheses and assumptions to falsify: 3 to 5, each verifiable in the conversation with the observable signal that would confirm or refute it.
3. Opening and consent: framing, permission to record, "there are no right answers".
4. Warm-up: 2 context questions about role and routine.
5. Central block: 8 to 12 open questions, in a funnel from general to specific, anchored to the last time the behavior occurred, each with 1-2 follow-up probes in parentheses, and linked to COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE when it exists.
6. Closing: 2 questions (what was not asked + referrals).
7. Prohibited formulations: table with anti-pattern and its open rewrite.
8. Hypothesis -> question matrix: which central block question tests each hypothesis (serves as a coverage checklist).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: set the learning objective and derive falsifiable hypotheses from DECISION_A_INFORMAR; for each one define the observable signal that refutes it.
Phase 2 - Architecture: order the central block in a funnel (general > specific), anchoring each question to a real past episode and avoiding all hypothetical or solution language.
Phase 3 - Probes: add follow-ups that deepen motivation, context, and consequence ("what happened next", "why that way", "what did it cost you").
Phase 4 - Hygiene: review each question against the prohibited list; eliminate double-barreled, leading, yes/no, and adjective-loaded questions. Calibrate the number of questions and probes to DURACION_OBJETIVO.
Phase 5 - Coverage: complete the hypothesis -> question matrix and confirm that no hypothesis is left without at least one question that falsifies it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each central block question is open (cannot be answered with yes/no) and contains a single idea.
- At least 70% of the questions are anchored to a specific past episode, not to future intentions.
- Zero hypothetical questions ("would you use", "would you pay", "would you like") and zero mention of the solution before exploring the problem.
- Each hypothesis is falsifiable, has an observable signal, and maps to at least one question in the coverage matrix.
- The prohibited list includes anti-pattern and rewrite for each case.
- Data not provided is asked for or flagged [ASSUMPTION]; nothing is invented. If COMPORTAMIENTO_CLAVE is missing, one is derived and flagged.
- Edge cases: if DECISION_A_INFORMAR is ambiguous, ask for clarification before deriving hypotheses; if the SEGMENT does not yet perform the behavior (new market), anchor to the closest current problem or workaround, not to intention.
Expected deliverable: a start-to-finish conductible guide, in neutral English, without internal jargon, reusable for future rounds with the same segment.
spec-producto_test_usabilidad_tareas:
[inputs]
- INTERFAZ: {{INTERFAZ}} > Product, screen, or prototype to evaluate (app, web, flow, prototype version); include fidelity level (sketch, navigable prototype, production)
- OBJETIVO_DECISION: {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} > Product decision the test must inform (e.g., validate checkout redesign before release); ideally with the deadline or gate it feeds
- PERFIL_USUARIO: {{PERFIL_USUARIO}} > Target user and relevant segments; novice vs. recurring, roles, domain experience level
- FLUJOS_CRITICOS: {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}} > Key flows or paths to cover in the tasks; mark which are make-or-break for the decision
- MODALIDAD_MUESTRA: {{MODALIDAD_MUESTRA}} > Modality (in-person / remote moderated / unmoderated) and number of available participants per segment; if comparative, indicate variants
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to evaluate the usability of {{INTERFAZ}} with real users before committing engineering and budget in {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}. A task-based test converts diffuse opinions into observable evidence: it shows where and why people get stuck, how much it costs them to achieve their goal, and how severe each problem is. The deliverable is a test plan ready to run that any team facilitator can conduct consistently, generating comparable and prioritizable findings that unlock the decision with data rather than intuition. A poor design wastes the scarcest resource of the study (sessions with users) and produces non-actionable findings: the plan must be shielded against this from the design stage.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX Researcher specialized in task-based usability testing, with mastery of usability metrics (task success, time on task, error rate, number of assists, SEQ, SUS, or UMUX-Lite) and of sampling for qualitative and comparative studies.

Produce a complete usability test plan with these numbered sections:
1. Research objectives: 3 to 5 questions the test must answer, each explicitly linked to {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, expressed as a falsifiable hypothesis, and accompanied by its decision criterion (what result triggers proceed, adjust, or halt).
2. Participants: profile derived from {{PERFIL_USUARIO}}; screener of 4 to 6 filter questions with disqualifying answers marked; recommended number per segment, justified by {{MODALIDAD_MUESTRA}} (practical rule: 5 per homogeneous segment in formative qualitative studies; larger and balanced n if comparative or summative); brief note on incentives and recruitment logistics.
3. Tasks and scenarios: 4 to 6 tasks covering {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}}, prioritizing make-or-break flows; for each task define a scenario narrated in user language (context plus goal, without naming buttons or revealing the path), initial state, required test data, and observable and unambiguous success criterion. Define the task order and whether to counterbalance to mitigate the learning effect.
4. Metrics per task: specify which apply among task success (binary or by levels), time on task, error rate, number of assists, and SEQ (1 to 7), with a target threshold per metric and how each is recorded. Distinguish primary metrics (decide) from secondary metrics (diagnose).
5. Facilitator script: introduction, consent and recording permission, think-aloud instruction, no-help rules and hint escalation protocol (what to do with prolonged blocking), post-task and post-test questions, and global satisfaction instrument (SUS or UMUX-Lite) if applicable.
6. Analysis plan: how to tabulate results by participant and by task (master table), severity scale (1 cosmetic, 2 minor, 3 major, 4 critical), prioritization criterion (severity by frequency), and findings report format (problem, evidence, severity, recommendation).
7. Study risks and mitigations: foreseeable biases (moderator, task order, sample bias), validity of the chosen modality against {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, and pilot plan with 1 participant before the full group to debug tasks and instruments.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: extract from {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} and {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}} the hypotheses to falsify and convert each into an actionable research objective with its associated decision criterion.
Phase 2 - Task design: for each critical flow write the scenario from the user's goal; verify that no statement filters the solution (no button names or steps). Associate metrics and thresholds consistent with the nature of the task and define order and counterbalancing.
Phase 3 - Instrumentation: build screener, script, and metrics capture template aligned with each other; include the hint escalation protocol to maintain comparability between facilitators.
Phase 4 - Analysis and risks: define the master table, the severity rubric, and the prioritization rule before the test so the analysis is reproducible; document biases and mitigations and reserve a pilot.
Phase 5 - Verification against C checklist. Flag with [ASSUMPTION] every data point not provided; if a critical input ({{INTERFAZ}}, {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, {{FLUJOS_CRITICOS}}, or {{MODALIDAD_MUESTRA}}) is missing, ask for it rather than inventing it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] 3 to 5 research objectives, each traceable to {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}}, as a falsifiable hypothesis with decision criterion.
- [ ] Screener with explicit disqualifying answers, justified n per segment, and recruitment note.
- [ ] 4 to 6 tasks; each scenario in user language, without naming buttons or revealing the path; order and counterbalancing defined.
- [ ] Each task has initial state, test data, and observable and unambiguous success criterion.
- [ ] Each task defines its metrics with a numerical target threshold and distinguishes primary from secondary.
- [ ] Script includes consent and recording, think-aloud, no-help rules, hint escalation, and global satisfaction (SUS or UMUX-Lite).
- [ ] Analysis plan with master table, severity scale 1 to 4, prioritization rule, and report format.
- [ ] Risks and mitigations documented, modality validity evaluated, and pilot planned.
- [ ] Assumptions flagged [ASSUMPTION]; no prices; neutral and professional English.
Expected deliverable: usability test plan document, ready to recruit and run, executable by any team facilitator consistently and reproducibly.
spec-producto_reclutar_screener:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO: {{OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO}} > Research question or product decision the study must inform
- PERFIL_OBJETIVO: {{PERFIL_OBJETIVO}} > Target user described by behavior, context, and experience — not only demographics
- TAMANO_MUESTRA: {{TAMANO_MUESTRA}} > Number of participants to recruit and method (interviews, usability test, survey)
- CUOTAS: {{CUOTAS}} > Desired distribution by segment (e.g., newcomers vs. advanced, region, device) (optional)
- CRITERIOS_EXCLUSION: {{CRITERIOS_EXCLUSION}} > Profiles to discard: industry, market research, media, competitor, recent participation, conflicts of interest (optional)
- MODALIDAD: {{MODALIDAD}} > Format and logistics: remote/in-person, duration, type of planned incentive (without amounts) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A weak screener contaminates the entire research effort: if participants who do not represent the target — or who lie to access the incentive — get through, the conclusions are expensive noise. This prompt produces the study entry filter for OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO: it guarantees a representative sample of PERFIL_OBJETIVO and blocks professional respondents, incentive fraud, and conflicts of interest. A well-designed screener unlocks reliable findings, reduces wasted sessions, and protects the product EstrategIA that will depend on those data. The cost of a false positive (someone who is not the target but gets in) typically exceeds that of a false negative (a real target who is rejected): when in doubt, the screener filters more strictly.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX research specialist in participant recruitment and screener design, with experience running panels, quotas, and anti-fraud controls for qualitative and quantitative studies.

Deliverable: a complete screener ready to load into a survey tool, plus its qualification logic and quota matrix. Steps:
1. Reframe OBJETIVO_ESTUDIO and translate PERFIL_OBJETIVO into observable and verifiable criteria: demographic quotas, real behavior (frequency, context, tools), experience level, and tenure as a user. Measure behavior, not abstract self-declared attitudes. Mark every inferred criterion with [ASSUMPTION] and [to_confirm] for anything you cannot resolve.
2. Convert each criterion into one or two closed-choice questions with an explicit decision rule per option (QUALIFIES / DISQUALIFIES / QUOTA per cell).
3. Insert a minimum of three controls: (a) plausibility trap (a non-existent but credible option within a list that disqualifies anyone who selects it); (b) conflict-of-interest filter based on CRITERIOS_EXCLUSION (industry, market research, media, competitor, recent studies); (c) internal consistency check (two questions that must align — e.g., frequency vs. last use) so you are not relying on honesty without cross-checking.
4. Order the flow from lowest to highest friction: fast disqualifiers first, quota next, fine profiling and sensitive data at the close, to avoid burning incentive or time on those who will be screened out.
5. Translate CUOTAS into concrete cells that sum to TAMANO_MUESTRA and include an over-recruitment buffer for no-shows; suggest the percentage based on MODALIDAD and justify the assumption.
6. Draft a neutral, non-leading introduction (without revealing the target profile or the desired answer) and a close that captures contact details, availability, and consent in line with MODALIDAD. The incentive is referred to as the planned incentive, without amounts.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate the objective and profile; list inclusion/exclusion as observable, verifiable statements.
Phase 2 - Operationalization: per criterion define the question, closed options, and QUALIFIES/DISQUALIFIES/QUOTA rule. Avoid leading questions that reveal the correct answer.
Phase 3 - Controls: insert the plausibility trap, conflict-of-interest filter, and internal consistency check; verify that no decision depends solely on the respondent's honesty.
Phase 4 - Sequencing and quotas: order from lowest to highest friction, calculate cells and buffer, draft the introduction and close.
Phase 5 - Packaging: deliver the numbered screener, the logic table (question | option | action), and the quota matrix with total and buffer.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every profile criterion has at least one question measuring it by observable behavior, not by abstract self-declaration.
- [ ] Every response option carries an explicit decision rule (QUALIFIES / DISQUALIFIES / QUOTA).
- [ ] There are >=3 controls: plausibility trap, conflict of interest, and internal consistency check.
- [ ] No question is leading or reveals the target profile or the qualifying option.
- [ ] The order minimizes friction: disqualifiers > quota > profiling > sensitive data.
- [ ] Quotas sum to the sample size and include an over-recruitment buffer for no-shows with a justified percentage.
- [ ] Introduction and close are neutral; the close captures contact details, availability, and consent. Incentive without amounts.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] and pending items [to_confirm].
Expected deliverable: numbered screener ready to load into a survey + qualification-logic table + quota matrix with cells, target per cell, total, and buffer.
spec-producto_encuesta_producto:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_DECISION: {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} > Product decision the survey must enable (e.g., prioritize a feature, validate perceived pricing, measure satisfaction)
- PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION: {{PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION}} > Central question the survey answers
- PUBLICO_OBJETIVO: {{PUBLICO_OBJETIVO}} > Who answers: segment, role, relationship with the product
- CANAL_DISTRIBUCION: {{CANAL_DISTRIBUCION}} > Distribution channel (in-app, email, external panel) (optional)
- TAMANO_MUESTRA: {{TAMANO_MUESTRA}} > Expected or available responses (optional)
- DURACION_MAXIMA: {{DURACION_MAXIMA}} > Maximum acceptable response time (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to design a quantitative product survey whose sole purpose is to enable the decision {{OBJETIVO_DECISION}} with reliable data; this is not an exercise to collect scattered opinions. The central risk of any survey is bias: loaded questions, unbalanced scales, and carry-over order produce numbers that look valid but point to the wrong decision. A well-constructed survey unlocks decisions that are defensible to stakeholders and reusable in future waves; a biased one costs weeks of rework and credibility. If OBJETIVO_DECISION, PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION, or PUBLICO_OBJETIVO are missing, ask for them before continuing and do not invent them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior product researcher (quantitative UX researcher) grounded in psychometrics and questionnaire design.
Deliverable: the complete, bias-free, traceable survey instrument ready for field. Steps:
1. Translate OBJETIVO_DECISION and PREGUNTA_INVESTIGACION into a construct map: each measurable variable with its operational definition. Discard what cannot be measured and flag the uncertain items.
2. Draft the question block; for each item indicate type (single, multiple, scale, ranking, open-ended), options, and associated scale. Limit open-ended questions (costly to analyze) to those that provide the "why" that quantitative data cannot capture.
3. Design balanced scales: a justified number of points, symmetric labels at both ends, an explicit neutral point or its absence justified, and an exit option (Not applicable / Prefer not to answer) where appropriate.
4. Define the item order: general before specific, sensitive at the end, grouping by construct, with a note on why that sequence reduces carry-over effects and fatigue. Randomize options where applicable.
5. Document the biases avoided (acquiescence, social desirability, leading framing, double-barreled questions, order anchoring) and the technique used against each.
6. Attach a pre-field analysis plan: per construct, how each result will be read to make the decision and what threshold tips it. Setting the criterion before seeing the data prevents redefining success after the fact.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Constructs: decompose the objective into variables; discard what cannot be measured.
Phase 2 Drafting: one question = one concept; neutral language; no double negatives or loaded terms; avoid implicit assumptions about the respondent.
Phase 3 Scales: balance points and labels; justify even vs. odd based on whether you want to force direction or allow genuine neutrality.
Phase 4 Order: anti-carry-over sequence; randomize options where applicable; protect attention with a length appropriate to DURACION_MAXIMA and CANAL_DISTRIBUCION.
Phase 5 Sample: contrast segment cuts against TAMANO_MUESTRA; warn when the base is insufficient to conclude by segment.
Phase 6 Verification: run each item through the criteria checklist. Mark everything not provided as [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Every item measures one single concept (no double-barreled questions).
- Zero leading framings, loaded terms, or double negatives.
- Scales with symmetric labels and a justified number of points.
- Response options that are exhaustive and mutually exclusive (no overlap).
- Order documented with its anti-carry-over rationale and within DURACION_MAXIMA.
- Every construct traceable to OBJETIVO_DECISION.
- The analysis plan fixes, per construct, the threshold that tips the decision, defined before field.
- Segment cuts flagged when TAMANO_MUESTRA does not support them.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; missing data requested, not invented.
Edge cases: if OBJETIVO_DECISION mixes several decisions, separate them or prioritize one; if PUBLICO_OBJETIVO includes heterogeneous segments, flag which items require branching (skip logic).
Expected deliverable: survey document with construct map, numbered question block with type and scale, recommended order, register of biases avoided, and pre-field analysis plan, ready to load into the field tool.
spec-producto_sintesis_affinity_mapping:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_INVESTIGACION: {{OBJETIVO_INVESTIGACION}} > Question or decision that motivates the research (e.g., "why they abandon onboarding")
- OBSERVACIONES: {{OBSERVACIONES}} > Raw notes, verbatim quotes, behaviors, and complaints to synthesize
- NUM_PARTICIPANTES: {{NUM_PARTICIPANTES}} > Number of distinct participants represented in the material
- IMPACTO_PRODUCTO: {{IMPACTO_PRODUCTO}} > Product dimension to prioritize against (e.g., activation, retention, a feature) (optional)
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > executive summary of themes | full map with all notes (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You have raw research observations about {{OBJETIVO_INVESTIGACION}} scattered across notes, quotes, and behaviors. Without synthesis, the team decides by anecdote: the last noisy comment carries more weight than the real pattern, and the loudest voice bias contaminates the roadmap. Affinity mapping converts that raw material into emerging themes with traceable evidence, unlocking defensible roadmap decisions and a product EstrategIA anchored in what users actually do and say — not in assumptions. The value lies not in the quantity of clusters but in the quality of traceability: every assertion must be traceable to concrete observations and a verifiable participant count.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior UX researcher specializing in qualitative synthesis and affinity mapping, with judgment to separate signal from noise and resistance to comfortable narratives.
Deliverable: an affinity map with prioritized and traceable emerging themes. Steps:
1. Normalize each observation into an atomic note (one single idea, user's language without interpretation) and flag duplicates with their frequency.
2. Group bottom-up by semantic affinity (same need, friction, motivation, or context); DO NOT use predefined categories or imposed taxonomies.
3. Iterate: merge or split groups until each cluster is internally coherent and does not mix distinct needs.
4. Name each cluster with an insight label in the form of a statement that captures the tension — not a generic noun (bad: "navigation"; good: "users abandon when they cannot find the next step within 5 seconds").
5. Document each theme: insight name, number of observations, number of distinct participants, 2-3 representative pieces of evidence (verbatim quotes), and the underlying pattern.
6. Elevate 1-2 meta-themes that connect several clusters, only if the connection is supported by evidence.
7. Prioritize by evidence strength (frequency + dispersion across participants) and impact on {{IMPACTO_PRODUCTO}}; a theme cited by many participants carries more weight than one repeated by a single participant.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Atomization: decompose {{OBSERVACIONES}} into single-idea notes; preserve the literal voice; consolidate duplicates with a count; separate the observed data from the analyst's interpretation.
Phase 2 Emergent grouping: cluster related notes without a prior framework; allow a group to subdivide if it mixes distinct needs; leave an "ungrouped" cluster for notes that do not fit, rather than forcing them.
