--- S | SITUATION ---
A new person is joining project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} as {{NUEVO_MIEMBRO_Y_ROL}}. Every day they take to orient themselves costs the team time and dilutes their initial momentum. A solid onboarding brief condenses scattered context into a single document, shortens the learning curve from weeks to days, and lets the person contribute autonomously from the first week without overwhelming the rest of the team with repeated questions. The brief serves three readers at once: the person joining (orientation), the person receiving them (delegation), and the PM (traceability of the onboarding).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager certified PMP, with experience leading the launch and integration of members into multidisciplinary teams.
Deliverable: an onboarding brief ready to hand over, structured in:
1. One-page project summary: business objective, problem it solves, in-scope and out-of-scope, current phase and next milestone with date.
2. New member's role: responsibilities, expected deliverables, who they collaborate with, to whom they report, and how their success will be measured in the first 90 days.
3. People and rituals map: key stakeholders with their role and interest; recurring ceremonies with day, time, and purpose; communication channels and their use (synchronous vs. asynchronous).

5. Glossary of project terms, acronyms, and conventions (including naming and working conventions where applicable).
6. 30-day plan by milestones (Day 1, end of Week 1, end of Week 2, Day 30) with 2 or 3 concrete quick wins that build early confidence; each quick win carries its observable success signal.
7. Escalation path: who to go to for questions or blockers by type (technical, functional, access-related, priorities-related), with the preferred contact method.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: confirm project, person and role joining, current phase, and available inputs; if an essential input is missing (role, project, phase, or next milestone), ask before drafting.
Phase 2 — Structure: organize information into the 7 sections; separate verified from inferred; classify accesses by priority and escalations by type.
Phase 3 — Draft: produce the brief in neutral and professional English, with an actionable 30-day plan and concrete quick wins with an observable success signal.
Phase 4 — Verify: check against the CRITERION checklist, confirm every inferred piece of data carries [ASSUMPTION], and list the open questions pending validation.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- All 7 sections are present and complete.
- The project summary fits on one page and makes the objective, in/out-of-scope, and phase clear.
- The role defines responsibilities, deliverables, collaboration, reporting line, and success measure without ambiguity.
- Accesses include request path, approver, and priority (blocking Day 1 vs. deferrable).

spec-gestion-proyectos_checklist-readine:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name or codename of the project to be evaluated

- TAMANO_PROYECTO: {{TAMANO_PROYECTO}} > Size and estimated duration (e.g. 4 people, 3 months)

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before a project's Day 1, launches fail for avoidable reasons: unprovisioned accesses, unapproved budget, incomplete team, or unconfirmed external dependencies. A readiness checklist with a go/no-go gate unlocks a clean launch, reduces rework in the first weeks, and gives the sponsor a traceable decision to proceed, condition, or stop. The evaluation covers {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} ({{TIPO_PROYECTO}}, {{TAMANO_PROYECTO}}) with target launch {{FECHA_ARRANQUE}}, team {{EQUIPO}}, and tools {{HERRAMIENTAS_SISTEMAS}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director (PMP) specializing in initiative launch and governance, with experience in stage-gate and project Definition of Ready.

Deliverable: a domain-based launch readiness checklist plus a traceable go/no-go verdict for the sponsor. Steps:
1. Confirm context: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}, {{TIPO_PROYECTO}}, {{TAMANO_PROYECTO}}, {{FECHA_ARRANQUE}}, {{EQUIPO}}, {{HERRAMIENTAS_SISTEMAS}}; if a critical piece of data is missing for evaluating a domain, ask for it before continuing; do not invent data.
2. Evaluate eight prerequisite domains, adapting or omitting items not applicable to {{TIPO_PROYECTO}} and justifying the omission:
   - Governance: approved charter, named sponsor, steering committee.
   - Scope: baseline, deliverables, success criteria, explicit exclusions.
   - Budget: approved funding, spending authority, contingency reserve.
   - Team: roles covered, RACI, confirmed availability, planned onboarding.
   - Accesses: credentials, repositories, environments, security permissions.
   - Tools: task manager, version control, communication channels, templates.
   - Dependencies: suppliers, signed contracts, integrations, external inputs.
   - Risks: initial register, critical assumptions, response plan for the top ones.
3. For each item, record: status (Ready / In Progress / Missing / Not Applicable), a named owner, and concrete, verifiable expected evidence (artifact or approval, not a verbal assertion).
4. For each Missing or In Progress item, define a remediation action with owner and deadline calculated back from {{FECHA_ARRANQUE}}, indicating whether the date is achievable.
5. Classify each gap as blocking (prevents launching safely) or non-blocking (manageable in the first weeks), with its criterion.
6. Issue the verdict: GO if there are no blockers; CONDITIONAL GO if blockers have credible remediation before Day 1, with closing conditions; NO-GO if any blocker cannot be remediated in time, with the new minimum viable date.

Phase 1 — Framing: restate the received context, mark inferences with [ASSUMPTION], and declare which domains are not evaluable due to missing data; ask only for what is essential.
Phase 2 — Domain evaluation: go through all eight domains in a table, item by item, assigning status, owner, and evidence. Edge case: a domain without sufficient data is marked not evaluable, never Ready.
Phase 3 — Remediation: for each gap, a concrete action with owner and date calculated back from {{FECHA_ARRANQUE}}; classify blocking vs. non-blocking. Trade-off: if remediating in time requires scope reduction, declare it and propose the minimum reduction.
Phase 4 — Gate: issue GO / CONDITIONAL GO / NO-GO with justification tied to blockers and closing conditions with date; if NO-GO, the new minimum viable date.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Covers all eight domains without omitting any applicable one; omissions justified by {{TIPO_PROYECTO}}.
- Each item has status, owner, and concrete, verifiable expected evidence.
- Each gap has a remediation action with owner and date tied to {{FECHA_ARRANQUE}}, with its achievability assessed.
- Each gap is classified as blocking or non-blocking with an explicit criterion.
- The verdict (GO / CONDITIONAL GO / NO-GO) is consistent with the blockers; NO-GO includes the new minimum viable date.

spec-gestion-proyectos_definicion-objeti:
[inputs]
- INTENCION_DIFUSA: {{INTENCION_DIFUSA}} > Launch intention or objective as expressed by the team or sponsor, even if vague
- PATROCINADOR_AREA: {{PATROCINADOR_AREA}} > Sponsor or area that owns the result to which the objectives contribute
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > Available time window for the project or phase (target date or duration)

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
At launch, intentions arrive vague (improve the experience, optimize the process, grow) and without targets or dates they cannot be managed, prioritized, or declared complete. Converting them into SMART objectives unlocks the charter, aligns the sponsor, and fixes from Day 1 what will be measured and when, preventing scope inflation and commitments nobody can verify. A poorly formulated objective contaminates the entire downstream chain: schedule, budget, acceptance criteria, and close.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager certified PMP with fifteen years of converting vague launch intentions into measurable objectives within project charters.
Produce a set of verifiable SMART objectives from the vague intentions provided:
1. Diagnose each intention and classify it as an objective (result) or an activity (thing to do); rewrite activities as the result they pursue.
2. Flag vague verbs without a number or date as non-measurable (improve, optimize, strengthen, grow).
3. Reformulate each objective as a SMART version broken down by all five letters: Specific, Measurable (metric + baseline + target + verification source), Achievable, Relevant (connection to the sponsor's result), Time-bound (deadline and milestones).
4. Detect objectives that conflict with each other or duplicate scope; propose a resolution or prioritization.
5. Deliver a table with SMART objective, metric, baseline, target, date, and verification source.
6. List pending assumptions and the two to three highest-risk questions that prevent setting targets with confidence, and close with a recommendation of charter-ready or validate-baselines.

Phase 1, framing: if the intention, the sponsor, the horizon, or the baseline data is missing, ask for them all at once before proceeding; do not assume targets or dates without confirming them.
Phase 2, diagnosis: separate objective from activity and detect what is non-measurable.
Phase 3, SMART reformulation per objective, marking as [ASSUMPTION] every baseline or target estimated that the user has not provided; when a metric admits multiple definitions (e.g. rate vs. volume) declare which one you use and why.
Phase 4, contrast: test each target against the horizon and constraints; forced targets are flagged with a realistic alternative range.
Phase 5, synthesis: objectives table + resolved conflicts + pending assumptions + risk questions + recommendation.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- No objective is left without a numeric metric, a deadline, and a verification source.
- Every activity disguised as an objective was rewritten as a result.
- Each metric shows a baseline and a target; estimated values are marked [ASSUMPTION].
- Each ambiguous metric declares its operational definition (numerator, denominator, or unit).
- The Achievable criterion justifies realism against effort and constraints; forced targets carry an alternative range.
- Each objective is connected to a sponsor result (Relevant).
- Conflicts or duplications between objectives are flagged and resolved.
- No invented market or budget figures.
Expected deliverable: SMART objectives table (objective, metric, baseline, target, date, verification source) + resolved conflicts note + pending assumptions list + two to three highest-risk questions + recommendation of charter-ready or validate-baselines.
spec-gestion-proyectos_mapa-vision-porta:
[S·SITUATION]
Role: Senior strategy and portfolio management consultant with 15 years aligning organizations from the executive layer down to operational teams.
Activation context: The organization has a declared strategic vision (or one in the process of refinement) and a set of projects or initiatives underway, but teams operate in silos, are unaware of how their work contributes to the strategic "north" and leaders have no unified visibility of the cascade alignment.

- The active portfolio contains between 5 and 25 initiatives/projects.
- There are between 3 and 12 execution teams with differentiated responsibilities.

[P·REQUEST]
Build a Vision→Portfolio→Team Cascade Alignment Map that:
1. Links each strategic objective with the portfolio initiatives that drive it.
2. Links each initiative with the teams responsible for executing it.
3. Identifies gaps: objectives without supporting initiatives, initiatives without a clear team, teams with no strategic link.
4. Detects overloads and cross-dependencies between teams.
5. Produces prioritized realignment recommendations.

[E·EXECUTION]
ROLE: You act as Principal Strategic Alignment Consultant. Your responsibility is to produce a high-credibility executive artifact that a C-level can present to the board and that a team leader can use as a daily reference.

OPERATING ASSUMPTIONS [ASSUMPTION]:
- Current strategic horizon: 3 years (adjust if the user indicates otherwise).
- Alignment methodology: OKR/BSC hybrid as conceptual reference.
- Organizational maturity level: medium (declared strategy exists, traceability is lacking).
- Output language: formal business English.

REQUIRED INPUTS (the user must provide at least one of the three levels; if any is missing, infer with [ASSUMPTION] and flag it):
- Level 1 — Vision/Strategy: mission, vision, strategic objectives or pillars.
- Level 2 — Portfolio: list of active projects/initiatives with name, brief description, status and owner.
- Level 3 — Teams: team names, each team's mission and approximate available capacity.

EXECUTION STEPS:
Step 1 — Inventory and normalization
  1.1 List strategic objectives numbered (OE1…OEn). If not provided, derive them from the vision with [ASSUMPTION].
  1.2 List portfolio initiatives (P1…Pm) with status (active/paused/proposed).
  1.3 List teams (E1…Ek) with their mission summarized in one line.

Step 2 — Traceability matrix
  Build a cross-reference table OE × P with cells: ● strong, ◑ partial, ○ weak, — no link.
  Build a cross-reference table P × E with cells: R responsible, C collaborator, — no link.

Step 3 — Gap analysis
  3.1 Orphan objectives: OE with no P linked (● or ◑).
  3.2 Floating initiatives: P with no link to any OE.
  3.3 Disconnected teams: E with no P assigned (R or C).
  3.4 Overloads: E with more than [ASSUMPTION: 4] projects in simultaneous R role.
  3.5 Cross-dependencies: pairs (Pi, Pj) that share E in C role and have overlapping dates.

Step 4 — Cascade narrative map
  Draft an executive synthesis of at most 400 words describing the complete cascade: how strategic intent flows from the vision down to each team, with the 3 most critical gaps highlighted.

Step 5 — Prioritized recommendations
  Produce between 3 and 7 recommendations in format:
  [Rn] Concrete action — Expected impact — Suggested deadline — Suggested owner.
  Ordered from highest to lowest urgency.

Step 6 — Portfolio health indicators
  Calculate (or estimate with [ASSUMPTION] if no numerical data is available):
  - % of strategic objectives with at least one active linked initiative.
  - % of initiatives with a clear team owner.
  - Average overload index per team (projects in R / declared capacity).

EXPECTED OUTPUT (in this exact order):
1. "Normalized Inventory" section — three numbered sublists.
2. "Vision→Portfolio Matrix" table (markdown).
3. "Portfolio→Team Matrix" table (markdown).
4. "Gap Analysis" section with subsections 3.1–3.5.
5. "Cascade Narrative Map" section (executive paragraph).
6. "Prioritized Recommendations" section (table R1…Rn).
7. "Portfolio Health Indicators" section (3 metrics with calculated or estimated value).

EDGE CASES:
- If the user only provides the vision without a portfolio: infer 6–8 typical initiatives for that type of organization, mark all with [ASSUMPTION] and request validation before continuing with step 3.
- If there are more than 25 initiatives: group by thematic cluster before building the matrices; document the grouping criterion.
- If teams are not defined: derive them from the initiative owners; note that the team structure requires formalization.
- If both vision and portfolio are absent: halt execution, ask for at least one of the two levels with a direct question.

[C·SUCCESS CRITERIA]
✓ Each OE has at least one linked P or appears as a documented gap.
✓ Each P has at least one E in R role or appears as a floating initiative.
✓ Gaps are expressed in terms of business risk, not just as technical observations.
✓ Recommendations are actionable within ≤90 days for high-urgency ones.
✓ The narrative map can be read autonomously without the tables.
✓ No claims without evidence or without [ASSUMPTION] marker.

TRADE-OFF: Depth vs. speed — If the user needs the map in <30 minutes of work, skip step 6 and reduce recommendations to 3. If the user has a workshop session available, execute the full step and include facilitation notes for each recommendation.

DEFINITION OF DONE: The artifact is ready when: (a) both matrices are complete with no unexplained empty cells, (b) the gap analysis covers all 5 points, (c) recommendations have an owner and deadline, and (d) the user confirms that the normalized inventory reflects their organization's reality.

spec-gestion-proyectos_declaracion-alcan:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Project name and one-line purpose
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > Business objective, problem it solves, and expected result
- ENTREGABLES: {{ENTREGABLES}} > List of deliverables or expected products
- PLAZO_Y_ESFUERZO: {{PLAZO_Y_ESFUERZO}} > Target date and available effort in person-months
- INTERESADOS: {{INTERESADOS}} > Sponsor and key stakeholders who approve (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES_EXCLUSIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES_EXCLUSIONES}} > Known constraints, assumptions, and exclusions (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are defining the scope baseline for {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}. A well-built Scope Statement unlocks planning (WBS, schedule, budget in person-months) and protects the team from scope creep: it precisely separates what is delivered from what is not, sets verifiable acceptance criteria, and puts assumptions and constraints in writing before committing resources. It is the formal agreement between the sponsor and the team, and the reference against which every future change is assessed. The most frequent source of disputes is not what is included but what each party assumed was included without writing it down: that is why explicit exclusions and assumptions with impact are as valuable as deliverables.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Director (PMP) expert in scope management according to PMBOK, with practice in technology and transformation projects.
Draft a Project Scope Statement ready for the sponsor's signature, with this structure:
1. Product and project scope description, connected to {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} and the problem it solves.
2. Main deliverables (from {{ENTREGABLES}}), each with a verifiable acceptance criterion, acceptance owner, and definition of done.
3. Project boundaries: what IS included, without ambiguity.
4. Explicit exclusions: what is left out, including what is typically assumed included but is not, to neutralize assumptions.
5. Assumptions: each marked [ASSUMPTION] with impact if it proves false and validation event/date where applicable.
6. Constraints of scope, time, cost (in person-months, never prices), quality, resources, and external dependencies, using {{PLAZO_Y_ESFUERZO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES_EXCLUSIONES}}, with their effect on scope.
7. Full-project acceptance criteria and approval process with {{INTERESADOS}}: who reviews, who signs, in what order, and what happens if rejected.
8. Scope change control log.
Close with three to five open scope risks the sponsor must know before signing. Consider {{ADJUNTOS}} as context if provided.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: confirm business objective, deliverables, and constraints; if any piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask for it all at once and do not invent figures or dates (mark what is not confirmed as [ASSUMPTION]).
Phase 2 — Structure: derive deliverables from the objective and write a measurable or binary acceptance criterion for each one, avoiding "improve" or "optimize" without a metric; assign an acceptance owner.
Phase 3 — Delimit: contrast included vs. excluded until they are mutually consistent; declare assumptions and constraints with their impact and external dependencies.
Phase 4 — Close: write full-project acceptance criteria, approval process, change control log, and the open scope risk note.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every deliverable has a verifiable acceptance criterion (measurable or binary), an acceptance owner, and a definition of done; nothing descriptive.
- Boundaries and exclusions are consistent: nothing included appears excluded and vice versa; exclusions cover at least the typical false assumptions.
- All assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION] with impact if they fail and, where applicable, a validation event or date.
- Cost constraints expressed in person-months; zero prices and zero "free"; external dependencies declared with their effect.
- No vague verbs without a metric; every claim traceable to the business objective.
- Approval process names who signs, in what order, and the rejection path; change control log with columns (id, date, requestor, change, impact on scope/schedule/effort, decision).
- Closes with three to five open scope risks.
Expected deliverable: Project Scope Statement in sections 1 through 8 plus risk note, ready for sponsor review and signature.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estructura-desglo:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project to be decomposed
- ENUNCIADO_ALCANCE: {{ENUNCIADO_ALCANCE}} > Objective and scope statement (expected final deliverable)
- ENTREGABLES_PRINCIPALES: {{ENTREGABLES_PRINCIPALES}} > Known Level 1 deliverables or phases (optional)
- CRITERIO_DESCOMPOSICION: {{CRITERIO_DESCOMPOSICION}} > Decomposition axis: by deliverables, by phases, or by sub-projects
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Work package closing rule (e.g. estimable, single owner, 8/80 rule) (optional)
- EXCLUSIONES: {{EXCLUSIONES}} > Known out-of-scope work (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to convert the scope of {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} into a deliverable-oriented Work Breakdown Structure (WBS). The WBS is the scope baseline: effort is estimated on it, the schedule is built from it, owners are assigned through it, and progress is controlled against it. A well-built WBS unlocks reliable estimation, scope-creep prevention, and a shared language between team and stakeholders; a poorly built one propagates errors throughout the entire plan and makes them expensive to correct downstream.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director certified PMP, specializing in scope management and deliverable-oriented WBS construction.
Deliverable: numbered WBS tree + WBS dictionary + scope exclusions list. Steps:
1. Confirm the final deliverable and Level 1 deliverables from {{ENUNCIADO_ALCANCE}} and {{ENTREGABLES_PRINCIPALES}}; if the scope statement, the deliverables, or {{CRITERIO_DESCOMPOSICION}} is missing, ask before decomposing.
2. Decompose top-down in 3 to 4 levels following {{CRITERIO_DESCOMPOSICION}}, down to work packages that meet {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}: estimable, assignable to a single owner, and of a reasonable duration for control (8/80 rule as a reference, not a dogma).
3. Number with a hierarchical code (1, 1.1, 1.1.1), identify each node as a branch or leaf work package, and mark with a control account code the nodes where budget management is aggregated.
4. Write the WBS dictionary per leaf package: code, name, scope description, deliverable, verifiable acceptance criterion, owner, and assumptions.
5. Declare explicit scope exclusions from {{EXCLUSIONES}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpretation: restate the objective, list the detected Level 1 deliverables, and flag missing data; integrate {{ADJUNTOS}} as a scope source.
Phase 2 — Top-down decomposition: derive each level from the parent deliverable according to {{CRITERIO_DESCOMPOSICION}}; decompose by deliverable-nouns or phases, never by standalone actions; stop when the package is estimable and assignable.
Phase 3 — 100% rule verification: verify that the sum of children equals exactly the parent's scope, with no extra work, no overlaps between branches, and no gaps; correct before delivering.
Phase 4 — Edge cases: if a component is shared by two branches, extract it to its own package or document the interface to avoid double-counting; if a deliverable is uncertain, model it as a planning package pending refinement.
Phase 5 — Dictionary and exclusions: document each leaf package and declare what is out of scope. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] every piece of data not provided; do not invent owners or dates. Trade-off: prioritize depth sufficient for estimation over low-value exhaustiveness; exceed 4 levels only if control demands it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- WBS oriented to deliverables (nouns), not standalone activities.
- 100% rule verified level by level; no overlaps or gaps.
- Each leaf package is estimable, has a single owner, and a reasonable duration for control (8/80 reference).
- Consistent hierarchical coding (1, 1.1, 1.1.1); nodes marked as branch/leaf and control accounts identified.
- Shared components resolved without double-counting; uncertain deliverables marked as planning packages.
- Complete dictionary per package (code, name, scope, deliverable, verifiable acceptance criterion, owner, assumptions).
- Scope exclusions explicitly declared.
- Every piece of data not provided marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented data; missing data that limited detail flagged.
Expected deliverable: numbered hierarchical WBS tree, WBS dictionary table per work package, and exclusions list, ready to move to estimation and scheduling.
spec-gestion-proyectos_diccionario-wbs:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project whose scope is being documented
- OBJETIVO_PROYECTO: {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}} > Project objective or expected result, to anchor scope interpretation
- PAQUETES_WBS: {{PAQUETES_WBS}} > List of work packages at the lowest level of the WBS, with their account codes if they exist
- ROLES_EQUIPO: {{ROLES_EQUIPO}} > Roles or people available to assign as accountable owner and supports for each package
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Desired depth per card: summary or exhaustive (optional; exhaustive by default)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am documenting the scope of project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}, whose objective is {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}}. I have a decomposed WBS but its work packages only have names: without a common definition, every team member interprets the scope their own way, phantom deliverables appear, and scope creep erodes the schedule and budget. The WBS Dictionary converts each package into a verifiable contract: it is clear what is done, what is NOT, who is accountable, what is delivered, and when it is considered approved. This unlocks the scope baseline, reliable estimation, and formal change control (every request is measured against this baseline).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Director (PMP) expert in scope management and baseline construction according to PMBOK.
Generate the complete WBS Dictionary:
1. Restate the objective and list the packages from {{PAQUETES_WBS}} you will document; flag any ambiguous or inadequately granular package (heuristic: a package should be estimable and assignable to a single owner; if it requires multiple owners or more than one reporting period, it is probably too coarse; if it is an atomic task of a few hours, too fine).
2. For each package, produce a card with: (a) account code and name; (b) work description, with included scope and explicit exclusions; (c) verifiable and measurable acceptance criteria; (d) a single accountable owner plus supporting roles from {{ROLES_EQUIPO}}; (e) concrete resulting deliverable; (f) assumptions and constraints; (g) dependencies or predecessors.
3. Build a summary table: code, package, owner, deliverable, main acceptance criterion.
4. List gaps, overlaps, and ambiguities detected, marked as {to_confirm} to resolve with the team.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpretation: anchor each package to the objective; detect packages that are too coarse or too fine and scope overlaps between neighboring packages (two packages claiming the same deliverable = overlap; a deliverable from the objective with no package covering it = gap).
Phase 2 — Definition: write each card applying level {{NIVEL_DETALLE}}; assign a single owner per package (single-throat-to-choke rule); write explicit exclusions in every package whose boundary is typically confused with a neighboring one; formulate acceptance criteria as verifiable conditions (with metric, threshold, or verifiable evidence), never as opinions.
Phase 3 — Consolidation and verification: build the summary table, validate that each package has a single owner, that there are no deliverables without a package or packages without a deliverable, and report risky dependencies and potentially critical paths.
Edge cases: if a package has no account code, assign a provisional hierarchical one (e.g. 1.2.3) and mark it {to_confirm}; if {{ROLES_EQUIPO}} is insufficient to cover all packages, leave the owner as {to_confirm} instead of inventing names; if two packages share an owner, it is valid, but flag it if it concentrates risk.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each package has all 7 fields complete (code and name, description with exclusions, criteria, accountable owner and supports, deliverable, assumptions and constraints, dependencies).
- Each package has exactly ONE accountable owner; all other roles are support.
- Acceptance criteria are verifiable and measurable (metric, threshold, or evidence), not subjective.
- Explicit exclusions appear where the scope boundary is typically confused.
- Each package produces at least one concrete and identifiable deliverable; no deliverable is left without a package.
- The summary table covers all packages without omissions or duplicates.
- Gaps, overlaps, and ambiguities are listed as {to_confirm} with the pending decision.
Expected deliverable: WBS Dictionary in package cards + summary table + gap list to resolve, ready to fix the scope baseline and enable change control.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-trazabilid:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name and objective of the project whose scope is to be traced
- REQUISITOS: {{REQUISITOS}} > List of requirements (business, stakeholder, functional, non-functional, transition); with or without prior ID
- ALCANCE_ENTREGABLES: {{ALCANCE_ENTREGABLES}} > Committed scope and deliverables or work packages of the project
- CASOS_PRUEBA: {{CASOS_PRUEBA}} > Available test cases or acceptance criteria (optional; if missing, verification gaps are flagged)
- NIVEL_PRIORIDAD: {{NIVEL_PRIORIDAD}} > Prioritization scheme to use, MoSCoW by default (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Scope bleeds when requirements do not trace to a source, a test, and a deliverable: orphan requirements appear, verification gaps emerge, and gold-plating that nobody requested accumulates. A bidirectional Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) turns scope into auditable evidence: every line of work is justified backward to a need and forward to a test and a deliverable. This unlocks defensible change control, quality audits, and phase closing without surprises.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager specializing in scope management, with command of the Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) according to the PMBOK Guide and BABOK.
Deliver a bidirectional auditable RTM for {{PROYECTO}}. Steps:
1. Normalize {{REQUISITOS}}: assign a stable, unique ID (REQ-001…), rewrite each requirement in atomic and verifiable form, deduplicate overlaps, and classify by type (business, stakeholder, functional, non-functional, transition) and priority {{NIVEL_PRIORIDAD}} (MoSCoW by default: Must, Should, Could, Won't).
2. Trace backward: link each requirement to its source (business need, stakeholder, or source document). Mark as Orphan every requirement without a source.
3. Trace forward: link each requirement to its design or decision, its test case in {{CASOS_PRUEBA}}, and its deliverable in {{ALCANCE_ENTREGABLES}}.
4. Evaluate coverage: mark Gap if a test or deliverable is missing; mark Gold-plating if a design or deliverable traces to no requirement; assign each gap a risk (high/medium/low) according to the priority of the affected requirement.
5. Produce the table, the executive count summary, and the phase-closing recommendation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Inventory: consolidate and deduplicate requirements, assign IDs, types, and priority.
Phase 2 Trace backward: confirm the source of each requirement; list orphans.
Phase 3 Trace forward: map design, test, and deliverable per requirement.
Phase 4 Coverage: classify status (Covered, Gap-no-test, Gap-no-deliverable, Orphan, Gold-plating), assign risk to each gap, and record every inference as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 5 Synthesis: issue table, executive summary, prioritized remediation actions, and phase-closing recommendation.
Edge cases: requirement without a prior ID -> generate an ID; compound requirement -> split into atomic ones; no {{CASOS_PRUEBA}} -> mark all rows Gap-no-test; Won't priority (MoSCoW) -> exclude from active scope and annotate; missing essential input -> ask for it before executing, do not invent.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each requirement has a unique ID, type, priority, and coverage status; no requirement is left unclassified.
- Complete bidirectional traceability: no requirement without a source or without a destination is left unmarked as gap or orphan.
- Every assumption is tagged [ASSUMPTION]; no requirements or test codes are invented; missing inputs are requested, not filled in.
- Gold-plating (design or deliverable without a requirement) is explicitly flagged.
- Each gap carries an associated risk (high/medium/low) consistent with the requirement's priority.
- Expected deliverable: (a) RTM table with columns ID | Requirement | Type | Priority | Source | Design | Test Case | Deliverable | Coverage Status | Risk; (b) executive summary with totals (total requirements, covered, with gap by type, orphans, gold-plating) and coverage percentage; (c) prioritized remediation actions; (d) phase-closing recommendation: Ready / Ready with conditions / Not Ready, with justification.
spec-gestion-proyectos_proceso-control-c:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Project to which the scope change control process applies
- METODOLOGIA: {{METODOLOGIA}} > Management approach: predictive, agile, or hybrid (defines how the baseline and backlog are handled)
- ROLES_AUTORIDAD: {{ROLES_AUTORIDAD}} > Who approves at each level: PM, sponsor, Change Control Board (CCB), and its members (optional: if missing, propose a minimum structure [ASSUMPTION] and mark it for validation)
- UMBRALES_IMPACTO: {{UMBRALES_IMPACTO}} > Criteria separating minor, moderate, and major change (impact on schedule, cost, and scope) (optional: if missing, propose thresholds [ASSUMPTION] and mark them for validation)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
In project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}, scope changes arrive through informal channels and are accepted without measuring their impact, which erodes the schedule and budget (scope creep). A formal, lightweight, and operable change control process is needed that distinguishes routine decisions from those requiring a committee, protects the approved baseline, and leaves auditable traceability. Having this process in place unlocks shorter governance meetings, decisions defensible to the sponsor, and a stable scope for the team. Limit: the process designs change governance; it does not replace the scope management plan or the already-approved WBS/backlog it operates on.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director (PMP) expert in scope management and change integration under PMBOK (Integrated Change Control) and ISO 21500, with experience operating Change Control Boards.
Design a complete and operable scope change control process for {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}, coherent with methodology {{METODOLOGIA}}. Produce:
1. Textual flow diagram across phases (Request > Registration and triage > Impact evaluation > Decision by threshold > Baseline update > Communication and close), indicating inputs, outputs, and the responsible role per phase from {{ROLES_AUTORIDAD}}.
2. Change Request (CR) format in a table, with minimum fields: CR-ID, requestor, date, change description, business justification, affected scope/deliverables, urgency, and status (suggested states: registered > under evaluation > approved / rejected / deferred / regularized).
3. Authority-threshold matrix according to {{UMBRALES_IMPACTO}}: minor / moderate / major ranges crossing impact on schedule, cost, and scope, with the approver for each range. Aggregation rule: if a change falls in two different ranges, the higher one governs. Avoid everything escalating to the CCB.
4. Impact evaluation across the triple constraint (scope, schedule, cost) plus quality, risks, resources, and dependencies, with responsible party, response deadline (SLA), and response options (approve, reject, defer, or approve with conditions).
5. Approved-baseline update and traceability mechanism: CR number, baseline version (vX.Y scheme), link to the affected WBS/backlog item, and stakeholder communication record.
6. Anti-scope-creep control: how changes introduced without going through the process (gold-plating, verbal changes, scope expanded in execution) are detected and regularized or reversed.
7. Emergency path: how an urgent change is processed outside the committee cadence with traceable verbal approval and mandatory documentary regularization within a fixed deadline.
8. Example change log with 2 illustrative rows (one approved, one rejected or deferred).
Brand restriction: do not express real monetary amounts; use relative ranges, percentages, or levels. Mark all unconfirmed data as [ASSUMPTION].

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: confirm project type, methodology, and who serves as PM, sponsor, and CCB; if {{UMBRALES_IMPACTO}} or {{ROLES_AUTORIDAD}} is not defined, propose initial values and mark them as [ASSUMPTION] for validation.
Phase 2 — Design the flow: define the 6 phases with inputs, outputs, and responsible role; ensure triage filters duplicates, out-of-governance requests, and incomplete submissions before consuming evaluation effort.
Phase 3 — Calibrate authority: build the threshold matrix so that minor changes are resolved by the PM, moderate ones by the sponsor, and only major ones go to the CCB; document the aggregation rule and the emergency path.
Phase 4 — Integrate baseline and traceability: specify how the baseline is versioned, how the CR is linked to the WBS/backlog item, and how stakeholders are notified after each approval.
Phase 5 — Close anti-scope-creep: define the rule for unauthorized changes and the change log format with the 2 example rows; verify coherence with {{METODOLOGIA}}.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The 6 phases have an explicit responsible role from {{ROLES_AUTORIDAD}} and clear inputs/outputs.
- [ ] The CR format includes the 8 minimum fields and the status cycle, and allows a request to be submitted without ambiguity.
- [ ] The threshold matrix prevents everything from escalating to the CCB (PM for minor, sponsor for moderate, CCB for major only) and declares the aggregation rule.
- [ ] The evaluation covers the triple constraint plus quality, risks, resources, and dependencies, with responsible party, SLA, and response options.
- [ ] Baseline versioning and stakeholder communication are traceable (CR-ID + version + WBS/backlog item).
- [ ] Anti-scope-creep control defines what happens with unauthorized changes and how they are regularized or reversed.
- [ ] An emergency path exists with traceable verbal approval and subsequent regularization within a fixed deadline.
- [ ] The example change log has 2 coherent rows (one approved, one rejected/deferred).
- [ ] Coherence with methodology {{METODOLOGIA}} (formal baseline in predictive; backlog/refinement in agile; both in hybrid).
- [ ] No real monetary amounts; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: scope change control process document with a phased flow diagram, CR format, threshold matrix, impact evaluation scheme, baseline/traceability mechanism, emergency path, and example change log, ready to incorporate into the project management plan.
spec-gestion-proyectos_solicitud-cambio-:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Project the change is being requested for and its minimum context (e.g. "migration of the customer portal to the cloud")
- CAMBIO_PROPUESTO: {{CAMBIO_PROPUESTO}} > What is to be changed, in one or two concrete sentences (e.g. "add multi-factor authentication to all profiles")
- ORIGEN_DISPARADOR: {{ORIGEN_DISPARADOR}} > Why the change arises: defect, materialized risk, new requirement, regulatory or business change
- ALCANCE_ACTUAL: {{ALCANCE_ACTUAL}} > Scope committed in the current baseline that the change would affect
- CRONOGRAMA_ACTUAL: {{CRONOGRAMA_ACTUAL}} > Milestones, dates, or phases currently in the schedule baseline
- ESFUERZO_COMPROMETIDO: {{ESFUERZO_COMPROMETIDO}} > Effort or budget already committed, in hours, FTE-weeks, or relative range (optional)
- APROBADORES: {{APROBADORES}} > Sponsor, CCB, or roles who approve the decision (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to convert a change idea into a formal Change Request that the sponsor or change control committee (CCB) can decide on with full information in view. A well-formulated CR protects the project baselines: it makes explicit what is being altered, why, how much it costs in scope, time, and cost, and what happens if nothing is done. This unlocks a traceable, auditable decision, prevents silent scope creep, and leaves a governance record that sustains the integrity of the schedule and budget. The value lies in the approver not needing to ask for clarifications: the CR must be self-sufficient to decide.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager (PMP), expert in integrated change control per PMBOK, scope, schedule, and cost baselines, impact analysis, and CCB operation.

Produce a formal change request with these components:
1. CR Header: unique identifier, date, requester, project, priority (high/medium/low), change type (defect, requirement, risk, regulatory/business), affected baseline, and status (proposed).
2. Change Description: what is being changed, what explicitly falls within and outside the scope of the change, and which baseline it touches (scope, schedule, cost, or several).
3. Justification of 4 to 6 lines: problem or opportunity, expected benefit, urgency or decision window, and the explicit consequence of not approving (do-nothing scenario).
4. Triple-constraint impact table: rows for scope, time, and cost; columns for before state, after state, magnitude of change (delta), traceability (verified data or [ASSUMPTION] with its basis), and confidence (high/medium/low). Express cost in effort (hours or FTE-weeks) or relative range, never in monetary amounts.
5. Secondary impact: brief effect on quality, resources/team, dependencies, and risk, including new risks the change introduces or mitigates.
6. Alternatives considered: at least the recommended option versus doing nothing, with its trade-off; add an intermediate option (reduced or deferred version) if applicable.
7. Recommendation: a single clear option among approve, approve with conditions, defer, or reject, with its rationale, the conditions or assumptions supporting it, and next steps with an owner.
8. CCB Decision Row: approved / rejected / deferred, decision owner, date, and space for conditions, ready for signature.

--- E | EXECUTION ---

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to rigorously evaluate how a requested change affects my project before approving, rejecting, or deferring it. A change never touches a single variable: it moves the schedule, consumes effort, opens or aggravates risks, puts pressure on quality, and reshuffles dependencies. An honest impact analysis converts a request into a traceable decision: it exposes the real cost of saying yes, the cost of saying no, and the conditions under which the change is viable. This prevents silent scope creep, protects the baseline, and gives the change control committee the evidence it needs to decide. The value of the analysis is not in recommending yes or no, but in making the reasoning that leads to the decision auditable.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Certified senior Project Manager (PMP), expert in Integrated Change Control management, multi-dimensional impact analysis, and scope decomposition (WBS).

Produce a change impact analysis with these components:
1. Executive summary of 5 to 7 lines with the change, its dominant effect (the most affected dimension), and the preliminary recommendation.
2. Change framing: what is requested, its origin, the problem it solves, and what falls within and outside its scope against the current baseline.
3. Affected dependencies table: touched deliverable or task, link type (upstream/downstream), whether it is on the critical path, available float, and expected effect.
4. Impact table by dimension, one row each: schedule, cost, risk, quality, and scope, with quantified effect, evidence or [ASSUMPTION], severity (high/medium/low), and reversibility (reversible/irreversible once executed).
5. Comparative table of at least three scenarios (approve now, reject and maintain baseline, intermediate alternative or defer to later phase) with consequences by dimension and the objective trigger that would activate each.
6. Close: grounded recommendation, conditions and assumptions supporting it, implementation plan if approved (steps, sequence, and baseline re-planning), and open validation questions for the committee.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: delimit the change, its origin, and the problem it solves; confirm what falls within and outside its scope against the current baseline.
Phase 2 — Dependency tracing: walk through the WBS and the task network; identify which deliverables, tasks, teams, systems, and third parties are affected upstream and downstream, mark the critical path, and record available float.
Phase 3 — Evaluation by dimension: estimate schedule (days/weeks and consumed float), cost (incremental person-days and opportunity cost, never monetary prices), risk (new or aggravated risks with probability and impact), quality (acceptance criteria and technical debt), and scope (what is added, modified, or displaced). Note the reversibility of each impact.
Phase 4 — Scenarios: contrast approve, reject, and an intermediate or deferred alternative, with consequences by dimension and the objective trigger for each.
Phase 5 — Recommendation: integrate the analysis into a grounded decision with conditions, assumptions, and implementation plan.
Cross-cutting rules: label each statement as verified data or as [ASSUMPTION] and never present inferences as facts; when a piece of data is missing to quantify, declare it as [ASSUMPTION] with the value you assume instead of omitting the row; if an essential input is missing or ambiguous, ask for it before executing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
The analysis is complete when:
- It includes an executive summary of 5 to 7 lines with dominant effect and preliminary recommendation.
- The framing explicitly separates what falls within and outside the scope of the change.
- The dependencies table marks which ones touch the critical path and records float.
- The impact table covers all five dimensions (schedule, cost, risk, quality, scope), each with quantified effect, evidence or [ASSUMPTION], severity, and reversibility.
- Cost is expressed in effort (person-days/person-months) and opportunity cost, never in monetary prices.
- It compares at least three scenarios with consequences by dimension and an objective trigger for each.
- It closes with a conditioned recommendation, explicit assumptions, implementation plan if approved, and open questions for the committee.
- Each statement is labeled as verified data or as [ASSUMPTION].

Phase 3 · Quantification: estimate impact on schedule/effort/dependencies; all unconfirmed data goes as [ASSUMPTION]. Flag hidden dependencies where a minor deviation enables or blocks others.

The team needs a single, shared agreement that settles the question "is this done?" with evidence, not opinion. Archetype: Senior Agile Delivery Lead, team quality agreement facilitator, with mastery of Scrum, acceptance criteria, and scope management.
Deliver an actionable, verifiable Definition of Done document. Steps:
1. Distinguish three concepts to avoid the most common confusion: Definition of Done (applies across all increments), acceptance criteria (specific to each story), and Definition of Ready (entry condition for work). Explain what belongs to each and where the boundary lies.
2. Draft the DoD organized by verifiable categories, prioritizing {{DIMENSIONES}}: code and review, tests (unit, integration, regression), quality and security, documentation, deployment and observability, business acceptance.

You will draft the acceptance criteria for {{ENTREGABLE}} within {{CONTEXTO_PROYECTO}}. These criteria are the verification contract: the set of objective conditions {{CLIENTE_APROBADOR}} will use to formally accept the deliverable and close that portion of the scope. Well-crafted criteria unlock the milestone without friction, shield the project against scope creep, and eliminate the ambiguity that generates claims, rework, and payment disputes. Subjective or incomplete criteria produce the opposite: endless acceptances, disagreements about what was promised, and tacit acceptance through silence. The dividing line is one: each condition must be answerable with yes or no without two reasonable people disagreeing.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: PMP-certified senior Project Manager, specialist in scope management and formal deliverable verification, with experience translating vague client expectations into auditable acceptance conditions.

1. Header: deliverable, approver, unlocked milestone, and reference standard ({{ESTANDAR_REFERENCIA}}).
2. 6 to 12 numbered criteria. Each criterion: binary wording (passes / fails), measurable verb, concrete threshold or evidence; no subjective adjectives (translate "fast" to a time, "intuitive" to an observable test). Each criterion is independent: does not presuppose another is met.

- Every threshold or assumption NOT derived from {{ESTANDAR_REFERENCIA}} is marked [assumption to confirm] instead of being set unilaterally.
- If two criteria overlap, merge them into one; if a criterion is not binary or cannot be verified independently, rewrite or discard it.

Archetype: Senior Project Manager specialized in scope management, with mastery of MoSCoW (DSDM) and PMBOK scope planning.
