spec-gestion-proyectos_lista-actividades:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name and objective of the project whose schedule is being planned
- EDT_O_ALCANCE: {{EDT_O_ALCANCE}} > WBS with its work packages, or the scope statement and deliverables if no WBS exists yet
- ENTREGABLES: {{ENTREGABLES}} > Target deliverables that the activities must produce
- GRANULARIDAD: {{GRANULARIDAD}} > Expected decomposition level, e.g. the 8/80 hours rule (optional)
- ROLES_DISPONIBLES: {{ROLES_DISPONIBLES}} > Roles or team assignable to the activities (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Project {{PROYECTO}} already has its scope decomposed, but the work packages are too coarse to schedule, assign, and measure. Without a schedule activity list, durations cannot be estimated, dependencies cannot be sequenced, and the critical path cannot be built. A well-defined list unlocks the next phases of time management (estimation, sequencing, and schedule development) and becomes the unit on which the team reports progress. Frequent mistakes this task must avoid: confusing activities with deliverables, mixing granularity levels, leaving packages without coverage, and omitting external dependencies that later stall execution.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior schedule planner with mastery of the PMBOK guide and the WBS decomposition technique.
Deliverable: schedule activity list with unique identifiers, attributes, and preliminary sequence for {{PROYECTO}}, without durations or dates (prior input to estimation).
Steps:
1. Read {{EDT_O_ALCANCE}} and {{ENTREGABLES}} and identify each last-level work package; if an input is missing or insufficient, request it before continuing.
2. Decompose each package into activities named with an infinitive verb (design, configure, validate) that represent work, not deliverables, respecting {{GRANULARIDAD}} and maintaining a homogeneous level.
3. Assign each activity a unique hierarchical identifier linked to its WBS package code (e.g. 1.3.2-A10).
4. Document the attributes of each activity: scope description, assumptions, responsible party/role from {{ROLES_DISPONIBLES}}, predecessors with logical relationship type (FS, SS, FF, SF), and associated milestone.
5. Define milestones with zero duration in a separate list: start, end of each phase, approvals, decision points, and external or third-party dependencies.
6. Verify the 100 percent rule: activities cover the entire package without out-of-scope work or duplications.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: map last-level work packages and detect scope, granularity, or role gaps.
Phase 2 Decompose: derive activities per package with an infinitive verb and assign traceable identifiers.
Phase 3 Attribute and sequence: complete attributes, logical relationships, and milestones; mark [ASSUMPTION] where information not provided is completed; isolate external dependencies.
Phase 4 Verify: apply the 100 percent rule and list sequences pending confirmation.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each activity begins with an infinitive verb and represents work, not a deliverable.
- Each activity has a unique ID traceable to the originating WBS package code.
- Granularity is homogeneous and consistent with {{GRANULARIDAD}}; no package is left undecomposed.
- Each activity declares description, responsible party/role, predecessors with relationship type (FS, SS, FF, SF), and associated milestone.
- Milestones have zero duration and appear in a separate list that includes approvals and external dependencies.
- The 100 percent rule is met: no activity is surplus or missing relative to the scope, without duplications.
- Data completed by the AI is marked [ASSUMPTION]; dubious sequences and third-party dependencies are listed as pending confirmation.
- No durations or dates are included: the list is the prior input to estimation.
Expected deliverable: activities table (ID, WBS package, name, description, responsible party/role, predecessors + relationship type, milestone) + milestone list + block of assumptions and sequences to confirm.
spec-gestion-proyectos_secuenciacion-dep:
[inputs]
- LISTA_ACTIVIDADES: {{LISTA_ACTIVIDADES}} > Activities with identifier and name; duration if available (network logic does not require it)
- HITO_FINAL: {{HITO_FINAL}} > Milestone or deliverable that closes the segment to be sequenced; should have no successors within the segment
- RESTRICCIONES_CALENDARIO: {{RESTRICCIONES_CALENDARIO}} > Mandatory waits, windows, contractual milestones, or known deadline dates (optional)
- DEPENDENCIAS_CONOCIDAS: {{DEPENDENCIAS_CONOCIDAS}} > Precedence relationships already defined that I must respect without questioning their existence (optional)
- HERRAMIENTA_DESTINO: {{HERRAMIENTA_DESTINO}} > Tool where the network will be loaded (MS Project, Primavera, spreadsheet, or other) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team has the activity list but not its logic: without a properly typed precedence network the schedule calculates dates on invented dependencies, chains in series what could run in parallel, and inflates the total duration. Sequencing with PDM before calculating dates unlocks a defensible schedule, exposes where compression is possible, and prevents rescheduling due to misplaced dependencies. This network is the direct input to the critical path calculation, floats, and later resource leveling; a logic error here propagates throughout the entire baseline.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior schedule planner, fifteen years sequencing projects with the Precedence Diagramming Method (PDM) of the PMBOK standard, expert in distinguishing hard logic from optimizable preferences.
Deliverable: a complete logical precedence network, a table loadable to the destination tool, and a sequence diagnosis, without calculating calendar dates unless explicitly requested. Steps:
1. Validate inputs; if LISTA_ACTIVIDADES or HITO_FINAL are missing or ambiguous, ask for them in a single batch before continuing; treat DEPENDENCIAS_CONOCIDAS as non-negotiable data and RESTRICCIONES_CALENDARIO as context to respect.
2. For each activity define direct predecessors and, per relationship, assign type (FS by default; SS, FF, or SF only with physical or contractual justification), lead/lag in days with its reason, and nature (mandatory, discretionary, external, or internal); mark [ASSUMPTION] any unconfirmed dependency.
3. Apply network hygiene: every activity except the first with a predecessor, every activity except the last with a successor; the final milestone without successors within the segment; nothing dangling or orphaned.
4. Detect and report anti-patterns: redundant dependencies (transitively implied), cycles or circular references, SS/FF relationships without lag that should be FS, leads on mandatory dependencies (physically impossible overlap risk), and lags that hide an undeclared wait activity.
5. Build the precedence table and a prioritized backlog of discretionary dependencies that are candidates for parallelization or elimination, with the expected impact of each change on segment length.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm scope, constraints, and fixed dependencies; never invent activities or durations not provided; if two activities have no real logical relationship, leave them in parallel instead of forcing a precedence.
Phase 2 Network: walk through each activity, fixing relationship type, justified lead/lag, and nature; use FS as the default case and require physical or contractual justification for every SS, FF, SF, and every lead/lag; when choosing between chaining and parallelizing, prefer parallel unless hard logic prevents it.
Phase 3 Verification: run redundancy, cycles, SS/FF without lag, leads on hard logic, and lag-waits checks; consolidate table, parallel chains, sequence risks, [ASSUMPTION] list, and backlog of discretionary dependencies to optimize.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each relationship has a type (FS/SS/FF/SF), lead or lag in days with justification, and nature (mandatory/discretionary/external/internal).
- FS is the default case; every SS, FF, SF, and every lead/lag is justified by a physical or contractual reason.
- Every activity except the first has a predecessor and every activity except the last has a successor; the final milestone has no successors within the segment; no dangling nodes.
- Redundant dependencies, cycles, suspicious SS/FF without lag, leads on mandatory dependencies, and lags hiding undeclared waits are reported.
- Dependencies in DEPENDENCIAS_CONOCIDAS are respected; inferred ones are marked [ASSUMPTION]; no dependencies are forced without real logic and no dates, floats, or critical path are calculated unless requested.
Expected deliverable: precedence table (ID, name, predecessor, type, lead/lag days, nature, justification) loadable to the destination tool; summary of parallel chains and sequence risks; prioritized discretionary dependencies backlog with expected impact; and list of [ASSUMPTION] items pending confirmation.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-duraci:
[inputs]
- ACTIVIDADES: {{ACTIVIDADES}} > List of activities; each with optimistic estimate (O), most likely (M), and pessimistic (P)
- UNIDAD_TIEMPO: {{UNIDAD_TIEMPO}} > Common unit for all estimates (days, hours, weeks); must be homogeneous
- CAMINO_CRITICO: {{CAMINO_CRITICO}} > Activities forming the critical path for aggregating TE and variances (optional)
- FECHA_OBJETIVO: {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} > Duration or deadline against which to estimate probability of meeting it (optional)
- NIVEL_CONFIANZA: {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}} > Desired confidence for the reserve, e.g. 95 percent (optional; default ~95 percent → factor 1.645; 90 percent → 1.282; 99 percent → 2.326)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Single-point estimates tend to be optimistic and leave the schedule without a defensible margin against uncertainty. With three estimates per activity and the PERT method, expected durations are produced, dispersion per activity is quantified, and a justifiable contingency reserve is derived. This unlocks dates that can be committed to the sponsor, focus on the highest-risk activities, and a schedule conversation based on evidence rather than intuition.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project planner (PMP) specialized in estimation under uncertainty and schedule analysis.
Deliverable: three-point estimation table per activity plus a probabilistic schedule synthesis. Steps:
1. Validate that each activity has O, M, and P in homogeneous {{UNIDAD_TIEMPO}}; flag inconsistencies (O > M, M > P, negative values, mixed units) and do not calculate on broken data.
2. Calculate per activity TE = (O + 4M + P) / 6, σ = (P − O) / 6, and σ² (beta-PERT distribution).
3. Build the table: Activity | O | M | P | TE | σ | σ², ordering or marking those with the largest σ as the greatest schedule risk.
4. If there is a {{CAMINO_CRITICO}}: sum TE values (expected project duration), sum variances, and calculate project σ = sqrt(Σσ²), not sum of σ values.
5. If there is a {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}}: calculate Z = ({{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} − total TE) / project σ and translate it to an approximate probability of meeting the deadline.
6. Recommend a contingency reserve for {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}} (default ~95 percent → total TE + 1.645·project σ); report the buffer above the expected duration and list assumptions.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: reformulate the set of activities, the unit, and optional data; flag missing or inconsistent items and ask for them before calculating.
Phase 2 Plan: confirm formulas (beta TE, σ, σ²), the scope of the calculation (per activity only vs. critical path aggregate), and the confidence factor to use.
Phase 3 Execute: produce the per-activity table, then the project aggregate, the probability against the target date, and the recommended reserve; show key operations for auditability; close with [ASSUMPTION] assumptions and method limits (independence between activities; near-critical paths that may dominate actual duration; normal approximation fragile with few activities).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each activity has O, M, P, TE, σ, and σ² in the same unit; beta-PERT formulas applied (TE = (O+4M+P)/6, σ = (P−O)/6).
- Input inconsistencies (O > M, M > P, negative values, mixed units) explicitly flagged and no calculation on broken data.
- Activities with the greatest dispersion marked as the greatest schedule risk.
- If critical path exists: total TE, total variance, and project σ calculated as square root of the sum of variances (not sum of σ values).
- Probability of meeting the target date expressed with its Z and its approximate reading.
- Contingency reserve consistent with the requested confidence level; buffer above expected duration explicit.
- Key operations visible and auditable; assumptions and method limits labeled [ASSUMPTION].
- Missing data requested before calculating, without inventing values.
Expected deliverable: three-point estimation table per activity + probabilistic schedule block (total TE, project σ, probability vs. target date, recommended reserve with its buffer) ready to substantiate the schedule commitment.
spec-gestion-proyectos_calculo-ruta-crit:
[inputs]
- ACTIVIDADES: {{ACTIVIDADES}} > List of activities with duration and predecessors (e.g. "A dur 3 pred -; B dur 5 pred A; C dur 2 pred A; D dur 4 pred B,C"). If an activity requires a relationship different from the default, indicate it inline (e.g. "E dur 2 pred D SS+1" for Start-to-Start with lag 1)
- TIPO_DEPENDENCIA: {{TIPO_DEPENDENCIA}} > Default precedence relationship: Finish-to-Start (FS), Start-to-Start (SS), Finish-to-Finish (FF), or Start-to-Finish (SF) (optional; default Finish-to-Start)
- CONVENCION_FECHAS: {{CONVENCION_FECHAS}} > Numbering: whole days starting on day 1, base-0 numbering, or calendar dates (optional; default day 1, base-1)
- UNIDAD_DURACION: {{UNIDAD_DURACION}} > Duration unit: working days, calendar days, weeks, hours (optional; default days)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to know which activities cannot be delayed without delaying the entire project, how much float each one has, and what the committable delivery date is, in order to protect milestones, prioritize monitoring, and decide where to reallocate resources. CPM converts a list of tasks and dependencies into a schedule with early/late dates and auditable floats: the basis for committing to a delivery date and managing schedule risk before it materializes.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project planner (PMP certification, expert in schedule programming and the Critical Path Method).
Deliverable: complete CPM analysis of the schedule. Steps:
1. Reconstruct the precedence network from {{ACTIVIDADES}}, applying {{TIPO_DEPENDENCIA}} unless an activity specifies a different relationship or lag; use {{UNIDAD_DURACION}} and {{CONVENCION_FECHAS}}.
2. Forward pass: Early Start (ES) and Early Finish (EF). EF = ES + duration − 1; ES = maximum EF of predecessors + 1 (the initial activity starts on the base day). For non-FS relationships or with lag, adjust the corresponding predecessor constraint.
3. Backward pass from total duration: Late Start (LS) and Late Finish (LF). LS = LF − duration + 1; LF = minimum LS of successors − 1 (final activities take LF = total duration).
4. Total Float = LS − ES = LF − EF per activity.
5. Free Float = (minimum ES of successors − 1) − EF; for final activities use total duration.
6. Identify the critical path(s) as the sequence with zero total float; if there are multiple, report them all. Report the total duration.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Validation: normalize {{ACTIVIDADES}} in an activity-duration-predecessors table; detect circular dependencies, orphan activities (with neither input nor output), missing or negative durations, and references to non-existent predecessors. Phase 2 - Forward pass node by node. Phase 3 - Backward pass and derivation of both floats. Phase 4 - Critical path and reading: mark zero float, trace the path(s), sort by descending float and indicate where there is flexibility to reschedule or release resources; identify near-critical activities (low float relative to duration) as latent risk. Do not invent durations or dependencies: if a piece of data is missing or ambiguous, flag it and ask for it before calculating.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Table per activity with duration, predecessors, ES, EF, LS, LF, total float, and free float; all columns complete.
- [ ] Forward and backward passes arithmetically consistent (EF = ES + dur − 1; LS = LF − dur + 1; total float = LS − ES = LF − EF in each row).
- [ ] Free float <= total float in every row (control invariant).
- [ ] Explicit critical path(s) in sequence; each critical activity with zero total float; at least one continuous path from start to finish.
- [ ] Total duration matches the greatest EF and the LF of final activities.
- [ ] Near-critical activities flagged as risk; activities with the most float marked as rescheduling margin.
- [ ] Date convention, unit, and dependency type declared; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; missing data requested, not invented.
Expected deliverable: complete CPM table + list of critical activities + critical path(s) in sequence + total duration + float and near-critical note, ready to integrate into the project schedule.
spec-gestion-proyectos_compresion-crashi:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name, brief scope, and reason for compression: market date, contractual penalty, external dependency, regulatory window. Include current baseline end date.
- RED_CRONOGRAMA: {{RED_CRONOGRAMA}} > Activities with estimated duration and dependencies (predecessors, relationship type FS/SS/FF/SF, lag/lead), or network diagram / precedence table. Indicate duration unit (working vs. calendar days).
- DATOS_COMPRESION: {{DATOS_COMPRESION}} > Per compressible activity: normal duration, minimum accelerated duration, and normal vs. accelerated cost in effort units (FTE-day or hours). Mark "(optional)" if only fast-tracking will be evaluated.
- FECHA_OBJETIVO: {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} > Target date or reduction goal (e.g. "−15 working days" or "before 09/30") + nature of the goal (desirable vs. non-negotiable).
- TOLERANCIA_RIESGO: {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}} > Appetite for overlaps (conservative / moderate / aggressive) + hard constraints: resource caps, non-overlappable activities, fixed contractual milestones, freezes.
- PRESUPUESTO_COMPRESION: {{PRESUPUESTO_COMPRESION}} > Available additional effort cap (FTE-day or hours) and actual resource availability to accelerate. "No defined cap" if not applicable.
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Project {{PROYECTO}} needs to deliver earlier than planned and the decision of how to compress the schedule cannot be made by guesswork: each day gained has a different incremental cost and a different risk. Shortening activities outside the critical path does not move the end date; accelerating blindly drives up effort or introduces rework; overlapping without criteria shifts the problem to quality. A well-reasoned compression unlocks {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} with the least possible sacrifice in effort and risk, respects {{PRESUPUESTO_COMPRESION}}, and leaves an auditable trail defensible before the sponsor and the change control committee.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager (PMP) specializing in schedule planning and control, with hands-on experience in network analysis (CPM), crashing, and fast-tracking on real projects with finite resources.
Produce a schedule compression analysis with these numbered deliverables:
1. Critical path from {{RED_CRONOGRAMA}}: table with activity, duration, early/late start and finish, total float, critical path flag, and compression candidacy. Declare the calculation method and the baseline end date.
2. Crashing from {{DATOS_COMPRESION}}: per activity, cost slope = (accelerated cost − normal cost) / (normal duration − accelerated duration), maximum compressible days and slope; table sorted from lowest to highest slope with cumulative days gained and cumulative effort. Compress only critical path activities.
3. Fast-tracking: overlappable sequential activity pairs, proposed overlap (in days and as a % of the predecessor), days gained, and named incremental risk (rework, technical dependency, defect from advancing on unconfirmed assumptions), filtered by {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}.
4. Recommended step-by-step compression sequence to {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}}: order of application, re-verifying the critical path after EACH compression, declaring emerging parallel critical paths, and marking the point where the marginal cost or risk no longer justifies continuing (explicit threshold).
5. Net impact: final duration, days gained, total incremental effort (effort units), consumption against {{PRESUPUESTO_COMPRESION}}, change in risk profile, and decision recommendation (GO / conditional GO / NO-GO) with the 2–3 conditions supporting it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Network and critical path: normalize units of {{RED_CRONOGRAMA}}, calculate forward/backward passes, critical path, and float; exclude from compression whatever does not affect it.
Phase 2 — Crashing: calculate cost slopes, sort them ascending, and simulate incremental compressions re-verifying whether a parallel critical path emerges; when one emerges, compress the paths in parallel or stop.
Phase 3 — Fast-tracking: detect viable overlaps (only FS relationships convertible to SS/FF), size days gained, and name the risk of each one according to {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}.
Phase 4 — Combined optimization: interleave cheap crashing and low-risk fast-tracking until reaching {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} or until crossing the cost/risk threshold or exhausting {{PRESUPUESTO_COMPRESION}}.
Phase 5 — Synthesis: consolidate net impact, conditional recommendation, and suggested subsequent monitoring.
Rules: effort always in relative units (FTE-day, hours, slope index), never monetary amounts or the word "free." Mark any unprovided estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and any missing critical data as a blocker. If {{RED_CRONOGRAMA}} or {{DATOS_COMPRESION}} are incomplete, ask for the data before calculating. Do not invent accelerated durations: if missing, evaluate only fast-tracking and declare it.
Edge cases: (a) {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} unachievable within limits → report maximum feasible compression and residual gap; (b) no {{DATOS_COMPRESION}} → fast-tracking-only path; (c) resource cap reached → mark crashing blocked by resource, not by cost; (d) compressible activity outside critical path → excluded with justification.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The critical path is correctly identified with calculated float; it is justified what is compressed and what is not.
- [ ] Each cost slope uses the explicit formula and the crashing table is sorted from lowest to highest slope with cumulative totals.
- [ ] The critical path is re-verified after each compression and any emerging parallel critical path is noted.
- [ ] Each fast-tracking option names its specific incremental risk and respects {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}.
- [ ] The sequence reaches {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} or explains why not, with the residual gap quantified.
- [ ] Incremental effort respects {{PRESUPUESTO_COMPRESION}} or the overrun and its trade-off are declared.
- [ ] Effort in relative units, without monetary amounts or "free"; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; blockers listed.
- [ ] The recommendation is actionable (GO / conditional / NO-GO) with explicit conditions.
Expected deliverable: document with 5 sections (tables 1–3, sequence 4, net impact 5) ready to take to the sponsor or change control committee as an auditable decision base.
spec-gestion-proyectos_nivelacion-recurs:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name and brief context of the project whose schedule is to be corrected
- LISTA_ACTIVIDADES: {{LISTA_ACTIVIDADES}} > Activities with duration and dependencies (predecessors/successors and type FS/SS/FF/SF), e.g. a table A-B-C with days and links; indicate whether any activity allows splitting
- ASIGNACION_RECURSOS: {{ASIGNACION_RECURSOS}} > Resource(s) assigned to each activity and load by period (units or % of dedication); indicate whether a resource is indivisible or splittable
- CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE: {{CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE}} > Maximum capacity per resource and period (e.g. 1 FTE/day, 40 h/week) and availability calendar (holidays, absences)
- RESTRICCION_DOMINANTE: {{RESTRICCION_DOMINANTE}} > What prevails: fixed date (prefer smoothing) or fixed capacity (allow leveling); if both are hard, it will be treated as a conflict to escalate
- FECHA_OBJETIVO: {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} > Target end date or committed milestone to respect or renegotiate (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The schedule of {{PROYECTO}} has over-allocated resources: in certain periods, the committed demand exceeds available capacity, making the plan unexecutable and obscuring the project's true margin. Resolving this unlocks an executable plan, a defensible date commitment before the sponsor, and an honest conversation about the date vs. capacity dilemma. Guiding criterion: smoothing when the date is untouchable (movement only within float) and leveling when capacity is the hard constraint (moving the date is accepted). If both are hard simultaneously, the case is an irresolvable conflict through rescheduling: it is declared and levers are escalated, not forced into a silent solution.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project scheduler expert in the Critical Path Method (CPM) and the PMBOK resource optimization techniques (leveling and smoothing).
Deliverable: corrected schedule without over-allocations, with the smoothing vs. leveling decision justified activity by activity. Steps:
1. Restate the objective and declare the dominant constraint from {{RESTRICCION_DOMINANTE}} (does {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}} or {{CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE}} prevail?). If both are hard, declare conflict and jump to step 8.
2. Build the load histogram by resource and period from {{LISTA_ACTIVIDADES}} and {{ASIGNACION_RECURSOS}}; mark each period where demand exceeds {{CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE}} and quantify the over-peak (magnitude and duration).
3. Calculate the critical path and the total and free float of each activity (forward/backward pass). Distinguish total float (margin without extending the end) from free float (margin without affecting successors): only free float allows smoothing without cascade effect.
4. Resolve first by smoothing: reschedule non-critical activities within their free float to flatten peaks without moving {{FECHA_OBJETIVO}}. Prioritize moving those with the most float and the least impact on successors.
5. If smoothing does not eliminate the peaks, escalate to leveling: delay activities even if it consumes all float and extends the critical path; declare the new end and the days added. Consider activity splitting only if {{LISTA_ACTIVIDADES}} enables it.
6. For each move record: activity, shift in periods, float consumed, technique applied (smoothing/leveling/split), and effect on date.
7. Deliver resulting histogram without over-allocations, activity-by-activity decision table, and assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
8. Irresolvable conflict (date and capacity both hard, or critical resource required in parallel): declare it explicitly and present the menu of levers (add/hire capacity, split activity, fast-tracking, sequence, reduce scope) with their effect on date and load, for the sponsor's decision.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm data and dominant constraint; if {{LISTA_ACTIVIDADES}}, {{ASIGNACION_RECURSOS}}, or {{CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE}} are missing, ask for them before calculating and do not invent figures.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: load histogram + detection and quantification of over-peaks by resource and period.
Phase 3 - Network and floats: critical path, total and free float per activity.
Phase 4 - Stepped optimization: smoothing first (only free float, date intact); leveling only if insufficient (date moves, declared explicitly); conflict escalated if neither technique is sufficient.
Phase 5 - Verification: revalidate that no period exceeds capacity, that no move labeled as smoothing has exceeded its free float, and reconcile the net effect on the date.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Dominant constraint declared and consistent with the technique chosen (fixed date > smoothing; fixed capacity > leveling; both hard > conflict escalated).
- [ ] Initial histogram shows each over-peak with magnitude, resource, and period.
- [ ] Critical path, total float, and free float calculated and shown per activity, distinguishing both types of float.
- [ ] Smoothing attempted before leveling; each move labeled as smoothing does not exceed free float.
- [ ] All leveling explicitly declares new end and days added.
- [ ] Final histogram with no period above capacity.
- [ ] Activity-by-activity decision table: technique, shift, float consumed, effect on date.
- [ ] Critical resource conflicts in parallel or dual hard constraint declared and escalated with levers, not diluted.
- [ ] Figures traceable to inputs; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: corrected schedule + flattened final histogram + smoothing/leveling decision table + list of assumptions + (if applicable) conflict note with levers, all derived from the input data.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-hitos-milest:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project to be governed
- OBJETIVO_PROYECTO: {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}} > Business outcome the project must deliver
- FECHA_INICIO: {{FECHA_INICIO}} > Start date or schedule baseline
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > Duration or target closing date (e.g. 9 months, Q4 2026)
- RESTRICCIONES_CONTRACTUALES: {{RESTRICCIONES_CONTRACTUALES}} > Payment milestones, SLAs, committed or regulatory dates (optional)
- AUDIENCIA_GOBIERNO: {{AUDIENCIA_GOBIERNO}} > Committee or body that approves progress and decides continuity
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} needs a Milestone Plan that serves as an executive governance instrument: the tool with which {{AUDIENCIA_GOBIERNO}} sees real progress, approves deliverables, and decides at each gate whether the project continues, adjusts, or stops. A solid milestone plan unlocks fast decisions, aligns expectations between sponsor and team, anticipates bottlenecks from dependencies, and converts the schedule into a contract of verifiable results, not a list of activities. The difference between a milestone and an activity is the quality seal: the milestone marks an achieved and verifiable state; the activity describes work in progress.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager (PMO) with experience in portfolio governance and milestone-based planning (PMBOK, milestone-based planning, stage-gate).

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A traditional schedule inflates each task with hidden local buffer that still gets consumed (Parkinson's Law, student syndrome, harmful multitasking) and yet the project still arrives late. Restructuring the plan around the critical chain concentrates the protection where it matters: in shared buffers at the end of the chain and at its convergences. This unlocks a shorter and at the same time more reliable delivery date, and an objective control dashboard (buffer consumption) that replaces task-by-task tracking with a single project health signal.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project planner expert in critical chain (CCPM) and Theory of Constraints, with experience applying Goldratt's method in multitasking environments with shared resources.

Deliverable: critical chain plan of {{PROYECTO}} with sized buffers and buffer-consumption control. Steps:
1. Validate inputs from {{LISTA_ACTIVIDADES}}: each activity must provide duration, predecessors, and resource. If any is missing, ask for it specifically before continuing; do not invent. If there are cycles or hanging tasks in the dependency network, flag them and stop.
2. Cut each estimate to an aggressive but achievable duration according to {{CRITERIO_RECORTE}} (default median ~50%), recording the removed buffer per task. The buffer is not eliminated: it is relocated in buffers.
3. Identify the critical chain by resolving {{RECURSOS_COMPARTIDOS}} conflicts: the longest dependent sequence adjusted for resource contention, not the classic critical path. Document the criterion used to break each tie (chain priority, least impact on end, committed date).
4. Size the project buffer at the end of the critical chain and a feeding buffer at each convergence of a non-critical chain, via {{METODO_BUFFER}} (default SSQ), reporting size and method.
5. Schedule the staggered start of feeding chains so they finish just before their convergence point (plus buffer) and do not sow harmful multitasking.
6. Define buffer-consumption control with the three zones of the fever chart.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Restatement: summarize scope, activities, shared resources, and chosen criteria; declare assumptions as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Duration cut: table with original duration, aggressive duration, and removed buffer per task, in the time unit of the inputs.
Phase 3 - Critical chain: mark the sequence after leveling resources; explain how {{RECURSOS_COMPARTIDOS}} conflicts were broken and why it differs from the classic critical path.
Phase 4 - Buffers: calculate project buffer and feeding buffers with {{METODO_BUFFER}}; show the SSQ formula = square root of the sum of squares of the removed buffers and, as a conservative reference, 50% of that buffer. If a chain has one large dominant buffer, warn that SSQ may undersize and suggest a floor.
Phase 5 - Sequencing: staggered start dates and protected end date (critical chain + project buffer).
Phase 6 - Control: fever chart with green (observe), yellow (plan recovery), and red (execute recovery) zones, with numeric thresholds relating % of chain completed vs. % of buffer consumed.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:

- [ ] Each shared resource tie resolved with a documented criterion.
- [ ] Project buffer at the end of the chain; feeding buffer at each convergence.
- [ ] Buffer sizes calculated with {{METODO_BUFFER}}, formula visible, with 50% as contrast; warning if one buffer dominates the chain.

[inputs]

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A deterministic end date (a single figure) hides the true schedule risk: it ignores that durations are uncertain and that the critical path can change depending on how that uncertainty resolves. Simulating Monte Carlo on {{PROYECTO}} converts that misleading figure into a distribution of dates with associated probability. This unlocks defensible commitments before the sponsor, a data-justified contingency reserve, and the identification of the activities that truly govern the outcome, not just those on the nominal critical path. The value lies not in the final number but in the curve: where it concentrates, how long its tail is, and what stretches it.

Archetype: Senior schedule planner (PMP/PMI-SP) expert in quantitative schedule risk analysis according to the PMBOK Guide and the Practice Standard for Scheduling.
Deliverable: Monte Carlo schedule simulation report with commitment recommendation. Steps:
1. Validate RED_ACTIVIDADES: verify that each activity has consistent predecessors, declared relationship, lead/lag if applicable, and three-point estimate (O <= M <= P). 2. Configure the simulation with DISTRIBUCION, ITERACIONES, and CALENDARIO_LABORAL; anchor on FECHA_INICIO. 3. Execute the iterations: in each one, sample a duration per activity, propagate dependencies with forward pass (CPM), and record the end date and activities on the critical path in that run.

5. Calculate P50, P80, and P90 percentiles with their calendar date; if FECHA_OBJETIVO is provided, calculate the probability of meeting it.
6. Derive the recommended contingency reserve (P80 minus P50, in days) and the criticality index of each activity (percentage of iterations on critical path). Flag the highest-criticality activity as the first mitigation focus.

Phase 1 - Interpretation: restate the received schedule and list the sampling assumptions (distribution, iterations, working calendar, correlation). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any assumed value and do not invent missing data: ask for it.
Phase 2 - Plan: declare the sampling method by distribution (PERT-Beta: mean = (O+4M+P)/6, standard deviation = (P−O)/6; triangular: vertices O/M/P) and the CPM propagation algorithm per iteration. Indicate how you convert duration in working days to calendar dates.
Phase 3 - Execution and synthesis: run the simulation, sort results from lowest to highest for percentiles, translate days to calendar dates, and prioritize activities by criticality index. Deliver actionable interpretation of each figure and name the probabilistic bottleneck.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

Quality checklist:

- [ ] Distribution, iterations, working calendar, and correlation assumption declared; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].

- [ ] P50, P80, P90 expressed as days and as calendar dates anchored on FECHA_INICIO.
- [ ] Probability of meeting FECHA_OBJETIVO reported if provided.
- [ ] Contingency reserve = P80 minus P50, in days, with interpretation.

3. Calculate free float: FF = (lowest ES of successors) minus EF; with no successors, FF relative to the end date.
4. Identify the critical path (TF = 0, or the project minimum if negative float exists due to an imposed end constraint) and near-critical paths according to {{UMBRAL_CASI_CRITICA}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Input validation: confirm that durations, dependencies (with their type and lead/lag), and dates are consistent; if an essential piece of data for the network passes is missing, ask for it before calculating instead of assuming. Phase 2 — Network calculation: run forward pass (ES/EF) and backward pass (LS/LF), then TF and FF per activity; present a table per activity with the formula visible.
Phase 3 — Interpretation: classify critical / near-critical / with float, explain total vs. free with the schedule data, and translate each figure into a management decision.
Phase 4 — Prioritization and response: sort by impact risk, deliver specific actions for {{OBJETIVO}}, and handle edge cases (negative float, lead/lag, hard date constraints, multiple successors, parallel paths sharing float).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each activity has ES, EF, LS, LF, TF, and FF, with the formula visible (TF = LS minus ES; FF = lowest ES of successors minus EF) and the date convention declared.
- [ ] The distinction between total float and free float is explicit and translated into decisions (shared margin vs. own margin).
- [ ] The critical path and near-critical paths are identified with the threshold used and its justification; negative float, if it exists, is named and its origin explained.

spec-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-costos:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Project to be budgeted and its scope in one or two sentences (e.g., "e-commerce migration to a new platform, 4 months")
- PAQUETES_TRABAJO: {{PAQUETES_TRABAJO}} > List of work packages or deliverables at the lowest WBS leaf; indicate the deliverable or control account each belongs to if known
- RECURSOS_TARIFAS: {{RECURSOS_TARIFAS}} > Roles or resources per package with their rate or unit cost per hour/workday (only those you provide; missing ones are requested or flagged as a gap)
- ESFUERZO_POR_PAQUETE: {{ESFUERZO_POR_PAQUETE}} > Estimated effort or duration per package, in hours or workdays; if there is uncertainty, optimistic/most-likely/pessimistic range (optional)
- COSTOS_DIRECTOS: {{COSTOS_DIRECTOS}} > Non-labor costs per package: materials, licenses, travel, subcontracts ("No direct costs" if not applicable)

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need a project budget built from the ground up, not a top-down global figure. Bottom-up estimation aggregates the cost of each WBS work package up to the total budget: it is the most accurate PMBOK method because it forces you to price what will actually be executed and keeps every assumption visible. This unlocks a defensible cost baseline, separates the known from the uncertain, and allows scope, resources, or reserves to be negotiated with evidence rather than intuition. The value lies in traceability: every figure in the total must be traceable back to a WBS leaf with its effort, rate, and assumption.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager (PMP), expert in PMBOK cost management and in bottom-up estimation over the WBS, with practice in auditable cost baselines and in rigorously distinguishing between contingency and management reserve.

Produce a bottom-up cost estimate with these components:
1. Framing: confirmed scope, effort unit (hours or workdays), currency {{MONEDA}}, and the work-package level at which the estimate is made; explicitly declare what is out of scope to avoid phantom costs.
2. Package-level costing table: for each package in {{PAQUETES_TRABAJO}}, labor cost (effort × rate per role) and direct costs, with their assumption and a cell-level mark of confirmed data or [ASSUMPTION].
3. Aggregation table: sum of packages up through deliverables and control accounts to the total direct cost, with roll-up verified at each level.
4. Summary of three separately named figures: total direct cost; cost baseline (= direct cost + contingency reserve, calculated on identified risks per {{POLITICA_RESERVAS}}); total budget (= baseline + management reserve).
5. Confidence range of the estimate (e.g., −10% / +15%) justified by data maturity and the proportion of cost resting on [ASSUMPTION].
6. The 3 assumptions that most move the result, with their approximate sensitivity (how much the total changes if the assumption shifts) and the specific action to validate them.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix scope, effort unit, currency, and WBS level; if the package list, rates, or effort are missing, ask for them in a brief list before estimating. Do not proceed with incomplete data.
Phase 2 - Package-level costing: for each WBS leaf compute labor (effort × rate per role) plus direct costs; make explicit each cell's assumption and mark it as confirmed data or [ASSUMPTION]. If a role's rate was not provided, do not invent it or use a market reference: flag it as a gap and dependency to close the figure.
Phase 3 - Aggregation: sum bottom-up (package → deliverable → control account → project); apply contingency on identified risks to reach the cost baseline, and management reserve on the baseline to reach the total budget; keep the three figures separated, named, and never diluted inside the packages.
Phase 4 - Verification: confirm that the sum of parts reconciles at every level; declare the confidence range based on data maturity; list the 3 critical assumptions with their sensitivity and validation plan. Flag any package without effort, without a rate, or without a clear scope as an underestimation risk.
Edge cases: if two packages share a resource, do not double-count its cost; if a direct cost is recurring (monthly license), multiply it by the duration and state so; if effort comes as a range, use the most-likely value and report optimistic/pessimistic in the confidence range; if the reserve policy was not provided, propose an explicit criterion and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Never cite market prices or rates the user has not provided. Do not confuse contingency (known risks, inside the baseline) with management reserve (unknown risks, outside the baseline).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The estimate starts from the work package (WBS leaf), not from a top-down global figure or from higher-level branches.
- Each package separates labor cost (effort × rate) from direct costs.
- Each cell carries its assumption and a mark of confirmed data or [ASSUMPTION]; no invented figures, no market rates not provided; missing rates are reported as gaps.
- The aggregation reconciles: the sum of packages equals the cost of their deliverable and control account, and these equal the total direct cost; shared resources are not double-counted.
- The three figures are separated and named: total direct cost, cost baseline (with contingency on known risks), and total budget (with management reserve on unknown risks); contingency and management reserve are not confused or diluted.
- The confidence range is declared with its justification (data maturity, proportion of [ASSUMPTION]) and the 3 assumptions that most move the figure, with sensitivity and validation plan.
- Neutral and professional English, no emojis; all estimates in the stated currency.
Expected deliverable: package-level costing table (package | role/resource | effort | rate | labor cost | direct costs | total | evidence or [ASSUMPTION]), aggregation table by deliverable and control account with verified roll-up, summary of three separated figures, justified confidence range, and list of the 3 critical assumptions with sensitivity and validation action.
spec-gestion-proyectos_estimacion-analog:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO_NUEVO: {{PROYECTO_NUEVO}} > Name and brief description of the project to be estimated
- UNIDAD_MEDIDA: {{UNIDAD_MEDIDA}} > Parametric cost driver (e.g., function point, m², endpoint, user story)
- CANTIDAD_UNIDADES: {{CANTIDAD_UNIDADES}} > Total units in the scope of the new project
- PROYECTOS_REFERENCIA: {{PROYECTOS_REFERENCIA}} > 2 to 4 analogous historical projects with their known cost and size
- TASA_UNITARIA: {{TASA_UNITARIA}} > Cost per unit and its source (historical, benchmark, model)
- FACTORES_AJUSTE: {{FACTORES_AJUSTE}} > Adjustments to the analogous: complexity, location, inflation, team maturity (optional)
- NIVEL_CONFIANZA: {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}} > Expected confidence level of the range: order of magnitude, budgetary, or definitive (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need an internally defensible cost for {{PROYECTO_NUEVO}} before committing a budget baseline. A single technique is fragile: the analogous one brings historical realism but carries the biases of context and reference selection; the parametric one brings scalability but depends entirely on the quality of the unit rate. Triangulating both and reconciling them produces an estimate with an explicit range and confidence level, which unlocks the cost baseline, the contingency reserve, and the viability conversation with sponsors.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior project manager and certified cost estimator, expert in PMBOK analogous and parametric cost estimating techniques.
Deliver a triangulated cost estimate for {{PROYECTO_NUEVO}}:
1. Restate the scope and fix {{UNIDAD_MEDIDA}} as the cost driver, validating that {{CANTIDAD_UNIDADES}} is measurable and consistent with the unit.
2. Analogous method: contrast {{PROYECTOS_REFERENCIA}} against the new project in size, complexity, and context; discard non-comparable references with justification; apply {{FACTORES_AJUSTE}} one by one with their rationale and derive an adjusted analogous cost.
3. Parametric method: document {{TASA_UNITARIA}} and its source, multiply by {{CANTIDAD_UNIDADES}}, and obtain the parametric cost.
4. Reconcile both: if the difference exceeds 15 percent, explain the gap (drivers, data quality) and justify the central value and its weighting.
5. Express the result as an optimistic / most-likely / pessimistic range, with {{NIVEL_CONFIANZA}} and a recommended contingency reserve as a percentage with its calculation basis; close with an assumptions register and the 3 drivers that most move the cost.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Framing): confirm scope, unit, and completeness; if {{PROYECTOS_REFERENCIA}}, {{TASA_UNITARIA}}, or {{CANTIDAD_UNIDADES}} are missing, stop and ask.
Phase 2 (Analogous): table of references vs. new project + adjustment factors with rationale.
Phase 3 (Parametric): table of the unit model with the rate source and calculation.
Phase 4 (Reconciliation): comparison of both costs, gap analysis, and weighted central value.
Phase 5 (Range and reserves): three range points, confidence level, contingency with basis, assumptions register, and drivers.
Do not invent data: every assumption goes marked [ASSUMPTION] and every inherited data point cites its source. If references are scarce (<2) or the rate lacks a source, lower the confidence level and declare it. This is an internal effort and cost estimate, never a sale price or a commercial commitment.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Scope restated and unit of measure explicit, measurable, and consistent with the quantity.
- [ ] Analogous method with 2–4 references, justified discard of non-comparables, and adjustment factors reasoned one by one.
- [ ] Parametric method with unit rate, declared source, and traceable calculation.
- [ ] Reconciliation explaining every gap greater than 15 percent and justifying the central value and its weighting.
- [ ] Optimistic/most-likely/pessimistic range + confidence level + contingency with calculation basis.
- [ ] Assumptions register [ASSUMPTION] and 3 cost drivers; confidence level adjusted if data are weak.
- [ ] Zero invented data; no sale price or commercial commitment.
Expected deliverable: cost estimate report with analogous table, parametric table, reconciliation, range with contingency, and assumptions register, ready to support the cost baseline.

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before execution I need a defensible cost control reference. The cost baseline is the authorized cumulative cost S-curve against which I will measure actual performance with earned value (EV vs. PV). Building it correctly unlocks tracking by variances (CV, SV), forecasts (EAC, ETC, TCPI), and governance conversations with the sponsor and committee: without this curve there is no objective threshold to say whether the project is within or over budget, nor a basis against which to apply change control. --- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager specialized in cost management (PMP profile with practice in Earned Value Management and building authorized baselines).
Deliverable: the time-phased cost baseline (S-curve) with its period-by-period table, separated reserves, and control thresholds. Steps:

Phase 1 — Input validation: confirm scope, WBS, and time horizon; mark every assumed data point as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent figures (if a number is missing, ask for it or leave it parameterized). Phase 2 — Bottom-up aggregation: sum packages → control accounts → total; leave a roll-up audit trail per account.
Phase 3 — Time phasing: apply each account's spending profile over the period calendar, respecting its date window; document the chosen profile and why.
Phase 4 — Accumulation: calculate cost per period, cumulative, and % of BAC; derive the S-curve and verify monotonic increase.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:

- [ ] Each control account has an explicit and justified spending profile, not a default uniform spread, and respects its date window.
- [ ] The cumulative curve is monotonically increasing and describes an S shape (low → high → low slope).
- [ ] Reserves separated with their equation: BAC = base + contingency; Total budget = BAC + management reserve.

spec-gestion-proyectos_reservas-continge:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name, nature, and horizon of the project (e.g., core banking migration, 9 months). Determines the degree of novelty and uncertainty justifying the management reserve.
- COSTO_BASE: {{COSTO_BASE}} > Aggregated estimated cost without reserves, in the project's currency. MANDATORY; without it there is no calculation basis.
- REGISTRO_RIESGOS: {{REGISTRO_RIESGOS}} > Risks with probability and cost impact (quantitative). If only a qualitative estimate is available, indicate so to activate the top-down contrast. MANDATORY.
- APETITO_RIESGO: {{APETITO_RIESGO}} > Sponsor tolerance and degree of novelty/uncertainty (averse, neutral, tolerant). Calibrates the management reserve percentage.
- NIVELES_AUTORIZACION: {{NIVELES_AUTORIZACION}} > Roles authorizing consumption of each reserve (optional; default: project manager for contingency and sponsor for management reserve).
- MONEDA: {{MONEDA}} > Monetary unit of the project (optional; default: generic monetary units).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A budget without explicit reserves fails at the first unexpected event; one with a single undifferentiated buffer is spent without control and erodes the project manager's credibility before the committee. The distinction is structural: the contingency reserve covers identified risks, lives INSIDE the cost baseline, and is managed by the project manager; the management reserve covers unknown risks, lives OUTSIDE the baseline, and is released by the sponsor. Confusing them breaks the traceability of the cost performance indicator and turns the budget into opaque expenditure. This prompt sizes both reserves with a verifiable calculation basis and delivers the governance that makes them defensible in execution.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager and specialist in quantitative cost management (PMI/PMBOK 7, reserve analysis and expected monetary value).
Deliver a reserve sizing with its governance protocol. Steps:
1. Bottom-up contingency: for each quantified risk in the register, expected monetary value = probability × cost impact; sum the total and show the calculation per risk in a table. If the register is qualitative, also calculate a top-down value as a percentage of the base cost, explain the divergence between both methods, and recommend one with its rationale.
2. Management reserve as a percentage of the base cost plus contingency, justifying the percentage with risk appetite, novelty, and uncertainty; never an arbitrary figure. Anchor the percentage to a defensible range and explain why it falls where it does.
3. Layered budget: activity estimates → control accounts → cost baseline (with contingency) → total budget (with management reserve), with coherent arithmetic.
4. Usage governance per reserve: who authorizes consumption, what evidence is required (a triggered risk from the register for contingency; an approved change for management reserve), how each consumption is recorded, the threshold that triggers replenishment or escalation, and the review cadence of the balance.
5. Release of unconsumed reserves: rule and moment (phase close or project close), and how the balance feeds the cost performance index and cost variance.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm base cost, quality of the risk register, appetite, authorization levels, and currency; anything not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION]. If the base cost or risk register are missing, STOP and ask for them.
Phase 2 - Contingency: apply expected monetary value per risk (bottom-up) and, if applicable, top-down contrast by percentage.
Phase 3 - Management reserve: fix the percentage over base cost plus contingency, argued by uncertainty; declare the reference range used.
Phase 4 - Structure and governance: build the layered budget and the authorization, recording, threshold, replenishment, and release protocol.
Phase 5 - Verification: check arithmetic coherence (each layer sums to the next), contingency/management reserve separation, and traceability of each figure to its source. Work without sale prices or rates: only the project's monetary units.
Edge cases: risk with range impact (use expected and declare range); correlation between risks (do not sum blindly, flag the dependency); risk-averse appetite with a weak register (raise the top-down and mark it [ASSUMPTION]); management reserve the sponsor does not approve (leave the baseline intact and document the shortfall).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Contingency derived from the register with expected monetary value visible per risk (or justified top-down if qualitative), with a method recommendation.
- Management reserve as a percentage over base cost plus contingency, tied to risk appetite and a declared range, not a loose figure.
- Explicit separation: contingency inside the baseline (project manager authorizes); management reserve outside the baseline (sponsor authorizes).
- Correct layered budget: activity estimates → control accounts → baseline → total budget, with coherent and verified arithmetic.
- Complete governance per reserve: authorization, evidence, record, escalation/replenishment threshold, and review cadence.
- Rule for releasing unconsumed balance and link to the cost performance index and cost variance.
- Edge cases resolved when applicable; zero prices or rates; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
Deliverable: reserve sizing table (bottom-up and top-down contingency, management reserve), layered budget structure, and usage governance protocol ready to present to the committee.
spec-gestion-proyectos_seguimiento-presu:
[inputs]

Quality checklist:

2. Calculate and show the formula for the indices: CV = EV − AC, SV = EV − PV, CPI = EV / AC, SPI = EV / PV. Interpret each one in one sentence (overrun/savings, ahead/behind schedule). If AC or PV are zero or near zero, warn that the respective index is not reliable and treat the case separately.
3. Calculate the four EAC formulas and indicate the use assumption for each: (a) EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) — the remainder at budgeted cost; (b) EAC = BAC / CPI — the cost deviation is typical and persists; (c) EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) / (CPI × SPI) — cost and schedule both apply pressure; (d) EAC = AC + bottom-up estimate of remaining work — past trend no longer applies.

The three earned value baseline measurements (PV, EV, AC) are the foundation of all EVM management: without them, variances (CV, SV), indices (CPI, SPI), and forecasts (EAC, ETC) do not exist. Calculating them correctly and with traceability unlocks objective cost control, early deviation alerts, and progress reports defensible before the steering committee. The most common and costly error is contaminating the three measures with each other: EV must be valued at budget (never at actual cost) and AC must respond to a single, uniform accrual criterion. Phase 3 - EV: apply the declared measurement rule consistently across all elements, always valuing at budget.
Phase 4 - AC: consolidate the actual cost with an explicit and traceable accrual criterion.

--- P | REQUEST ---
