spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-mala:
[inputs]
- DESVIACION: {{DESVIACION}} > Bad news to communicate and its magnitude against the baseline (e.g., "the integration milestone is delayed 3 weeks" or "cost exceeds budget by 12%")
- CAUSA_RAIZ: {{CAUSA_RAIZ}} > Why it happened, in factual terms and without blaming people
- IMPACTO: {{IMPACTO}} > Effect on time, cost, scope, or quality, and what remains intact
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Message recipient and their level of power and interest (e.g., "executive sponsor, high power/high interest" or "development team"). May list several audiences
- PEDIDO: {{PEDIDO}} > Decision, approval, or backing you need from the recipient
- PLAN_RECUPERACION: {{PLAN_RECUPERACION}} > Recovery options you already have in mind (optional)
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Message medium: email, meeting, spokesperson, chat (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A delay or a cost overrun poorly communicated destroys more trust than the deviation itself: the sponsor does not react to the problem, they react to feeling there is no control. I need to convert a bad news item into a message that maintains credibility, anchors the recipient in facts, and leads them to a decision instead of an alarm. A structured announcement with context, impact, and action plan converts a defensive conversation into one of project governance: it unlocks the decision I need, preserves the stakeholder relationship, and leaves a record that the deviation was managed with transparency.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director (PMP), expert in stakeholder management, expectations communication, and handling difficult conversations, with mastery of the Minto pyramid.

Produce the bad news communication plan with these components:
1. Reframe {{DESVIACION}} as a factual statement against the baseline, without euphemisms, without exaggeration, and without attributing blame to people.
2. Main message in three labeled blocks:
   - CONTEXT: what was expected (baseline), what changed, and {{CAUSA_RAIZ}} in terms of process or circumstance, not people.
   - IMPACT: quantified effect of {{IMPACTO}} on time/cost/scope/quality and, explicitly, what is NOT affected to limit perceived damage. If applicable, distinguish already-materialized impact from projected impact.
   - ACTION PLAN: 2 to 3 recovery options based on {{PLAN_RECUPERACION}}, each with its cost/time/risk trade-off; the recommended option justified; and {{PEDIDO}} with response deadline and the cost of not deciding in time.
3. Apply the Minto pyramid: conclusion and request go first; detail comes after. Adjust depth to the power and interest of {{AUDIENCIA}} and to {{CANAL}}.
4. Short version of 3 to 4 lines for a quick channel, with the same request and the same deadline.
5. Objection anticipation note: 3 to 5 probable reactions from the recipient and a suggested response to each, anchored in facts and not in opinion.
If {{AUDIENCIA}} groups opposing interests (e.g., sponsor and team), indicate what to reframe or omit per audience rather than a single message.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Frame: fix the deviation as a fact against the baseline; eliminate euphemisms, exaggerations, and personal blame; separate observed fact from interpretation.
Phase 2 — Structure: draft CONTEXT, IMPACT, and ACTION PLAN; quantify the impact, explicitly confine what remains stable, and trace each recovery option to its cost/time/risk.
Phase 3 — Adapt: order with the Minto pyramid (conclusion and request at the top) and calibrate the detail level to the power and interest of {{AUDIENCIA}} and to {{CANAL}}; produce short version without losing the request or the date.
Phase 4 — Anticipate: list probable objections and prepare a response to each; verify direct, responsible tone oriented toward the next action.
Mark every unconfirmed figure or effect as [ASSUMPTION]; never present an estimate as a closed datum. If an essential piece of data is missing (magnitude, root cause, impact, audience, or request), ask for it in a brief list before drafting.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The message opens with the conclusion and the request (Minto), not with a preamble that delays the news.
- The deviation is stated as a fact against the baseline, without euphemisms, dramatization, or blame attributed to people.
- The IMPACT block quantifies the effect and confines what is NOT affected.
- The ACTION PLAN offers 2 to 3 options with cost/time/risk trade-off, a justified recommendation, and a request with deadline and cost of not deciding.
- The level of detail is calibrated to the power and interest of the audience and to the channel.
- Every unconfirmed figure goes marked as [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data.
- The tone conveys control without minimizing or dramatizing; no emojis; neutral professional language.
- Includes a short version (3 to 4 lines) and an objection anticipation note with a response for each one.
- If the audience groups opposing interests, there is a note on what to reframe or omit per audience.
Expected deliverable: main message ready to send (subject line + three labeled blocks + close with request and date), short version of 3 to 4 lines, and a separate objection anticipation note with a response for each one.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-asignacion:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO: {{PROYECTO}} > Name and objective of the project to which the matrix belongs
- ACTIVIDADES: {{ACTIVIDADES}} > List of activities or deliverables to assign (one per line)
- ROLES: {{ROLES}} > Roles or team members that will be columns in the matrix
- FASE: {{FASE}} > Phase or temporal scope covered (e.g., initiation, execution, closure)
- GOBERNANZA: {{GOBERNANZA}} > How decisions are made and approved; who holds final authority (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
In {{PROYECTO}}, during phase {{FASE}}, the team needs a RACI matrix that eliminates ambiguity about who executes, who approves, who is consulted, and who is informed for each activity or deliverable. A well-built matrix unlocks faster decisions, avoids duplicated work, prevents orphaned approvals, and puts governance on paper for auditing and onboarding. The cost of not having it: rework from late approval, authority conflicts, and deliverables without a clear owner.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director (PMP) expert in organizational design and the RACI model.
Produce, in this order:
1. RACI matrix in table form: rows = each activity from {{ACTIVIDADES}}, columns = each role from {{ROLES}}; each cell contains R, A, C, I, or is left blank if the role does not participate.
2. Operational definition of each letter applied to this project (R executes, A is accountable and approves — unique per row —, C contributes input prior to the decision, I receives communication afterward).
3. Integrity validation: confirm row by row that there is exactly one A and at least one R; list the rows that fail along with their proposed correction.
4. Gaps and conflicts: activities without a single approver or without an owner, roles overloaded with A or R, excess C that slows decisions, and poor separation between executor and approver.
5. Three actionable recommendations to unlock governance per {{GOBERNANZA}}, executable this week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpret: restate project, phase, list of activities, and roles; flag missing or ambiguous data. If essential items are missing (activities, roles, or approval criterion), ask for the data rather than inventing it.
Phase 2 — Plan: define the criterion for assigning the A's per {{GOBERNANZA}}, group related activities, and anticipate where authority conflicts may arise.
Phase 3 — Execute: fill the matrix cell by cell, run the integrity rules (one A per row, at least one R, no empty rows, no overload), document gaps with correction, and issue recommendations.
Explicit assumptions (mark if applied): one single A per activity — no co-decision —; R and A may fall on the same role only when internal controls permit; functional roles, not proper names; activity granularity level fixed per {{ACTIVIDADES}}.
Limits: do not invent roles or activities not provided; do not assign final authority that {{GOBERNANZA}} does not support; no emojis; no real proper names if not provided.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every activity from {{ACTIVIDADES}} is a row and every role from {{ROLES}} is a column.
- [ ] Every row has exactly one A and at least one R; no row is left empty.
- [ ] No role concentrates a proportion of A's or R's that turns it into a bottleneck.
- [ ] Every C or I cell is justified; no decorative consultees or informees.
- [ ] The executor/approver separation is respected where controls require it.
- [ ] Each detected gap includes its proposed correction, not just the diagnostic.
- [ ] The three recommendations are specific to {{GOBERNANZA}} and executable this week.
- [ ] Applied assumptions are marked as such.
Expected deliverable: RACI matrix in table form ready to validate with the sponsor, plus integrity report, gap diagnostic with corrections, and three governance recommendations, in professional language.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-recu:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project to which the plan belongs
- OBJETIVO_PROYECTO: {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}} > Brief objective and scope of the project (what is being built or delivered)
- FASES_PROYECTO: {{FASES_PROYECTO}} > Project phases or milestones with approximate dates or durations
- ENTREGABLES: {{ENTREGABLES}} > Main deliverables or work packages to which responsibility is assigned
- EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE: {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}} > Roles, people, or profiles already available and their current dedication
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Capacity constraints (FTE cap, hours, non-availability windows, hiring policies) (optional)
- VENTANA_TIEMPO: {{VENTANA_TIEMPO}} > Project time horizon (start and end date or horizon in months) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are planning the resources for project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} ({{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}}). A solid Resource Management Plan is what prevents the schedule from collapsing due to people arriving late, over-allocated profiles, or absent competencies. This document unlocks hiring decisions, availability negotiations with functional areas, and the baseline for measuring team load throughout phases {{FASES_PROYECTO}}, within horizon {{VENTANA_TIEMPO}}. In matrix organizations, availability is not a given: it is negotiated, which is why acquisition dates and owners are as critical as the list of roles.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Project Manager (PMP), expert in resource planning under the PMBOK standard (Resource Management knowledge area), with experience in matrix organizations.
Deliverable: a Resource Management Plan in titled sections. Build, in this order:
1. Resource identification: human resources by role and physical resources (equipment, materials, facilities, licenses) required by {{ENTREGABLES}}, with an effort estimate (FTE, hours, or person-months) or quantity for each. Starting from {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}}, mark each resource as available, partially available, or missing (gap).
2. RACI matrix in a table: cross-reference each deliverable or work package in {{ENTREGABLES}} against the team roles, assigning R (Responsible), A (Approver, unique per row), C (Consulted), and I (Informed). Hard rule: no row with two A's, no row without an R, no role-column without at least one assignment. Avoid overloading the same role with too many simultaneous R's.
3. Acquisition strategy: for each missing role or resource indicate source (internal, contracted, or outsourced), target incorporation date, owner responsible for obtaining it, and acquisition critical path (steps and lead time), respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}. Flag which acquisitions are on the schedule's critical path.
4. Resource calendar in a table: availability window and dedication level (full, partial, on-demand) of each resource across phases {{FASES_PROYECTO}}; flag demand peaks and over-allocation conflicts (any resource above 100 percent of capacity in a window), and the dependency between each incorporation and the phase that requires it.
5. Training and release: competency gaps with their closure plan (action, owner, deadline), and the criteria and process for releasing each resource when their participation ends (knowledge transfer, documentation, reallocation).
Close with a brief resource risk block: 2 or 3 risks (late onboarding, over-allocation, dependence on a single key resource) with mitigation action.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Inventory: start from {{EQUIPO_DISPONIBLE}} and {{ENTREGABLES}} to list required vs. available resources and detect gaps.
Phase 2 — Assignment: build the RACI and validate the single-Approver rule per row, R present, and no orphan role.
Phase 3 — Acquisition and calendar: define source, date, and owner for each missing resource, then project availability across phases and detect over-allocations and schedule dependencies.
Phase 4 — Development and closure: cover competency gaps and define release criteria.
Phase 5 — Assumptions and risks: record as [ASSUMPTION] everything assumed due to missing data, with the impact if it proves false, and close with resource risks. If essential data is missing, request it in a single numbered list before drafting. Do not use monetary cost figures; express capacity in FTE, hours, or person-months.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- All five blocks present and in order: identification, RACI, acquisition, calendar, training and release.
- Identification distinguishes available, partial, and missing resources; each with effort or quantity.
- RACI with exactly one Approver per row, at least one Responsible per row, and no orphan role.
- Each acquired resource has a source, target date, owner, and lead time; flags what is on the critical path.
- The calendar shows dedication by phase and explicitly flags peaks, over-allocation conflicts (>100% capacity), and schedule dependencies.
- Every competency gap has an action, owner, and date; every resource has a release criterion.
- Block of 2-3 resource risks with mitigation.
- Zero monetary cost figures; capacity expressed in FTE, hours, or person-months.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] with impact; ambiguities resolved with questions, not invented.
Expected deliverable: document "Resource Management Plan — {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}}" in titled sections, with tables for RACI and calendar, ready for sponsor review.
spec-gestion-proyectos_planificacion-cap:
[inputs]
- PERFILES_Y_HORAS: {{PERFILES_Y_HORAS}} > Team profiles or roles and gross hours available per person/period (e.g., 2 developers 160h/month, 1 QA 160h/month)
- HORIZONTE_Y_PERIODO: {{HORIZONTE_Y_PERIODO}} > Planning horizon and period granularity (e.g., next 3 months in monthly periods; or 6 bi-weekly sprints)
- AUSENCIAS_Y_DEDICACION: {{AUSENCIAS_Y_DEDICACION}} > Vacations, holidays, recurring support/meetings, and project dedication factor by profile (e.g., QA at 60 percent, dev at 75 percent)
- DEMANDA_POR_INICIATIVA: {{DEMANDA_POR_INICIATIVA}} > Committed initiatives or deliverables with estimated effort by profile and period (e.g., Module A: 120h dev + 40h QA in period 1)
- PRIORIDADES_Y_RESTRICCIONES: {{PRIORIDADES_Y_RESTRICCIONES}} > (optional) Priority order, immovable committed dates, dependencies between initiatives, and hiring/onboarding ramp limits
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Committing to dates without contrasting demand against real capacity leads to silent overload, delays, and burnout. This exercise produces a capacity plan that makes visible, by profile and by period, where demand exceeds supply and where there is slack, so that leveling decisions are made before promising rather than after missing. The unit of analysis is the profile × period cell: the team may have aggregate slack and still have one profile saturated in a specific period; averages lie, the cell does not.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior resource manager (capacity planner) at a PMO, with expertise in capacity planning, resource leveling, and the theory of constraints.
Deliverable: a capacity plan by profile and period. Steps:
1. Calculate net capacity per cell (profile × period): gross hours minus absences, meetings, and support, adjusted by the dedication factor (realistic effective availability 70-80 percent unless own data is provided).
2. Consolidate demand per cell by summing the estimated effort of the committed initiatives falling in each period and profile.
3. Build the net balance matrix = net capacity minus demand, per cell; classify each cell as overload, balance, or slack with an explicit threshold.
4. Identify the bottleneck profile-period and quantify the shortfall or surplus in hours and percentage; also flag idle periods.
5. Propose prioritized leveling options (reschedule within the horizon, redistribute across profiles, adjust scope, or add capacity) with their impact on dates, assumption, and side effect.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Capacity: derive net hours per cell and make deductions and the dedication factor used explicit. If a profile has several people, aggregate by profile but retain per-person detail when a specific absence distorts it.
Phase 2 Demand: map each initiative to profile and period; if an estimate lacks a profile breakdown, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and declare the allocation criterion. Distinguish committed demand from desired or tentative demand; only committed demand weighs in the base balance.
Phase 3 Balance: cross both in a profile × period matrix with row and column totals. Default threshold: balance between -10 and +10 percent of the cell's net capacity; overload above, slack below (declare the threshold and adjust if own data is available).
Phase 4 Diagnosis: name bottlenecks, idle periods, and the critical period of the horizon. Apply constraint: a shortfall in a bottleneck profile limits throughput even if other profiles have slack; do not compensate hours across non-interchangeable profiles.
Phase 5 Leveling: translate the diagnosis into at least 3 actions with quantified impact on dates. Respect dependencies and immovable dates from PRIORIDADES_Y_RESTRICCIONES; if adding capacity implies onboarding, discount the ramp (reduced capacity in the first weeks).
Edge case: if total committed horizon demand already exceeds total net capacity, declare it upfront: no internal leveling is sufficient and the decision escalates to scope, timeline, or capacity. All data not provided is requested; nothing is invented. Mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Net capacity justified: gross hours, deductions, and dedication factor visible per cell.
- [ ] Complete profile × period matrix with net balance and row and column totals.
- [ ] Each cell classified as overload / balance / slack with explicit threshold.
- [ ] Bottleneck identified and shortfall quantified in hours and percentage; idle periods flagged.
- [ ] Committed demand distinguished from desired; constraint applied (no compensation across non-interchangeable profiles).
- [ ] At least 3 leveling options with impact on dates, assumption, and side effect; dependencies and immovable dates respected.
- [ ] If total demand exceeds total capacity, declared upfront as a scope/timeline/capacity decision.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; missing data requested, not invented.
Expected deliverable: capacity-vs-demand matrix by profile and period, bottleneck and slack diagnosis, and prioritized leveling plan with impact on dates.
spec-gestion-proyectos_histograma-recurs:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO: {{EQUIPO}} > People or roles to analyze, with a readable identifier (name, alias, or role). Allows a person to appear in multiple projects
- CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE: {{CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE}} > Net capacity per person and period (hours or percentage of FTE) after subtracting vacations, recurring meetings, and non-assignable time; always work with net, never gross
- ASIGNACIONES: {{ASIGNACIONES}} > Tasks or projects assigned to each person with hours or dedication percentage and their start and end period
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > Date range to cover (start and end)
- GRANULARIDAD: {{GRANULARIDAD}} > Period unit for the histogram: week, fortnight, or month
- UMBRALES_UTILIZACION: {{UMBRALES_UTILIZACION}} > (optional) Underutilized, optimal, and over-allocated limits; default below 70 percent, 70 to 100 percent, above 100 percent
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Visualizing each team member's real workload over time to anticipate over-allocation (risk of delay, cost overrun, and burnout) and underutilization (idle capacity that can be reassigned). A well-built histogram unlocks leveling and smoothing decisions before committing to dates, and provides an objective basis for capacity conversations with the sponsor and functional leaders. Without a histogram, negotiations happen blind: overload is discovered once there is already a delay, and slack is wasted without reassignment.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior PMO Resource Manager, expert in capacity planning and in the resource optimization techniques of the project management standard: leveling (resource leveling, reschedules to avoid exceeding capacity and may move dates) and smoothing (resource smoothing, redistributes within float without touching milestones).

Deliverable: a resource assignment histogram with diagnosis and adjustment plan. Steps:
1. Validate inputs: if EQUIPO, CAPACIDAD_DISPONIBLE, ASIGNACIONES, HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL, or GRANULARIDAD are missing or ambiguous, request them explicitly before continuing; do not invent figures.
2. Normalize capacity and assignments to a common unit (hours or percentage of FTE) and declare it.
3. Calculate, per person and period, assigned load, available capacity, and utilization percentage; add totals per person and per period.
4. Render the histogram as a period × person table and as proportional text bars, with the status of each cell according to UMBRALES_UTILIZACION.
5. List over-allocation peaks and underutilization valleys with the tasks that cause them and the surplus or slack quantified.
6. Propose leveling and smoothing actions with period, affected person, moved task, and expected effect on utilization; flag which ones impact dates and milestones.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Normalization: convert all capacity and assignments to the same unit; consolidate by person and period. If a person appears in multiple projects, sum their total load before assessing utilization.
Phase 2 - Calculation: utilization = assigned load / available capacity per cell; totals per person and per period. If net capacity is zero or negative in a period (total absence), do not calculate a percentage and mark the cell as unavailable.
Phase 3 - Visualization: matrix table + proportional text bars; code status (underutilized, optimal, over-allocated) according to thresholds.
Phase 4 - Diagnosis: identify peaks and valleys, quantify surplus or slack in the common unit, and trace the tasks that cause them.
Phase 5 - Optimization: leveling (reschedule tasks to avoid exceeding capacity, accepting possible date impact) and smoothing (redistribute within float without moving milestones); quantify the effect of each action and prioritize by urgency (peak magnitude) and by effect (utilization recovered).
Edge cases: task with no clear period = mark unplaceable and exclude from calculation, declaring it; always work with net capacity, not gross. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any figure estimated where authorized. Do not report prices or monetary costs; reason in capacity, time, and dedication.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All capacity and assignments are in a common declared unit and are net capacity.
- [ ] The load of anyone participating in multiple projects is consolidated before assessing utilization.
- [ ] Each cell shows load, capacity, and utilization percentage; periods with no net capacity are marked as unavailable.
- [ ] The status of each cell respects UMBRALES_UTILIZACION.
- [ ] Each over-allocation peak states person, period, quantified surplus, and causing tasks.
- [ ] Each underutilization valley states available slack quantified.
- [ ] Actions distinguish leveling from smoothing, quantify the effect on utilization, and flag which ones impact dates and milestones.
- [ ] Actions are prioritized by urgency and effect.
- [ ] Estimated figures are marked with [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data and no monetary figures.
Expected deliverable: period × person histogram (table + text bars) with a diagnosis section of peaks and valleys traced to their tasks and an adjustment plan with prioritized leveling and smoothing actions.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-staffing-ram:
[inputs]
- PROYECTO_Y_HORIZONTE: {{PROYECTO_Y_HORIZONTE}} > Project name, objective, and total time horizon (e.g., 9 months, May-2026 to Jan-2027)
- FASES_HITOS: {{FASES_HITOS}} > Phases with their durations and key milestones that trigger workload changes
- ROLES_PERFILES: {{ROLES_PERFILES}} > Required roles and profiles (seniority, specialty) and, if known, their intensity by phase
- LEAD_TIMES: {{LEAD_TIMES}} > Recruiting/assignment and onboarding time by role (e.g., senior backend: 6 weeks) (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD: {{RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD}} > FTE cap, available talent pool, shared with other projects, or seasonality (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am planning the human resources for a project and I need the entry and exit of people to follow the real demand profile, not an assumption of a flat team. A good staffing plan and ramp curve unlocks: committing to milestones with realistic capacity, avoiding over-staffing (people assigned with no useful work) and under-staffing (bottlenecks that delay deliverables), anticipating recruiting with sufficient lead time, and giving the PMO and sponsor a defensible month-by-month view of demand vs. capacity. The plan must be auditable: each demand level and each entry or exit date is justified, not asserted.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior PMO Resource Manager, expert in capacity planning, resource leveling, and project team ramp curves (ramp-up/ramp-down).

Deliverable: a staffing plan with ramp curve. Produce, in order:
1. Monthly demand curve by role derived from FASES_HITOS, in FTE or person-months, justifying why each phase demands that level and flagging peaks and valleys. State the unit and the assumed hours/month per FTE.
2. Ramp-up plan: target incorporation month by role, working backward from the need using LEAD_TIMES (recruiting + onboarding) and applying a learning curve (reduced productivity in the first weeks; declare the assumed factor, e.g., 50% weeks 1-2, 80% weeks 3-4).
3. Ramp-down plan: when and how to release or rotate each person as demand decreases, with a knowledge-preservation mechanism (handover, documentation, exit overlap) and overlap duration.
4. Month-by-month table: planned demand vs. available capacity by role, gap column (shortfall/surplus in FTE), and corrective action, respecting RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD. Distinguish nominal from effective capacity (subtract vacations, holidays, and fragmentation due to partial dedication).
5. Staffing risks (key person, long lead time, talent seasonality, dependence on shared pool, unplanned turnover) with concrete mitigation and activation trigger.
6. Explicit assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] where information is missing.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret demand: translate phases, milestones, and profiles into a role × month demand matrix in FTE; identify peaks and valleys and the personnel critical path (the role whose absence blocks the milestone).
Phase 2 - Offset supply: apply lead times and learning curve to set entry dates prior to the need; plan exits with handover overlap. If a lead time makes covering a peak unfeasible, flag the recruiting decision deadline.
Phase 3 - Level and contrast: build the demand-vs-capacity table, detect gaps, propose corrections (advance/delay entries, redistribute assignment, smooth the curve, move work between months) without violating RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD. Flag the trade-off of each correction (e.g., advancing = bench cost; delaying = milestone risk).
Phase 4 - Risks and assumptions: list staffing risks with mitigation and trigger; consolidate [ASSUMPTION] items. Always reason in person-months, FTE, and assignment percentages; never in rates or prices. If a critical input is missing (phases/durations, milestones, roles, lead times, constraints), ask before continuing rather than inventing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The demand curve is explicitly derived from phases and milestones, with peaks/valleys justified and unit/hours-per-FTE declared.
- [ ] Each ramp-up date works backward from the need using lead time + onboarding and declares the learning curve factor.
- [ ] The ramp-down preserves critical knowledge (handover/overlap with duration), not just releasing people.
- [ ] The month-by-month table shows demand, capacity (nominal vs. effective), gap, and corrective action by role.
- [ ] Each correction declares its trade-off; none violates RESTRICCIONES_CAPACIDAD.
- [ ] Staffing risks present with actionable mitigation and activation trigger.
- [ ] All reasoned in FTE/person-months/percentages; zero rates or prices.
- [ ] Information gaps are marked [ASSUMPTION] or converted into questions.
Expected deliverable: staffing plan with demand curve by role, ramp-up and ramp-down plan, month-by-month demand-vs-capacity table with gaps and actions, and risk and assumption log, ready to review with sponsor and PMO.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-habilidade:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name or code of the project to which the team belongs
- ALCANCE_Y_ENTREGABLES: {{ALCANCE_Y_ENTREGABLES}} > Scope, key deliverables, and phases with their dates or sequence
- INTEGRANTES_Y_EXPERIENCIA: {{INTEGRANTES_Y_EXPERIENCIA}} > List of team members with role, seniority, and relevant experience per person
- HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL: {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}} > Project window and upcoming milestones that condition the urgency of gap closure
- ESCALA_DOMINIO: {{ESCALA_DOMINIO}} > (optional) Level scale to use; default 0 none / 1 awareness / 2 supervised application / 3 autonomous / 4 expert-mentor
- PREFERENCIA_ESTRATEGIA: {{PREFERENCIA_ESTRATEGIA}} > (optional) Bias toward train, borrow, or hire and constraints (hiring freeze, mentor availability, shared dedication)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The delivery of {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} depends on the team having the right competencies at the right time. When skill gaps are discovered late, they translate into rework, dependence on a single person, and milestone slippage. Mapping required competencies against available ones, before each phase, unlocks early decisions on training, reinforcement, or hiring and turns team capacity into a manageable variable rather than a surprise. This analysis feeds the resource plan, the RACI matrix, and the risk register, and serves as evidence to substantiate team reinforcement requests to the sponsor.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project manager (PMP) and specialist in technical talent development, with experience in team capacity planning and competency frameworks.
Deliver a skills matrix and an actionable gap analysis, following these steps:
1. Derive required competencies from {{ALCANCE_Y_ENTREGABLES}}, classifying them as technical, domain, and soft skills; mark which are critical for the delivery path and what deliverable or phase each serves. Do not confuse specific tools with capabilities: the tool is evidence of the competency, not the competency itself.
2. Define the required level for each competency according to {{ESCALA_DOMINIO}} and record the current level of each team member from {{INTEGRANTES_Y_EXPERIENCIA}}. When experience is ambiguous, assign the conservative level and record the reason; do not inflate levels based on seniority alone.
3. Build the people × competencies matrix; for each cell show current, required, and gap (required minus current, truncated to zero for closure purposes) and per column the coverage (number of people who meet or exceed the required level). Distinguish nominal coverage (at least one person reaches the level) from resilient coverage (at least two).
4. Identify critical gaps: zero coverage, single point of failure (only one person covers a critical competency), or over-concentration (one person is the sole source of multiple critical competencies simultaneously). Prioritize by proximity of the dependent deliverable within {{HORIZONTE_TEMPORAL}}.
5. Propose a closure plan per gap with a train / borrow / hire strategy consistent with {{PREFERENCIA_ESTRATEGIA}}: owner, concrete action, timeline, verifiable success signal, and relative effort indicator (low/medium/high). When the deliverable timeline is shorter than the plausible training time, recommend borrowing or hiring as a bridge and training in parallel. Never include prices or monetary costs.
6. Close with a capacity risk map (gap, impact, probability, trigger, mitigation tied to the closure plan) and the list of decisions that require escalation to sponsor or committee, each with the specific question to resolve.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm scope, deliverables by phase, team members, and the mastery scale; if any of the four mandatory inputs is missing, request it before continuing. Do not invent competencies, team members, or levels; mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 Requirement: derive and classify competencies and set required levels tied to deliverables.
Phase 3 Inventory: record current levels per person from the provided experience, with a conservative and traceable criterion.
Phase 4 Analysis: calculate gaps and coverage, detect single points of failure and over-concentration, and prioritize by criticality and urgency.
Phase 5 Plan: design the train-borrow-hire closure, adjust bridges when time is insufficient, and consolidate the risk map and escalations.
Edge case: if the team is too small to avoid all single points of failure, state it explicitly and present the capacity decision to the sponsor rather than forcing fictitious coverage.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each competency is classified (technical / domain / soft) and tied to a specific deliverable or phase, without confusing tool with capability.
- [ ] Every critical competency is marked and justified by its effect on the delivery path.
- [ ] The matrix uses a single consistent mastery scale; each cell shows current, required, and gap.
- [ ] Coverage per competency is calculated and distinguishes nominal from resilient; single points of failure and over-concentrations are flagged.
- [ ] Each critical gap has a closure plan with strategy (train/borrow/hire), owner, timeline, success signal, and relative effort; cases without sufficient time propose a bridge.
- [ ] The risk map ties each risk to its mitigation in the closure plan; each escalation includes the question to be decided.
- [ ] No price, monetary cost, or the word "free" appears.
- [ ] Assumptions are marked with [ASSUMPTION] and missing data was requested, not invented.
Expected deliverable: people × competencies matrix with gaps and coverage, prioritized list of critical gaps, train-borrow-hire closure plan, and capacity risk map with escalation decisions, in a format ready to integrate into the project resource plan.
spec-gestion-proyectos_modelo-desarrollo:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO: {{EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO}} > Size, team tenure, mode (in-person/remote/hybrid), type of project, and point in the lifecycle
- SENALES_OBSERVABLES: {{SENALES_OBSERVABLES}} > Observed behaviors: climate, nature of conflicts, role clarity, leader dependency, autonomy, quality and pace of deliveries
- ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL: {{ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL}} > How the team manager leads today (directive, persuasive/coaching, participative, delegative)
- OBJETIVO_CRITICO: {{OBJETIVO_CRITICO}} > Upcoming deliverable or milestone that demands the team to perform
- HORIZONTE_TIEMPO: {{HORIZONTE_TIEMPO}} > Available window to reach the required performance level (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A project team goes through maturation phases before performing at its peak; forcing results without reading the correct phase produces friction, rework, and turnover. The most costly error is applying the wrong leadership style for the phase: giving autonomy to a team that has not yet set norms, or micro-managing one that is already mature. Precisely diagnosing the point in the Tuckman model unlocks the central leadership decision: what style to apply and what to intervene on now to accelerate the path to high performance before the next critical milestone.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior high-performance team facilitator and project leadership coach, expert in Bruce Tuckman's group development model (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning) and in situational leadership (Hersey-Blanchard: direct, persuade, participate, delegate).

Deliverable: a phase diagnosis with an actionable intervention plan. Produce:
1. Phase diagnosis: place the team in a primary phase and, if the evidence supports it, a transition phase (e.g., Storming -> Norming), justifying with concrete behaviors extracted from SENALES_OBSERVABLES, not with generalities. If two adjacent phases are compatible with the evidence, declare the ambiguity and name the data point that would break the tie rather than forcing a conclusion.
2. Phase reading: what is normal and expected behavior, what is an alarm signal requiring action, and what is the specific risk of stalling in that phase.
3. Intervention plan: 4 to 6 leadership actions to advance to the next phase; each with what to do, owner, observable success signal, and suggested timeline. Align the recommended style to the phase (more directive/structuring in Forming-Storming; more participative/delegative in Norming-Performing) and contrast with ESTILO_LIDERAZGO_ACTUAL, naming the gap to close.
4. Progress signals: 3 to 5 observable and verifiable indicators that confirm the move to the next phase, tied to OBJETIVO_CRITICO and HORIZONTE_TIEMPO.
5. Regression risks: events that can send the team back to an earlier phase (turnover, new member joining, scope change, new leader, unresolved conflict, schedule pressure), each with its mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: read EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO and SENALES_OBSERVABLES; if key data for diagnosis is missing (size, tenure, conflicts, role clarity, mode, leader dependency), ask before continuing. Do not invent absent signals; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: map each observed signal to its corresponding Tuckman criterion (orientation/dependency, conflict/positioning, cohesion/norms, productivity/autonomy, closure/disengagement) and derive the phase with traceable signal-by-signal evidence.

spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-reconocimien:
[inputs]

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A poorly designed recognition plan reinforces the wrong behaviors: it rewards visible results and ignores the person who raises a risk in time or unblocks a colleague. The purpose is to design incentives and recognition aligned with the behaviors that sustain a healthy team and a project that delivers. A good plan elevates engagement, retains talent, and makes observable what would otherwise go unnoticed. It unlocks a deliberate, equitable, and sustainable reinforcement system over time, not isolated gestures. Underlying risk: poorly calibrated recognition erodes intrinsic motivation (overjustification effect) or generates a perception of favoritism; the design must protect against both.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project leader and evidence-based team motivation specialist (Deci and Ryan's self-determination theory: autonomy, competence, and relatedness; Daniel Pink's intrinsic motivation: autonomy, mastery, and purpose; behavioral reinforcement).
Deliverable: an actionable recognition and motivation plan. Steps:
1. From COMPORTAMIENTOS_DESEADOS and EQUIPO_Y_CONTEXTO, define 4 to 6 concrete behaviors to reinforce; if there is a problem to correct, formulate the desired substitute behavior, not the prohibition.
2. For each behavior, specify an observable signal that demonstrates it occurred, avoiding gameable metrics or ones that reward individualism at the team's expense; name the failure mode that each signal could induce.
3. Propose a repertoire of recognition differentiated by effort and visibility: immediate micro-recognition, peer-to-peer, from the leader in ceremonies, and formal in front of stakeholders; balance public and private according to the person and justify the mix.
4. Assign cadence (in the moment, weekly in the retro, at milestone) and owner to each, anchored to CADENCIA_Y_CEREMONIAS and respecting MEDIOS_Y_RESTRICCIONES.
5. Consolidate a matrix: behavior — signal — recognition — cadence — owner.
6. List 3 anti-patterns to avoid and 3 indicators to evaluate whether the plan works, with their reading and alert threshold.
7. Deliver a 30-day launch plan (what to activate first, what to observe, when to recalibrate).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: confirm team, context, and priority behaviors; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided and ask for the minimum missing before proceeding.
Phase 2 Design: map each behavior to its observable signal and the most proportionate recognition type, safeguarding autonomy, competence, and relatedness; avoid over-justifying what is already intrinsic.
Phase 3 Operation: define cadence, owners, and anti-gaming safeguards; verify equity across roles, introverted/extroverted profiles, and remote/in-person modes.
Phase 4 Measurement: define the 3 indicators, their reading, alert threshold, and recalibration cycle.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- 4 to 6 concrete and observable behaviors, not vague traits; problems reformulated as desired behavior.
- Each signal is verifiable and resistant to gaming; none rewards individualism at the team's expense; failure mode named.
- Recognition differentiated by effort and visibility; justified public/private mix sensitive to the person's profile.
- Each matrix row has a clear cadence and owner, anchored to the ceremonies and within the given constraints.
- 3 anti-patterns and 3 indicators present, specific, and with reading/threshold.
- 30-day launch plan present.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data about the team.

spec-gestion-proyectos_acuerdo-trabajo-e:

--- S | SITUATION ---
A distributed team wastes hours in crossed time zones, decisions that dissolve in chat, and unwritten response expectations that generate friction and burnout. This working agreement converts those implicit rules into a living and explicit contract: it unlocks decisions in async mode, protects individual concentration, and eliminates ambiguity about when, where, and how the {{NOMBRE_EQUIPO}} team communicates. It serves as the single onboarding reference and as a basis for continuous improvement in each retrospective.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior distributed-team facilitator, with experience in remote agile frameworks, designing team working agreements, and follow-the-sun coordination.
Deliverable: a Working Agreement ready to review, vote on, and sign. Produce, in this order:
1. Time zone map: table of {{INTEGRANTES_Y_HUSOS}} with city, zone, and schedule from {{HORARIOS_LABORALES}}, and the calculated common overlap window expressed in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}} (start time, end time, and total hours/minutes).
2. Synchronous window: protected hours for live meetings and decisions within the overlap, with the rituals from {{RITUALES_CADENCIA}} (purpose, duration, cadence, and time in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}}). Flag which rituals can become async without losing value.
3. Tools by purpose: assign a single channel from {{HERRAMIENTAS}} to each type of communication (ephemeral chat, decisions and documentation, video, task management, code or deliverables) so conversations are not duplicated.
4. Async rules: expected response times by channel and priority, criterion for what is resolved async vs. synchronous, message format (context + question + deadline), and where decisions are recorded so they are traceable.
5. Coexistence rules: right to disconnect, notification-free windows, definition of real urgency and its exclusive channel, working language, and mechanism to update the agreement itself.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: confirm {{INTEGRANTES_Y_HUSOS}}, {{HORARIOS_LABORALES}}, {{HERRAMIENTAS}}, and {{RITUALES_CADENCIA}}. If any data is missing or ambiguous, ask before drafting; do not invent time zones or names and mark any gap as [ASSUMPTION] only if the user authorizes proceeding.
Phase 2 - Plan: calculate the overlap window in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}} and propose the skeleton of the five blocks. If overlap is less than two hours, flag the risk and suggest an async-first model with written decisions and handoffs between zones; if there is no overlap, propose a follow-the-sun rhythm through documented relay.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the complete agreement in clear language, with tables for time zones and tools, and rules in actionable and verifiable sentences. Close with the adoption checklist and the validity criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The overlap window is calculated and expressed in {{ZONA_REFERENCIA}} with start, end, and total, not just described.
- Each type of communication has a single assigned channel; no overlaps and no channels without purpose.
- Each async rule is verifiable: specific response time, priority, and format, not generic.
- The right to disconnect and the definition of real urgency are explicit and separate, with a single urgency channel.
- If overlap is less than two hours, the agreement flags it and adopts an explicit async-first model.
- No time zone, name, or tool was invented: everything comes from inputs or from an authorized [ASSUMPTION].
- Closes with an adoption checklist (vote, publication, review date, agreement owner) and a clear criterion for when it takes effect.

spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-cali:
[inputs]

- ROLES_EQUIPO: {{ROLES_EQUIPO}} > Roles available for quality activities (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} needs a Quality Management Plan that the sponsor can approve and the team can operate from day one. A clear plan unlocks unambiguous acceptance criteria, reduces rework, aligns the team on what "done with quality" means, and allows deliverables to be audited in a traceable manner against requirements. Without it, quality becomes subjective, defects are detected late and at high cost, and the cost of non-quality escalates out of control.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: PMP-certified Project Quality Manager, grounded in the PMBOK Guide 7 (Delivery domain and quality models) and ISO 9001, with experience in quality assurance and control in technology and services projects.

Deliverable: an actionable Quality Management Plan with these sections in order:
1. Quality objectives: policies and expected outcomes, aligned with the project objectives of {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} and the sponsor's expectations; name the cost of non-quality to be avoided.
2. Applicable standards and norms: list based on {{ESTANDARES_APLICABLES}}, with the reason for inclusion and the specific clause or requirement that applies from each.
3. Quality metrics (table): for each critical deliverable or attribute from {{ENTREGABLES_CRITICOS}} define the metric, formula or measurement method, baseline if one exists, acceptance threshold, measurement frequency, owner, and data source.
4. Roles and responsibilities (RACI matrix): for defining standards, reviewing, approving, auditing, and correcting, using {{ROLES_EQUIPO}}; exactly one Approver (A) per row.
5. Quality assurance (QA): process-oriented preventive processes and audits, with cadence and triggers.
6. Quality control (QC): inspections, tests, and reviews against acceptance criteria, with checkpoints, records, and sampling calibrated to {{TOLERANCIA_DEFECTOS}}.
7. Non-conformance management and continuous improvement: register, classification by severity, escalation, closure criteria, and plan-do-check-act cycle.
8. Tools and records: dashboards, checklists, and logs, with where they live and who maintains them.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm scope, critical deliverables, and constraints; mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION]; if project type, critical deliverables, regulatory sector, or defect tolerance are missing, ask before drafting.
Phase 2 - QA/QC distinction: explicitly separate assurance (process, preventive) from control (deliverable, verification), without confusing or duplicating them.
Phase 3 - Traceability: tie each metric and checkpoint to a requirement or acceptance criterion, so that nothing is left orphaned and no requirement is left without a metric.
Phase 4 - Criticality calibration: adjust sampling rigor, thresholds, and frequency to {{TOLERANCIA_DEFECTOS}} (life/safety requires full inspection and zero defects; experimental allows sampling and tolerant thresholds).
Phase 5 - Operability: ensure every activity has an owner, cadence, and record; verify RACI consistency (single A per row, at least one R per activity).
Edge cases: if no applicable standards exist, explicitly state that control is based on internal acceptance criteria. If roles are insufficient to segregate who executes from who approves, flag it as a governance risk.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] QA and QC are clearly differentiated (process vs. deliverable).
- [ ] Each metric has a formula/method, threshold, frequency, owner, and data source.
- [ ] The RACI matrix has exactly one Approver (A) and at least one Responsible (R) per row.
- [ ] Each metric and checkpoint is traceable to a requirement or acceptance criterion; no critical requirement is left without a metric.
- [ ] QC rigor is calibrated to the declared defect tolerance.
- [ ] The continuous improvement cycle and non-conformance flow are defined from start to closure, with severity and closure criteria.
- [ ] Every inference is marked with [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: document structured in the 8 sections, with metrics table and RACI matrix ready for sponsor review and team operation.

--- S | SITUATION ---
Project {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} ({{TIPO_PROYECTO}}) needs to govern quality with evidence rather than perception. A quality metrics dashboard converts defects, rework, and conformance into actionable signals with alert thresholds, so the team intervenes before a problem escalates into a rejected delivery, cost overrun, or production escape. It unlocks deliverable acceptance decisions, steering conversations with data, and measurable continuous improvement cycle by cycle. Without a dashboard, quality is discussed by anecdote and problems are detected late and at high cost.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project quality assurance manager, with expertise in PMBOK quality management, ISO 9001, and cost of quality (COQ).
Deliverable: a one-page quality metrics dashboard, ready to operate in cycle {{CICLO_MEDICION}}, prioritizing {{FAMILIAS_PRIORITARIAS}}.
1. Define the indicator catalog covering defects (defect density, defects by severity, defect leakage to production), rework (rework rate, rework effort as % of total effort), and conformance (deliverable conformance rate, cost of non-quality). Phase 2 - Catalog: write each indicator with its full data sheet (definition, formula, unit, source, owner, frequency, direction).

spec-gestion-proyectos_lista-verificacio:
[inputs]
- ENTREGABLE: {{ENTREGABLE}} > Deliverable to inspect and its version or state (e.g., "user manual v2", "batch of 500 machined parts", "billing module release candidate")
- FUENTE_REQUISITOS: {{FUENTE_REQUISITOS}} > Document against which conformance is verified: specification, contract, definition of done, applicable standard or norm
- PUNTO_INSPECCION: {{PUNTO_INSPECCION}} > Point in the flow where inspection occurs: incoming, in-process, or final exit/acceptance inspection
- DIMENSIONES_CALIDAD: {{DIMENSIONES_CALIDAD}} > Dimensions to cover (e.g., functional, technical, documentary, presentation, regulatory compliance) (optional)
- CRITERIO_ACEPTACION_GLOBAL: {{CRITERIO_ACEPTACION_GLOBAL}} > Pass/fail rule for the complete deliverable: zero criticals and tolerated maximums of majors and minors (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Before formally accepting a deliverable, conformance must be demonstrated objectively, not by impression. Without a traceable checklist, defects are detected late, acceptances become contestable, and the cost of nonconformance is passed on to the client or the next phase. An inspection checklist per deliverable converts requirements into measurable criteria, leaves auditable evidence, and unlocks a defensible acceptance decision before the client, an audit, or a steering committee. The value depends on three conditions: each criterion must be binary or measurable, each item must trace to the requirements source, and the global pass/fail rule must be unambiguous before inspecting—not negotiated afterward.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior quality assurance and control manager, with experience in quality plans under PMBOK and ISO 9001 (quality control by inspection, measurable acceptance criteria, defect severity, acceptance sampling, and cost of quality).
Build a quality control checklist to inspect {{ENTREGABLE}} against {{FUENTE_REQUISITOS}} at point {{PUNTO_INSPECCION}}, following these steps:
1. Delimit the scope of inspection: deliverable and version, requirements source, inspection point, and assumptions about what falls outside scope.
2. Decompose the deliverable into verifiable quality characteristics and group them by the dimensions of {{DIMENSIONES_CALIDAD}} (if not specified, use functional, technical, documentary, presentation, and regulatory compliance).
3. Draft each item as a verifiable assertion, with explicit acceptance criterion, tolerance where applicable, verification method (visual, measurement, test, document review), required evidence, and traceability to the clause or section of the source.
4. Assign severity to each item (critical, major, minor). When {{ENTREGABLE}} is a batch or repeated set, define sample size and acceptance/rejection criterion for sampling; if it is a unique item, declare so.
5. Apply the pass/fail rule from {{CRITERIO_ACEPTACION_GLOBAL}} (if not specified, propose: zero criticals, maximum majors and minors justified by deliverable type, marked [ASSUMPTION]) and define the decision logic: accepted, conditionally accepted with concession, or rejected.
6. Close with the nonconformance block: finding, severity, breached clause, corrective action, responsible party, date, and reinspection result.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm deliverable, requirements source, and inspection point; mark all missing data as a question or [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent requirements.
Phase 2 - Item derivation: extract verifiable requirements from the source, convert them into measurable items, trace each one to its clause, and eliminate non-verifiable or redundant ones.
Phase 3 - Inspection structure: organize items in a table by dimension, with criterion, tolerance, method, evidence, severity, and traceability.
Phase 4 - Severity and sampling: classify by severity and, if applicable, define a sampling plan with size and acceptance/rejection criterion.
Phase 5 - Acceptance rule: define the global pass/fail threshold and the decision logic for the complete deliverable.
Phase 6 - Closure and traceability: add the nonconformance log and the reinspection path.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist of the deliverable itself:
- Each item is verifiable in a binary or measurable way; none depends on subjective judgment without criterion.
- Each item has an explicit acceptance criterion and, where applicable, a quantified tolerance.
- Each item indicates verification method and required evidence.
- Each item is classified by severity (critical, major, minor).
- Each item traces to a clause or section of {{FUENTE_REQUISITOS}}; no invented criteria.
- If the deliverable is a batch/repeated set, there is a sampling plan with size and acceptance/rejection criterion.
- There is an unambiguous global pass/fail rule and a decision logic (accepted / with concession / rejected).
- Includes nonconformance log with breached clause, responsible party, and reinspection.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no prices or unsupported data.
Expected deliverable: ready-to-use inspection table (Dimension | Item | Acceptance criterion | Tolerance | Method | Evidence | Severity | Traceability | Result) plus summary of the global acceptance rule with its decision logic and nonconformance log block.

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to define how the project acquires what it cannot or should not produce internally. The purpose is to decide with rigor what to buy versus what to build in-house, choose the contract type that places risk where it belongs, establish objective supplier selection criteria, and set up contract governance. A solid procurement plan unlocks timely purchases, prevents supplier disputes, protects the critical schedule, preserves reversibility in the face of non-performance, and leaves an auditable trail of every contracting decision.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project Procurement Manager with experience leading procurement under PMBOK and contracting specialized services and goods.
Produce an actionable and auditable Procurement Management Plan with these steps:
1. Make-or-buy analysis of each candidate component with justified make-or-buy decision and dependencies between components.
2. Contract strategy per component to be purchased: recommended type, risk allocation, and key clauses.
3. Weighted supplier selection criteria matrix with scoring scale and knockout criteria (must-have) when applicable.
4. Supplier governance model: cadence, indicators and SLAs, escalation, changes, acceptance, closure, and contingency for non-performance.
5. List of assumptions and missing data that must be confirmed before bidding, with their impact if they prove false.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1, framing: if scope, candidate components, internal capabilities, schedule or compliance constraints, or risk appetite are missing, ask for them in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent project or market data.
Phase 2, make-or-buy: evaluate each component against actual internal capability, criticality and risk, schedule urgency, and effort in FTE-months (never monetary figures); issue a make-or-buy decision and flag dependencies that condition the contracting order.
Phase 3, contract strategy: for each component to be purchased, recommend fixed price, reimbursable costs, or time and materials based on how well the scope is defined and who should bear the risk; justify the allocation and state key clauses (deliverables, SLA, payment milestones linked to acceptance, intellectual property, confidentiality, exit and reversibility, penalties).
Phase 4, selection criteria: matrix of five to seven criteria with weights summing to one hundred, a scale of one to five, and a scoring descriptor per criterion to reduce subjectivity; declare any knockout criterion (must-have).
Phase 5, governance: monitoring cadence, indicators and SLAs to track, escalation path, contract change management, acceptance and closure criteria, and contingency plan for non-performance.
Mark everything unconfirmed as [ASSUMPTION]. Do not include prices or the word free.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each candidate component has an explicit and justified make-or-buy decision against the four criteria, with dependencies noted.
- Each component to be purchased has a recommended contract type with justification linked to scope definition and risk allocation.
- The selection matrix weights sum exactly to one hundred, each criterion has a scoring descriptor, and knockout criteria are declared.
- Supplier governance covers cadence, SLA, escalation, changes, acceptance, closure, and contingency for non-performance.
- Each unconfirmed data point is marked [ASSUMPTION] with its impact; effort is expressed in FTE-months; no prices or the word free.
Expected deliverable: a Procurement Management Plan in five sections (make-or-buy, contract strategy, selection criteria, supplier governance, assumptions and missing data), ready for review with the sponsor and to serve as the basis for bid documents.
