--- S | SITUATION ---
I am going to select a supplier for {{OBJETO_CONTRATACION}} and I need the decision to be objective, traceable, and defensible before an audit, procurement committee, or steering body. The risk to neutralize: selecting by affinity, by the best commercial presentation, or by subjective impression—and then being unable to justify the why. A well-built weighted matrix unlocks apples-to-apples comparison among shortlisted suppliers, consensus among evaluators, and a file that sustains the decision if anyone questions it later. Prices are not evaluated here: the focus is on value, capability, and risk. The commercial criterion is governed separately to avoid contaminating the technical evaluation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior procurement and contract management specialist (Procurement Lead), with experience in competitive supplier evaluation under PMBOK practices (Source Selection Criteria) and weighted multi-criteria scoring models.

Deliverable: a complete, ready-to-use weighted evaluation matrix. Steps:
1. Propose 6 to 9 criteria grouped into dimensions (technical capability and experience; quality and verifiable references; delivery capacity and schedule compliance; financial soundness and business continuity; compliance, legal risk, and security; post-sale support and service; cultural and governance fit). For each criterion, define the objective evidence that supports it and how it is requested or verified (document, demo, contactable reference, valid certification).
2. Assign each criterion a percentage weight summing exactly to 100%, calibrated against {{PRIORIDADES_CRITICAS}}, and justify each weight in one line. Equal distribution without justification is not allowed; concentrate weight on what decides success and assign lesser weight to hygiene factors.
3. Define a common scale of 1 to 5 with anchor descriptors per level for each criterion, so that two evaluators with the same evidence reach the same score. Avoid even scales to prevent forcing an artificial midpoint.
4. Deliver the matrix as a table ready to fill: criterion, dimension, weight, scale, required evidence, and one column per supplier from {{PROVEEDORES_FINALISTAS}}.
5. Explain the weighted score calculation (score × weight), its totalization, the resulting ranking, and the tie-breaking rule (e.g., higher score in the highest-weight dimension).
6. Define knockout criteria from {{RESTRICCIONES_NO_NEGOCIABLES}} and a minimum acceptance threshold below which no supplier advances even if it leads the ranking.
7. Indicate how to document the final recommendation so that it is auditable: who evaluated what, traceability of each score to its evidence, record of discrepancies between evaluators, and declaration of conflicts of interest.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm OBJETO_CONTRATACION, TIPO_PROVEEDOR, PRIORIDADES_CRITICAS, RESTRICCIONES_NO_NEGOCIABLES, and PROVEEDORES_FINALISTAS. If anything is missing or arrives empty, ask for it before continuing. Do not invent project data; mark each assumption as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Criteria and weights design: derive criteria from the supplier type and calibrate weights against the critical priorities; verify they sum to 100%.
Phase 3 - Scale anchoring: draft 1-to-5 descriptors that eliminate ambiguity between evaluators, with an example of what evidence justifies a low, medium, and high score.
Phase 4 - Assembly: build the table, define knockouts and threshold, and explain the scoring method, tie-breaking rule, and ranking.
Phase 5 - Auditability: close with the traceable recommendation format and a self-check against the quality criterion checklist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Between 6 and 9 criteria, each with a dimension and associated, verifiable objective evidence.
- Weights sum exactly to 100% and each weight is justified against the priorities; no unjustified equal distribution.
- Scale of 1 to 5 with anchor descriptors per level that allow replicating the score across evaluators.
- Table ready to fill with a column per supplier, explicit weighted scoring method, and tie-breaking rule.
- Knockout criteria and minimum acceptance threshold defined and traceable to the non-negotiable requirements.
- No reference to prices; focus on value, capability, and risk. Assumptions marked as [ASSUMPTION].
- Auditable final recommendation: scores traceable to evidence, discrepancies recorded, conflict of interest declared.
Expected deliverable: weighted supplier evaluation matrix, in table form, with criteria, justified weights, anchored scales, knockouts, threshold, scoring formula, tie-breaking rule, and auditable recommendation template.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-cont:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_CONTRATO: {{NOMBRE_CONTRATO}} > Name or object of the contract to administer
- PROVEEDOR: {{PROVEEDOR}} > Supplier or contractor responsible for delivery
- TIPO_CONTRATO: {{TIPO_CONTRATO}} > Modality (fixed price, time and materials, reimbursable cost, managed service)
- VIGENCIA: {{VIGENCIA}} > Start and end date, or duration and renewals
- ENTREGABLES_CLAVE: {{ENTREGABLES_CLAVE}} > Contractual deliverables or milestones to track
- SLAS: {{SLAS}} > Service levels to measure (availability, response time, quality, schedule)
- CADENCIA_GOBIERNO: {{CADENCIA_GOBIERNO}} > Rhythm of governance meetings and reports (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A signed contract without an active administration plan leaves the project at the mercy of the supplier's goodwill: deliverables arrive late, SLAs are breached without consequence, and closure turns into a dispute over bonds and retentions. This plan converts the contract into a living governance instrument, from signing through formal closure. It unlocks objective compliance tracking, traceable application of penalties, severity-based escalation, and a clean closure that releases bonds, transfers knowledge, and captures lessons.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior contracts and procurement administrator, with experience in supplier governance under PMBOK (Procurement Control) and ISO 37500.
Deliverable: Administration plan for contract {{NOMBRE_CONTRATO}} with {{PROVEEDOR}} ({{TIPO_CONTRATO}}, validity {{VIGENCIA}}). Steps:
1. Contract summary card: object, validity period, parties, contract manager, change authority, and approval thresholds by level.
2. Deliverables matrix: for each one in {{ENTREGABLES_CLAVE}}, verifiable acceptance criteria, review responsible party, required evidence, committed date, and dependencies between deliverables.
3. SLA catalog: for each level in {{SLAS}}, metric, calculation formula, target, measurement window, auditable data source, and treatment of missing or degraded data (do not penalize without reliable data).
4. Penalty and credit regime: link each SLA or deliverable breach to its consequence (discount, service credit, remediation plan, termination cause), with caps, cure period, and notification process. Distinguish isolated failure from recurring failure.
5. Monitoring cadence (use {{CADENCIA_GOBIERNO}} if provided): governance meetings, compliance dashboard, trend indicators, and escalation paths by severity.
6. Change and dispute management: how changes to scope or SLA are requested, approved, recorded, and resolved; resolution ladder (operational > committee > formal proceedings) before litigation.
7. Contract risks: supplier dependency, obsolescence, service continuity, and exit or reversibility plan.
8. Closure checklist: final acceptance, settlement, bond and retention release, knowledge transfer, lessons learned, and file archiving.
Do not include amounts or rates; express penalties as percentages or relative credits. Mark as [ASSUMPTION] any threshold, target, or cap you assume, with its impact.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: confirm contract type, deliverables, SLAs, and validity period; if an essential data point is missing, ask for it before drafting and do not assume silently.
Phase 2 Design the framework: define governance with approval thresholds, deliverables matrix with dependencies, and SLA catalog with formulas, data sources, and handling of degraded data.
Phase 3 Articulate consequences: connect each SLA or deliverable to its penalty/credit, caps, cure period, notification process, and distinction between isolated and recurring failure.
Phase 4 Operate and close: detail cadence with severity-based escalation, change/dispute management, contract risks, and the closure checklist with final acceptance criteria and bond release.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each deliverable has a verifiable acceptance criterion, responsible party, evidence, and dependencies—not just a date.
- [ ] Each SLA includes metric, formula, target, measurement window, auditable data source, and rule for missing or degraded data.
- [ ] Each penalty or credit is linked to a specific breach, with a cap, cure period, and notification process, distinguishing isolated from recurring failure.
- [ ] The cadence defines severity-based escalation and dispute management has a resolution ladder before formal proceedings.
- [ ] There is a contract risks section with an exit or reversibility plan.
- [ ] Closure covers final acceptance, settlement, bond and retention release, knowledge transfer, lessons learned, and file archiving.
- [ ] No amounts or rates; consequences as percentages or relative credits; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] with their impact.
Expected deliverable: contract administration plan in sections (summary card, deliverables matrix, SLA catalog, penalty regime, monitoring cadence, change and dispute management, contract risks, closure checklist), ready to attach to the contract file.
spec-gestion-proyectos_matriz-make-or-bu:
[inputs]
- COMPONENTE: {{COMPONENTE}} > Component, module, or capability being evaluated for development or acquisition
- CRITICIDAD: {{CRITICIDAD}} > How central it is to the project outcome (differentiating core vs. support function)
- CAPACIDAD_INTERNA: {{CAPACIDAD_INTERNA}} > Internal team skills, people, and availability to develop it
- HORIZONTE_USO: {{HORIZONTE_USO}} > How long and intensively it will be used (one-time, recurring, long-term platform)
- RESTRICCIONES_TIEMPO: {{RESTRICCIONES_TIEMPO}} > Deadlines or delivery windows that condition the decision (optional)
- CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS: {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}} > Criteria or weights most valued by the committee (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project must decide between building {{COMPONENTE}} internally or acquiring it. This decision conditions total cost of ownership, delivery speed, supplier risk exposure, and control over future capability. A well-executed make-or-buy analysis unlocks a traceable and defensible decision before the project committee, prevents involuntary lock-in, and aligns team effort investment with what truly differentiates the project. Common error this analysis prevents: building what is a market commodity (wastes scarce effort) or buying what is a differentiating core (gives the competitive advantage away to the supplier).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior procurement manager with experience in technology outsourcing, contract management, and supplier negotiation, anchored in the PMBOK Procurement knowledge area.

Deliverable: make-or-buy analysis with weighted decision matrix and conditioned recommendation. Steps:
1. Restate what is being evaluated ({{COMPONENTE}}), its {{CRITICIDAD}}, and its {{HORIZONTE_USO}}, and classify the component as differentiating core or support function: this classification governs all subsequent weights.
2. Define 6 to 7 decision criteria with their relative weight (summing to 100%): total cost of ownership, time to availability, technical risk, supplier risk, internal capability, strategic fit, and intellectual property control. Justify each weight in one line. Adjust weights per {{CRITERIOS_PRIORITARIOS}}; if {{RESTRICCIONES_TIEMPO}} is active, raise the weight of time to availability.
3. Build the matrix: score MAKE and BUY on each criterion on a scale of 1 to 5 with one line of justification per cell; calculate the weighted score of each option and show the subtotal per criterion.
4. Estimate relative effort in person-months and calendar per option; distinguish initial build effort from recurring maintenance effort. Mark each non-verifiable estimate as [ASSUMPTION].
5. Analyze key risks by path with qualitative probability and impact: for MAKE technical debt, schedule overrun, team opportunity cost; for BUY supplier dependency and lock-in, loss of internal knowledge, scalability limits. Associate a mitigating contractual clause to each BUY risk (SLA, exit clause, escrow, data portability).
6. Deliver the recommendation with validity conditions, signals that would force its revision, and, when appropriate, a hybrid path (internal core + acquired periphery) with the explicit integration boundary.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm component, criticality, internal capability, and horizon; if CRITICIDAD, CAPACIDAD_INTERNA, or HORIZONTE_USO are missing or ambiguous, ask before proceeding.
Phase 2 Criteria: fix criteria and justified weights; differentiating core tilts weights toward control and strategic fit, support toward cost and time.
Phase 3 Matrix: score each option cell by cell with justification and obtain the weighted score.
Phase 4 Effort and risk: estimate person-months and calendar (initial and recurring), label assumptions, and analyze risks by path with mitigants.
Phase 5 Decision: draft conditioned recommendation with review triggers; if the difference between weighted scores is < 10%, declare a technical tie and resolve by the highest-weight criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The component is classified as core or support and that classification governs the weights.
- Criteria sum exactly to 100% and each weight has a one-line justification.
- Each matrix cell has a 1-to-5 score and justification; weighted scores are correctly calculated and a technical tie (< 10%) is declared when applicable.
- Cost is expressed in person-months and relative effort, never in monetary figures or with the word free; initial effort is separated from maintenance.
- Every non-verifiable estimate is marked [ASSUMPTION].
- Risks of lock-in, technical debt, knowledge loss, and scalability are covered; each BUY risk has a mitigating contractual clause.
- The recommendation is unambiguous and includes validity conditions and review signals; the hybrid path, if applicable, defines the integration boundary.
Expected deliverable: document with framing and classification, weighted criteria table, MAKE vs. BUY decision matrix with scores and subtotals, effort analysis (initial and recurring) and risk with mitigants, and conditioned recommendation (with hybrid path if applicable).
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-direccion-pr:
[inputs]
- NOMBRE_PROYECTO: {{NOMBRE_PROYECTO}} > Name of the project to integrate (e.g., "Core banking migration to the cloud")
- OBJETIVO_PROYECTO: {{OBJETIVO_PROYECTO}} > Business objective and expected project outcome
- ENFOQUE_CICLO_VIDA: {{ENFOQUE_CICLO_VIDA}} > Life cycle and development approach: predictive, agile, or hybrid
- ALCANCE_ENTREGABLES: {{ALCANCE_ENTREGABLES}} > Main scope and major project deliverables
- HITOS_FECHAS: {{HITOS_FECHAS}} > Milestones, anchor dates, and known schedule constraints
- RESTRICCION_COSTO: {{RESTRICCION_COSTO}} > Budget or cost constraint (without invented figures; "to be confirmed" if unknown)
- PLANES_EXISTENTES: {{PLANES_EXISTENTES}} > Subsidiary plans or baselines that already exist and must be consolidated (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to consolidate the subsidiary management plans and baselines of a project into a single project management plan: the master document that defines how work is executed, monitored, controlled, and closed. Without this integration, plans live scattered, contradict each other, and the team has no single source of truth for decision-making. A coherent, integrated plan unlocks the performance measurement baseline, establishes the change control rules, and allows management to confidently approve a stable baseline against which to measure actual progress.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior project director with PMP certification, expert in PMBOK PMI integration management, consolidation of subsidiary plans, and definition of scope, schedule, and cost baselines.

Produce an integrated project management plan with these components:
1. Executive summary of 5 to 7 lines: objective, life cycle, major scope, and the dominant constraint.
2. Table of the ten subsidiary plans (scope, requirements, schedule, cost, quality, resources, communications, risks, procurement, stakeholders): approach, responsible party, tool or cadence per plan; mark as missing any plan that does not exist.
3. Table of baselines (scope with WBS and dictionary, schedule and milestones, phased cost, performance measurement): content and control mechanism for each.
4. Table of the change control process: flow step, variation threshold that triggers action, approval authority (PM, CCB, sponsor), and decision record.
5. Coherence matrix crossing scope against schedule against cost and flagging conflicts or assumptions that break consistency.
6. Closure: life cycle plan and management reviews, open assumptions [ASSUMPTION], dependencies, integration risks, and approval path.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing and integration: confirm objective, life cycle, constraints, and assumptions; inventory which subsidiary plans and baselines exist and which are missing.
Phase 2 — Subsidiary plans: consistently synthesize the ten management plans, each with its approach, roles, and tools, aligned to the chosen life cycle (in agile/hybrid, translate to backlog, cadences, and Definition of Done without abandoning baseline traceability).
Phase 3 — Baselines and integration: define the scope, schedule, and cost baselines, and the performance measurement baseline; specify the change management plan with its flow, variation thresholds, and authority by level.
Phase 4 — Coherence and closure: verify cross-consistency between scope, schedule, and cost; resolve or flag contradictions; name integration risks (absent plans, unvalidated assumptions, external dependencies); establish management reviews and the approval path.
Label each unconfirmed data point as [ASSUMPTION]; never present inferences as facts or invent dates or figures. If an essential data point is missing, ask for it in a brief list before executing.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The framing establishes objective, life cycle, constraints, and assumptions before integrating.
- All ten subsidiary plans are present; missing ones are explicitly marked, not silently omitted.
- Each baseline (scope, schedule, cost, performance) declares its content and its control mechanism.
- Change control defines flow, variation thresholds, and approval authority—not just "changes are evaluated".
- The coherence matrix crosses scope, schedule, and cost and names the conflicts, instead of assuming they fit.
- Integration risks (absent plans, dependencies, unvalidated assumptions) are explicit.
- Every unconfirmed data point is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented dates or figures.
- Neutral and professional English; the result is an integrated plan, not a list of disconnected plans.
Expected deliverable: an integrated project management plan with executive summary, table of the ten subsidiary plans, table of baselines, table of change control with thresholds and authority, scope-schedule-cost coherence matrix, and closure with assumptions, dependencies, integration risks, and approval path.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-bene:
[inputs]
- BENEFICIOS_ESPERADOS: {{BENEFICIOS_ESPERADOS}} > Expected business value (savings, revenue, time, quality, risk, satisfaction); may arrive diffuse
- ENTREGABLES: {{ENTREGABLES}} > What the project produces (products, capabilities, systems), to separate outputs from benefits
- DUENOS_CANDIDATOS: {{DUENOS_CANDIDATOS}} > Roles or areas that could take responsibility for capturing each benefit after delivery
- LINEA_BASE: {{LINEA_BASE}} > Current value of the indicators before the project (optional; if missing, the model asks or marks [ASSUMPTION])
- HORIZONTE_REALIZACION: {{HORIZONTE_REALIZACION}} > Window in which value is expected to materialize: closure, 30/60/90 days, 6-12 months
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team is closing or planning a project that produces {{ENTREGABLES}}, but delivering is not the same as generating value: the benefit materializes after delivery, when someone adopts the outcome and an indicator moves. The purpose of this plan is to transform {{BENEFICIOS_ESPERADOS}} from vague promises into measurable commitments, with an owner and a date. A well-built plan unlocks the investment decision, holds someone distinct from the project team accountable for capturing value within the {{HORIZONTE_REALIZACION}}, and leaves evidence to defend the return before the sponsor. Without it, the project is declared successful upon delivery and no one verifies whether the value arrived. Underlying risk to neutralize: confusing outputs with benefits, unmeasurable optimism, and benefit orphans (no one responsible after the transition to operations).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior benefits realization manager, expert in benefits management per PMBOK, benefits realization management (Cranfield Process Model), and Managing Successful Programmes, with practice in benefit maps and transition-to-operations plans.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate the business purpose in one sentence: "This project exists to achieve [outcome] measured by [indicator]".
2. Separate outputs (from {{ENTREGABLES}}), outcomes (behavior or capability change), and benefits (captured value); list 3 to 6 benefits stated as measurable changes, not as activities. Explicitly discard any activity or deliverable disguised as a benefit.
3. For each benefit, define in a table: metric and unit, baseline (from {{LINEA_BASE}}), quantified target, formula or data source, type—tangible/intangible (with measurement proxy if intangible), and financial/non-financial classification.
4. Assign each benefit a nominal owner from {{DUENOS_CANDIDATOS}} (role responsible for capturing it after delivery), explicitly distinct from the delivery owner; if there is no clear candidate, record it as a governance gap to resolve before closure.
5. Build the realization timeline within {{HORIZONTE_REALIZACION}}: which benefits are realized at closure, at 30/60/90 days, and at 6-12 months, with measurement milestone, expected ramp-up period, and, where applicable, temporary disbenefit (dip before rise) or adoption cost.
6. Map dependencies and adoption or process-change assumptions required for each benefit; mark [ASSUMPTION] where there is no data and identify the most fragile benefit and the condition that would leave it unrealized.
7. Define the post-delivery monitoring cadence (who reviews, how often, against what threshold) and the explicit criterion that would declare a benefit as unrealized and trigger corrective action.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Value framing: fix the business purpose and validate that benefits, deliverables, candidate owners, and baseline exist; if an essential data point is missing, ask before executing and do not invent figures.
Phase 2 - Value chain: trace output > outcome > benefit for each deliverable and discard as a benefit any activity or disguised deliverable.
Phase 3 - Quantification: define metric, baseline, target, and formula per benefit; convert intangibles to measurable proxies and declare the data source.
Phase 4 - Accountability and timeline: assign a benefit owner (not the project owner) and place each benefit in the timeline with its measurement milestone and ramp-up; name temporary disbenefits if any.
Phase 5 - Robustness: review adoption dependencies and assumptions, identify the most fragile benefit, define monitoring cadence, alert threshold, and non-realization criterion.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The business purpose was restated in one sentence with outcome and indicator before listing benefits.
- Outputs, outcomes, and benefits are explicitly distinguished; no benefit is stated as an activity or deliverable.
- There are 3 to 6 benefits, each with metric, unit, baseline, quantified target, and formula or data source.
- Intangible benefits have a declared measurement proxy; each benefit is classified as financial/non-financial.
- Each benefit has a nominal owner by role, distinct from the delivery owner; benefits without a clear owner are marked as governance gaps.
- The timeline places each benefit (closure, 30/60/90 days, 6-12 months) with a measurement milestone and ramp-up within the horizon; temporary disbenefits are named when applicable.
- Adoption dependencies and assumptions are mapped; assumptions without data are marked [ASSUMPTION]; the most fragile benefit is identified.
- A post-delivery monitoring cadence was defined (responsible party, frequency, threshold) and a non-realization criterion with associated corrective action.
Expected deliverable: benefits management plan in tables (benefits register + realization timeline + monitoring cadence), with traceable owners and metrics, in neutral and professional English, no prices.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-gestion-camb:
[inputs]
- CAMBIO: {{CAMBIO}} > Specific change to adopt: from what current state to what future state and for what business outcome
- GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS: {{GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS}} > Groups of people whose day-to-day changes (departments, roles, teams, locations)
- SPONSOR: {{SPONSOR}} > Executive sponsor who backs and communicates the change
- GO_LIVE: {{GO_LIVE}} > Date or window when the change takes effect (temporal reference for interventions)
- RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA: {{RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA}} > Already observed resistance, objections, or adoption risk (optional; if missing, inferred and marked [ASSUMPTION])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project is going to introduce {{CAMBIO}} and the real risk is not delivering the solution but having the impacted people adopt it: most projects that fail do not fail because of the technology, they fail because the human side of the change was managed late or not managed at all. The purpose of this plan is to convert a diffuse transition into a traceable change management plan, anchored in the ADKAR model, that connects each individual adoption gap of the {{GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS}} with an intervention, a responsible party, and a metric. Such a plan unlocks the change being sustained after {{GO_LIVE}} instead of reverting to the previous state, and gives {{SPONSOR}} evidence to defend the investment. Change management applied with discipline is what separates an installed tool from an adopted tool.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior change management leader (change manager), certified in the Prosci ADKAR model, expert in stakeholder mapping, audience-specific communication plans, and resistance management.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate {{CAMBIO}} in a single sentence: "Move from [current state] to [future state] for [business outcome]". If the business outcome is not explicit, propose one and mark it [ASSUMPTION].
2. Map of impacted stakeholders from {{GRUPOS_IMPACTADOS}}, in a table: by group, approximate size, what changes in their day-to-day, influence (high/medium/low), disposition (champion/neutral/resistant), and priority management action (engage/communicate/train/contain); mark [ASSUMPTION] where there is no data.
3. ADKAR diagnosis of the most impacted group: green/yellow/red traffic light on Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, and Reinforcement, with one line per color justifying the color. Identify the first red/yellow stage as the barrier (barrier point), because ADKAR is sequential and you do not advance by skipping a weak stage.
4. Interventions by ADKAR stage (Awareness, Desire, Knowledge, Ability, Reinforcement), each with a nominal responsible party and timing relative to {{GO_LIVE}} (before/during/after); concentrate effort on the identified barrier and distinguish point-in-time training (Knowledge) from sustained adoption (Ability + Reinforcement).
5. Communication plan by stage: message, correct sender ({{SPONSOR}} communicates the why and the vision; the direct manager communicates "what this means for you"), channel, timing, and expected receipt signal (how you will know the message landed).
6. Resistance map from {{RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA}}: 3 to 5 likely objections, root cause, and concrete response, distinguishing lack of information (resolved by communicating) from real loss of power, status, or workload (resolved by negotiating or redesigning). If {{RESISTENCIA_CONOCIDA}} arrives empty, infer and mark [ASSUMPTION].
7. Adoption metrics with baseline, target, measurement frequency, and reinforcement milestones after {{GO_LIVE}}; they must measure usage/compliance/productivity, not activity.
Operational closure: top 3 adoption risks with alert trigger, consolidated assumed assumptions, and the pending data to confirm.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: fix the business outcome of the change and validate that change, groups, sponsor, and go-live exist; if an essential data point is missing, ask before executing and do not invent groups or sponsors.
Phase 2 · Stakeholders: identify and characterize the impacted groups by influence and disposition, prioritizing the one most exposed to the change and naming the priority management action for each.
Phase 3 · ADKAR diagnosis: evaluate the five stages in order and locate the first barrier; intervention concentrates there, stages are not skipped, and effort is not spent on later stages still blocked.
Phase 4 · Interventions and communication: design actions by stage with responsible party and timing, align the message to the correct sender per stage, and define the receipt signal for each communication.
Phase 5 · Resistance and measurement: anticipate objections by root cause, define adoption metrics (not activity metrics) with baseline, target, and frequency, and establish post-go-live reinforcement to prevent reversion; close with top 3 risks and assumptions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The change was restated in a sentence from current state to future state with business outcome before planning.
- Each impacted group has size, concrete day-to-day impact, influence, disposition, and management action; estimates without data are marked [ASSUMPTION].
- The ADKAR diagnosis covers all five stages with a justified traffic light and names the first barrier stage; interventions respect the sequential order and concentrate on the barrier.
- Each intervention by stage has a nominal responsible party and timing relative to the go-live; training (Knowledge) is not confused with sustained adoption (Ability + sustained Reinforcement).
- The communication plan assigns the correct sender by stage (sponsor communicates the why; direct manager the personal impact) and includes a receipt signal.
- The resistance map distinguishes lack of information from real loss and gives a concrete response per objection.
- Metrics are adoption metrics (usage, compliance, productivity), not activity metrics, and have baseline, target, frequency, and post-go-live reinforcement milestones.
- The closure lists top 3 adoption risks, consolidated assumptions, and the pending data to confirm.
Expected deliverable: change management plan with stakeholder map in a table, ADKAR diagnosis with traffic light and identified barrier, interventions and communication by stage with responsible parties, resistance map, adoption metrics with baseline and target, and closure block with risks and assumptions, in neutral and professional English.
spec-gestion-proyectos_plan-transicion-o:
[inputs]
- ENTREGABLE: {{ENTREGABLE}} > Product, system, or service being handed over to operations (e.g., payments platform, mobile app, SAP integration)
- EQUIPO_OPERACION: {{EQUIPO_OPERACION}} > Receiving team or area that will operate and support it on a daily basis (e.g., internal service desk, managed service provider)
- NIVELES_SERVICIO: {{NIVELES_SERVICIO}} > SLA or committed service objectives (optional; e.g., 24x7, P1 response in 30 min). If empty, propose baseline and mark [ASSUMPTION]
- VENTANA_HYPERCARE: {{VENTANA_HYPERCARE}} > Duration of the reinforced stabilization period (optional; e.g., 2 weeks, 30 days). If empty, propose baseline and mark [ASSUMPTION]
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A project enters its final phase and must be formally handed over to the team that will operate it in production. Without a transition plan, knowledge remains trapped in the project team, incidents have no owner, there is no objective way to revert if something fails, and closure becomes ambiguous. This plan unlocks an orderly handover: {{EQUIPO_OPERACION}} receives {{ENTREGABLE}} documented, with support defined, with a stabilization window, and with objective criteria to declare closure, releasing the project team without leaving operational debt.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Transition and Operations Manager (Service Transition Manager) with experience in ITIL v4 (Service Transition, incident and problem management) and PMI (project closure, deliverable transfer).

Produce a transition-to-operations plan with these numbered sections:
1. Handover scope: what is included and what is excluded (with an explicit boundary), interdependencies with neighboring systems, and assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION] when data is missing.
2. Support model by level (L1, L2, L3): responsibilities, channels, coverage hours, and escalation path aligned to {{NIVELES_SERVICIO}}. Distinguish incident management (restore service) from problem management (root cause). Define a severity/priority matrix (P1–P4) with target times.
3. Operations documentation inventory: operational run-book, incident procedures, recovery/rollback guide, access and credentials management (referenced in a vault, never secrets in plaintext), escalation contacts. Indicate responsible party, status (pending/draft/approved), and target date per artifact.
4. Knowledge transfer plan: sessions, shadowing, reverse-shadowing, and receiving team competence verification with explicit approval criterion (what must be demonstrated to consider the team ready).
5. Hypercare period: duration {{VENTANA_HYPERCARE}}, reinforced coverage (who, in what schedule), metrics to monitor (incident volume, MTTR, backlog, project escalations), and measurable exit conditions (thresholds that trigger the end of hypercare).
6. RACI matrix for key activities between project and operations: a single Accountable per activity; no rows without a Responsible.
7. Acceptance criteria and closure: transition Definition of Done, initial service metrics (response and resolution times), and a nominated acceptance signature from the operations responsible party with date.
8. Transition risks and mitigations: explicitly include the reversion risk, its trigger, and the rollback plan, plus critical dependencies (key people, access, deployment windows).

Limits: do not propose prices or monetary cost estimates. Unknowns are marked [ASSUMPTION], never invented. If {{NIVELES_SERVICIO}} or {{VENTANA_HYPERCARE}} arrive empty, propose a reasonable baseline and mark it [ASSUMPTION] for validation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm the nature of {{ENTREGABLE}}, {{EQUIPO_OPERACION}}, {{NIVELES_SERVICIO}}, and {{VENTANA_HYPERCARE}}; review {{ADJUNTOS}} if they exist; if an essential data point is missing, ask for it before drafting.
Phase 2 - Service design: define scope/boundary, support model by level with severity matrix, and required documentation.
Phase 3 - Enablement: structure knowledge transfer and hypercare with metrics and measurable exit conditions.
Phase 4 - Governance and closure: build RACI, acceptance criteria, initial metrics, rollback plan, and risk log.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

- RACI with a single Accountable per activity and no rows without a Responsible.

- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data; no prices.
Expected deliverable: transition-to-operations plan document in neutral and professional English, ready for change committee or operations responsible party review, with an actionable closure DoD.

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to focus my B2B prospecting on the accounts with the highest probability of closing fast, paying well, and staying, instead of scattering effort across an undifferentiated universe that burns out the commercial team and dilutes the pipeline. Defining a firmographic and technographic Ideal Customer Profile (ICP) unlocks segmenting the market, prioritizing target accounts, qualifying leads consistently, and giving the go-to-market strategy a defensible foundation for scaling. The ICP is a living hypothesis, not a dogma: it is born from the best current customers and validated with data before committing prospecting budget.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Revenue Operations strategist expert in Ideal Customer Profile construction, firmographic and technographic segmentation, and target account design for B2B sales.
Deliver an actionable ICP through these steps:
1. Derive the common patterns from MEJORES_CLIENTES that explain why they are ideal, separating cause from correlation; if there are customers who left or never fit, use them as contrast to sharpen exclusion.
2. Build the firmographic block (industry/vertical, headcount and revenue size, geography, business model, organizational structure), each criterion with threshold, relative weight, and reason it matters.
3. Build the technographic and signals block (technology stack, digital maturity, intent triggers derived from SENALES_COMPRA), distinguishing observable signal from mere plausibility.
4. Synthesize explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria; a good ICP excludes as much as it includes.
5. Classify fit in an A/B/C level matrix with a reproducible assignment rule and a suggested commercial action per level.
6. Translate everything into a list of operational filters ready to apply in a CRM or prospecting tool, aligned to message fit with DECISOR_USUARIO.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Patterns: analyze MEJORES_CLIENTES and isolate the attributes that CAUSE good fit, not those that merely coexist by chance or by sales history bias; name the causal mechanism for each.
Phase 2 - Firmographics: tabulate each criterion with threshold, weight (high/medium/low), and justification, anchored to PRODUCTO_SERVICIO and PROPUESTA_VALOR; the weight reflects how much it moves the probability of success, not how easy it is to measure.
Phase 3 - Technographics and signals: identify stack and maturity that predict fit, and convert SENALES_COMPRA into observable and verifiable triggers (source and how to detect them), discarding generic non-actionable signals.
Phase 4 - Synthesis: define inclusion/exclusion, build the A/B/C matrix with assignment rule and action per level, and derive the actionable CRM filters.
Limits: mark every inference as [ASSUMPTION]; do not invent data, cost figures, or market sizes; use qualitative ranges when data is missing. Edge cases: if MEJORES_CLIENTES has fewer than 3 cases or they are very heterogeneous, warn of low statistical confidence and propose a provisional ICP with stricter validation criteria. Close with the assumptions to validate with real data (CRM, win/loss analysis, customer calls) ordered by impact on ICP quality.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Phase 1 patterns explicitly distinguish cause from correlation and name the mechanism of each attribute.
- Each firmographic and technographic criterion has a concrete threshold, relative weight, and reason it matters.
- Purchase signals are observable, verifiable, and come with a source or detection method—not generic.
- Explicit exclusion criteria exist, not only inclusion.
- The A/B/C matrix has a clear, reproducible assignment rule and a suggested commercial action per level.
- Final filters are directly applicable in a CRM or prospecting tool and align to the message toward DECISOR_USUARIO.
- Every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no prices or invented figures; low confidence is flagged when the customer sample is small.
Expected deliverable: structured ICP card (firmographics + technographics + signals), criteria table with threshold and weight, exclusion criteria list, A/B/C level matrix with its rule and action per level, actionable CRM filter list, and closure with assumptions to validate with real data—ordered by impact—before scaling.
spec-ventas_buyer_persona:
[inputs]
- SOLUCION: {{SOLUCION}} > Product or service you sell and the core problem it solves
- SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO: {{SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO}} > Sector, company size, and geography of the ideal customer
- TICKET_COMPLEJIDAD: {{TICKET_COMPLEJIDAD}} > Ticket size and purchase complexity (transactional, consultative, or strategic) to calibrate how many roles are involved

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You sell a B2B solution whose purchase is not decided by a single person but by a committee (Decision-Making Unit) with different — and sometimes opposing — interests. Without understanding what each role wants, prospecting fires generic messages that bounce and the deal stalls between stakeholders: the user requests it, finance freezes it, security vetoes it. Mapping the committee as buyer personas unlocks tailored messages by role, anticipates objections before they kill the deal, identifies the champion who drives it from within, and accelerates your commercial strategy. The most expensive mistake is confusing functional role with nominal title: the same person can be both User and Technical Buyer, and a CFO is not always the real Economic Buyer.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B sales strategist specializing in complex sales and Decision-Making Unit mapping, with mastery of Jobs-to-be-Done and actionable buyer persona design.

Deliverable: a set of buyer personas (one per committee role) plus a comparison table, decision journey, and message angles. Steps:
1. Derive committee roles from SOLUCION, SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO, and TICKET_COMPLEJIDAD using the DMU model: Economic Buyer, User(s), Technical Buyer / Gatekeeper, Internal Champion, and Brake / Blocker. Calibrate composition: a transactional ticket may collapse roles into one person; a strategic one adds a risk, finance, procurement, or legal committee. Merge or split according to complexity and integrate ROLES_CONOCIDOS without duplicating.
2. Per persona define nine attributes: label and typical title, business objective, motivations (personal and professional), current pain points and frustrations, evaluation criteria, success metrics they are measured by, likely objections, and action trigger.
3. Anchor every non-obvious attribute in FUENTES_EVIDENCIA citing the source; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference without backing and assign it a confidence level (high / medium / low).
4. Map the decision journey with the sequence initiates > influences > approves > vetoes; flag the typical bottleneck and the lever that unblocks it.
5. Close with a comparison table of roles and, per persona, a one-line prospecting message angle tied to their dominant pain point.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm SOLUCION, SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO, TICKET_COMPLEJIDAD, and the solidity of FUENTES_EVIDENCIA; if anything critical is missing or evidence is weak, ask for it or declare it before proceeding.
Phase 2 Roles: determine committee composition according to ticket complexity; distinguish functional role from nominal title and declare when one person carries two roles.
Phase 3 Personas: complete the nine attributes per role, anchoring in evidence and marking assumptions with their confidence level.
Phase 4 Dynamics: trace the decision journey, the bottleneck, and the unblocking lever.
Phase 5 Activation: produce the comparison table and message angles per persona.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- One persona per functional committee role, with no overlapping pain points or criteria across roles; if one person carries two roles, it is declared.
- All nine attributes complete in each persona (label, title, objective, motivations, pain points, criteria, metrics, objections, trigger).
- Every non-obvious attribute anchored in FUENTES_EVIDENCIA or marked [ASSUMPTION] with a confidence level.
- Explicit distinction between functional role and nominal title; the Champion identified by personal stake in the deal moving forward, not by likability.
- Decision journey with the sequence initiates > influences > approves > vetoes, bottleneck, and unblocking lever.
- Readable comparison table and a one-line message angle per persona connected to their dominant pain point; no generic catalog personas.
- No invented prices or figures; ambiguities flagged for confirmation.
Expected deliverable: document with N persona profiles + comparison table + decision journey map + N prospecting message angles, ready to feed into segmented outreach sequences.
spec-ventas_lista_cuentas_objetivo:
[inputs]
- PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL: {{PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL}} > Ideal customer profile (ICP): industry, size, geography, stack or maturity, business model (e.g., "LATAM fintech, 50–500 employees, already on a cloud core banking system")
- OFERTA_PROBLEMA: {{OFERTA_PROBLEMA}} > What you sell and the problem it solves, which gives meaning to the fit axis (e.g., "automated reconciliation platform to reduce manual month-end close")

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I have a broad universe of possible accounts and a team with limited capacity: chasing all of them disperses effort and burns time on accounts that were never going to buy. A target account list prioritized by fit and intent converts that flat universe into an attack queue: fit reveals which accounts resemble my best customers, but fit alone is not enough, because a perfect account with no recent activity can take years. Intent adds the when: which accounts are showing signs of being in motion right now. Crossing both axes unlocks a short, defensible list of where to start, concentrates the team on accounts with the highest probability and momentum, and structures the coverage conversation with each seller.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B sales leader, expert in target account strategy, ICP definition, and fit-and-intent scoring models (account-based marketing style).

Produce a prioritized target account list with these components:
1. Definition of the two axes: 4–6 fit criteria tied to PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL and OFERTA_PROBLEMA, and 3–5 observable intent signals from SENALES_INTENCION; each axis with its weighting (summing to 100% per axis) and a 1–5 scale with explicit anchors per level, plus the threshold that separates high from low on each axis.
2. Ranking table: account, fit score 1–5, intent score 1–5, combined score, evidence or [ASSUMPTION], assigned tier.
3. Tier classification: A (high fit, high intent, attack now), B (high fit, low or latent intent, nurture), C (medium or opportunistic fit), discard (low fit, do not pursue).
4. A-tier account list capped at what CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO can cover, with entry angle and trigger to cite per account; if there are more A-tier accounts than slots, declare which enter the active cycle and which remain on a prioritized waitlist.
5. Treatment of B and C accounts: how to nurture them, what concrete and observable condition promotes them to A, and what to delegate or leave opportunistic.
6. Open questions to validate criteria, weightings, and signals before committing the team.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Define axes: derive fit criteria from PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL and OFERTA_PROBLEMA, and intent signals from SENALES_INTENCION; assign weighting to each criterion and set 1–5 scales with anchors and the high/low threshold per axis. Distinguish hard intent signals (verifiable triggering event) from soft ones (proxy or inference) and weight accordingly.
Phase 2 — Score: evaluate each account in CUENTAS_CANDIDATAS on fit and intent using available evidence; when you infer, mark it [ASSUMPTION] and do not present inferences as facts or invent account figures. If an account lacks sufficient evidence to score an axis, assign it to "to be qualified" instead of forcing a number.
Phase 3 — Rank and classify: calculate the combined score, sort the accounts, and assign them to tier A/B/C or discard; on ties, break by intent then by fit. Verify that each account falls in only one tier consistent with its scores and thresholds.
Phase 4 — Attack plan: limit A-tier accounts to what CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO can sustain, define entry angle and trigger per A-tier account, set B and C treatment with their promotion condition, and declare open questions.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
The target account list is complete when:
- Both axes have criteria tied to PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL and OFERTA_PROBLEMA, observable signals, weightings that sum to 100% per axis, and 1–5 scales with explicit anchors and a high/low threshold.
- Each account has a fit, intent, and combined score, with evidence or a visible [ASSUMPTION]; no inference is presented as fact and no figures are invented; accounts without evidence remain in "to be qualified".
- The ranking table and the classification are consistent: each account falls in only one tier consistent with its scores and thresholds.
- The A-tier account list respects CAPACIDAD_EQUIPO, declares active vs. waitlist if there is excess, and each A-tier account has an entry angle and trigger; B and C accounts have explicit treatment with an observable promotion condition.
- Open questions are listed to validate criteria, weightings, and signals.
- Text in neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis and without invented data.
Expected deliverable: document with the definition of the two axes, ranking table by combined score, A/B/C and discard classification, A-tier account list with angle and trigger (active and on waitlist), B and C treatment with promotion condition, and open validation questions.
spec-ventas_research_cuenta:
[inputs]
- CUENTA: {{CUENTA}} > Name of the target company to research

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are preparing the first contact with a target account in a B2B consultative selling process. The first message is rarely won with product: it is won with relevance. This pre-call research converts scattered data (website, news, job postings, LinkedIn, CRM) into an intelligence sheet that unlocks a credible entry angle, prioritizes the commercial effort, and reduces the risk of opening with a generic pitch that closes doors. The deliverable directly feeds the opening message and the discovery call, so its value depends on the traceability of every claim, not on the volume of data.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B commercial intelligence analyst, specialist in account-based selling and strategic account design.

Deliverable: an actionable one-page account sheet with these numbered sections:
1. Executive summary (3 lines): who the account is, its current moment, and why to contact it now.
2. Recent signals within the indicated window: funding rounds, key hires, launches, expansion, leadership changes, regulatory or market news. Each signal with its source or source type and a recency marker (recent / old / undated).
3. Priorities and initiatives declared by the account (website, reports, interviews, open job postings).
4. Purchase triggers: the event or combination that makes the timing opportune and the latent need it connects to, with confidence level (high / medium / low).
5. Tentative power map: economic buyer, internal champion, and affected user, with typical title for each role.
6. Value hypotheses: 2–3 falsifiable hypotheses ("we believe they face X, which costs Y, and the proposal changes it like this").
7. Entry angle: a single concrete hook for the first message, anchored in the strongest and most real signal.
8. Open questions to confirm in discovery.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Framing: confirm account, proposal, buyer profile, and time window. If an essential data point is missing (account, proposal, or decision-maker profile), ask for it before proceeding.
Phase 2 — Collection: order available signals by type (financial, talent, product, market, leadership). Cite source or source type and mark recency on each one.
Phase 3 — Synthesis: connect signals with declared priorities and identify the purchase trigger(s); assign confidence based on how many independent signals support it.
Phase 4 — Hypotheses and angle: derive falsifiable value hypotheses and a single entry angle anchored in the strongest and most recent signal. If two signals compete, choose the most recent and best-supported one.
Phase 5 — Control: separate fact from inference, mark [ASSUMPTION] for every unverified claim, list open questions, and flag low-confidence or outdated signals.
Cross-cutting rules: do not invent figures, names, or dates; gaps are declared as data to confirm. If there are not enough signals for a credible angle, state it explicitly and suggest what data to look for instead of forcing a weak hook.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- All 8 sections present and in order.
- Each signal has an explicit source or source type and a recency marker.
- Verified fact and inference are differentiated; every assumption carries [ASSUMPTION].
- Zero invented figures, names, or dates; gaps are declared to confirm.
- At least one purchase trigger connected to a latent need, with a confidence level.
- Value hypotheses formulated as falsifiable statements.
- A single entry angle, anchored in a real signal and not a generality.
- Power map covers economic buyer, champion, and user.
- If evidence is insufficient for a credible angle, it is declared and data to look for is suggested.
Expected deliverable: one-page account sheet, ready to prepare the opening message and the discovery call.

Detecting it in time is what separates outreach the buyer perceives as pertinent from outreach they ignore. This prompt converts scattered signals into prioritized and actionable contact angles for {{CUENTA_OBJETIVO}}, aligned with {{OFERTA}} and directed at {{PERFIL_COMPRADOR}}. Archetype: Senior B2B prospecting strategist specializing in trigger event selling, with experience in intent signals and outreach timing.

1. Restate the account(s), the offer, and the buyer profile. If {{CUENTA_OBJETIVO}}, {{OFERTA}}, or {{PERFIL_COMPRADOR}} are missing or ambiguous, ask for them before continuing.

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Starting a cold conversation with a prospect who does not know me. The goal of the first touch is not to sell but to earn a reply: to make the prospect feel the email was written for them and not for a list. A good cold email unlocks the first meeting and opens the pipeline; a generic one burns the contact and, worse, flags the domain as spam. The email will be sent as-is, without further editing: it must be flawless and self-sufficient.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior B2B outbound copywriter with a proven track record in high-response-rate cold email campaigns and mastery of prospecting copywriting.
Deliverable: a cold email in neutral, professional Spanish without emojis, ready to send, with subject and body separated plus a subject line variant for A/B testing.
Steps:
1. Subject of 4 to 7 words: curiosity or relevance anchored in the prospect's context — never clickbait, all-caps, or an empty promise. Avoid spam trigger words (urgent, offer, free, guaranteed).
2. Personalized opening anchored in DETALLE_PERSONALIZACION; no generic greeting or compliment. The first sentence must be impossible to reuse with another prospect.
3. Bridge: connect that detail to a concrete pain point or ambition of ROL_PROSPECTO; calibrate depth based on NIVEL_CONCIENCIA (more context if fully cold, more direct if they know the problem).
4. Value proposition in one or two sentences about RESULTADO_PROMETIDO; describe the measurable result, not the features of OFERTA. No unverifiable superlatives.
5. Proof: include PRUEBA_CREDIBILIDAD in one concrete line; if it arrives empty, omit it and mark [ASSUMPTION] omitted due to missing data. Never invent figures or client names.
6. Close with a single low-friction CTA; offer a tentative date only if CTA requests a meeting. If there are ADJUNTOS, mention them in one line without opening a second CTA.
7. Clean one-line signature, without inflated titles.

spec-ventas_secuencia_cadencia:

I need an outbound prospecting cadence to approach {{SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO}} and offer {{OFERTA}}, leveraging {{GATILLO_RELEVANCIA}} as the entry angle. A well-designed cadence over {{CANALES_DISPONIBLES}} and {{DURACION_DIAS}} unlocks systematic contact, messages that progress instead of repeating, and clear rules for what to do with every type of reply — so an SDR can load it into a sequencer and execute it while optimizing {{META_CONVERSION}}. The output must be self-executable: nothing that depends on context that only lives in my head.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior head of sales development with fifteen years designing high-performance outbound prospecting cadences for B2B SDR teams, expert in the multichannel sequencing models of Salesloft and Outreach.
Deliverable: a complete multichannel cadence with calendar, base messages, branching rules, and metrics. Steps:
1. Parameters: define total number of touches, duration in business days per {{DURACION_DIAS}}, mix of {{CANALES_DISPONIBLES}}, and spacing pattern (denser at start, sparser at end); justify the pattern in one sentence. 2. 3. Base messages: draft each written touch; email with subject and short body, a single idea and a single call to action; short call and voicemail scripts; social note. Chain a narrative that progresses from providing context to providing proof to creating urgency without repeating the same argument, speaking to {{SEGMENTO_OBJETIVO}} about {{OFERTA}}.

Phase 3 Content: execute step 3 drafting the messages in the calendar sequence, validating that each touch adds something new and does not repeat the previous one. spec-ventas_guion_llamada_fria:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO_SERVICIO: {{PRODUCTO_SERVICIO}} > What you sell: name and brief description of the product or service
- PROSPECTO: {{PROSPECTO}} > Whom you are calling: role, industry, and company size of the target contact
- DISPARADOR: {{DISPARADOR}} > Event, change, or relevant prospect/industry data point that justifies calling now
- PROPUESTA_VALOR: {{PROPUESTA_VALOR}} > Concrete problem you solve and result you enable for this profile
- OBJETIVO_LLAMADA: {{OBJETIVO_LLAMADA}} > (optional) Commitment you want to close (20-min meeting, demo, discovery); default: a short 20-minute discovery meeting
- CANAL_PRUEBA: {{CANAL_PRUEBA}} > (optional) If the prospect hangs up or does not answer, preferred follow-up channel (email, LinkedIn, another call); default: a short multichannel sequence
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am going to cold-call {{PROSPECTO}} to sell {{PRODUCTO_SERVICIO}} and I need a script that survives the first ten seconds — the part where most cold calls die. The challenge is to earn permission to speak, connect with {{DISPARADOR}} so the call feels relevant and not random, and transition to {{OBJETIVO_LLAMADA}} without pressuring. A good script unlocks real meetings with qualified prospects, reduces dial anxiety, and makes repeatable a conversation that today depends on luck or the caller's mood. Assumption: this is a first cold-door contact, not a follow-up to inbound or a referral.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior outbound sales representative (SDR/AE) with more than ten years closing cold meetings for B2B solutions, expert in permission-based openings and Jeb Blount's objection-handling structure (Fanatical Prospecting).
Deliverable: a cold call script ready to read aloud — conversational and not sounding like a script — with tone notes and success criteria. Build it in this order, in numbered blocks:
1. Permission-based opening: greeting, clear identification, honest acknowledgment that this is an unexpected call, and a request for thirty seconds with an easy-yes question.
2. Hook anchored in {{DISPARADOR}} that answers why this person and why now; never open with product features.
3. Value message in a single sentence based on {{PROPUESTA_VALOR}}: names the problem and the result, without jargon.
4. A single open discovery question that confirms relevance and invites {{PROSPECTO}} to speak.
5. Transition to agenda toward {{OBJETIVO_LLAMADA}}: micro-commitment with two concrete time options.
6. Four objection branches (validate + redirect to agenda): "no time", "we already have a solution", "send me an email", "I am not the right person".
7. Voicemail script of fifteen seconds with a single reason to return the call, aligned with {{CANAL_PRUEBA}}.
Accompany each block with a brief tone or rhythm note. Close with three usage notes: (a) what to adapt live based on the response, (b) the single metric to watch (rate of connected calls that convert to a meeting), and (c) a reminder that the script is a map, not a monologue: the goal is to listen more than talk.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Interpretation: confirm product, prospect, trigger, value proposition, and objective; if any is missing, ask for it before drafting. Do not invent the trigger or the value proposition: they are the foundation of relevance.
Phase 2 — Architecture: define the call's promise in one sentence and the single yes you are seeking (the meeting), so every block pushes toward it and nothing is superfluous.
Phase 3 — Conversational drafting: write in short sentences, readable aloud, with marked pauses; avoid superlatives, jargon, monologues, and any price promises.
Phase 4 — Resilience: draft the four objection branches and the voicemail maintaining tone and direction toward the agenda; each objection is validated first and redirected after, without arguing.
Phase 5 — Polish: review against the checklist, verify time limits (10 s to permission, 15 s voicemail), adjust rhythm, and deliver with the three usage notes.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The opening asks permission and can be answered with a yes in under ten seconds.
- The hook starts from {{DISPARADOR}}, not from the product, and justifies why this person and why now.
- The value proposition fits in one sentence and names problem + result, without jargon.
- There is exactly one open discovery question before asking for the meeting.
- The transition to agenda offers two concrete time options and asks for a single micro-commitment.
- The four objections have a response that validates first and redirects after, without arguing.
- The voicemail lasts fifteen seconds and leaves a single reason to return the call.
- Each block has its tone or rhythm note; the script closes with the three usage notes (adapt, metric, no-monologue).
- Everything is readable aloud, neutral and professional Spanish, without emojis, without the word "free", and without price promises.
Edge cases to cover: if the trigger is generic to the industry (not specific to the prospect), the hook grounds it with a verifiable hypothesis; if the objective is not a meeting but a demo or discovery, the transition adjusts without losing the micro-commitment.
Expected deliverable: cold call script in numbered blocks, with tone notes per block and three usage notes at the close, ready to use in the next dialing session.

--- S | SITUATION ---
An outbound call reaches the voicemail. Most sales voicemails are ignored or deleted: they sound like a generic pitch, give no reason to call back, and burn the contact for future attempts. A well-constructed voicemail (20–30 seconds, opened with concrete relevance, curiosity seeded without burning the value, close with the number dictated twice) turns the mailbox into a second door: it unlocks the callback and keeps the prospect warm. This prompt produces that script ready to read aloud. Non-negotiable premise: the callback is born from genuine relevance of MOTIVO_RELEVANCIA; without a real trigger, no phrasing can save it.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior sales coach specializing in B2B outbound telephone prospecting, with a focus on voice messaging that maximizes callback rate.
Deliverable: a complete voicemail script. Steps:
1. Validate NOMBRE_PROSPECTO, EMPRESA_PROSPECTO, MOTIVO_RELEVANCIA, NOMBRE_VENDEDOR, ROL_VENDEDOR, and NUMERO_CALLBACK. If any is missing, ask for it one question at a time before writing; do not invent data. If MOTIVO_RELEVANCIA is generic or weak (e.g., "I wanted to introduce myself"), flag it and suggest how to strengthen it before drafting.
2. Draft the main script of 55–75 words (20–30 spoken seconds): open with NOMBRE_PROSPECTO + MOTIVO_RELEVANCIA in the first 5 seconds; seed curiosity by hinting at the value without fully revealing it; identify NOMBRE_VENDEDOR and ROL_VENDEDOR; close by saying NUMERO_CALLBACK twice, slow and grouped in digit blocks.

4. Produce an alternate version of ~15 s (30–40 words) for mailboxes that cut off quickly: sacrifice curiosity before the number; the close with NUMERO_CALLBACK is non-negotiable in both versions.

Phase 1 Interpret: confirm data, evaluate the strength of the relevance angle and the attempt number.
Phase 2 Plan: define the opening hook, the curiosity to seed (what is hinted / what is reserved), and the close with the double number.
Phase 3 Execute: write main script, short version, and delivery notes; verify word count, estimated duration, and that the number appears twice.

I need to break the ice with a cold or follow-up prospect through a short 1:1 video of 30 to 90 seconds. A well-structured script unlocks a higher response rate than a mass message and leaves a reusable asset for prospecting campaigns. Phase 2 Structure: draft the five blocks ensuring they center the message on the prospect and not the sender, open with their name and not "I", and that the full text reads aloud in 90 seconds or less.

If {{METRICA_RESULTADO}} is not verifiable, flag it and propose a qualitative replacement rather than inventing figures.

Phase 3 Execute: draft the message (neutral, professional, warm Spanish, no pressure), the three subject lines, and the timing note. Attach {{ADJUNTOS}} only if they reinforce proof of the achievement. Never mention prices or use the word free; do not exaggerate the metric.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- [ ] Opens with a specific, recent achievement backed by {{METRICA_RESULTADO}}, not a generic compliment.
- [ ] Makes ONE single concrete, low-friction ask anchored in {{PERFIL_CLIENTE_IDEAL}} (role, sector, challenge).
- [ ] Offers at least two comfortable ways to facilitate the introduction (includes a forwardable-message option).
- [ ] Makes it explicit that there is no obligation and offers a dignified exit; zero pressure or sense of calling in a favor.

- [ ] Neutral, professional, warm Spanish; no emojis; no prices; no word "free".
- [ ] Length appropriate for {{CANAL}} (brief email / shorter LinkedIn / telegraphic WhatsApp).

spec-ventas_reactivacion_lead_frio:
[inputs]
- PROSPECTO: {{PROSPECTO}} > Name and role of the lead to reactivate, and company if applicable
- OFERTA_CONVERSADA: {{OFERTA_CONVERSADA}} > What was offered or discussed in the last exchange
- ULTIMO_CONTACTO: {{ULTIMO_CONTACTO}} > How long ago the last contact was, and why it went cold if known
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Sending channel (email, LinkedIn, WhatsApp)
- DISPARADOR: {{DISPARADOR}} > New and legitimate reason to reconnect now (news, event, prospect milestone, use case)
