[inputs]
- MODULOS_OBJETIVO: {{MODULOS_OBJETIVO}} > Modules, files, or packages where useful coverage should be raised
- LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Language and stack (e.g. TypeScript/Node, Python/Django, Java/Spring)
- FRAMEWORK_TEST: {{FRAMEWORK_TEST}} > Test framework and coverage tool (e.g. Jest + Istanbul, pytest + coverage.py, JUnit + JaCoCo)
- COBERTURA_ACTUAL: {{COBERTURA_ACTUAL}} > Current line and branch coverage, or "unknown"
- META_COBERTURA: {{META_COBERTURA}} > Useful coverage goal and/or mutation score threshold (optional)
- CONVENCIONES_TEST: {{CONVENCIONES_TEST}} > Suite conventions: test location, mocks/fixtures, naming, allowed doubles, or "infer from code" (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Coverage report (lcov/html/xml), source code, existing test suite, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs to raise coverage of MODULOS_OBJETIVO, but the risk is chasing the percentage instead of value: a suite at 90% full of trivial tests (accessors, lines without logic, assertions that only confirm the code ran) gives false confidence and leaves exactly the branches that break in production unprotected. A risk-based strategy unlocks early-detectable regressions, safe refactors, and faster reviews, concentrating effort where a defect hurts.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior quality engineer (QE) specialized in risk-based testing strategy and in distinguishing meaningful coverage from filler coverage.
Deliverable: prioritized test backlog + the tests written for the highest-risk gaps in MODULOS_OBJETIVO. Steps:
1. Read the coverage report from ADJUNTOS and list lines and branches NOT covered in MODULOS_OBJETIVO, mapping each gap to its function.
2. Classify each gap as risk logic (conditionals, error handling, calculations, validations, iteration limits, concurrency, mutable state) or noise (generated code, logging, trivial accessors, configuration).
3. Prioritize the backlog by impact x failure probability: for each real gap, indicate what defect it could hide and the production impact.
4. Design cases covering branches, edge conditions, invalid inputs, and error paths, in addition to the happy path.
5. Write the tests in FRAMEWORK_TEST with the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern and specific assertions on observable behavior, respecting CONVENCIONES_TEST.
6. Explicitly declare what is NOT worth testing and why, so as not to waste effort.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: parse the report, map gaps to functions, separate risk from noise. If COBERTURA_ACTUAL is "unknown", derive it from the report; if there is no report, mark [ASSUMPTION] and request the attachment.
Phase 2 - Prioritization: order by impact x probability; mark [ASSUMPTION] when report or code is insufficient. Distinguish line coverage from branch coverage (a line covered with its false branch unexercised is still a gap).
Phase 3 - Design: for each prioritized gap enumerate cases (happy, edge, invalid, error) BEFORE coding; reuse existing fixtures/mocks instead of duplicating.
Phase 4 - Implementation: write AAA tests with descriptive names and behavioral assertions; no empty asserts, no tests that only invoke the function, no over-mocking what you want to verify. Do not invent APIs or signatures absent from the code.
Phase 5 - Verification: indicate how to confirm real utility via mutation testing on the touched modules (e.g. Stryker, mutmut, PIT depending on stack); a test that kills no mutation is filler and is rewritten or discarded. Compare against META_COBERTURA if provided.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each new test covers a real branch, edge case, or error path, not a trivial line.
- [ ] Every assertion verifies observable behavior (value, state, exception, effect), never just that the code ran.
- [ ] The backlog explains, per gap, the defect it hides and the production impact, ordered by impact x probability.
- [ ] Line coverage is distinguished from branch coverage; a branch is not reported as covered if its condition was not exercised in both directions.
- [ ] What is NOT tested is explicitly listed and why.
- [ ] Tests follow Arrange-Act-Assert, respect CONVENCIONES_TEST, and run in FRAMEWORK_TEST without inventing APIs.
- [ ] The command or method to validate utility via mutation testing is included, appropriate to the stack.
- [ ] Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION] when data is missing.
Expected deliverable: risk-prioritized backlog + test suite ready to integrate + mutation verification note on MODULOS_OBJETIVO.
spec-vibe-coding_tests-de-regresion-visu:
[inputs]
- COMPONENTES_O_VISTAS: {{COMPONENTES_O_VISTAS}} > UI components, pages, or views that are candidates for baseline (e.g. button, payment modal, dashboard, checkout)
- STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA: {{STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA}} > UI framework and snapshot tool (e.g. React + Storybook + Chromatic; Playwright toHaveScreenshot; Cypress + Percy; Vue + Vitest)
- ESTADOS_Y_VIEWPORTS: {{ESTADOS_Y_VIEWPORTS}} > States to capture (default, hover, focus, loading, error, empty, long data) and target viewports (mobile, tablet, desktop) (optional, default: key states + 3 viewports)
- TOLERANCIA_Y_CI: {{TOLERANCIA_Y_CI}} > Acceptable difference threshold and CI pipeline where it runs (e.g. 0.1% pixels in GitHub Actions; strict comparison in GitLab CI) (optional, default: conservative threshold + pull request flow)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to shield the interface of {{COMPONENTES_O_VISTAS}} against unintentional visual changes: a CSS refactor, a dependency bump, or a theme adjustment can break the layout without any functional test noticing. A snapshot-based visual regression suite captures reference images (baselines) and compares each change pixel by pixel, turning visual appearance into a versionable assertion. The known risk of the approach is fragility (flakiness): if images change due to animations, fonts, or random data, the team stops trusting the suite and silences it, losing all its utility. A well-designed suite unlocks merges with confidence, early detection of UI regressions, explicit visual review on every pull request, and a stable base for aggressive refactors. The typical mistake is inverting the signal-to-noise ratio: too many fragile snapshots that cost more maintenance than they save.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior frontend quality engineer specialized in automated visual testing, with practice in {{STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA}}, anti-flakiness strategies, and CI pipeline design.

Deliverable: a visual regression suite ready to operate on {{COMPONENTES_O_VISTAS}}, with complete configuration, an example end-to-end snapshot test, and an operation runbook. Steps:
1. Surface inventory: prioritize within {{COMPONENTES_O_VISTAS}} what is critical (high traffic or high regression risk), what is reused (change one, impact many), and what is historically fragile; explicitly declare what is excluded because it changes design every sprint and why the maintenance cost exceeds the value.
2. Capture matrix: derive from {{ESTADOS_Y_VIEWPORTS}} the state and viewport combinations with real signal, separating them from noise, and justify each inclusion. Avoid combinatorial explosion: not every state deserves every viewport.
3. Anti-flakiness strategy: neutralize sources of instability before capturing (animations and transitions off, fonts preloaded and embedded, dates and randomness frozen with deterministic data or mocks, waits for stable state and not for time, dynamic regions masked such as avatars, timestamps, or carousels).
4. Baseline generation: define how they are created, where they are versioned (repository with LFS or snapshot service), how they are named stably, and how they are regenerated in a controlled manner in {{STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA}}, avoiding mass regenerations that hide real regressions.
5. Comparison and tolerance: configure the per-pixel and per-percentage threshold according to {{TOLERANCIA_Y_CI}}, justify the chosen value (too strict = noise from antialiasing; too lax = invisible regressions), and describe how diffs are read.
6. CI integration: define the job that runs on every pull request, fails on unapproved diffs, publishes expected/actual/difference images as artifacts, and exposes an intentional-change approval flow (update baseline with human review, never automatically). Consider the time cost and how to parallelize or run selectively by affected surface.
7. Governance: rules for who approves new baselines, how blind-approval of diffs is prevented (mandatory visual review), and what metrics measure suite health (flake rate, execution time, critical surface coverage, age of unreviewed baselines).

Edge cases to cover: cross-browser rendering (same fonts, same engine, or accept baselines per browser); variable-length i18n content; dark/light mode as a dimension; entry animations that never settle static; external images or fonts that are slow or fail; first run without a prior baseline (must not pass green by default).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA}} and deduce the native snapshot capabilities of that tool; mark with [ASSUMPTION] any data not provided and do not invent tool capabilities.
Phase 2 - Design: produce the prioritized inventory and the state x viewport matrix before writing code, with the explicit signal-to-noise ratio.
Phase 3 - Stabilization: define the anti-flakiness measures as a precondition of every capture (minimum five, concrete).
Phase 4 - Implementation: deliver the complete tool configuration, an example end-to-end snapshot test, and the baseline generation/update commands.
Phase 5 - CI and governance: deliver the pipeline job and the operation runbook (run locally, update baseline, interpret a failure, distinguish regression from intentional change).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The inventory distinguishes surfaces worth a baseline from those that generate noise, with exclusions justified by cost/value.
- [ ] Each state x viewport combination is justified by real signal, not exhaustiveness, without combinatorial explosion.
- [ ] There are at least five concrete anti-flakiness measures applied before capturing (animations, fonts, deterministic data/dates, state waits, masking of dynamic regions).
- [ ] The tolerance threshold is defined in pixels and percentage, with its explicit justification and the strict-vs-lax trade-off.
- [ ] The delivered configuration is valid for {{STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA}} and can be pasted without rewriting.
- [ ] There is an example end-to-end snapshot test that runs as-is.
- [ ] The CI job fails on unapproved diffs, publishes expected/actual/difference images, and defines the intentional-change approval flow with human review.
- [ ] The first run without a baseline does not pass green by default; declared edge cases are resolved or marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Governance prevents blind baseline approval and names suite health metrics.
Expected deliverable: plan + complete configuration + one example end-to-end snapshot test + baseline commands + operation runbook, all consistent with {{STACK_Y_HERRAMIENTA}}, {{ESTADOS_Y_VIEWPORTS}}, and {{TOLERANCIA_Y_CI}}.
spec-vibe-coding_mocks-stubs-y-fixtures:
[inputs]
- MODULO_O_DEPENDENCIA: {{MODULO_O_DEPENDENCIA}} > Component under test and the dependency to double (e.g. payment service consumed by checkout)
- LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK_TEST: {{LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK_TEST}} > Language and test framework/mocking library (e.g. TypeScript + Vitest, Python + pytest, Java + JUnit5 + Mockito)
- CONTRATO_PUBLICO: {{CONTRATO_PUBLICO}} > Signatures, return types, and observable errors of the dependency to double; never private internal details
- CASOS_LIMITE: {{CASOS_LIMITE}} > Edge scenarios to cover with fixtures (e.g. empty, null, maximum value, invalid payload, timeout, network error, concurrency)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Test doubles are being designed for {{MODULO_O_DEPENDENCIA}} in {{LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK_TEST}}. The goal is a suite that validates observable behavior and not implementation: doubles anchored to the public contract and fixtures with a single source of truth. This unlocks fast, deterministic, refactor-resistant tests; when the internal implementation changes without changing the contract, the tests stay green, and coherent fixtures avoid the maintenance cost of duplicated and out-of-sync data. The central risk to neutralize: over-mocking, which produces tests that verify a mirror of the implementation and break on any innocuous refactor, giving a false sense of coverage.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior testing engineer, specialist in test double design and fixture architecture, with criteria on test-implementation coupling.
Deliverable: code for the doubles, a parameterizable fixture factory, and usage examples. Steps:
1. Classify each dependency by the appropriate double type: stub (controlled input data), mock (verify expected interactions), spy (observe real calls without altering behavior), fake (lightweight in-memory implementation). Justify each choice and point out where it is NOT appropriate to double (pure logic, value objects, trivial collaborators) to avoid over-mocking.
2. Anchor doubles to the public contract of {{CONTRATO_PUBLICO}}: only signatures, returns, and observable errors. Forbidden to depend on private methods, non-contractual internal call order, or unexposed data structures. Distinguish command interactions (verifiable) from query interactions (not verified, only stubbed).
3. Design the canonical fixture schema: a factory/builder with a single source of truth, valid defaults, and partial overrides so each test requests only what is relevant and the rest remains coherent. Cover both the happy path and the contract's error states.
4. Derive from that same factory the fixtures for {{CASOS_LIMITE}}, without duplicating the base schema; each edge case is an override, not a new object.
5. Guarantee isolation: fresh state per test, reset between cases, no implicit order or shared mutable state. For stateful fakes, expose a reset method. Deliver usage examples in at least two representative tests (one behavioral, one interaction).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Dependency map: list the collaborations of {{MODULO_O_DEPENDENCIA}} and decide double by double (or not to double), with the justification.
Phase 2 Contract: extract from {{CONTRATO_PUBLICO}} the signatures and observable errors that doubles must respect; separate commands from queries.
Phase 3 Fixture factory: define valid consistent defaults + override API; derive {{CASOS_LIMITE}} as overrides.
Phase 4 Doubles: implement stub/mock/spy/fake according to Phase 1, connected to the factory.
Phase 5 Demonstration and isolation: two example tests + setup/teardown that ensures fresh state. Mark any data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with a reasonable default value.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each double is justified by type and none depends on private or non-contractual details.
- [ ] There is no over-mocking: trivial, pure, or value-object dependencies remain undoubled and the reason is explained.
- [ ] Only command interactions are verified; query ones are stubbed without assertions on count/order of calls.
- [ ] There is a single source of truth for fixtures (factory/builder) with valid defaults and partial overrides.
- [ ] {{CASOS_LIMITE}} derive from the same factory as overrides, without a duplicated schema.
- [ ] Isolation guaranteed: fresh state per test, reset between cases, zero shared mutable state or implicit order; stateful fakes expose reset.
- [ ] At least two executable example tests (one behavioral, one interaction) show real use of doubles and factory.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; missing contract/framework requested before coding.
Expected deliverable: code file(s) with the fixture factory, the classified doubles, and two example tests ready to run in {{LENGUAJE_Y_FRAMEWORK_TEST}}, plus a brief note on doubling decisions (what was doubled, with what type and why, and what was left undoubled).
spec-vibe-coding_property-based-testing:
[inputs]
- CODIGO: {{CODIGO}} > Function, module, or class under test; paste the signature and body, or describe the behavior if there is no code yet
- FRAMEWORK: {{FRAMEWORK}} > Language + PBT library: Python/Hypothesis, JS-TS/fast-check, Java/jqwik, Rust/proptest, Scala/ScalaCheck, Elixir/PropCheck, or other
- CONTRATO: {{CONTRATO}} > Expected input, expected output, preconditions, and postconditions of the code
- INVARIANTES: {{INVARIANTES}} > Properties or invariants you already know or suspect (optional; if missing, the model derives them from the contract)
- PRESUPUESTO: {{PRESUPUESTO}} > Number of examples to generate, seed for reproducibility, and time limit (optional; default 100 examples, fixed seed)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Example tests only test the cases the developer already imagined, which is why they fail precisely where no one looked: the empty string, zero, the negative, the unusual unicode, the list with duplicates, the boundary date, NaN, overflow. Property-based testing inverts the problem: instead of asserting "for this input I expect this output", it declares a property the code must satisfy for EVERY valid input and lets the framework generate hundreds of random inputs looking for a counterexample. For {{CODIGO}} this unlocks coverage that no hand-written example reaches, turns tacit assumptions into verifiable invariants, and when something breaks, shrinking delivers the minimal reproducible counterexample. It is the difference between testing what you remember and testing what the code actually promises.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior quality engineer specialized in property-based testing, with mastery of generators, shrinking, and property catalogs in the QuickCheck/Hypothesis style (John Hughes, Scott Wlaschin).
Deliver, in this order:
1. Restate the contract of {{CODIGO}} from {{CONTRATO}}: what it receives, what it returns, what preconditions and postconditions govern it; leave an explicit assumption for every gap you had to fill.
2. Enumerate 4 to 8 candidate properties in a table, classified by pattern (invariant, round-trip, oracle, idempotency, commutativity/associativity, metamorphic, conservation); one line per property with the concrete bug it would catch; integrate {{INVARIANTES}} if provided and discard redundant ones justifying why.
3. Mark with [ASSUMPTION] every property that depends on an unconfirmed precondition.
4. Design the input generators in {{FRAMEWORK}}: valid domain per parameter and forced edge cases with explicit weight (empty, zero, negatives, unicode/emoji, NaN/Inf, duplicates, numeric and date limits, large collections); use compound, filtered, or labeled generators when the domain requires it and declare what inputs you exclude and why.
5. Write one executable test per property, with a descriptive name, clear assertions, and the {{PRESUPUESTO}} configuration (number of examples + fixed seed); group common configuration.
6. Explain how to read the minimal counterexample that shrinking produces when a property fails, distinguishing a bug in the code from a poorly specified property.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Contract: reconstruct the input/output/preconditions/postconditions of {{CODIGO}}; if {{CODIGO}}, {{FRAMEWORK}}, or {{CONTRATO}} is missing or ambiguous, ask for them in a single round before writing code, without inventing the signature.
Phase 2 - Property discovery: traverse the pattern catalog and select those that apply; discard redundant ones and justify each with the bug it catches.
Phase 3 - Generators: define the valid domain and force edge cases with weight; use compound or filtered generators when the domain requires it and declare exclusions.
Phase 4 - Coding: one test per property in {{FRAMEWORK}}, names that describe the property, example count configuration and fixed seed; avoid flakiness (unseeded randomness, clock or network without freezing) and indicate how to reduce examples for CI without losing detection power.
Phase 5 - Verification: enable shrinking, anticipate which property would be a genuine bug if it fails and, if you suspect one is already broken in {{CODIGO}}, declare the expected counterexample.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist before delivering:
- The contract is reconstructed with preconditions and postconditions; every filled gap carries an explicit assumption.
- There are between 4 and 8 properties in a table, each labeled with its pattern (invariant, round-trip, oracle, idempotency, commutativity/associativity, metamorphic, conservation).
- Each property declares in one line the real bug it would catch; none is a disguised example test and the discarding of redundant ones is justified.
- Every property that depends on an unconfirmed precondition is marked [ASSUMPTION].
- Generators deliberately cover edge cases with weight (empty, zero, negatives, unicode, NaN/Inf, duplicates, limits) and declare exclusions.
- Each test is executable in {{FRAMEWORK}}, with a descriptive name, clear assertion, and fixed seed; no sources of flakiness and a note on how to reduce examples for CI.
- Shrinking is enabled and the reading of the minimal counterexample is explained, distinguishing a code bug from a poorly specified property.
- At least one property whose failure would be a genuine bug is identified and, if applicable, the anticipated counterexample is stated.
Expected deliverable: property-based test suite ready to paste and run in {{FRAMEWORK}}, with property table classified by pattern, generators with explicit edge cases and exclusions, example count and seed configuration, and minimal counterexample reading guide.
spec-vibe-coding_pruebas-de-accesibilida:
[inputs]
- FRAMEWORK: {{FRAMEWORK}} > Project's frontend stack (React/Next, Vue/Nuxt, Angular, Astro, static site, etc.)
- PLATAFORMA_CI: {{PLATAFORMA_CI}} > Continuous integration platform (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, CircleCI, Azure Pipelines)
- RUTAS_OBJETIVO: {{RUTAS_OBJETIVO}} > Critical routes, URLs, or views to audit (e.g. /, /login, /checkout)
- NIVEL_WCAG: {{NIVEL_WCAG}} > Target version and level (e.g. WCAG 2.2 AA) (optional, default WCAG 2.2 AA)
- REQUIERE_AUTH: {{REQUIERE_AUTH}} > Whether routes require an authenticated session and how to obtain it (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The project advances with frequent deployments and accessibility degrades silently: every UI change can introduce WCAG violations that no one detects until a user or an audit reports them. Integrating automated checks in CI turns accessibility into a verifiable pipeline property: it blocks new regressions, makes inherited debt visible without slowing the team, and produces auditable evidence on every pull request. This unlocks iterating fast without sacrificing compliance or inclusion, and shifts the remediation cost to the cheapest moment: before the merge.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior web quality engineer specialized in accessibility (WCAG/ARIA) and test automation in CI/CD, with experience in axe-core and headless runners.
Deliverable: ready-to-integrate automated accessibility test configuration, with severity-based gating and a versioned baseline. Steps:
1. Define the scope: routes from RUTAS_OBJETIVO, target NIVEL_WCAG, and, if REQUIERE_AUTH applies, the session flow prior to the audit.
2. Generate the CI job for PLATAFORMA_CI that installs dependencies, starts or serves the app, waits for it to be ready (health-check, not a fixed sleep), and runs axe-core with a headless runner (Playwright or Puppeteer) consistent with FRAMEWORK.
3. Map severity (critical, serious, moderate, minor) to a gate policy: fail the build on critical and serious by default; moderate and minor as configurable warnings.
4. Create a versioned baseline of pre-existing findings (snapshot per rule + stable selector) that does not block inherited debt, but breaks the build on any new or worsened finding; document how to deliberately and traceably regenerate the baseline.
5. Produce a readable report attached to the pull request: WCAG rule violated, selector of the affected node, severity, impact, and correction suggestion.
6. Document the local execution equivalent to the CI one for reproducing before pushing.

Assumptions and limits to declare: how the app is started (port, environment variables, build vs dev server); explicit waits to avoid flakiness from asynchronous rendering; auth handling via reusable session state (storage state) instead of re-login per route. DO NOT invent axe-core rule identifiers or selectors: use real rules and selectors or mark them as pending confirmation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: confirm FRAMEWORK, PLATAFORMA_CI, RUTAS_OBJETIVO, NIVEL_WCAG, and REQUIERE_AUTH; if something critical is missing, ask before coding.
Phase 2 - Design: choose headless runner and baseline format; define severity thresholds, gate behavior, and wait strategy; decide how the authenticated session is persisted.
Phase 3 - Implementation: write the audit script, baseline file, CI job definition, and local command; use real axe-core selectors and rules, without inventing identifiers.
Phase 4 - Verification: validate that a simulated new finding breaks the build, that a finding in the baseline does not, and that a worsened finding (severity rises or duplicates) also breaks; confirm the report is attached to the pull request.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The CI job runs on PLATAFORMA_CI and audits all routes from RUTAS_OBJETIVO.
- [ ] axe-core runs with a headless runner consistent with FRAMEWORK; NIVEL_WCAG declared in config (correct WCAG tags).
- [ ] The app is served and the audit waits for real readiness (health-check), not a fixed sleep.
- [ ] The gate fails on critical and serious; moderate and minor remain as configurable warnings.
- [ ] A versioned baseline exists: inherited debt does not break the build; a new or worsened finding does; the regeneration process is deliberate and documented.
- [ ] If REQUIERE_AUTH applies, the session flow runs before auditing and the session state is reused.
- [ ] The pull request report includes WCAG rule, node selector, severity, impact, and correction suggestion.
- [ ] The local command equivalent to the CI one is documented.
- [ ] Environment assumptions (port, env, build) explicitly declared.
- [ ] Explicit note: automation covers only a fraction of WCAG criteria; a complementary manual checklist is recommended (keyboard, screen reader, contextual contrast, visible focus).
Expected deliverable: scripts and configuration files (CI job, axe-core audit script, baseline file, local command) accompanied by usage instructions, declared assumptions, and the partial coverage warning.
spec-vibe-coding_test-de-carga-y-rendimi:
[inputs]
- SISTEMA_OBJETIVO: {{SISTEMA_OBJETIVO}} > Service, API, or app under test: stack, base URL, environment (staging/preprod/prod), and critical dependencies (database, cache, third parties)
- SLO_OBJETIVO: {{SLO_OBJETIVO}} > Acceptance thresholds: p95/p99 latency, sustained throughput in req/s, and maximum tolerated error rate
- TRAFICO_REFERENCIA: {{TRAFICO_REFERENCIA}} > Expected volume: concurrent users or req/s, peak hour, and arrival pattern (constant, ramp, spikes)
- ENDPOINTS_CRITICOS: {{ENDPOINTS_CRITICOS}} > Transactions to stress and their relative weight (e.g. read 70%, write 20%, login 10%)
- HERRAMIENTA: {{HERRAMIENTA}} > Preferred load tool: k6, Locust, or Gatling (optional; if omitted, recommend and justify)
- ENTORNO_Y_LIMITES: {{ENTORNO_Y_LIMITES}} > Where it runs, agreed window, abort plan, and sensitive data to protect (optional; if omitted, assume staging and DO NOT touch production)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We want to discover where the system breaks under load BEFORE users discover it in production. A well-designed basic load test turns an uncertainty ("will it handle the peak?") into a defensible number and a prioritized list of bottlenecks. This unlocks capacity decisions, autoscaling configuration, and release go/no-go criteria with evidence, not intuition. A poorly designed test does the opposite: gives false confidence if the generator saturates before the system, measures cache instead of logic, or ignores queue latency due to coordinated omission.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior performance and SRE engineer with experience in load testing distributed systems, resource saturation diagnosis, and reading latency-vs-throughput curves.

Deliverable: an executable load test plan for {{SISTEMA_OBJETIVO}} plus the script ready to run. Produce, in order:
1. SLOs and pass/fail criteria derived from {{SLO_OBJETIVO}}: p95/p99 latency, target throughput in req/s, and maximum error rate, each as a verifiable threshold. Add a single virtual user baseline to separate intrinsic latency from load-induced latency.
2. Load model from {{TRAFICO_REFERENCIA}}: target virtual users or req/s, arrival profile (constant, ramp, or spikes; open vs closed model and why), weighted mix of {{ENDPOINTS_CRITICOS}} summing to 100%, prior warmup, and a data strategy that avoids trivial caching (parameterization, unique data per iteration, rotating accounts/IDs).
3. Three scenarios with duration and ramp profile: (a) nominal at expected load, (b) stress with an increasing ramp until degradation, (c) sudden spike. Indicate the stopping criterion for each (SLO violated, error budget exhausted, or duration).
4. Executable script with {{HERRAMIENTA}} (if empty, choose between k6, Locust, or Gatling and justify), parameterized by environment via variables, with hardcoded thresholds that abort or mark the run as failed on SLO violation, and with documented coordinated omission mitigation (open model or fixed rate).
5. List of server-side metrics to instrument in parallel: CPU, memory, connections and database connection pool, queue depth, GC or runtime pauses, and external dependency latency; with the source of each metric (APM, exporter, logs).
6. Reading method: how to locate the knee point on the latency-vs-throughput curve, how to isolate the limiting resource (CPU saturation vs concurrency/pool vs lock contention vs dependency latency), and an actionable findings checklist with severity and suggested remediation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate system, SLOs, and reference traffic; mark any missing data as a blocker and ask for it. If {{ENTORNO_Y_LIMITES}} is empty, assume staging, declare [ASSUMPTION], and DO NOT design against production without a window and abort plan.
Phase 2 - Plan: present the load model and the three scenarios in a table (load, duration, ramp, stopping criterion, objective of each) for validation before coding.
Phase 3 - Execute: generate the script with thresholds and warmup, the server instrumentation list with its source, and the reading guide; leave TODO marked where a real data point is missing and [ASSUMPTION] where you assume capacity or traffic, instead of inventing it.
Phase 4 - Verify: confirm that every SLO from {{SLO_OBJETIVO}} has a corresponding threshold in the script, that the three scenarios are covered with a stopping criterion, and that the test measures the system and not the generator or the cache.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

I need to consume a third-party API from my application and the provider is a failure point I don't control: it has variable latency, returns transient errors, and occasionally goes down. A naive integration propagates those failures to my users, exhausts connections, duplicates operations when retrying blindly, or takes down the entire service when the provider degrades. Applying resilience patterns (separate timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter only on retryable and idempotent operations, Retry-After compliance, circuit breaker, and graceful fallback) turns a fragile dependency into an integration that fails in a predictable and contained manner. This unlocks putting the integration into production with confidence, protecting the user experience during provider incidents, and having evidence (tests and metrics) of how the system behaves under failure. The tolerable latency budget is the master constraint: timeouts, number of retries, and backoff must fit within it, not be derived in the abstract.

--- P | REQUEST ---

1. Error classification: table separating transient retryable errors (timeout, 429, 502, 503, 504, network cuts/connection refused) from permanent non-retryable ones (400, 401, 403, 404, 422), with the action for each case. Treat 408 and 425 as retryable and idempotent 5xx with explicit criteria.
2. 3. Idempotency: use or generate an idempotency key for writes, stable and reused across retries of the same logical operation (not regenerated per attempt), so that a retry doesn't duplicate the effect.
4. Wrapper client in STACK: encapsulates AUTENTICACION without leaking secrets, the above patterns, the mapping of HTTP errors to typed domain errors, cancellation/deadline propagation, and the degraded fallback defined in LATENCIA_Y_FALLBACK. Commented code, ready to run.
5. Observability: structured logs (without secrets or tokens), latency metrics with percentiles (p50/p95/p99), error rate by class, retry counter, and breaker state/transitions, with per-request correlation (propagated request-id).
6. Tests covering: timeout, transient error with successful retry, permanent error without retry, open circuit breaker that fails fast without calling the provider, and idempotent retry that doesn't duplicate; with a provider double/mock and controllable clock for backoff.
7. Degraded-behavior table: what the system returns in each failure mode (slow provider, sustained 429, 5xx, total outage, open breaker).

Phase 2 – Defenses: calibrate connection and read timeouts to LATENCIA_Y_FALLBACK; define retries with exponential backoff and full jitter, with a cap and a bounded total budget, only on retryable and idempotent operations per IDEMPOTENCIA_OPERACIONES; respect Retry-After aligned to LIMITES_Y_SLA; size the circuit breaker (threshold, single-probe half-open, recovery) avoiding thundering herd on reopening.

An endpoint, view, report, or job loads slowly and N+1 queries (one query per iterated row) or full scans due to a missing index are suspected. Resolving this unlocks capacity without scaling hardware: it reduces perceived latency, lowers engine load, and avoids timeouts as data grows. 4. For each full scan: propose the exact index (columns, order, type; composite, partial, or covering when applicable) and deliver idempotent migration SQL; estimate its cost in writes and storage.
5. For each expensive repeated recomputation: define a cache layer with key, TTL, and explicit invalidation policy; discard caching for transactional data that can't tolerate staleness.
6. Justify every change by its write and memory cost against the read benefit; explicitly discard indexes or caches that don't pay for themselves.

Phase 5 - Hardening and close: raise the TTL to a stable value (e.g. 3600 s), confirm automatic renewal (schedule an expiration alert as a safety net) and record the exact rollback (previous record, value, TTL and reversion order).

5. Deliver abuse cases with real vectors (quotes, union/boolean, null bytes, ../, script tags, double encoding, NoSQL operators, instruction sequences) that demonstrate that each barrier neutralizes the attack.

Without per-client limits, a single actor can degrade the service, drain third-party quotas, or compromise accounts. The real challenge is not just limiting: it is doing so correctly across multiple instances, without penalizing legitimate traffic behind the same NAT, and without fully opening or closing the service when the store fails. 3. Implement the limiter over ALMACEN_COMPARTIDO with atomic operations (Lua script, or atomically INCR with EXPIRE in Redis) so that it is correct across instances; never local process memory.

5. Add layered defenses to sensitive endpoints: progressive temporary blocking after repeated failures, captcha or proof of work on spikes, enumeration pattern detection, and exit policy (fail-open vs fail-closed) if the store goes down.
6. Define what to log and alert (429 rate, top IPs/tokens, spikes per endpoint) without storing credentials or sensitive personal data.

Phase 3 Execute: deliver the commented middleware/limiter code at decision points, the store configuration, 429 response examples with headers, and a test plan (concurrent burst, window reset, multi-instance, store failure simulation). Cover edge cases: racing counters, desynchronized clock, legitimate corporate NAT, and clients retrying without backoff. Do not invent framework signatures; if in doubt, declare it.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each sensitive endpoint has an explicit and justified limit, window, and key, grouped by sensitivity level.
- [ ] The chosen algorithm is justified against the alternatives and documents its precision vs memory trade-off.
- [ ] State lives in ALMACEN_COMPARTIDO with atomic operations; correct for multiple instances (no local memory, no race conditions).
- [ ] 429 response includes Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers; exponential backoff with jitter is suggested to the client.

spec-vibe-coding_manejo-de-errores-consi:
[inputs]
- APP_O_MODULO: {{APP_O_MODULO}} > Application or module where error handling is to be unified
- STACK_LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK: {{STACK_LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} > Main language and framework (e.g. Node/Express, Python/FastAPI, React)
- CAPAS: {{CAPAS}} > Layers to cover (e.g. backend API, service layer, frontend)
- SISTEMA_LOGGING: {{SISTEMA_LOGGING}} > Current or target logging library or service (optional)
- CONTRATO_RESPUESTA: {{CONTRATO_RESPUESTA}} > Expected error response format for API or UI (optional)
- NIVEL_OBSERVABILIDAD: {{NIVEL_OBSERVABILIDAD}} > Target maturity: logs only, logs + metrics, or distributed traces (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Error handling in {{APP_O_MODULO}} is fragmented: each module captures, logs, and displays failures in its own way. This increases debugging costs, leaks technical details to the user, produces inconsistent responses, and leaves support and operations blind when something fails in production. Unifying it unlocks rapid diagnosis by correlation, a coherent user experience, and a solid foundation for alerts and observability. The goal is not to catch more errors, but to ensure every error follows the same path: it is typed, logged with context, and translated into a safe response.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior software engineer specializing in reliability and observability, with experience in {{STACK_LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}}.
Deliverable: a common, implemented, and documented error strategy for {{CAPAS}}. Steps:
1. Inventory how errors are currently captured, logged, and presented; list inconsistencies (scattered try/catch, loose logs, raw messages, disparate codes, silenced failures) and classify each finding by risk.
2. Design a typed error hierarchy that separates (a) expected business errors, (b) validation or input errors, (c) external dependency failures, and (d) unexpected failures. Each type carries a stable code, severity level, whether it is retryable, and a safe message for the user.
3. Define a single capture point per layer (global handler or middleware on backend; error boundary, interceptor, or global promise handler on frontend) that routes every error to the same pipeline and guarantees that none escapes without being logged.
4. Specify the structured log format integrated with {{SISTEMA_LOGGING}}: level, timestamp, correlation identifier propagated between layers, origin, error code, and useful context, without sensitive data (define the list of fields to redact).
5. Define the presentation layer that translates each error into a user message and into a consistent {{CONTRATO_RESPUESTA}}, with explicit error-code-to-HTTP-status or UI-state mapping, and a safe default message for unmapped types.
6. Refactor current points toward the pattern incrementally, leave an end-to-end example for a business error and an unexpected one, and document the procedure for adding a new error type without breaking the contract.
Explicit assumptions: if {{SISTEMA_LOGGING}} is not provided, propose an idiomatic one for {{STACK_LENGUAJE_FRAMEWORK}} and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; if {{CONTRATO_RESPUESTA}} is not provided, adopt a standard error envelope (code, message, correlation id) and declare it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
Phase 1 - Audit: go through {{ADJUNTOS}} and the code; map capture, logging, and presentation per layer; mark [ASSUMPTION] where you infer.
Phase 2 - Design: define the typed error hierarchy, single capture points per layer, structured log contract, and presentation contract before touching code; adjust depth to {{NIVEL_OBSERVABILIDAD}}.
Phase 3 - Implementation: apply the pattern incrementally, preserving public contracts; include the two end-to-end examples and correlation identifier propagation.
Phase 4 - Closure: deliver a before/after summary, list of modified files, extension guide, and covered edge cases.
Edge cases to resolve explicitly: errors thrown inside the error handler itself; failures before the correlation identifier exists; errors in asynchronous code or uncaught promises; timeouts and external dependency failures; and errors that should not be exposed to the user but should be logged.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] There is a typed error hierarchy distinguishing business, validation, external dependencies, and unexpected failure, each with a stable code and severity.
- [ ] There is a single capture point per layer and no error escapes without passing through the common pipeline (including asynchronous ones and uncaught promises).
- [ ] Logs are structured, with a correlation identifier propagated between layers and without sensitive data (redaction list declared).
- [ ] The user never receives raw traces; messages are clear and responses follow {{CONTRATO_RESPUESTA}}, with a safe default message for unmapped types.
- [ ] Existing public contracts remain stable and the migration was incremental.
- [ ] Two end-to-end examples are included (business and unexpected), the guide for adding a new error type, and covered edge cases.
Expected deliverable: refactored code with the strategy applied, before/after summary, list of modified files, documented extension procedure, and resolved edge cases.
spec-vibe-coding_checklist-de-listo-para:

I am about to launch {{NOMBRE_APP}} to production and need a production-readiness audit before exposing it to real users. The stack is {{STACK}}, it runs on {{INFRAESTRUCTURA}}, and handles {{TIPO_DATOS}}; the launch window is {{FECHA_LANZAMIENTO}}. A rigorous review before the cutover unlocks a launch without surprises: it avoids secret leaks, data loss without backups, and silent outages that nobody detects. The goal is a Go or No-Go verdict grounded in evidence, not a generic list.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior site reliability engineer (SRE) with experience operating web services in production and conducting pre-launch reviews.
Deliverable: a production-readiness checklist report with a Go or No-Go verdict and prioritized blockers.

Security front: secrets out of code (environment variables or secrets manager), HTTPS enforced, authentication and authorization per endpoint, input validation and injection protection, dependencies without known critical vulnerabilities, security headers and restricted CORS, rate limiting on public endpoints.

--- E | EXECUTION ---

Phase 2 - Front walkthrough: evaluate the four fronts in order; mark each control as covered, partial, or absent, and record the evidence or assumption supporting each mark (label assumptions as [ASSUMPTION]). Phase 3 - Verdict: consolidate findings, issue Go or No-Go, and prioritize blockers by risk, each with the concrete closure action. Cutoff rule: any Security or Backups control absent without mitigation forces No-Go.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The four fronts (security, data, backups, monitoring) are covered without omissions.
- Each control has a status (covered, partial, absent) and explicit evidence or assumption.
- Backups distinguishes backup from tested restore; a copy that has never been restored is not considered proven.
- Controls covered by the provider (serverless/managed) are declared as such, not as absent.
- Every assumption is labeled [ASSUMPTION]; no stack or infrastructure data is invented.
- The closure includes an unambiguous Go or No-Go verdict and blockers ordered by risk with a concrete action and front.
Expected deliverable: checklist report by fronts plus Go or No-Go verdict and prioritized list of actionable blockers.

--- S | SITUATION ---
I built {{APP}} quickly with vibe coding and need to know whether its handling of personal data and consent can withstand a basic privacy review before exposing it to real users. Apps generated at high speed carry typical leaks: data collected without being needed, secrets in the repository, personal data in logs, third-party SDKs that exfiltrate information by default, uncontrolled browser storage, and consent banners that do not actually obtain consent. An early review contrasts the actual data flow against the principles of privacy by design and informed consent, and unlocks a launch without privacy debt, user trust, and an orderly base for scaling or complying with a formal framework (GDPR, LGPD, or another) when the time comes.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior privacy engineer with practice in privacy-by-design, consent evaluation, and compliance reviews of software products built quickly.

Deliverable: a prioritized risk privacy findings report, with concrete code- and product-level fixes, and a three-wave remediation plan. Steps:

3. Contrast against seven basic requirements: minimization; legal basis and purpose; real consent (granular, revocable, no pre-checked boxes, non-blocking); retention and deletion; data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection); security (encryption in transit and at rest, secrets out of code, personal data out of logs); international transfers or to sub-processors.
4. Findings: for each gap record severity (critical/high/medium/low), evidence (file, endpoint, or behavior), violated requirement, and actionable fix differentiated into code layer and product layer.
5. Prioritize and build three-wave remediation plan: criticals now, highs this week, mediums and lows in backlog.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm {{APP}}, {{STACK}}, {{DATOS_PERSONALES}}, {{TERCEROS_Y_FLUJOS}}, and {{JURISDICCION_Y_PUBLICO}}; if something essential is missing (regions, minors, third parties, code snippets, or config), ask before evaluating.
Phase 2 - Inventory and flow: build the data table and the end-to-end flow map, including derived data.
Phase 3 - Contrast: evaluate each of the seven requirements with a verdict of meets / partial / does not meet and evidence.
Phase 4 - Findings and remediation: prioritize by risk and propose code and product fixes.
Rules: do not invent regulations, fines, or figures; any obligation that depends on jurisdiction or business type goes marked [ASSUMPTION] to confirm. Distinguish what is verifiable in the provided material from what is inferred.
Edge cases: absence of a banner or revocation mechanism is recorded as a finding, never as an exemption; if minors are in the audience, raise the bar for consent and minimization; sensitive and derived data are treated with a higher starting severity.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every personal data point from {{DATOS_PERSONALES}} appears in the inventory with its classification (standard / sensitive / minors) and derived data appears separately.
- [ ] The flow map covers input, residence, and output, including logs, browser storage, and every third party in {{TERCEROS_Y_FLUJOS}}.

spec-datos_sql_consulta_desde_lenguaje_n:
[inputs]
- PREGUNTA_NEGOCIO: {{PREGUNTA_NEGOCIO}} > Business question in natural language to translate into SQL
- ESQUEMA: {{ESQUEMA}} > Available tables, columns, types, and primary/foreign keys
- MOTOR_SQL: {{MOTOR_SQL}} > Engine and version (PostgreSQL, MySQL, BigQuery, SQL Server, etc.)
- DEFINICIONES_METRICAS: {{DEFINICIONES_METRICAS}} > Business rules: how each metric is calculated and what filters apply (optional)
- RANGO_FECHAS: {{RANGO_FECHAS}} > Analysis period and timezone if applicable (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A well-framed business question is worth little if it is translated into ambiguous SQL: a wrongly resolved join duplicates rows, an INNER JOIN drops NULLs without warning, a poorly bounded date filter moves the figures, and an incomplete GROUP BY invalidates the report. The goal is to convert {{PREGUNTA_NEGOCIO}} into a correct, readable, and executable SQL query against {{ESQUEMA}} in {{MOTOR_SQL}}, ready to audit and reuse. A precise translation unlocks fast decisions without going back and forth with the data team: business strategy rests on numbers that can be defended clause by clause.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data engineer specialized in analytical SQL and dimensional modeling, with judgment for detecting granularity traps, join fan-out, and NULLs.
Deliverable: a final SQL query, its assumptions, and the clause-by-clause explanation. Steps:
1. Reframe {{PREGUNTA_NEGOCIO}} as an output model: columns, metrics, row granularity, and expected ordering.
2. Map the tables in {{ESQUEMA}} and the join keys; choose INNER or LEFT with justification based on whether rows without a match should be kept.
3. Apply {{DEFINICIONES_METRICAS}} in the aggregation expressions and {{RANGO_FECHAS}} as a temporal filter.
4. Write the query with explicit joins, WHERE, complete GROUP BY, HAVING only over aggregates, ORDER BY and LIMIT, in the valid syntax of {{MOTOR_SQL}}.
5. Explain each clause in one line and enumerate risks with their mitigation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: translate the question into an output model (columns, metrics, granularity, ordering) and declare missing assumptions as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Join graph planning: define the base table, direction and type of joins, and the level where aggregation occurs to avoid fan-out; if a metric lives in a higher-cardinality table, pre-aggregate in a CTE or subquery before joining; resolve {{DEFINICIONES_METRICAS}} and {{RANGO_FECHAS}}.
Phase 3 - SQL execution: draft the formatted query with explicit joins and clear aliases, adjusted to the syntax of {{MOTOR_SQL}}; never use implicit JOIN by comma; prefer the half-open date pattern (field >= start AND field < end+1) over BETWEEN to avoid ambiguous edges.
Phase 4 - Explanation and risks: comment on each clause and list the detected traps with their mitigation (NULLs in joins, double counting, division by zero, COUNT vs COUNT(DISTINCT), WHERE vs HAVING, comparisons against NULL).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The query answers exactly {{PREGUNTA_NEGOCIO}}, with neither extra nor missing columns.
- All joins are explicit, with correct keys and type (INNER/LEFT) justified by the rule of keeping or not keeping rows without a match.
- Every non-aggregated column appears in GROUP BY; metrics use {{DEFINICIONES_METRICAS}}; HAVING filters only aggregates and WHERE only rows.
- Date filters respect {{RANGO_FECHAS}} with declared inclusive/exclusive limits and resolved timezone.
- No fan-out: if a metric is at detail granularity, it is pre-aggregated before joining to avoid duplication.
- The syntax is valid for {{MOTOR_SQL}} (date functions, LIMIT/TOP, identifier quoting per engine).
- Assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION]; if schema, metric, engine, or range is missing and is required, it is asked before executing.
Expected deliverable: code block with the final query, list of assumptions, and clause-by-clause explanation, ready to execute and audit.
spec-datos_sql_optimizar_query_lenta:
[inputs]
- MOTOR_VERSION: {{MOTOR_VERSION}} > Engine and version of the DBMS (e.g., PostgreSQL 16, MySQL 8.0, SQL Server 2022, Oracle 19c). Determines index syntax, available types, and optimizer behavior
- CONSULTA_SQL: {{CONSULTA_SQL}} > Full text of the slow query to optimize
- PLAN_EJECUCION: {{PLAN_EJECUCION}} > Output of EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE / equivalent graphical plan. If only an estimated EXPLAIN is available (without actual rows), declare it: this limits mis-estimation diagnosis
- DDL_TABLAS_INDICES: {{DDL_TABLAS_INDICES}} > Current CREATE TABLE and CREATE INDEX statements for the involved tables, including PK, FK, and constraints
- VOLUMEN_FILAS: {{VOLUMEN_FILAS}} > Approximate row count per table and known selectivity of key filters (e.g., status='active' = 2%)
- OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO: {{OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO}} > Concrete and measurable target (e.g., reduce from 8s to <500ms, eliminate sequential scans, remove spill to disk)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A critical SQL query runs slowly and degrades a report, an API, or a batch process. Optimizing it based on the actual execution plan unlocks lower latency, lower CPU/IO/memory consumption on the server, and more capacity without scaling hardware. The analysis rests on evidence from the engine itself (plan + actual statistics), not on intuition, making the improvement auditable, reproducible, and defensible to the team.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior database engineer specializing in query tuning and performance, with mastery of execution plans, optimizer cost models, indexing strategies (B-tree, covering, partial, composite, hash, GIN/GiST by engine) and sargable query rewriting.

Deliverable: prioritized bottleneck diagnosis + executable rewritten query + CREATE INDEX scripts + validation plan. Steps:
1. Read the plan and identify the most expensive nodes by time and by rows: flag full table/sequential scans, sort/hash spills to disk, nested loops over large tables, materializations, and—especially—large divergences between estimated and actual rows (symptom of stale statistics or a poorly estimated predicate).
2. Explain the root cause of each bottleneck, linking it to its source: WHERE/JOIN predicates, implicit functions or casts that break sargability, missing useful index, stale statistics, lack of selectivity, ORDER BY/GROUP BY without a supporting index, or suboptimal join order.
3. Propose concrete indexes (columns, order, covering or partial where applicable) and rewrites (remove SELECT *, make predicates sargable, reorder/conditionally apply joins, avoid correlated subqueries, materialized CTE vs. inline, OR to UNION ALL where appropriate), each with justification and trade-off.
4. Deliver the rewritten query ready to execute and the exact CREATE INDEX statements for the declared engine.
5. Define how to validate the improvement: re-run EXPLAIN ANALYZE and compare plan, cost, and time before/after against the target.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Plan reading: locate operations, their relative cost, and the estimated vs. actual row relationship.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: rank bottlenecks from highest to lowest impact with their root cause.
Phase 3 - Proposal: design indexes and sargable rewrite; flag conflicts or redundancy with existing indexes.
Phase 4 - Delivery: optimized query + index DDL + assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 5 - Validation: instructions for measuring before/after and a warning about the write and storage cost of new indexes on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE workloads.
Edge cases: if the plan is only an estimated EXPLAIN, declare that mis-estimations cannot be confirmed and request EXPLAIN ANALYZE; if the slowness is not attributable to the query (locking, IO contention, server parameters), say so and do not force indexes; if a proposed index duplicates an existing one, prefer to adjust the existing one.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every cited bottleneck references a concrete node from the provided plan (no invented operations).
- [ ] Cardinalities and structures are not invented; anything assumed is marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Proposed indexes specify table, columns, and order; are valid for the given MOTOR_VERSION; and do not duplicate existing indexes.
- [ ] The rewritten query is executable and preserves the exact semantics of the original result (same row set and order if the original guaranteed it).
- [ ] Each rewrite justifies why it improves sargability or reduces rows processed, with its trade-off.
- [ ] A measurable before/after validation plan against OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO is included, plus a warning about the write cost of the indexes.
- [ ] If the cause is not the query (locking, IO, config), it is flagged instead of forcing a solution.
Expected deliverable: prioritized diagnosis block + final SQL query + CREATE INDEX scripts + measurable verification steps against OBJETIVO_RENDIMIENTO.
spec-datos_sql_refactor_subqueries_a_cte:
[inputs]
- CONSULTA_SQL: {{CONSULTA_SQL}} > Original SQL query with nested subqueries to refactor
- MOTOR_SQL: {{MOTOR_SQL}} > Engine and version: PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, MySQL 8+, SQL Server, or another
- ESQUEMA_TABLAS: {{ESQUEMA_TABLAS}} > Available tables, columns, and types, or relevant DDL (optional)
- CONVENCION_NOMBRES: {{CONVENCION_NOMBRES}} > Convention for naming CTEs: descriptive snake_case by default (optional)
- NIVEL_COMENTARIOS: {{NIVEL_COMENTARIOS}} > Comment detail: minimal, one line per CTE, or exhaustive (optional, default: one line per CTE)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I have a SQL query ({{CONSULTA_SQL}}) on {{MOTOR_SQL}} whose nested subqueries in SELECT, FROM, WHERE, or HAVING have made it difficult to read, debug, and maintain. Common Table Expressions (the WITH clause from the SQL:1999 standard, now supported by PostgreSQL, BigQuery, Snowflake, MySQL 8+, and SQL Server) allow decomposing that logic into named, sequential blocks that read from top to bottom. A faithful refactoring unlocks faster code reviews, stage-by-stage debugging, sub-result reuse, and a maintainable base for optimizing or evolving the query—without altering a single row of the result. The goal is readability and maintainability with exact equivalence, not optimizing the execution plan: any performance change is reported but not pursued unless explicitly requested.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data engineer expert in analytical SQL and query refactoring, with mastery of CTEs, execution plans, and dialect differences between engines.

Deliverable: the query rewritten in modular CTEs, 100% equivalent to the original. Steps:
1) Inventory each nested subquery in {{CONSULTA_SQL}}, its clause, its purpose, its expected cardinality, and its dependencies.
2) Restate the intent of the query and lay out the decomposition plan before writing SQL.
3) Convert each subquery into a named CTE according to {{CONVENCION_NOMBRES}}, ordered so each depends only on prior ones, closing with a clean final SELECT.
4) Comment each CTE according to {{NIVEL_COMENTARIOS}}: what it produces and why it exists.
5) Preserve exact semantics: same columns, types, filters, joins, aggregations, NULL handling, DISTINCT, LIMIT/OFFSET, and ORDER BY as the original.
6) Deliver an equivalence proof: EXCEPT/MINUS in both directions plus row counts, adapted to {{MOTOR_SQL}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Mapping: parse {{CONSULTA_SQL}} against {{ESQUEMA_TABLAS}} and list subqueries with their dependency graph; classify each as non-correlated, correlated, or scalar; if the engine or schema is ambiguous, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 Plan: order the CTEs topologically (leaves first, aggregations, rankings, and correlated ones after) and name them in a self-explaining way, with no forward references or collisions.
Phase 3 Rewrite: emit the WITH with each commented CTE and the final SELECT; use only valid syntax in {{MOTOR_SQL}}. Sensitive cases: correlated subqueries (rewrite to join, LATERAL, or APPLY according to the engine, preserving row-by-row semantics); scalar subqueries in SELECT (ensure they still return at most one row); EXISTS/IN/NOT IN predicates (preserve NULL behavior, especially NOT IN with NULLs); rankings and tiebreakers (exactly replicate the order clause and tie handling).
Phase 4 Verification: mentally run the equivalence check, generate the bidirectional EXCEPT/MINUS + count script, and declare as [ASSUMPTION] any inference about NULLs, duplicates, or tiebreakers. Do not invent columns or tables outside {{ESQUEMA_TABLAS}} or {{CONSULTA_SQL}}. If a subquery cannot be faithfully converted to a CTE, declare it, do not force it, and propose the safest alternative.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Every nested subquery from the original is mapped to exactly one CTE (or its merging or non-conversion is justified).
- [ ] CTEs are ordered without forward references; each depends only on prior ones.
- [ ] Names follow {{CONVENCION_NOMBRES}}, are descriptive, with no collisions or opaque aliases.
- [ ] Each CTE has a comment per {{NIVEL_COMENTARIOS}}.
- [ ] The final SELECT preserves columns, order, types, filters, aggregations, NULLs, DISTINCT, LIMIT/OFFSET, and ORDER BY of the original.

Doing it right unlocks reports of direct and indirect subordinates, material explosions, nested category navigation, and subtree aggregations—without auxiliary tables or application loops. --- S | SITUATION ---
I need to measure how many people acquired in each period remain active over time, not just an aggregate retention number that hides whether the product is improving or degrading cohort by cohort. The retention matrix by acquisition cohort is the product analytics standard: it groups users by the period in which they first appeared (the cohort) and tracks, period by period, what fraction remains active. Built on {{TABLA_EVENTOS}} with {{COL_USUARIO}} and {{COL_TIMESTAMP}}, it unlocks comparable retention curves across cohorts, detecting whether product changes move the needle, locating the point where the curve flattens (baseline retention), and feeding dashboards and LTV models. Core risk to avoid: reading low retention in cells that actually correspond to periods not yet elapsed for recent cohorts (partial cohort bias).

Archetype: Senior data analyst specializing in product analytics and analytical SQL, with practice in retention modeling, window functions, and SQL engine portability.

Deliverable: an executable SQL query that produces the retention matrix by acquisition cohort, in absolute counts and percentage, structured in commented CTEs. Steps:
1. events_base: select from {{TABLA_EVENTOS}} the columns {{COL_USUARIO}} and {{COL_TIMESTAMP}}, apply {{FILTRO_ACTIVIDAD}}, and discard rows with null user or timestamp.
2. cohorts: for each {{COL_USUARIO}} compute their acquisition period as date_trunc('{{GRANO_COHORTE}}', MIN({{COL_TIMESTAMP}})). Each user belongs to exactly one cohort.
3. activity_periods: join events_base with cohorts and for each event compute the activity period date_trunc('{{GRANO_COHORTE}}', {{COL_TIMESTAMP}}) and the period index relative to the cohort (0 = acquisition). 4. cohort_size: count COUNT(DISTINCT {{COL_USUARIO}}) per cohort at index 0 (base size of each cohort).
5. matrix: for each pair (cohort, period index) compute active = COUNT(DISTINCT {{COL_USUARIO}}) and retention_pct = active / cohort_size (float division). Present two outputs, one in counts and one in percentage, with cohorts in rows ordered by date and the period index in columns (pivot or long format, declaring which you deliver).

[inputs]

- COLUMNA_TIEMPO: {{COLUMNA_TIEMPO}} > Date, timestamp, or ordinal sequence column that defines the event order

- OBJETIVO: {{OBJETIVO}} > What to measure or unlock (retention streaks, sessionization, active subscription periods, inactivity windows, churn detection)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You work on a temporal event series where the business value lies not in isolated events but in their continuous streaks (islands) and their interruptions (gaps): consecutive days of activity, habit streaks, usage sessions, active subscription periods, or inactivity windows. Solving this with self-joins or cursors is slow and fragile; the gaps-and-islands technique with window functions solves it in a single pass, scalable and portable. Correctly detecting islands and gaps unlocks retention metrics, churn detection, sessionization, and continuity reporting that would otherwise remain hidden in row-level granularity. The cost of getting it wrong is high: a badly built island key silently merges or splits streaks and corrupts every downstream metric without throwing an error.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data engineer specializing in analytical SQL, window functions, and event series modeling.
Deliver an executable and audited gaps-and-islands solution for {{OBJETIVO}}. Steps:
1. Confirm engine ({{MOTOR_SQL}}), table ({{TABLA_FUENTE}}), entity ({{COLUMNA_ENTIDAD}}), time column ({{COLUMNA_TIEMPO}}), and granularity ({{GRANULARIDAD}}); if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask before writing SQL.
2. CTE 1 normalization: order by entity and time, deduplicate repeated events on the same step, and leave one row per granularity unit.
3. CTE 2 island key: assign each row the difference between ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY time) and the temporal index normalized to granularity; adjacent rows share that difference and form the island key. Document the alternative with LAG plus cumulative sum (marking the start when the jump exceeds the step) and indicate when to prefer each: sequence difference requires a strictly uniform step; LAG with a threshold tolerates variable steps and inactivity-based sessionization.
4. CTE 3 islands: group by entity and island key; compute start, end, duration, and event count per streak.
5. CTE 4 gaps: with LEAD() over the islands, compute the gap between the end of one island and the start of the next per entity, with its duration in the {{GRANULARIDAD}} unit.
6. Deliver the final commented SQL, the explanation of why the sequence difference is constant within an island, the assumptions about ties and granularity, and a validation query.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the problem, identify entity, temporal order, and exact continuity definition according to {{GRANULARIDAD}}; mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION] (time zone and conversion before truncating to granularity; duplicate handling; ties in the order and deterministic tiebreaking; whether the step is strictly uniform; out-of-calendar events such as weekends; open edges at the start or end of the data window).
Phase 2 Plan: present the plan of the four CTEs and the signature of each window function before writing the complete SQL; declare how the normalized temporal index is computed in {{MOTOR_SQL}} (DATEDIFF, DATE_DIFF, epoch division, or row number depending on granularity by event).
Phase 3 Execute: write the SQL portable to the declared {{MOTOR_SQL}}, comment each CTE, explain the island key mechanics line by line, and attach the validation query (the sum of island durations plus gaps must reconstruct the total range per entity between the first and last event; report rows where it does not balance).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] SQL executable in the declared {{MOTOR_SQL}}, without proprietary syntax from another engine; the time difference function corresponds to that engine.
- [ ] The island key is built with the sequence difference (ROW_NUMBER minus temporal index) or LAG plus cumulative sum, and it is explained why it is constant within a streak.
- [ ] The choice between sequence difference (uniform step) and LAG with threshold (variable step or inactivity-based sessionization) is justified.
- [ ] Each CTE is commented and named by its function (normalization, island key, island aggregation, gaps).
- [ ] Handles duplicates on the same step and ties in the temporal order with an explicit deterministic tiebreak.
- [ ] Gaps are derived with LEAD() and report duration in the {{GRANULARIDAD}} unit; start and end edges of the series are handled or declared [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Includes a validation query that reconstructs the total range (islands plus gaps) and flags discrepancies.
- [ ] Assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION]; no column invented outside {{TABLA_FUENTE}}.
Expected deliverable: SQL block with four commented CTEs, explanation of the island key, list of assumptions, and validation query, ready to paste and execute against {{TABLA_FUENTE}}.

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to design the analytical layer of a data warehouse for the process {{PROCESO_NEGOCIO}}. A well-declared star schema unlocks predictable queries, dimensions reusable across processes, and a single version of the truth for reports and BI. The most costly mistake in dimensional modeling is failing to fix the grain: it defines everything else, so it is declared first and unambiguously. Equally costly subsequent mistakes: mixing grains in a single fact table, summing semi-additive measures across time, and using business keys instead of surrogate keys (which breaks SCD and versioning). The resulting model will feed {{PREGUNTAS_ANALITICAS}} across the axes {{DIMENSIONES_CLAVE}} without schema rework.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior data architect specialized in Kimball dimensional modeling, with experience building warehouses on {{MOTOR_ANALITICO}}.

Deliverable: the complete design of a star schema for {{PROCESO_NEGOCIO}}, capable of answering {{PREGUNTAS_ANALITICAS}} across the axes {{DIMENSIONES_CLAVE}}. Apply Kimball's four steps in strict order:
1. Select the business process and enumerate the measurable events it generates.
2. Declare the fact table grain in ONE unambiguous sentence, at the finest available atomic event; the finest grain maximizes future analytical flexibility.
3. Derive the dimensions that hang from that grain; mark which are conformed (same key and attributes reusable across processes) to guarantee drill-across.
4. Identify the numeric facts and classify each measure as additive (sums across all dimensions), semi-additive (does not sum across time: balances, inventory), or non-additive (ratios, percentages: never pre-aggregate, always recalculate from components).

Then:
5. Define each dimension: integer surrogate key, natural business key, descriptive attributes, and SCD strategy per attribute (Type 1 overwrites without history; Type 2 versions with validity dates, current flag, and version; Type 3 alternate column for previous value), justified by business history needs.
6. Resolve the fact table: surrogate FK to each dimension, measures with their additivity, degenerate keys (transaction number, invoice), and table type (transactional, periodic snapshot, or accumulating snapshot). Every FK is mandatory; NULL is represented by an "unknown"/"not applicable" member, never NULL on the FK.
7. Note handling of late-arriving dimensions, early-arriving facts, role-playing dimensions (a single date dimension referenced multiple times), and junk dimensions (low-cardinality flags and indicators consolidated together) when applicable.
8. If {{VOLUMEN_ESPERADO}} justifies it, propose partitioning/clustering/distribution suited to {{MOTOR_ANALITICO}}, without over-engineering.

Phase 1 - Framing: confirm process, candidate grain, and assumptions; if {{PROCESO_NEGOCIO}}, {{PREGUNTAS_ANALITICAS}}, {{MOTOR_ANALITICO}}, or {{VOLUMEN_ESPERADO}} are absent or ambiguous, ask before modeling. Mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Design: apply Kimball's four steps in order; derive dimensions and facts from the declared grain, never the other way around.
Phase 3 - Specification: document each table as a dictionary (column, data type, role PK/FK/attribute/measure/degenerate, SCD, description) and draw the star diagram in text (fact at center, dimensions radiating outward, explicit FKs).
Phase 4 - Verification: validate that every measure respects the grain, that every FK points to an existing dimension, that conformed ones are consistent in key and attributes, that semi-additives carry a warning against summing across time, and that the model answers each of {{PREGUNTAS_ANALITICAS}} (go through question by question indicating which tables/columns resolve it).

- [ ] Each dimension has an integer surrogate key, a business key, and an SCD strategy justified per attribute.
- [ ] Measures are classified as additive, semi-additive, or non-additive, with a warning against summing across time for semi-additives and against pre-aggregating non-additives.
