Eisenhower matrix: place each task in one quadrant — Q1 important and urgent (crises, decisions only the leader can make, immovable deadlines), Q2 important and not urgent (strategy, planning, team development, process improvement), Q3 urgent and not important (interruptions, avoidable meetings, low-value requests that press), Q4 neither urgent nor important (distractions, work that does not contribute).
3. Disposition by quadrant: Q1 the leader does it now; Q2 schedule and protect in the calendar; Q3 delegate or automate; Q4 eliminate or decline. Justify each decision in one sentence.
4. Decision table: one row per task with columns task, quadrant, action (do / schedule / delegate / automate / eliminate), responsible party, and hours/week freed for the leader.
5. Delegation plan: for each delegated task, to whom based on their maturity, what authority level they receive (consult, recommend, decide and inform, decide autonomously), the expected outcome, the control point, and the risk that is covered; if nobody has the maturity, propose delegation with scaffolding (support + review) rather than retaining by default.
6. Impact summary: weekly hours the leader recovers and what to reinvest them in (Q2 quadrant); explicitly name the cost of not delegating (what Q2 work keeps being postponed).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Inventory: list each task from the received material and estimate its weekly consumption; if the time is missing, flag it [ASSUMPTION] with your best estimate and state what would be needed to refine it.
Phase 2 - Classification: evaluate each task on two axes — importance (does it contribute to the leader's results and mission?) and urgency (does it have a pressing deadline?) — and assign it to a quadrant; watch for the trap of treating everything urgent as important. Edge case: if a task is urgent because a Q2 job was postponed (manufactured urgency), flag it and address the root cause, not just the symptom.
Phase 3 - Disposition: apply the per-quadrant rule (Q1 do, Q2 schedule, Q3 delegate/automate, Q4 eliminate) and justify each decision; between delegating and automating, prefer automating what is repeatable and rule-based and delegating what develops a person. If a Q1 task is recurring, signal how to convert it to Q2 (train someone, document the criterion) so it stops being a crisis.
Phase 4 - Delegation and close: for what is delegated, match task to person by maturity, set authority level, expected outcome, and control point, and name the risk to cover; avoid over-control (high authority to someone who has already demonstrated) and under-support (high authority to someone who has not yet). Close with the decision table and the summary of hours recovered and their reinvestment in Q2.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
The classification is complete when: (a) every task in the inventory appears in one quadrant, without any left unclassified or duplicated; (b) each task has an explicit action (do/schedule/delegate/automate/eliminate) consistent with its quadrant; (c) the decision truly separates importance from urgency and does not send everything urgent to the leader; (d) what is delegated states to whom, with what authority level, expected outcome, and control point; (e) the distinction between delegating and automating is justified (repeatable and rule-based -> automate; develops someone -> delegate); (f) Q4 proposes to eliminate or decline with a concrete exit, not "do it later"; (g) there is a summary of weekly hours recovered and their reinvestment in Q2, with the cost of not delegating named; (h) manufactured urgency (recurring Q1 or Q3 from postponing Q2) is flagged with its root cause; (i) inferred data is flagged [ASSUMPTION]; (j) neutral professional English, no emojis. Expected deliverable: a task-by-task decision table with its quadrant matrix and a brief delegation plan, ready for the leader to execute this week.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_brief_resultad:
[inputs]
- ENCARGO: {{ENCARGO}} > Name and brief description of the assignment to delegate
- COLABORADOR: {{COLABORADOR}} > Person or role receiving the assignment, with their relevant experience level for this assignment
- RESULTADO_ESPERADO: {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}} > The finished deliverable in observable terms (what exists and is true when it is done)
- PLAZO: {{PLAZO}} > Target date or available time window
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable boundaries: time, brand, sensitive data, dependencies, reserved decisions (optional)
- NIVEL_AUTONOMIA: {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} > Desired level among tell, sell, consult, agree, advise, inquire, delegate (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am going to delegate the assignment {{ENCARGO}} to {{COLABORADOR}}, with deadline {{PLAZO}}. I want to empower, not micromanage: I need a brief that fixes the WHAT and the WHY with total clarity and leaves the HOW to the person. A good brief transfers ownership, reduces rework, frees my supervision time, and develops the collaborator's decision-making capacity. When the assignment is properly framed, the person moves forward alone without coming back to ask the basics, and I avoid both micromanagement and delegation-and-abandonment. The risk to neutralize: ownership ambiguity, reverse delegation (the work comes back to me), and a brief that describes activities instead of outcomes.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader expert in effective delegation and the seven-level autonomy model (Management 3.0 delegation levels).
Draft a delegation brief with these seven numbered sections:
1. Expected outcome: a single sentence describing the finished deliverable in observable terms based on {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}}; describe the outcome, never the activity (what exists and is true when it is done).
2. Why it matters: impact on team, customer, or business and what is unlocked by achieving it; connect to a real priority, not a generic justification.
3. Success criteria: three to five verifiable conditions that allow the collaborator to self-assess quality; standards, not tasks. Calibrate their granularity to the profile: pure outcome if the person is senior, more explicit if junior.
4. Restrictions and non-negotiable boundaries: based on {{RESTRICCIONES}}; if empty, propose typical boundaries (time budget, brand, sensitive data, dependencies, reserved decisions) and flag them as [ASSUMPTION] for me to confirm. Explicitly separate the closed (non-negotiable) from the open (at the person's discretion).
5. Authority level: fix {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} among the seven levels; if empty, propose the level coherent with {{COLABORADOR}}'s profile and flag it [ASSUMPTION]. Explain for this specific case who decides and who is informed, and what would change if the level moved up or down one.
6. Control points: by milestone or by risk, never by arbitrary calendar; for each state the concrete question that will be answered and who convenes the check (preferably the collaborator, to reinforce ownership).
7. Resources and who to contact: what is available, who decides on dependencies, and who is the unblocking contact.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1, Framing: confirm outcome, purpose, {{COLABORADOR}}'s profile, and deadline; if a critical data point is missing (what exists at the end, experience level, hard boundaries), ask before drafting rather than assuming.
Phase 2, Drafting the WHAT and WHY: write expected outcome and why it matters; verify that no verb dictates the method.
Phase 3, Calibrating the HOW: define success criteria, restrictions, and authority level consistent with the profile; the more experience, the greater autonomy and more outcome-focused criteria; the less experience, bounded autonomy and more explicit criteria, without converting them into a task list.
Phase 4, Close: add control points by milestone or risk and resources; verify that the brief enables autonomous action and note at the end the main delegation risk to watch for.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The expected outcome is a single observable sentence describing the finished deliverable, not the activity.
- The why connects to a concrete impact on team, customer, or business and names what is unlocked.
- There are three to five verifiable, self-assessable success criteria (standards, not tasks), calibrated to the profile.
- Restrictions distinguish the non-negotiable from the open; proposed boundaries are flagged [ASSUMPTION].
- The authority level is explicit (one of the seven), justified by the profile, and clarifies who decides and who is informed.
- Control points are by milestone or risk, each with its question; none is an arbitrary calendar.
- No verb prescribes the method; the HOW stays in the collaborator's hands.
- The brief closes by noting the main delegation risk to watch for.
- Professional, neutral, enabling tone; no emojis.
Expected deliverable: a one-page delegation brief in the seven numbered sections, ready to send to the collaborator.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_monkey_managem:
[inputs]
- COLABORADOR_ROL: {{COLABORADOR_ROL}} > Collaborator and their role or seniority on this topic
- PROBLEMA_Y_DIALOGO: {{PROBLEMA_Y_DIALOGO}} > The problem and the conversation: what the collaborator raised and what I responded
- SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL: {{SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL}} > Where the next move of the problem currently sits (who owns it)
- NIVEL_AUTONOMIA: {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} > How autonomous the collaborator is on this topic: low / medium / high
- RESTRICCION: {{RESTRICCION}} > Real constraint of time, risk, compliance, or quality to respect (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A problem has just bounced back, or is about to bounce back, from a collaborator to the leader: the conversation ended with a "let me check", "I'll review it", or "I'll handle it", and the next move of the problem is on the leader's desk instead of the one who brought it. Every problem carries with it a "monkey" — the next step to take — and the leader's role is not to feed other people's monkeys but to keep them where they generate initiative and learning. Fixing this unlocks leadership time, avoids the bottleneck where everything passes through one person, and raises team autonomy conversation by conversation. What is at stake is not a loose task: it is the pattern of who systematically holds the next step.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach specialized in delegation, trained in the framework Management Time: Who's Got the Monkey? by William Oncken and Donald Wass (Harvard Business Review, 1974, revised 1999), with the 5-level initiative scale.
Deliverable: a rewrite of the leader's response that returns the next move to the collaborator, plus a mini-plan for sustaining the delegation. Steps:
1. Identify the "monkey": name the concrete next move of the problem and who owns it today per {{SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL}}. If there are several steps mixed in, separate the one that belongs to the collaborator from the one that legitimately belongs to the leader (approve, escalate, protect a boundary).
2. Diagnose the current initiative level on the Oncken scale (1 wait for instruction; 2 ask what to do; 3 propose and then act; 4 act and report immediately; 5 act and report routinely) and set a realistic target level given {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}}. Move at most one level per conversation when autonomy is low; do not jump to 4-5 if the collaborator has never operated at that level on this topic.
3. Rewrite the leader's response in 2 to 4 sentences that: acknowledge the person, reassign the next step, set the agreed initiative level, and schedule a check-in (when, in what format, with what progress criterion), respecting {{RESTRICCION}}. Spoken language, not a written memo.
4. Anticipate 2 or 3 typical maneuvers by which the monkey jumps back to the leader (e.g. "just a quick question", bringing the problem without options, manufactured urgency, seeking the leader to decide for them) and deliver a brief reply to return it in each case without damaging the relationship.
5. Close with a memorable pocket rule for the next conversation.
Assumptions and limits: assume the problem is delegable and the collaborator has basic competence on the topic; if {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}} is low, prioritize level 3 (propose and act) over higher levels. Do not turn returning the monkey into abandonment: the leader retains supervision, not execution. Do not reassign steps that are non-delegable in the leader's role (budget decisions outside the collaborator's mandate, people management, legal risks). If the case reveals a repeated pattern, note it in one line without turning the response into an extended feedback session.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the case in one sentence — who brought what problem and where the monkey sits — and declare the observed initiative level. If {{PROBLEMA_Y_DIALOGO}} or {{SIGUIENTE_PASO_ACTUAL}} do not allow you to locate the monkey or who owns the next step, ask for only that data before continuing.
Phase 2 Plan: define the target initiative level and the check-in design (the check-in is the leader reaching out to the person on an agreed date and format, not the person reporting to the leader so the leader decides). Verify that the target respects {{RESTRICCION}} and {{NIVEL_AUTONOMIA}}.
Phase 3 Execute: produce the rewrite, the replies to the bounce-backs, and the pocket rule. Maintain care for the person; returned initiative is not abandonment: the leader retains supervision, not execution.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The "monkey" (next move) is named and reassigned to the collaborator, not the leader; what is non-delegable in the role is explicitly separated.
- [ ] The current and target initiative levels are named using Oncken's 1-5 scale, with a realistic jump (max +1 if low autonomy).
- [ ] The rewrite acknowledges the person, reassigns the step, sets the level, and schedules the check-in with when + format + progress criterion, in spoken language.
- [ ] The check-in is the leader reaching out to the person, not the person asking the leader for a decision.
- [ ] There are 2-3 anticipated bounce-backs with a brief reply for each, without damaging the relationship.
- [ ] {{RESTRICCION}} is respected and abandonment or delegation of non-delegable role items is not suggested.
- [ ] Closes with a memorable pocket rule.
- [ ] If a repeated pattern was detected, it is noted in one line without becoming extended feedback.
Expected deliverable: block with (a) the monkey identified and who owns it, (b) current to target level, (c) rewritten response ready to say, (d) 2-3 bounce-backs with reply, (e) pocket rule.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_seguimiento_si:
[inputs]
- TAREA_ENTREGABLE: {{TAREA_ENTREGABLE}} > Delegated task or deliverable and its scope
- FECHA_LIMITE: {{FECHA_LIMITE}} > Deadline or cycle duration of the task
- NIVEL_RIESGO: {{NIVEL_RIESGO}} > Criticality or impact of the deliverable if it goes wrong (high/medium/low and why)
- MADUREZ_PERSONA: {{MADUREZ_PERSONA}} > Technical competence and autonomy demonstrated by the person on similar tasks
- ANTECEDENTES: {{ANTECEDENTES}} > Relationship context, delivery history, or prior friction (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You delegated a task and need to supervise it without smothering the person. Over-control erodes trust, autonomy, and speed; under-control lets risks slip through until it is too late to correct. The lever is to design control points proportional to the task's risk and the executor's maturity: enough supervision with minimum intrusion, so the person advances with autonomy, you sleep soundly, and the relationship strengthens rather than degrades. The plan is an agreement with the person, not a surveillance system imposed on them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior team leader with experience in effective delegation and people development, trained in situational leadership and risk management.
Deliverable: a proportional follow-up plan. Steps:
1. If TAREA_ENTREGABLE, NIVEL_RIESGO, or MADUREZ_PERSONA are empty or ambiguous, ask for them before continuing; without them the plan would be invented.
2. Diagnose the risk-maturity combination: cross the situational leadership framework (direct, coach, support, delegate) with an impact x probability-of-deviation matrix. Declare the recommended supervision style and its justification in one sentence.
3. Define the control rhythm: how many check-ins, at what moments in the cycle (start, intermediate milestones, pre-delivery), and for how long. For each specify what is reviewed, what evidence or partial deliverable the person brings, and what decision is made.
4. Explicitly separate reporting (information flowing to the leader) from delegated autonomy (decisions that stay in the person's hands without asking permission).
5. List early warning signals that justify increasing control and good-progress signals that justify reducing it, each with a concrete, observable threshold.
6. Draft a 5-to-8-line script for the initial alignment conversation, in an enabling-partner tone, not an auditor's.
Decision rules:
- High risk + high maturity: prioritize verification points at milestones over process intervention; more evidence, less how-control.
- High risk + low maturity: increase frequency and co-working in the early stretches, with an explicit plan to withdraw scaffolding.
- Low risk + high maturity: minimize check-ins to start and delivery; the rest is pure autonomy.
- Low risk + low maturity: use the task as a development opportunity with frequent feedback and low cost of error.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: classify risk and maturity, locate the case in the matrix, and set the style.
Phase 2 Design: derive rhythm, focus, and evidence of each check-in directly from the diagnosis, never by default or indiscriminate daily control.
Phase 3 Boundaries: draw the reporting / delegated autonomy line and the escalation or relaxation thresholds.
Phase 4 Alignment: convert the plan into an agreed conversational script, not an imposed one.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Number and depth of controls are justified by the risk-maturity diagnosis, not by habit or indiscriminate daily control.
- Each check-in indicates moment, focus, expected evidence, and decision.
- Reporting and delegated autonomy are separated without ambiguity.
- There are concrete, observable thresholds for raising and for lowering the control level.
- The alignment script sounds like an enabling partner, not surveillance, and opens space for the person to adjust the plan.
- Zero invented data; assumptions are flagged as [ASSUMPTION].
- If ANTECEDENTES reveals prior friction, the plan names it and proposes how to avoid repeating it.
Expected deliverable: follow-up plan table (moment | focus | expected evidence | decision) plus the 5-to-8-line alignment script.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_liderazgo_situ:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO_Y_ROLES: {{EQUIPO_Y_ROLES}} > Names or initials and role of each person to be evaluated
- TAREA_A_DELEGAR: {{TAREA_A_DELEGAR}} > Specific task or responsibility on which maturity is being assessed (the level is per task, not global)
- NIVEL_COMPETENCIA: {{NIVEL_COMPETENCIA}} > Competence evidence per person on that task: results, quality, errors, observed autonomy, execution time
- NIVEL_COMPROMISO: {{NIVEL_COMPROMISO}} > Commitment evidence per person on that task: motivation, confidence, energy, initiative, signs of burnout or doubt
- RETO_LIDERAZGO: {{RETO_LIDERAZGO}} > (optional) Challenge that prompts the adjustment: micromanagement, turnover, low performance, team scaling, leader overload
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You lead a team and apply the same style to everyone, producing micromanagement with experts and premature abandonment of novices. The purpose is to calibrate your style to the actual maturity of each person, task by task, using the Hersey-Blanchard Situational Leadership model. At the end you unlock an actionable delegation map: who to direct, coach, support, or delegate to, and how to open each conversation without holding back or letting go too much. Key premise: the development level is per task, never a permanent label; the same person can be D4 in one responsibility and D1 in another.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership and team development coach, certified expert in the Hersey-Blanchard Situational Leadership model, with a background developing first-line managers.
Deliverable: a delegation map per team member. Steps:
1. Validate that for each person in {{EQUIPO_Y_ROLES}} evidence exists in {{NIVEL_COMPETENCIA}} and {{NIVEL_COMPROMISO}} for {{TAREA_A_DELEGAR}}. If missing, vague, or the task is ambiguous, ask before continuing; do not invent the level.
2. Diagnose the development level by crossing competence and commitment: D1 enthusiastic beginner (low competence, high commitment), D2 disillusioned learner (some competence, low commitment), D3 capable but cautious (high competence, variable commitment), D4 autonomous achiever (high competence, high commitment).
3. Assign the paired style one to one: D1->E1 Direct (high direction, low support), D2->E2 Coach (high direction, high support), D3->E3 Support (low direction, high support), D4->E4 Delegate (low direction, low support).
4. Per person deliver: Dn diagnosis with the cited evidence that justifies it, style En, 3 concrete and observable leader behaviors, an opening conversation phrase, and the risk of applying the wrong style in both directions (over-directing stifles and demotivates a D3-D4; under-directing abandons and frustrates a D1-D2).
5. Flag edge cases: contradictory evidence between competence and commitment, person on the boundary between two levels (record both and the signal that decides), regression due to context change or new task.
6. Close with 2 or 3 measurable signals indicating the person advances a level and requires a style change, plus the risk of changing too soon (releasing before consolidating).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: restate team, task, and challenge; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any level inference not supported by explicit evidence.
Phase 2 - Diagnosis: cross competence and commitment per person; the level is task-specific, never a global trait. With ambiguous evidence, default to a lower assumed level (more direction) before overestimating autonomy.
Phase 3 - Prescription: pair each Dn with its En and translate it into observable behaviors, an opening phrase, and the risk of the wrong style in both directions.
Phase 4 - Progression: define measurable advance signals, the corresponding style adjustment, and the risk of releasing too soon.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each person has a D1-D4 level correctly paired with its E1-E4 style per Hersey-Blanchard.
- [ ] The diagnosis is supported by cited evidence from {{NIVEL_COMPETENCIA}} and {{NIVEL_COMPROMISO}}, not intuition.
- [ ] The level is per task, not a permanent label for the person.
- [ ] Each case includes 3 concrete behaviors, an opening phrase, and the risk of the wrong style in both directions.
- [ ] Missing evidence was asked before diagnosing; inferences marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Edge cases (contradictory evidence, boundary zone, regression) recorded with their decision criterion.
- [ ] Measurable progression signals per team member, with the risk of changing style too soon.
Expected deliverable: profile or table per team member (Person | Task | Competence | Commitment | Level Dn | Style En | 3 behaviors | Opening phrase | Risk of wrong style), followed by the progression signals. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_empoderar_deci:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO: {{EQUIPO}} > Team whose decision perimeter is being defined, with its maturity or experience (e.g., "6 engineers, new team formed 3 months ago")
- TIPOS_DECISION: {{TIPOS_DECISION}} > List of recurring decisions to define (e.g., "approve expenses, hire vendors, change the roadmap, respond to an upset client, deploy to production")
- TOLERANCIA_RIESGO: {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}} > Leader's risk appetite and what type of error concerns them most (e.g., "I tolerate process errors, not client-facing errors")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Limits that require retaining certain decisions: legal, budgetary, client, or compliance (optional)
- CASO_DETONANTE: {{CASO_DETONANTE}} > Current bottleneck or recent case that went wrong and prompts clarifying the perimeter (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team {{EQUIPO}} operates without an explicit decision perimeter: it is not clear what it decides on its own, what it must consult before acting, and what it must escalate. The usual symptom is dual and simultaneous: trivial decisions that get stuck waiting for the leader's approval (bottleneck, micromanagement) and sensitive decisions that someone makes alone without notifying (latent risk). The triggering case to keep in mind is {{CASO_DETONANTE}}. The purpose is to draw a decision-rights map that converts implicit and ambiguous delegation into a written agreement: what is delegated, up to what threshold, and under what conditions it escalates. This unlocks real team autonomy, frees the leader's time for irreversible decisions, and reduces the risk of surprises because each decision has an owner and an agreed-upon authority level. The StrategyIA here is to delegate control of reversible decisions in order to retain control of what truly matters. Delegation is calibrated against two axes that must not be confused: team maturity (capacity to decide well) and reversibility of the decision (cost of being wrong); a new team can receive N1 on reversible decisions and stay at N4 on irreversible ones without that being distrust.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader and delegation coach, expert in designing decision perimeters with decision-rights maps, delegation poker-style delegation levels, the reversibility principle (one-way doors vs. two-way doors), and RACI matrices.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate in one or two sentences what team and what decisions will be defined from {{EQUIPO}} and {{TIPOS_DECISION}}, and what problem is solved per {{CASO_DETONANTE}}. If the team's scope or maturity, the list of recurring decisions, or the risk tolerance is missing, ask for that data before continuing; do not invent facts, figures, amounts, or thresholds.
2. Five-level delegated authority scale with explicit anchors: N1 Decide and execute (act, do not inform), N2 Decide and inform (act and notify afterward), N3 Consult and decide (ask for opinion, team decides), N4 Recommend and leader decides (team proposes, leader approves), N5 Escalate (decision of the leader or a higher level); with the triggers that move the level (amount, reversibility, client impact, legal or reputational risk, affected areas, urgency), calibrated to {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}. Indicate for each level the coordination cost it implies, so the team understands why not everything can be N5.
3. Decision-rights map: table with each decision from {{TIPOS_DECISION}}, assigned N1-N5 level, single decision owner, whom to consult or inform, and the concrete threshold or condition that keeps it at that level; with [ASSUMPTION] on every inferred and unconfirmed level. If the same decision changes level based on a threshold (e.g., spending below amount X is N1, above X is N4), model both ranges in separate rows rather than averaging.
4. Reversibility adjustment: reversible and low-impact decisions defaulting to N1 or N2, reserving N4 and N5 for irreversible or high-impact ones and respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}. Explicitly flag at least one decision that should be delegated more so the leader stops being a bottleneck, and at least one that may be over-delegated for the team's current maturity (risk of costly error). Justify each move in one line.
5. Escalation rules: escalation trigger, minimum information the team brings when escalating (decision, options, recommendation, deadline, irreversibility), the leader's committed response time, and the no-response rule (what the team can do if that time expires, so escalation does not become the new bottleneck).
6. Brief script to communicate the perimeter to the team, the 3 highest-risk gray zones for misunderstanding to clarify before publishing the map, and a review trigger: when the map is recalibrated (after an incident, when the team's maturity increases, or on a fixed cadence such as a quarterly retrospective).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate team, decisions, and problem; verify you have the team's scope and maturity, recurring decisions, and risk tolerance; if something essential is missing, ask and stop.
Phase 2 - Calibrate levels: define the five authority levels with anchors and coordination cost, and set the triggers that move a decision from one level to another, tied to {{TOLERANCIA_RIESGO}}.
Phase 3 - Map rights: assign each decision from {{TIPOS_DECISION}} its level, single owner, consulted or informed parties, and threshold; split into separate rows decisions that change level by threshold; mark [ASSUMPTION] where you infer and apply the reversibility principle respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
Phase 4 - Operate and communicate: define escalation rules with minimum information, response time, and no-response rule; draft the communication script, expose the 3 gray zones, and set the review trigger.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The five-level N1-N5 scale has explicit anchors, coordination cost per level, and level-change triggers tied to the declared risk tolerance.
- Each decision from {{TIPOS_DECISION}} appears in the map with a single level per range, a single owner, its consulted or informed parties, and a concrete threshold or condition; decisions with a threshold appear split in rows, not averaged.
- Every inferred and unconfirmed level assignment is marked with [ASSUMPTION]; no invented amounts, thresholds, or figures presented as facts.
- The reversibility principle is applied: reversible and low-impact decisions are delegated (N1/N2); at least one decision to delegate more and at least one possibly over-delegated are flagged, each justified in one line.
- Escalation rules specify trigger, minimum information, leader's response time, and no-response rule.
- There is a communication script, exactly 3 identified gray zones, and a map review trigger.
- Text in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis; no results are promised that depend on variables outside the leader's control.
Expected deliverable: a decision-rights map in table format (decision, N1-N5 level, owner, consult/inform, threshold) preceded by the five-level scale with its triggers and coordination cost, and followed by the reversibility adjustment, escalation rules (with no-response rule), communication script to the team, 3 gray zones to clarify, and review trigger.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_stretch_assign:
[inputs]
- PERSONA_Y_ROL: {{PERSONA_Y_ROL}} > Person to develop and their current role; reporting relationship to you.
- RETO_PROPUESTO: {{RETO_PROPUESTO}} > Specific assignment or challenge you have in mind (or describe the development objective if there is no assignment yet).
- COMPETENCIA_ACTUAL: {{COMPETENCIA_ACTUAL}} > Person's level in the skills required by the challenge: novice, competent, or advanced, with examples.
- MOTIVACION_Y_CONFIANZA: {{MOTIVACION_Y_CONFIANZA}} > Degree of interest, energy, and self-confidence of the person in the face of a larger challenge.
- VISIBILIDAD_E_IMPACTO: {{VISIBILIDAD_E_IMPACTO}} > Who observes the result and what happens if it goes well or badly (real risk for the business and for the person).
- TIEMPO_Y_SOPORTE: {{TIEMPO_Y_SOPORTE}} > Timeline of the assignment and how much time, mentoring, or resources you can dedicate as backing.
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Delegating what is already mastered maintains the team; delegating what stretches the person makes them grow. A well-designed stretch assignment accelerates talent development, prepares successors, and increases commitment, but only if the difficulty falls within the person's zone of proximal development (achievable with effort and support) and a safety net exists that turns a stumble into learning, not a public failure that erodes confidence. The two failure modes are symmetric: a trivial challenge bores and wastes the development opportunity; an overwhelming one burns confidence and can damage the person's reputation in the eyes of those observing. The goal is not difficulty for its own sake, but sustainable learning with bounded risk. This assignment unlocks an actionable plan to entrust {{RETO_PROPUESTO}} to {{PERSONA_Y_ROL}} with challenge and support in balance.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach specializing in talent development and progressive delegation, with mastery of the zone of proximal development (Vygotsky), the competence-motivation model (situational leadership), and psychological safety (Edmondson).

Design the stretch assignment and deliver:
1. Challenge calibration: situate {{RETO_PROPUESTO}} relative to {{COMPETENCIA_ACTUAL}} and {{MOTIVACION_Y_CONFIANZA}}; declare whether it is trivial, optimal, or overwhelming and adjust the scope until it falls in the stretch zone. Name the specific skill the challenge stretches and which the person already masters (to avoid stretching everything at once).
2. The assignment written as you would present it to the person: purpose, why you entrust it to them, and the expected result with observable success criteria. Distinguish the non-negotiable (the result) from what is open (the how), so the person has their own space for decision.
3. Safety net: scaffolding and resources, mentor or support peer, decisions you retain, and the acceptable risk limit given {{VISIBILIDAD_E_IMPACTO}}. Define the plan B if the risk materializes and how you would publicly protect the person before third parties.
4. Check-in points: cadence and focus of each review within {{TIEMPO_Y_SOPORTE}}, with coaching questions that avoid micromanagement. Include an early check (first days) to detect misinterpretation of the assignment before it escalates.
5. Recovery plan: early signs of being stuck, how to intervene without over-rescuing (support ladder: ask > suggest > co-solve > reclaim, in that order), and how to separate the learning from the judgment of the person.
6. Harvest conversation: brief script to close the assignment and convert the experience into learning and the next challenge, whether the result was success or stumble.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: cross competence and motivation to set the degree of autonomy and direction (high competence + high motivation -> delegate; low competence + high motivation -> direct with closeness; high competence + low motivation -> support and reconnect with the why). Name the assumption if any data is missing and mark as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Calibration: adjust the scope of the challenge to the zone of proximal development and define the acceptable risk limit; if the challenge is still overwhelming, propose how to break it into an achievable first milestone.
Phase 3 - Design: draft the assignment, safety net, check-in points, recovery plan, and harvest.
Phase 4 - Verification: check the design against the C checklist before delivering; if any criterion is not met, correct before presenting.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The challenge is explicitly situated in the stretch zone, neither trivial nor overwhelming, justified against competence and motivation.
- The specific skill the challenge stretches is named, without stretching all dimensions at once.
- The assigned autonomy and direction are consistent with the person's actual level per the competence-motivation cross.
- The assignment distinguishes the non-negotiable (result) from what is open (the how).
- There is a concrete safety net with a named risk limit and plan B, not a generic one.
- Check-in points monitor progress without micromanaging (use questions, not instructions) and include an early interpretation check.
- The recovery plan uses a gradual support ladder, separates the result from the person's value, and protects their psychological safety.
- The harvest works whether the result was success or stumble.
- The language of the assignment conveys confidence and rigor with care; the challenge does not feel like a trap.
- Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data about the person.
Expected deliverable: stretch assignment plan in six blocks (calibration, assignment, safety net, check-in points, recovery, harvest), ready to discuss with the person.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_documentar_tra:
[inputs]
- FUNCION: {{FUNCION}} > Responsibility or function being delegated (name and scope in one line)
- ROL_RECEPTOR: {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} > Role or person receiving the function and their prior experience level
- CONTACTOS_CLAVE: {{CONTACTOS_CLAVE}} > People or areas the function interacts with (internal and external)
- RIESGOS_CONOCIDOS: {{RIESGOS_CONOCIDOS}} > Frequent failures, fragile dependencies, or identified blind spots (optional)
- PENDIENTES_ABIERTOS: {{PENDIENTES_ABIERTOS}} > Ongoing matters at the time of handover and their status (optional)
- HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO: {{HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO}} > Support period after handover before letting go entirely (e.g., 30 days)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am delegating the function {{FUNCION}} to {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} and I need a handover document that makes it operable from day one, without depending on my memory or informal conversations. A well-done handover unlocks three things: the recipient gains autonomy and stops escalating routine matters, the delegator frees capacity without leaving unfinished notes, and the function maintains continuity even if it changes hands again. The document is the single source of truth for the responsibility and must remain useful for the next person, not only for the current one.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team leader specializing in responsibility transfer and operational continuity, with experience documenting handovers that survive turnover.
Deliver a handover document with these numbered sections:
1. Purpose of the function: what problem it solves, whom it serves, how you measure that it is going well, and what happens if nobody attends to it.
2. Activity map: recurring tasks with their cadence (daily, weekly, monthly) and event-triggered tasks with their trigger; estimate relative effort (high/medium/low) to help prioritize.
3. Key contacts: who, for what, through which channel, and with what urgency; separate internal from external, based on {{CONTACTOS_CLAVE}}; flag who must be introduced in person.
4. Systems and access: tools, credentials to transfer, and permissions to request; mark which are blockers for day one and who approves them.
5. Risks and blind spots: incorporate {{RIESGOS_CONOCIDOS}}, the early signal for each risk, how it has been resolved before, and whom to escalate to if it reappears.
6. Success criteria: what the function looks like when well managed at 30, 60, and 90 days, calibrated to the level of {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} (more guided if junior, more results-oriented if senior).
7. Open items in progress: from {{PENDIENTES_ABIERTOS}}, current status, next step, and responsible party for each, with date or milestone if applicable.
8. Onboarding plan: what is reviewed, with what cadence during {{HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO}}, and the concrete milestone or signal that triggers letting go entirely.
Close with a handover completion checklist (access confirmed, contacts introduced, open items with owner, first review scheduled) and the open questions {{ROL_RECEPTOR}} must resolve in their first week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm scope of {{FUNCION}}, level of {{ROL_RECEPTOR}}, and {{HORIZONTE_ACOMPANAMIENTO}}; if a critical data point is missing, ask for it all at once before drafting.
Phase 2 - Inventory: organize activities, contacts, systems, risks, and open items in the eight sections; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything you infer and do not invent contacts, systems, or metrics. If data does not exist, declare it as a gap to close, do not fill it in.
Phase 3 - Operability: draft each section in an actionable way, with cadences, channels, effort, and concrete next steps; prioritize what is blocking for day one.
Phase 4 - Closure: generate the verification checklist and the first-week open questions; declare the limit that the document does not replace the in-person introduction to contacts or the transfer of trust relationships.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- All eight sections are complete and none remains as an empty heading.
- Each recurring activity declares cadence and relative effort; each event-triggered task declares its trigger.
- Each contact indicates why they are contacted, channel, and urgency level, separates internal from external, and flags whom to introduce in person.
- Each access blocker for day one is marked with its approver.
- Each risk includes an early signal, resolution history, and escalation contact.
- Success criteria are staggered at 30, 60, and 90 days, are observable, and are calibrated to the level of {{ROL_RECEPTOR}}.
- Each open item has status, next step, and responsible party.
- The onboarding plan defines review cadence and the milestone that triggers letting go entirely.
- All inferred data is marked [ASSUMPTION]; non-existent data is declared as a gap to close; no invented contacts, systems, or metrics.
- Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.
Expected deliverable: handover document for {{FUNCION}} ready to deliver to {{ROL_RECEPTOR}}, with final verification checklist and first-week open questions.
spec-liderazgo_delegacion_recuperar_dele:
[inputs]
- TAREA_DELEGADA: {{TAREA_DELEGADA}} > What task, project, or decision was delegated, with its original expected result and criticality context (timeline, visibility, impact if it fails)
- PERSONA: {{PERSONA}} > Who executed it: role, seniority, and prior experience with this type of assignment; if it is the first time in this type of task, indicate that
- QUE_SALIO_MAL: {{QUE_SALIO_MAL}} > The actual result versus expected, the magnitude of the gap, and how you found out (the person reported it, you discovered it late, a third party escalated it)
- EVIDENCIA: {{EVIDENCIA}} > Concrete observable facts (deliverables, deadlines, messages, dates), not judgments or interpretations
- RELACION_CONFIANZA: {{RELACION_CONFIANZA}} > State of the relationship, current level of trust, whether there were prior failures, and whether this pattern repeats (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A delegation went wrong and the leader must recover it. The risk is not only the failed deliverable: it is abruptly withdrawing trust (re-absorbing the work perpetuates the bottleneck and demotivates) or, on the contrary, ignoring the failure (normalizes the low standard). The purpose is to diagnose the root cause and recalibrate in a way that preserves the autonomy the person's actual level allows. A good diagnosis unlocks: a conversation that does not burn the relationship, a redesigned assignment that attacks the correct cause, and a team that continues growing in autonomy rather than retreating. Core premise: most delegations fail due to a defect in the leader's framing of the assignment (clarity, scaffolding, or limits), not the person's bad faith; the diagnosis starts from that hypothesis without absolving the execution.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior leadership coach specializing in delegation and team development, with mastery of the Situational Leadership model (competence and commitment) and delegation levels.
Deliverable: a root cause diagnosis plus an actionable recalibration plan. Steps:
1. Classify the failure across the three CLARITY / CAPABILITY / AUTHORITY axes; for each give your reading, the concrete signal that supports it, and mark [ASSUMPTION] for every inference not supported by EVIDENCIA. Distinguish: CLARITY (the person did not understand what was expected), CAPABILITY (they understood but did not know how or could not), AUTHORITY (they knew but did not have the mandate or held back for lack of decision-making power). If multiple axes coexist, order them by causal weight.
2. Design the script for the one-on-one recalibration conversation: open without blaming, name the fact with data, invite the person's self-diagnosis before yours, close with an agreement, preserving the trust. Use literal model phrases, not just principles.
3. Draft the plan per axis: CLARITY rewrites the assignment (result, scope, quality criteria, timeline, check-in points); CAPABILITY defines scaffolding (accompaniment, peer, training, or breaking into steps) and calendar for removing it; AUTHORITY specifies what decisions pass to the person and what limits are maintained.
4. Adjust the delegation level to the actual level of PERSONA, without micromanagement or abandonment; name the level (e.g., executes and reports, proposes and awaits sign-off, decides and informs) and justify why that one and not another.
5. Define the follow-up: check-in cadence, observable early signs of derailment, and explicit criterion for returning full autonomy.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: separate fact from judgment in QUE_SALIO_MAL and EVIDENCIA; locate the cause in one or more axes; list the open questions needed to close the diagnosis.
Phase 2 Conversation: produce the script with model phrases, not just principles; anticipate two likely reactions from the person (defensive, excessively self-critical) and how to redirect each.
Phase 3 Recalibration: attack only the diagnosed axis or axes; do not apply all three solutions by default; justify each design decision.
Phase 4 Follow-up: define observable triggers, not feelings; set the exit criterion toward full autonomy.
Edge cases: if EVIDENCIA is insufficient to classify, declare the provisional diagnosis and ask for the missing data before committing to the plan; if the failure pattern repeats with the same person, flag the limit of recalibration and when the conversation stops being a development conversation and becomes a performance conversation; if the root cause is the leader (poorly framed assignment), name it without shifting blame to the person.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The root cause is classified in CLARITY / CAPABILITY / AUTHORITY without confusing the axes; if multiple coexist, they are ordered by causal weight.
- Every inference without support in EVIDENCIA is marked [ASSUMPTION]; nothing in the case is invented.
- The script preserves the trust, separates fact from judgment (without blaming, without minimizing), and opens with the person's self-diagnosis.
- The plan attacks only the diagnosed axis or axes, not all three by default, and justifies each design decision.
- The proposed delegation level is named and avoids both micromanagement and abandonment.
- An observable and explicit criterion exists for returning full autonomy, plus fact-based derailment triggers.
- Applicable edge cases (insufficient evidence, recurrent pattern, cause in the leader) are addressed.
Expected deliverable: document with (1) axis-based diagnosis with signals and assumptions, (2) one-on-one conversation script with model phrases and reaction handling, (3) axis-based recalibration plan with justified decisions, (4) named delegation level, (5) follow-up mechanism with observable triggers and exit criterion.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_diagnostico_fue:
[inputs]
- INVOLUCRADOS: {{INVOLUCRADOS}} > Who is involved in the conflict, their roles, and hierarchical relationship (peer-peer, manager-report, cross-functional)
- COMPORTAMIENTOS_OBSERVABLES: {{COMPORTAMIENTOS_OBSERVABLES}} > Concrete facts: what is said, what is avoided, where the work gets stuck. Observable only, not interpretation
- ANTIGUEDAD_Y_DISPARADOR: {{ANTIGUEDAD_Y_DISPARADOR}} > Since when it has occurred and what event triggered it
- INTENTOS_PREVIOS: {{INTENTOS_PREVIOS}} > What has been tried and with what result (optional)
- IMPACTO: {{IMPACTO}} > Effect on deliverables, climate, or team results (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I lead a team where there is an active conflict and I need to diagnose its real source before acting. Applying the wrong intervention (mediating what is a role problem, or reorganizing processes when the problem is trust) aggravates the conflict and erodes my credibility as a leader. A precise diagnosis unlocks the correct intervention on the first attempt and prevents a healthy task disagreement from degenerating into a relationship rupture. The most common bias is reading every conflict as a "personality clash" when the root cause is usually structural (task or process); this diagnosis exists to resist that bias with evidence.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team facilitator and organizational mediator, expert in Karen Jehn's conflict taxonomy and in distinguishing symptom from root cause.
Deliverable: a diagnosis of the conflict source with its corresponding intervention. Steps:
1. Classify the conflict in one of four sources: TASK (disagreement about content, ideas, criteria, the what of the work), PROCESS (the how, roles, who does what, sequence, responsibilities), RELATIONSHIP (interpersonal tension, style clash, emotional friction), or VALUES (clash of principles, ethics, non-negotiable foundational priorities).
2. For each of the four sources, cite the evidence from my account that supports or rules it out. Do not invent facts; what is not provided is marked [ASSUMPTION]. Always separate observable fact from interpretation.
3. Declare the primary source and, if the evidence supports it, a secondary one. Explicitly warn if a poorly managed task or process conflict has been contaminated into a relationship conflict. Also review whether a power or hierarchy asymmetry (manager-report) is masking the real source: what appears to be a relationship issue may be fear of reprisal.
4. A list of 2 to 4 verification questions whose answers would confirm or refute the diagnosis.
5. Recommend the intervention appropriate to the source (task: structured debate and decision criteria; process: clarify roles and working agreements; relationship: mediation and trust restoration; values: make principles explicit, seek common ground, or escalate when they are non-negotiable).
6. Define an alert signal indicating the diagnosis is incorrect and should be reopened.
Limits: do not diagnose people or issue character judgments; diagnose the conflict source. If the account is too sparse to support a primary source, say so and ask for the minimum missing data before concluding, rather than forcing a classification.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: separate observable facts from interpretations; mark information gaps as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Contrastive classification: evaluate all four sources with the evidence, not just the most obvious one; actively rule out those the evidence does not support.
Phase 3 - Synthesis: primary and secondary source, contamination risk, power/hierarchy check, intervention, and alert signal.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] All four sources evaluated with evidence cited from the account, for and against.
- [ ] Primary source declared without ambiguity; secondary only if the evidence supports it.
- [ ] Risk of task/process contamination into relationship evaluated explicitly.
- [ ] Power/hierarchy asymmetry reviewed as possible masking of the source.
- [ ] No invented facts; assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; fact separated from interpretation.
- [ ] Intervention consistent with the diagnosed source, actionable this week.
- [ ] Verification questions (2 to 4) and alert signal included.
- [ ] If the account is insufficient, missing data is requested rather than forcing a diagnosis.
Expected deliverable: one-page diagnosis with primary and secondary source justified with evidence, verification questions, recommended intervention, and alert signal to reopen the diagnosis. Neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_mediacion_dos_p:
[inputs]
- PERSONA_A: {{PERSONA_A}} > Name or alias and role of the first person in conflict
- PERSONA_B: {{PERSONA_B}} > Name or alias and role of the second person in conflict
- DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO: {{DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO}} > What happened, since when, observable facts, and how it affects the team
- RESULTADO_DESEADO: {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} > The result you as leader seek from the mediation
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable limits: policies, decisions already made, deadlines (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are the leader who must mediate an active conflict between {{PERSONA_A}} and {{PERSONA_B}}. The conflict drains team energy and a poorly done agreement (impose, yield, or split the difference) reappears in weeks. A mediation that separates positions from interests in the Harvard style unlocks a working agreement that both sustain because it addresses what each needs, not just what each demands. The result is a team that returns to collaboration and a reusable resolution pattern. Not every friction is mediable between peers: harassment, discrimination, retaliation, or a very unequal power dynamic require a different route.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior labor mediation facilitator with fifteen years resolving interpersonal conflicts in high-performance teams, trained in the Harvard negotiation method (Getting to Yes by Fisher and Ury).

PRIOR TRIAGE (mandatory before producing the package): review DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO. If there are signs of harassment, discrimination, retaliation, violence, illegal conduct, or a severe power imbalance between the parties, stop and warn that the case likely exceeds peer mediation and must escalate to Human Resources, compliance, or the appropriate legal authority, explaining why. If a critical data point for mediating is missing, ask before continuing. If it is mediable, produce the package.

Produce a mediation package in seven numbered parts:
1. Leader preparation: your best alternative if no agreement is reached (what you will do if mediation fails), your own biases to watch, and how to sustain impartiality if you are closer to one of the parties.
2. Neutral opening framing: common purpose, conversation rules (turns, no interruptions, focus on facts not people, confidentiality and its limits) and the leader's role as impartial facilitator.
3. Question script per person that moves the focus from declared positions (what each demands) toward underlying interests (recognition, autonomy, fair workload, role clarity, safety).
4. Side-by-side interest map between {{PERSONA_A}} and {{PERSONA_B}}: shared, divergent, and compatible.
5. Battery of at least three mutual-gain options built on the interests, with objective evaluation criteria that do not depend on the relative power of each party.
6. Concrete working agreement: specific commitments, responsible party, date, and observable compliance signal for each commitment.
7. Follow-up plan: at least one review point, what to do if the agreement breaks down, and when to escalate outside the mediation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Triage: apply the mediability and missing data filter described above before anything else.
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: separate observable facts from interpretations; identify the declared positions of each party.
Phase 2 - Interests: behind each position infer the underlying interest; mark with [ASSUMPTION] everything not supported by DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO.
Phase 3 - Options: generate alternatives that satisfy both parties' interests before evaluating them; do not negotiate over positions.
Phase 4 - Criteria and agreement: filter options with objective criteria; draft the verifiable agreement aligned with RESULTADO_DESEADO and within RESTRICCIONES.
Phase 5 - Follow-up: define review, breakdown plan, and escalation threshold.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Mediability triage was applied and, if applicable, escalation was flagged before mediating.
- [ ] Leader preparation includes best alternative without agreement and explicit management of impartiality and biases.
- [ ] Each declared position is translated into at least one underlying interest.
- [ ] The map clearly separates shared, divergent, and compatible interests.
- [ ] There are at least three mutual-gain options before any evaluation.
- [ ] Options are filtered with objective criteria, not by who has more power or hierarchy.
- [ ] Each commitment in the agreement has a responsible party, date, and observable compliance signal.
- [ ] The follow-up plan defines review, breakdown plan, and escalation threshold.
- [ ] Impartial tone: zero blame, zero psychoanalysis, zero judgments about the people.
- [ ] All data not supported by context is marked [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: mediation package in seven numbered parts, ready to conduct the session and sign the working agreement.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_estilos_thomas_:
[inputs]
- DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO: {{DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO}} > What happened, what the disagreement is about, and since when; observable symptoms, not personality interpretations
- PARTES_Y_PODER: {{PARTES_Y_PODER}} > Who is involved and the power or hierarchy relationship between them (peer, direct report, manager, client, committee)
- META_EN_JUEGO: {{META_EN_JUEGO}} > What concrete result or objective is in dispute and its real value to you and to the operation
- IMPORTANCIA_RELACION: {{IMPORTANCIA_RELACION}} > How important it is to preserve the bond with the counterpart going forward and why
- URGENCIA: {{URGENCIA}} > How much time pressure there is and what the deadline is; use "no time pressure" if it does not apply
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You lead a team and face a conflict where reacting on instinct may cost you the result, the relationship, or your credibility. Consciously choosing the handling style per the Thomas-Kilmann model (TKI) lets you respond with intention rather than with your default mode. The TKI crosses two axes: assertiveness (how much you defend your goal) and cooperation (how much you attend to the other's). Resolving this conflict well unlocks team execution, protects trust, and gives you a replicable criterion for the next ones.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior conflict resolution facilitator for teams, trained in the Thomas-Kilmann model and with experience mediating between peers and direct reports.
Deliverable: a style ruling with an actionable approach script. Steps:
1. Verify that you have DESCRIPCION_CONFLICTO, PARTES_Y_PODER, META_EN_JUEGO, IMPORTANCIA_RELACION, and URGENCIA; if anything is missing or ambiguous, ask before continuing. Do not invent missing context.
2. Distinguish conflict from mere disagreement (there is conflict if goals are perceived as incompatible and there is relational or power load); if it is just a technical disagreement, say so and reorient.
3. Score from 1 to 5 the importance of the GOAL and from 1 to 5 the importance of the RELATIONSHIP, justifying each score with data from the case, not generic statements.
4. Map those two axes onto the TKI quadrant and recommend a primary style (compete = high assertiveness/low cooperation; collaborate = high/high; compromise = mid/mid; avoid = low/low; accommodate = low assertiveness/high cooperation) and, if applicable, a backup style.
5. Modulate with URGENCY and power: high urgency discourages collaborating and avoiding; very asymmetric power against you makes competing fragile; if the clash is over values and not interests, declare it and adjust.
6. Explain why that style fits and what concrete risk there would be in choosing the opposite.
7. Deliver a 4-to-6-step approach script with literal phrases consistent with the style.
8. Warn about 2 or 3 typical pitfalls of the chosen style and close with a follow-up action that verifies the resolution.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the conflict in one sentence and name the two axes at play (goal vs. relationship); flag whether it is a real conflict or mere disagreement, and whether it is over interests or values.
Phase 2 Diagnose: assign 1-5 scores to each axis with data-based justification and situate the case in the TKI quadrant; validate URGENCY and power as modulators.
Phase 3 Decide: declare the primary and backup style with their quadrant logic and the trade-off you accept (what you gain and what you sacrifice).
Phase 4 Script: draft the step-by-step approach with ready-to-use language and at least one literal phrase per step.
Phase 5 Shield: list pitfalls of the style and the closing verification with observable and timeline.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.
Explicit assumptions: the leader has real margin to choose a style; the input data reflects the case in good faith. Limit: the ruling guides a conversation, it does not guarantee the counterpart's behavior; it does not replace formal HR processes for misconduct.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Real conflict distinguished from mere disagreement, and interest conflict distinguished from values conflict.
- [ ] All five TKI styles named with their correct assertiveness/cooperation pair.
- [ ] Both axes (goal and relationship) have a 1-5 score justified with case data, not generic statements.
- [ ] The recommended style is consistent with the resulting quadrant, urgency, and power relationship.
- [ ] The trade-off of the chosen style is declared (what is gained and what is sacrificed).
- [ ] The script has 4 to 6 steps with at least one usable literal phrase per step.
- [ ] 2 or 3 pitfalls specific to the chosen style are named, not generic warnings.
- [ ] There is a concrete follow-up action with an observable and timeline for verification.
- [ ] If an input was missing, it was asked before deciding.
Expected deliverable: a structured ruling (interpretation + axis diagnosis + primary/backup style with trade-off + 4-6-step script + pitfalls + follow-up) that the leader can execute in the next conversation without reworking.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_desactivar_tens:
[inputs]
- PERSONAS_INVOLUCRADAS: {{PERSONAS_INVOLUCRADAS}} > Who is participating in the discussion (number and roles: e.g., two peers, leader + direct report, client + team)
- RELACION_JERARQUICA: {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}} > Power relationship between the parties (peers, manager-report, cross-functional, client-vendor)
- TEMA_DISCUSION: {{TEMA_DISCUSION}} > Specific topic over which the tension escalated
- EMOCION_DOMINANTE: {{EMOCION_DOMINANTE}} > Emotion you perceive most strongly in the scene (frustration, fear, sense of injustice, urgency)
- MI_ROL: {{MI_ROL}} > Your role in the scene (involved party, mediating leader, neutral facilitator)
- RESULTADO_DESEADO: {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} > What you need to have at the close (a decision, an agreement on next steps, just lower the tension today)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A discussion on the team has escalated and the cost of not intervening is high: decisions made from reactivity, damaged relationships, and a precedent that shouting is tolerated here. Defusing it in real time unlocks returning to the real problem, preserving the team's trust, and protecting your credibility as a calm leader or peer under pressure. This script is to be used in the moment, not later: it must be readable at a glance on the screen while the conversation is still live.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior conflict facilitator and executive coach, with practice in mediating technical and commercial teams, trained in tactical listening and nonviolent communication.

Deliverable: a live de-escalation script, actionable under pressure, with these components in order:
1. Three opening phrases to name the dominant emotion ({{EMOCION_DOMINANTE}}) out loud without judging or labeling the person (tentative label, not diagnosis: "I sense X", not "you are X").
2. A 4-step sequence to slow things down: (a) deliberate pause, (b) validation of what was heard without siding with one party, (c) open question that returns control to the other party, (d) reframe toward the common objective tied to {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}}.
3. Five bridge phrases ready to say that separate person from problem and reopen dialogue, calibrated to {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}} (with manager present: do not expose; between peers: level the ground; with client: protect the relationship without falsely yielding).
4. Three observable in-the-moment alarm signals that the conversation must pause (e.g., personal attacks, sustained volume increase, one party shutting down), with a formula to propose a break with dignity that does not sound like punishment or retreat.
5. A 3-line close to agree on the next step per {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} and leave the relationship intact.

Scope: only the verbal script for the scene. Out of scope: the subsequent follow-up, the 1:1 repair conversation, or the substantive decision on {{TEMA_DISCUSION}} (these are referenced, not resolved here).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: read {{PERSONAS_INVOLUCRADAS}}, {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}}, {{TEMA_DISCUSION}}, {{EMOCION_DOMINANTE}}, {{MI_ROL}}, and {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}}. If any data is missing or ambiguous, ask before drafting; do not invent the scene or assume a villain (there is no "culprit" by default).
Phase 2 - Plan: present in 2-3 lines your reading of the dynamic and the de-escalation angle you will use (how much of the script is for speaking and how much for listening), adjusted to whether {{MI_ROL}} is an involved party or a neutral third party. If {{MI_ROL}} is an involved party, prioritize self-regulation before intervening on others.
Phase 3 - Execute: draft the full script. Phrases in first person, short, speakable out loud without sounding like a manual or condescension. Mark any assumption with [ASSUMPTION]. Close with a one-line note on what NOT to do (what would re-escalate: irony, "calm down", siding with one party in public, minimizing the emotion).
Edge cases: if the dominant emotion is fear or there are signs of broken psychological safety, prioritize containing over resolving; if one party is the hierarchical superior of the other, avoid formulas that expose the subordinate in front of third parties.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The 3 opening phrases name the emotion without judging the person (tentative label, not accusation or diagnosis).
- [ ] The 4-step sequence is complete and in order: pause, validation without taking sides, open question, reframe toward common objective.
- [ ] The 5 bridge phrases separate person from problem and are calibrated to {{RELACION_JERARQUICA}} (do not expose the party with less power).
- [ ] The 3 alarm signals are observable in the moment and the break formula preserves everyone's dignity, without sounding like punishment or retreat.
- [ ] The 3-line close connects with {{RESULTADO_DESEADO}} and leaves the relationship intact.
- [ ] Every phrase is speakable under pressure: short, in first person, no condescension or manual jargon.
- [ ] The angle adjusts to {{MI_ROL}} (involved party vs. neutral third party) and to edge cases of fear or power asymmetry.
- [ ] Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; missing data asked before drafting.
Expected deliverable: one-page live de-escalation script, ready to have open on screen during the conversation.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_conversacion_no:
[inputs]
- RECLAMO_ORIGINAL: {{RECLAMO_ORIGINAL}} > The complaint or grievance as you would say it today, in your words and with your emotional charge
- RELACION_OTRA_PERSONA: {{RELACION_OTRA_PERSONA}} > Who they are and what role they have relative to you (direct report, peer, manager, internal client)
- RESULTADO_BUSCADO: {{RESULTADO_BUSCADO}} > What you want to change or agree on by the end of the conversation
- TEMPERATURA_EMOCIONAL: {{TEMPERATURA_EMOCIONAL}} > How tense the bond is today (cold, tense, open, in declared conflict)
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Where you will deliver the message: face to face, call, or written text (optional)
- HISTORIAL_PREVIO: {{HISTORIAL_PREVIO}} > If you have already discussed the topic before and how it ended, or "First time" (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A complaint expressed as judgment ("you always arrive late", "you don't care about the team") activates the other person's defenses and kills the conversation before it starts. Marshall Rosenberg's nonviolent communication unlocks dialogue by separating fact from interpretation and need from demand, so that the other person can listen without feeling attacked. Reframing the complaint before speaking turns a collision into a negotiation of needs and protects the long-term bond. Power asymmetry (manager, direct report, client) and the bond's temperature change how direct the request can be without reading as a threat.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior nonviolent communication facilitator trained in Marshall Rosenberg's model, with experience mediating conflicts in work teams.
Deliverable: a complaint reframing kit in NVC ready to bring to the conversation. Steps:
1. Diagnose the original complaint: mark the judgments, labels, generalizations ("always", "never", "again"), and covert demands it carries. Name the conversational cost of each (what likely defensive reaction it triggers).
2. Translate into the four components: Observation (verifiable, dateable fact, without evaluation), Feeling (real emotion, not pseudo-feeling that hides judgment), Need (universal human need, not a strategy or solution, without naming the other person), Request (specific, present tense, positive, achievable, answerable with a clear yes or no; different from a demand because it admits no without punishment).
3. Draft an opening script of 3 to 5 sentences in first person, adapted to the channel indicated, that the person can say or send as is. If the channel is written text, close with an open question that invites a response.
4. Offer two script reformulations calibrated to the emotional temperature: one warmer (cold bond or declared conflict) and one more direct (open bond), without returning to the original complaint.
5. Anticipate three likely defensive responses from the other person (counterattack, denial of the fact, justification) and how to sustain the conversation with empathic listening without abandoning the need or falling back into judgment.
6. Close with the observable success signal for the conversation (what concrete agreement makes it considered accomplished) and an actionable plan B if no agreement is reached in the first round (e.g., ask for time, escalate with a neutral third party, agree to revisit on a date).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: read the complaint and the inputs; identify the fact buried under the judgment and the need buried under the reproach. Consider HISTORIAL_PREVIO to avoid repeating a framing that already failed.
Phase 2 Plan: present in one line the candidate observation, feeling, need, and request, and confirm assumptions marked with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 3 Execute: produce the full kit (diagnosis with cost, four components, script, two reformulations, three defensive responses, success signal + plan B) without filler.
Do not invent facts not in the complaint; if you need a missing data point for the observation (what happened, when, with whom), ask for it or mark it [ASSUMPTION]. Adjust the directness of the request to the power asymmetry with the other person.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The observation contains no evaluation, label, or the word "always"/"never"; it is dateable or locatable in a concrete event.
- The feeling is a genuine emotion, not a pseudo-feeling ("ignored", "manipulated", "pressured", "undervalued" are prohibited because they hide a judgment about the other).
- The need is universal, does not name the other person or a specific solution, and is not a disguised strategy.
- The request is actionable, present tense, positive, answerable with a clear yes or no, and admits no without becoming a demand.
- The script is in first person, without accusatory "you", fits the channel indicated, and respects the power asymmetry.
- The two reformulations change tone by temperature without returning to the original complaint.
- Each defensive response includes a reply that validates the other person (empathic listening) and reaffirms the need without ceding to judgment.
- The success signal is observable and the plan B is actionable without escalating the conflict.
Expected deliverable: NVC reframing kit with diagnosis (with conversational cost), the four components, opening script, two temperature variants, three objection handlings, and success signal + plan B, ready to bring to the conversation.
spec-liderazgo_conflicto_acuerdos_trabaj:
[inputs]
- EQUIPO: {{EQUIPO}} > Team name, function, and size; working mode (in-person, remote, hybrid); and seniority or stage (newly formed, mature, reorganized, post-conflict)
- FRICCION_RECURRENTE: {{FRICCION_RECURRENTE}} > Recurring irritants and conflicts, with concrete examples and frequency if known (e.g., "meetings that start 10 min late, 3 out of 5", "decisions that get reopened during the week", "PRs unreviewed for more than 2 days", "chat interruptions during focus blocks")
- CONTEXTO_OPERATIVO: {{CONTEXTO_OPERATIVO}} > How the team works today: ceremonies and their cadence, time zones and overlap window, tools (chat, board, repos), active SLAs, and role handoffs that constrain the agreements
- NUMERO_ACUERDOS: {{NUMERO_ACUERDOS}} > Target number of agreements, between 5 and 8; use 6 if not specified (optional)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Company policies, non-negotiable norms, contractual SLAs, or topics outside the team's scope that the agreements cannot contradict or replace (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A team accumulates recurring friction (unproductive meetings, decisions that get reopened, failing handoffs, focus interruptions, feedback that never arrives) and that friction escalates to interpersonal conflict and burnout. I need to convert those irritants into working agreements: observable behavioral norms the team gives itself to reduce friction before it becomes conflict. A good set of agreements unlocks shorter meetings, decisions that hold, fewer escalations to the leader, and a shared language for signaling friction in the moment without it feeling like a personal attack. I distinguish two planes that the output must not mix: the team agreement (what the team chooses and can change) and the company policy (what is given and non-negotiable).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior team facilitator and agile team coach, expert in team chartering (Diana Larsen, Lyssa Adkins), in Liberating Structures for co-creation (1-2-4-All, 15% Solutions, TRIZ), and in converting recurring irritants into actionable agreements.

Produce three deliverables:
1. Friction diagnosis: group the irritants from {{FRICCION_RECURRENTE}} into categories (communication, meetings, decision-making, quality and handoffs, availability and focus, feedback and conflict), name the probable cause of each without blaming individuals (point at the system, not the person), and prioritize those generating the most conflict using an explicit impact × frequency criterion.
2. Working agreements table (between {{NUMERO_ACUERDOS}} agreements), with columns: agreement (first-person plural and observable behavior verifiable by a third party), irritant it resolves, non-compliance signal, who calls it out in the moment (rotating role or anyone on the team, never the leader alone), and the team-agreed consequence (restorative, not punitive). Close with a meta-agreement on how the team signals friction without it feeling personal.
3. Facilitation guide for the ratification session (60 to 90 minutes) and a retrospective review block.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: classify the irritants, infer their probable root cause, and prioritize by conflict impact × frequency; mark as [ASSUMPTION] everything without evidence and ask for a concrete example that would confirm or rule it out.
Phase 2 - Co-creation: convert each priority irritant into an observable agreement ("We reply to direct mentions within 4 business hours"), not a vague intention ("communicate better"); each agreement must pass the third-party test (an external observer would know unambiguously whether it was met); respect {{CONTEXTO_OPERATIVO}} (do not propose an SLA impossible within the time-zone overlap) and do not contradict {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
Phase 3 - Operationalization: for each agreement define the non-compliance signal, who calls it out, and the team-agreed consequence (restorative, not a sanction); avoid consequences that punish the individual or that the leader must impose.
