spec-finanzas_presupuesto_anual_base_cer:
[inputs]
- UNIDAD_O_AREA: {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}} > Department, division, or business unit whose budget will be built
- PERIODO_FISCAL: {{PERIODO_FISCAL}} > Fiscal year or budget period and its temporal breakdown
- DRIVERS_DE_NEGOCIO: {{DRIVERS_DE_NEGOCIO}} > Candidate activity drivers that explain resource consumption
- TECHO_PRESUPUESTAL: {{TECHO_PRESUPUESTAL}} > Total resource limit available for the priority cut-off (optional; if missing, it is requested)
- OBJETIVOS_ESTRATEGICOS: {{OBJETIVOS_ESTRATEGICOS}} > Objectives or targets for the period (optional)
- DATOS_BASE: {{DATOS_BASE}} > Historical volumes, known unit costs, or restrictions (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The annual budget of {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}} for {{PERIODO_FISCAL}} will be built using Zero-Based Budgeting: unlike incremental budgeting, no line item starts from prior spend or is adjusted by default for inflation. Every dollar is re-justified from zero against an activity driver and an objective. The result unlocks defensible resource-allocation decisions, exposes spending that adds no value, and allows reallocation to the highest-return activities instead of applying linear cuts.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Director, expert in Zero-Based Budgeting and management control, able to translate operational activity into a defensible cost structure and sustain each line item before a committee.
Deliverable: zero-based annual budget of {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}}, with prioritized decision packages, monthly consolidated by unit, strategy narrative, and risk register.
Steps:
1. Define the decision units to be budgeted separately; justify the disaggregation level chosen.
2. For each unit, identify the activity driver from {{DRIVERS_DE_NEGOCIO}} that best explains resource consumption and establish the cost-driver relationship; use {{DATOS_BASE}} where available.
3. Build at least three incremental packages per unit (minimum viable, current operations, enhanced): driver volume, justified cost, benefit or risk, and dependency on prior packages.
4. Rank all packages in a single list by value-cost and mark the cut-off per {{TECHO_PRESUPUESTAL}}; state what is inside, outside, and the opportunity cost of the first excluded package.
5. Consolidate by unit and by month aligned with {{OBJETIVOS_ESTRATEGICOS}}, distributing per driver seasonality, and close with estimation risks and monitoring metrics.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Structure: break down {{UNIDAD_O_AREA}} into budgetable decision units.
Phase 2 - Drivers: map activity driver and unit cost per unit; document cost-driver logic and source of each figure.
Phase 3 - Packages: define incremental service levels; a higher package is only costed on top of the prior one.
Phase 4 - Prioritization and cut-off: rank by value-cost, apply ceiling, state inside/outside with opportunity cost.
Phase 5 - Consolidation and risks: build monthly tables with explicit seasonality, narrate strategy, list 3 to 5 estimation risks with monitoring metrics.
Hard rules: do not invent figures; ask for missing ceiling/volumes/unit costs before calculating; mark own estimations [SUPUESTO]; zero carry-forward and zero default inflation unless documented; verify consolidated total matches approved packages.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reformulate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every line item justified against a driver and objective; zero carry-forward or default inflation.
- Each decision unit has 3 or more incremental packages with explicit volume, cost, and value, without duplicating the base.
- Single prioritized list by value-cost with cut-off aligned to ceiling and opportunity cost of first excluded package.
- No figures invented: missing data requested and estimations labeled [SUPUESTO].
- Consolidated by unit and month matches sum of approved packages; monthly distribution reflects driver seasonality.
- 3 to 5 estimation risks including single-driver dependence, each with monitoring metric.
Expected deliverable: decision units table; prioritized packages table with cut-off; monthly consolidated by unit; brief strategy narrative; risks table with monitoring metrics.
spec-finanzas_presupuesto_incremental_hi:
[inputs]
- PERIODO_OBJETIVO: {{PERIODO_OBJETIVO}} > Period to budget and its granularity (e.g., FY2027, Q1 2027, monthly 2027)
- MONEDA: {{MONEDA}} > Working currency and number format (e.g., COP, USD, EUR)
- HISTORICO_LINEAS: {{HISTORICO_LINEAS}} > Actuals by line for the prior period; ideally 2–3 periods to detect trends (revenue and expenses). Indicate whether figures are final actuals or estimates
- INFLACION_ESPERADA: {{INFLACION_ESPERADA}} > Inflation assumption or general adjustment index (optional; if missing, marked [ASSUMPTION] with value and source)
- METAS_CRECIMIENTO: {{METAS_CRECIMIENTO}} > Growth or cut targets by line or category (optional)
- EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS: {{EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS}} > Additions, removals, new contracts, seasonality, or other one-time events, with amount and recurring/non-recurring nature (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- [S·SITUATION] ---
The budget for {{PERIODO_OBJETIVO}} in {{MONEDA}} is needed for committee submission. The method is incremental based on historical data: starting from the actual close of the prior period and adjusting each line by inflation, growth, and explicit assumptions. A fully traceable line-by-line budget enables its defense before the committee, resource allocation, and subsequent variance tracking against the plan. The strength of the method is its traceability; its risk is perpetuating inefficiencies from the base period, so assumptions must be visible and auditable.

--- [P·REQUEST] ---
Archetype: senior FP&A manager with experience in incremental budgeting and scenario building for committee review.
Deliverable: projected line-by-line budget with three scenarios and prioritized assumptions. Steps:
1. Verify inputs: confirm HISTORICO_LINEAS, INFLACION_ESPERADA, METAS_CRECIMIENTO, and EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS. Ask for anything missing; data not available is declared [ASSUMPTION] with assumed value and source. Do not invent figures.
2. Classify each line as fixed, variable, or semi-variable and assign its adjustment driver (general inflation, revenue growth, headcount, volume, indexed contract). A line without a clear driver is documented as such.
3. Project line by line: adjusted base = prior actual × (1 + inflation) × (1 + growth) ± one-time events. Show formula and absolute and percentage delta versus the prior period.
4. Build base, conservative, and aggressive scenarios by varying inflation and growth; summarize the impact on total revenue, total expenses, and margin, and identify the assumption that most separates the scenarios.
5. Prioritize assumptions by sensitivity (impact on results from a 1-point change) and include a risk note and recommendations.
Edge cases: (a) negative or zero base → adjust on the absolute amount, not the percentage; (b) non-recurring event → exclude it from the next period's base and state it explicitly; (c) line with no history → build it bottom-up and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; (d) volatile history across periods → use average or trend and declare the criterion.

--- [E·EXECUTION] ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: restate the objective, period, currency, and scope of line items; list information gaps and preliminary assumptions.
Phase 2 - Plan: present the line classification, proposed drivers, and inflation and growth ranges per scenario, before calculating.
Phase 3 - Execute: apply the formulas line by line, build the table, run the three scenarios, and consolidate assumptions and risks. Each figure must trace to a provided input or to an [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- [C·CRITERION] ---
- Each line shows: prior actual, classification, driver, % adjustment, projected amount, absolute delta, and % delta.
- The adjustment formula is explicit and reproducible for each line.

4. Build the recalculable budget in {{HORIZONTE}} and {{MONEDA}}, showing per line: associated driver, unit rate, fixed component, formula, and base-scenario amount. Calculate contribution margin (revenue minus variable costs) and EBITDA.
5. Deliver a sensitivity table showing revenue, costs, contribution margin, and EBITDA against the variations in {{RANGOS_SENSIBILIDAD}} for key drivers; identify the driver with the greatest operational leverage.

[inputs]

--- [S·SITUATION] ---
The organization needs to convert a global budget into governed departmental pools — not a simple arithmetic split. The deliverable unlocks three things: clear accountability (every monetary unit has a named owner), spending control (caps and alerts before overspending), and disciplined agility (reallocation rules that avoid bottlenecks without losing traceability). It serves to submit for financial committee approval and to operate month-by-month tracking. Without explicit governance, the budget becomes unreadable mid-period: no one knows who authorized what, pools run dry without warning, and reallocations happen by email without a trail.

--- [P·REQUEST] ---
Archetype: senior financial controller specialized in FP&A and cost-center budgeting, with experience in spending governance and zero-based budgeting.
Deliverable: departmental budget plan with owners, caps, and reallocation rules. Steps:
1. Build the master allocation table by cost center: name, allocated amount, percentage of total, a single named owner, and the criterion that justifies the amount. The sum must equal PRESUPUESTO_GLOBAL; report the reconciliation and any residual.
2. Break each cost center into expense lines (personnel, operations, technology, marketing, local contingency, or other relevant lines). Distinguish committed fixed spending from discretionary spending, because only discretionary spending is truly reallocatable.
3. Define for each line a hard cap (not to be exceeded without approval) and a soft cap (alert threshold, e.g., 80 percent) with the concrete action each one triggers (who receives the alert, within what timeframe, what they decide).
4. Specify reallocation rules at three levels: what the owner can move unilaterally, what requires the superior's approval, and what escalates to committee; each level with a limit in amount AND percentage of the pool, and with the data that must be recorded to leave a trail (date, source, destination, reason, approver).
5. Reserve a central contingency (percentage of the global total) and define its release criterion, its approver, and what happens to the remainder at period close.
6. Define the review cycle (monthly/quarterly), the budget approval workflow, and, if HORIZONTE_FASEADO applies, the fund-release calendar by phase.

Phase 4 Governance: write the three-level reallocation rules, the central contingency, and the traceability log requirements.
Phase 5 Close: consolidate the master table, verify the reconciliation to the cent, and issue the risk note.
Edge cases: if the sum of criteria does not reach 100 percent, allocate the residual to contingency and report it; if a cost center has no owner, mark it {to_be_confirmed} and do not close; if CRITERIOS_ASIGNACION contradict each other (e.g., headcount vs. strategic priority), present both readings and ask for a tiebreak.

I need to allocate my marketing budget {{PRESUPUESTO_PERIODO}} across the channels {{CANALES_HISTORICO}} to maximize the projected return per unit invested at the margin — not to distribute by inertia or by last period's spending. The purpose is to put every monetary unit where it yields the most, respecting my cash position, my payback tolerance, and each channel's capacity. A good allocation unlocks four decisions: where to scale, where to sustain, where to cut, and how much to reserve for learning. The result will guide the investment decision for the period and must be defensible before a committee.

--- [P·REQUEST] ---
Archetype: Marketing Finance Director (Marketing Finance / growth finance lead) with expertise in unit economics, marginal-return budget allocation, and channel saturation models.

2. Diagnosis by channel: for each channel in {{CANALES_HISTORICO}} calculate CAC = investment / acquired customers, ROAS = attributed revenue / investment, LTV/CAC using {{LTV_MARGEN}}, and payback = CAC / monthly contribution margin per customer. Show formula and data.
3. Marginal return: estimate the effect of the next unit invested in each channel, acknowledging diminishing returns and saturation; do not assume the historical average holds at scale. Distinguish average CAC from marginal CAC and make explicit the inflection point where marginal efficiency crosses the threshold.
4. Allocation: rank channels by marginal efficiency and allocate from highest to lowest return, stopping at each channel when its marginal return falls below the threshold or its capacity cap is reached; respect contractual minimums and explicitly reserve a fraction (suggested 5–15%, adjustable) for experimentation in channels without sufficient history.

With it I unlock decisions on supplier payments, bridge financing needs, and collections conversations with sufficient lead time, seeing from today the lowest-balance week and how much cushion remains. The direct method (actual receipts and payments, not accrual) is what connects to the bank account and enables decisions.

Archetype: senior treasurer (cash manager) specialized in liquidity management for SMEs and mid-sized companies, expert in direct-method cash projections and liquidity contingency plans.

1. Fix the W1 opening balance using SALDO_INICIAL and build the weekly calendar W1 to W13 from FECHA_INICIO_S1 (each week with its date range).
2. Project weekly receipts from CALENDARIO_COBROS (cash sales, receivables by aging bucket, other income), recognizing the receipt in the week of actual cash inflow, not billing.
3. Project weekly payments from CALENDARIO_PAGOS (payroll and payroll taxes, suppliers, taxes, rent and utilities, debt principal and interest, other items).
4. Compute per week: net flow, opening balance, closing balance, and available cushion (closing minus COLCHON_MINIMO).
5. Identify the minimum-balance week and flag an alert for every week that breaches COLCHON_MINIMO, quantifying the deficit and the first breach week.
6. Deliver a liquidity traffic light, 3 actionable levers prioritized by impact and speed (accelerate collections, defer payments, bridge financing) with estimated impact and timeframe, and the list of assumptions that most move the result.

Phase 1 - Framing: confirm currency, SALDO_INICIAL, COLCHON_MINIMO, and the 13-week window. If the opening balance, cushion, or receipts/payments calendar is missing, ask for it before projecting; do not invent figures.
Phase 2 - Classification: separate committed items (contracts, firm orders, known payroll, debt installments) from estimated ones; each key estimate carries an explicit assumption marked [ASSUMPTION]. If a receipt has low probability, project it in its realistic scenario and declare it.
Phase 3 - Direct projection: build the W1-to-W13 table with receipts, payments, net flow, and chained balances (one week's closing = the next week's opening). Cutoff rule: payments or receipts falling on a weekend or holiday are shifted to the next business day within their week; if they cross into the next week, flag it.
Phase 4 - Risk reading: locate the minimum cash week, detect cushion breaches, quantify the deficit, and translate to green/yellow/red traffic light (green: no breach or close call; yellow: available cushion approaching zero; red: cushion breached).
Phase 5 - Action and rolling: propose 3 levers prioritized by impact and speed, and explain how to roll the horizon (when a real week closes, a new one enters at the end to always maintain 13 weeks). If data only permits a partial projection, deliver what is possible and flag the pending gaps.

spec-finanzas_forecast_rolling_12_meses:
[inputs]

- HISTORIAL_PRECISION: {{HISTORIAL_PRECISION}} > Track record of prior forecast accuracy (optimistic or conservative bias, typical error) to calibrate the new one (optional; if missing, bias calibration is omitted and noted)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I maintain a rolling P&L forecast that always looks 12 months ahead. Each month that closes stops being a projection and becomes actual: I release that first cell, add a new month at the end of the horizon, and rebuild the projections with what I just learned. A well-maintained rolling forecast avoids the cliff effect of a fixed annual budget, which shortens toward December; it always preserves 12 months of visibility, captures in the run-rate what the close just taught us, and separates transitory noise from permanent changes. This unlocks cash, hiring, and investment decisions with a live, defensible number — not a plan frozen at the start of the year.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Analyst, expert in P&L rolling forecasts, driver-based modeling, and variance analysis with bridges/walks; with the judgment to distinguish signal from noise in a close and translate it into a defensible re-forecast.
Deliverable: updated 12-month rolling forecast, with decomposed close variance, driver-based re-forecast, a tying NTM walk, and an executive read calibrated by historical bias.
Components:
1. Close-and-add: mark {{MES_CIERRE}} as actual, shift the window, and add the new month 12, keeping 12 live, contiguous periods.
2. Close variance: compare {{REALES_MES_CIERRE}} against the projection in {{FORECAST_VIGENTE_12M}} line by line, decomposing each deviation into price/volume/mix/timing/one-off and labeling it permanent (moves the run-rate) or transitory.
3. Driver-based re-forecast: rebuild the remaining 11 months and the new month from {{DRIVERS_POR_LINEA}}, propagating close learnings and {{SUPUESTOS_EVENTOS}}; no line without an explicit driver or assumption.
4. NTM walk: bridge from the previous next-12-months forecast to the new one, quantifying each movement (carryover from close, driver changes, new month, management decisions).
5. Synthesis: executive read of the new number, bias per {{HISTORIAL_PRECISION}}, live risks and opportunities, and assumptions requiring validation.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Window roll: lock the closed month as actual, reorder the horizon to 12 contiguous periods, and declare which is the new month 12; verify no orphan cell or duplicated period remains.
Phase 2 – Close variance and interpretation: for each line calculate actual minus forecast, attribute the cause (price/volume/mix/timing/one-off), and decide whether the effect persists; permanent effects recalibrate the future run-rate, transitory ones do not. When the cause is ambiguous, declare the criterion used instead of guessing.
Phase 3 – Driver-based re-forecast: project each line from its driver, not by inertia; apply the corrected run-rate and known events; label each cell as [ACTUAL], [PROJECTION] with its driver, or [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 4 – Walk and reconciliation: build the prior-NTM-to-new bridge so that the sum of movements explains exactly the delta, with no unexplained residual; verify in each month that revenue minus COGS = gross margin and gross margin minus OPEX = EBITDA.
Phase 5 – Calibration and close: contrast historical bias, adjust for optimism or conservatism, and summarize the new NTM with its risks, opportunities, and pending validations. Do not invent figures: ask for missing data before calculating.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The window has exactly 12 contiguous months: the closed one as actual, one new month at the end, no orphan cell or duplicated period.
- Every figure is labeled [ACTUAL], [PROJECTION] with driver, or [ASSUMPTION]; no estimate presented as fact, no line without a driver.
- Close variances are decomposed into price/volume/mix/timing/one-off and classified permanent or transitory; only permanent effects moved the future run-rate.
- NTM walk ties: prior forecast + sum of movements by cause = new forecast, no residual.
- P&L is internally consistent each month: revenue – COGS = gross margin; gross margin – OPEX = EBITDA.
- Historical bias was considered in calibration; if {{HISTORIAL_PRECISION}} is missing, it is noted that no calibration was performed.
- Missing data was requested before calculating; every estimate is labeled [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: (1) 12-month rolling P&L table by month (revenue, COGS, gross margin, OPEX by block, EBITDA) flagging actual vs. projected; (2) close variance table with decomposition and permanent/transitory label; (3) NTM walk table (prior forecast, +/– by cause, new forecast); (4) list of drivers and assumptions by line; (5) 6-to-8-line executive close with the new number, its historical bias, and 3-to-5 pending decisions or validations. 5. Reality check against {{CAPACIDAD_ENTREGA}}: if the forecast exceeds capacity, mark the break-even point (period and volume), cap it at the deliverable level, and report the gap and the capacity increase needed to sustain the base scenario.
6. Deliver three scenarios (conservative, base, optimistic) with explicit differential assumptions and 3–5 highest-sensitivity levers (move one lever, observe the revenue delta).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Market funnel: decompose TAM>SAM>SOM with each cut's rationale and its [ASSUMPTION]s; validate orders of magnitude against a bottom-up when data exists.
Phase 2 – Adoption and capture: model the non-linear share ramp and apply the capture rate by funnel stage, including the sales-cycle lag.
Phase 3 – Monetization: translate customers/accounts into revenue via ticket or ARPA; separate new vs. recurring and apply churn.
Phase 4 – Capacity cross-check: compare revenue against installed capacity; cap the forecast at the deliverable level and quantify the gap.
Phase 5 – Scenarios and sensitivity: build conservative/base/optimistic, isolate critical levers, declare risks, and state the concrete condition that invalidates the forecast (revision trigger).
Data rule: never invent market figures, tickets, or capacity; if an essential input is missing, ask before calculating.
Edge case: if TAM and capacity point to incompatible ceilings (huge market, small operation), the SOM is determined by capacity, not by share, and is reported as the dominant constraint.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Explicit, auditable TAM>SAM>SOM chain; each cut justified with its declared method.
- Every estimate without a source labeled [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented market or ticket figures.
- Non-linear adoption curve with justified shape (not a simple proportional ramp).
- Capture rate discounts real funnel losses and the sales-cycle lag, not the direct share.
- Revenue separates new from recurring; churn incorporated if the model is subscription-based.
- Capacity cross-check present: break-even point, gap, and dominant constraint reported if the forecast exceeds capacity.
- Three scenarios with explicit differential assumptions and 3–5 quantified sensitivity levers.
- Forecast risks and invalidation condition (revision trigger) declared.
Expected deliverable: top-down revenue projection by scenarios, with step-by-step traceable calculation, forecast capped to deliverable capacity, and a log of assumptions, risks, and revision triggers.
spec-finanzas_forecast_demanda_serie_tem:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO_O_SKU: {{PRODUCTO_O_SKU}} > Product, SKU, family, or aggregate whose demand is being forecasted
- SERIE_HISTORICA: {{SERIE_HISTORICA}} > Period-by-period historical volumes (paste a date-quantity table or attach a file); ideally >= 2 complete seasonal cycles
- FRECUENCIA: {{FRECUENCIA}} > Time granularity: daily, weekly, or monthly (defines the seasonal period: 7, 52, or 12)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > How many periods ahead to project (e.g. 12 months)
- EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS: {{EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS}} > Past and future promotions, holidays, launches, price changes, or stockouts to consider (optional)
- DECISION_OBJETIVO: {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}} > Inventory, capacity, or purchasing decision that depends on the forecast and its target service level
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to project the future demand of {{PRODUCTO_O_SKU}} from its historical series to decide with a basis, not by intuition. A solid forecast unlocks {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}: sizing safety stock, planning capacity and purchases, and reducing both stockouts and overstock. The value is not the point estimate — it is the decision the range enables and the risk it avoids.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Demand Planning Analyst (S&OP) with expertise in time-series forecasting and classical decomposition.

Deliverable: {{HORIZONTE}}-period forecast with confidence bands, numbered assumptions, and a monitoring plan. Steps:
1. Diagnose the series {{SERIE_HISTORICA}} at frequency {{FRECUENCIA}}: length (available seasonal cycles), gaps, zeros, outliers, and level shifts; flag questionable data and declare how you treat them.
2. Decompose into trend + seasonality + residual; fix the seasonal period and decide additive (constant amplitude) or multiplicative (amplitude grows with the level); justify.
3. Select and apply the smoothing method per the pattern: moving average or simple exponential without trend or seasonality, Holt with trend, Holt-Winters with trend and seasonality; explain why that method.
4. Project {{HORIZONTE}} point by point with low/mid/high bands derived from residual dispersion; translate the interval into recommended coverage for {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}.
5. Validate with backtesting (holdout of last periods): MAPE, MAE, and over/under-forecast bias; honest accuracy read.
6. Synthesize forecast table, numbered assumptions, model limits vs. {{EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS}}, and re-forecast plan.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: profile the series and clean/adjust questionable data before modeling; do not model on dirty data. If fewer than 2 seasonal cycles are available, warn that seasonality will be tentative.
Phase 2 Decomposition: separate trend, seasonality, and residual; fix the seasonal period and type (additive if amplitude does not vary with the level, multiplicative if it grows).
Phase 3 Modeling: apply the smoothing method consistent with the pattern; estimate level, trend, and seasonal factors. Treat outliers and events as exceptions, not as recurring signal.
Phase 4 Projection: generate point estimate and bands from residual dispersion, not from free estimates; wider bands at longer horizons. Convert the interval into coverage/safety stock per the service level.
Phase 5 Validation: backtesting with holdout; report MAPE, MAE, and bias. If the error exceeds the threshold useful for the decision, say so and propose an alternative method, more data, or a different granularity.
Phase 6 Delivery: table + numbered assumptions + limits + re-forecast cadence (when to recalculate) and triggers (sustained deviation, major event, level shift).
Truthfulness rule: every number comes from the provided series or is labeled [ASSUMPTION] with its rationale; never invent figures. Do not confuse the forecast interval with safety stock: state the service-level assumption if you use one.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Frequency, length (seasonal cycles), and anomalies diagnosed; questionable data flagged and their treatment declared.
- [ ] Explicit decomposition; type of seasonality (additive/multiplicative) justified against amplitude behavior.
- [ ] Smoothing method chosen with justification against the observed pattern (and why the others were discarded).
- [ ] Period-by-period forecast with low/mid/high bands derived from real error, not from free estimates.
- [ ] Band translated into coverage or safety stock for {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}, with the service level as an explicit assumption.
- [ ] Backtesting with MAPE, MAE, and bias reported; honest read and usefulness threshold for the decision.
- [ ] Numbered assumptions and events not captured by the model ({{EVENTOS_CONOCIDOS}}) listed as limits.
- [ ] Re-forecast plan with cadence and triggers included.
- [ ] Zero invented figures; all data traceable or labeled [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: {{HORIZONTE}}-period forecast table with low/mid/high bands, numbered assumptions block, model limits list, backtesting metrics, and monitoring plan, ready to feed {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}.
spec-finanzas_forecast_accuracy_tracking:
[inputs]
- HISTORICO_FORECAST_VS_REAL: {{HISTORICO_FORECAST_VS_REAL}} > Period-by-period forecast and actual series (table, spreadsheet, or reference to attachment). Recommended minimum: 6–8 periods to read the tracking signal meaningfully.
- GRANULARIDAD: {{GRANULARIDAD}} > Temporal analysis level: monthly, quarterly, or weekly
- DRIVERS: {{DRIVERS}} > Dimensions to decompose the error: business line, region, volume vs. price (optional; if empty, aggregate analysis only)
- META_ACCURACY: {{META_ACCURACY}} > Accuracy target or tolerable MAPE, e.g. MAPE below 10% (optional; if empty, use 10% as the reference and declare it [ASSUMPTION])
- MONEDA: {{MONEDA}} > Reporting currency; default COP (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The finance team needs to know how reliable their forecast is before supporting inventory, hiring, or cash decisions on it. Measuring the error in a disciplined way and decomposing it by driver enables a forecast that improves cycle over cycle instead of repeating the same bias. The result is used at the monthly FP&A close and feeds the projection model review. A measured but uncorrected forecast is just error accounting; the value lies in closing the loop.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Analyst specializing in forecast accuracy and demand planning, with expertise in forecast error metrics (MAPE, MPE, MAD, WAPE, tracking signal) and in distinguishing systematic bias from random error.

Deliverable: forecast accuracy diagnostic with an iterative improvement plan. Steps:
1. Validate HISTORICO_FORECAST_VS_REAL: confirm forecast-actual pairs by period; flag periods where the actual is zero, gaps, and outliers. Actuals at zero: exclude from MAPE (division breaks) and report separately with WAPE; declare it [ASSUMPTION].
2. Calculate by period and in aggregate at the given GRANULARIDAD: MAPE = average |actual – forecast| / |actual|; WAPE = sum|actual – forecast| / sum|actual| (more robust when actuals are small or zero); MAD = average |actual – forecast|.
3. Calculate bias with MPE = average (actual – forecast) / actual; interpret the sign: positive = the forecast understates, negative = overstates. Distinguish bias (error with a consistent direction) from dispersion (error without direction).
4. Calculate tracking signal = signed cumulative error / MAD; flag if it exceeds +/–4 (bias out of control: the model must be recalibrated, not just adjusted).
5. Decompose the error across DRIVERS to locate the greatest concentration (which segment contributes the most absolute error and which has the most bias).
6. Identify the top 3 error sources (optimistic bias, poorly captured seasonality, unmodeled events, data lag, mix change) with numerical evidence supporting them — not generic labels.
7. Propose model adjustments prioritized by expected error reduction (MAPE/WAPE), aligned to META_ACCURACY, and define for each one the next-cycle validation metric and how it will be measured to confirm it worked.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Cleansing: verify the series for completeness and consistency; flag zeros, gaps, and outliers; declare assumptions with [ASSUMPTION]. If the series has fewer than 4 periods, warn that the tracking signal and bias read will be indicative, not conclusive.
Phase 2 – Metrics: calculate MAPE, WAPE, MPE, MAD, and tracking signal by period and in aggregate; show at least one formula solved with real numbers for traceability; never invent missing data.
Phase 3 – Diagnostic: decompose error by DRIVERS, separate bias from dispersion, read tracking signal, isolate top 3 sources with evidence.
Phase 4 – Iterative improvement: propose adjustments prioritized by expected error reduction and set their validation metric; distinguish a model adjustment (structural) from a manual override (point patch).
Report amounts in MONEDA (default COP). Error metrics go in percentage or units, not in currency.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] MAPE, WAPE, and MPE calculated with explicit formulas, by period and in aggregate, with at least one solved numerical example.
- [ ] Periods where the actual is zero treated explicitly (excluded from MAPE, included in WAPE) and declared [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Bias interpreted by sign (under/overforecast) and separated from dispersion; tracking signal contrasted against +/–4 with its implication.
- [ ] Error decomposed by the indicated DRIVERS, flagging which segment concentrates the most absolute error and which has the most bias.
- [ ] Top 3 error sources backed by numerical evidence, not generic statements.
- [ ] Each proposed adjustment has an expected error reduction, distinguishes model adjustment from manual override, and sets a validation metric for the next cycle.
- [ ] Assumptions labeled [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data; consistent currency; short series warned.
Expected deliverable: error table by period + MAPE/WAPE/MPE/MAD/tracking signal aggregate block with its read + decomposition by driver + top 3 error sources + iterative improvement plan with validation metric.
spec-finanzas_forecast_gastos_run_rate:
[inputs]
- UNIDAD: {{UNIDAD}} > Unit, area, or company whose expenses are being projected (e.g. operations, the whole company, a team)
- PERIODO_PROYECTADO: {{PERIODO_PROYECTADO}} > Future period to project (e.g. H2 2026, FY2026, the next 12 months) and its sub-periods (month or quarter)
- PERIODO_BASE: {{PERIODO_BASE}} > Recent, closed, and stable period that serves as the run-rate base (e.g. last closed quarter); if it had distortions, declare them
- MONEDA_PERIODICIDAD: {{MONEDA_PERIODICIDAD}} > Output currency and periodicity (e.g. COP monthly, USD quarterly); if there is expense in another currency, provide the rate or it will be labeled [ASSUMPTION]
- GASTO_BASE: {{GASTO_BASE}} > Base-period expense broken down by category, separating recurring from one-off; include known seasonality if any
- COMPROMISOS: {{COMPROMISOS}} > Signed contracts: amount, start/end date, periodicity, and escalation (or "No new commitments")
- NUEVAS_CONTRATACIONES: {{NUEVAS_CONTRATACIONES}} > New roles: fully-loaded cost, estimated start date, and close probability if applicable (or "No new hires")
- AJUSTES: {{AJUSTES}} > (optional) Salary increases, renewals with price changes, confirmed departures, inflation escalation, FX effect
- POLITICA_CONTINGENCIA: {{POLITICA_CONTINGENCIA}} > (optional) Buffer range or rule and the base it applies to (or use 3–8% of variable OpEx as the declared default)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The finance lead needs to project the expenses of {{UNIDAD}} for {{PERIODO_PROYECTADO}} with a figure defensible before management, a committee, or investors — not a back-of-the-envelope estimate. The purpose is to transform the historical expense of {{PERIODO_BASE}} into a forward-looking forecast built in traceable layers: what is already running (recurring run-rate), what is already signed (contractual commitments), and what is about to be added (new hires), all in {{MONEDA_PERIODICIDAD}}. A well-built forecast unlocks budget approval, anticipates cash needs, and detects early if the expense plan is sustainable. The typical error is double-counting (including a one-off in the run-rate and also as a commitment) or assuming all new headcount starts on day one; both inflate or distort the figure.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Analyst, expert in OpEx forecasting by run-rate method, contractual commitments, headcount planning with fully-loaded cost, and bottom-up vs. top-down reconciliation.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate the task in one sentence: "Project the expenses of {{UNIDAD}} for {{PERIODO_PROYECTADO}}, starting from {{PERIODO_BASE}}, in {{MONEDA_PERIODICIDAD}}". If {{GASTO_BASE}}, {{COMPROMISOS}}, or {{NUEVAS_CONTRATACIONES}} is missing, ask before executing; do not invent figures or contracts. If {{PERIODO_BASE}} is not stable, state how you normalize it.
2. Calculate the base run-rate from the recurring costs of {{GASTO_BASE}}; separate and exclude one-offs, listing them by name and amount to prevent double-counting, and carry the result to the target periodicity. If the base period had seasonality or an atypical month, adjust and declare it.
3. Incorporate {{COMPROMISOS}}: add only the portion that falls within {{PERIODO_PROYECTADO}}, prorate starts/ends at mid-period (declared convention), and apply contractual escalations on the agreed date. A contract starting mid-horizon does not contribute prior periods.
4. Model {{NUEVAS_CONTRATACIONES}} with fully-loaded cost (salary + payroll taxes + benefits + equipment/onboarding if applicable) and a ramp per start date; a role starting mid-period only contributes the remaining months. If there is a close probability, show the committed case and the probability-adjusted case separately.
5. Apply {{AJUSTES}} to the run-rate (salary increases, renewals with price changes, confirmed departures, inflation escalation, FX effect if there is expense in another currency); label [ASSUMPTION] where no data was given and indicate the source or rate used.
6. Add contingency as its own line per {{POLITICA_CONTINGENCIA}} (declared default: 3–8% of variable OpEx, not of the total), justifying the percentage by horizon uncertainty and plan maturity. Never dilute the buffer into the categories.
7. Present the forecast in a table by category and sub-period, separating base run-rate, commitment delta, hiring delta, adjustments, and contingency, with row and column totals that tie.
8. Reconcile the bottom-up total against the simple annualized run-rate, explain the delta (= commitments + hires + adjustments + contingency) component by component, declare the 3 most sensitive assumptions with their approximate impact (+/–), and close with the main risk of the forecast coming in short or over and what data would resolve it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Framing: fix the unit, projected period, base period, and periodicity; validate that a detailed base expense, commitments, and hiring plan exist; if an essential data point is missing or the base period is not stable, resolve or ask before executing.
Phase 2 – Base run-rate: isolate the recurring costs of {{GASTO_BASE}}, exclude and list one-offs, adjust seasonality, and normalize to the target periodicity.
Phase 3 – Incremental layers: add prorated commitments with escalation, then new hires with loaded cost and ramp, then known adjustments with [ASSUMPTION] and source where applicable; watch for double-counting against the run-rate.
Phase 4 – Contingency and consolidation: add the buffer as its own line over the correct base and build the table by category and sub-period with totals that tie.
Phase 5 – Reconciliation and sensitivity: compare bottom-up vs. top-down, verify the delta ties with its components, declare the 3 assumptions that most move the total with their impact range, and name the dominant risk.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The task was restated in one sentence with unit, projected period, base period, and periodicity before calculating.
- The base run-rate was built from recurring costs only; one-offs were listed and excluded explicitly (no double-counting) and seasonality was adjusted if present.
- Contractual commitments are prorated to the projected period, with escalations on their agreed date and no contribution to periods prior to their start.
- New hires use fully-loaded cost and a ramp per start date, not all starting on day one; if a close probability exists, committed vs. adjusted cases are shown.
- Every adjustment or figure without supporting data is labeled [ASSUMPTION] with its source or rate.
- Contingency appears as its own line, with a justified percentage and declared base, never diluted into categories.
- The table separates base run-rate, commitments, hires, adjustments, and contingency, with row and column totals consistent with each other.
- The bottom-up vs. top-down reconciliation ties, the delta is decomposed by component, the 3 most sensitive assumptions are declared with their impact, and the dominant risk is named.
- No selling prices or commercial rates appear: this is an internal expense projection.
Expected deliverable: expense forecast table by category and sub-period with base run-rate + commitments + hires + adjustments + contingency decomposition, plus bottom-up vs. top-down reconciliation, the 3 key assumptions with sensitivity, and the main risk, in {{MONEDA_PERIODICIDAD}}, neutral professional Spanish.

--- S | SITUATION ---
The team needs to anticipate the total payroll cost month by month to support the annual budget, validate the growth plan, and detect cash pressure before committing to hires. A rigorous headcount forecast unlocks decisions on hire pace, runway sizing, and budget negotiation with management — separating the inertial cost of existing headcount from the incremental cost of growth. The value lies in traceability: every figure must be reconstructable from its source rate and its assumption.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Director specializing in workforce planning and fully-loaded personnel costing.
Produce a labor cost forecast model with these steps:
1. Normalize the hiring plan into cohorts (role, positions, base salary, start month, contract type, FTE) and consolidate payroll tax, statutory contribution, and benefit rates by component, noting caps and non-monthly payments.
2. Calculate beginning-of-month and end-of-month active headcount and average FTE, reflecting staggered hires, proration of the start month (declared days-or-fraction convention), and departures from attrition.
3. Apply a salary or productivity ramp where one exists and model expected attrition with its replacement, coverage lag, and recruiting cost per vacancy; if the policy is not to replace, reflect the net contraction.
4. Calculate the fully-loaded labor cost by month, quarter, and total horizon, broken down by component (base, taxes, benefits, bonuses, recruiting) and separating existing headcount from new hires; isolate non-monthly payments (bonuses, holiday pay) in their accrual month.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: confirm the horizon, start month, currency, jurisdiction, and completeness of taxes, hiring plan, and attrition; if an essential data point is missing, ask before calculating and never invent rates, benefits, or market prices. Phase 2 Structure: define the monthly proration mechanics, the FTE base, the treatment of non-monthly payments, and the formula for each cost component.

Phase 4 Scenarios and read: run the three scenarios, quantify the cost and cash delta, and write the actionable findings.

>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---

- Existing headcount and new hires appear separated by month, quarter, and total.
- Assumptions listed upfront; every figure not provided labeled [ASSUMPTION] with justification; no market prices, vendor rates, or legal rates invented.

spec-finanzas_forecast_estacional_ajusta:
[inputs]
- TOTAL_ANUAL: {{TOTAL_ANUAL}} > Annualized total to distribute, in revenue and costs, with the currency and the forecast year.
- HISTORICO_MENSUAL: {{HISTORICO_MENSUAL}} > Monthly series covering at least one complete cycle (ideally 2–3 years of the same months), used as the basis for the indices.
- ANIOS_HISTORICO: {{ANIOS_HISTORICO}} > Number of complete years available in the history (optional; inferred from the series by default).
- COSTOS_SIGUEN_INGRESOS: {{COSTOS_SIGUEN_INGRESOS}} > Whether cost seasonality mirrors revenue seasonality or uses its own pattern (optional).
- COSTOS_FIJOS: {{COSTOS_FIJOS}} > Fixed costs to distribute as linear and exclude from seasonalization (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A correctly annualized forecast can be poorly planned if it is spread in flat twelfths: it ignores real peaks and troughs and distorts cash, purchasing, and staffing. Distributing the annual total using seasonal indices derived from historical data converts an aggregated figure into an operable month-by-month calendar, the basis for treasury budgeting, commercial targets, and variance control. It unlocks inventory, hiring, and financing decisions aligned to the actual business rhythm. The risk to control: a pattern biased by an atypical year or a short historical series is propagated across twelve months; that is why input validation precedes calculation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Analyst specializing in financial planning and seasonality modeling.
Deliverable: seasonalized monthly forecast table reconciled to the annual total.
1. Request TOTAL_ANUAL, HISTORICO_MENSUAL, and if not present, ANIOS_HISTORICO, COSTOS_SIGUEN_INGRESOS, and COSTOS_FIJOS; do not calculate with missing data.
2. Validate the quality of the historical data: month coverage, gaps, zeros, negative values, and atypical years from non-recurring events; propose excluding or adjusting the atypical year explaining the impact before calculating.
3. Calculate the seasonal index for each month using the ratio-to-moving-average method: divide each month by the average monthly value of its cycle and average the result across the available years.
4. Normalize the indices so they average 1 (sum 12) and correct the rounding deviation in the highest-weight month.
5. Apply the indices to TOTAL_ANUAL to obtain revenue and cost for each month; leave COSTOS_FIJOS as linear and seasonalize only the variable component. If COSTOS_SIGUEN_INGRESOS indicates its own pattern, derive a second set of indices using the same mechanics.
6. Reconcile that the twelve-month sum equals the annual total; show the tie-out adjustment if any.
7. Calculate the monthly margin and flag peak and trough months.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Inputs and validation: confirm totals, historical series, and cost rules; measure coverage and gaps; label with [ASSUMPTION] any inferred data point and declare excluded years.
Phase 2 Indices: derive raw indices using the ratio-to-moving-average method and average them across years; if costs follow their own pattern, calculate their separate set.
Phase 3 Normalization: scale the indices to average 1 and document the rounding adjustment.
Phase 4 Distribution and tie-out: apply indices to the total, separate fixed linear from variable seasonalized, reconcile against the annual total, and build the monthly table with margin.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The twelve-month sum equals exactly TOTAL_ANUAL (difference 0 after the tie-out adjustment).
- Normalized indices average 1 (sum 12); each index is traceable to the historical data and the ratio-to-moving-average method.
- Historical data quality declared: coverage, gaps, zeros, negatives, and atypical years excluded or adjusted with justification.
- COSTOS_FIJOS remain linear; only the variable portion is seasonalized; if costs use their own pattern, their index set is reported separately.
- Table with columns: month, normalized index, revenue, cost, margin, plus a totals row.
- Assumptions labeled [ASSUMPTION]; peak and trough months identified; index method declared; explicit warning if the historical data covers only one cycle or is insufficient to sustain the pattern.
- No invented figures: missing data is requested, not silently assumed.
Expected deliverable: 12-row-plus-totals monthly table reconciled to the annual total, with a brief note on method, assumptions, excluded years, peak/trough months, and confidence limits of the pattern.
spec-finanzas_forecast_reforecast_trigge:

--- S | SITUATION ---
Waiting for the regular planning cycle when the business has already changed turns the forecast into a historical document rather than a decision tool. This re-forecast trigger policy defines in advance which deviations require re-forecasting out of cadence, separating normal noise from structural signal. By codifying it, timely decisions are unlocked on cash, costs, and investment; the ad-hoc discussion of "should we or shouldn't we re-forecast" in every meeting is eliminated; and the credibility of the finance team before the committee and board is protected. Without this policy, two failures alternate: reactive re-forecasts triggered by every data point (team fatigue, loss of the planning anchor) or blindness to structural breaks detected too late.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Director with experience in rolling forecasts, monthly closes, and variance governance in {{TIPO_NEGOCIO}}, accustomed to defending thresholds before a committee and a board.

Deliver a re-forecast trigger policy with these components:
1. Monitoring metrics map {{METRICAS_VIGIA}}: each with reading frequency (daily, weekly, monthly), comparison base (vs. plan, vs. current forecast, vs. same period prior year), and data owner.
2. Quantitative triggers: deviation thresholds in percentage and absolute value, differentiating point deviation for the period from year-to-date accumulated, with a persistence rule (how many consecutive periods or what point magnitude trigger) to avoid reacting to a single outlier. Link each threshold to its rationale: historical volatility of the line item, materiality relative to the result, irreversibility of the associated decision.
3. Qualitative or event-based triggers: facts that require a re-forecast regardless of the number — loss of anchor client, regulatory change, FX shock, merger or acquisition, pricing change, rupture of a base assumption.
4. Three-level severity matrix — watch / partial re-forecast of the affected line / full re-forecast — each level with its governance: who detects, who validates, who approves, and by what deadline, using {{GOBIERNO}} if defined.
5. Step-by-step activation protocol, from detection of the signal to publication of the revised forecast and stakeholder communication, with an auditable log (date, metric, deviation, decision, responsible party, version of the resulting forecast).

Decisions and trade-offs to make explicit: loose threshold (fewer re-forecasts, higher blindness risk) vs. tight (more timely, higher operational cost and fatigue); and how the persistence rule balances both. Edge cases to cover: deviations that offset each other across line items but hide a mix break; correlated metrics that must not be double-counted; months of strong seasonality; and expected reversal vs. permanent change.

--- E | EXECUTION ---

Phase 2 – Threshold calibration: for each monitoring metric define the noise band, signal threshold, and persistence rule; justify each number with its financial rationale. Label [ASSUMPTION] any volatility or materiality assumed without data.
Phase 3 – Severity and governance: build the three-level matrix and assign detection, validation, approval, and deadline to each level; flag the escalation path if the approver does not respond within the deadline.
Phase 4 – Protocol and log: draft the step-by-step activation flow and the auditable record template, including how the revised forecast is versioned and archived.
Phase 5 – Stress test: run 2 to 3 illustrative scenarios showing each trigger firing or not; include at least one false positive avoided by the persistence rule and one real break that should trigger. Verify no threshold generates trivial noise or blindness to breaks.

The analysis does not replace the income statement: it measures contribution, not net profit.

2. Calculate per product: unit contribution margin = PRECIO_UNITARIO minus unit variable cost.
3. Calculate the contribution ratio = unit margin / PRECIO_UNITARIO, as a percentage.

1. Unit and scope: declare the transaction as the unit of analysis, identify the two sides (supply and demand) from DESCRIPCION_MARKETPLACE, mark the implied period and currency, and list what revenue and what cost touches each side and what is shared.
2. Take rate: calculate gross take rate (marketplace revenue over GMV_POR_TRANSACCION) and effective take rate (after INCENTIVOS_POR_LADO), broken down into supply commission, demand commission, and other revenue from COMISIONES_POR_LADO; separate the percentage component of GMV from the fixed fee component.
3. Cost per transaction: disaggregate COSTOS_VARIABLES, assign each cost to the originating side and to the shared portion with an explicit proration criterion (assignment driver), and total the variable cost per transaction with no orphan costs. Exclude fixed costs and acquisition costs: this model measures contribution margin per transaction, not CAC or payback.
4. Contribution: calculate total contribution per transaction (effective revenue minus variable costs) and contribution per side (revenue of the side minus attributable costs and incentives of that side), explicitly declaring how you split the shared portion between sides.
5. Cross-subsidy: make explicit whether one side operates with a negative contribution financed by the other, quantify the subsidy per transaction, indicate its direction (who finances whom), point to the unit break-even with the lever that closes it (take rate, incentive, or variable cost) and the magnitude of the required adjustment, weighted by VOLUMEN_MEZCLA if available.
6. Sensitivity: show how total contribution moves when the dominant lever is varied across a reasonable range (at least one conservative case and one optimistic case), and identify the threshold at which total contribution crosses to positive.
7. Model risks and open questions for validating it (missing data, semi-variable costs treated as variable, volatile mix).
Mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION]; never present an estimate as a closed fact. If GMV_POR_TRANSACCION, COMISIONES_POR_LADO, COSTOS_VARIABLES, or INCENTIVOS_POR_LADO are missing, ask for them before modeling instead of inventing them.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix the transaction as the unit, name the two sides, declare period and currency, and map revenues and costs to each side and to shared. Phase 2 - Take rate: compute gross and effective, separating revenue components by side and percentage of GMV from fixed fee. Phase 3 - Costing: assign variable costs by side and to shared with their proration driver, and total them. Phase 4 - Contribution: calculate total and per-side contribution after splitting the shared portion. Phase 5 - Subsidy and break-even: quantify the cross-subsidy with its direction, solve the unit break-even identifying the lever and its magnitude, and run sensitivity against the dominant lever. Always distinguish verifiable data from [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist: (a) the unit of analysis is the transaction, the two sides are named, and period and currency are declared; (b) gross and effective take rate are calculated on GMV, broken down by side and separated into percentage component and fixed fee; (c) each variable cost is assigned to a side or to shared with an explicit proration driver, with no orphan costs, and fixed costs and CAC are excluded; (d) there is total contribution per transaction and separate per-side contribution, with a declared rule for splitting shared costs; (e) the cross-subsidy is explicit, with amount, direction (who finances whom), and a signal of which lever and at what level the unit break-even closes; (f) there is sensitivity of total contribution against the dominant lever with the threshold for crossing to positive; (g) every inferred figure carries [ASSUMPTION] and no inference is presented as fact; (h) zero mentions of selling prices or the word for something unpaid; (i) neutral, professional language, no emojis. 2. Total billing hides the truth: in most portfolios a minority of customers generates the bulk of the margin while another segment destroys it through discounts, intensive support, small orders, returns, and long payment terms. This analysis, for {{PERIODO}}, unlocks high-impact decisions — who to renegotiate with, surcharge, migrate to self-service, or de-scale — freeing margin without raising sales. --- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior financial controller in customer profitability and cost-to-serve, with expertise in activity-based costing (ABC) and contribution margin.

2. Profitability cascade by customer: net revenue − direct cost = gross margin − assigned cost to serve = contribution margin, in value and percentage of revenue.
3. Whale curve: customers sorted from highest to lowest by accumulated margin; reading of the maximum-margin point (where serving additional accounts destroys value) and the % of customers that concentrates 100% of the margin.

Phase 1 Structure: normalize {{DATOS_CLIENTES}} to the same {{PERIODO}}; declare units, currency, and assumptions; separate assignable from structural costs; mark every estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and never invent figures.
Phase 2 ABC Costing: assign each component of {{COSTOS_DE_SERVIR}} with its driver from {{DRIVERS_ASIGNACION}}; declare driver, rate (cost/driver unit), and basis of each assignment — no black boxes; validate that the total assigned sums to the full pool (±1%).

- [ ] Each customer has a complete cascade through contribution margin in value and %.

--- P | REQUEST ---

Deliverable: comparative channel profitability analysis with mix recommendation. Steps:

For any shared cost, declare the proration basis and its driver and mark it [ASSUMPTION]. spec-finanzas_cohortes_retencion_ingreso:
[inputs]
- UNIDAD_COHORTE: {{UNIDAD_COHORTE}} > Sign-up grouping axis (month or quarter); defines the row grain of the matrix
- FUENTE_DATOS: {{FUENTE_DATOS}} > Customer and revenue source (CRM export, billing table, spreadsheet) with its currency and periodicity
- DEFINICION_ACTIVO: {{DEFINICION_ACTIVO}} > What counts as an active customer in a period (with revenue > 0, active contract, minimum usage); basis of logo retention
- NRR_OBJETIVO: {{NRR_OBJETIVO}} > Net revenue retention threshold that defines health (e.g., 110%)
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > Decision the analysis must support (prioritize retention, expansion, or acquisition)

- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to understand the true quality of my customer base beyond gross growth. By grouping customers by sign-up date into cohorts and following them over time I separate new from retained revenue, see whether recent cohorts retain better or worse than older ones, and detect revenue leaks that acquisition conceals. This unlocks unit economics decisions: where to invest between retention, expansion, and acquisition, and whether the business grows healthily (NRR > 100%) or sustains itself only by buying new customers. The risk to avoid is reading an immature cohort as a trend or incorrectly squaring the revenue bridge.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior SaaS finance and RevOps analyst specialized in unit economics, revenue cohort models, and NRR/GRR reading.
Deliverable: cohort report with matrices, revenue bridge, trend reading, and prioritized recommendations.
1. Validate integrity: confirm sign-up date per customer, recurring revenue by period, observation period, and {{DEFINICION_ACTIVO}}. If anything is missing, ask for it before calculating; never invent figures.
2. Fix and declare conventions: currency and periodicity of {{FUENTE_DATOS}}, revenue normalization (MRR/ARR), treatment of reactivations, upgrades/downgrades, prorations, and customers with zero revenue but an active contract.
3. Build the matrix by {{UNIDAD_COHORTE}}: rows = sign-up cohort, columns = tenure (0, 1, 2, …). Mark as immature the cells with few observed periods; do not project them as a trend.
4. Calculate per cell logo retention (active/initial) and revenue retention (revenue for period/initial cohort revenue), using {{DEFINICION_ACTIVO}}.
5. Separate GRR (only churn and contraction, capped at 100%) from NRR (includes expansion); make the formula and basis of each explicit.
6. Decompose the movement of each period into opening base + expansion − contraction − churn (revenue bridge) and verify it reconciles against observed revenue.
7. Identify the logo curve stabilization period and estimate average customer lifetime with its logic; if {{SEGMENTO}} applies, compare segments.
8. Compare NRR of recent (mature) cohorts vs. older ones, evaluate against {{NRR_OBJETIVO}}, and triangulate with GRR to distinguish whether health comes from low leakage or from expansion that masks it.
9. Deliver three actionable findings aligned with {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} and a warning if NRR < 100%, < {{NRR_OBJETIVO}}, or if expansion conceals growing contraction.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: restate objective, {{UNIDAD_COHORTE}}, {{VENTANA_OBSERVACION}}, and {{SEGMENTO}}; list available and missing data.
Phase 2 - Conventions: document currency, normalization, active definition, reactivations, upgrades/downgrades, and prorations before calculating.
Phase 3 - Construction: build logo and revenue retention matrices; mark immature cells.
Phase 4 - Decomposition: GRR and NRR by cohort + opening base/expansion/contraction/churn bridge squared against observed revenue.
Phase 5 - Reading: stabilization, average lifetime, recent vs. older comparative, and NRR/GRR triangulation against the threshold.
Phase 6 - Synthesis: three actionable findings, NRR warning, and assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- [ ] Data validated; missing data requested before calculating; zero invented figures.
- [ ] Conventions declared: currency, MRR/ARR normalization, active definition, reactivations, upgrades/downgrades, prorations.
- [ ] Matrix by {{UNIDAD_COHORTE}} with logo and revenue retention in readable tables; immature cells marked and not projected.
- [ ] GRR (capped at 100%) and NRR differentiated, with explicit formula and basis per cohort.
- [ ] Revenue bridge with the four components (base, expansion, contraction, churn) squared against observed revenue.
- [ ] Stabilization period and average lifetime estimated with explicit logic; comparison by {{SEGMENTO}} if applicable.
- [ ] Recent vs. older comparison + NRR/GRR triangulation + evaluation against {{NRR_OBJETIVO}}.

spec-finanzas_kpi_tree_financiero:
[inputs]
- METRICA_NORTE: {{METRICA_NORTE}} > Apex metric to decompose and its accounting formula if known (e.g., EBIT = Revenue − COGS − Operating expenses; contribution margin; LTV; operating cash flow)
- SECTOR_NEGOCIO: {{SECTOR_NEGOCIO}} > Sector and business model, to anchor the controllable operational drivers (e.g., retail, SaaS, manufacturing, services, marketplace)
- CIFRAS_BASE: {{CIFRAS_BASE}} > Current values of the north-star metric and its known components, with unit and source; "(optional)" if only the tree structure is needed without numbers
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Period of the figures' analysis (e.g., current quarter, fiscal year, closed month)
- HORIZONTE_ACCION: {{HORIZONTE_ACCION}} > Window in which the owner of each lever can move the driver (e.g., this week, this month, this quarter)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The executive team looks at the north-star metric {{METRICA_NORTE}} but does not know which operational lever to pull or who controls it. A KPI tree translates that aggregate figure into a chain of drivers, from the accounting root to actions that an area owner executes within {{HORIZONTE_ACCION}}. Building it unlocks actionable management meetings: every gap at the top is traced to its operational root cause and its owner, and the conversation shifts from "margin fell" to "conversion on channel X fell 2 points and the owner is commercial."

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A Director with experience building management control models (driver trees) for executive committees in {{SECTOR_NEGOCIO}}.
Deliver a KPI tree of {{METRICA_NORTE}} for {{PERIODO}}. Steps:
1. Confirm the north-star metric and write its exact accounting formula; if it has multiple valid definitions, choose one and declare which.
2. Decompose level 1: arithmetic components directly derived from the north-star metric (addends/subtractors).
3. Decompose level 2: each component into its drivers (e.g., revenue = volume × price; cost = units × unit cost). Separate volume, price, and mix: never fuse them in the same node.
4. Drill down to level 3 or 4 until reaching controllable operational metrics specific to {{SECTOR_NEGOCIO}} (e.g., conversion, shrinkage, days outstanding, occupancy, churn, average ticket, productivity per FTE).
5. For each node declare: formula, mathematical relationship with the parent node (addend, multiplicative factor, or divisor), and primary owning area (note co-owners if applicable).
6. For each leaf driver mark the direct or inverse relationship with the north-star metric and its relative elasticity (high/medium/low) with its rationale.
7. Deliver a table of 3 to 5 highest-leverage levers: KPI, owner, formula, base value per {{CIFRAS_BASE}}, concrete action for {{HORIZONTE_ACCION}}, and warning signal with numeric or percentage threshold.
If {{METRICA_NORTE}}, {{SECTOR_NEGOCIO}}, {{CIFRAS_BASE}}, or {{PERIODO}} are missing, ask before proceeding; do not invent figures.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: fix the north-star metric, its formula, and the available data; mark each absent figure as an input gap and note its unit and source.
Phase 2 Structure: build the tree top-down ensuring each level multiplies or sums exactly to the parent node (arithmetic consistency root-to-leaf). If a residual component does not reconcile, declare it as an "other/reconciliation" node instead of forcing the close.
Phase 3 Operationalize: translate the leaf nodes into metrics an area moves, assign owner, and classify direction and elasticity. If a driver has no clear owner, mark it as "owner unassigned" (a governance finding, not omitted).
Phase 4 Prioritize: rank levers by leverage on the north-star metric (impact × controllability × speed within {{HORIZONTE_ACCION}}) and draft action and warning signal for each.
Edge cases: if two drivers cancel each other out, flag it; if elasticity depends on the current level (non-linear), declare it in the rationale.
Always distinguish what is calculated from what is assumed: mark every assumption with [ASSUMPTION] and its calculation basis.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The tree is arithmetically consistent: every node reconstructs exactly from its children up to the root; residuals declared as "other/reconciliation."
- Every node declares formula, relationship with the parent (addend/factor/divisor), and primary owning area.
- Volume, price, and mix live in separate nodes; no node fuses two effects.
- The leaf nodes are controllable operational metrics, not accounting aggregates.
- Each leaf driver indicates direction (direct/inverse) and elasticity (high/medium/low) with its rationale.
- The lever table has 3 to 5 rows with KPI, owner, formula, base value, action for {{HORIZONTE_ACCION}}, and warning signal with threshold.
- Every assumption carries [ASSUMPTION] with calculation basis; no invented figures presented as real.
Expected deliverable: hierarchical KPI tree (root {{METRICA_NORTE}} to operational leaves) plus prioritized table of actionable levers.

A well-structured dashboard unlocks proactive daily management: it detects the problem while it is still cheap to correct, assigns the right owner to each alert, and replaces the status meeting with a traffic light readable in seconds. The frequent trap is the museum-dashboard: many pretty figures that nobody uses to decide. MetodologIA contributes here the rigor of management control applied to the real pace of operations: few metrics, each with an owner, band, and action.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior operations director, expert in management control, operational KPI design, command dashboards (operational balanced scorecard), and statistical process control (traffic-light threshold bands and escalation rules).
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate {{AREA_OPERATIVA}} in one sentence: "Monitor [process] for [daily decision it enables]". Name the decision before any metric.
2. Select 5 to 8 metrics from {{METRICAS_CLAVE}} (if empty, propose them and mark them as proposed), classifying them as leading (predict the outcome, provide reaction time within {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}}) or lagging (confirm an already-occurred outcome); for each one give a one-line operational definition, unit, and formula. Explicitly discard those that do not trigger an action, naming them.
3. Define the desired direction (more is better / less is better / target band) and three threshold bands green / amber / red per metric, derived from {{UMBRALES}}; mark [ASSUMPTION] thresholds without a historical basis and state what evidence would confirm them.
4. Associate with each amber and red band a concrete action, an owner named by role (not by person), and a response deadline; define the escalation logic for a sustained amber to red (how many readings or how much time in amber triggers red).
5. Set the update and reading cadence per metric according to {{CADENCIA}} and the source of each number according to {{FUENTES_DATOS}}; flag instrumentation gaps (desired metric without a reliable source) and the real latency of each source if it differs from the reading cadence.
6. Propose the dashboard layout in a table: metrics actionable today at the top, context metrics below; identify the "10-second glance" of exactly 3 metrics that summarize the state of operations.
7. Close with: (a) a stale-data control (what is shown and what happens when a number has gone beyond its cadence without refreshing), (b) a note on what the dashboard does NOT measure and what risk it leaves out, and (c) an anti-gaming check: per metric, how it could be inflated without improving operations and what counter-metric protects it.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: set the daily decision the dashboard enables and validate that candidate metrics, cadence, reference thresholds, and sources exist; if an essential datum is missing, ask before executing.
Phase 2 - Metric selection: classify as leading vs. lagging using {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}} as an anchor, apply the actionability rule (every metric must trigger an action when a threshold is crossed) and the anti-redundancy rule (if two metrics measure the same thing or one is a linear function of the other, consolidate and explain why). Define each one with unit and formula.
Phase 3 - Bands and thresholds: assign direction and green/amber/red traffic light derived from normal vs. critical levels; mark [ASSUMPTION] where there is no historical basis and name the evidence that would confirm it.
Phase 4 - Actions and escalation: link each amber/red band to action, owner by role, and deadline, and formalize when a sustained amber becomes red (explicit persistence threshold).
Phase 5 - Instrumentation and layout: associate cadence and source per metric, flag instrumentation gaps and latencies, order the dashboard by actionability, define the 10-second glance (3 metrics), and add the stale-data control, the coverage limit (what it does NOT measure), and the anti-gaming check per metric.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The process was restated in one actionable sentence that names the daily decision before listing metrics.
- There are between 5 and 8 metrics, each classified as leading or lagging, with operational definition, unit, and formula; the leading ones provide real reaction time within {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}}.
- Every metric triggers a concrete action when a threshold is crossed; those that do not were explicitly discarded and named.
- No redundant metrics: any consolidation of metrics that measured the same thing was justified.
- Each metric has a declared direction and three green/amber/red bands; thresholds without a historical basis are marked [ASSUMPTION] with the evidence that would confirm them.
- Each amber and red band has an action, owner by role, and deadline, and there is an explicit escalation rule from a sustained amber to red with a persistence threshold.
- Each metric indicates update and reading cadence and data source; non-existent sources are flagged as instrumentation gaps and relevant latencies are declared.
- The table layout prioritizes actionable today at the top and declares the 10-second glance (exactly 3 metrics).
