spec-finanzas_semaforos_umbrales:
[inputs]
- INDICADORES: {{INDICADORES}} > List of indicators to traffic-light, with formula and unit for each.
- METAS_REFERENCIA: {{METAS_REFERENCIA}} > Target, budget, objective band, or comparison period against which each indicator is measured.
- SENTIDO_MEJORA: {{SENTIDO_MEJORA}} > For each indicator, whether higher is better or worse (defines towards which direction red is triggered). Include a double band if the indicator has a central optimum (neither high nor low).
- APETITO_RIESGO: {{APETITO_RIESGO}} > Risk tolerance: what deviation is acceptable (green), concerning (yellow), or unacceptable (red). Indicate whether expressed as percentage, absolute value, or number of standard deviations.
- CADENCIA_DUENOS: {{CADENCIA_DUENOS}} > Review frequency (daily, weekly, monthly) and possible owners of each indicator. (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We want to move from a dashboard that only shows numbers to a control system that alerts by itself and dictates the reaction. By defining traffic lights with clear thresholds and predefined actions, the team stops debating whether a value is good or bad in every meeting: the color decides, the owner acts, and the escalation is triggered without friction. This unlocks early reaction to deviations, consistent performance governance, and exception-based management meetings (only what is in yellow or red is discussed). The risk to avoid is the opposite: arbitrary thresholds that generate noise (everything in red) or complacency (everything in green), and alarms that oscillate from normal volatility instead of signaling real deterioration.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior financial controller, expert in management control and scorecard design with a RAG (Red-Amber-Green) alert system and KPIs under the SMART principle.
Deliverable: an actionable traffic-light table plus a summary of indicators in alert and a governance note. Steps:
1. For each indicator in {{INDICADORES}}, confirm formula, unit, direction of improvement ({{SENTIDO_MEJORA}}), and comparison reference ({{METAS_REFERENCIA}}). An indicator without a reference or direction of improvement cannot be traffic-lighted: flag it, declare it blocked, and ask for the datum; do not invent a target for it.
2. Set two cut-points per indicator: green-yellow and yellow-red, expressed as deviation from the reference, consistent with direction of improvement and {{APETITO_RIESGO}}; briefly justify each cut-point (where the number comes from) and avoid arbitrary thresholds. For indicators with a central optimum use a double band (red for excess and for deficit).
3. Guarantee full domain coverage: three contiguous ranges with no gaps or overlaps, and explicitly declare to which color the exact value at each cut-point belongs (border convention, e.g., the limit counts as the more conservative color).
4. Define the transition rule for each state, including persistence (e.g., two consecutive periods in zone) to filter false alarms; distinguish a one-time crossing from a sustained deterioration and, if applicable, hysteresis so the indicator does not oscillate between two colors at the border.
5. Assign each state (green, yellow, red) a predefined action, an owner, and a deadline; red must include an explicit escalation path (to whom and by when). Reuse {{CADENCIA_DUENOS}} where it exists; if owner or frequency is missing, propose one as [ASSUMPTION].
6. Assemble the table, the summary of indicators in alert, and the governance note on threshold recalibration.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Normalization: standardize each indicator (formula, unit, direction, reference). Mark with [ASSUMPTION] any missing datum; do not invent figures. Flag non-traffic-lightable indicators and explain why.
Phase 2 - Thresholds: derive the green-yellow and yellow-red cut-points from {{METAS_REFERENCIA}} and {{APETITO_RIESGO}}, respecting {{SENTIDO_MEJORA}}; verify coverage with no gaps or overlaps and set the border convention.
Phase 3 - Rules and actions: define triggers, persistence or hysteresis, action-owner-deadline per state, and red escalation path, using {{CADENCIA_DUENOS}} where it exists.
Phase 4 - Assembly: build the table (indicator, unit, direction, target or reference, green range, yellow range, red range, transition rule, owner, frequency, action per state) and the summary of the 3 to 5 indicators in red or yellow, ordered by severity.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each traffic-lightable indicator has three contiguous ranges with no gaps or overlaps and consistent with its direction of improvement; the border convention is declared.
- Each threshold is justified against target and risk appetite (it is visible where the number comes from); none is arbitrary.
- Indicators with a central optimum use a double band; non-traffic-lightable ones are flagged and blocked with the missing datum.
- Transition rules include persistence (and hysteresis where applicable) to avoid false alarms and border oscillation.
- Each state has an action, owner, and deadline; red has an explicit escalation path.
- Missing data marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented figures.
- Includes a governance note: how often and under what triggers thresholds are recalibrated, and who approves the change.
Expected deliverable: traffic-light table ready to paste into a scorecard, with the indicated columns, plus an actionable summary of indicators in alert (ordered by severity) and a closing section with open questions or assumptions.
spec-finanzas_reporte_gestion_mensual:
[inputs]
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Month and year of the report (e.g., May 2026); indicate whether preliminary or final close
- UNIDAD_NEGOCIO: {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}} > Company, unit, or cost center being reported; currency and P&L units

--- S | SITUATION ---
The executive committee of {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}} reviews the close of {{PERIODO}} and needs a management report that explains what happened, why it happened, and what will be done about it, not just a table of figures. A well-structured report turns the meeting into decisions: it unlocks approval of corrective actions, forecast adjustments, and resource allocation. Poorly done, it triggers a number hunt that consumes the meeting with no conclusions. The committee has no time to reconcile sources live: it trusts that every figure closes and every variance is explained.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Director of Financial Planning (FP&A) who assembles and defends the monthly management report before the executive committee, with mastery of price-volume-mix variance analysis, management control, and executive narrative.
Deliverable: the complete monthly management report of {{PERIODO}} for {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}}, ready for committee. Sections:
1. Executive summary: maximum five bullets with the month's verdict on revenue, gross margin, EBITDA, net income, and cash, each with its figure and key variance; one final bullet with the overall reading.
2. Results table: material P&L lines with columns Actual, Budget, Absolute variance, Variance %, Prior year, and Variance vs. prior year, according to the comparatives in {{LINEA_BASE}}; includes a totals row that closes.
3. Classification: flag each variance as favorable or unfavorable by its effect on the result (a cost overrun is unfavorable even if the number is higher; a saving is favorable even if the number falls), not by its arithmetic sign; flag those that exceed {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}}.
4. Management commentary: for the most material variances, separate root cause (price, volume, mix, unit cost, timing, or reclassification), quantified effect, and classify as recurring or one-time (timing that reverses next month vs. structural deterioration).
5. Corrective actions: table with action, owner, target date, and expected recovery amount, prioritized by impact and aligned with {{FOCO_DECISION}}; distinguish what recovers the result from what merely mitigates.
6. Control dashboard: {{KPIS_CONTROL}} with value, target, and traffic light; green/amber/red is set against the target and its band, not by judgment.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Input validation: confirm period (preliminary or final), unit, currency, available comparatives, and threshold; if the baseline, the period, or the detail of a material line item are missing, ask before calculating.
Phase 2 - Variance calculation: derive absolute and percentage variance against each comparative in {{LINEA_BASE}}; decompose into price-volume-mix where price and quantity data exist; verify that the sum of line variances reconciles with the total variance; never invent absent figures, mark any estimate as [ASSUMPTION] and isolate it from real data.
Phase 3 - Diagnosis: prioritize variances by materiality, attribute root cause and recurrence; when a cause is uncertain, declare it as a hypothesis to confirm, not as fact.
Phase 4 - Narrative and actions: write a concise management commentary and derive corrective actions with owner, date, and expected recovery; avoid generic actions without an owner or amount.
Phase 5 - Dashboard and close: assemble KPIs with traffic light and write the executive summary as a final defensible synthesis figure by figure.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Executive summary of maximum five bullets, each with a figure and variance.
- [ ] Results table with the comparative columns from {{LINEA_BASE}} and a totals row that closes.
- [ ] Every variance classified favorable/unfavorable by effect on result, not by sign.
- [ ] Material variances (above {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}}) flagged and explained with price-volume-mix-cost-timing root cause.
- [ ] Each material variance distinguishes recurring vs. one-time.
- [ ] Each corrective action has an owner, target date, and expected recovery amount.

spec-finanzas_variance_analysis_presupue:
[inputs]
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Period analyzed (e.g., May 2026, Q2 2026, YTD cumulative)
- UNIDAD_NEGOCIO: {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}} > Unit, cost center, or line of business under analysis
- DATOS_PLAN_REAL: {{DATOS_PLAN_REAL}} > Budget and actual amounts by line, or reference to the attachment containing them
- UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD: {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}} > Threshold for flagging a variance as material: percentage of the line or amount (optional; default 5% of the line with a relevance floor for small lines)
- DETALLE_PRECIO_VOLUMEN: {{DETALLE_PRECIO_VOLUMEN}} > Actual vs. budgeted units and rates that enable separating price, volume, and mix (optional; "not available" if it does not exist)
- PRESUPUESTO_ANUAL: {{PRESUPUESTO_ANUAL}} > Annual target or current forecast against which fulfillment risk is assessed (optional)
- BASE_COMPARACION: {{BASE_COMPARACION}} > What "plan" means: original budget, revised forecast, or both; and whether the actual is preliminary or closed (optional; default: original budget vs. closed actual)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Management receives a budget and an actual close for {{PERIODO}} for {{UNIDAD_NEGOCIO}}, but raw numbers do not explain why the result deviated or where to act. A well-done variance analysis converts the difference between plan and reality into decisions: which line to correct, which trend to stop, and which risk to escalate before it compromises the year. What is unlocked is an FP&A commentary that a committee can read in minutes and act on the same day.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A (Financial Planning & Analysis) analyst with mastery of budgetary management control and price-volume-mix decomposition.
Deliver a budget vs. actual variance analysis with root cause by line, in these steps:
1. Build a table by line (revenue, direct costs, operating expenses, margin) with budget, actual, absolute variance, and percentage variance, in the currency of the data; verify that the lines sum to the subtotals and totals (closing check).
2. Apply {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}} to flag material variances; combine percentage and amount criteria to avoid flagging as material a high % over a trivial line or omitting a large amount with a low %. Immaterial ones are aggregated in a single row to avoid diluting focus.
3. Classify each material variance as favorable or unfavorable by its impact on the result, not by its arithmetic sign (lower cost = favorable; lower revenue = unfavorable; higher expense = unfavorable).
4. For revenue and variable costs, decompose the deviation into price effect, volume effect, and mix effect using {{DETALLE_PRECIO_VOLUMEN}}; make explicit the formula for each effect (price = (Pr-Pp)×Qr; volume = (Qr-Qp)×Pp; mix according to composition) and verify that the sum of effects reconstructs the total variance of the line.
5. For each material variance write the root cause: why it occurred, verifiable against the data, not a restatement of the number. Distinguish structural/recurring cause from a one-time event (one-off) and indicate whether the variance advances or defers expense/revenue (timing) rather than creating it.
6. Close with an executive commentary: top 3 variances by absolute impact on the result, reading of whether the trend puts {{PRESUPUESTO_ANUAL}} at risk (run-rate projection to year-end), and the next control action for each, with suggested owner and time horizon.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate period, unit, comparison base, threshold, and whether there is or is not price-volume detail; confirm currency, scale (thousands/millions), and sign convention for variances.
Phase 2 Plan: list the lines to compare, the decomposition method, how you will filter what is material, and how you will handle lines with plan or actual at zero (% variance not calculable); declare assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 3 Execute: calculate variances, decompose effects where data exist, assign root cause, separate timing from permanent impact, and write the executive commentary.
Analytic honesty rule: if the data do not allow separating price from volume, say so and deliver the total variance without inventing the decomposition; when figures are inconsistent or do not balance, flag the discrepancy rather than forcing the total; never invent figures or causes.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each line has absolute and percentage variance balancing against subtotals and totals; lines with a zero base are treated explicitly (no silent %DIV0).
- [ ] The materiality threshold combined % and amount consistently and immaterial items were aggregated in one row.
- [ ] Favorable/unfavorable reflects impact on result, not arithmetic sign.
- [ ] The price-volume-mix decomposition shows its formula and the sum of effects reconstructs the total variance, or it is explicitly declared "not separable".
- [ ] Each root cause explains the why, is verifiable against the data, and distinguishes structural vs. one-off vs. timing; zero invented causes.

spec-finanzas_descomposicion_precio_volu:
[inputs]
- METRICA: {{METRICA}} > What is decomposed: revenue or cost. Includes currency and unit. The sign interpretation depends on this: for cost, an increase is unfavorable; for revenue, favorable.
- PERIODO_BASE: {{PERIODO_BASE}} > Reference period (month, quarter, or comparison year)
- PERIODO_ACTUAL: {{PERIODO_ACTUAL}} > Period to explain relative to the base
- NIVEL_DESAGREGACION: {{NIVEL_DESAGREGACION}} > Unit of analysis: SKU, product line, segment, or region
- DATOS: {{DATOS}} > For each line and period: quantity (units) and price or unit cost. Mark lines present in only one of the periods.
- MONEDA_REPORTE: {{MONEDA_REPORTE}} > Currency for the final table; if multi-currency, indicate the rate or whether the FX effect is decomposed separately
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The total variation of a revenue or cost between two periods is often read as a single number that hides opposing levers: a price increase can mask a volume decline, or a mix shift toward cheaper products can simulate non-existent price weakness. Decomposing the variation into volume, mix, and price effects exposes the true cause and unlocks the right decision: defend price, recover volume, or recompose the portfolio. The output feeds the variation commentary in the close, the business review, and the conversation with commercial and operations teams. The technical challenge is that price, volume, and mix share a cross term: if the formulas are not anchored to a consistent base, the bridge does not close or one effect absorbs what belongs to another.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior FP&A financial analyst specializing in revenue and cost variation analysis, fluent in price-volume-mix bridge reconciliation and cross-effect treatment.
Produce the decomposition of the variation of {{METRICA}} between {{PERIODO_BASE}} and {{PERIODO_ACTUAL}} at the level {{NIVEL_DESAGREGACION}}, in {{MONEDA_REPORTE}}, with these numbered deliverables:
1. Bridge table starting from {{METRICA}} base, summing in order Volume Effect, Mix Effect, Price Effect, and, if applicable, Line Additions/Removals, closing at {{METRICA}} current.
2. Percentage weight of each effect over total variation and closing residual if any.
3. The 2 or 3 lines that contribute most to each effect, with their signed contribution.
4. Executive narrative of 3 to 5 sentences naming the dominant lever, correctly interpreting the sign according to whether {{METRICA}} is revenue or cost, and stating the actionable business implication.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Validate inputs: confirm whether {{METRICA}} is revenue or cost (defines the sign interpretation), periods, level, currency, and that {{DATOS}} includes quantity and price or unit cost per line in both periods. Isolate new lines (current only) and discontinued lines (base only). If anything is missing, ask before calculating; do not invent figures; mark each assumption as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Calculate effects on a consistent base (convention anchored to base, controlled cross residual). Work first on lines present in both periods:
  - Volume Effect = (total current quantity / total base quantity - 1) x base {{METRICA}} of comparable lines. Measures volume growth keeping the base mix and prices.
  - Mix Effect = sum per line of (current share - base share) x total current quantity x (line base unit price or cost - total base average unit price or cost). Measures the composition shift valued at base prices.
  - Price Effect = sum per line of (current - base unit price or cost) x current quantity. Also captures the price x volume cross term by using current quantity; declare this convention to avoid duplicating it in another effect.
Phase 3 - Handle additions and removals: New line entries = sum of their current {{METRICA}}; discontinued line exits = minus their base {{METRICA}}. Report in their own column, never dilute into the three effects.
Phase 4 - Verify closure: Volume + Mix + Price + Additions/Removals must equal (current {{METRICA}} - base {{METRICA}}). If there is a residual, report it and explain its origin (rounding, cross convention, missing data) instead of forcing the reconciliation.
Phase 5 - Build bridge, weights, and top lines per effect; draft the executive narrative watching the sign (for cost, higher is unfavorable; for revenue, favorable).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- The effects (volume, mix, price, additions/removals) sum exactly to total variation, or the residual is reported and explained.
- Each effect uses the declared consistent base; the price x volume cross term is explicitly assigned to one effect only, without double counting.
- New and discontinued lines go in their own column, never ignored or forcibly allocated.
- The sign is interpreted according to {{METRICA}}: for cost an increase is unfavorable, for revenue favorable.
- Every figure comes from {{DATOS}}; assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented data; if multi-currency, the FX effect is isolated or declared out of scope.
- The executive narrative names a dominant lever and an actionable implication.
Expected deliverable: bridge table in {{MONEDA_REPORTE}} with verified closure + percentage weights + top lines per effect + executive narrative of 3 to 5 sentences.
spec-finanzas_costeo_abc:
[inputs]
- COSTOS_INDIRECTOS: {{COSTOS_INDIRECTOS}} > Amount and composition of the indirect costs to assign (plant overhead, support, quality, logistics), their reference period, and whether the figure is actual, budgeted, or normalized
- ACTIVIDADES_Y_DRIVERS: {{ACTIVIDADES_Y_DRIVERS}} > Activities that consume resources and cost driver candidates per activity (e.g., number of setups, purchase orders, inspection hours, warehouse movements)
- DATOS_POR_PRODUCTO: {{DATOS_POR_PRODUCTO}} > By product: period volume, consumption of each driver, selling price, and direct cost (material + direct labor)
- BASE_TRADICIONAL: {{BASE_TRADICIONAL}} > Current traditional allocation base (single rate on machine-hours, units, or direct labor) for comparison
- DECISION_OBJETIVO: {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}} > Decision the analysis must support (pricing, mix, minimum lot size, discontinuation, SKU rationalization)
- LINEA_O_PLANTA: {{LINEA_O_PLANTA}} > Analysis scope (line, plant, product family, or service unit)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Traditional costing spreads overhead with a single rate (machine-hours, units, or direct labor) and distorts margins: high-volume products subsidize low-volume, high-complexity ones, because single rates reward volume and ignore complexity (setups, small batches, inspections, handling). Migrating to activity-based costing (ABC) reveals true profitability by product and unlocks decisions on pricing, mix, batch size, and discontinuation based on causal figures, not averages. Applies to {{LINEA_O_PLANTA}} with focus on {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior cost controller / cost accountant with experience designing and implementing ABC models in manufacturing and service operations.
Deliverables:
1. Activity map by level (unit, batch, product, plant support) with the overhead pool assigned to each, from {{COSTOS_INDIRECTOS}} and {{ACTIVIDADES_Y_DRIVERS}}; the sum of pools must reconcile with total overhead.
2. Selection of one cost driver per activity with causal justification (resource-activity-product, not volume correlation) and rate per driver = pool / total driver volume; when the driver depends on capacity, distinguish practical vs. used capacity and isolate idle capacity.
3. Overhead assignment to each product using {{DATOS_POR_PRODUCTO}} and fully loaded unit cost (direct + ABC indirect).
4. Comparison of ABC margin vs. traditional costing margin ({{BASE_TRADICIONAL}}) by product, quantifying cross-subsidies: at least one over-costed and one under-costed product under the traditional method, separating material from immaterial distortions.
5. Actionable recommendations tied to {{DECISION_OBJETIVO}} (price adjustment, mix recomposition, minimum economic lot size, discontinuation, or renegotiation), each with estimated impact, explicit assumption, and warning about committed overhead that does not disappear when discontinuing.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 0 - Input validation: confirm that COSTOS_INDIRECTOS, ACTIVIDADES_Y_DRIVERS, DATOS_POR_PRODUCTO, BASE_TRADICIONAL, and DECISION_OBJETIVO are available. If anything is missing, ask before calculating; do not invent figures. Mark all assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 1 - Model design: group activities by cost hierarchy and assign each overhead pool to its activity; validate that the sum of pools = total overhead (no unassigned overhead or double counting).
Phase 2 - Drivers and rates: choose one causal cost driver per activity and calculate the rate (pool / driver volume); isolate idle capacity when applicable.
Phase 3 - Assignment and costing: distribute overhead to each product according to its driver consumption and obtain the fully loaded unit cost and ABC margin (unit and total).
Phase 4 - Contrast: replicate traditional costing with the single base, compare cost and margin, quantify the cross-subsidy by product, and flag material distortions.
Phase 5 - Decision: translate findings into prioritized recommendations for DECISION_OBJETIVO, with estimated impact and associated assumption.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Every activity is classified by level and each pool reconciles with total COSTOS_INDIRECTOS (no unassigned overhead or double counting).
- Each cost driver has explicit causal justification, not just volume correlation.
- Rates show the formula (pool / volume) and unit costs separate direct vs. ABC indirect; idle capacity isolated when applicable.
- The ABC vs. traditional comparison identifies at least one over-costed and one under-costed product, with the magnitude of the cross-subsidy and its materiality.

- Zero invented figures; missing data was requested before calculating; external or publishable figures are flagged for validation.

spec-finanzas_costeo_estandar_desviacion:
[inputs]
- PRODUCTO: {{PRODUCTO}} > Product or line whose standard cost and variances are analyzed
- PERIODO: {{PERIODO}} > Period of the actual production to evaluate (month, week, or batch)
- ESTANDARES: {{ESTANDARES}} > Unit standards: standard material quantity and price per unit; standard labor hours and rate per unit; if applicable, indirect cost base and standard rate
- DATOS_REALES: {{DATOS_REALES}} > Period actuals: units produced, material consumed and actual cost, hours worked and actual direct labor cost; if applicable, actual indirect costs
- UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD: {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}} > Threshold for prioritizing relevant variances in amount or % (optional; if empty, suggest one and mark it [ASSUMPTION])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Standard costing is the management control system that sets a target cost per unit and confronts it with reality to explain why the result deviated. Clearly defining the standards for {{PRODUCTO}} and decomposing the variances for the period {{PERIODO}} unlocks concrete decisions: renegotiate with suppliers, adjust the labor learning curve, review scrap rates, or correct an obsolete standard. Without this decomposition, management only sees an aggregated cost overrun, without knowing whether it originated from price or consumption, or whether a favorable variance hides a problem (cheaper material of worse quality that drives up consumption).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior cost controller with experience in manufacturing and standard costing, trained in management accounting under the price/rate plus efficiency/usage framework.
Deliverable: variance analysis for direct material and direct labor (and indirect costs if {{DATOS_REALES}} includes them) with causes and actions. Steps:
1. Establish or confirm the unit standard from {{ESTANDARES}}: standard material quantity/unit, standard price/material unit, standard hours/unit, standard rate/hour.
2. Load {{DATOS_REALES}} for {{PERIODO}}: units produced, material consumed and actual cost, actual hours and actual direct labor cost. Calculate the allowed standard quantity and hours = actual units x unit standard (flexed to actual volume, NEVER the original budget).
3. Material variance: price = (actual price - standard price) x actual quantity; quantity/efficiency = (actual quantity - allowed standard quantity) x standard price. If there are multiple substitutable materials and the data permits, separate mix and yield within the quantity variance.
4. Labor variance: rate = (actual rate - standard rate) x actual hours; efficiency = (actual hours - allowed standard hours) x standard rate.
5. Label each variance F/U (F = lowers cost; U = raises it), verify that price + quantity = total material variance and rate + efficiency = total labor variance, and reconcile the sum of ALL variances against the total cost variance (actual cost - standard cost of actual production). If it does not reconcile, stop and report the discrepancy before concluding.
6. Consolidate the impact against {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}}; for each relevant variance draft a probable cause and actionable corrective action, flag any standard that looks obsolete, and expose any misleading offset between an F and a U.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: restate product, period, standards, and actuals received; list missing data and ask for it; declare the scope (material + labor only, or also indirect costs) and mark each numerical assumption as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Plan: present the calculation scheme (allowed standard, the four base variances, possible mix/yield, F/U rule, reconciliation verification, and reconciliation to total) before executing.
Phase 3 - Execution: run the calculations showing formula and numerical substitution, build the variance table, reconcile to the total, and close with the management narrative; do not invent absent figures or sign off on external data without verification.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- The four base variances (material price and quantity; labor rate and efficiency) are calculated with visible formula and numerical substitution; if mix/yield or indirect costs were separated, those too.
- Allowed standard quantity/hours are based on units actually produced (flexed), not the budget.
- Each variance is marked F or U according to its effect on cost, with the sign rule declared and consistent.
- Reconciliation verified: price + quantity = total material; rate + efficiency = total labor; and the sum of all variances reconciles with the total cost variance (actual - standard). Any discrepancy is reported, not hidden.
- Every datum not provided is listed as [ASSUMPTION] or as a question, never invented; no external figure is signed off without verification.
- Each relevant variance (above {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}}) has a probable cause and corrective action; obsolete standards and misleading offsets between F and U are flagged.
Expected deliverable: variance table (concept | formula | value | F/U) with totals that reconcile to the total cost, followed by a management narrative paragraph that prioritizes according to {{UMBRAL_MATERIALIDAD}}.
spec-finanzas_analisis_cvp:
[inputs]
- LINEA_PRODUCTO_SERVICIO: {{LINEA_PRODUCTO_SERVICIO}} > Product, service, or business line to analyze and reference period (month, quarter, year)
- PRECIO_UNITARIO: {{PRECIO_UNITARIO}} > Unit selling price or average ticket per unit/transaction

- UTILIDAD_OBJETIVO: {{UTILIDAD_OBJETIVO}} > Target operating profit for the period (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
It is necessary to understand how the operating profit of {{LINEA_PRODUCTO_SERVICIO}} reacts to movements in volume, price, and cost structure, so as to decide with evidence where to move the levers before committing resources or setting targets. A solid CVP analysis unlocks decisions on pricing, capacity sizing, realistic sales targets, and reading the operating risk associated with the fixed-variable mix. The goal is a reusable model that separates what is an assumption from what is verified data, so that the conclusions withstand management scrutiny.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior financial analyst in management accounting and cost-volume-profit modeling, with experience in pricing, capacity, and profit planning decisions.
Deliver a complete CVP analysis of {{LINEA_PRODUCTO_SERVICIO}} with these steps:
1. Classify each cost item as fixed or variable; if mixed, separate it with the high-low method and declare the assumption. Consolidate the resulting unit variable cost.
2. Calculate the unit contribution margin (PRECIO_UNITARIO minus COSTO_VARIABLE_UNITARIO) and the percentage margin (margin ratio over price).
3. Determine the break-even in units (COSTOS_FIJOS_PERIODO / unit contribution margin) and in revenue (COSTOS_FIJOS_PERIODO / contribution margin ratio). If there is a UTILIDAD_OBJETIVO, calculate units and revenue to reach it ((COSTOS_FIJOS_PERIODO + UTILIDAD_OBJETIVO) / margin).
4. Calculate the safety margin (VOLUMEN_ACTUAL relative to break-even, in units and as %) and the degree of operating leverage (total contribution margin / operating profit); interpret how sensitive profit is to volume.
5. Build three scenarios (pessimistic, base, optimistic) varying volume, price, and costs with explicit assumptions per lever, and a double-entry sensitivity table of profit at variations of -10%, -5%, +5%, and +10% in price and in volume.
6. Identify the 2-3 highest-impact levers (by profit elasticity), name the cross effect between them, and deliver an actionable recommendation with its validity condition.
Rules: mark every datum not provided as [ASSUMPTION] with assumed value and justification, and flag assumptions whose change reverses the conclusion. Do not invent figures as actuals; do not include specific selling prices or promises of free services in conclusions; reason in variables and percentages. Declare the model's limits: linearity of costs and revenues, constant product mix, fixed capacity within the relevant range, and validity only within that range.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm scope, period, and unit of measurement; list available and essential missing data (unit price, unit variable cost, fixed costs, volume). If anything is missing, ask before calculating.
Phase 2 - Cost structure: classify fixed/variable, separate mixed items with high-low (declaring the two activity levels used), and consolidate the unit variable cost.
Phase 3 - Core calculations: contribution margin, break-even, units for target profit, safety margin, and operating leverage, showing formula and calculation for each.
Phase 4 - Scenarios and sensitivity: build the three scenarios with assumptions per lever and the double-entry sensitivity table; highlight the threshold where profit crosses zero.
Phase 5 - Synthesis: prioritize levers by impact, name trade-offs (e.g., lowering price raises volume but compresses margin), and draft the recommendation with its validity condition.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Costs classified fixed/variable; mixed items decomposed with method and declared activity levels; unit variable cost consolidated.
- [ ] Unit and percentage contribution margin with visible formula and calculation.
- [ ] Break-even in units and revenue; units and revenue for UTILIDAD_OBJETIVO if applicable.
- [ ] Safety margin and degree of operating leverage calculated from VOLUMEN_ACTUAL, with risk interpretation.
- [ ] Three scenarios with explicit assumptions per lever and sensitivity table -10/-5/+5/+10% in price and volume, with zero-profit threshold.
- [ ] 2-3 levers prioritized by impact, trade-offs named, and recommendation with validity condition.
- [ ] Every missing datum marked [ASSUMPTION] with value and justification; assumptions that reverse the conclusion flagged; zero invented figures.
- [ ] Model limits declared (linearity, constant mix, relevant range).
- [ ] No specific selling prices or promises of free services in conclusions; reasoning in variables and percentages.
Expected deliverable: CVP document with formula, calculation, and executive narrative per block, scenario table, double-entry sensitivity table, and close with the prioritized cost StrategyIA.
spec-finanzas_analisis_costo_servir:
[inputs]

- UNIDAD_ANALISIS: {{UNIDAD_ANALISIS}} > Calculation level: by total segment, by average customer of the segment, or by order. Determines how drivers are normalized

--- S | SITUATION ---
Gross margin by segment hides the truth: two segments with the same gross margin can have opposite profitability once the cost of serving them is accounted for. Small and frequent orders, intensive support, volume discounts, and slow collections erode margin without appearing in COGS. Calculating the cost to serve unlocks defensible portfolio decisions: with whom to renegotiate conditions, whom to migrate to a different channel, whom to protect. The output feeds commercial reviews, budgeting, and pricing discussions with evidence, not intuition.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Director of Operational Finance with experience in activity-based costing (ABC) and customer profitability analysis, accustomed to defending the model in front of the commercial team.
Deliver a cost-to-serve model by segment:
1. Confirm the segments in {{SEGMENTOS}}, the {{UNIDAD_ANALISIS}}, the period, the currency, and the units.
2. Calculate gross margin by segment from {{DATOS_INGRESOS_COSTO}}.
3. Assign each block of {{BLOQUES_COSTO_SERVIR}}: logistics/distribution, service/support, commercial, and portfolio capital cost (DSO x rate, using {{DIAS_COBRO_TASA}}).
4. Link each block to the driver from {{COST_DRIVERS}} that best explains its consumption; calculate the rate per driver unit (total block cost / total driver volume) and assign by driver, NEVER by flat allocation on sales.
5. Calculate the contribution margin after cost to serve and its % of revenue by segment.
6. Position the segments on a gross margin vs. cost-to-serve matrix (high/low) and classify quadrants: profitable (high margin, low cost), low maintenance (low margin, low cost), costly to serve (high margin, high cost), margin drains (low margin, high cost).
7. Derive 3 to 5 prioritized actions (renegotiate conditions, rationalize service, reprice minimum order, migrate channel, adjust credit terms) with the segment they apply to and their estimated impact on margin.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: validate segments, unit, period, currency, and units; list available vs. missing cost blocks and drivers. If an essential datum is missing (cost pools, driver volumes, DSO/rate), ask before calculating.
Phase 2 - Gross margin: tabulate net revenue and COGS by segment.
Phase 3 - ABC assignment: for each block define the driver, rate per driver unit, and cost assigned by segment; the capital cost comes from DSO x financing rate on the segment's receivables (prorate the annual rate to the period). After assigning, verify that the sum of assigned costs reconciles with the total for each pool.
Phase 4 - Net contribution: subtract the blocks from gross margin; calculate % of revenue and real profitability ranking.
Phase 5 - Matrix, sensitivity, and actions: classify quadrants, identify the 3 drivers that most explain the differences, flag the segment where a driver change would move the result the most, and prioritize actions by impact on margin.
Rules: do not invent figures; mark every intermediate estimate and each driver rate as [ASSUMPTION]; maintain consistent currency and units; distinguish gross from net revenue and be explicit about whether discounts are already in the revenue or assigned as a commercial block (avoid double counting); do not suggest selling prices or fees.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each cost block is assigned by an explicit cost driver with its declared rate per unit, not by flat allocation on sales.
- [ ] The portfolio capital cost is included and traceable (DSO x rate, rate prorated to the period).
- [ ] The sum of assigned costs per block reconciles with the pool total (sanity check).
- [ ] No double counting of discounts (declared whether they go in net revenue or in the commercial block).

- [ ] All estimates and rates marked as [ASSUMPTION]; missing data asked before calculating.

spec-finanzas_optimizacion_costos_estruc:
[inputs]
- ALCANCE_GASTO: {{ALCANCE_GASTO}} > Perimeter of the cost base to optimize: unit, area, categories, or accounts included, with amounts if available
- PERIODO_BASELINE: {{PERIODO_BASELINE}} > Reference period against which savings are measured (e.g., last 12 months, fiscal year)
- OBJETIVO_AHORRO: {{OBJETIVO_AHORRO}} > Target savings sought as a percentage or amount, and the time horizon
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable limits: untouchable areas or contracts, service levels to preserve, workforce sensitivities (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Linear cuts destroy value: they slash muscle along with fat and the cost returns within one or two quarters. A structural optimization program is needed that sustainably reduces the cost base, protecting operational capacity and service level. A well-designed program unlocks reinvestable margin, improves resilience against revenue pressure, and gives leadership a defensible roadmap with quantified savings and explicit risk, instead of a reactive across-the-board cut.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior Director of Finance and Operations, specialist in cost transformation, with mastery of zero-based budgeting, lever analysis (value levers), and StrategyIA applied to prioritization.

Deliverable: a prioritized, wave-based cost optimization program. Steps:
1. Decompose ALCANCE_GASTO by category, nature (fixed/variable, direct/indirect, discretionary/committed), and process; identify concentrations (80/20 rule) and pools of avoidable spending against PERIODO_BASELINE.
2. Build the inventory of candidate structural levers: contract renegotiation, supplier consolidation, process redesign and automation, portfolio/SKU rationalization, energy efficiency, workforce reallocation, elimination of duplications, demand optimization, and specification optimization (should-cost).
3. Quantify each lever: estimated annual savings, recurring vs. one-time, implementation cost (one-off), effort, time to first impact, and risk level (operational, contractual, service, reputational).
4. Prioritize with an impact-effort matrix; separate quick wins (high impact, low effort) from structural initiatives (high impact, high effort) and discard traps (low impact, high effort).
5. Organize the program into waves (0-3, 3-9, 9-18 months) with cumulative savings target against OBJETIVO_AHORRO, dependencies, suggested owner, and monitoring signal per lever.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Mapping: structure the cost base and locate where spending lives.
Phase 2 Diagnosis: cross each spending pool against applicable levers and rule out anything that violates RESTRICCIONES.
Phase 3 Quantification: estimate net savings (gross minus implementation cost) and risk per lever; every figure not provided by the user is marked [ASSUMPTION] with its calculation logic and range.
Phase 4 Prioritization: apply the impact-effort matrix and build the wave sequence until the gap against OBJETIVO_AHORRO is closed; if it does not close, declare the shortfall and propose additional levers or a target adjustment.
Phase 5 Packaging: consolidate the program, dependencies, residual risks, and monitoring plan (KPI and cadence).
Edge cases: if ALCANCE_GASTO comes without amounts, work with percentages and structure, and ask for the data to quantify; if OBJETIVO_AHORRO is unachievable without touching RESTRICCIONES, state it explicitly and show the trade-off.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate your understanding and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Cost base decomposed by category, nature, and process, with concentrations flagged.
- [ ] Each lever quantified in annual savings, recurring vs. one-time, implementation cost, effort, time to impact, and risk.
- [ ] Net savings (not just gross) used for prioritization; every figure not provided marked [ASSUMPTION] with logic and range; zero invented amounts.
- [ ] Impact-effort matrix with quick wins, structural initiatives, and traps separated.
- [ ] Wave program with cumulative savings against OBJETIVO_AHORRO, dependencies, and owner per lever.
- [ ] RESTRICCIONES respected; gap against target resolved or declared; residual risks explicit.
Expected deliverable: prioritized lever table + impact-effort matrix + wave plan with cumulative savings targets and suggested owner, ready for committee decision.
spec-finanzas_cost_to_serve_logistico:
[inputs]
- ALCANCE: {{ALCANCE}} > Channel/segment and period to cost (e.g., "B2C e-commerce, Q1 2026"). Defines the costing unit (one order) and the time window of the costs.
- VOLUMEN_PEDIDOS: {{VOLUMEN_PEDIDOS}} > Number of orders for the period and average ticket; if contribution margin per order is available, include it.
- COSTOS_LOGISTICOS: {{COSTOS_LOGISTICOS}} > Period cost pools: storage, picking/labor, last-mile, reverse logistics. Indicate whether these are direct costs or include prorated fixed costs.

--- S | SITUATION ---
An average logistics cost per order hides where the margin truly goes: two orders with the same ticket can cost very differently depending on how much space they occupy in the warehouse, how many lines their picking has, which zone they are shipped to, and whether they end up returned. Costing each order by activity unlocks decisions on shipping pricing, returns policy, network design, and profitable customer segmentation. This analysis converts aggregated operational figures into an actionable unit cost per component, with the traceability needed to defend each figure in front of finance and operations.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior cost-to-serve and logistics operations analyst, expert in activity-based costing (ABC) applied to e-commerce fulfillment and distribution.

Phase 2 - ABC assignment: map each pool to its driver, justify the choice, calculate activity rates and unit costs per component.
