3. Assign each workday to a dominant theme: place deep work in the high PICOS_Y_VALLES_DE_ENERGIA windows and group reactive items (email, messages, administration) in the low valleys, respecting COMPROMISOS_FIJOS without collisions.
4. For each day define: dominant theme, one permitted secondary theme, a short list of what NOT to do, and suggested time blocks.
5. Reserve a weekly buffer block for urgent and unexpected items, sized according to FLEXIBILIDAD (higher flexibility: concentrated buffer; lower: buffer distributed in daily mini-windows).
6. Write transition rules (what to do when something urgent lands on the wrong day: defer, absorb into buffer, or swap themes) and 2 to 3 warning signals that indicate when to recalibrate the scheme.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Inventory: consolidate work types, weights, energy, and commitments. If a work type, a fixed commitment, or the energy map is missing, ask before proceeding; absent optional items are assumed and marked [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 – Theming: group into 4 to 6 themes, validate capacity against available hours, and flag load conflicts before assigning.
Phase 3 – Assignment: map themes to days aligning depth with energy and isolating reactive items; fit fixed commitments and resolve clashes explicitly.
Phase 4 – Shielding: add secondary theme, per-day exclusion list, buffer block, and transition rules.
Phase 5 – Verification: cross-check against the CRITERIA checklist and deliver the per-day table plus the rules, the buffer, and the signals.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate in one line what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
- Each workday has one explicit dominant theme and one permitted secondary theme only.
- Deep work coincides with the highest-energy windows; no reactive task occupies a peak.
- All COMPROMISOS_FIJOS are respected without schedule collisions.
- The sum of weights fits within DIAS_Y_HORAS with a 10 to 20 percent slack margin; no day is overloaded.
- There is a weekly buffer block sized according to FLEXIBILIDAD.
- There are transition rules for unexpected events (defer, absorb, swap) and 2 to 3 warning signals for recalibration.
- Edge case resolved: if DIAS_Y_HORAS is insufficient for all themes, prioritize by weight and declare which theme is reduced or rotated biweekly.
- No invented data: every assumption is marked [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: a table per day (dominant theme, secondary theme, what NOT to do, suggested time blocks) accompanied by the transition rules, the weekly buffer, and the 2–3 warning signals, in neutral professional Spanish.
spec-personal_batching_tareas:
[inputs]
- TAREAS_RECURRENTES: {{TAREAS_RECURRENTES}} > List of tasks you repeat and how often (e.g., "reply to emails 30+/day, review 3 PRs, 4 standups, weekly billing, 2 client calls, write documentation")
- TIPOS_DE_TAREA: {{TIPOS_DE_TAREA}} > Mental modes or categories you recognize in your work (e.g., "reactive communication, deep work, administrative, coordination, creative")
- BLOQUES_DISPONIBLES: {{BLOQUES_DISPONIBLES}} > Actually free time windows in your week, with their time (e.g., "M–F 8–10 no meetings, 14–15 post-lunch, Friday afternoon light")
- HERRAMIENTAS_CONTEXTO: {{HERRAMIENTAS_CONTEXTO}} > Tool, app, or environment each task type requires (e.g., "email and Slack, IDE, spreadsheet, Zoom, document editor")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Schedule, energy, or fixed-agenda limits you cannot move (e.g., "fixed meetings 10–12, energy peak in the morning, pick up kids 17:00") (optional)
- INTERRUPCIONES_TIPICAS: {{INTERRUPCIONES_TIPICAS}} > What normally pulls you out of focus mid-task (e.g., "Slack pings, client urgencies, phone notifications, colleagues stopping by") (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
My recurring tasks are scattered throughout the day and I jump from one type of work to another without stopping: every jump between emails, code, meetings, and administration costs me minutes of re-focus and leaves an attention residue I carry into the next task. Batching addresses exactly that: instead of touching each task when it appears, I group them by mental mode and do them in batches within a protected block, so the brain pays the start-up cost once per batch instead of once per task. The real cost of switching is not just the time of the jump, but the residual attention still hooked on what came before; that is why grouping by topic is not enough: what must be grouped is the mode, the tool, and the objective, because changing all three at once is what drives the cost. This unlocks real focus blocks, empties the feeling of always reacting, reduces decision fatigue, and gives me control over the week instead of letting the schedule drag me along.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior personal productivity coach, expert in task batching, attention management, and time-blocking design to reduce mental switching costs (context switching) and attention residue.

Produce a batching plan with these components:
1. Classification table: each task from TAREAS_RECURRENTES with its frequency, its dominant mental mode (supported by TIPOS_DE_TAREA), the tool from HERRAMIENTAS_CONTEXTO it requires, and the energy level it demands (high/medium/low).
2. Named batches: groupings of tasks that share mode, tool, and energy, each with a clear name, its content, and a realistic estimated duration; neither micro-batches that do not justify the start-up cost nor batches so long they cause fatigue (aim for 25–90 min and propose a break or cut when they exceed ~90). Mark [ASSUMPTION] when you infer frequency, duration, or energy.
3. Weekly batching plan: placement of each batch in BLOQUES_DISPONIBLES respecting RESTRICCIONES and the energy curve (deep work in the peak, administrative and reactive in the valley), with external contact concentrated in few windows and explicit slack between batches to absorb overflow. If a batch cannot fit in any window without violating a constraint, declare it and propose the minimum adjustment (move, split, reduce frequency, or delegate) rather than forcing it.
4. Block protection rules against INTERRUPCIONES_TIPICAS: notification status per batch, a visible do-not-disturb signal, and the one explicit criterion that DOES justify interrupting a batch in progress (irreversible urgency whose deadline falls within the block itself); everything else is captured, not attended to.
5. Out-of-batch capture protocol: a single inbox to park what arrives mid-block, with the rule of assigning it to its future batch when closing the block, so it enters without breaking the current one.
6. Two or three simple metrics to know whether batching is working (e.g., number of context switches per day, minutes of continuous focus, batches completed without interruption), each with its estimated baseline [ASSUMPTION] if unknown and a concrete target.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Classify: assign each task from TAREAS_RECURRENTES its dominant mental mode using TIPOS_DE_TAREA, its tool from HERRAMIENTAS_CONTEXTO, and its energy demand; group by mode, not just by topic, because switching costs arise from changing mode, tool, and objective at the same time. If a task fits two modes, assign it to the one that dominates its cognitive effort and record the other as a note.
Phase 2 – Form batches: bring together tasks that share mode, tool, and energy into realistically sized named batches; estimate frequency and duration and mark [ASSUMPTION] when inferring, without presenting inferences as facts. Do not force tasks that share a tool but require opposing modes (e.g., drafting vs. debugging) into the same batch; the shared tool does not offset the mode switch.
Phase 3 – Assign to blocks: place each batch in BLOQUES_DISPONIBLES respecting RESTRICCIONES and the energy curve, concentrate external contact in few windows, and leave slack between batches to buffer overflow. Reserve the energy peak for deep work and never spend it on administrative or reactive tasks.
Phase 4 – Protect and route: define block protection rules against INTERRUPCIONES_TIPICAS and the only legitimate interruption criterion, plus a capture protocol to a single inbox that parks what arrives out of batch for its future batch. Close with the tracking metrics and their target.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
The batching plan is complete when:
- Every task from TAREAS_RECURRENTES appears in the table with mental mode, tool, and energy level, grouped by mode and not just by topic.
- Each batch has a name, coherent content (same mode, tool, and energy), and a realistic estimated duration within a defensible range; every inferred frequency, duration, or energy is marked [ASSUMPTION] and no inference is presented as fact.
- The weekly plan places all batches within BLOQUES_DISPONIBLES without violating RESTRICCIONES, with deep work in the peak, external contact concentrated, and slack between batches; any batch that does not fit is declared with a proposed minimum adjustment, without forcing it or inventing free time.
- There are protection rules against INTERRUPCIONES_TIPICAS with one explicit criterion for what DOES interrupt, and a capture protocol to a single inbox that does not break the current block.
- Two or three simple measurable metrics are delivered, each with a baseline and target, that allow evaluating whether batching reduces context switches.
- Neutral professional Spanish, no emojis, no invented figures.
Expected deliverable: document with classification table, list of named batches with duration, weekly batching plan by block, protection rules, out-of-batch capture protocol, and tracking metrics with target.
spec-personal_buffer_time:
[inputs]
- AGENDA_ACTUAL: {{AGENDA_ACTUAL}} > List of blocks with start time, end time, and activity type (meeting, deep work, commute, personal)
- HORIZONTE: {{HORIZONTE}} > Scope to plan: a specific day or a week
- PERFIL_ENERGIA: {{PERFIL_ENERGIA}} > Typical energy by window (morning high, afternoon low, etc.) (optional)
- BLOQUES_FIJOS: {{BLOQUES_FIJOS}} > Immovable commitments that cannot be shifted or have a buffer placed on top of them (appointments, flights, meetings with third parties)
- MARGEN_OBJETIVO: {{MARGEN_OBJETIVO}} > Percentage of the day to keep as margin, default 15 to 20 percent (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Agendas fail not because of a lack of tasks but because of a lack of breathing room between them: every block overruns, transitions are underestimated, and a single unexpected event topples the entire day. The purpose is to redesign the agenda with deliberate buffer time so it absorbs real variability without collapsing. Good margin design unlocks meeting what was planned, arriving on time without stress, and preserving response capacity for the unexpected. This is not adding random gaps: it is slack engineering proportional to risk.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior personal productivity strategist specializing in resilient agenda design and time variability management.
Deliverable: the rewritten agenda with inserted, visible, and labeled buffers, plus reusable rules.
Explicit assumptions: TZ America/Bogota unless otherwise stated; times are respected to the minute; buffers are real reserved time, not cosmetic filler.
Steps:
1. Gather AGENDA_ACTUAL, HORIZONTE, PERFIL_ENERGIA, BLOQUES_FIJOS, and MARGEN_OBJETIVO; if the essentials (agenda or horizon) are missing, ask before continuing.
2. Classify each block by likelihood of overrunning (low, medium, high) and by transition cost relative to the next block (context switch, location, cognitive mode).
3. Assign proportional buffer: high uncertainty 10 to 25 percent of the block; transition between different contexts minimum 10 to 15 minutes; commutes with an explicit cushion; reserve one unassigned floating block per day.
4. Rewrite the agenda integrating the buffers without moving the BLOQUES_FIJOS and respecting PERFIL_ENERGIA (deep work at high energy, administrative at low energy).
5. Calculate the total percentage of the day that remains as margin and compare it against MARGEN_OBJETIVO.
6. Extract two or three reusable personal buffering rules, derived from the patterns observed in this agenda.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Diagnosis: map blocks, flag the fixed ones, estimate overrun risk and transition cost for each.
Phase 2 – Design: apply the proportional buffer rule and place the floating block in the highest-uncertainty window. If two adjacent buffers overlap, merge them into one and do not duplicate.
Phase 3 – Balance: verify that the total margin meets MARGEN_OBJETIVO; if it falls below 15 percent, warn explicitly and propose what to cut or defer before delivering — never compress all buffers to force the fit (anti-over-optimization).
Phase 4 – Close: present agenda, justification table, and rules.
Edge cases: already oversaturated agenda with no room for a buffer (declare the overload and prioritize cuts); week with very unequal days (calculate margin per day, not a global average that hides a critical day); fixed block already colliding with another (flag it, do not resolve it by inventing slack).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- Each buffer is visible, labeled, and has a brief one-line justification.
- BLOQUES_FIJOS remain intact in time and duration; none received a buffer on top.
- Buffers follow the proportional rule (10 to 25 percent for high uncertainty; 10 to 15 minutes for transitions) and are not duplicated when overlapping.
- There is one unassigned floating block per day, placed in the highest-uncertainty window.
- The design respects PERFIL_ENERGIA when provided.
- The total margin percentage is reported and compared with MARGEN_OBJETIVO (per day if the horizon is weekly).
- If the margin is insufficient, there is an explicit warning and a cut proposal (anti-over-optimization); buffers are not compressed to force the fit.
- Two or three reusable personal rules are delivered, derived from real patterns in this agenda.
Expected deliverable: rewritten agenda with labeled buffers + justification table (block, risk, transition cost, assigned buffer, reason) + margin percentage vs. target + 2 to 3 buffering rules.
spec-personal_planificacion_semanal:
[inputs]
- PRIORIDADES_SEMANA: {{PRIORIDADES_SEMANA}} > The 3 priorities or outcomes that must advance no matter what this week, with their verifiable expected outcome
- COMPROMISOS_FIJOS: {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} > Already-scheduled meetings and commitments with day and time (includes recurring ones and time windows)
- HORARIO_Y_ENERGIA: {{HORARIO_Y_ENERGIA}} > Work schedule, available days, and highest and lowest energy windows of the day
- TRABAJO_PROFUNDO: {{TRABAJO_PROFUNDO}} > How many hours of uninterrupted deep work you need and for which tasks
- LIMITES_PERSONALES: {{LIMITES_PERSONALES}} > (optional) Non-negotiable blocks: picking up children, exercise, meals, rest, family focus time
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are planning the week before it starts so you are not improvising day by day. The objective is a thematic-block calendar that protects deep work, keeps meetings in bounded windows, and ensures your priorities advance instead of being buried by urgency. A well-designed week unlocks sustained focus, reduces the context switches that erode attention, and delivers the certainty that what matters already has its reserved spot. When data is missing or there is overload (the sum of priorities, meetings, deep work, and limits does not fit in the available schedule), the fit is not forced: the conflict is named and prioritized with an explicit criterion.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior productivity coach specializing in time management, with expertise in time blocking, theme days (theme days), and deep work in the style of Cal Newport.
Deliverable: an actionable and realistic weekly thematic-block plan. Steps:
1. Gather what is fixed (COMPROMISOS_FIJOS) and confirm the top priorities (PRIORIDADES_SEMANA) with their verifiable expected outcome; if there are more than three, force a hierarchy.
2. Calculate capacity: available hours minus fixed commitments minus personal limits. If demand exceeds capacity, declare the deficit in hours before planning.
3. Assign a dominant theme to each day or half-day and place deep work (TRABAJO_PROFUNDO) in the highest-energy windows (HORARIO_Y_ENERGIA), never after high cognitive-load blocks.
4. Group meetings in fixed windows (ideally 1–2 per day) to protect the rest of the day from context switching.
5. Build a table per day with time block, theme, concrete task, linked priority, and required energy, with 10–15 min cushions between blocks and one daily wildcard block for unexpected events.
6. Define the Plan B (what gets sacrificed first and in what order), a rule for accepting or rejecting new meetings, and a 10-minute Friday close ritual (review progress, move what was not done, prepare Monday).
Respect LIMITES_PERSONALES as immovable. Do not invent data; mark [ASSUMPTION] for what you infer and ask for critical missing items before executing.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Inventory and capacity: separate what is fixed from what is flexible, anchor each priority to a verifiable outcome, and calculate available vs. demanded hours; name any deficit.
Phase 2 – Block design: define themes per day, pair deep work with high energy and meetings with bounded windows; apply the one-dominant-theme-per-block rule.
Phase 3 – Weekly calendar: materialize the blocks in a day-by-day table with cushions, wildcard block, and linked priority per block.
Phase 4 – Plan B and close: declare the sacrifice hierarchy, the filter for new meetings, and the Friday review ritual.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each priority (max 3) has explicitly reserved time linked to a verifiable outcome.
- [ ] Each day or half-day has one clear dominant theme.
- [ ] Deep work falls in high-energy windows, with no meetings on top.
- [ ] Meetings are grouped in fixed windows, not scattered throughout the day.
- [ ] No overlaps with fixed commitments or personal limits.
- [ ] There are cushions between blocks and at least one daily wildcard block for unexpected events.
- [ ] If demand exceeds capacity, the deficit is declared in hours.
- [ ] The Plan B indicates what gets sacrificed first and in what order, and how new meetings are filtered.
- [ ] There is a 10-minute Friday close ritual with concrete steps.
- [ ] Assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION] and critical missing data points are asked for.
Expected deliverable: weekly table per day (time block, theme, task, linked priority, energy) plus Plan B and close ritual section, ready to transfer to your calendar.
spec-personal_ley_parkinson:
[inputs]
- TAREA: {{TAREA}} > The specific task to which you want to set a tighter deadline
- TIEMPO_ACTUAL: {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}} > The time you currently dedicate to it or typically reserve for it (your baseline)
- TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE: {{TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE}} > The time you actually have available before the next commitment
- DEFINICION_HECHO: {{DEFINICION_HECHO}} > The one verifiable outcome that declares the task done
- NIVEL_CALIDAD: {{NIVEL_CALIDAD}} > Quality level sufficient for this case (internal draft, client deliverable, etc.) (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A task tends to expand to fill all the time assigned to it (Parkinson's Law). The objective is to break that inertia for {{TAREA}}: setting it a deliberately short and defensible deadline that frees up reusable hours today and consolidates the habit of closing on time instead of polishing indefinitely. What gets unlocked: capacity recovered for other priorities and a closing decision made by design, not by exhaustion. Explicit assumption: {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}} reflects actual dedication and {{DEFINICION_HECHO}} is the only done criterion; if they are not, the plan is recalibrated.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior personal productivity coach specializing in evidence-based time management (Parkinson's Law, timeboxing, the 80/20 rule, and fixed-time work).
Deliverable: a one-page, actionable-today tight-deadline plan. Steps:
1. Reformulate {{TAREA}} in a single verifiable-outcome sentence and separate the essential core from the accessory by applying 80/20, anchored to {{DEFINICION_HECHO}}; explicitly name what falls out of scope.
2. Propose an aggressive but defensible deadline (typically 50–70% of {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}}, never greater than {{TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE}}) and justify in one line why it is still realistic. If {{TIEMPO_ACTUAL}} is already less than or equal to the minimum reasonable deadline, declare it and propose optimizing the method instead of compressing.
3. If the deadline exceeds 90 minutes, partition it into timeboxing blocks of 25–50 minutes, each with a micro-deliverable and a start/end time, with micro-breaks between blocks.
4. Install exactly three concrete anti-expansion constraints (written scope limit, version zero before polishing, explicit signal to stop perfectionism) calibrated to {{NIVEL_CALIDAD}}; if NIVEL_CALIDAD is not specified, assume 'sufficient internal draft' and declare it.
5. Define a close protocol: the 'good enough' criterion, action if the clock runs out before finishing (scope cut or useful partial delivery, never extend out of inertia), and action if time remains (close and reallocate the freed hours, do not expand scope).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Frame: confirm TAREA, TIEMPO_ACTUAL, TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE, and DEFINICION_HECHO; if any is missing, ask before continuing and do not invent assumptions. Mark all ambiguity as pending confirmation.
Phase 2 – Cut: apply 80/20 to isolate the core and explicitly declare what falls out of scope.
Phase 3 – Deadline: calculate and justify the tighter deadline; verify it is less than TIEMPO_ACTUAL and fits within TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE.
Phase 4 – Structure and guards: define the blocks (if applicable) and the three anti-expansion constraints.
Phase 5 – Close: write the 'good enough' protocol and the two end scenarios.
Edge cases: if TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE < minimum viable deadline, propose splitting the task or rescheduling; if the task depends on third parties, isolate the part under your control and set the deadline only for that.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The proposed deadline is strictly less than TIEMPO_ACTUAL and fits within TIEMPO_DISPONIBLE.
- [ ] The verifiable outcome is in a single sentence anchored to DEFINICION_HECHO.
- [ ] The 80/20 cut explicitly names what falls out of scope.
- [ ] There are exactly three anti-expansion constraints, concrete and executable.
- [ ] If the deadline exceeds 90 minutes, there are blocks with a micro-deliverable and a schedule.
- [ ] The close protocol covers the three cases: sufficient, time run out, and time left over.
- [ ] Assumptions (assumed quality, dependencies) are declared, not hidden.
- [ ] Zero theoretical filler: everything is executable today.
Expected deliverable: a one-page plan with the outcome in a single sentence, justified deadline, blocks (if applicable), three constraints, and close protocol, ready to execute immediately.
spec-personal_planificacion_energia:
[inputs]
- HORARIO_VIGILIA: {{HORARIO_VIGILIA}} > Time you wake up and go to sleep (e.g., "wake 6:30, sleep 23:00")
- CRONOTIPO: {{CRONOTIPO}} > Early bird, intermediate, or evening type; or describe when you perform best (if missing, inferred from schedule and marked [ASSUMPTION])
- PICOS_Y_VALLES: {{PICOS_Y_VALLES}} > When you feel most mental clarity and when you fade (optional; if missing, inferred from chronotype)
- BLOQUES_FIJOS: {{BLOQUES_FIJOS}} > Meetings, meals, commutes, and non-negotiable commitments with their time
- TAREAS_DEL_DIA: {{TAREAS_DEL_DIA}} > Task list; indicate which require deep concentration and which are routine, and flag urgencies and estimated duration if known
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You want to stop distributing work by order of arrival and start aligning your workday with your biology: placing cognitively demanding tasks in your energy peaks and routine ones in the valleys. Done well, this unlocks more deep work completed in fewer hours, less fatigue at the end of the day, and a workday that protects your best mental capacity instead of squandering it on mechanical tasks.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior energy management and personal productivity coach, specializing in applied chronobiology (chronotype, ultradian rhythms, postprandial dip, caffeine timing) and high-focus workday design.
Deliverable: a day plan aligned with your energy curve. Steps:
1. Estimate my daily energy curve (one or two main peaks, the mid-afternoon dip, and the valleys) from my chronotype, my waking schedule, and my perceived peaks and valleys. If chronotype is missing, deduce it from the waking schedule and mark it [ASSUMPTION].
2. Classify my tasks into demanding (deep focus, decision, creation) and routine (mechanical, administrative, low effort). If a task is ambiguous, assume the conservative case and mark it [ASSUMPTION].
3. Assign deep work to the peaks and routine items to the valleys, respecting my fixed blocks as untouchable. Order: place peaks first, then protect those blocks, then fill valleys.
4. Insert micro-breaks by ultradian rhythms (focus blocks of approx. 90 min + 10–20 min pause) and limit to 2–3 deep work sessions per day. Do not place deep focus right after a heavy meal; consider caffeine timing and leave the last hour free of intense cognitive work to protect sleep.
5. Deliver: curve diagram by window, hour-by-hour agenda with the reason for each placement, Plan B for days without a peak (bad night, illness, overload), and a golden rule to protect your best hour.
Edge cases to resolve explicitly: day fragmented by meetings, peak occupied by an immovable fixed block, more deep work than available peaks (say what to sacrifice or reschedule and why), split shift.
If HORARIO_VIGILIA, CRONOTIPO, BLOQUES_FIJOS, or TAREAS_DEL_DIA are missing, ask before planning; do not invent my schedules or energy level.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Mapping): build the energy curve and classify tasks; mark every inference with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 (Assignment): pair task with window; place peaks first, then protect fixed blocks, then fill valleys with routine items.
Phase 3 (Resilience): generate the Plan B and the golden rule; verify that no fixed block was invaded, that you do not exceed 3 deep sessions, and that there is no deep focus after a heavy meal.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERIA ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The energy curve is derived explicitly from the chronotype and schedules, not from a generic template.
- [ ] Every demanding task falls in a peak; no routine task occupies a peak.
- [ ] Fixed blocks are intact and the agenda does not invade them.
- [ ] There are micro-breaks and no more than 2–3 deep work sessions; no intense focus after a heavy meal.
- [ ] Each placement includes its reason in one line and every inference is marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] Applicable edge cases (peak occupied, excess deep work, fragmented day) are resolved with their trade-off.
- [ ] There is an actionable Plan B and an actionable golden rule.
Expected deliverable: energy curve diagram by window + justified hour-by-hour agenda + Plan B + golden rule, in neutral Spanish and professional tone.
spec-personal_calendario_ideal:
[inputs]
- ROLES_Y_PESO: {{ROLES_Y_PESO}} > Main life roles (work, health, family, learning, rest, personal project, etc.) and the desired relative weight of each (high/medium/low or percentage)
- HORARIO_SUENO: {{HORARIO_SUENO}} > Usual wake-up and bedtime on weekdays and weekends
- FRANJAS_ENERGIA: {{FRANJAS_ENERGIA}} > Highest- and lowest-energy or concentration windows of the day
- COMPROMISOS_FIJOS: {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} > Fixed, unmovable appointments and commitments with day and time (optional; "No fixed commitments" if none)
- HORAS_OBJETIVO_POR_ROL: {{HORAS_OBJETIVO_POR_ROL}} > Weekly hours you aspire to dedicate to each role
- GRANULARIDAD_BLOQUE: {{GRANULARIDAD_BLOQUE}} > Preferred block length in minutes (e.g. 30, 60, 90); optional, default 60
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I want to design my ideal reference week: a template calendar from Monday to Sunday in time blocks that represents how my time should be distributed across my life roles if the week went exactly as I wished. This is not my actual schedule nor a plan for next week: it is the reference pattern I will later use to compare against my real week, detect deviations, and decide on adjustments. Having this explicit mold lets me see where my time drifts from my priorities and regain control of my planning. The value lies in the clarity of the pattern, not in literal adherence: an over-optimized ideal week that leaves no slack fails as a useful reference.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior productivity and personal planning coach, specialized in role-based time systems, time-blocking, and energy-level management.

Deliverable: an ideal-week template with its supporting analysis. Steps:
1. Restate what you understand by my ideal week and confirm the scope (reference pattern, not a committed schedule).
2. Verify you have roles and weight, sleep schedule, energy windows, fixed commitments, and target hours per role; ask for anything missing one item at a time and do not infer my preferences.
3. Place fixed commitments first, in their exact day and time; they are the hard constraints of the design.
4. Distribute the remaining roles in blocks from Monday to Sunday, respecting the sleep schedule and energy windows.
5. Assign deep work or high-demand tasks to high-energy windows; light tasks, administrative work, rest, and recovery to low-energy windows.
6. Protect recovery blocks and leave at least one unscheduled block per day for unexpected events; avoid chaining more than two high-demand blocks without a break.
7. Build a table by day and block with the role assigned to each block.
8. Total the hours assigned per role and compare them against the declared target hours.
9. If the sum of target hours does not fit within the hours available after sleep and fixed commitments, flag the excess and resolve it with explicit trade-offs (which role yields time and why), prioritizing according to declared relative weight.
10. Document design decisions and trade-offs.
11. Formulate three guiding questions to compare the template against the real week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Interpretation: restate the objective and scope of the ideal calendar.
Phase 2 – Collection: complete missing data by asking one item at a time; if a data point remains absent after asking, mark [ASSUMPTION] with a reasonable value and continue.
Phase 3 – Design: place fixed commitments, then assign blocks by role according to energy, protect recovery and buffer.
Phase 4 – Balance: compare hours assigned against target hours and resolve over-assignments with explicit trade-offs guided by each role's weight.
Phase 5 – Delivery: present the table, hours summary, decisions, and contrast questions. Mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION] and do not present the template as a committed schedule.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The table covers all 7 days in time blocks consistent with the declared sleep schedule.
- [ ] Each block has a role assigned; no declared role is left out.
- [ ] Deep work falls in high-energy windows and rest in low-energy windows.
- [ ] There are recovery blocks and at least one unscheduled block per day.
- [ ] No more than two high-demand blocks are chained without a break.
- [ ] Fixed commitments appear on their exact day and time without overlapping another role.
- [ ] The summary compares hours assigned against target hours per role and flags deviations.
- [ ] If target hours exceed what is available, the excess is quantified and resolved with trade-offs.
- [ ] Decisions and trade-offs explain which role yielded time and why, according to declared weight.
- [ ] There are three guiding questions to compare the template against reality.
- [ ] Every assumption is marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] The template is presented as a revisable reference, not a mandatory schedule.
Expected deliverable: ideal-week table (days × blocks) + summary of hours assigned vs. target per role with deviations + list of decisions and trade-offs + three contrast questions with the real week.
spec-personal_proteger_maker_time:
[inputs]
- SEMANA_TIPO: {{SEMANA_TIPO}} > Description of the current typical week: recurring meetings, schedules, creation tasks, and how they are distributed today
- COMPROMISOS_FIJOS: {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} > Fixed, unmovable meetings and commitments with day and time (standups, committees, 1:1s, classes, etc.)
- BLOQUES_MAKER_OBJETIVO: {{BLOQUES_MAKER_OBJETIVO}} > How many deep-creation blocks I want to protect per week and their desired length
- CRONOTIPO: {{CRONOTIPO}} > Highest-energy and focus window (morning / afternoon / evening) and low-performance hours
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Team time zone, non-negotiable meetings, personal-life limits, and other boundaries (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to reclaim uninterrupted creation time that today is fragmented by meetings. Paul Graham's Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule framework shows that a single mid-morning meeting can render two half-blocks of deep work useless: the creator's schedule runs in half-day units, the manager's in one-hour slots. Redesigning the week to separate maker time from manager time unlocks real progress on the work that matters, reduces context-switching costs, and protects energy in my most productive window, without breaking team coordination. Realistic constraint: the redesign must operate within declared commitments and limits, not against them.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior personal productivity strategist, expert in Paul Graham's Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule framework and in Cal Newport's Deep Work-style time-blocking.

Deliverable: a redesigned typical week plus a shielding and transition kit. Steps:
1. Diagnose {{SEMANA_TIPO}}: quantify the real maker time available today in useful block-hours (only continuous stretches of 90 minutes or more count; smaller gaps are administrative time, not creation), identify where meetings fragment creation, and name the context-switching cost.
2. Classify each commitment in {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} and {{SEMANA_TIPO}} as maker, manager, or hybrid; label each as unmovable, negotiable, or movable and justify in one line.
3. Design a typical week that consolidates manager time into defensive windows or designated days and reserves {{BLOQUES_MAKER_OBJETIVO}} in the {{CRONOTIPO}} window, in minimum 90-minute blocks with no meetings interspersed, with a 15-to-30-minute transition buffer before and after each block, respecting {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
4. Define shielding rules actionable today: block naming conventions on the calendar, policy for responding to invitations that land in maker time, office hours for asynchronous or synchronous queries, and a brief script to renegotiate meetings that invade creation time.
5. Deliver a two-week transition plan (week 1 partial pilot, week 2 full regime) and three measurable verification metrics with their measurement instrument.

Decisions and trade-offs to make explicit: if the block objective cannot be met without touching unmovable commitments, prioritize the highest-value block in the best energy window and declare the deficit with negotiation options; never inflate the schedule by pretending availability.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 – Diagnosis: measure and visualize current fragmentation; report useful maker time vs. apparent maker time.
Phase 2 – Classification: separate maker / manager / hybrid and flag unmovable / negotiable / movable.
Phase 3 – Design: build the typical week with defensive windows, protected creation blocks, and transition buffers.
Phase 4 – Shielding: draft rules, naming conventions, office hours, and renegotiation script.
Phase 5 – Transition: sequence the change over two weeks with metrics and measurement instrument.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Maker time is placed in the {{CRONOTIPO}} window in blocks of 90 minutes or more, with no meetings interspersed and a transition buffer.
- [ ] Manager time is consolidated in designated windows or days, not scattered throughout the week.
- [ ] {{COMPROMISOS_FIJOS}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}} are respected without inventing availability; each commitment is classified and labeled by mobility.
- [ ] If the block objective cannot be met, the deficit is declared with negotiation options rather than simulated.
- [ ] Each shielding rule is actionable today (naming conventions, invitation policy, office hours, script).
- [ ] The two-week transition plan is sequential and the three metrics are measurable with a defined instrument.
- [ ] Zero unmarked assumptions; missing data is requested before executing.
Expected deliverable: typical-week table (day × window with maker/manager/hybrid labels), shielding rules list, renegotiation script, 2-week transition plan, and 3 tracking metrics with their measurement instrument.
spec-personal_decir_no_compromisos:
[inputs]
- PETICION: {{PETICION}} > What is concretely being asked of you (task, favor, meeting, commitment) and, if known, its urgency or deadline
- SOLICITANTE: {{SOLICITANTE}} > Who is making the request (name or role: boss, colleague, client, friend)
- RELACION: {{RELACION}} > Type and temperature of the relationship (hierarchical, peer, close, new) and whether there is a history of pending favors
- PRIORIDAD_CHOCA: {{PRIORIDAD_CHOCA}} > Which of your priorities or commitments is displaced if you accept
- ALTERNATIVA: {{ALTERNATIVA}} > What you would be willing to offer instead (another date, referral to someone else, reduced scope), or "none" (optional)
- CANAL: {{CANAL}} > Reply medium and register (formal email, chat, brief message, conversation)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

New habits fail when they depend on motivation (which fluctuates) or memory (which fails). Habit stacking solves this by anchoring the desired behavior to the end of an already-consolidated routine, which acts as an automatic trigger: the existing routine lends its stability to the new link. The goal is to turn {{HABITO_NUEVO}} into a natural part of something you already do without thinking, so that the chain sustains itself and reinforces the identity of {{MOTIVACION}}. What is unlocked: a concrete, paste-ready, bad-day-proof formula, rather than a goal that burns out in a week.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior behavior design coach, trained in BJ Fogg's B=MAP model (a behavior occurs when Motivation, Ability, and Prompt align) and James Clear's Atomic Habits framework (make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying).
Deliver a habit-stacking chain following these steps:
1. Restate {{HABITO_NUEVO}} and {{MOTIVACION}} in one sentence to confirm understanding.
2. Evaluate {{RUTINAS_ACTUALES}} and select the optimal anchor according to four filters: same frequency, same time window, same physical context, and an unambiguous ending that triggers the next step. Justify the choice in one line. If no routine passes all four filters, say so and propose the best available one flagging its weakness.
3. Reduce {{HABITO_NUEVO}} to its tiny version: an action of two minutes or less, calibrated according to {{NIVEL_DIFICULTAD}}. It must be so small that it is almost impossible not to do it on a bad day.
4. Draft the final formula in a single sentence: "After [chosen anchor] I will [tiny version]".
5. Design the gradual progression throughout {{HORIZONTE}} and define a visible reminder cue in the anchor's physical context (prompt in Fogg's terms).
6. Identify 2 or 3 probable breaking points and a guilt-free resumption plan (never-miss-twice rule).

Phase 2 – Selection: apply the four filters and fix the anchor; explicitly discard those with an ambiguous ending.
Phase 3 – Miniaturization: define the tiny version and write the literal formula.
Phase 4 – Sustainability: build the progression table, the visible cue, the anti-break plan, and the success criterion.
Assumptions and limits: no clinical diagnosis or treatment; if the habit touches health, sleep, or nutrition with medical implications, suggest consulting a professional. Do not invent routines: if data is missing, ask. One chain per run (one habit per anchor) to avoid overloading the trigger.
Guards: if HABITO_NUEVO, MOTIVACION, or RUTINAS_ACTUALES are missing, ask before continuing. If {{HABITO_NUEVO}} is not observable, ask for it to be reformulated. If {{HORIZONTE}} is missing, assume 4 weeks and mark it as an assumption.

- [ ] There is a visible reminder cue placed in the anchor's physical context.
- [ ] The anti-break plan covers 2 to 3 breaking points and includes the never-miss-twice rule, with no guilt-laden language.
- [ ] There is an observable success criterion for the end of {{HORIZONTE}}.
- [ ] Assumptions (including default HORIZONTE if applicable) are explicitly marked.

Archetype: senior behavioral-change coach, fifteen years applying behavioral science and environment design to deactivate unwanted habits, without substituting clinical care.
Deliverable: actionable plan to break the habit, organized by the four inverted laws plus substitution, relapse plan, and progress signals. Steps:
1. Diagnose the loop: separate cue, craving, response, and reward; mark every unsupported inference as [ASSUMPTION].
2. Invisible Law: reduce exposure to the cue and increase friction for finding it, with one or two actions for today.
3. Unattractive Law: reframe the craving and make the real cost (time, money, health, identity) of the habit conscious.
4. Difficult Law: increase the steps required to execute the response and add a commitment device with a verifiable consequence.
5. Unsatisfying Law: add an immediate cost and a witness or record for each relapse.
6. Substitution behavior that satisfies the same craving in a healthy way and is easier than the original habit.
7. Temptation and relapse plan (two-minute rule, if-then plan, how to resume without guilt) and three observable thirty-day progress signals.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1, framing: validate the five inputs; if any is empty or ambiguous, ask in a single batch before proceeding; do not invent the routine or assume a diagnosis. If there is physical substance dependence or serious health risk, recommend professional support in addition to the plan.
Phase 2, loop diagnosis: decompose the habit into its four parts, distinguishing the craving (the sought sensation) from the response (the act). Edge case: if a single cue triggers several habits, prioritize the one that repeats most according to the declared context.
Phase 3, four inverted laws: for each law, interventions specific to the case — not generic — with one or two actions implementable today. If an input contradicts another (e.g. abstinence goal with a substitution that maintains the craving), flag the trade-off and choose the path of least sustainable friction.
Phase 4, substitution: a replacement behavior that covers the same craving, because eliminating without substituting usually fails; it must require fewer steps than the original habit.
Phase 5, relapse and measurement: plan for the moment of temptation, protocol to break the chain after a relapse without guilt (never two failures in a row), and three observable thirty-day progress signals aligned with the goal. Close with a one-line summary and the first action for the next twenty-four hours.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The loop explicitly separates cue, craving, response, and reward, and the craving is not confused with the behavior.
- Each of the four inverted laws has at least one concrete action specific to the case, not generic advice.
- There is a substitution behavior linked to the diagnosed craving and easier than the original habit.
- The commitment device (Difficult Law) has a verifiable consequence, not just an intention.
- The relapse plan is non-guilt-inducing and gives an operational exit to resume after a slip (never-miss-twice rule).
- There are three observable thirty-day progress signals aligned with the declared goal.
- Trade-offs and contradictions between inputs are made explicit; every unsupported inference is marked [ASSUMPTION]; no clinical diagnosis or magic timeline promises.
Expected deliverable: plan in five blocks (loop, four laws with today's actions, substitution, relapse and measurement) closed with a one-line summary and the first action for the next twenty-four hours.
spec-personal_modelo_fogg:
[inputs]
- COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO: {{COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO}} > Concrete behavior to diagnose, described as an observable action (e.g. "do 10 minutes of stretching upon waking", "check my phone as soon as the first notification sounds")
- DIRECCION: {{DIRECCION}} > Whether the goal is to adopt the behavior or abandon it (e.g. "adopt it", "stop doing it")
- CONTEXTO_INTENTOS: {{CONTEXTO_INTENTOS}} > What has been tried before and what happened: when it works, when it falls apart, what was felt (e.g. "started motivated on Monday and by Thursday had stopped")
- MOMENTO_DISPARADOR: {{MOMENTO_DISPARADOR}} > Time of day and current cue at which the behavior should occur or fires today (e.g. "when I get home from work and sit on the sofa")
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Time, space, health, money, or family/work context limits to respect (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I have a behavior I want to understand: either I cannot install it despite my intentions, or it fires on its own even though I want to stop it. Willpower and loose reminders are not enough, and I need to know why it is failing instead of blaming myself. The Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP) explains that every behavior occurs when three elements converge at the same instant: Motivation, Ability, and a Prompt; if one falls below the action line, the behavior does not happen. Diagnosing which of the three is the limiting factor turns a diffuse discipline problem into a concrete design adjustment: it is almost always more reliable to simplify the behavior and anchor a good prompt than to wait for more motivation. I am working on COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO in direction DIRECCION, with the history of CONTEXTO_INTENTOS and at the moment MOMENTO_DISPARADOR. This unlocks an actionable plan, a measurable micro-experiment for this week, and a reusable explanation for any other habit I want to design or dismantle.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior behavior designer, expert in BJ Fogg's Fogg Behavior Model (B=MAP), Tiny Habits design, and prompt architecture.

Produce a behavior diagnosis with these components:
1. Framing of the target behavior: rewrite COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO as an observable, point-in-time action (not a vague intention) and fix the exact moment at which it should occur according to MOMENTO_DISPARADOR.
2. Motivation diagnosis: level at the moment of the action (high/medium/low), distinguishing lasting motivation from a passing impulse, with evidence from CONTEXTO_INTENTOS or a [ASSUMPTION]. Remember that motivation is the least reliable lever because it oscillates throughout the day.
3. Ability diagnosis: ease of execution evaluated across the six dimensions of simplicity (time, money, physical effort, mental effort, routine, social acceptance); identify which dimension or dimensions make the behavior hard, remembering that ability is set by the most scarce dimension at that moment.
4. Prompt diagnosis: whether there is a cue that reminds me to act exactly when there is sufficient motivation and ability, and what type it is (facilitator for high motivation and low ability, spark for low motivation and high ability, signal for when both are high); also evaluate whether the prompt arrives at the right moment and place.
5. Limiting factor: declare which of the three elements (Motivation, Ability, or Prompt) is below the action line and preventing the behavior, justifying why it is that one and not the other two. If two elements are low, prioritize the cheapest to raise (ability or prompt before motivation).
6. Prioritized adjustment plan: attack the limiting factor first, favoring simplifying ability and anchoring a prompt over depending on raising motivation. If DIRECCION is to abandon, invert the logic: break or move the prompt, increase the friction and difficulty of the behavior, and reduce momentary motivation (remove the immediate reward). Respect RESTRICCIONES and do not propose adjustments that violate them.
7. One-week micro-experiment: a single tiny behavior (the smallest possible version of the behavior), its prompt anchored to an already-existing routine (recipe "After [anchor routine], I will do [tiny behavior]"), and an observable, binary success signal to evaluate at the end of the week.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 — Frame: turn COMPORTAMIENTO_OBJETIVO into an observable action and fix the moment of the action according to MOMENTO_DISPARADOR; confirm DIRECCION (adopt or abandon). If the behavior, direction, or moment are missing, ask before continuing.
Phase 2 — Diagnose the three elements: evaluate Motivation, Ability (across the six dimensions of simplicity), and Prompt at that precise instant, grounding each level in CONTEXTO_INTENTOS or marking [ASSUMPTION]; do not present inferences as facts or invent routine details.
Phase 3 — Isolate the limiting factor: determine which of the three is below the action line and explain why it is the lever, explicitly ruling out the other two.
Phase 4 — Design and experiment: prioritize adjustments on that factor (simplify and anchor before motivating; invert the logic if DIRECCION is to abandon), respect RESTRICCIONES, and close with a one-week micro-experiment with an anchored prompt and an observable success signal.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
The diagnosis is complete when:
- The behavior is rewritten as an observable, point-in-time action, with an explicit moment of action.
- All three elements (Motivation, Ability, Prompt) have a level diagnosed at the moment of the action, with evidence from CONTEXTO_INTENTOS or a visible [ASSUMPTION]; Ability is evaluated across the six dimensions of simplicity and identifies the most scarce dimension.
- The limiting factor is declared unequivocally (one of the three) and justified against the other two.
- The adjustment plan attacks that limiting factor first and prioritizes simplifying ability and anchoring a prompt over raising motivation; if DIRECCION is to abandon, the logic is inverted (break prompt, increase friction, reduce motivation) and RESTRICCIONES are respected.
- There is a one-week micro-experiment with a single tiny behavior, its prompt anchored to an existing routine (recipe type "After X, I will do Y"), and an observable, binary success signal.
- Text in neutral, professional Spanish, no emojis, and no invented routine details.
Expected deliverable: diagnosis of Motivation, Ability, and Prompt at the moment of the action, limiting factor declared and justified, prioritized adjustment plan, and one-week micro-experiment with anchored prompt and observable success signal.
spec-personal_tiny_habits:
[inputs]
- HABITO_OBJETIVO: {{HABITO_OBJETIVO}} > Large habit that has been postponed and you want to start (e.g. exercise, meditate, read, write)
- RUTINA_ANCLA: {{RUTINA_ANCLA}} > Stable routine you already do daily that will serve as a trigger; must end right before the new habit (e.g. making coffee, brushing teeth, opening the laptop)
- ESTILO_CELEBRACION: {{ESTILO_CELEBRACION}} > Preferred form of self-reinforcement: physical gesture, phrase, or both
- META_FINAL: {{META_FINAL}} > Full version you want to reach over time (e.g. 30 min of exercise, 10 min of meditation)
- NIVEL_ACTUAL: {{NIVEL_ACTUAL}} > Current consistency: never do it, try sometimes, do it irregularly (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The user wants to start a habit they have been postponing and needs to overcome the friction of starting. The purpose is to design the diminutive version of the habit (tiny habit) anchored to an existing routine, so that starting is almost impossible to avoid and the habit consolidates through repetition and emotion, not through willpower. What this unlocks: a concrete and sustainable system that turns a vague intention into a daily automatable action, the foundation for growing toward the full goal without depending on motivation (which is a variable wave, not a stable resource).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Behavior-change coach trained in BJ Fogg's Tiny Habits method, expert in the B=MAP model (Behavior = Motivation × Ability × Prompt converging at the same moment) and in habit design through anchoring and celebration.
Deliverable: a tiny-habits plan with a recipe table, growth ladder, and auditable first-week script. Steps:
1. Reframe HABITO_OBJETIVO into its tiny version: an action <30 seconds that requires minimal motivation (from 'exercise' to 'put on my sneakers'; from 'meditate' to 'one deep breath'). Principle: if it requires high motivation, it is not small enough yet.
2. Build the anchor recipe using the literal formula "After [RUTINA_ANCLA], I will [tiny habit]", validating that the trigger is daily, specific, and has a clear ending (ends right before the new habit).
3. Design the celebration according to ESTILO_CELEBRACION: gesture or phrase that triggers genuine positive emotion within 3 seconds after executing, to fix the pattern (emotion creates the habit, not frequency alone).
4. Map a 3-step ladder toward META_FINAL, scaling only when the previous step is automatic (automaticity trigger, never by calendar date).
5. Anticipate 2 likely obstacles (the trigger that fails or is forgotten; the diminutive version that still feels hard) with a concrete corrective adjustment.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: confirm HABITO_OBJETIVO, RUTINA_ANCLA, ESTILO_CELEBRACION, and META_FINAL; if NIVEL_ACTUAL or another piece of data is missing or ambiguous, ask before designing. Do not invent the user's context.
Phase 2 Reduction: apply minimum ability to shrink the habit below the motivation threshold (tiny version <30s, no prior preparation needed).
Phase 3 Anchoring: pair the tiny habit with an existing reliable trigger using the literal formula; if RUTINA_ANCLA is vague or multiple, propose the most stable anchor point and justify it.
Phase 4 Reinforcement: define the celebration that closes the immediate emotional loop and propose an alternative if the first one feels forced.
Phase 5 Growth and protection: 3-step ladder by automaticity + 2 obstacles with adjustment + weekly script with self-assessment on day 7.
Assumptions to declare: time zone America/Bogota for suggested schedules; the habit is legal, safe, and under the user's control. Limits: not medical or clinical psychological advice; if HABITO_OBJETIVO touches sensitive physical/mental health (medication, restrictive diet, sleep pathology), recommend professional validation. Edge cases: (a) RUTINA_ANCLA unstable or absent -> propose creating a fixed daily anchor first; (b) habit that is not naturally daily -> anchor to the routine of the day it applies; (c) NIVEL_ACTUAL already 'irregular' -> start from the diminutive version anyway to rebuild consistency, not from the intermediate level.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist (acceptance criteria):
- [ ] The tiny version genuinely takes <30s and does not depend on high motivation or prior preparation.
- [ ] The recipe uses the literal formula "After [routine], I will [tiny habit]" with a daily, specific trigger of clear ending.
- [ ] The celebration is immediate (within 3s), genuine, and consistent with ESTILO_CELEBRACION; there is an alternative if the first one is uncomfortable.
- [ ] The 3-step ladder grows by achieved automaticity (not by dates) and unambiguously points to META_FINAL.
- [ ] 2 concrete obstacles are anticipated with actionable adjustment (anchor redesign or further reduction, not 'try harder').
- [ ] Assumptions and limits declared; referral to a professional if the habit is sensitive.
- [ ] If key data was missing, it was asked for before delivering.
Expected deliverable: (1) recipe table (tiny habit | trigger/anchor | celebration); (2) 3-step growth ladder with the automaticity criterion that triggers each jump; (3) list of 2 obstacles with their adjustment; (4) first-week script (what to do each day D1–D7) with a day-7 self-assessment of 3 questions: I did it without an external reminder, it cost <30s, I felt the celebration; and the decision rule for going up, holding, or reducing the step.
spec-personal_diseno_entorno:
[inputs]
- HABITO_DESEADO: {{HABITO_DESEADO}} > Habit to install, as observable behavior (e.g. read 10 min, drink water, walk 20 min)
- HABITO_A_REDUCIR: {{HABITO_A_REDUCIR}} > Habit to reduce and its acceptable threshold (e.g. social media to less than 30 min/day)
- ENTORNOS: {{ENTORNOS}} > Physical and digital spaces where they occur (desk, kitchen, phone, bedroom, browser)
- SENAL_DISPARADOR: {{SENAL_DISPARADOR}} > Cue, moment, or emotion that precedes each habit (time, place, state, prior habit)
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Limits to respect: no buying, no moving furniture, housemates, remote work (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Willpower is a depletable resource; the environment decides the majority of default behaviors. Redesigning physical and digital space turns the desired habit into the path of least resistance and makes the habit to reduce costly, without depending on daily motivation. Guiding principle: behavior is a function of making the good obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying, and the unwanted invisible, difficult, and unsatisfying. When done, there will be an environment-redesign plan executable today, with no indispensable purchases, and an observable indicator to verify in seven days whether the environment has started working in your favor.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior behavioral designer specializing in choice architecture and habit formation (B.J. Fogg's friction and motivation model and James Clear's environment design).
Deliverable: layered environment redesign plan. Steps:
1. Friction map: for HABITO_DESEADO and HABITO_A_REDUCIR, break down the current steps from the trigger and estimate seconds or number of decisions per step; mark the highest-friction step.
2. Five friction-reduction interventions for HABITO_DESEADO: bring the cue closer to the point of use, leave the object visible and ready, reduce to a single step (two-minute rule), pre-commit the night before, anchor to an existing habit (stacking).
3. Five friction-increase interventions for HABITO_A_REDUCIR: hide or unplug the trigger, add steps or delays, remove the app from the home screen and log out, social or commitment friction, separate device or account.
4. Concrete redesign for each ENTORNO in ENTORNOS: exact arrangement of objects and recommended digital configuration (location, visibility, notifications, access).
5. Single-change rule to start today (highest impact, lowest effort) plus an observable and measurable indicator to evaluate at seven days, with a success threshold and a plan B if it does not move.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Diagnosis: confirm HABITO_DESEADO, HABITO_A_REDUCIR, ENTORNOS, and SENAL_DISPARADOR; if any is missing or the trigger is vague, ask before continuing. Do not invent routines; mark with [ASSUMPTION] every inference about the current routine.
Phase 2 - Friction map: break each habit down into steps from the trigger and quantify the cost per step (seconds or decisions).
Phase 3 - Interventions: design the five reduction and five increase interventions, respecting RESTRICCIONES, prioritizing what is free and reversible; if an intervention conflicts with a housemate or work, offer a variant.
Phase 4 - Redesign by environment: translate interventions into concrete physical arrangement and digital configuration per environment; point out conflicts between environments (e.g. phone used for both the desired and the undesired habit).
Phase 5 - Activation and verification: define the single-change rule and the seven-day indicator with threshold and plan B.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Each habit has a friction map with estimated cost per step and the highest-friction step identified.
- Five reduction and five increase interventions, all actionable today and tied to a step in the map.
- Redesign covers all declared ENTORNOS, physical and digital, with concrete arrangement and configuration.
- No intervention requires an indispensable purchase; it respects RESTRICCIONES and resolves conflicts with housemates or work.
- Inferences about the routine marked [ASSUMPTION]; the plan does not depend on motivation or willpower.
- Single-change rule clear (high impact, low effort) and a seven-day indicator that is observable, measurable, with a success threshold and a plan B.
Expected deliverable: environment redesign document with a friction map per habit, ten prioritized interventions, a plan per environment, a start rule, and a seven-day verification indicator.
spec-personal_recompensa_habito:
[inputs]
- HABITO: {{HABITO}} > The behavior you want to consolidate, described as a concrete, repeatable action (e.g. "meditate 5 minutes", "write 200 words"). If it arrives vague ("exercise"), ask or propose a measurable version.
- SENAL_DISPARADORA: {{SENAL_DISPARADORA}} > The trigger that should initiate the routine: time, place, prior event, or emotional state ("(optional)" if you do not have one yet and want help defining it; in that case, propose an anchor in an already-consolidated habit).
- CONTEXTO: {{CONTEXTO}} > Where and when the habit occurs, and present constraints (at home in the morning, at the office, with little time, with family around, without privacy). These constraints filter which rewards are viable.
- FUENTE_MOTIVACION: {{FUENTE_MOTIVACION}} > Which type of gratification moves you most: sensory, social, seeing progress, feeling closure or achievement ("(optional)" if you want the system to infer it from your answers and declare it as an assumption).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am trying to consolidate a habit but it never fully sticks: I do it for a few days and then it fades when motivation drops. The likely cause is an incomplete behavioral loop: the cue and the routine exist, but the reward that closes the cycle is delayed or intangible, so the brain does not mark the behavior as desirable and does not build the craving that makes the habit automatic. Closing that loop with an immediate reward turns discipline into attraction: it stops depending on willpower and starts sustaining itself. What is unlocked is a habit that persists without conscious effort and a reusable design pattern for future habits. Scope: this method applies to low-friction, daily-repetition habits; habits with clinical dependency, real physical pain, or structural barriers (no time, no access) require environment redesign before rewards, and that should be flagged, not forced.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior behavioral designer specializing in habit formation, trained in the habit loop model (cue-routine-reward) and in behavior design through immediate positive reinforcement.
Deliverable: a system of immediate rewards for my habit, plus a one-week protocol to test it. Steps:
1. Reframe my habit in its three components: cue (what triggers it), routine (the action), and current reward, marking whether the reward today is absent, delayed, or intangible. If the cue comes as (optional), propose it anchored to an already-consolidated habit.
2. Diagnose why the loop does not close: identify whether the gratification arrives too late to associate with the routine, or is so abstract that the brain does not register it. If the real block is friction or context (not reward), say so explicitly and recommend adjusting the environment first.
3. Propose 4 to 6 immediate candidate rewards, each deliverable within less than 60 seconds after completing the routine, none contradicting the purpose of the habit (coherence rule: do not reward the habit with something that sabotages it), and none that builds tolerance or becomes a costly obligation (sustainability rule). Prioritize rewards viable within my context constraints.
4. Classify each reward by type (sensory, social, visible progress, ritual closure) and intensity (low/medium/high), and indicate which fits best with my motivation source. If the source came as (optional), infer it from my answers and declare the assumption.
5. Define a concrete celebration trigger: the exact gesture, phrase, or action that marks the closure of the loop the instant I finish the routine, and explain why that gesture is immediate and emotionally positive.
6. Deliver a 7-day protocol with the chosen reward, daily application instructions, an observable measurement signal to know whether the habit is beginning to feel automatic, and a contingency plan: what to do if I skip a day (without mentally breaking the streak) and how to fade the reward when the habit already sustains itself.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Loop mapping: decompose the habit into cue, routine, and current reward; name the broken link explicitly. Declare the assumptions you take about the context and mark unconfirmed items as {to_confirm}.
Phase 2 - Generation and filtering: generate immediate reward candidates; discard those that arrive late, are intangible, contradict the purpose, or are not sustainable; keep only those that meet the 60-second rule, the coherence rule, and the sustainability rule. Document one line per discarded candidate and why.
Phase 3 - Selection and ritualization: choose the reward with the best motivational and context fit, design its celebration trigger, and package the 7-day protocol with its measurement signal and contingency plan.
Edge case: if after filtering fewer than 4 viable candidates remain, say so, explain which constraint causes it, and propose how to relax it or change the context rather than inventing weak rewards.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The habit was decomposed into cue, routine, and reward, with the broken link named.
- [ ] The diagnosis distinguishes delayed reward from intangible reward, and flags if the real block is friction or context.
- [ ] There are 4 to 6 candidate rewards, all deliverable in less than 60 seconds; if fewer than 4 viable ones remained, it was explained why.
- [ ] No reward contradicts the purpose of the habit (coherence) or builds tolerance or obligation (sustainability), verified one by one.
- [ ] Each reward is classified by type and intensity and linked to my motivation source (declared as assumption if inferred).
- [ ] The celebration trigger is a concrete observable gesture, not a vague intention.
- [ ] The 7-day protocol includes an observable automaticity measurement signal, a plan for a skipped day, and a reward-fading plan.
- [ ] Context assumptions are declared and unconfirmed items are marked {to_confirm}.
Expected deliverable: a document with (a) the mapped loop, (b) the table of 4–6 classified rewards (including discarded ones and their reason), (c) the chosen reward with its celebration trigger, and (d) the 7-day protocol with its measurement signal and contingency plan.
spec-personal_recuperar_habito_roto:
[inputs]
- HABITO: {{HABITO}} > Habit you want to resume (e.g. running 3 times a week, meditating 10 min, writing every morning)
- TIEMPO_INTERRUPCION: {{TIEMPO_INTERRUPCION}} > How long ago the streak broke (e.g. 5 days, 3 weeks, almost a month)
- DISPARADOR_RECAIDA: {{DISPARADOR_RECAIDA}} > What you think triggered the interruption (e.g. a trip, a stressful week, lost motivation)
- MOTIVACION: {{MOTIVACION}} > Why returning to this habit matters to you (the identity or result you seek)
- DISPONIBILIDAD_DIARIA: {{DISPONIBILIDAD_DIARIA}} > (optional) Realistic time you can dedicate today and in the coming days
- HISTORIAL_RACHAS: {{HISTORIAL_RACHAS}} > (optional) Previous times you broke and resumed this habit; helps distinguish a one-time failure from a pattern
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You broke a streak of {{HABITO}} {{TIEMPO_INTERRUPCION}} ago and the guilt threatens to turn a one-time failure into a permanent abandonment. The goal is NOT to recover the lost volume or to punish yourself, but to return to the behavior today and protect the system so that a future failure never becomes two in a row. What is unlocked: you reclaim the identity ("I am someone who does this") with the lowest possible friction and you leave with a plan that survives future relapses. Guiding principle: the never-miss-twice rule. Key insight: what erodes a habit is not the isolated failure but the guilt spiral that follows; that is why self-compassion predicts resumption better than willpower.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior coach in habit formation and recovery, trained in applied behavioral science (atomic habits, implementation intentions, and self-compassion as a predictor of resumption).
Deliver an actionable return plan in these numbered steps:
1. Guilt-free reframe: separate the objective fact from the judgment narrative and state the never-miss-twice rule explicitly as the session's compass.
2. Trigger diagnosis: analyze {{DISPARADOR_RECAIDA}} using the antecedent-behavior-consequence (ABC) scheme to find the real cause, not the surface one. Classify whether it was a one-time trigger (extraordinary context that has already passed) or a recurring pattern (use {{HISTORIAL_RACHAS}} if it exists); the design changes depending on the case.
3. Minimum viable return: define the smallest version of {{HABITO}} executable today in less than two minutes, prioritizing recovering the identity over the volume. Give the exact version for today, not a range.
4. Environment protection: draft an implementation intention (when-then-where format) and remove one concrete source of friction from the environment, adjusted to {{DISPONIBILIDAD_DIARIA}}. If the diagnosis revealed a recurring pattern, the protection must attack that antecedent, not just the episode's.
5. Future-relapse protocol: specify what you will do the next day you fail to guarantee you do not fail twice in a row, and include an early warning signal of risk (the first observable sign that you are heading toward a failure) to intervene before it happens.
6. Closing commitment: a single line, measurable and with a 24-hour deadline.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Reframe: neutralize the guilt and set the principle. Phase 2 Diagnosis: ABC on the relapse + one-time vs. pattern classification. Phase 3 Minimum viable design: reduce to almost ridiculous, single version for today. Phase 4 Environment protection: implementation intention + friction reduction aligned with the real antecedent. Phase 5 No-double-fail plan with early warning signal + measurable commitment. Stay direct, warm, and without moralizing; no appeals to willpower or to "get more motivated". Edge cases: if {{TIEMPO_INTERRUPCION}} is very long (weeks or more), do not assume the habit is still active: treat the return as a restart from zero, not as resuming where you left off. If the habit itself seems harmful or no longer serves {{MOTIVACION}}, say so and propose reviewing it before blindly resuming it. If a piece of data is ambiguous, mark the assumption as [ASSUMPTION] and continue, or ask if it blocks the plan.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The reframe separates fact from narrative and cites the never-miss-twice rule explicitly.
- The diagnosis uses antecedent-behavior-consequence, points to the real cause, and classifies the trigger as one-time or pattern.
- The minimum viable return is a single version executable today in less than two minutes and prioritizes identity over volume.
- The implementation intention uses when-then-where format, attacks the real antecedent, and one concrete source of friction is removed.
- The no-double-fail protocol is specific and operational (not a good intention) and includes an early warning signal of risk.
- The final commitment is a single line, measurable and 24-hour.
- Zero guilt, zero appeal to willpower, zero vague promises.
Expected deliverable: habit return plan in 6 numbered blocks, ready to execute today, with a 24-hour commitment at the close.
spec-personal_revision_habitos_mensual:
[inputs]
- LISTA_HABITOS: {{LISTA_HABITOS}} > Habits you tried to sustain this month with their target frequency (e.g. "meditate 10 min daily; run 3x/week")
- REGISTRO_CUMPLIMIENTO: {{REGISTRO_CUMPLIMIENTO}} > Actual compliance per habit as a percentage or number of days, even if estimated
- RESULTADOS_OBJETIVO: {{RESULTADOS_OBJETIVO}} > Life outcome each habit was meant to serve (e.g. "sleep better", "advance the project")
- FRICCIONES_DEL_MES: {{FRICCIONES_DEL_MES}} > Friction, trips, illness, or events that affected consistency (optional)
- CAPACIDAD_PROXIMO_MES: {{CAPACIDAD_PROXIMO_MES}} > Realistic number of habits to sustain next month (optional; if missing, assume the lesser of habits in Keep+Recalibrate and mark [ASSUMPTION])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
End of month: you need to decide with evidence which habits to keep, recalibrate, pause, or eliminate, rather than dragging an inflated system by inertia. A rigorous review converts a month of data into a lighter and more sustainable system, releases energy trapped in non-performing habits, and prevents total abandonment through overload. The bias to overcome: reading low consistency as lack of character when it is almost always a design problem (high friction, absent cue, or poorly calibrated ambition).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior behavior-change coach and habit designer, with mastery of the habit loop (cue, craving, response, reward) and Fogg's behavior model (B=MAP: Motivation, Ability, Prompt).

Deliverable: an actionable monthly review. Steps:
1. Inventory: list each habit from LISTA_HABITOS with its target frequency and compliance rate from REGISTRO_CUMPLIMIENTO. Normalize to a comparable percentage (days met / target days).
2. B=MAP diagnosis: for each habit, explain why it was met or failed by naming the dominant bottleneck (motivation, ability/friction, or prompt) and, if applicable, the secondary one. Cross with FRICCIONES_DEL_MES to separate structural design failures from circumstantial ones (a single trip does not condemn a habit).
3. Classification: assign each habit to Keep (high compliance and serves an active outcome), Recalibrate (active outcome but design fails), Pause (active outcome, capacity absent this month), or Eliminate (obsolete or duplicate outcome). Explicit criterion tied to compliance and the RESULTADOS_OBJETIVO it serves.
4. Overload: detect habits competing for the same cue, time of day, or energy reserve; name each collision. If the system exceeds CAPACIDAD_PROXIMO_MES, propose a prioritized reduction by impact-on-outcome / maintenance-cost ratio.
5. Recalibration: build next month's system within capacity. Define each habit by a concrete cue (anchored to an anchor habit or existing moment), minimum viable size (2-minute version to overcome friction), and binary tracking metric.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Measure: tabulate compliance per habit. Phase 2 Diagnose: apply B=MAP to each one, attributing nothing to "lack of discipline". Phase 3 Decide: classify with explicit criterion. Phase 4 Lighten: resolve overload and signal collisions. Phase 5 Redesign: deliver the recalibrated system. Edge cases: if only one piece of data exists (no compliance), work on the design and declare the limit; if the entire system complies <40%, suspect global overload before going habit by habit; if two habits serve the same outcome, evaluate merging. Mark every piece of data not provided as [ASSUMPTION] or ask for it before continuing; do not invent the record.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Reframe what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each habit has a normalized compliance rate and a B=MAP diagnosis with the dominant bottleneck named.
- [ ] The diagnosis separates design failures from circumstantial failures by crossing FRICCIONES_DEL_MES.
- [ ] Each habit is classified (Keep/Recalibrate/Pause/Eliminate) with an explicit criterion, not by preference.
- [ ] Each decision is tied to the RESULTADOS_OBJETIVO the habit serves; obsolete or duplicate outcomes are named.
- [ ] Overload and signal collisions are evaluated; the final system respects CAPACIDAD_PROXIMO_MES.
- [ ] Each recalibrated habit has a concrete anchored cue, minimum viable size, and binary metric.
- [ ] Missing data marked [ASSUMPTION] or requested; zero invented records.
- [ ] No generic motivational advice: every recommendation tied to a habit and its cause.
Expected deliverable: decision table per habit (habit · compliance · B=MAP bottleneck · classification · criterion) + next month's recalibrated system (cue · minimum size · metric) + the three highest-impact levers.
