[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need a fast, reusable operational prompt that produces predictable output without rewriting instructions each time. The RTF pattern (Role, Task, Format) compresses intent into three minimal blocks: it unlocks immediate execution, consistent output, and easy templating for {{TAREA_OPERATIVA}} directed at {{PUBLICO}}. RTF works best for single-step, high-frequency tasks; if the task requires multi-step reasoning or examples, it is appropriate to escalate to RACE or CRISPE (a conscious limit, not a pattern defect).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer specialized in compact patterns (RTF, RACE, CRISPE) for high-frequency operational tasks.
Deliverable: a compact RTF prompt (under 120 words) ready to paste and run. Steps:
1. Role block: specific and credible expert aligned to {{ROL_EXPERTO}}; if missing, propose one justified in one sentence. Never a generic "helpful assistant".
2. Task block: a single concrete action on {{TAREA_OPERATIVA}}, with its explicit input and the {{RESTRICCIONES}}. If you detect two actions, split and keep only the main one.
3. Format block: exact output structure according to {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} (type, length, sections, required fields, tone).
4. Assemble the three blocks into a continuous prompt, without visible R/T/F labels, and deliver it in plain copiable text.
5. Add a one-sentence note about which variable to change to reuse the prompt for another task.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Interpret: restate the need and tag with [ASSUMPTION] any inferred data (proposed role, assumed format).
Phase 2 Plan: show in three lines how you will populate Role, Task, and Format; if {{TAREA_OPERATIVA}}, {{PUBLICO}}, or {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} is missing, ask for them before continuing (they are required; {{ROL_EXPERTO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}} are optional).
Phase 3 Execute: draft the RTF prompt, verify the word count, and deliver the copiable block plus the reuse note.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] The three blocks (Role, Task, Format) are present, integrated in continuous prose, and do not overlap.
- [ ] The Role is specific and credible, never a generic "helpful assistant".
- [ ] The Task expresses a single concrete action with its input; any second action was discarded or redirected.
- [ ] The Format fixes the structure, length, and tone of the output without ambiguity.
- [ ] The final prompt is under 120 words and in plain copiable text.
- [ ] Assumptions are tagged [ASSUMPTION]; required missing data is asked for, not invented.
- [ ] If the task exceeds a single step, the RTF limit is noted and RACE/CRISPE is suggested.
Expected deliverable: a compact, copiable, reusable RTF prompt block, followed by a one-sentence note indicating which variable to swap to adapt it to another operational task.
spec-ia-automatizacion_tecnica-tag:
[inputs]
- PROMPT_ACTUAL: {{PROMPT_ACTUAL}} > The prompt used today or the task to be automated (the material to rewrite)
- RESULTADO_ESPERADO: {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}} > The concrete deliverable needed (what the model must produce)
- OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} > What the result is for: the decision it enables, the metric it moves, or the success criterion; must not be invented
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Tone, length, output format, and what not to do (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The user has a prompt or automation intent that produces inconsistent results because it mixes three distinct planes in a single instruction: the task (what), the way to execute it (how), and the objective the result must serve (why). The purpose is to rewrite {{PROMPT_ACTUAL}} with the TAG framework (Task, Action, Goal), which separates those planes and anchors the prompt to the business outcome instead of leaving it hanging. By separating the Goal from the Task, the model stops optimizing for "completing the task" and starts optimizing for "serving the objective," which is what the user actually needs. The result is an outcome-oriented, reusable prompt that unlocks reliable automations instead of prompts that need correcting on each execution. The strategy is to make the why explicit before the how.
Assumptions: the material delivered is rewritable text; if the objective cannot be expressed as a decision, metric, or criterion, the prompt is not ready for TAG and this is declared. TAG orders planes; it does not by itself guarantee the quality of the input data.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer, expert in the TAG framework (Task, Action, Goal) and in designing instructions oriented toward business outcomes.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate in one sentence what {{PROMPT_ACTUAL}} is trying to achieve; if {{PROMPT_ACTUAL}}, {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}}, or {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} is missing, ask for them before executing and do not invent the business objective. If {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} is generic ("improve", "optimize", "make it good"), demand that it be made concrete as a decision, metric, or criterion.
2. Diagnose in 2 or 3 lines what {{PROMPT_ACTUAL}} mixes or lacks: vague task, undefined action, absent objective, or missing success criteria. Name the affected plane (T, A, or G).
3. Rewrite the prompt in three labeled, separated, non-overlapping blocks:
   - T · Task: the scoped, unambiguous instruction derived from {{RESULTADO_ESPERADO}} (a single main deliverable).
   - A · Action: expert role or archetype, method or steps, output format and tone per {{RESTRICCIONES}}, and what to do if data is missing.
   - G · Goal: {{OBJETIVO_NEGOCIO}} translated into the decision it enables, the metric it moves, or the criterion by which success will be known.
4. Add 3 to 5 acceptance criteria derived from the Goal: how to verify that the output meets the objective, not just the task. Each criterion must be observable.
5. Explain in 2 or 3 lines why the TAG version surpasses the original, anchoring each improvement to T, A, or G in a concrete way.
6. Close with a variant of the TAG prompt with {{UPPERCASE}} variables for data that changes between executions, reusable as a template.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: validate that the current prompt or task, the expected result, and the business objective exist; if a key piece of data is missing or the objective is generic, ask for or demand it before executing.
Phase 2 · Diagnosis: identify which planes are mixed or absent in the original (Task, Action, Goal) and name them.
Phase 3 · TAG Rewrite: draft the three separate blocks, ensuring the Goal is a business objective and not merely a restatement of the Task.
Phase 4 · Objective-based verification: derive the acceptance criteria from the Goal, not the Task, and verify that the prompt can satisfy them.
Phase 5 · Template: parameterize with {{UPPERCASE}} variables to leave the prompt reusable.
Edge cases: if the Task already contains multiple deliverables, split and prioritize one main one. If the Goal is identical to the Task, warn that a real objective is missing and ask for it. If {{RESTRICCIONES}} is empty, propose a default format and tone and mark them as editable.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The intent was restated in one sentence before rewriting, and missing data was asked for rather than invented.
- The diagnosis explicitly names which plane (Task, Action, or Goal) was missing or mixed in {{PROMPT_ACTUAL}}.
- The three T, A, and G blocks are labeled and separated, with no overlap between them.
- The G · Goal block expresses a business objective (decision, metric, or success criterion), not a restatement of the Task.
- The Action includes the expert role, method, format, and the rule for what to do if data is missing.
- There are 3 to 5 acceptance criteria derived from the Goal, observable and verifiable.
- The explanation of the why anchors each improvement to T, A, or G in a concrete way.
- A parameterized variant with {{UPPERCASE}} variables reusable as a template was delivered.
Expected deliverable: the prompt rewritten in TAG format (three labeled blocks) + acceptance criteria + justification anchored to TAG + parameterized variant ready to paste, in neutral Spanish and professional tone.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-chaining:
[inputs]
- TAREA_COMPLEJA: {{TAREA_COMPLEJA}} > Task you today try to solve in a single monolithic prompt and want to convert into a chained pipeline
- ENTREGABLE_FINAL: {{ENTREGABLE_FINAL}} > Concrete output the complete pipeline must produce and its observable success criterion
- NUMERO_ESLABONES: {{NUMERO_ESLABONES}} > Desired number or range of links (optional; default 3 to 6)
- FORMATO_SALIDA: {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} > Output contract format between links, e.g. JSON, Markdown, table (optional; default JSON)
- RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS: {{RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS}} > Environment limits: model, token window, orchestration tool, latency, or cost (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A monolithic prompt that loads decomposition, reasoning, and formatting into a single step produces inconsistent, hard-to-debug results: when it fails, you cannot tell which part failed. Converting that task into a pipeline of chained prompts (prompt chaining) isolates each responsibility in a link, and the structured output of one becomes the input of the next. This unlocks link-by-link traceability, validation at every junction, and the ability to retry or correct a single step without redoing the entire flow. Explicit trade-off: chaining adds cumulative latency, cost per call, and contract surface to maintain; it is justified when reliability and debuggability outweigh the simplicity of a single step.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer and AI flow orchestration expert, with experience designing productive pipelines where the output of one model feeds the next under strict data contracts.
Deliverable: complete pipeline design for TAREA_COMPLEJA that produces ENTREGABLE_FINAL, ready to implement in an orchestrator. Steps:
1. Restate the full task and its final deliverable; state the observable and measurable success criterion for the pipeline (what is inspected to declare it correct).
2. Decompose the task into NUMERO_ESLABONES sequential single-responsibility links; justify why that cut reduces error compared to the monolithic prompt and why each boundary is a good cut point (change of reasoning type, format, or source of truth).
3. For each link define: purpose in one line, input contract (fields received from the previous link, with types), output contract in FORMATO_SALIDA (exact schema with types and required vs. optional fields), and the drafted ready-to-use prompt.
4. Define the control checkpoints between links: what to validate before advancing (schema, ranges, non-empty), failure policy (retry with attempt limit, degrade to partial output, or stop), idempotency guarantee of the retry, and the mechanism for preventing error propagation downstream (e.g. flag the payload as invalid and abort).
5. Deliver the flow diagram in text format (link 1 > link 2 > ...) and a summary table of inputs and outputs per link.
Edge cases to cover: a link that returns an invalid format or broken JSON; an empty or out-of-range field; conditional branching (a link decides to skip another); the need for fan-out/fan-in (a link produces N items the next one processes). Address each in the design or tag [ASSUMPTION] if it is out of scope.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Framing): fix the task, deliverable, and success criterion; if a critical piece of data for chaining (deliverable, contract format, or number of links) is missing, ask before proceeding. Respect RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS when sizing links and payload sizes; if not provided, assume reasonable limits and tag them [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 (Decomposition): trace the cut into single-responsibility links and verify that the output of each is sufficient input for the next (no missing fields).
Phase 3 (Contracts and prompts): draft the input/output schema and the prompt for each link; ensure field names and types match between adjacent links.
Phase 4 (Control and assembly): define validations, failure policy, idempotency, and deliver the diagram and summary table.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each link has a single responsibility and a purpose in one line.
- [ ] The output contract of each link matches field by field and type by type with the input contract of the next.
- [ ] Schemas are in FORMATO_SALIDA, distinguish required from optional fields, and are parseable without ambiguity.
- [ ] Each link includes its drafted ready-to-paste prompt.
- [ ] There are control checkpoints with an explicit failure policy (retry/degrade/stop) and retry idempotency.
- [ ] Edge cases (invalid format, empty field, branching, fan-out/fan-in) are covered or tagged [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] The design respects RESTRICCIONES_TECNICAS or tags [ASSUMPTION] when assuming a limit.
- [ ] A text-format flow diagram and inputs/outputs summary table are included.
- [ ] The pipeline success criterion is observable and measurable, not subjective.
Expected deliverable: document with success criterion, N links (purpose + input contract + output contract + prompt), a control-checkpoint section with failure policy, a text-format flow diagram, and an inputs/outputs summary table per link, ready to implement in an orchestrator.
spec-ia-automatizacion_self-consistency:
[inputs]
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > Question or task to solve with reasoning (calculation, classification, logic, decision)
- TIPO_RESPUESTA: {{TIPO_RESPUESTA}} > Form of the expected final answer: number, category, yes/no, or brief text
- NUM_RUTAS: {{NUM_RUTAS}} > Number of independent reasoning chains to generate (optional; default 5; use 7-9 if the problem is ambiguous or high-impact)
- FORMATO_NORMALIZACION: {{FORMATO_NORMALIZACION}} > Rules for making answers comparable: units, rounding, capitalization, category synonyms (optional)
- UMBRAL_ACUERDO: {{UMBRAL_ACUERDO}} > Minimum coincidence percentage to declare high confidence (optional; default 60%)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A single reasoning chain can fail due to a defective intermediate step, and the model delivers it with a confident tone anyway. Self-consistency attacks that: it generates several independent routes for the same problem and votes for the most repeated answer, because correct answers tend to converge by different paths while errors disperse. Applying it unlocks more reliable answers in calculations, classifications, and logical decisions, and delivers an explicit confidence signal to know when to rely on the result and when to doubt. It does not replace factual verification: it votes on what the model believes, not on external truth.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompting engineer specialized in reasoning techniques (chain-of-thought, self-consistency, ensemble voting) of language models.

Deliverable: consensus answer by majority vote over multiple reasoning routes, with vote count and confidence level.

Steps:
1. Confirm PROBLEMA and TIPO_RESPUESTA; if missing, ask before continuing. If NUM_RUTAS is empty use 5; if UMBRAL_ACUERDO is empty use 60%.
2. Generate NUM_RUTAS independent chains, each with a different focus or order of steps, without one consulting another. Number each route and show its reasoning and its isolated final answer.
3. Normalize the final answers according to FORMATO_NORMALIZACION (units, rounding, capitalization, synonyms) so they are comparable. If a route does not reach an answer of TIPO_RESPUESTA, mark it as a null vote and do not count it in the denominator.
4. Tabulate the frequency of each normalized answer and apply majority voting; declare the most frequent one the winner.
5. Report the consensus answer, vote count, agreement level (percentage of valid coincident routes), and confidence note (high if UMBRAL_ACUERDO is exceeded; medium or low if there is a tie or dispersion). If there is a tie, do not invent a winner: show it and recommend more routes or reformulating.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: fix the problem, type of answer, and parameters; tag every assumption with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Diversification: produce the routes in isolation, varying the angle (different decomposition, reverse order, cross-check) so errors do not correlate. Nearly identical routes inflate agreement in a misleading way: if two routes share the same critical step, replace one.
Phase 3 - Normalization: bring all final answers to a common format before comparing; discard null routes from the count.
Phase 4 - Voting and reporting: count, choose the majority, calculate the agreement over valid routes, and translate into an actionable confidence note.
Edge cases: tie -> declare a tie and recommend 2-4 more routes or reformulating. High dispersion (no answer dominates) -> low confidence and signal that the problem may be poorly defined. Strong majority but all with the same premise error -> warn that self-consistency does not detect shared systematic biases.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Exactly NUM_RUTAS routes were generated, each with visible reasoning and an isolated final answer.
- [ ] The routes use distinct approaches, not paraphrased copies of the same chain; none shares a critical step with another.
- [ ] Answers were normalized to a comparable format before voting; null routes were excluded from the denominator.
- [ ] The vote table shows each unique answer and its frequency.
- [ ] The agreement level is in percentage over valid routes and translates to high/medium/low confidence against UMBRAL_ACUERDO.
- [ ] Ties, high dispersion, or shared premise bias are declared without inventing a winner, with an action recommendation.
- [ ] Assumptions carry the [ASSUMPTION] tag; no invented data.
Expected deliverable: final block with the recommended answer, vote count (e.g. "4 out of 5"), agreement percentage, confidence note, and one line about when to trust the result and when to escalate to external verification.
spec-ia-automatizacion_react-pattern:
[inputs]
- TAREA_OBJETIVO: {{TAREA_OBJETIVO}} > Specific task the agent must resolve that exceeds its internal knowledge or requires several steps with tools (e.g. "answer a factual query verified with citable sources")
- HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES: {{HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES}} > List of tools with signature and what each returns (e.g. search(query)->list of snippets+urls; open(url)->page text; calculate(expression)->number)
- FORMATO_ACCIONES: {{FORMATO_ACCIONES}} > Exact syntax for each Action (e.g. JSON {"tool":"","args":{}} or name[args]); includes the syntax of the closing Action (Finish/Answer)
- LIMITE_ITERACIONES: {{LIMITE_ITERACIONES}} > Maximum number of Thought-Action-Observation cycles before forcing an honest close or escalation
- CRITERIO_TERMINACION: {{CRITERIO_TERMINACION}} > Condition that defines sufficient evidence to close (e.g. "data confirmed by at least one citable source with no contradiction detected")
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
An agent must resolve a task that exceeds its internal knowledge and requires consulting external tools step by step. Free reasoning hallucinates data; blind action does not reason. The ReAct pattern (Reasoning + Acting, Yao et al. 2022) interleaves both: the agent thinks about what it is missing, acts with a tool, reads the real result, and thinks again, leaving an auditable trace. A well-designed contract unlocks agents that ground every claim in verifiable evidence instead of inventing it, and that stop when — and only when — they have gathered what is needed. The central risk to neutralize is twofold: fabricated Observations (the agent predicts what the tool would say) and premature or late closing (answering without evidence or spinning in loops without converging).

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior agentic systems engineer, specialized in reasoning and tool-use orchestration under the ReAct pattern.

Deliver the system prompt and the loop contract that make an agent operate in ReAct mode on {{TAREA_OBJETIVO}}. Steps:
1. Define the cycle with three unambiguously labeled turns in a fixed order: Thought (what is known, what is missing, what to do now), Action (a single call in {{FORMATO_ACCIONES}}), and Observation (the real result returned by the tool and injected by the orchestrator, never written by the agent).
2. Specify the catalog {{HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES}}: each tool's signature, what it returns, and the criterion for when to invoke it versus its alternatives (avoid redundant tools in a single step).
3. Codify the termination rule based on {{CRITERIO_TERMINACION}}: the agent emits the closing Action (Finish/Answer) only when an explicit Thought confirms sufficient evidence; the final answer must cite the Observations that support it.
4. Establish guardrails: forbidden to fabricate Observations; exactly one Action per turn; cap of {{LIMITE_ITERACIONES}} iterations with defined behavior when exhausted (honest close that declares uncertainty and what was gathered, never invent); and protocol when a tool fails, times out, or returns empty (one retry with corrected arguments, then alternate tool, then honest close with what is available).
5. Cover edge cases: Observation that contradicts a previous Thought (revise the hypothesis, do not ignore the data); loop detection (same Action with same arguments repeated) and strategy change; partial or conflicting results between sources (declare the conflict in the Thought and decide if one source dominates or if evidence is lacking).
6. Include a complete, executable example trace (Thought/Action/Observation × N plus close) that resolves {{TAREA_OBJETIVO}} and shows at least one annotated edge-case handling.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpretation: confirm {{TAREA_OBJETIVO}}, {{HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES}}, {{FORMATO_ACCIONES}}, {{LIMITE_ITERACIONES}}, and {{CRITERIO_TERMINACION}}; review {{ADJUNTOS}}. If any is empty or ambiguous, ask before drafting.
Phase 2 - Contract design: draft the system block with the three-turn cycle, the tool catalog, and the exact grammar for each turn (including the closing Action).
Phase 3 - Guardrails and termination: add the iteration limit with its behavior when exhausted, the no-fabrication policy, failure/timeout/empty handling, loop detection, and the closing condition with evidence citation.
Phase 4 - Demonstration: build the executable example trace, include an annotated edge case, and review it against the criterion checklist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The three turns (Thought, Action, Observation) are unambiguously distinguishable and follow a fixed order.
- There is exactly one Action per turn, expressed in {{FORMATO_ACCIONES}}, with the closing syntax defined.
- Observations come only from the tool; the prompt explicitly prohibits fabricating them.
- A stopping condition derived from {{CRITERIO_TERMINACION}} exists, and a budget of {{LIMITE_ITERACIONES}} with explicit behavior when exhausted (honest close, without invention).
- There is a defined protocol for failure, timeout, or empty result, and repetitive loop detection.
- Handling of a contradictory Observation and conflicting sources is codified.
- The close cites the Observations that support the answer.
- The example trace is executable end to end, shows an edge case, and ends with the closing Action.
Expected deliverable: ready-to-paste ReAct system prompt block for the orchestrator, plus an annotated example trace that demonstrates the complete cycle and at least one edge case on {{TAREA_OBJETIVO}}.
spec-ia-automatizacion_tree-of-thought:
[inputs]
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > Planning or design problem to solve: what to design or plan and what for
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Non-negotiable constraints: time budget, capacity, mandatory requirements, hard dependencies
- CRITERIO_EXITO: {{CRITERIO_EXITO}} > How it will be known the solution is good (the success signal that guides the evaluation)
- DESCARTADOS: {{DESCARTADOS}} > Already-tried or discarded approaches that must not reappear (optional; if missing, write "none")
- NUM_RAMAS: {{NUM_RAMAS}} > Number of branches to explore, between 3 and 5 (optional; if missing, the model uses 4)
- HORIZONTE_DECISION: {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}} > When to decide and how reversible the choice is (optional; if missing, assume a relevant and partially reversible decision)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
The solver faces {{PROBLEMA}}, a planning or design problem where the first idea is rarely the best and choosing blindly is costly. The purpose is to apply Tree of Thought: instead of committing to a single line of reasoning, open several solution branches, develop them enough to judge them, prune the weak ones with an explicit criterion, and converge on the strongest. What is unlocked is a defensible, traceable design decision — the tree is visible, not just the winning leaf — under the given {{RESTRICCIONES}}, measurable against {{CRITERIO_EXITO}}, and calibrated to {{HORIZONTE_DECISION}} (the more irreversible the decision, the more demanding the pruning). AI strategy contributes here by providing deliberate exploration rather than improvisation.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior reasoning architect, expert in Tree of Thought (ToT), deliberate search for alternatives, multi-criteria evaluation, and pruning of dominated hypotheses.
Deliver the following, in this order:
1. Restate {{PROBLEMA}} in one sentence: "Design/plan [what] for [purpose], respecting [hard constraint]".
2. Generate 3 to 5 branches (use {{NUM_RAMAS}} if provided; if not, 4): genuinely distinct approaches, each with a short name and a one-sentence thesis. Exclude what is in {{DESCARTADOS}}.
3. Expand each branch one or two levels: implementation steps, assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION], and the breaking point where it would fail.
4. Define 3 to 5 criteria derived from {{CRITERIO_EXITO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}}; if one criterion dominates, assign weights and declare them. Score each branch from 1 to 5 per criterion with a supporting note and tag [ASSUMPTION] when the note depends on an unconfirmed piece of data.
5. Pruning: explicitly discard branches that violate a non-negotiable or are dominated (equal or worse in all criteria), naming each and the reason. A branch is not pruned just for being ambitious: distinguish infeasible from demanding.
6. Deepen the surviving branch or the two strongest: execution plan, risks, and mitigations.
7. Recommend a winning branch, its margin over the second, the early signal that would indicate error, and the specific condition for rolling back to a pruned branch. If two branches tie, declare the tie and resolve it by the criterion of greatest weight or by lowest breakage risk, not randomly.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 · Framing: fix the objective and validate that the problem, non-negotiable constraints, and success criterion exist; if a key piece of data is missing, ask before executing and do not invent constraints.
Phase 2 · Branching: generate 3 to 5 distinct approaches (not variants of a single one), each with a thesis; exclude what is already discarded.
Phase 3 · Expansion: develop each branch one or two levels with steps, assumptions [ASSUMPTION], and breaking point.
Phase 4 · Evaluation and pruning: define criteria with weights if applicable, score 1 to 5 per criterion with support, apply non-negotiables, and prune dominated branches declaring the reason for each cut.
Phase 5 · Convergence: deepen the winning branch (and at most the second), recommend with margin, early error signal, and rollback condition; show the complete tree for audit.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The problem was restated in one actionable sentence before branching.
- There are between 3 and 5 genuinely distinct branches, each with a name and thesis; none repeats what is in {{DESCARTADOS}}.
- Each branch was expanded with steps, assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION], and a breaking point.
- The evaluation criteria derive from {{CRITERIO_EXITO}} and {{RESTRICCIONES}}, carry weight when one dominates, and each 1-to-5 score has a supporting note.
- Pruning is explicit: each eliminated branch is named and the reason stated (constraint violated or dominance), distinguishing infeasible from demanding.
- The winning branch includes an execution plan, risks and mitigations, margin over the second, early error signal, and rollback condition; ties are resolved with a declared criterion.
- The complete tree (branches, prunings, winner) remains visible for auditing the reasoning, not just the result.
Expected deliverable: Tree of Thought reasoning tree with evaluated and pruned branches + single defensible recommendation with plan, error signal, and rollback condition, in neutral Spanish and professional tone.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-descomposi:
[inputs]
- PROBLEMA: {{PROBLEMA}} > Complex problem to solve, with its parts and how they relate
- OBJETIVO_FINAL: {{OBJETIVO_FINAL}} > Result or final deliverable to be reached
- DATOS_Y_RESTRICCIONES: {{DATOS_Y_RESTRICCIONES}} > Available data, constraints, assumptions, or rules to respect
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Level of reasoning shown: summarized or complete (optional, default summarized)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to solve a complex problem whose parts depend on each other. Attacking it all at once produces errors and logical jumps; solving it from simple to complex (least-to-most) makes each step verifiable and unlocks the next. A good decomposition converts an intractable problem into a chain of auditable steps, where the exact point where the reasoning breaks can be identified and corrected without redoing everything.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompting and structured reasoning engineer, expert in the least-to-most technique and in decomposing problems with dependencies.
Deliverable: the complete solution to {{PROBLEMA}} built step by step up to {{OBJETIVO_FINAL}}, plus the subproblem chain that supports it.
Steps:
1. Validate that {{PROBLEMA}} has real dependencies that justify decomposing; if it is atomic, declare it and solve it directly without forcing the technique.
2. Decompose {{PROBLEMA}} into subproblems ordered from simplest to most complex; for each one declare its specific question, its inputs (dependencies), and its done criterion. Mark the independent ones.
3. Define the resolution order (topological): nothing is solved before what it depends on.
4. Solve each subproblem in order, explicitly reusing previous outputs and respecting {{DATOS_Y_RESTRICCIONES}}.
5. Integrate the partial results into the final solution that fulfills {{OBJETIVO_FINAL}}.
6. Verify dependencies, completeness, and consistency; trace any contradiction to the step that caused it and correct from there.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 (Decomposition): map subproblems and dependencies in a list or simple graph; order from simple to complex; mark independent ones and declare the done criterion per subproblem. Practical limit: group to maintain between 3 and 9 subproblems; more granularity is consolidated.
Phase 2 (Chained resolution): solve one by one in topological order; each step cites the inputs it uses, shows reasoning at {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} (default summarized), and leaves a verifiable partial result. If an input is a blocking ASSUMPTION, stop and ask.
Phase 3 (Integration and verification): assemble the final solution, verify that every dependency was respected and that no subproblems are left open. Missing or ambiguous data are tagged [ASSUMPTION]. Edge cases: dependency cycle (declare it, break by justified assumption or ask for the data), irreducible circular dependency (escalate to the user), subproblem with no data (tag [ASSUMPTION] and isolate its impact).
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] It was validated whether the problem warrants decomposition before applying it.
- [ ] Each subproblem has an explicit question, declared dependencies, and a done criterion.
- [ ] The resolution order respects all dependencies (nothing before its input).
- [ ] Each step visibly reuses the outputs of previous steps.
- [ ] No jumps: no subproblem is left unsolved.
- [ ] The final solution fulfills {{OBJETIVO_FINAL}} and is consistent with {{DATOS_Y_RESTRICCIONES}}.
- [ ] Contradictions are traced to the originating step and corrected from there.
- [ ] Assumptions tagged [ASSUMPTION]; blocking assumptions asked for before executing.
Expected deliverable: ordered list of subproblems with dependencies and done criterion + step-by-step chained resolution citing inputs + final integrated and verified solution.
spec-ia-automatizacion_role-prompting-ex:
[inputs]
- DOMINIO: {{DOMINIO}} > Field or discipline where the expert persona is needed (e.g. web application security, legal contract drafting, B2B growth marketing). The narrower, the better the role conditioning.
- OBJETIVO_TAREA: {{OBJETIVO_TAREA}} > Concrete task and expected deliverable that the expert persona must resolve (verb + object + success criterion).
- NIVEL_EXIGENCIA: {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} > Expected quality standard: working draft, client-delivery quality, or auditable/publishable level. The rubric is calibrated to this level (optional, default: client-delivery quality).
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Limits to respect: length, format, regulations, audience, prohibited data, banned tools (optional).
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments".

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to resolve {{OBJETIVO_TAREA}} in the domain {{DOMINIO}} with specialist quality, not generalist quality. Role prompting elevates domain quality only when the profile contributes real procedural knowledge (mental models, heuristics, anti-patterns, and quality criteria), not a decorative title. A well-built profile functions as a system layer: it conditions the reasoning space, activates the correct vocabulary and criteria, and unlocks more precise, defensible deliverables that are reusable as the foundation of a permanent system prompt. Explicit assumption: the model does not hold real credentials; the role is a reasoning scaffold, not a guarantee of expertise, which is why all unverifiable identity data is marked [ASSUMPTION] and verification rests on the rubric, not the title.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer specialized in role prompting and high-fidelity expert persona design, with practice in model conditioning for technical and professional domains.

Deliverable: an operational expert persona plus the task resolved from that role. Proceed as follows:
1. Build the optimal persona for {{OBJETIVO_TAREA}} in {{DOMINIO}}, with five layers: (a) Identity and credentials (precise senior title, years of practice, domains; unverifiable data as [ASSUMPTION]); (b) Mental models (3 to 5 frameworks, principles, or real theories named explicitly); (c) Decision heuristics (rules "if X then prioritize Y", with the trade-off each one resolves); (d) Anti-patterns (3 to 5 errors the expert avoids by trade, each with its warning signal); (e) Quality rubric calibrated to {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}}, with observable criteria and an approval threshold.
2. Verify that each layer changes how the task is resolved (not just the tone); discard every decorative layer and declare what you discarded.
3. Execute {{OBJETIVO_TAREA}} by embodying the persona: apply its mental models and heuristics visibly, avoid its anti-patterns, and respect {{RESTRICCIONES}}.
4. Self-evaluate the deliverable against the rubric; if it does not reach {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}}, iterate and re-evaluate before delivering (maximum two iterations; if a gap persists after the second, declare it as an open limit).
5. Close with a quality delta note: what the role contributed versus a generic response.
Data gate: if DOMINIO or OBJETIVO_TAREA are ambiguous, request clarification before drafting; do not invent context.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Persona design: derive the most specific role that masters {{OBJETIVO_TAREA}}; draft the five layers with density, without filler; mark assumptions with [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 Profile validation: confirm that mental models, heuristics, and anti-patterns are real, actionable, and field-specific, not generic; prune decorative elements.
Phase 3 Embodied execution: resolve the task from the role, citing which heuristic or model guides each key decision.
Phase 4 Self-evaluation: score the deliverable against the rubric; iterate until {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}} is met or declare the open limit.
Phase 5 Delta and reuse: deliver the card, response, and delta note; offer the card as a reusable system prompt.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- The persona has a specific senior title (not "generic expert") coherent with {{DOMINIO}}.
- All five layers are complete; mental models and heuristics are named and real (uncertain data marked [ASSUMPTION]).
- Each heuristic has actionable form "if X then Y" and declares the trade-off it resolves; anti-patterns are concrete errors with their warning signal, not platitudes.
- The rubric is calibrated to {{NIVEL_EXIGENCIA}}, has observable criteria and an approval threshold, and was actually used in the self-evaluation.
- The response shows traceability: at least the key decisions cite which heuristic or model guided them.
- {{RESTRICCIONES}} are respected and there is no decorative role prompting (every layer changes the result; discarded elements are declared).
- The delta note explains the role's contribution verifiably, without empty self-praise.
- Edge cases resolved: domain too broad (role is narrowed and justified), insufficient data (requested before drafting), quality gap persisting after two iterations (declared as open limit).
Expected deliverable: (1) five-layer expert persona card, (2) task resolved from the role with heuristic traceability, (3) quality delta note and the card offered as a reusable system prompt.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-contraste-:
[inputs]
- TAREA: {{TAREA}} > Target task or instruction of the prompt to be fixed (e.g. classify tickets, write email subject lines, extract data)
- COMPORTAMIENTO_DESEADO: {{COMPORTAMIENTO_DESEADO}} > Observable behavior the model must reproduce (what you want to see in the output)
- ANTIPATRON: {{ANTIPATRON}} > Recurring error or behavior to be eliminated (what must NOT appear)
- CASOS_PRUEBA: {{CASOS_PRUEBA}} > Real sample inputs to build the pairs from; at least one ambiguous
- FORMATO_SALIDA: {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} > (optional) Target format of the model's output (JSON, list, paragraph, single label)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I want a model to perform {{TAREA}} stably, reproducing {{COMPORTAMIENTO_DESEADO}} and stopping committing {{ANTIPATRON}}, which currently appears recurrently. Instructions alone are not enough: the model understands the rule but violates it in edge cases. A block of positive-negative contrastive examples, where each input is shown resolved correctly and incorrectly side by side, anchors behavior by demonstration and makes the anti-pattern evident. The operative principle is the minimal pair: two outputs identical except in the target dimension, so that the model attributes the contrast to that dimension and not to noise. This unlocks a reusable prompt that can be pasted into production, versioned, and expanded with new pairs when a new error appears.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer specialized in few-shot with contrastive examples to fix model behavior in repeatable tasks.
Deliverable: a block of contrastive demonstrations ready to insert into the prompt for {{TAREA}}, with its rules, the closing instruction, and a placement note. Steps:
1. Operationalize: rewrite {{COMPORTAMIENTO_DESEADO}} and {{ANTIPATRON}} as observable behaviors in the output, not as vague adjectives; name the exact dimension that distinguishes one from the other and verbalize why the model confuses both today.
2. Contrastive pairs: from {{CASOS_PRUEBA}} build three to five pairs; each pair starts from the same input and presents a CORRECT and an INCORRECT version, labeled, where the only difference is the dimension from step 1 (minimal pair), so the contrast is clean and attributable.
3. Rule per pair: below each pair add a Rule line drafted as an actionable instruction derived from the contrast, not as a description.
4. Limit coverage: ensure the set includes an ambiguous input, one that invites the anti-pattern, and one where the desired behavior seems not to apply (non-application case), to avoid overfitting to a single mold.
5. Anti-leak audit: verify that no INCORRECT version is so plausible that it teaches the error as acceptable, and that no CORRECT version carries a second unlabeled difference; discard or rewrite any failing pair.
6. Closing instruction and placement: draft the final block that orders the model to always imitate the CORRECT versions, never the INCORRECT ones, respect {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} if applicable, and generalize the rules to new inputs; indicate where to place the block (after the instructions, before the real input) and warn not to leave the last example in the INCORRECT version.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Definition: convert desire and anti-pattern into observable behaviors; mark as [ASSUMPTION] any inference without the user's evidence. Phase 2 Construction: generate the pairs minimizing all differences unrelated to the target dimension, because a pair that varies in two things at once teaches ambiguously; label CORRECT and INCORRECT explicitly. Phase 3 Coverage: verify that the pairs cover ambiguity, trap case, and non-application case, not just the easy case. Phase 4 Audit: apply step 5 (anti-leak and single difference) and verify that the Rules do not contradict each other. Phase 5 Assembly and test: assemble the complete block, add the closing instruction with placement note, and propose a new test input not in the pairs to validate that the behavior generalizes; make the expected result of that input explicit.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist: (1) Desired behavior and anti-pattern expressed as observable behaviors, not adjectives. (2) Three to five pairs, each with CORRECT and INCORRECT versions explicitly labeled. (3) In each pair the only difference is the target dimension (minimal pair); the contrast is attributable. (4) Each pair closes with an actionable Rule derived from the contrast. (5) The set covers at least one ambiguous input, one that invites the anti-pattern, and a non-application case. (6) Anti-leak audit passed: no INCORRECT version is plausible to the point of teaching the error, no CORRECT version carries unlabeled differences, no Rule contradicts another. (7) Closing instruction orders imitating the CORRECT, avoiding the INCORRECT, and generalizing; includes placement note and does not leave the last example in INCORRECT version. (8) Respects {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} when specified. (9) Includes a new test input outside the pairs, with its expected result. (10) Assumptions marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented examples presented as real. (11) Neutral professional language, no emojis or prices. Expected deliverable: block of three to five labeled contrastive pairs with their Rule each, closing instruction with placement note, and a generalization test input with expected result, all ready to paste into the prompt for {{TAREA}}.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-rubrica-au:
[inputs]
- ENTREGABLE: {{ENTREGABLE}} > What you will produce (email, proposal section, summary, code, etc.)
- AUDIENCIA_Y_USO: {{AUDIENCIA_Y_USO}} > Who reads it and for what decision or action it is used
- CRITERIOS_CALIDAD: {{CRITERIOS_CALIDAD}} > 4-6 criteria that matter here (optional; if missing, the model proposes and asks for confirmation)
- UMBRAL: {{UMBRAL}} > Approval rule (optional; default: minimum 4/5 per criterion and weighted average >= 4.3)
- MAX_ITERACIONES: {{MAX_ITERACIONES}} > Cap on rewriting cycles (optional; default 3)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to deliver {{ENTREGABLE}} for {{AUDIENCIA_Y_USO}} with verifiable, not assumed, quality. The risk of the first draft is that it is delivered without control: errors, filler, and omissions reach the reader. Converting quality into an explicit gate (a rubric the model itself applies before delivering) unlocks deliverables that hold up on the first try and an auditable trace of why this result is good.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior editor and evaluation rubric designer, expert in model self-critique and in quality control of deliverables.
Produce the deliverable and, before showing it, subject it to a self-evaluation rubric. Steps:
1. If {{CRITERIOS_CALIDAD}} or {{UMBRAL}} are empty, propose 4-6 reasoned criteria for this type of deliverable, with weights summing to 100%, and a default threshold; ask for confirmation before continuing.
2. Define the rubric: each criterion with its weight and a 1-5 scale with a concrete descriptor per level (what a 3 vs a 5 looks like), so that the score is defensible, not impressionistic.
3. Generate an internal draft of the deliverable.
4. Score criterion by criterion with a justification sentence anchored in evidence from the text itself, and calculate the weighted average.
5. Identify the lowest score and rewrite ONLY what is necessary to raise it without breaking what already meets the standard. When tied, prioritize the criterion with the highest weight.
6. Repeat 4-5 until meeting {{UMBRAL}} or exhausting {{MAX_ITERACIONES}}.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Framing: confirm criteria, weights, and threshold; do not assume a draft is enough.
Phase 2 - Rubric: criterion / weight / 1-5 descriptors table.
Phase 3 - Improvement cycle: draft > justified scoring > targeted rewriting at the lowest score, iterating to the threshold. If an iteration raises no score, change tactics (restructure instead of touching up) in the next one.
Phase 4 - Closure: final version + table of final scores + a line of what improved between iterations.
Hard rules: never invent data or cite unverifiable metrics to raise a score; what is missing is marked [ASSUMPTION] or asked. If the threshold is not reached in {{MAX_ITERACIONES}}, deliver the best achieved and declare which criterion fell short, by how much and why.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Criteria, weights (summing 100%) and threshold confirmed (or proposed set confirmed if they were empty).
- [ ] Rubric with weight and 1-5 descriptors per criterion, not just labels.
- [ ] Each score carries justification anchored in the text; weighted average calculated.
- [ ] Rewriting targeted the lowest score in each iteration, not everything at once.
- [ ] No data invented to raise a score; missing items marked [ASSUMPTION].
- [ ] If the threshold was not reached, it is declared which criterion fell short and by how much.
Expected deliverable: final version of the deliverable + rubric table with final scores + a line of what improved between the first and the last iteration.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-step-back:
[inputs]
- PROBLEMA_CONCRETO: {{PROBLEMA_CONCRETO}} > Specific case to resolve, stated exactly as the model will receive it
- DOMINIO: {{DOMINIO}} > Knowledge area of the problem (physics, finance, law, code, business logic, etc.)
- NIVEL_DETALLE: {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} > Expected depth of reasoning (executive synthesis or exhaustive step-by-step development)
- FORMATO_SALIDA: {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} > Format of the final result (prose, table, numbered list, JSON) (optional; default: prose with three blocks)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
Language models fail more when they attack a concrete case without anchoring the principle that governs it: they drag in irrelevant details and reason on sand. Step-back prompting (Zheng et al., 2024, "Take a Step Back") corrects this by forcing a prior abstraction: deriving the general law, formula, or pattern and only then landing on the case. Applying it in {{DOMINIO}} unlocks more accurate and transferable responses, reduces hallucinations, and leaves an auditable reasoning trace, reusable in analogous cases. The risk to avoid: abstracting to a principle so generic it decides nothing (over-abstraction) or so narrow it does not apply to the case.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior prompt engineer specialized in reasoning techniques (chain-of-thought, abstraction, self-verification).
Deliverable: resolution of {{PROBLEMA_CONCRETO}} via step-back prompting, in {{FORMATO_SALIDA}}, with three named blocks (GENERAL PRINCIPLE, APPLICATION TO THE CASE, VERIFICATION). Steps:
1. Restate {{PROBLEMA_CONCRETO}} and classify which family of problems in {{DOMINIO}} it belongs to; name what is being solved and what would decide the result.
2. Step back: state the general principle, law, formula, or applicable framework, drafted in an abstract and reusable form, WITHOUT using the case data yet. Choose an abstraction level that is operative: neither trivial nor inapplicable.
3. Declare boundary conditions, assumptions of the principle, and relevant exceptions; indicate when the principle does NOT apply.
4. Application: resolve the case by reasoning step by step at the {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} level, showing how each conclusion anchors in a concrete part of the principle (substitution of variables one by one).
5. Verification: confirm that the solution does not contradict the principle or introduce unjustified assumptions; review units, magnitudes, or logical coherence; list which datum or condition would invalidate the result.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Abstraction: identify the type of problem before the concrete numbers or names; name the general principle explicitly and justify why it governs this case.
Phase 2 - Landing: instantiate the principle over {{PROBLEMA_CONCRETO}}, substituting general variables with real data one by one; if two principles compete, declare which prevails and why.
Phase 3 - Control: contrast result against the principle; mark each absent datum as [ASSUMPTION] and do not invent values; if an assumption changes the conclusion, state it explicitly. Consider {{ADJUNTOS}} if they exist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- The GENERAL PRINCIPLE block is abstract and reusable: it does not mention the concrete data of the case.
- The abstraction level is operative: the principle decides the case, it is neither trivial nor inapplicable.
- The step back precedes the application; the order is not reversed.
- Each conclusion in the APPLICATION explicitly cites the part of the principle that supports it.
- The boundary conditions, assumptions, and exceptions of the principle are declared, including when it does NOT apply.
- Missing data are marked [ASSUMPTION]; zero invented values; assumptions that move the conclusion are flagged.
- The VERIFICATION block confirms internal consistency, reviews units or coherence, and lists what would invalidate the result.
- The deliverable respects {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} and the {{NIVEL_DETALLE}} level.
Expected deliverable: document with blocks GENERAL PRINCIPLE, APPLICATION TO THE CASE, and VERIFICATION, ready to audit and reuse in analogous cases of {{DOMINIO}}.
spec-ia-automatizacion_prompt-restriccio:
[inputs]
- CONTENIDO_O_TAREA: {{CONTENIDO_O_TAREA}} > What the prompt to be corrected produces (e.g. support responses, copy, legal summaries)
- PROHIBICIONES: {{PROHIBICIONES}} > List of what the model must NOT do (one per line)
- RIESGO_TIPICO: {{RIESGO_TIPICO}} > Real undesired behavior already observed, if any ("(optional)")
- AUDIENCIA: {{AUDIENCIA}} > Target audience and tone of the final result
- FORMATO_SALIDA: {{FORMATO_SALIDA}} > Expected format of the result produced by the corrected prompt
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
A production prompt violates its own prohibitions: isolated negations ("don't use jargon", "don't invent data") fail because the model processes the prohibited concept without internalizing the boundary, and because they typically lack a measurable threshold and an actionable alternative. Redesigning these constraints unlocks reliable outputs, reduces manual correction, and makes the prompt auditable. Context: task {{CONTENIDO_O_TAREA}} for {{AUDIENCIA}}, with output in {{FORMATO_SALIDA}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: senior prompt engineer specialized in language model behavior control (guardrails).
Deliverable: (1) rewritten constraints block ready to paste + (2) mapping table original prohibition > reinforced version > type of failure resolved.
Steps:
1. Inventory each item in {{PROHIBICIONES}} and pair it with its manifestation in {{RIESGO_TIPICO}}.
2. Reframe each prohibition as an affirmative directive (the desired behavior, not the prohibited one).
3. Add to each constraint: explicit substitution ("instead of A, do B"), one-line justification, and observable detection criterion (threshold or verifiable signal, not diffuse judgment).
4. Build a contrast pair per critical constraint: prohibited example vs. acceptable version, consistent with {{AUDIENCIA}}.
5. Draft a final self-check block where the model verifies its draft against each constraint and corrects before delivering in {{FORMATO_SALIDA}}.

Explicit assumptions: the declared prohibitions are real and complete; if {{RIESGO_TIPICO}} is empty, infer the most probable failure and mark it as a hypothesis to confirm, not as fact.
Limits: do not add undeclared constraints; do not tighten to the point of making the task infeasible; flag conflicts between prohibitions instead of resolving them silently.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Diagnosis: classify each prohibition by type of failure (ignored negation, ambiguity without threshold, lack of alternative).
Phase 2 Rewriting: apply positive reframing + substitution + justification + detection criterion to each item.
Phase 3 Anchoring: place each constraint next to the relevant instruction and repeat the 2-3 critical ones at the close of the prompt, where the model fixes its output.
Phase 4 Verification: integrate the self-check block and validate with the contrast pairs.
Edge cases: ambiguous prohibition that cannot be reinforced without context > mark it {to_confirm} instead of guessing; two prohibitions that contradict each other > expose the trade-off; already well-formulated prohibition > preserve it and note why.
If {{CONTENIDO_O_TAREA}} or {{PROHIBICIONES}} are missing, request them before executing; do not invent undeclared constraints.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Each prohibition from {{PROHIBICIONES}} appears reformulated as an affirmative directive.
- [ ] Each constraint includes substitution, justification, and observable detection criterion with a threshold or verifiable signal.
- [ ] The 2-3 critical constraints are repeated at the close of the prompt.
- [ ] There is at least one prohibited/acceptable contrast pair aligned with {{AUDIENCIA}}.
- [ ] The self-check block requires verifying and correcting before delivering.
- [ ] Conflicts between prohibitions and ambiguous items are flagged, not silently resolved.
- [ ] No constraints not mentioned by the user were added.
Expected deliverable: rewritten constraints block (pasteable) + mapping table original > reinforced > type of failure, in {{FORMATO_SALIDA}}.
spec-ia-automatizacion_arquitectura-agen:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO: {{OBJETIVO}} > What task the agent automates, for whom, and how success is measured (observable metric). If it arrives as a vague desire ("I want an agent to help with X"), the model grounds it to task + actor + metric before proceeding
- HERRAMIENTAS: {{HERRAMIENTAS}} > APIs, databases, search, and available actions (optional; if missing, the model proposes the minimum and sufficient set and marks it [ASSUMPTION]; never invents integrations with specific names/credentials without data)
- MEMORIA: {{MEMORIA}} > What the agent must retain within the turn, during the task, and between sessions (optional; if missing, the model derives the default policy from the MODELO_ENTORNO horizon)
- MODELO_ENTORNO: {{MODELO_ENTORNO}} > Environment and horizon: single turn or long-horizon multi-step task; time, iteration, or token budget limits; whether the environment is real write or sandbox
- GUARDRAILES: {{GUARDRAILES}} > Actions requiring human approval, what the agent must never do, and when to escalate to a human (optional; if missing, the model proposes a conservative security floor and marks it [ASSUMPTION])
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
We need to go from the intention "I want an agent that does {{OBJETIVO}}" to an implementable architecture of a single autonomous agent (one agent, no multi-agent orchestration). This architecture fixes the five decisions that determine whether an agent works in production or goes off the rails: what objective it pursues and how it is measured, what tools it can invoke and with what permissions, what it remembers in each memory layer, how its reason-act-observe control loop works, and under what criteria it stops or escalates to a human. A well-defined design unlocks implementation with clear cost and risk limits, and prevents the three canonical failures of the autonomous agent: the infinite loop (doesn't know when to stop), the unauthorized destructive action (writes/deletes without approval), and the objective drift (accumulates context and drifts from the goal). The strategy contributes here the rigor of agent patterns (ReAct, tool calling, layered memory, verifiable stopping) applied to a real case, not a demo.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior AI agent architect, expert in single autonomous agent design, ReAct pattern (reason-act-observe), function/tool calling, layered memory design (context, episode, persistent), and stopping and escalation policies. Thinks in terms of tool contracts, iteration budgets, and risk surface, not "magic prompts".
Deliver an architecture document in this order:
1. Restate {{OBJETIVO}} in a sentence: "An agent that [does what] for [whom], measuring success as [observable metric]".
2. Objective: inside/outside scope (what the agent does NOT do), observable success metric, explicit failure criterion, and the sole closing task (what it delivers when done); distinguish single-turn task from long-horizon task per {{MODELO_ENTORNO}} and justify the classification.
3. Tools: from {{HERRAMIENTAS}}, for each tool indicate name, function, input/output contract, read vs. write (side effect), required permission, idempotency/reversibility, and human confirmation flag. Apply the principle of least privilege: minimum and sufficient set, no tools "just in case". If {{HERRAMIENTAS}} is empty, propose the minimum and mark it [ASSUMPTION]; never invent concrete integrations.
4. Layered memory from {{MEMORIA}}: (a) turn working context (instruction + immediate state), (b) task episode/scratchpad (plan, observations, partial results), (c) persistent memory between sessions (what is saved, where, how retrieved and with what key). Include truncation/summary policy when approaching the window limit and what is discarded first.
5. Control loop: reason > select tool > execute > observe > decide next step; define maximum iterations, tool error handling (retry with backoff / alternate route / abort), and how it decides it is done. Accompany with a textual diagram of the loop.

spec-ia-automatizacion_agente-multiagent:
[inputs]
- TAREA_A_AUTOMATIZAR: {{TAREA_A_AUTOMATIZAR}} > The task or workflow the multi-agent system must resolve end-to-end
- FRAMEWORK: {{FRAMEWORK}} > Target framework or environment (e.g. LangGraph, CrewAI, Agents SDK, custom orchestration) (optional)
- HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES: {{HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES}} > Tools, APIs, or data sources workers can access (optional)
- PRESUPUESTO_LATENCIA_TOKENS: {{PRESUPUESTO_LATENCIA_TOKENS}} > Latency, cost, or token limits the architecture must respect (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I need to automate a complex task that a single agent resolves poorly: it either runs out of context, mixes responsibilities, or fails without recovery. The orchestrator-workers pattern distributes the work across specialized sub-agents coordinated by an orchestrator. Well designed it unlocks parallelism, context bounded per worker, and recovery from partial failures; poorly designed it produces agents that step on each other, inflated contexts, uncapped costs, and a system that falls apart entirely when a worker returns garbage. A precise design delivers a blueprint implementable directly in the framework, with contracts, budget, and failure handling closed before writing code.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior AI agent systems architect, with experience in orchestration, typed agent input/output contracts, and fault-tolerant design.
From {{TAREA_A_AUTOMATIZAR}} (and, if provided, {{FRAMEWORK}}, {{HERRAMIENTAS_DISPONIBLES}}, and {{PRESUPUESTO_LATENCIA_TOKENS}}), deliver the multi-agent architecture with:
1. Decomposition of the task into atomic subtasks (parallel or sequential) with an explicit dependency graph.
2. Catalog of worker sub-agents: each with unique responsibility, permitted tools or sources (closed list), and typed input/output contract with preconditions and postconditions.
3. Orchestrator logic: delegation criterion (to whom and in what order), minimum context passed to each worker, and how it avoids work overlap.
4. Aggregation strategy: how it receives, validates, and merges partial outputs into a coherent result, and explicit rule to resolve contradictions between workers (priority, voting, escalation, or business rule).
5. Layered failure handling: timeouts, retries with backoff and retry cap, idempotency, fallbacks, partial degradation, and abort criterion; what the orchestrator does when a worker is down or returns invalid output.
6. Textual flow diagram of the orchestrator-workers-aggregation journey.
7. Minimum observability: what to log per delegation (delegation and trace id, worker, input, output, latency, attempt, result, approximate cost).
8. Risk closure: residual single points of failure, fit with the latency/token budget, and assumptions to validate before implementing.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 - Interpret: extract the verifiable final objective, the inputs, and the expected output. If the objective, target framework, or latency/token budget are missing, ask before assuming; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION].
Phase 2 - Decompose: split the task into atomic subtasks (one responsibility each), declare dependencies, and mark which run in parallel. A subtask is atomic if a worker completes it without delegating again. Flag maximum fan-out and graph depth to anticipate cost.
Phase 3 - Contract: for each subtask define a worker with a typed input/output contract (what it receives, what it returns, format, preconditions, postconditions) and its closed list of tools; the orchestrator never executes domain work, only coordinates.
Phase 4 - Coordinate and aggregate: define the delegation criterion, the minimum context per worker (do not pass the full state), and how the aggregator validates each output against its contract before merging, with explicit rule and priority for contradictions.
Phase 5 - Harden and bound: add timeouts, retries with backoff with cap, idempotency, fallbacks, and partial degradation per layer; define when the orchestrator aborts vs. delivers partial result, and verify the design fits the budget. Close with the flow diagram, the observability fields, and residual single points of failure.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
- Each subtask is atomic and has a unique responsibility; the dependency graph indicates what runs in parallel and what in sequence, with explicit fan-out and depth.
- Each worker has a typed input/output contract with preconditions/postconditions and a closed list of tools; no worker shares responsibility with another.
- The orchestrator only coordinates (does not execute domain work) and passes minimum context, not the full state, to each worker.
- Aggregation validates each partial output against its contract before merging and includes an explicit rule with priority to resolve contradictions.
- Failure handling covers, per layer, timeout, retry with backoff with cap, idempotency, fallback, and abort vs. partial degradation criterion; no single worker failure takes down the entire system without a defined rule.
- The flow diagram reflects the full journey and is consistent with the decomposition and aggregation.
- Observability logs at least delegation/trace id, input, output, latency, attempt number, result, and approximate cost per delegation.
- The closure names residual single points of failure and confirms fit with the latency/token budget.
- Assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION]; no invented data presented as true.
Expected deliverable: an architecture blueprint in numbered sections 1-8, directly implementable in the indicated framework without pending design decisions.
spec-ia-automatizacion_agente-definicion:
[inputs]
- OBJETIVO_AGENTE: {{OBJETIVO_AGENTE}} > What the agent must achieve and for whom (e.g. "support assistant that queries orders and opens tickets")
- TAREAS_OBJETIVO: {{TAREAS_OBJETIVO}} > List of user intentions or tasks the agent must resolve
- SISTEMAS_Y_APIS: {{SISTEMAS_Y_APIS}} > Systems, APIs, functions, or actions the agent can call
- RESTRICCIONES: {{RESTRICCIONES}} > Permissions, costs, latency, and irreversible actions to consider (optional)
- PLATAFORMA: {{PLATAFORMA}} > Tool-calling environment: OpenAI, Anthropic, custom framework, or other (optional)
- ADJUNTOS: {{ADJUNTOS}} > Attached files, URLs, or "No attachments"

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
You are going to define the tool catalog of an LLM agent. An agent's reliability does not depend only on the model: the model decides which tool to call by reading names and descriptions as if they were its selection prompt, and fills arguments by inferring from the schema. An ambiguous catalog produces the typical failure pattern: wrong tool chosen, invented parameters, redundant tools chained, and irreversible actions executed without confirmation. A well-designed catalog unlocks an agent that picks the right tool, does not invent parameters, does not call competing tools, and stops to ask or confirm when appropriate. The agent's objective is {{OBJETIVO_AGENTE}}, it must cover {{TAREAS_OBJETIVO}} using {{SISTEMAS_Y_APIS}}, subject to {{RESTRICCIONES}}, and running on {{PLATAFORMA}}.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior LLM agent engineer specialized in tool-calling design and function schemas (JSON Schema), with judgment for naming, delimiting, and disambiguating tools and for separating reads from mutations.
Deliver an actionable tool catalog. Steps:
1. Reconstruct the task model from {{TAREAS_OBJETIVO}}: list each user intention and the tool or combination of {{SISTEMAS_Y_APIS}} that resolves it; flag gaps without coverage, overlaps where two tools would compete, and tasks requiring chaining multiple tools (indicate the order and data dependency).
2. For each tool deliver a card with: (a) canonical name in snake_case, verb+object, unambiguous among the others; (b) decision-oriented description that says WHAT it does, WHAT it returns, and WHEN to choose it; (c) typed parameter schema in JSON Schema style with type, enum for closed domains, format, required vs. optional, defaults, range or pattern constraints, and one valid example per field; (d) preconditions and effects: reads or mutates, idempotent or not, requires human confirmation, cost or latency per {{RESTRICCIONES}}; (e) return shape: key fields it returns and, if applicable, expected errors and their handling; (f) "when NOT to use" block that distinguishes it from its neighboring tools by name.
3. Apply the minimum catalog principle: merge nearly identical tools, split an overloaded tool that mixes intentions, and justify each merge or split decision in one line. If two systems from {{SISTEMAS_Y_APIS}} do the same thing, decide which one to expose and why.
4. Define disambiguation rules between competing tools and a fallback policy: missing parameter > ask, do not invent; no tool applies > respond without tool; irreversible or mutating action > confirm first; empty or error tool result > retry, degrade, or escalate as appropriate; respect {{PLATAFORMA}} conventions.
5. Close with an intent > tool matrix and 3 to 5 selection test cases, each with the user's phrase, the expected tool, the expected arguments, and the reason for the choice; include at least one trap case where the correct answer is to call no tool and one ambiguous request that requires asking for a parameter before acting.

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Coverage: map intentions against tools; every intention must have an owner, no tool pair can remain indistinguishable, and multi-step tasks must have an explicit order.
Phase 2 Specification: draft the cards; the description is the selection prompt, so prioritize the WHEN over the internal how and name the neighboring tools in the "when NOT to use".
Phase 3 Robustness: add disambiguation, fallback, confirmation for mutating or irreversible actions, and error or empty result handling.
Phase 4 Verification: mentally run the test cases; if a case would be ambiguous, adjust the name, description, or schema and run it again until the selection is deterministic.
Use only the information provided; mark all inferences as [ASSUMPTION].
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- Every intention from {{TAREAS_OBJETIVO}} has at least one covering tool; gaps and overlaps are resolved or flagged.
- Every name is snake_case, verb+object, and unambiguous among the others.
- Every description states WHAT it does, WHAT it returns, and WHEN to choose it; includes "when NOT to use" naming the neighboring tools.
- Every parameter has type, required/optional status, default when applicable, enum for closed domains, and one valid example; return shape and expected errors are described.
- Tools that mutate or are irreversible mark their effect and idempotency and require confirmation.
- The catalog is minimal: no redundant tools, no tool mixing intentions; every merge or split is justified.
- There is a fallback policy for missing parameter, no applicable tool, irreversible action, and error or empty result.
- There is an intent > tool matrix and 3 to 5 test cases, with at least one where the correct answer is to call no tool and one that requires asking for a parameter.
- All inferences appear as [ASSUMPTION].
Expected deliverable: tool catalog with per-tool cards, disambiguation and fallback rules, intent > tool matrix, and selection test cases, ready to register on {{PLATAFORMA}}.
spec-ia-automatizacion_agente-memoria-co:
[inputs]
- CASO_USO_AGENTE: {{CASO_USO_AGENTE}} > Purpose and domain of the agent (e.g. support assistant, sales copilot, personal productivity agent)

[prompt]

--- S | SITUATION ---
I am designing an agent for CASO_USO_AGENTE that must maintain coherence over time. Without an explicit memory architecture the agent repeats already-answered questions, forgets user preferences, inflates the context to the point of degradation, or, worse, persists sensitive data it should never have saved. A clear memory contract unlocks continuity between sessions, controlled context costs, and auditable privacy compliance, distinguishing what the agent remembers within a session (short-term) from what it learns and retains between sessions (long-term). The design must be implementable on BACKEND_MEMORIA and withstand real failures: store unavailable, stale memory retrieved, PII leak.

--- P | REQUEST ---
Archetype: Senior AI agent systems architect, specialized in conversational and persistent memory management (working memory, episodic, semantic, and procedural).
Deliver the complete memory design of the agent with these components:
1. Short-term memory: effective context window (in turns and tokens), what is kept literal vs. summarized, and the compaction strategy when the context fills (incremental summary, thread synthesis, old-turn discard always preserving the state of the task in progress: objective, completed steps, pending steps, decisions made).
2. Long-term memory in three types: episodic (dated events and interactions), semantic (stable facts about user, domain, and preferences), and procedural (learned routines and templates); with the data schema of each (fields, keys, indices, and search type) according to BACKEND_MEMORIA.
3. Write policy: what is written, with what trigger (explicit order, durable fact detection, task closure), and deduplication and reconciliation rules to avoid duplicating or contradicting what is stored.
4. Retrieval policy: selection signals (semantic relevance, recency, importance), injected token budget per turn, priority order when the budget is exceeded, and citation of the origin of each memory (id + type + date).
5. Forgetting policy: TTL per memory type, decay by disuse, merger of redundant items, and privacy boundary honoring RESTRICCIONES_PRIVACIDAD and POLITICA_RETENCION (what is NEVER persisted, what requires consent, how deletion at user request is executed).
6. Consistency contract: short vs. long-term conflict resolution (which wins and why), versioning of a fact that changes over time (reversed preference, corrected datum), and explicit promotion criterion from short to long-term.
7. Validation and resilience: test case set (input > expected memory behavior) covering write, retrieval, forgetting, and privacy; plus behavior on failures (store down, stale memory retrieved, attempt to persist prohibited PII).

--- E | EXECUTION ---
Phase 1 Framing: restate the use case, volume, backend, and constraints; mark assumptions as [ASSUMPTION] and formulate missing questions before designing.
Phase 2 Modeling: define short-term and the three long-term types; produce the architecture diagram in Mermaid syntax (turn > write/retrieval > stores flow) and the data schema of each type.
Phase 3 Policies: draft the write, retrieval, and forgetting policies in a table, with concrete triggers and thresholds; integrate the privacy and retention gates as blocking rules.
Phase 4 Consistency and testing: define conflict resolution, versioning, and promotion criterion; build the test cases, behavior on failures, and a closure checklist.
>> MetodologIA Protocol: Interpret > Plan > Execute. Restate what you understand and present your plan before executing.

--- C | CRITERION ---
Quality checklist:
- [ ] Short and long-term are separated without ambiguity, with explicit promotion criterion from one to the other.
- [ ] The three long-term types (episodic, semantic, procedural) have their own data schema with fields, keys, indices, and search type.
- [ ] Each policy (write, retrieval, forgetting) has concrete triggers and thresholds, not generic descriptions.
- [ ] The privacy boundary explicitly declares what is NEVER persisted, what requires consent, and how deletion at user request is executed, honoring RESTRICCIONES_PRIVACIDAD.
- [ ] The compaction strategy preserves the state of the task in progress (objective, pending items, decisions) when discarding turns.
- [ ] Retrieval declares token budget and priority order when exceeded.
- [ ] The consistency contract resolves short vs. long-term conflicts and versions facts that change.
- [ ] The Mermaid diagram renders and reflects the write and retrieval flow.
- [ ] Test cases cover all four fronts (write, retrieval, forgetting, privacy) and include behavior on failures.
- [ ] Assumptions are marked [ASSUMPTION] and there is no invented data.
